--- Page 9 ---
<meta>Following the heraldic frontispiece dedicated to the patron, we now encounter the illustrated title page for Athanasius Kircher’s monumental study of the "Pamphilian Obelisk." This engraving serves as a visual manifesto for Kircher’s theories on the universal origins of wisdom.</meta>

*This elaborate engraving serves as the formal gateway to the book. In the center, the messenger god Mercury—associated here with Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom—soars through the air. He holds an unfurling scroll containing ancient <term>hieroglyphs</term> (the sacred carvings of Egypt), which he points toward with a sense of revelation.*

*To the left, a winged figure representing Wisdom or History records these secrets, while above her, Father Time watches with his scythe, signifying that these ancient truths are being rescued from oblivion. At the base, we see the infant god Harpocrates, gesturing for silence to protect these mysteries, sitting near symbols of the many languages Kircher studied to unlock the past.*

->PAMPHILIAN OBELISK<-

->**HARMONY**<-
->**SMALL THINGS**<-
<note>original Latin: "CONCORDIA PARVAE." These words are the start of the Roman historian Sallust’s famous motto: *Concordia parvae res crescunt*—"Small things grow through harmony." In the context of this book, it suggests that even the smallest fragments of ancient wisdom, when brought together in harmony, reveal the grand design of God's truth.</note>

<margin>
The Scepter of Power
The Majesty of the Lion
</margin>
<note>The scepter and the lion are traditional symbols of sovereignty and strength, likely paying tribute to the Pope or the noble Pamphili family who sponsored Kircher’s research.</note>

-><term>Chi-Rho</term><-
<note>original: ☧. This is a "Christogram," a monogram formed from the first two letters of the Greek word for Christ (XPIΣTOΣ). By placing this on a foundation stone at the base of the image, the artist indicates that all the "Small Things" of Egyptian, Greek, and Chaldean wisdom are ultimately supported by the foundation of the Christian faith.</note>

<meta>This page continues from the frontispiece and title page. It is the beginning of the formal dedication (page signature a 2) to Pope Innocent X, the patron who commissioned the restoration of the obelisk in the Piazza Navona.</meta>

<image-desc>Intricate woodcut headpiece featuring a symmetrical arrangement of stylized floral scrolls and vine patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>Emblems</margin>

# TO INNOCENT X.
## PONTIFF
### BEST AND GREATEST.

->*LIFE AND HAPPINESS.*<-

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'O' set within a square frame decorated with elaborate acanthus-style leaves and scrollwork.</image-desc>

THIS OBELISK, illustrious with its mystic Sphinxes, which Your Holiness <note>original: "BEATITVDO" (Your Beatitude/Holiness)</note> not long ago erected in the Agonal Forum <note>The *Agonali Foro* is the modern-day Piazza Navona in Rome, built on the site of the ancient Stadium of Domitian (Circus Agonalis).</note> with a magnificence rivaling the Ancients, I now present to your Most Sacred feet. It stands as one of the greatest survivors from the world of Antiquity, now unrolled and explained from the unknown secrets in which it was wrapped. I come as a new Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx. Kircher often used this metaphor to describe his work deciphering hieroglyphs.</note>, so that it may be clear to posterity that these mysteries of ancient wisdom—unknown until now—have, after the passing of so many centuries, shone forth upon the world having been discovered at that very time when a "Friend of All" <note>original Greek: "Π Α Μ Φ Ι Λ Ο Σ" (Pamphilos). This is a pun on the Pope's family name, Pamphili. In Greek, it means "beloved by all" or "friend of all."</note> presided over it. And although I recognize that the burden imposed upon me is indeed heavier than Mount Etna, and a weight to be feared even by the shoulders of Hercules, such was the force and efficacy of your command that you have drawn out by a single nod those things which seemed to exceed the limits of human genius. This work came forth at that very time when, amidst such great disturbance of the Christian Republic, You, MOST BLESSED FATHER, were elected as the Supreme Admiral <note>original: "Nauarchum," a Greek-derived term for a ship's captain or commander.</note>—not without the admirable counsel of divine providence—to command the Ship of St. Peter so that you might come to the aid of a shipwrecked world. It was at that time, I say, when INNOCENT <note>The author is making a wordplay between the Pope's name, *Innocentius*, and the Latin *nocentium*, meaning "the guilty" or "the harmful."</note> [was chosen] for the [restraining] of the guilty...

<summary>This is the opening of Athanasius Kircher's dedication to Pope Innocent X, celebrating the Pope's restoration of the "Pamphilian Obelisk" in Piazza Navona. Kircher styles himself as a "new Oedipus" capable of solving the "riddles" of the Egyptian hieroglyphs under the Pope's enlightened patronage.</summary>
<keywords>Innocent X, Athanasius Kircher, Obeliscus Pamphilius, Piazza Navona, Oedipus, Sphinx, hieroglyphs, Papal patronage, Ship of St. Peter</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication to Pope Innocent X. The previous page ended mid-sentence, describing how the Pope's command compelled Kircher to undertake the daunting task of deciphering the obelisk's hieroglyphs to aid in the removal of ancient errors.</meta>

[uprooting of all error]; the **TENTH** of this name <note>Pope Innocent X (reigned 1644–1655)</note>, for the integrity of the World; **PAMPHILIUS** <note>The Pope’s family name, which Kircher interprets via the Greek *Pan-philos*</note>, that is, the "Love of All," for the harmony of mutual Love, was given by **GOD** with a lucky omen and a purposeful sign. By this name, the Dove <note>The dove with an olive branch is the central heraldic symbol of the Pamphili family.</note>—conspicuous with its green olive branch—arises to appease the angered Deity and bring the tranquility of peace. By this name, the **LILIES** <note>Lilies also appeared on the Pamphili coat of arms.</note> bloom for the delight of the World; the Basilicas of the City <note>Rome</note> and the Prince of the World are restored for the increase of Religion; and finally, for the perfect administration of justice, the Capitoline Citadel <note>The *Arx Capitolina* refers to the Capitoline Hill, which Innocent X continued to renovate and embellish.</note> is restored to its former splendor. Thus, nothing is present, whether in **YOUR** heraldic emblems or in your glorious actions, that is not full of arguments for good omens and happy portents.

Therefore, under this most sacred Auspice of **YOUR** Name, this Hieroglyphic Work comes forth into the light: what you commanded, I have performed according to the smallness of my talent, **GOD** granting it. And if I find this work to be not at all unworthy in the eyes of **YOUR HOLINESS**, you will add a spur and wings to my spirit to explain the remaining surviving Obelisks of the City with equal daring. In the meantime, I pray to **GOD, BEST AND GREATEST**, whose place you hold on earth and who has signaled **YOU** with so many signs for the happiness of the World, that He may also prolong your life for many years, so that we may see with joy the fulfillment of all those things indicated by **YOUR** family emblems.

**FAREWELL, FOUNDATION AND SUPPORT OF THE WORLD**, and may you not disdain to cherish with fatherly care my Religious Order <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits)</note>, bound to **YOU** by so many titles, and me along with it under the shadow of the wings of the **PAMPHILI DOVE**.

Rome, October 4, 1650.

->**OF YOUR HOLINESS**<-

->Prostrate at your most sacred feet,<-

->The most humble and obedient servant,<-

->*Athanasius Kircher, of the Society of JESUS.*<-

<summary>Athanasius Kircher concludes his dedication to Pope Innocent X, interpreting the Pope's names and heraldic symbols (the dove and lily) as divine omens of peace and restoration for Rome. He officially presents his decipherment of the Pamphili Obelisk and asks for continued papal patronage to study Rome's other Egyptian monuments.</summary>
<keywords>Pope Innocent X, Athanasius Kircher, Pamphili family, heraldry, symbolism, Rome, obelisks, Jesuits, restoration, justice</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>The catchword "Ita" from the previous page leads into the continuation of the formal introductory sequence. This page serves as a poetic "vestibule" or entrance to the work, transitioning from Kircher’s prose dedication to the Pope to a laudatory poem by James Alban Gibbes, a prominent English physician in Rome.</meta>

### EXPLANATION OF THE VESTIBULE
# OF THE PAMPHILI OBELISK
->Through which one enters into the deserved praises<-
->Of the Very Reverend Father ATHANASIUS KIRCHER,<-
->AUTHOR OF THIS BOOK,<-

## JAMES ALBAN
## GIBBES,
->Doctor of Medicine.<-

---

### LIMPING IAMBICS
<note>original: "SCAZON." A "limping" Greek poetic meter often used for satirical or personal verse, though here used for sophisticated praise.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut historiated initial 'G' depicting a figure and architecture within the letterform.</image-desc>
LEARN, Reader, what is meant by the winged race <note>Likely referring to the personification of Fame or the Pamphili dove depicted in the book's frontispiece.</note> which you see at the first front of Kircher's book—a work worthy of cedar <note>The Romans used cedar oil to preserve precious manuscripts from decay; "worthy of cedar" means "worthy of immortality."</note>, learned and polished.
<margin>Saturn</margin>
That one, that reaper of towers, that voracious abyss—never sated by the loss of the ages, a merchant of oblivion for great things, the thin posthumous moth of eternity—see what Saturn <note>The god of Time, often depicted as a destructive force.</note> builds, or rather, what he overthrows. Hovering high, with a cruel joke he overturned the Egyptian <note>original: "Phariæ," referring to Pharos, the lighthouse of Alexandria.</note> trophies which Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt said to have conquered the world.</note> and Lagus <note>Ptolemy I, son of Lagus, founder of the Greek dynasty in Egypt.</note> established—not so that they might merely rival the heavens in beauty, but so they might make their names famous to the world forever. But a greater King <note>God</note> suppresses the foolish vows of kings: God allows nothing to be born equal to the divine—certainly not to endure. He will give an end to all things. Thus, neither the proud Pyramid nor the Colossus (whether it be made of marble or cast by Corinthian bronze)
<margin>Fame</margin>
avoids Necessity <note>The personification of inescapable Fate.</note>. O, brief Fame! Wherefore, though fitted with wings, yet she is chained; she cannot wander or send forth her ringing cry—that Virgin through the cities with her trumpet—by the command of Cronus <note>Saturn/Time.</note>. Sad because of the obliterated signs of Coptos <note>A city in Egypt; here referring to the lost Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, those wise signs, the veils of nature, and the magic of the gods; she appears with a tearful face, carrying her wings and her trumpet drooping, because she is not permitted to carry the sacred symbols abroad. 
But sometimes the Sun <note>original: "Titan."</note> shines through black clouds, and the whirlpool itself often provides a safeguard to the one tossed by waves. There is always a crack of hope. Who would have believed, while the daughter of Cepheus <note>Andromeda.</note> stood bound as prey for the fierce dragon to atone for a crime not her own, that she would be freed by the son of Jove <note>Perseus.</note> to become his wife, and later shine equally as a star in the heavens?

<summary>This page contains a celebratory poem by James Alban Gibbes that personifies Time (Saturn) as a destroyer of monuments and Fame as a chained figure mourning the lost wisdom of Egypt, setting the stage for Kircher to act as the "Perseus" who rescues these secrets.</summary>

<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, James Alban Gibbes, Saturn, Fame, Egypt, hieroglyphs, Sesostris, Andromeda, Perseus, obelisk, symbolism</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded by describing the Egyptian trophies as symbols of beauty meant to rival the heavens. This page continues the poetic tribute by James Alban Gibbes, transitioning from the destruction caused by Time (Saturn) to the restorative power of Athanasius Kircher’s scholarship.</meta>

And so, who would have thought that for the struggling glory
of the Egyptians—with their Obelisk <note>original: "Obelum"</note> left to 
barely a faint fame—a heavy champion from the land 
<margin>The Author</margin> of the Teutons <note>Kircher was German; "Teutonum" refers to his Germanic origins.</note> would be born, near to those 
whom the Earth's axis once feared, a man who would know 
how to bring forth these wonders into eternity, even though the towers fall?
This is **ATHANASIUS KIRCHER**, a name built up by deeds. 
Henceforth, O grateful crowd of learned men, 
rise for the man; and you, the Younger ones, rejoice 
<margin>or</margin> in your luck, having found the ring of the snake <note>Likely referring to the Ouroboros, the snake eating its tail, a symbol of eternity and cyclical time common in Kircher's iconography.</note>.
That which was fouled by filth and suffered blind confinement, 
he insists on restoring to brilliance, and he restores 
the fame of the open path of heaven, so long delayed.
Observe the shape of the face, and both hands, 
and survey the foot, together with the whole manner 
<margin>Love of Learning</margin> of the figure, my Friend. The face of the woman <note>A description of the personification of "Philomathia" appearing in the book's frontispiece.</note> denotes 
an untiring desire for learning (which the Greek orator 
would call *Philomathia*).
Feathers upon her shoulders indicate the difficult task 
<note>original: "Spartam," referring to the proverb "You have found Sparta, now adorn it," meaning one must work hard at the task they have been given.</note> she must cultivate; a stylus holds her right hand, 
and a tablet her left, so that she may reveal the secrets 
of Memphis <note>Egypt</note>, consecrated to books destined to live, through her cleverness.
She rests upon a hundred arts of the masters.

## INTRODUCTORY
# E P I S T L E
### TO THE READERS SKILLED
### IN HIDDEN LITERATURE.

In which, within a four-part structure of paragraphs, the reasoning, manner, division, style, and method of the entire planned work are set forth. Furthermore, it explains the process by which the Author proceeded in the restoration of hieroglyphic literature, together with a catalog of Authors, Printers, Manuscripts, Libraries, Workshops, Museums, and all those who contributed some help toward advancing the expedition of both this present Work and the *Oedipus* <note>A reference to Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempted to "solve" the riddle of the Egyptian Sphinx.</note>. Finally, it concludes that the interpretation of the present Obelisk has been carried out with such rigor according to the mind of the ancients that it is demonstrated by a singular proof that the context of said interpretation can signify nothing other than what the Author has explained in it.

---

->§. I.<-
->The Occasion of this Work.<-

It has been nearly twenty years now <note>original: "Quatuor lustra"—a lustrum is a five-year period.</note>, Kind Reader, since I was summoned from France to Rome during the papacy of Urban VIII to present a certain specimen of hieroglyphic interpretation on the Roman Obelisks. Rumor had it that I was attempting the restoration of this hitherto unknown literature based on a very ancient Arabic Manuscript. This business was ardently pushed by that Great Patron of Letters, Nicolas Peiresc <note>Nicolaus-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a famous French polymath and one of Kircher’s most important early supporters.</note>, a Senator of the Parliament of Aix in Narbonese Gaul <note>Modern-day Provence, France.</note>. While I struggled in this "hieroglyphic dust" <note>A metaphor for the difficult, exhausting labor of scholarly research.</note>, it can hardly be said how great was the expectation of nearly all the learned for the success of such an unusual undertaking, and how much curiosity there was in exploring my mode and reasoning. 

And just as I seemed to be attempting things impassable to human estimation and genius, there was no lack of diverse judgments from critics <note>original: "Momorum," referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism.</note>. Some approved the care of the undertaking, while others laughed at it and sang to me that "the mountains are in labor" <note>A reference to the Latin proverb "parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus"—the mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born—implying a great effort for a meager result.</note>. Some even, as often happens in the efforts of such arduous negotiations, thrust "impossibility" <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαν"</note> upon me. Finally, others barked other things, with whom I had to struggle perhaps more than with the hieroglyphic monsters themselves. Indeed, things had come to such a point that, in my defense and to blunt the burning judgments of my adversaries, there was a need for a public Specimen. Therefore, I thought it best to send ahead to the learned of all Europe the *Coptic Precursor* <note>The *Prodromus Coptus* (1636), Kircher's work arguing that the Coptic language was a late stage of ancient Egyptian.</note>, in which I held the reason and method of my plan in the interpretation of hieroglyphics. Convinced by its force and efficacy, they might judge the undertaking a little more mildly. And truly, the matter turned out as desired. For this work was received everywhere with such applause as the letters of the greatest learned...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces his work on Egyptian obelisks, recounting how he was called to Rome under Pope Urban VIII and the initial skepticism he faced from critics before publishing his "Coptic Precursor."</summary>
<keywords>Pope Urban VIII, Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, hieroglyphics, Coptic language, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, academic criticism, Rome, Egyptology</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>The previous page concludes the start of the word "EPISTOLA" (Letter), which continues here as the address to the readers.</meta>

...[of the let]ters given to me testifies, was received [so well] that, beyond my hope, it achieved so much that those whom I first found as detractors, I now find as solicitors—indeed, as promoters of the undertaken task. Enticed by the small sample of my *Preliminary Study*<note>original: "Prodromi"; referring to Kircher's 1636 work *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus*, which argued that Coptic was the key to understanding hieroglyphs.</note>, they have openly testified that I found the key to this kind of hidden literature, not only through manuscripts (which we will bring to light more opportunely in due time) but also through printed books.

Encouraged by their solicitation, I turned my pen more boldly to the task. First, I published the *Arabic-Latin-Egyptian Treasury of the ancient Pharaonic language*<note>original: "Thesaurum Arabico-Latino-Aegyptiacum"; this refers to his work *Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta* (1643), a Coptic grammar and dictionary.</note>, together with a supplement to the *Preliminary Study*. I did this so that the restoration of the ancient language of the Egyptians—unknown for so many centuries—might be followed by a fitting explanation of their doctrinal and symbolic language. I wished to ensure that nothing necessary for our arduous labors would seem to have been omitted.

And so, from the universal wisdom and doctrine of the Ancient Orientals, I composed the *Egyptian Oedipus*<note>original: "Oedipum Aegyptiacum"; Kircher’s most famous work, where he attempted to "solve" the riddle of the hieroglyphs as Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx.</note>. In this work, divided into three volumes, I intended to demonstrate the origin, progress, destruction, and restoration of hieroglyphic literature from its very foundations. However, since Italy was shaken by a sudden whirlwind of wars, a <term>Maecenas</term><note>A wealthy and influential patron of the arts or sciences, named after Gaius Maecenas, the advisor to Augustus.</note> for such a great work was lacking. Men of distinction, authority, and power, burdened by the various and long-lasting calamities of the world, were unable to lend their "midwife hands" to such a costly undertaking. Thus it happened that the Work, as if stunned by the inconveniences of war, has remained suspended until this very day.

Finally, by the singular providence of GOD, it happened that **POPE INNOCENT X** was raised to the world. Following the glorious footsteps of **POPE SIXTUS V**, of happy memory—after erecting remarkable monuments of both Sacred and Profane magnificence—he turned his Heroic Mind toward the erection of an Obelisk for the adornment of the City. But since nothing was lacking for the final completion of the Work except for the knowledge of the symbols contained upon it, and for that reason a priestly interpreter and translator of such mysteries was sought; it finally pleased His Holiness to make use of my humble service in the exposition of this most unknown and subtle literature. And so, I approached the commands of a Great Soul—that is, the interpretation of the Obelisk committed to me—with a great spirit. I now present this to the Republic of Letters in this present Work as a second specimen of the *Oedipus*. Furthermore, let the judgment of the learned, who deign to read this work, determine how skillfully I have performed the office of interpreter. Certainly, whatever good emerges for the public from this, I wish the Reader to credit entirely to His Holiness, under whose happy auspices it is produced.

To this, I join the **Most August Emperor**<note>Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1637–1657.</note>, who for many years now has shown himself to be a promoter both of this volume and of the remaining volumes on Egyptian literature. When he understood that, due solely to a lack of foreign characters, the said Works were suffering a delay perhaps harmful to the Republic of Letters, he—out of his immense and innate generosity—soon provided enough funds to produce the necessary types for Oriental languages and to complete the remaining begun works. He administered this with an annual subsidy, most largely and munificently. I mention this here so that the Reader may understand the incomparable virtues of this Imperial and truly invincible spirit; though overwhelmed by the immense cruelty of wars and enemies rushing in from all sides, he yet studies **Mars**<note>The Roman god of war.</note> in such a way that he by no means excludes **Pallas**<note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and craftsmanship.</note> from his threshold—an example rarely set by Princes. How much my unworthy Person and the pursuit of the studies I have undertaken were a care to his Imperial kindness, I wished to testify by a Letter sent to me of his own accord; which I have thought fit to join here for the memory of posterity.

<summary>Kircher describes the challenges of publishing his Egyptian studies during wartime and praises the patronage of Pope Innocent X and Emperor Ferdinand III, which allowed him to interpret the Roman obelisks and print Oriental languages.</summary>

# L E T T E R
## OF FERDINAND III,
## EMPEROR
### TO THE AUTHOR

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' with foliate motifs.</image-desc>
Reverend Father in Christ, I have heard, not without my great pleasure, with what laudable beginning and successful progress Your Reverence has for several years now spent labor in unearthing, along with other monuments of antiquity, especially the signs and characters for explaining the Oriental languages. Therefore, since I understand that the completion of what you have so nobly begun pertains not only to public utility, but also to the praise and honor of the German Nation, Your Reverence will do rightly if you persist in your undertaking and take care that the fruit of this labor comes to light in public as soon as possible. In this matter, you have and shall have me not only as a supporter and encourager of a good work, but also as a protector. I wished to make this clear to you by these presents, furthermore most kindly offering you my Imperial favor. Regensburg, October 3, 1640. Ferdinand.

*But when the Egyptian Works encountered longer delays than usual, and His Imperial Majesty understood that the sole cause of such slowness was a shortage of Arabic characters<note>The Emperor refers here to the physical lead type needed to print Arabic script, which was rare in 17th-century European printing houses.</note>, he sent another letter to the Grand Duke of Tuscany (as he knew him to possess Arabic characters of proven quality surviving from the Medici Press<note>The Typographia Medicea was a famous press in Rome, founded by Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici in 1584, specifically to print books in Oriental languages.</note>), in which he urged His Serenity to grant such characters for the publication of the work. I have thought it appropriate to subjoin the text of those letters here as well, so that others may learn from the Emperor's example what befits Princes in promoting the business of letters.*

I do not wish to hide from Your Dearness that Father Athanasius Kircher, a Priest of the Society of Jesus<note>The Jesuits, the religious order to which Kircher belonged.</note> and a German by birth, has for some time now, at my encouragement, been toiling to illustrate the secrets of Oriental languages and antiquities. ->E P I S T O L A<-
§. III.

## Method and distribution of the Work.

Furthermore, *the Method which we have thought should be maintained in the arrangement of the entire Work is as follows.*

*This present Work—which we have named the* Pamphilian Obelisk *after the glorious* Pamphilian *family, from which* INNOCENT X, Supreme Pontiff, <note>original: "INNOCENTIVS X. P. M." Referring to Giovanni Battista Pamphilj, who was Pope from 1644 to 1655.</note> *ascended to the highest peak of human affairs—we have divided first into five books, and each of these into decades, that is, fifty chapters; just as the upcoming Jubilee <note>The Holy Year or Jubilee of 1650, for which this book was prepared as a centerpiece of the celebrations in Rome.</note> serves as a sacred symbol, so we have taken it as a happy omen for our division. And since a very high structure requires the deepest foundations as if by its own right, it seemed best to begin the* First Book *from the primeval Origin of letters; and since those first inventors of letters, men of long life, entrusted the sciences they received by tradition not to papers or scrolls of flexible material, but to stones well-protected against all injuries of time, we have woven together the Origin and erection of Obelisks from the beginnings of things even to the times of Cambyses, the destroyer of ancient literature <note>original: "Cambysis literaturæ priscæ destructoris." Cambyses II was the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; Kircher follows the tradition that he destroyed the ancient monuments and records.</note>, according to the succession of the ages; so that whatever happened worth remembering concerning the erection of individual Obelisks, both here in Rome and surviving elsewhere, would by no means remain hidden from the Curious Reader.*

*But since the history of the erected Obelisks seemed to be useless unless the logic and Method of the Literature carved upon them were established, we thought it necessary to connect a most extensive argument—which the* Second Book *presents—concerning the first institution and progress of* <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>From the Greek 'hieros' (sacred) and 'glypho' (to carve). Kircher viewed these not as an alphabet for sounds, but as symbols of divine mysteries.</note> *symbols, the structure and propagation of sacred letters, and the ancient Writers of all ages. In this book, we bring back to the anvil for reshaping the sacred doctrine that was nearly abolished by the injuries of time; though it remains pure in various monuments of the Ancients, it was variously dispersed into only the smallest fragments according to the knowledge each Author was able to obtain. We have selected this doctrine from the inner chambers of all surviving monuments and restored it to its integrity after it was renewed. With what incredible labor and how much effort of mind and body this was done, I believe can only be understood by one who weighs this Work in his mind and, with equal daring, enters this inaccessible darkness of Antiquity and attempts to open the most hidden recesses of a most abstruse literature, penetrated by no one until now.*

*Furthermore, since the Greeks, those Apes of the Ancient Egyptians <note>Kircher frequently argued that Greek philosophy, religion, and science were merely distorted imitations of much older Egyptian "wisdom."</note>, compiled many things and made the doctrine of the Egyptians their own by transforming it with various methods and names, it seemed right to present a Greco-Egyptian* <term>Mystagogia</term> <note>A 'Mystagogy' is an interpretation of mysteries or a guide for those being initiated into sacred rites.</note> *in which we have extensively pursued a certain parallel comparison of the fables of the Greeks to those of the Egyptians, as well as the rites and ceremonies observed in sacrifices related under various allegories; this is what the* Third Book *presents.*

*This being finished, there remained the interpretation of our present Obelisk. In order to set this before the eyes of the curious Reader without confusion, we thought that individual Hierogrammatisms <note>Kircher's term for the specific clusters of sacred symbols or "sacred carvings" that make up an inscription.</note> of greater importance should be explained separately, so that the genius, skill, logic, and Method in the architecture of the devised symbols might shine forth as if in a model. Once this was performed, we hoped it would come to pass that the Reader, in the actual interpretation, would proceed without confusion—*

->P A R Æ N E T I C A<-
<note>original: "Parænetica"; Introductory or exhortatory remarks intended to advise or instruct the reader.</note>

...proceeding, so that whatever could be desired concerning the intimate knowledge of any sacred writing <term>Hierogrammatismus; the system of sacred Egyptian script or the act of writing holy symbols</term> might find here a doctrine gathered together, confirmed and established by the monuments of all the ancient authors. This is the idea that the Fourth Book presents to us. Therefore, having first laid out these preparations for the study of hieroglyphics—which are absolutely necessary to firmly establish our undertaking—we finally proceed to the actual interpretation of the Obelisk, which the Fifth Book presents. In this, with the assistance of God, the Father of Lights <note>original: "Deo Patre luminum"; a biblical reference to James 1:17, suggesting that all true knowledge and clarity descend from God.</note>, we shall apply ourselves with that sincerity and honesty which befits a faithful interpreter. We do not rely on mere and pure conjectures, as many wrongly believe, but we shall untie the knots using the doctrines found in the monuments of the most approved Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, Syrian, Arabic, Egyptian, Persian, Ethiopian, and other Eastern authors. We shall establish these points so firmly that no room will remain for anyone to doubt the truth of the matter in the future. Indeed, I would wish all fair judges of these things to be persuaded that we shall provide as much in this work as the cited authorities have proven.

->§. III.<-

*In which the reasoning, Method, and manner maintained in the interpretation of this Obelisk proposed in Book 5 is explained; the resources of the Libraries, the workshops of antiquities, and the learned men by whose counsel and help the author was supported are cited; and it is demonstrated through various examples that this interpretation of ours, proposed in the last book, is carried out so according to the mind of the ancients that it can signify nothing other than what we have explained there.*

Since we may seem to have attacked a difficult task—one unattempted until these times—not without a mark of rashness, I therefore foresee that there will not be wanting those who, spurred on by a dog’s tooth <note>original: "canino dente"; a Latin idiom referring to malicious, snapping, or cynical criticism.</note>, will object that this interpretation proposed by us in the Fifth Book was invented by our own imagination. They will argue this chiefly on the grounds that symbolic figures are so composed that a sense can easily be drawn and twisted from them by anyone into whatever they wish; and that this must be felt regarding hieroglyphics just as it is regarding all other symbols. And therefore, they may claim that no one can yet be certain of the truth of an exposition made in this way. To show that their complaint is unjust, right at the entrance of this book, in order to restrain the accusations of detractors, we have thought it timely to demonstrate here that our exposition (once the necessary foundations are laid) so squares with the mind of the ancient sages that it is clear they intended to signify nothing else through said symbols except what has been stated. So that this might be done as well as possible, it seemed best to begin the matter from the egg <note>original: "ab ouo"; a classical idiom meaning to start from the very beginning or the earliest origin.</note>.

A triple kind of demonstration, by the unanimous consensus of philosophers, is known to have been employed at all times in the acquisition of the sciences: mathematical, physical, and moral. Just as mathematical demonstration investigates the affections and properties of both types of quantity <note>referring to continuous quantity (geometry) and discrete quantity (arithmetic)</note> through principles known by the light of nature and eternal truth, free from all deception, so it also produces a certain and properly called science, with every scrap of doubt removed. Physical demonstration, since it arrives at the knowledge of hidden causes through experiments with things, does indeed produce science, but because of the experi—

<meta>catchword: mentum, [ment]</meta>

<summary>Kircher defends his interpretive method against potential critics, arguing that his decoding of the obelisk is not mere conjecture but is based on a vast array of ancient languages and "demonstrations" equivalent to mathematical and physical proofs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s defense of his interpretive method. He moves from discussing the types of intellectual certainty to the "moral demonstration" provided by historical authority. He argues that his decoding of the obelisk is not mere guesswork but is grounded in the established wisdom of the ancients, specifically the "Egyptian wisdom" credited to figures like Moses and Solomon.</meta>

# E P I S T O L A
<note>Epistle or Letter; likely part of the Dedicatory Epistle or the Preface to the Reader.</note>

...evidence, which, just as it is for the most part exposed to the phantasms <note>mental images or impressions</note> of the senses, and thus is not free from deception, does not reach the certainty of the former <note>referring to mathematical or metaphysical certainty discussed on the previous page</note>; yet, as **Aristotle** testifies, it triumphs under the title of true science. Finally, **moral demonstration**, since it depends on the experience of human actions, produces knowledge indeed, but only of such a kind as the condition of moral things permits, which is also called "human faith" <note>credibility based on human testimony</note>. It is in this sense that I accept it in this place, as it relies for the most part on the Authority of the speaker. For a similar reason, the **Authority of God** the revealer produces faith more certain than all science; for it relies solely, as I have said, on the Authority of God revealing, who, since He is infinitely wise and good, can neither be deceived nor deceive. There is a certain human Authority that is an imitator of this, which must be insisted upon unless we wish to invalidate and annihilate the histories of all past things.

This certainty has its own validity, approved by the unanimous judgment and testimony of all learned men and accepted up to this day. It contains all secular and ecclesiastical histories, as well as the monuments of ancient authors accepted everywhere by posterity. Since these have been accepted by everyone for many centuries up to these present times, they also deserve a necessary faith; without which, as I said, the actions of all human affairs would rightly collapse, nothing certain could be written or said, and all things would be neglected, entangled in doubts. I do not speak here of authors and histories of suspect reliability, but of those who have established their authority for many centuries with excellent reputation. 

And so, insisting upon this Authority of ancient and approved writers, which we call **moral or Authoritative demonstration**, we have demonstrated the interpretation of the things contained in this present **Obelisk** in such a way—unless I am mistaken—that, as long as the said Authority stands, any sensible person would be forced to admit that this exposition is both just and could not possibly exhibit anything other than what has been stated. I am speaking always of the essential meaning of the things; for in more minute matters, I do not deny that they could have had one meaning or another. However, I say that such a meaning was of a kind that would not differ in the least from the essential meaning of the things. Nevertheless, in all these matters, I would not wish to constrain the Reader to my interpretation so as to take away their free will of judging; rather, I wished to bring forward to the fair Reader only such reasons as could prove the proposed truth.

These things being proposed, let us now approach our demonstration with the help of the good God. It is admitted by everyone, and I assume as certain from the proofs in the first book: that the **Egyptians** were the first of mortals after the **Cataclysm** <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note> to discourse on the highest mysteries, both of nature and of divinity. Indeed, this method of philosophizing was of such fame and celebrity that none of the ancient Sages seemed to have achieved anything great in the acquisition of the sciences unless he had been imbued in some way with the **wisdom of the Egyptians**. The sacred text of **Acts 7** teaches that **Moses** was specifically instructed in this, above all other sciences, in these words: *And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.* Concerning this wisdom, it is also held in **1 Kings chapter 4**: *And the wisdom of Solomon preceded the wisdom of all the Egyptians.* It is assumed, therefore, even from the Sacred Scriptures themselves, that the Egyptians possessed a certain method of philosophizing which they called "wisdom." Since, therefore, wisdom is the knowledge of excellent things and the highest causes, it is first asked: what was that wisdom? Certainly, by the consensus of all Authors, it was nothing other than the knowledge of God, of Angels or demons, of the divine ministers in the World, and of the various worlds—

<meta>catchword: diuersi- (diverse-)</meta>

<summary>Kircher defines "moral demonstration" as proof based on historical authority and applies it to his Egyptian studies. He argues that Egyptian wisdom, praised in the Bible through Moses and Solomon, is the key to understanding the obelisk's mysteries.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, moral demonstration, historical authority, Egyptian wisdom, Moses, Solomon, Cataclysm, Obelisk interpretation</keywords>

Having established "moral certainty" on the previous page, he now cites specific ancient authorities—Hermes Trismegistus and Iamblichus—to prove that the obelisks were intended as permanent storehouses of this sacred knowledge, intended to survive the eventual downfall of Egyptian civilization.</meta>

-># P A R Æ N E T I C A <-
<note>An introductory exhortation or advisory address.</note>

...by their diversity and the order in which they flow into them; concerning the attraction of the Gods and Genii <note>protective spirits or divine agencies</note> and their descent into the individuals of the said Worlds; concerning astrological elections <note>choosing auspicious times based on the stars</note>; and concerning the rites and ceremonies by which each individual, through the proper application of things suitable for sacrifices, may attract the good and put the evil to flight. Finally, how through the knowledge of divine operations of this kind, individuals raised above the wheel of fortune <note>the unpredictable turns of fate</note> may become god-like and partakers of all good things—which is the ultimate goal and fulfillment of all Egyptian wisdom. Since I have discussed all these matters everywhere throughout this work, I have deemed it superfluous to repeat them here with tediousness. Let the reader consult the entire second book, and chapters 6, 7, 8, and 9 of the third book, as well as many things handed down here and there in the remaining books, where we confirm the doctrines of the Egyptians by the authors of all ages so thoroughly that no one can any longer rightly doubt the truth of the matter.

Secondly, I assume from the authors cited a little earlier that this Wisdom was nothing other than the sacred and symbolic science of the aforementioned things, carved into Obelisks, as has been demonstrated everywhere in this whole Work. This is so true that if anyone should dare to contradict it, they should know that with the same rashness they would be opposing the authors of all ages, who called this aforementioned wisdom "hieroglyphic"—that is, "sacred carving"—for no other reason than that they regarded it as a sacred and divine science, known only to the Priests, yet to be venerated by the common people at a mere glance, and left behind as a permanent monument and the sole defense of their homeland, inscribed on stones and obelisks to last forever. **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Egyptians attributed their sacred writings</note>, foreseeing by some instinct the future ruin of these Obelisks and of the ancestral religion, cried out thus:

> *O* **Egypt**, **Egypt**, *of your religions only fables will remain, and equally incredible to your posterity; only words carved into stones will remain, telling of your pious deeds. And the Phoenician or the Indian, or some such person, will inhabit Egypt; for divinity will return to heaven, and all deserted men will die, and thus Egypt, widowed of God and men, will be abandoned.* <note>original: "O Aegypte, Aegypte, religionum tuarum solæ supererunt fabulæ..." This famous passage is known as the "Lament of Hermes."</note>

This means that the doctrine received from the ancient Fathers concerning God will remain alone, carved into stones—that is, into the Obelisks—hidden as if in symbolic <note>Latin: "subtropicis," referring to tropes or figurative coverings</note> coverings. But as men dissolve into the stain of superstitions and vices, Egypt, destitute of divine help, will finally crumble and fall into ultimate ruin. Regarding these words, see **St. Augustine** discussing them more at length in book 17 of *The City of God*. 

Thus we have testimony even from **Mercury** <note>The Roman name for Hermes/Thoth</note> himself that his sacred doctrine was carved into stones. Indeed, **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> describes this truth more vividly than all others at the very beginning of his philosophy *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*. **Egyptian** writers, believing that all things were discovered by **Mercury**, dedicated their books to **Mercury**; **Mercury** presides over wisdom and eloquence. **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, **Democritus**, **Eudoxus**, and many others went to the **Egyptian** priests; the dogmas of this book are of the **Assyrians** and **Egyptians**. **Pythagoras** and **Plato** learned philosophy from the columns of **Mercury** in **Egypt**; the columns of **Mercury** are full of doctrines. But see what we have handed down extensively on these matters in book 1, chapters 2 and 3, likewise in book 2, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, etc.

Thus it is clear by the consensus of Authors that this hieroglyphic wisdom, as something sacred...

He is establishing that because the physical monuments (obelisks) and the ancient textual accounts of Egyptian philosophy both survive, a "mutual comparison" between the two should logically reveal their secrets—a task he claims no one has successfully achieved before him.</meta>

-># E P I S T O L A <-
<note>Latin: "Epistle" or "Letter." This serves as the formal introductory address to the reader.</note>

...that a certain doctrine worthy of eternity was carved into stones—that is, into Obelisks, Sphinxes, <term>Abaci</term> <note>In this context, architectural tablets or flat decorative surfaces</note>, and statues. This indeed requires no proof, since the Obelisks themselves and the fragments of countless statues brought from Egypt to Rome by the Emperors testify to it more than enough. These are visible everywhere in this "theater of the world" to the eyes of learned men, as was made clear in Book 2. Among these, our own **Pamphilian Obelisk** <note>The obelisk currently standing atop Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona, recovered and erected by Pope Innocent X (Pamphilj)</note>, the interpretation of which we have presented in this work, is a primary example.

We hold, therefore, from these premises: that the Egyptians possessed a hidden science regarding the deepest mysteries of divinity and nature; we also hold that this same science was inscribed by the Egyptians upon Obelisks and other monuments; furthermore, we hold that most of the Greek philosophers—the very leaders of all Greek wisdom—derived their own knowledge from stones of this kind. Since, therefore, the doctrine handed down by ancient Authors survives to this very day, and the stones of the Obelisks themselves also survive—immune to the ravages of time and still conspicuous and admirable for the splendor of their hieroglyphs after so many centuries—they must secretly contain that handed-down doctrine under the hidden veils of various symbols. Since, I say, all these things remain (as has been demonstrated throughout this Work), nothing else could be desired except that the aforementioned doctrine be aptly combined with the inscriptions on our Obelisk and others. Finally, through a mutual comparison of the two, performed with singular industry, the <term>sacramentum</term> <note>The "sacred secret" or inner mystery</note> of the hidden truth might be unfolded. Since no one before us, as far as I know, has attempted this, no one should wonder that the hieroglyphic doctrine was hitherto thought to have been lost to the world—until we, finally, with God as our guide, adapted the meanings of the Authors to the figures and brought the hidden truth into that light which we have exposed in this work for the judgment of the fair-minded Reader.

Lest I seem to seek wisdom beyond the limits of modesty, or to attribute more to myself than is proper, I have decided to reveal here to the honest Reader, with appropriate candor and sincerity, how I first came to think of this matter, and by what means I finally pressed this intended Work into execution.

Since from my early youth I always possessed an incredible desire for knowledge of hidden things, and my mind was most set on fire for the study of foreign languages, it happened that after completing my studies in Philosophy and Theology, I came upon a volume regarding the Obelisks erected by **Sixtus V** <note>Pope Sixtus V (reigned 1585–1590), who famously re-erected four ancient Egyptian obelisks in Rome, including the one in St. Peter's Square</note>, which was filled with exotic figures. I was stunned by the sight of them. While I understood from my reading that these Obelisks were marked with the hieroglyphs of ancient wisdom—though they had been penetrated and explained by no one until now—I was inflamed with the greatest desire to hunt for the truth. I reasoned thus with myself: the characters remain, and indeed have stayed pure and uncorrupted through so many centuries; the doctrine which they signify must undoubtedly lie hidden somewhere. If it is not in the hidden monuments of the Latins or Greeks, then at least some traces of it must still survive in the records of the Orientals <note>Kircher refers here to Coptic, Arabic, and Ethiopic sources</note>. Driven, therefore, by these hidden and powerful urges, I first commended the project I was undertaking to God through constant prayers and orisons, knowing by some hidden premonition that by His help I would undoubtedly achieve something. On the other hand, I clearly saw that without a knowledge of Oriental languages (of which I had already acquired some small knowledge), I would labor in vain. Armed with the support of both divine help and linguistic study, I applied myself with all my strength and the most intense study and sleepless nights to the study of hieroglyphic literature and idioms...

### E N C O U R A G E M E N T
<meta>catchword: scattered</meta>

...I applied myself. It happened in the meantime, at that very time, when I was driven from **Germany** by the tumults of war, that while I traveled through various nations, I intended this one thing: that wherever it was permitted, I might receive even the smallest information regarding **Egyptian** matters and the Authors who looked back upon my purpose. Nor did divine goodness fail my prayers, for I happened upon various books and aids by an unexpected chance—a true symbol of the divine will urging me on. 

Therefore, by the labor of many years—both through seeing and surveying the principal libraries of **Germany**, **France**, and **Italy**, and especially here in **Rome**—I weighed and read through all those authors, whether in manuscript or printed form, in **Latin**, **Greek**, **Hebrew**, **Arabic**, **Chaldean** <note>original: "Chaldaeos"; in Kircher's time, this often referred to Aramaic</note>, **Egyptian**, **Syriac**, **Armenian**, **Ethiopian**, and others published in the common languages of **Europe**. These were hidden in the **Vatican**, **Angelica**, **Barberini**, and **Sforza** libraries, the **Colleges of the Society of Jesus** <note>The Jesuits, Kircher's own religious order</note>, and other private museums, and made some mention of Egyptian matters. With intense study and persistent speculation, I took care to excerpt the specific passages into certain series of subjects, not without great expense. Thus, whatever I found concerning hieroglyphic animals, plants, instruments, sacrifices, rites, stones, crowns, stars, and other figures serving the sacred doctrine, I set aside individually into classes, as I have said. 

Then, from all the **Egyptian** monuments I could obtain, I likewise drew out the hieroglyphic characters according to their classes. By this method, through the help of the analytical art and by an ingenious combination, I compared the individual figures with the texts of the Authors and their corresponding figures, through the unceasing labor of many years and a process known and attempted by few. Indeed, by this singular industry, it happened that I gradually arrived at a hidden knowledge of things and clearly recognized the logic of the hieroglyphic context. And once these foundations were happily laid, I finally progressed so far that I no longer found any difficulty at all in the meanings of the more common hieroglyphs.

However, since many truly abstruse and nearly impassable symbols occurred here and there—whose shapes resembled neither man, nor animal, nor plant, nor any certain figure from those that could be known to us, but rather referred to unknown vessels and various utensils used in sacred rites, and there were no books that might suggest even a shadowy knowledge of them—I had to consult and excerpt the idols and images, fragments of stone, gems, amulets, charms, **Cameos**, and **Gnostic Talismans** <note>original: "Telismata"; likely referring to magical or astronomical charms</note> surviving in all the Treasuries of Antiquities both in **Rome** and elsewhere. From the continuous and incredible labor of combining these—while I studiously compared figures with figures, marks <note>original: "apices"; literally 'points' or the small details of characters</note> with marks, and instruments with instruments—by the grace of God, I perfectly understood that which I had doubted. For whatever had been carved here and there upon the Obelisks in a confused, obscure, and imperfect manner, I found expressed so clearly, expressly, and perfectly in the said monuments of statues, or tablets, and cameos, that it was no longer permitted to doubt the truth of their meanings. By finally comparing these new findings with the passages and texts of the Authors through combination, I at last attained the truth of things by the grace of God, the Father of Lights.

Therefore, having approached the interpretation of this present Obelisk as well as all the others with these labors and these aids, I finally completed it. From this, it also became brilliantly clear to me that **Egyptian** literature never perished, but had always lain hidden here and there, scattered among the monuments of Ancient Authors; all that was lacking until now was one who...

## E P I S T L E

->scattered<- doctrine, unearthed from obscure monuments, I have aptly compared with the hieroglyphic figures themselves. Because this has been done by no one before me until now, it is no wonder that this hieroglyphic doctrine was thought—as I have said—to have been almost entirely abolished in the opinion of nearly everyone. Secondly, it also became clear that whatever secrets are held and hidden in the monuments of **Hermes**, **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, and their followers, actually flowed from this same hieroglyphic doctrine. There is no difference between them, except that the **Egyptians** revealed this doctrine—wrapped in the "rind" <note>original: "cortice"; Kircher uses the metaphor of a tough outer shell or bark to describe the difficult symbolic layer of Egyptian wisdom</note> of obscure symbols—to only a few men of the priestly order who were distinguished in wisdom. Meanwhile, the **Hermetic**, **Pythagorean**, and **Platonic** followers handed it down to the men of their own sects in a way that was, so to speak, expanded and unfolded from those wrappings; I discuss these men throughout this entire book.

We have, therefore, the method, the industry, and the reasoning by which we proceeded in the restoration of hieroglyphic literature. Since this is established by the consensus of all the most approved **Authors**, and does not deviate in the slightest from the intention of the **Egyptians**, no one will doubt the truth of the interpretation I have made, unless perhaps they are an unbeliever or of a particularly stubborn brain. 

But at this point, some will object to my citation of certain **Authors** who, appearing to be of suspect reliability, might also make the interpretation doubtful. To respond more fully to their objection, I have seen fit to show what selection of **Authors** I have used. First, therefore, besides the volumes of the **Hermetics**, **Platonists**, and **Pythagoreans**—which I have turned over repeatedly with the greatest diligence and intense study—I have also weighed the whole of **Plotinus**, **Philo**, **Flavius Josephus**, **Porphyry**, **Iamblichus**, **Numenius**, **Synesius**, **Plutarch**, **Apuleius**, and other students of **Pythagorean** and **Platonic** science, comparing them with the figures with the greatest study. 

Afterward, I consulted the monuments of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The "SS. Patrum" or "Sancti Patres" are the early influential Christian theologians</note>: the volumes of **Dionysius**, **Tertullian**, **Origen**, **Justin Martyr**, **Clement of Alexandria**, **Arnobius**, **Lactantius Firmianus**, **Eusebius**, **Cyril**, **Athanasius**, **Augustine**, and others whom we have cited in the **Second Book**, regarding what they handed down in their works concerning **Egyptian** matters. I also separately excerpted passages from **Sanchuniathon**, **Zoroaster**, the **Sibylline oracles**, **Orpheus**, **Bitis**, **Artephius**, **Hecataeus**, **Pherecydes**, **Berosus**, **Manetho**, **Arius**, **Calosyrus**, and others whose works are lost at this time; the book will show how much I have progressed by stitching these together into a "cento" <note>A "cento" is a literary work made up of various fragments from other authors</note>. 

After these, I set upon the **Historians**, **Orators**, **Poets**, **Lexicographers**, and **Grammarians**. I approached **Herodotus**, **Stesichorus**, **Hesiod**, **Homer**, **Demetrius Phalereus**, **Pausanias**, **Athenaeus**, **Diodorus**, **Suidas**, **Harpocration**, **Photius**, **Julius Pollux**, **Cicero**, **Martianus Capella**, **Apuleius**, **Virgil**, **Ovid**, **Pliny**, **Lucian**, **Lucan**, **Lucretius**, **Juvenal**, **Persius**, **Statius**, and countless others concerning **Egyptian** matters, studiously noting individual passages. 

Truly, from the **Hebrews** and **Chaldaeans** <note>original: "Chaldaeis"; here referring to Aramaic sources</note>, I consulted the books of **Zohar**, written by the author **Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai**, the book **Yetzirah** <note>original: "Iezira"; a foundational work of Jewish mysticism</note>, the **Mikra Gedolot** <note>The "Great Scripture," a Rabbinic Bible featuring various commentaries</note> and its **Rabbinic** commentators **Ibn Ezra**, **Rashi**, **Radak**, **Ralbag**, **Baal Ha-Turim**, **Rabbi Menasseh**, and the work titled **Shilte Ha-Gibborim** <note>"Shields of the Mighty," a 16th-century Italian Jewish work on antiquities</note>, and finally **Rambam** <note>Moses Maimonides</note>, the "Doctor of the Perplexed" <note>Refers to his famous work "The Guide for the Perplexed"</note>. From the **Chaldaeans**, I used the **Babylonian** and **Jerusalem Targums** <note>Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible</note> and **Talmudic** works, especially the one titled **Avodah Zarah** <note>original: "gnabadah zarà"; a Talmudic tractate dealing with "Foreign Service" or idolatry</note>; also the **Zohar of Jochai**, the work called **Pardes** <note>likely "Pardes Rimonim" by Moses Cordovero</note>, along with the remaining **Cabalistic** monuments of the **Authors**, where the Reader will find many noteworthy **Rabbis** cited. When I found that they handed down many things by no means discordant with our argument,

...less worthy, I considered them worthy to be included in the registry of approved Authors; since even among dross, a precious pearl is occasionally discovered. Among the Arabs whom we cite throughout are Gelaldinus, Salamas, Aben Candathi, Algazel, Abenregel, Albuchasem, the *Geography of Nubia*, and that which Abulfeida produced; along with countless others we cite here and there. Among these, a truly principal place is held by Abenuafchia <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 10th-century author whose work on ancient scripts Kircher believed to be an authentic key to hieroglyphs</note> on the worship and religion of the ancient Egyptians, whom you will find cited by Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, known as Maimonides</note> in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nebuchim"</note>. Another is Abenephi, who stood out as a more curious investigator of Egyptian antiquity than the rest. His foundations truly "smell of the ancient lamp" <note>An idiom meaning they show signs of great midnight study and antiquity</note>, and he was quite skilled in the Egyptian language which we call Coptic, as is clear from his citation of names; he, above all others, handed me the torch to the inner sanctums of Egypt. 

When I once showed his manuscript to **Peiresc** <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a famous French astronomer and antiquarian who mentored Kircher</note>, he was immediately filled with such immense joy that from that time forward he "moved every stone" <note>did everything in his power</note> to promote the business of restoring the hieroglyphs. That this is so, **Gassendi** <note>Pierre Gassendi, a philosopher and scientist who wrote Peiresc's biography</note> confirms in his *Life of the Said Peiresc*, on page 265, with these words:

> "I was present, meanwhile, when he also wished to summon **Athanasius Kircher**, a German of the **Society of JESUS**, who was then staying at Avignon. He was reported to be exceptionally skilled in the mysteries of hieroglyphs; for which reason, to assist him, Peiresc had transmitted various books to him, as well as a copy of the **Isiac Table** described above. And since there was in Kircher's hands a distinguished manuscript—that is, the Arabic Author Rabbi Barachias Nephi (read *Abenephius*)—from whom the method of hieroglyphs was said to be handed down; for that reason, Peiresc entreated him to come to him, bringing both the manuscript itself and a certain specimen of his interpretation and notes. When he had done so, it cannot be said how ardently Peiresc encouraged him to finish the Coptic work and hasten its publication. The man was subsequently called to Rome; but Peiresc was not satisfied only with [appealing to] Mutio Vitelleschi, General of the Society of JESUS, but also to **Cardinal Barberini**, so that they might add a spur to him and provide enough leisure so that this work might come forth shortly." So says Gassendi.

I wanted to add these things here so that everything might stand with legitimate authentication. Furthermore, from the Syrians, **Saint Ephrem** was of great use, as was **Mor Isaac**, who was one of the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea and Bishop of Mesopotamia; his philosophy, extracted from the Library of the Maronites, is in my possession, along with other Syriac commentaries on Holy Scripture. From the Ethiopians, various letters sent from Ethiopia to Rome concerning Ethiopian matters and stored in the Vatican were used. From the Coptic, the support came from various fragments of Rituals, found both in the Vatican Library and kept by the Knight **Pietro della Valle**, as well as those brought to me from Egypt; finally, the work entitled *The Egyptian Language Restored* <note>original: "Lingua Aegyptiaca instaurata"</note>, published by us here in Rome in previous years, as well as the work called the *Great Scale* <note>original: "Scala magna"; a Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note>. From each of these, we have drawn material suitable for our purpose.

The "Treasuries and Workshops" <note>referring to private museums or cabinets of curiosities</note> of the Antiquarians were: first, that of the man worthy of eternal memory, **Nicolas Peiresc**, a most distinguished Senator at Aix-en-Provence <note>original: "Aquis Sextiis"</note> in the Narbonnese Province. Out of the zeal with which he was carried to promote these studies, whatever rare Egyptian thing was in his treasuries of antiquities, he sent a description of it to me in Rome to assist in the restoration of the hieroglyphs.

The second was that of **Cardinal Francesco Barberini**, whose curator was **Leonardo of Siena**; then that of **Claude Menestrier**, which was however dispersed after his death and came into the hands of various people. The third was that of **Francesco Angeloni** at the Pincian Gate, a man [renowned] for his writings...

<meta>bleed-through from reverse page</meta>

...less <note>original: "minus"</note> than those especially famous for their knowledge of ancient things, over which **Pietro Bellori** <note>Giovanni Pietro Bellori (1613–1696), a famous biographer of artists and a renowned antiquarian in Rome</note>, the nephew, presided. A fourth was that of **Francesco Gualdi**, Knight of St. Stephen, which was most richly furnished with Egyptian items, located in the Campo Carleo; in this very year, it passed by donation to the Most Christian King <note>The King of France</note>, under the care of the Minim Fathers on the Pincian Hill. Next to this is the collection of **Giovanni Battista Casali** at the foot of the Aventine Hill, which is particularly remarkable both for its Egyptian furnishings and for every kind of rarity. Then there is that of **Marcello Milesi**, a Roman Jurist, which after his death passed to the Theatine Fathers on the Quirinal Hill; and that of **Giovanni Battista Romano** of the Augustinian family, which upon his death was auctioned off and passed into other hands. Lest anyone say that I have worked with doubtful reliability in this project, I have placed the authentications made by these men themselves at the beginning of the Work.

There were also the private Museums <note>term: Museum - In the 17th century, this referred to a private collection of curiosities, books, and artifacts, often called a "Cabinet of Curiosities."</note> of **Pietro Stefanoni**, **Ippolito Vitelleschi**, and **Pietro della Valle**, Knights; and in Padua, that of **Johannes Rhode**, a man of refined wit and character. But above all others is the collection of the Illustrious **Cassiano dal Pozzo**, Knight, who acts as a common Patron and Maecenas <note>A generous benefactor of the arts and sciences</note> to all men of letters; he never ceases to promote the common good of the Republic of Letters <note>term: Republic of Letters - The international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 16th–18th centuries who corresponded across borders.</note> through both advice and assistance. To these, I could not fail to add the "Workshop" <note>original: "Ergasterion"</note> of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, most richly furnished with everything that could be desired in all of Italy—which they commonly call the "Gallery" <note>The Uffizi Gallery in Florence</note>—from which the Excellent Physician **Giovanni Nardi** extracted a vast supply of hieroglyphic material for my use. The same was provided in former times by **Ferrante Imperato** in Naples; in Palermo by the Most Illustrious **Carlo di Ventimiglia**; and in Malta by **Giovanni Francesco Abela**, Vice-Chancellor, all possessors of the rarest items. I come now to foreigners, among whom I first encountered the Imperial Treasury <note>original: "Gazophylacium Cæsareum"</note>, then the collections of the Most Serene Duke of Bavaria, Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, at Munich. From these, various materials were supplied both by **Jan Marek Marci**, a most famous physician and singular friend, and by various Fathers of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits</note>, which will be made clear in due time, God willing.

Added to these were the most learned records of famous men: **Lucas Holstenius** and **Leo Allatius**. The former, if anyone does, certainly possesses a most well-equipped museum of Platonic and Pythagorean manuscript volumes; he granted me the use of them not unwillingly, but with the greatest and most profuse liberality and zeal with which he urges the promotion of literature. Furthermore, in Paris, **Gabriel Naudé**, that indefatigable "glutton" for books and letters <note>original: "Helluo"</note>, was of no small help, providing various materials above all others. I also benefited from the various volumes filled with doctrine by the most learned **Petau** <note>Dionysius Petavius</note>; among the English, the works of **Selden** and **Greaves**; among the Dutch, the works of those most brilliant lights **Scaliger**, **Saumaise**, **Heinsius**, **Vossius**, and **Boxhorn**; and among the Danes, the liberality of **Bang**, **Bering**, and **Bartholin** in sending suitable aids for my undertaking. Finally, I add **Father Giacomo Viva** of our Society, a most faithful and loving coadjutor of my studies and a man tireless in his labors; broken at last by these efforts, he died while traveling to Loreto, entering a better life—a man worthy of a longer one. The line is finally closed by **Father Leo Sanchius**, Prefect of Superior Studies at the Roman College of the Society of Jesus, a man of sublime intellect and equipped with every kind of erudition, who never ceased to urge me toward the prosecution of the work I had begun, and to help me when I was roused by his timely advice. I wished to testify my due gratitude to all and each of these for posterity. Thus, with these aids sent to me by men of letters from every part of Europe, while I was examining each and every...

# EXHORTATIONS

*By aptly combining each element with one another, I have truly drawn an incredible light in unraveling the more secret Sphinxes <note>Here, "Sphinxes" is a metaphor for the profound riddles and enigmas of antiquity.</note>. However, modern critics might raise two objections against me: namely, the Hermetic works <note>term: Hermetica - A body of wisdom texts attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, a figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth.</note> and the mystic philosophy of Aristotle, and secondly, the Arabic authors whom I cite throughout. Regarding the Hermetic works, we have discussed this at length in Book 1, page 36; however, it should be noted there that some attribute them to the Gnostics <note>A diverse group of early religious thinkers who claimed secret "gnosis" or knowledge; Kircher, as a Jesuit, views them as heretics but acknowledges their scholarly reach.</note>. I would not entirely disagree with them; for, even if we grant (though not concede) that they were published by the Gnostics, it does not follow that they did not contain the genuine doctrine of Hermes. Since the Egyptian Gnostics possessed a remarkable knowledge of Egyptian matters beyond all others—as is evident from their surviving talismans <note>Amulets or charms believed to have magical properties.</note> engraved on various precious stones—and since their sole intention was to revive Egyptian dogmas and superstitions from the underworld, they surely must have sought out the books of the ancients with the greatest study and zeal to find support for their growing sect. They would have unearthed, transcribed, and published these from the libraries of Egypt, among which could be the Hermetic books I mentioned. Therefore, it is by no means to be inferred that these were fabricated by them or thrust upon the world as some sort of counterfeit offspring, since they contain a greater and more elevated doctrine than we would expect from such wicked men. But let us hear Iamblichus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher of the 4th century AD.</note> on these matters, who I trust will close the mouths of detractors with his own authority; for he says in his *On the Mysteries*, page 353 of the Basel edition:*

> *Once these things are distinguished, the doubts you say you conceived regarding the Egyptian books you read are easily solved. For those books circulated under the title of Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes.</note> contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers; for they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in philosophy.*

*I come now to that mystic philosophy of Aristotle, written according to the mind of the Egyptians, regarding which there is no less controversy among modern critics. According to the Arab Abenama, and as Francisco Rossi states in the preface, this was first detected and translated from Greek into Arabic; later, by the providence of the Divine Power, it was found in the library of Damascus (commonly called Schām). At that time, Nicolaus Rosius of Ravenna arranged for it to be translated word-for-word into the Italian language by Moses Rouasius, a physician then living in Cyprus who was well-versed in both Italian and Arabic. When it was brought to Italy, Pietro Nicolai Castellani, a philosopher and physician of Faenza during the time of Pope Leo X, translated it into Latin. This philosophy is such that it could deservedly be a model for hieroglyphic literature. Even if some attribute it to Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who linked Plato with ancient Eastern wisdom.</note>, and some to Ammonius Saccas <note>The teacher of Plotinus and the father of the Neoplatonic school.</note>—who likely hid this among other Platonic works as a secret treasure not to be revealed—nonetheless, that this was Aristotle’s and no other’s, gathered from the mouth of Plato, is asserted in Book 1, page 3 of the Roman edition of that same philosophy in these words:* Plato once gave many attributes to the soul, to which we are ear-witnesses, but he did not write them down, otherwise the reader would have grasped his mind; *and in many other places, he cites his Metaphysics, as well as his books on the soul, the world, and on coming-to-be and passing-away. From this, it is clear that Aristotle [produced] this philosophy in his old age and the final times of his life, and after the death of Plato, lest*

perhaps published while Plato was still living, he would have been convicted of plagiarism. This treasure, known to only a few, was later acquired by Ammonius Saccas <note>A third-century philosopher from Alexandria, often considered the teacher of Plotinus and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, or some other member of the Platonic school much later, who claimed it as his own. However, that this work can by no means be attributed to Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea, a philosopher who sought to link Plato with Pythagorean and even Eastern wisdom.</note> or Saccas, but is instead the **Platonic offspring of Aristotle**, is proven by the fact that it is written with such a subtlety of mind that it seems to yield to none of the Aristotelian works, whether you look at the sublimity of the subject matter or the knowledge of divine and most exalted things. It would therefore belong to a simple—not to say base—mind for someone like Numenius or Ammonius Saccas to suppress their own name and grant this glory to another, when by this work alone they could have secured the immortality of their own name.

As for the fact that some might object to certain <term>anachronisms</term> <note>Kircher uses the term "achronismos," meaning errors in the chronological order of events or the mention of things before they existed.</note> occurring in the text—that is, if they find certain discussions that suggest the book was written in the centuries following the Philosopher’s death—these are merely the persuasions of the critics of our time. For even if we grant (though do not concede) that some anachronism occurs in the said book, I nevertheless assert that one cannot conclude from this that the book is not by Aristotle. Such anachronisms are often added by later interpreters, as can be seen today in many ancient monuments, either to remove the obscurity of the context or by the prompting of their own imagination. From this source, too, came the division into books and chapters by later hands in those volumes which were originally written as a continuous text by the ancient authors. Thus, it is clear that anachronisms, if they ever appear in very ancient monuments, should be ascribed not to the Author, but to the Author’s **Scholiast** <note>An ancient or medieval commentator who added explanatory notes (scholia) to a text.</note> and interpreter.

Therefore, that this mystic philosophy contains the true doctrine of the ancient Egyptians—which Plato drew from them and then handed down orally to his disciples, and which Aristotle, after Plato’s death, was the first to capture in writing and make public—will be evident from what follows. Indeed, it touches upon <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>The sacred carvings of Egypt, which Kircher believed contained hidden, mystical truths rather than a phonetic language.</note> doctrine so precisely that it can be called an expanded interpretation of it. For by exactly combining the context of this said philosophy with the doctrine of the **Obelisks**, I have found them to be entirely the same. So that the reader may discover this **with their own eyes** <note>original: αὐτοψὶ (autopsi)</note>, let us present a specimen of this to the curious reader in the first four Diagrams of our Obelisk (the interpretation of which we have provided from page 308 to page 355 of this work); so that from this alone, the reader may gather what should be thought of the said Work.

But truly, so that the Truth may be revealed in parts, we shall prove the matter by example. What else does he do in the preface of Book 1, Chapter 1 of this said philosophy, except to show that he is emulating the most profound hieroglyphic doctrine—accessible only to the rarer and more sublime minds—with the said work? Indeed, to perform this more distinctly, he provides a sort of anatomy of the things to be said in the whole work, and a title for the entire work, which corresponds so closely to the first Diagrams of our Obelisk (which titles we have also called the summaries of the things contained in the whole Obelisk) that it can be called a living interpretation of them. But since these things can by no means be perceived without an exact comparison of the text with the hieroglyphic figures, we shall first provide the words of Aristotle himself (where in the beginning he cites both his *Metaphysics* and his books *On the Soul*), and then we shall apply the same to the first Diagrams of our Obelisk, so that the truth may become known part by part.

Similarly, we shall describe the base and contaminated soul, and then we will speculate on the disposition of the sensual and vegetative soul, as well as the quality of the soul of the earth, of fire, of water, and of the other elements. And these hidden matters, as we have stated before, we shall declare through figures sufficient for the purpose—thus far Aristotle.

And that He differs from others and moves all things without motion—is this not God considered in the solitary center of His unity, eternal, immense, and giving life to all things? And did he not speak of a Trinity when he said, "in Him, from Him, [and toward Him]"?*
