Secondly, what else is meant by the *Intellectual World* if not the *Angelic World*? Since this world is the nearest figure and exemplar of God's goodness, the Egyptians aptly placed it—using human figures—immediately after the Archetypal World, as is clear from the first diagrams. What else do they indicate through the variety of symbols with which these figures are equipped, if not the variety of divine forms inherent in them, through which they continually flow into lower things? These points also agree with the words of Aristotle: *Afterward, following the mind of the ancients, we shall consider the intellectual world, reflecting His goodness, and the inherent divine forms, and that goodness from it—namely, the intellectual world—flows into individual things,* etc.

Thirdly, when he says: *furthermore we shall relate the universal nature of heaven, how the power from the intellect exists within it, and also the dignity and light of the stars.* What else does he indicate but the *Sidereal World* <note>The world of the stars and planets</note>? Over this world the Intelligences preside. Its soul, as it were, and the moderator of all things, is Osiris under the form of a hawk—which is a symbol of light and life. This is indicated by his other properties, as well as by the serpent-bearing globe, by which the life and fertility he continually pours into the Sidereal World was signified.

Again, when he says: *We shall also relate the sublunary nature, how the power of Heaven is sent into it, which is manifested in sensible, material, changeable, and corruptible things.* What else does he point to but the fourth sacred engraving of the first Diagram—that is, the *material* <term>Hylean: from the Greek 'hyle' (matter), referring to the physical, elemental realm</term> or *Elemental World*? This is aptly indicated by angular figures, triangles, squares, and pyramids, as we have shown extensively in its proper place.

Just as they preside over the elements—air, water, fire, earth—and other mixtures, and over the sensory and vegetative nature, so they administer, order, and dispose all things toward a good or evil end. (none other than the hieroglyphic ones) are sufficient for our purpose. *Iamblichus* also bears witness to this in his work *On the Mysteries, folio 352*, with these words: (<note>original: "Atque ita Ægyptiorum tractatus..."</note> *And thus the Egyptian treatise on principles, proceeding from the highest down to the last, descends from the One into the multitude, a multitude governed by the one God; everywhere an infinite nature is imperiously contained within a certain defined limit, and especially by that Unit which is the exalted cause of all things.*)

You see, therefore, with what admirable connection our interpretation agrees with the words of *Aristotle* cited a little earlier. But someone might say at this point: if the *hieroglyphic* doctrine was already known in the times of *Plato and Aristotle*, then it is false (as we have said elsewhere) that it had already been lost before the time of *Alexander the Great*. I respond that the *hieroglyphic* doctrine can be considered in two ways in this context. First, in the abstract, without any reflection on the actual sacred carvings. Second, insofar as it is seen carved in the hieroglyphs themselves on *Columns* or *Obelisks*. If we consider it in the first way, it is certain that the aforementioned doctrine was never at any time abolished; rather, it was preserved and passed down, albeit in a scattered fashion, in the monuments of the *Hermetic, Pythagorean, and Platonic* authors and others, as has often been proven. But the other form of hieroglyphics—which was hidden secretly as if by a shell or a certain wrapping—was lost, since no one from the time of *Cambyses* <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; Kircher follows the tradition that the Persian conquest destroyed the Egyptian priestly tradition.</note> dared to perform anything in the way of its decoding. *Aristotle* himself testifies to this in his aforementioned *Mystical Theology, book 14, chapter 14*, with these words:

> The wise *Babylonians and Egyptians*, through the sharpness of their minds, looked into the forms of the intellectual World, having embraced a knowledge passed down from elsewhere or discovered by themselves—a profession which they even claimed for themselves. Indeed, when they were about to explain something, they used an "intellectual doctrine" rather than a human one like some others. For those who consulted them did not yet seem to themselves to learn firmly enough from opinions rendered in speech; therefore, they wrote down the concepts they had received in their minds—as we read with the evidence of our own eyes—upon stones through figures. They did the same in all sciences and arts, placing them in temples like pages to be read. Such were their useful books. They did this to indicate that the active, immaterial intellect created all things according to the specific reason and likeness of the essence of each thing. This was an excellent and most beautiful teaching, through which—would that they had also indicated by what means they reached those marvelous and hidden forms! For thus their Sacrament <note>Here used in the sense of a "sacred mystery" or "hidden ritual."</note> would be more worthy of praise, a condition that happens to few men.

From these words it is clearly gathered that *Aristotle*, with *Plato* as his guide, was imbued with the hieroglyphic doctrine and highly approved of it, yet he did not know the characters themselves. Thus, he seems to have wished for someone who might interpret them. He finally admits that their hidden sense is so sublime that it is granted to few, or hardly any, to reach such a great gift. And such men were *Pythagoras and Plato*; since *Iamblichus* asserts that they drew their doctrine from the columns of Mercury <note>The "Columns of Hermes/Mercury" were legendary pillars on which all ancient knowledge was said to be inscribed.</note>, there is no doubt that they drew some knowledge of these characters, even if it was not a universal one.

It is also clear (as we have always emphasized in the preceding pages) that these characters were by no means established by the wise so that they might compose words from them as if from an *alphabet*; but rather...

...that these were intellectual or "ideal" characters <note>The term "ideal" here refers to the Platonic theory of Ideas—universal archetypes rather than just mental concepts.</note>, under which they compressed many things into a few symbols. Consequently, Aristotle greatly approved of this method of writing, considering it close to the way "Angelic minds" understand things <note>Kircher suggests that angels perceive truth directly and holistically, without needing the step-by-step reasoning of human speech.</note>. > The Egyptians, imitating the very nature of the universe and the craftsmanship of the Gods, themselves also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions by creating symbols; just as nature expresses hidden principles in visible forms, as if through symbols, and the Gods express the truth of Ideas through manifest images.

Since, therefore, they perceive that all higher things are delighted by the likeness of lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness by those superior beings (insofar as they may imitate them to the best of their ability), they rightly offer to the High Ones a suitable mode of acting. They do this when they insert the hidden mysteries of secret things into manifest symbols. In interpreting these symbols, dismiss the words and receive the meanings. *And on page 354:* (*Now indeed, they are not accustomed to speculate on these things with bare speech and reason; but they further advise and teach that our nature—provided it carries no matter with it, nor anything else except the observation of the opportune time—proceeds toward God himself, the Creator of the World, toward things more sublime, universal, and superior to fate. They teach that we attain this through sacred works, and simultaneously they bring it about. Mercury <note>The legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note> himself also handed down this path to us, but the Prophet Bitis interpreted it for King Ammon, having found it in the inner sanctuaries of the temple in the City of Sais in Egypt; and inscribed in sacred letters—that is, hieroglyphics—he also provided to us the name of GOD running through the universe*) which is nothing other than that <term>Tautic character</term> <note>The "Tautic character" refers to the *Crux Ansata* or Ankh, which Kircher associated with both the name of God and the Christian cross.</note> so often described and celebrated in this work. These matters are so clear that they seem to have explained our entire purpose.

From all of this, it is clearly evident that we—following the hidden meanings of the Authors as if by Ariadne’s thread <note>A mythological reference to the thread used to navigate the Labyrinth; here, it refers to a guiding logic.</note>—have at last, with God as our guide and teacher, penetrated into the secret and hieroglyphic sacraments through many years of labor and speculation, aided by the <term>analytic or combinatorial art</term> <note>A system of logic, often associated with Ramon Llull, that seeks to find all possible truths by combining fundamental concepts.</note>. 

And although our present Obelisk contains innumerable mysteries of Theology most worthy of explanation, we have nevertheless reserved all of them for the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to "solve" the riddle of the hieroglyphs.</note>. In that work, while we aptly compare the secret and mystical meanings of the mentioned authors with the mystical figures of the Obelisks, we teach that the doctrine of entire ancient volumes is contained within just a few figures. Then, God willing, we demonstrate what use these characters have in natural or "theurgic" magic <note>Theurgy is a form of ritual intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits.</note>, in medicine, in the divinatory arts, in the right and blessed administration of the state, in chemistry, and other more hidden faculties. The reader will be able to consult it, if ever it should be brought to public light, where he will also find a perfect combination of all hieroglyphics discoverable at this time, arranged through skillfully organized tables. Thus, whatever we have produced in this Work may be seen as only a single ray of that doctrine which we are about to exhibit, God willing, in the *Oedipus*; but enough of these matters.

->§. IV.<-

## On the Ambiguity of Names, and the Style adopted both by the Author and by other Writers.

A great ambiguity of names *and* Divine Powers <note>original: "Numinum". In Latin, a "numen" refers to the spiritual force or divine will of a god, rather than just the god as a person.</note> occurs everywhere throughout this entire work. A critic will undoubtedly not be ashamed to quibble over this more than is fair. However, by doing so, he will immediately reveal his own ignorance, for he will demonstrate that he has not at all grasped the confusion and diversity of the ancients in their naming of the Powers and the Gods—which we explain and define in the third book of this work. For this was a specific trait of the Egyptians, from whom the Greeks derived it: *to apply the name of one God to various other Gods or Spirits* <note>original: "Genijs". Spirits or tutelary deities often associated with specific places or people.</note>; specifically, in that *one and the same Divine Power receives a different name based on the activities it performs*.

If, therefore, I occasionally confuse *Osiris* with *Momphta, or Hephta, or Nephta* <note>Kircher uses unique names for Egyptian gods: Osiris is the well-known god of the afterlife; Momphta, Hephta, and Nephta are likely his interpretations of Ptah and related creator deities.</note>, or similar names, I would not wish them to immediately condemn me for a distorted or confused judgment, or for being inconsistent in distinguishing things. Unless they have turned through the whole work from beginning to end, they should know they will never form a correct judgment on the teachings handed down here. Since it is not possible to repeat everything from the earlier books in every interpretation, it will be up to the reader’s wisdom to consult the cited pages and, from there, finally judge the truth or falsehood of the matter. But let this suffice regarding the ambiguity of names.

Finally, as pertains to the style of writing used in the course of this work, I clearly perceive that it will not please everyone equally, since I myself am occasionally displeased with it. For while I attempt to touch upon every detail in this richness of material—and to do so as briefly as possible—I am sometimes mixing *the profane with the sacred, medical with political, natural with metaphysical, historical with theological, Cabalistic with magical, foreign with foreign, mathematical with chemical*. While I strive to establish these things with various authorities—such as *Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Chaldean, Syrian, Arabic, Ethiopic, Persian, Armenian, Coptic, Samaritan, and Egyptian*—I could hardly escape a chaos of things. This was especially true when I lacked the leisure to explain what I have gathered through experience and reason in a subtle and concise speech suited for *refined Athenian ears* <note>original: "Atticorum aures teretes". "Attic" refers to the region of Athens, synonymous with the highest standard of refined, elegant, and clear literary taste.</note>. 

Often, I believe it is a mark of greater and more prudent genius—especially in such obscure and unexplored matter—to neglect polished refinement and instead indulge in Inspiration <note>original: "Enthusiasmo". In the 17th century, this meant a state of being "possessed by a god" or divine creative frenzy.</note> rather than observing rules too religiously in every instance. Indeed, it is more useful to take one's hand from the tablet <note>A classical metaphor for finishing a painting or a piece of writing.</note> at the right time than to linger so long over perfecting and polishing every single detail. Therefore, we do not always embrace *Ciceronian phrasing* <note>original: "Tullianam phrasin". Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the gold standard for Latin prose.</note> nor his rhythms; nor do we "swear by the words of another master," as the saying goes. Instead, so that the harmony between words and subjects might be greater, we indulge more in the *polychromatic style* <note>A musical metaphor: just as a "chromatic" scale uses many different notes to create color, Kircher's prose uses many disciplines and languages.</note>, as in music, according to the variety of the rising and falling themes. Thus, at times—as they say—*full of Apollo* <note>Inspired by the god of truth and prophecy.</note>, we may turn away from those deepest recesses of nature into *poetic fields*. One thing we wish to have clearly testified to everyone once and for all: we will bring forward no exotic language here of which we do not possess at least a moderate knowledge, by the grace of God; nor will we cite any authors whom we have not consulted in their original source...

<summary>Kircher defends the "confusing" naming conventions of Egyptian gods as a reflection of their functional nature and explains his dense, multi-lingual writing style as a necessary "polychromatic" approach to a vast subject.</summary>
<keywords>Osiris, Ptah, theology, writing style, linguistics, Cicero, multi-disciplinary, divine names, Egyptian mythology</keywords>

# E P I S T L E

...diligently, studiously, and by weighing it through frequent, repeated reading from the source itself. As for why we did not provide minute and precise citations for the *Eastern* books in works of this kind, you should know the cause was that confused writing method of the *Easterners* <note>original: "Orientalium". Kircher refers to writers of Arabic, Syriac, Hebrew, and Coptic manuscripts.</note>, by which many write their books without a title, or with the beginning of the volume worn away, and sometimes without any division, drafting their work in a continuous style throughout. To these was added another difficulty in citing authors such as *Hermes, Iamblichus, Plutarch, Eusebius, Herodotus*, and countless others like them. Most of these, published in different places and times, have received different arrangements and divisions due to the corrections of *Translators*. Because of this, it was not always possible to provide a precise text citation. Consequently, to prevent any discrepancy arising from different editions—and from this, a suspicion of bad faith—we were almost always forced to cite the page along with the location where the edition of the Author we used was published. This we have done for subjects written in a continuous style, such as *Plutarch's* history of *Osiris* and *Isis*, and all others we have cited. Since this is the case, nothing remains except that we begin the Work under the most fortunate *Auspices* of such a great Patron <note>original: "Mecænatis". A reference to Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of the arts; Kircher uses it as a title for his benefactor.</note>, with God's blessing. If anything worthy of praise should occur in it, I wish you to ascribe it solely to GOD, the GIVER of all good things, who alone makes the tongues of infants eloquent. But if there is less to praise in a task so arduous, difficult, and intricate, you will not find it burdensome to acknowledge my attempt and my ready will to advance the cause of literature, mindful of that saying: *In difficult matters, even to have willed [the attempt] is enough. Farewell.* <note>original: "In rebus arduis etiam voluisse tantùm, sat esse." A common Latin proverb derived from the poet Propertius.</note>

From the Roman College, September 19th in the Jubilee year of 1650; on that very day when the Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord CAMILLO ASTALLI <note>Camillo Astalli (1616–1663) was a relative of Pope Innocent X by marriage and was adopted into the Pamphili family.</note>, as he was a participant in my studies, so too was he their unique Favorer and Promoter, was admitted into the Sacred Senate of the Purple-clad Fathers <note>The College of Cardinals, so named for their red robes.</note> and named Cardinal PAMPHILIUS by INNOCENT X. I have no doubt that from his kindness, learning, prudence, and singular inclination toward men of letters, the greatest benefits will flow, not only to the Republic of Letters <note>original: "Rempublicam Literariam". The international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>, but to the entire Christian World. I therefore pray to God, Most High and Greatest, for his long life, happy rule, and finally, the enjoyment of blessed immortality.

# HISTORY
# OF THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK
### From its first erection in Egypt, until its final erection performed

->BY<-

->INNOCENT X, SUPREME PONTIFF<-
<note>Innocent X (reigned 1644–1655) commissioned the restoration of the obelisk now standing in Rome's Piazza Navona.</note>

->§. I.<-

->*Regarding the first Erection performed by Sothis, King of Egypt.*<-

I will undoubtedly be judged to have committed a bold act if I attempt to establish and determine anything certain regarding the first creator and erector of this Obelisk amidst such thick and shadowy mists of antiquity. But since it is so ingrained in my nature that I think nothing is more worthy of a human being than to test one's intellect, especially in hidden and secret things, I consider it necessary to cast the die in these matters; if it fails me, nothing remains except that I find credit in the attempt itself. Certainly, to arrive at at least some knowledge of it, I have left no stone unturned; I have poured over chronologists not only Latin, but also Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic with most persistent study; and I shall briefly reveal to the reader what I have observed among them regarding this present argument.

<margin>Manuphta was the first builder of obelisks after Moses.</margin>
In the year 2684 from the Creation of the World, according to the Hebrew calculation; 1028 years from the Great Flood; approximately 200 years from the departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt under the leadership of Moses; while Ehud, the Israelite Judge, was governing the people of God; and in the year 1366 before Christ—there arose in Egypt a certain king of lofty heart named Manuphta. Eusebius calls him Amenophis; Manetho calls him <gloss>Menuphthes</gloss> <note>original: "Μενεφθής"</note> Menuphti; and Africanus and Philo call him Ammenephthes—that is, they call him "Lord of Memphis." When this king saw the power of the Egyptians greatly diminished and weakened by a disaster memorable for all ages—partly through God's vengeance via Moses, and partly through the drowning of the Kingdom's leaders in the Red Sea—he summoned the priests. After holding councils on all sides, he first turned his mind toward ancestral religion and the worship of his fathers' gods, and then toward restoring the public monuments that his predecessors were accustomed to erecting in honor of the gods. While he was occupied with these noble efforts, he was overtaken by death, and he left his son Sothis, the heir to the kingdom, to carry out what he had so excellently decided in his mind. 
<margin>Sothis, son of Manuphta, carries out his father's intention.</margin>
This Sothis, not at all unlike his father in the generosity of his spirit, brought his parent's lofty thoughts (which had been suspended by death) back to the anvil, and finally completed them when he restored Egypt to its former beauty and magnificence.

<summary>Athanasius Kircher begins his history of the Pamphiljan Obelisk by identifying its original Egyptian patron as King Sothis, son of Manuphta, dating the work to the 14th century BCE following the Exodus.</summary>

# HISTORY

Here among other memorable things recounted by Manetho, he <note>Referring to King Sothis.</note> undertook with a great spirit both the restoration of the hieroglyphic learning—which had been almost abolished by so many disasters in Egypt—and especially the restoration of the Obelisks. He did this by the counsel and warnings of the priests, who still possessed the sacred volumes of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and father of Egyptian wisdom, to whom many mystical books were attributed.</note> concerning the highest and most difficult mysteries. Among these priests, there still flourished a significant use of the sacred characters, as well as knowledge of the ancestral rites, customs, and laws established by their predecessors and preserved in the inner sanctums.

First indeed, according to the testimony of Pliny (whom we cite in Book 1, folio 65), he erected eight Obelisks together with his son Rameses in the leading city, which was called Heliopolis <note>original: "Heliopolis" — Greek for "City of the Sun."</note> from the worship of the Sun; we describe the history of these in the place cited. Among these, our present Pamphiljan Obelisk is one, remarkable especially for the sublimity of its mysteries no less than for its apex <note>The pointed tip of an obelisk.</note>; it is a true symbol of ancient wisdom, the subject of which we place before the eyes of the curious Reader in Book 5, Chapter 3. Sothis, therefore, moved by these counsels, decided that his great efforts should be begun as if by a happy omen from the Supreme Deity. Thus, he erected many Obelisks, all of which were dedicated partly to the Supreme Deity and partly to the ancestral Spirits <note>original: "Genijs" — protective spirits or deities associated with a place or person.</note>, to demonstrate his zeal in restoring the religion of his forefathers. For he always conversed with the Priests, and he searched into the secrets of divinity with such great study above all others that he himself studiously pored over the sacred books sought from every quarter, and he took care that others should be composed; for this reason, he was called a "friend of the Gods." And Manetho expressly teaches that this is so in a fragment from the Library of Peiresc <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a famous French scholar and collector of ancient manuscripts.</note> found in Africanus, in which it is stated:

<note>original Greek: "Σώθις ἐβασίλευσε ἔτη ξγ΄ ὃς ἔγραψε πολλὰς τὰς πυραμίδας; ἔτος τὸ [solar symbol] ὑπροπιῆς εἰς Θεὸς ἐγένετο, καὶ τὴν ἱερὰν ἐντάλατο γράφειν βίβλον..."</note>
*Sothis, reigning for 63 years, erected many pyramids (understand these as Obelisks); for he was the first contemplator of the Gods—or what is the same, he wisely contemplated many things concerning the Gods—and he commanded a sacred book to be written, which I, while staying in Egypt, possessed as a thing of immense value.*

These matters are found slightly differently in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, folio 15, in a purely Greek copy:

<note>original Greek: "Ωὑτεῖτος Σῶθις, ὁ τὴν μεγίστην πυραμίδα ἐγείρας... ὃς καὶ ὑπόπτης εἰς Θεὸς γέγονε..."</note>
*The third King was Suphis (better Sothis), who raised the greatest pyramid, which Herodotus says was built by Cheops; he also became a contemplator of the Gods. Having reflected, he wrote the sacred book, which is said to be of great value and use among the Egyptians.* Truly, Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, though often identified with the 10th-century writer Ibn Wahshiyya.</note> describes these things even more expressly in these words:

<note>original Arabic: "في هذا الايام كان في مصر ملك سوطيس واقام كثيرين من المسلمات فرعون..."</note>
*Sauthis, indeed, the King of Egypt in those days, erected many "needles of Pharaoh"—that is, Obelisks—and he was a religious King. He carved upon them the mysteries of divinity and commanded the Priests to record whatever they found in the sacred books, and he was called the friend of the Gods.*

And although these cited testimonies could be more than sufficient to establish our purpose in such an abyss of antiquity, nevertheless, besides these...

<summary>This page argues that the Pamphiljan Obelisk was originally commissioned by the Egyptian King Sothis, a ruler noted for his religious devotion and efforts to restore ancient Egyptian wisdom and hieroglyphic writing with the help of the priests of Hermes.</summary>

# THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK II,

<margin>
Other arguments that this Obelisk was erected by Sothis.
</margin>
Likewise, three things especially lead us to believe that this Obelisk was erected by Sothis. The first of these is the Subject Matter of the Obelisk; the second corresponds to the dimensions handed down by Pliny; and the third is the Signature or inscription of the Obelisk itself. I demonstrate the first point as follows: since this Obelisk alone among the others surviving in Rome is inscribed to the supreme deity Hemphta <note>Kircher uses "Hemphta" to refer to a supreme Egyptian creator deity, often associated with Ptah or Kneph.</note>, as will be seen in its proper place, and it displays the highest mysteries of the triple-formed Divinity; and since Sothis, according to the cited authors, also dedicated his obelisks to the supreme Deity and carved the highest mysteries of the same upon them, certainly a great argument is supplied to us from this to believe that this obelisk was erected by Sothis. 

As for what pertains to the agreement of the dimensions, before we demonstrate that, the words of Pliny must first be cited from Book 36, Chapter 8. *Afterward,* he says, *other Kings also in the aforementioned city (namely Heliopolis) [and] Sothis erected four in number, forty-eight cubits in length; but Rameses, during whose reign Troy was captured, [erected ones of] forty cubits.* Thus Sothis, together with his son Rameses, his co-ruler, erected eight Obelisks, some of forty-eight cubits and some of forty cubits. When these are converted into palms <note>term: "palms" (palmi) — a unit of measurement used in Kircher’s time to bridge ancient cubits with contemporary Roman units.</note>, the former equal 96 and the latter nearly 80 palms in length; and our Obelisk contains just as many palms, if you subtract four from the total. Since, therefore, no other of the Roman Obelisks possess this measurement except ours, we are compelled to assert that this Obelisk is the same one that Sothis once erected at Heliopolis; see, Reader, folio 66, where we have followed all these things more extensively. 

But let us proceed to the "hypograph" <note>original: "hypographen" — the signature or closing mark.</note> of the Obelisk: 

<margin>
The aforementioned Sothis.
</margin>
Certainly the inscription of the Obelisk indicates it was erected by Sothis, for on the second Southern side, among the last characters near the base, the Obelisk displays the figure of a sitting dog with a handled cross <note>original: "cruce ansata" — better known today as the ankh, a symbol of life.</note>. This hieroglyphic is the symbol of the dog of Isis, or of Mercury translated into the heavens; and according to the testimony of Horus, it is called Sothis, in Greek *isokyon* <note>original: "ἰσοκύων" — meaning "equal to the dog."</note>, that is, the Dog-star <note>The star Sirius.</note>. Since King Sothis restored the sacred letters and disciplines from the books of Mercury, and indeed took his name from the name of Mercury—whom those worshipping him as Sothis in his celestial form under the figure of a dog (or, what is the same, they called him "dog" on account of his admirable sagacity in discovering things)—he placed the sign of Sothis, or of a sitting dog, at the end of the Obelisk as a kind of signature or subscription in memory of this deed. In this way, he secretly suggested both his own name and the Author of the sacred discipline, his own Guardian Spirit, by his own name, as if saying: "Sothis erected this to Sothis among the heavenly ones—the translated, fertile guardian Spirit of nature." For it has been proved in various places that Egyptian Kings, out of an extreme ambition for divinity, assumed the names of Gods and dedicated their great works to them, as will be shown in the interpretation of the remaining Obelisks. You see therefore, Reader, that we have been driven to assert these things not without reason.

But if anyone should object that this Obelisk could have been erected by other Kings, I shall satisfy this objection after I have first put forward some things for the greater clarification of the matter.

It must therefore be known that the Kings of Egypt, renowned for their power, undertook only the greatest and most unusual monuments worthy of royal magnificence, such as

# H I S T O R Y

...and the larger Obelisks were the focus of their attention; the care for erecting the smaller ones, however, was left both to the Priests and to private individuals. It is likely that these people were not equipped with such great wealth and power as to extract such vast and costly masses from the mountains, to engrave them with sacred letters <note>original: *sacris literis* — a reference to hieroglyphs, which Kircher and his contemporaries viewed as mystical symbols rather than an alphabet.</note> once extracted, and to erect them once engraved. Instead, these were arguments of power, ambition, glory, and the pursuit of immortality among posterity belonging to the most proud Kings. This fact can only be certain to one who has properly understood the high-mindedness of these Kings of Egypt in the marvelous constructions of their monumental masses. Thus, historians have sought to consign such extraordinary structures into their books, like something to be admired and remembered by all ages for the sake of posterity.

<margin>High-ranking citizens erect smaller Obelisks.</margin>
However, any prudent person will more easily conjecture than I could demonstrate even with many words, that private men of more ample fortune intended only the erection of smaller Obelisks, as well as images and hieroglyphic idols—of which a huge abundance is found everywhere in various places—tasks, obviously, proportioned to their power and strength.

Thus there is no doubt that the construction of such memorable works was held in the highest admiration at all times, both among the Egyptians and the other nations of the world. Indeed, the Roman Emperors, while they were undertaking the second erection in Rome of all the largest Obelisks they could find in Egypt, are reported by authors to have taken the greatest care—above all else—to send men famous for their skill in history and antiquities into Egypt (which was by then subjugated to the Roman Empire). These men were to obtain, as far as possible, exact information regarding the Kings who were the first Erectors of such great masses, their deeds, and the nature of the sacred letters, just as Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian whose work provides vital descriptions of the ancient world.</note> relates concerning Cornelius Gallus. Nor are these things inconsistent with the inquisitive nature of Augustus, nor were they hidden from Pliny, who lived forty years after the time of Augustus when light was dawning on the world. Therefore, I no longer wonder that he [Pliny] was so curious in his description of these Kings; for since he was a tireless investigator of such things, he was able to draw exact knowledge of individual matters both from those who had traveled through Egypt and had been present at the transport of the Obelisks, and from the very books which perhaps existed then but are unknown to us now.

<margin>Arguments concerning the Kings who were the erectors of other Obelisks.</margin>
There were, moreover, nine Kings of Egypt, as far as it has been possible to discover from the historians of all ages, celebrated for the erection of those Obelisks which Roman power brought into the City. Among these, it was proved in the first book that Misra, Hermes, and Mesramuthisin erected smaller ones. But Rameses erected the largest of all, which we still admire today, placed in the Lateran Field <note>The Lateran Obelisk, the tallest standing Egyptian obelisk in the world, brought to Rome by Constantius II.</note>. Nuncoreus, whom we also call Momphencur, erected the one which we look up to in our own times in the Vatican Field <note>The Vatican Obelisk, which stands in the center of St. Peter's Square; it was moved there by Domenico Fontana under the orders of Pope Sixtus V in 1586.</note>, having been erected by Sixtus V. Psammirtaus, whom Pliny calls Sennefertes, erected the Flaminian <note>Now located in the Piazza del Popolo.</note>; Sesostris erected the Campus Martius <note>The Obelisk of Montecitorio, used by Augustus as a giant sundial pointer.</note> and the Sallustian—otherwise known as the Ludovisi <note>The obelisk now at the top of the Spanish Steps (Trinità dei Monti).</note>. Truly, Simarres and

# THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK, BOOK II.

Ephies or Aphrius <note>Names of Egyptian kings derived from the chronologies of Manetho, often used by Kircher to identify historical periods.</note> erected two smooth obelisks, which Claudius Caesar once placed before the Mausoleum of his grandfather Augustus; one is currently buried near the Church of Saint Roch, while the other was erected on the Esquiline Hill by Sixtus Quintus <note>Pope Sixtus V (reigned 1585–1590), famous for re-erecting several fallen obelisks in Rome.</note>. Since, therefore, Sothis does not appear among the listed builders, yet it is established that Sothis, together with his son Ramesses, was an erector of obelisks; it certainly follows that the remaining obelisks—the Pamphilian, the Barberini, and perhaps also the Sallustian and the Campus Martius—were erected by no other than Sothis, since the names of no kings other than those mentioned are recorded by authors. Who the builders of the surviving obelisks in Egypt were will be discussed in its proper place; for in this place we are only debating the Roman obelisks, whose original builders the Emperors took great care and zeal to investigate through learned men. From this discourse, therefore, it is clear (unless I am mistaken) that this obelisk was truly erected by Sothis, and was one of the eight erected by Sothis and Ramesses at Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun," a major religious center in ancient Egypt and the source of many obelisks.</note>. This has already been made evident from the works of Africanus, Abenephius <note>Kircher's name for an Arabic source he believed held ancient Egyptian wisdom, likely Ibn Wahshiyya.</note>, and Pliny; it is also evident from the very subject matter and the hieroglyphic inscription, which the base of the southern side clearly shows in the symbol of the seated dog, or <term>Sothis</term> <note>Sothis is the Greek name for the star Sirius; Kircher interprets dog-headed figures as symbols of this star and the king associated with it.</note>. Since these things are so, nothing else remains but to follow the subsequent history at an equal pace.

## §. I I.
## Regarding the second erection performed at Rome by the Emperor Antoninus Caracalla.

<margin>
Caracalla was the second erector of the Pamphilian Obelisk.
</margin>

The first erection of the obelisks made in Egypt endured, as did the practice of the sacred disciplines, until the time of Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.</note>. He, as was narrated in the first book, turned everything upside down and caused a great slaughter of the obelisks, so that—according to Plutarch—he was not undeservedly called <term>Machaira</term> <note>original: *Machera siuè gladius* — "Machaira" is Greek for a sword or large knife.</note>, or "the Sword," by the Egyptians. From this time, with the Priests partly exiled and partly slain, Egypt, widowed of its sacred monuments, mourned until the times of the Roman Emperors. The first of these was Augustus, after Egypt was brought under the power of the Roman people. In the twenty-eighth year before the coming of our Salvation <note>28 BCE.</note>, in accordance with the grand scale of his imperial mind, he turned his attention to a new erection of obelisks. Having sent men skilled in antiquities from all over to gather information on each one, he saw to it that two were carried into the City as an unusual display of Imperial magnificence. Stimulated by his example, the succeeding Emperors in order each attempted something similar to achieve the immortality of their names. For after Augustus, his grandson Caius Caligula established the largest obelisk of Nuncoreus <note>A legendary Egyptian king mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note>, brought from Egypt in a ship of unusual design (which we have described below), in the Vatican Circus that he had newly built. After him, Claudius erected two others brought from Egypt before the Mausoleum of his grandfather Augustus, in the year 57 after Christ.

<meta>The text concludes mid-sentence with the catchword "erexit" (erected), indicating the narrative of Claudius's works continues on the next page.</meta>

erected it; following him nearly two hundred and two years later, Antoninus Caracalla <note>Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus (reigned 198–217 AD), commonly known as Caracalla.</note>, in the new Circus he had built at the Praetorian Camp <note>The headquarters of the Praetorian Guard in ancient Rome.</note> in the year 249 AD, erected this Pamphilian Obelisk of ours to be the glory of the Circus.

<margin>The location of the Obelisk.</margin>
Whether the said Obelisk was brought from Egypt by the aforementioned Emperor, or whether it had already been brought by others and remained inglorious and without the honor of this deification until that time, cannot be determined for certain from the records of Caracalla’s deeds. However, it is likely that, following the example of his predecessors, he had it brought over along with other monuments at that very time. The Circus of Caracalla was the best preserved of all the other Circuses (of which some traces still remain in Rome today); it was located at the Praetorian Camp on the Via Ardeatina, separated from the city walls by a distance of nearly a thousand paces. In this place, therefore, the present Obelisk was erected between two turning posts <note>original: "metas"; these were the conical pillars at each end of the central spine of a Roman circus.</note>, established like a Sun in the center of the World, shining with remarkable majesty. But in the course of time—whether by the hands of Barbarians or by an earthquake—it was cast down and remained so until our own times; the extent of the damage it suffered is shown clearly enough by its numerous fractures.

### §. III.

## Concerning the Third Erection performed in Rome by INNOCENT X, Roman Pontiff.

<margin>The restoration of the Obelisk.</margin>
In the year 1649, the most wise Pope INNOCENT X <note>Giovanni Battista Pamphili (reigned 1644–1655).</note>, having not long before ascended from the glorious *Pamphili* family to the supreme governance of the World, turned over in his heart noble thoughts worthy of a Pope. Following the glorious footsteps of his predecessor SIXTUS V <note>Pope Sixtus V was famous for re-erecting several fallen obelisks in Rome during the late 1500s.</note>, he desired to crown the city—already exceptionally ennobled by the public works and most splendid buildings of various Popes—with a new ornament. Among other monuments, both sacred and profane, which he was busy erecting for the splendor of the Jubilee Year <note>The Holy Year of 1650, a major pilgrimage event in the Catholic Church.</note>, he also destined the erection of this Obelisk. After various consultations were held, this particular obelisk was finally selected from among the others remaining in Rome (some of which were buried in the earth, others foully defaced). It was the one Caracalla had once erected in his Circus, and which we have chosen to title the *Pamphilian* after the family of the Pope. This choice was surely not without divine providence, as it contained mysteries of ancient religion and divine worship that were by no means unlike the orthodox <note>Kircher uses "orthodox" here to mean the true Christian faith.</note> religion. The most Reverend and Illustrious Lord Luca Torregiano, Archbishop of Ravenna, was appointed as the director of the entire operation; as a man of singular judgment and prudence, he was truly well-suited for bringing such matters into execution. For the Architect, however, the Knight *Lorenzo Bernini* <note>Gian Lorenzo Bernini (1598–1680), the preeminent sculptor and architect of the Roman Baroque.</note> was chosen. Because of his singular sharpness of mind, I consider him nearly equal to *Michelangelo Buonarroti*, whether you look at his excellence in the art of sculpture or architecture, as the most noble works with which he has adorned the City sufficiently demonstrate; to this task he applied a faithful hand...

# II. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK

Luigi Bernini, the brother [of Gian Lorenzo Bernini], a strenuous rival of his brother’s glory, assisted in the work. Finally, a suitable location for erecting the Obelisk was chosen: a place once distinguished by the name of the **Circus Agonalis**, but today known as the Roman Forum <note>Kircher refers here to the Piazza Navona, which served as a central "forum" or marketplace in his day, rather than the ancient Roman Forum (Forum Romanum).</note> located in the heart of the City. It is made illustrious by the magnificent Palace of the Pamphili, the Pope’s own family, and is furthermore very famous for its crowds of people and its markets.

<margin>The Transport of the Obelisk.</margin>
With matters thus prudently arranged, the Obelisk—which had been broken into five parts—was soon excavated with the greatest labor from the Circus of Caracalla. It was placed upon sledges and rollers, and, pulled by the various industrious applications of winches and other machines, it was transported to the designated location. And as the mass was exceedingly heavy, it demanded, as if by its own right, deep foundations upon which it might be placed. While these foundations were being strenuously laid, work was simultaneously carried out with unflagging sweat to restore the Obelisk, which had been so foully disfigured, to its original integrity. A significant difficulty arose in faithfully replacing those characters <note>The Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> that were missing from the variously damaged sections. For these either had to be supplied by one’s own ingenuity, or gaps devoid of characters had to be left on the Obelisk; the former course seemed difficult, if not to say rash, while the latter would bring an unseemly ugliness to the monument. Therefore, it was suggested by men skilled in antiquities that the pit from which the Obelisk had been dug should be explored with a new search; for they believed, led by certain clues, that such notable parts undoubtedly still lay hidden somewhere, buried in the earth in that same place. While this was attempted with truly immense labor, at last every single fragment was found—not without the singular providence of God. However, since these could not be aptly joined to the corresponding faces of the Obelisk without great deformity, it was achieved through the wisdom of the Architect that fragments of the same "Pyrite" stone <note>original: "lapide Pyrite"; Kircher likely refers to the red syenite or granite of Aswan, which was often called "pyropacilos" or "fire-speckled" stone in antiquity.</note> were inserted into those places with singular skill, restoring the Obelisk to its wholeness. Furthermore, it was my task to assign to each part its genuine hieroglyphs, excerpted from ancient fragments, and then to hand them over to be engraved; with what faith, care, diligence, and sincerity this was performed by Marcantonio Canini <note>A 17th-century artist and antiquarian who worked under Kircher's direction.</note>, the authentic testimonies affixed to the work will show. Moreover, the singular genius of the Architect shone forth in joining the parts together, as he connected them so subtly, without any iron clamps, that to those viewing it from a distance it appeared to be fashioned from a single stone. Meanwhile, as the mass of the foundation <margin>The Obelisk is placed upon a Rock distinguished by sculptures.</margin> emerged from the depths to the very surface of the earth in an oval shape to a height of thirty feet, other additions were prepared to secure reverence and ornament for the structure. For, so that this most celebrated place in the city might possess a remarkable utility joined with the ornament of splendor, it pleased *His Holiness* <note>Pope Innocent X (Giovanni Battista Pamphili).</note> to elevate the Obelisk above a fountain excavated in the form of a rock. On the four sides of the rock, he wished there to be four Colossi <note>These represent the four great rivers: the Danube, the Nile, the Ganges, and the Rio de la Plata.</note>, distinguished by a variety of symbolic apparatus, which would graphically display the fourfold face of the World through their symbols. From the bowls or vials which they grasp in their arms, a fourfold flow of water pours forth, as if through the rugged cataracts of the rock, into the vast basin situated beneath the rock with a pleasant...

And these are the inscriptions; indeed, because of the layout of the Forum <note>The Piazza Navona</note> to which the Architect had to adapt, they do not perfectly face the four cardinal points of the world on the Obelisk, but differ from the genuine points by almost half a quadrant; so that the four corners of the Obelisk almost correspond to the said points. And indeed, the first Inscription of the 1st side, the Eastern one, faces the Palaces of the Torres and Orsini families; the second Inscription, however, which is contained on the 2nd Southern side of the Obelisk, faces the side of the Forum conspicuous for the Pamphili Palace; and this inscription corresponds to the inscription which Sothis <note>A name associated with the star Sirius and the Egyptian personification of the same; Kircher interprets the ancient carvings as being originally dedicated to this deity</note> once executed in hieroglyphics on this same Southern side of the Obelisk. The third Inscription faces the Square distinguished by the Altemps and the German College buildings <note>The Collegium Germanicum, a Jesuit seminary for German-speaking priests</note>; finally, the fourth Inscription faces the side of the Forum celebrated for the Church of Saint James of the Spanish Nation. There were, furthermore, the intellectual tributes of certain other wits regarding such a noble and conspicuous work, some of which I have decided to include here.

# HISTORY

---

## INNOCENT X

*When, in the holy year of restored justice <note>The Jubilee Year of 1650.</note>, he poured out four rivers from the single source of the Virgo Water <note>The Aqua Virgo aqueduct, which feeds the fountain.</note>, he displayed a model of the ancient Paradise—that is, of justice—and renewed the age.*

---

## INNOCENT X

*With the four fountains of the Virgo Water opened for the decoration and convenience of the City, he revealed the Pontifical magnificence by introducing the secrets of the Egyptian Kings <note>original: "Regum Aegyptiorum arcanis." This refers to the hieroglyphs on the obelisk.</note>.*

---

## INNOCENT X

*Placing the Egyptian Obelisk upon the marble monument of the Virgo Water, he set the pinnacle of Roman Magnificence.*

---

> *While Rome brings the Egyptian Obelisk to its Fountains at the beginning of the year of expiation, the Virgo Water was able to wash even the very fingers of the Sun <note>Obelisks were historically considered "rays of the sun" solidified in stone; Kircher suggests the fountain's water now cleanses these solar symbols.</note>.*
>
> *Where once there was a struggle in the dust <note>A reference to the site's history as the Stadium of Domitian, where athletes competed.</note>, now there is play in the waters; oh, how pleasing is the change of times!*
>
> *The higher Memphis <note>A poetic metonymy for Egypt or the Egyptian obelisk itself.</note> raises itself here, the more submissively it adores Rome.*

---

### Enigma.

*A Roman Virgin carries a little black Egyptian on her white back to the market <note>This riddle describes the monument: the "Roman Virgin" is the Aqua Virgo aqueduct/fountain, the "white back" is the white marble base, and the "little black Egyptian" is the dark granite obelisk located in the Piazza Navona, which served as a marketplace.</note>.*

And this is the <term>PAMPHILI OBELISK</term>, destined to be memorable to all posterity, the most decorated and splendid of all those monuments that are in Rome. Indeed, nothing seemed to be lacking for its absolute perfection except for a true, certain, and faithful interpretation of the **hieroglyphic literature**, with which it struck the eyes and minds of everyone. It pleased HIS HOLINESS to entrust that task to my lowliness; how I have performed this duty, let the judgment be for the experts. I have endeavored to carry out the commands of a great soul as best I could—and as the subject matter, hitherto unattempted, allowed—according to my small measure. If the reader finds anything defective, mutilated, or imperfect in this, I would wish him to ascribe it solely to my insufficiency, but all that is good and worthy of praise, as I have also said above, to God alone, the Giver of all good things.

# CHRONOLOGY
## OF KINGS, EMPERORS, AND POPES

->*Those who, through the erection of Obelisks, secured for themselves eternal fame among posterity and immortality of name, extending from Mizraim* <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt, identified here as the son of Ham and the ancestor of the Egyptian people.</note> *son of Ham, up to* **INNOCENT X, Supreme Pontiff.**<-

---

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial T decorated with stylized scrolling vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>THREE intervals of the ages are especially worthy of consideration, in which the history and deeds of the human race have been displayed as if upon the stage-sets of different theaters. The first is from the creation of the world until the flood. The second is from the flood until the beginning of the Olympiads <note>The first recorded Olympic Games in 776 BCE, used by ancient Greeks as a chronological marker.</note>. The third continues from Iphitus, King of the Eleans and author of the Olympiads, through the succession of the following centuries. 

Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian who famously divided history into these three periods in his work "De Die Natali."</note> deservedly calls the first period "obscure" <note>original: "ἄδηλον" (adēlon)</note>; for just as the dominion of that era was lost in the transformation of the world <note>Referring to the physical and political destruction caused by the Great Flood.</note>, it likewise left no knowledge to posterity of the deeds done by those primeval men, except for what the Holy Scriptures teach us. 

The second period he calls "mythical" <note>original: "μυθικὸν" (mythikon)</note>, being so confused with the fables of Gods and Goddesses that there is nothing in it that aligns perfectly or exactly, and only a kind of analogical light shines upon writers who are inflamed with the desire for investigating the truth of things. 

The third period, however, is called "historical" <note>original: "ἱστορικὸν" (historikon)</note> by Censorinus for the best of reasons. For at its beginning, such an exact description of times and such a distinct knowledge of the deeds done in the world are presented that no room for doubting the truth of the things handed down by historians can remain. 

Following the better chronographers of this time, Salian and Tornielli <note>Jacques Salian and Agostino Tornielli were prominent Jesuit scholars of the 17th century who specialized in biblical and historical timelines.</note>, we define the first period as a span of 1,656 years; the second as 1,622 years; and the third, up to our current year, as a course of 2,421 years. Although we could indeed show in some way from the monuments of the Arabs that the erection of Obelisks or Pyramids was in use before the flood, nevertheless, since we discuss this chronological matter formally in our *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's encyclopedic work "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he attempted to decode hieroglyphs and Egyptian history.</note>—in addition to what has already been handed down in this present work—it seemed more advisable to refer the reader to those cited treatises, lest we confuse him with a manifold citation of authorities. Therefore, [we begin] our Chronology under good omens...

Kircher aligns biblical chronology with classical history, citing scholars like Censorinus and fellow Jesuits to establish the legitimacy of his historical account.</summary>

I declare in this prelude, however, that I have by no means determined the years of the Kings of Egypt with absolute precision, since in such a great confusion of historians holding diverse opinions, they can hardly be exactly determined. Also, Phoenix and Cadmus <note>Phoenix and Cadmus are credited in mythology with bringing the alphabet from the East to the Greeks.</note> were the first to transmit the native letters of Egypt to the Phoenicians and Greeks.

I have no doubt that future Popes, spurred on by his example, will be inspired to turn their minds toward similar glorious works of magnificence.

### *The total number of years elapsed from the first erection to the last.*

Thus, from the first erection of this obelisk by Sethi in Egypt until the final one made by **INNOCENT X**, Supreme Pontiff, in Rome in the year of Christ 1649, there have elapsed 2,985 years.

*Note to the Reader: In this chronology, we differ from others by three years in most of the "years of Christ" [AD dates]; we suggest the reason for this elsewhere.*

Since several theologians of our Society have reviewed this book by Father Athanasius Kircher, a priest of our Society, concerning the **Pamphilian Obelisk**, and have approved that it may be published, we grant permission for it to be printed—should it seem fit to those whom it concerns. # Giovanni Battista Rinalducci, <term>I.V.D.: Juris Utriusque Doctor, or "Doctor of Both Laws" (civil and church law).</term>

The noble mind of **INNOCENT X, Supreme Pontiff**, raised the Pamphilian Obelisk—notable for its hieroglyphic letters—from where it lay hidden among the ruins of the Hippodrome. He erected it in the Circus Agonalis itself <note>Now known as the Piazza Navona, built upon the site of the ancient Stadium of Domitian</note> as a symbol of peace and public magnificence. So that nothing might be lacking from the glory and happiness of the Pamphili reign, a man was also at hand who, almost surpassing the limits of natural genius, added a spirit to this mass, which was previously mere stone. He did this not like the fabled Prometheus, with fire stolen from the heavenly regions through a bold new trick; but rather as a devotee of true prudence, with a completely new discovery of wisdom drawn from heaven, from which a remedy for the errors of human minds might be prepared.

This man was Athanasius Kircher of the <term>Society of Jesus: The Jesuit Order, to which Kircher belonged.</term>, the author of this work. Searching out the wisdom of all the Ancients, and preserving the accounts not only of famous men but also of those unnamed in our regions, he applied himself to the intricacies of proverbs and parables with singular genius, long labor, and study—further aided by his knowledge of various languages. He has now made public the discipline of his teaching in explaining the marks on that stone. That which until now no one has dared or achieved—the confused, winding paths of hieroglyphs and their meanings, which were previously scattered according to the whim or nature of various thinkers—he has finally brought out of darkness into the light, to the astonishment and admiration of all, having collected them into one and restored them to the standard of a true interpretation.

All will therefore praise his wisdom and celebrate the benefit of such a great gift for ages to come; and, as is due to the piety and religion of such a great man, posterity will recount his praise in these writings as well. I offer this judgment and testimony regarding the release of this book to the press, which I have diligently examined according to the mandate of the Most Reverend Master of the Sacred Palace.

->*Giovanni Battista Rinalducci, I.V.D.*<-

# TESTIMONIALS
->*From Professors of Antiquarian Literature regarding the present Work.*<-

### Note to the Reader.

Although I am well aware that I did not require such a great authentication of these matters, we have nevertheless fallen into times in which the heat of intellects in literary affairs exerts itself more than ever. Furthermore, in matters that are new, difficult, and previously unattempted—such as the subject of the present Work promises—and amidst such a variety of antiquities and languages unknown to the general public, a suspicion of some fiction or bad faith could easily arise in the minds of critics. 

Therefore, lest they should rashly judge me guilty of such a shameful crime of bad faith, and having foreseen the arrows of the spiteful, I have chosen to set forth a "new Oedipus" <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the only one who could solve the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher casts himself as the solver of the "riddle" of Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> here in this theater of the World and the City <note>original: "Vrbis & Orbis"</note>, amidst such a crowd of learned men. I have concluded that I must proceed with the utmost caution and circumspection against the Sphinx. 

To this end, I saw fit to summon as witnesses men worthy of trust and instructed by long experience, who could form a perfect judgment of this work and who themselves struggle in the same arena against the forgetful antiquity of the ages. Just as they have first exactly discussed all my findings and compared individual points among themselves, they also wished to be witnesses of this, my faithful and sincere labor, for posterity, as follows.

<meta>This page provides official testimonials from prominent 17th-century antiquarians and collectors to verify the physical accuracy of Athanasius Kircher's work on the Pamphilian Obelisk. It follows the previous page’s "Note to the Reader," where Kircher anticipates skepticism regarding his "new discovery" and seeks to prove that his transcriptions of the hieroglyphs are faithful to the original stone fragments.</meta>

# I.

## Francesco Gualdo of Rimini, Knight of the Order of Saint Stephen.

Just as I have always been most devoted to the study of antiquities, I remember that some time ago, among other pursuits, I investigated with singular care the Obelisk (which was very recently erected in the Piazza Navona <note>original: "Foro Agonali," the site of the Stadium of Domitian, now Piazza Navona</note>). While it was still lying in the Hippodrome <note>the Circus of Maxentius on the Appian Way</note> broken into several pieces, I searched to see whether all the fragments—even the smaller ones containing hieroglyphic characters—still survived. I discovered, by a singular blessing of Providence <note>original: "Numinis," literally "of the Deity"</note>, that they did indeed still exist. 

I examined this even more studiously and exactly when, during the recent restoration of the same Obelisk, the hieroglyphic characters were being carved into the new stone pieces inserted into the Obelisk. There, I found that the very same figures or characters that existed on those ancient fragments had been carved into these recently substituted pieces with total faithfulness and sincerity. Furthermore, I assert that the Egyptian monuments which the Author cites as being drawn from my own Museum <note>In this period, a "museum" referred to a private collection of antiquities and curiosities</note> were described faithfully and sincerely in my presence. In order that the truth of this matter might be clear to posterity, I have not hesitated to testify with this, my own hand and seal. I so testify.

->Francesco Gualdo of Rimini, Knight of the Order of Saint Stephen.<-

---

# I I.

## Francesco Angeloni.

The hieroglyphs, which were gathered from the ancient fragments of this present Obelisk and placed onto the new fragments by which the Obelisk has been restored to its integrity, are well known to me through many years of investigation and examination while they still lay in the ruins of the Hippodrome. I, the undersigned, wished to testify by these words that they have been drawn forth with the greatest faith and sincerity, and with the extraordinary diligence of the Author, and rendered in their genuine places so that one can scarcely discern any difference between the new and the old figures. 

Furthermore, I bear witness that the Egyptian hieroglyphic monuments which the Author cites in this work as being drawn from my Museum were likewise sincerely and faithfully drawn and carved according to the originals, as befits an honorable man <note>original: "germanum virum," implying a man of true or authentic character</note>. This is done lest any suspicion of doubtful faith in an argument of such great importance should creep in for posterity. I so testify. Rome, August 14, 1650.

->Francesco Angeloni.<-
->To which I also concur, Giovanni Pietro Bellori.<-

### III.

### Giovanni Battista Casali of Rome.

I, the undersigned, by this my handwritten testimony, wish to attest for posterity that I have diligently and studiously examined the characters or figures newly carved into the Pamphilian Obelisk. I have compared them with the figures that were still visible on the ancient fragments and have discovered that nothing new has been added, fabricated, or mutilated; but that everything corresponds faithfully to those first characters and figures of the ancient fragments, produced under the direction of the Author of this Work <note>Athanasius Kircher</note>. I likewise attest the same regarding the Egyptian fragments taken by the Author from my own Museum <note>In the 17th century, a "Museum" referred to a private collection of antiquities and curiosities</note>. The Kalends of August <note>August 1st</note>, in the year of Christ's birth, 1649.

So I testify.
->*Giovanni Battista Casali of Rome.*<-

---

### IV.

### Leonardo Agostini of Siena, Antiquarian.

While the present Obelisk was still lying in the Hippodrome <note>The Circus of Maxentius on the Appian Way</note>—which is situated near the Praetorian Camp and the tomb of Caecilia Metella, daughter of Metellus—it was not unknown to me through many years of inspection. However, it became even better known to me during its restoration carried out this past year. I testify that its hieroglyphics, which were contained in the fragments, have been transferred into the new sections by which the Obelisk was made whole with such faithfulness that no suspicion of any deception <term>fuco</term> <note>original: "fuco," literally a seaweed dye, used metaphorically to mean a "varnish" or "disguise" intended to deceive</note> should arise in any of posterity, seeing as I stood by the engraver almost every day. Furthermore, those Egyptian fragments granted to the Author from the Workshop <note>original: "Ergasterio"</note> of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, over which I preside, were also extracted with such integrity <note>original: "candore," literally "whiteness" or "brightness"</note> that no one can doubt the truth of the matter; which things I have also wished to subscribe with my own hand.

->*Leonardo Agostini of Siena.*<-

### V I.

## Authentic Testimony concerning the fragments of the restored Pamphilian Obelisk, given by Father Jacopo Viva of the Society of Jesus, Associate of the Author.

I think it is not unknown to you, Friend Reader, that the Obelisk recently erected in the *Foro Agonali* <note>Piazza Navona</note>, while it still lay in the Hippodrome <note>The Circus of Maxentius on the Appian Way</note>, formerly consisted of one whole stone. Afterward, however, by the fury of the Barbarians <note>A common 17th-century term referring to the Germanic tribes whose invasions were blamed for the destruction of Roman monuments</note>, it was dashed to the ground and prostrated, broken into many pieces. Some of these suffered so much damage in this fall that they could no longer be of any use in the restoration of the Obelisk. Therefore, it was necessary to substitute other pieces in their place from a similar stone (which is commonly called <term>red granite</term> <note>original: "Granito rosso" — the distinctive Aswan granite used by ancient Egyptians</note>), which would fill the gaps of the previous ones. This was done with such industry by the craftsmen that it seems to have grown together again into one single and whole stone, with the joints being scarcely visible. 

Furthermore (which is most relevant to our matter), each and every image and figure of the <term>Hieroglyphics</term> <note>Sacred carvings; at this time, they were believed to be purely symbolic and mystical rather than phonetic</note> that were missing were carved into these newly added fragments, and indeed in exactly the same manner, position, order, and place which they once held in the whole Obelisk. Thus, the Honest Reader may know that absolutely nothing has been added anew, changed, or fabricated from one's own imagination (except in one single small space for a certain reason mentioned in the Work), but all things have been gathered from the ancient fragments with great care and study, and have been faithfully inscribed and transferred to their respective places, etc. This could be done without much difficulty, since by a singular providence of the Divine Will, it happened that all the aforementioned ancient fragments were still found in that very place where the mass lay prostrated on the ground. From these, as I said, it was easy to extract the aforementioned Hieroglyphic figures; and these fragments, to provide greater credibility and lest any opening be left for the cavils of the malevolent...

place, they are still preserved with singular care for posterity, so that they may be shown to anyone who requests it hereafter, and so it may be more certainly known to the World that this recently erected Obelisk is in every way entirely similar to the one that the Emperor Antoninus Caracalla <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, known as Caracalla (reigned 198–217 AD). In the 17th century, the circus on the Via Appia where the obelisk was found was often attributed to him rather than its actual builder, Maxentius.</note> once placed in the Hippodrome. The same must be judged regarding the other monuments of antiquity drawn from various Roman workshops <note>original: "Ergasterijs" — referring to the studios of stonecutters and restorers where ancient fragments were studied and reconstructed.</note> and scrupulously presented by the Author.

All of which, as I have recounted so far, I, Jacopo Viva of the Society of Jesus, testify and affirm with sincere faith, as an eyewitness to all these things and a constant companion and Associate of the Author. I provide this testimony all the more promptly and gladly because I see my efforts being placed in a most distinguished Work, one that has long been most eagerly desired by the entire community of Scholars with the most urgent hopes; and therefore I hope that the Fair Reader will by no means call the aforementioned things into doubt hereafter. January 10, 1650.

->Jacopo Viva, of the Society of Jesus.<-

# The Reverend Father Antonius of Aquila, of the Order of Friars Minor, Reformed Observant.

I have seen and thoroughly read the outstanding work entitled *The Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>The Obeliscus Pamphilius (1650) was Kircher's major study of the hieroglyphs on the obelisk now standing in Rome's Piazza Navona</note>, authored by the Reverend Father Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus. In it, besides the faithful citation and translation of Arabic texts, I found many other excellent, hidden, and most worthy documents of antiquity, drawn from the secret inner chambers of Oriental authors, especially the Arabs. These findings are able to confer the greatest benefit to the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" refers to the international community of scholars and intellectuals during the Enlightenment and Renaissance</note> and may provide a stimulus to others to venture something in a similar subject. This is my opinion and testimony. At Rome, in the Convent of Saint Peter on the Golden Mountain <note>San Pietro in Montorio</note>, on the 11th day of September, in the Jubilee Year of 1650.

->*Friar Antonius of Aquila, of the Strict Order of Friars Minor Observant,*<-
->*Professor of Theology and the Arabic Language.*<-

---

# Testimony of the Maronites.

Since we, the undersigned, have compared the Arabic and Syriac testimonies cited in this work word-for-word with the original Arabic manuscripts of Abulheſſan, Mahumed, Abnabdalla, Elheſſedi, Salamas, Alenephi, and other Arabic authors (some of whom were drawn from our own library); and since we found no discrepancy, and indeed acted as typesetters for the Syriac passages from the authors known to us from whom they were taken, we have found that all things have been cited with the highest faith and integrity. We have desired that the testimony of this matter be signed by our own hands. Rome, September 5, 1650. Thus we, the undersigned, testify.

->**Petrus Domitius of Keserwan.**<-
->**Petrus of Tula, Maronites from Mount Lebanon, Alumni of the College.**<-

# THE PAMPHILJ OBELISK
## BOOK I.
### On the Origin of Letters and Obelisks.
## PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting two infant figures or cherubs sitting amidst dense foliage and vines.</image-desc>

WE are undertaking a task that is truly all the more difficult because so few aids remain for us due to the extreme rarity of authors. It is a matter of great regret that, regarding the ancient cycles of ages, nothing is left to us except the desire to restore a fleeting antiquity. For although what exists today among the Eastern peoples <note>Kircher refers to scholars and manuscripts from the Near East and Levant</note> regarding the deeds of the first humans contains many excellent things worthy of knowing, it must by no means be hidden that many things are found in them which do not entirely satisfy more refined judgments. Let the proof be the total disagreement of all those who have commented on chronological matters, so that among so many, two can hardly agree on the same point.

<margin>The greatest difficulty of the undertaking.</margin>
This literary disaster is also noted in the records of Egyptian writers; among whom the discrepancy is so great—regarding the names of kings, their order, sequence, and the time each presided over Egypt with power, as well as their deeds and memorable works—that you can hardly discern which one you should follow.

<margin>The corruption of names.</margin>
Indeed, I have found no other reason for this matter than the great ambiguity of times and names, to which was added an ignorance of languages. By this, it happened that the Greeks so foully corrupted Hebrew names, the Persians corrupted <term>Chaldean</term> <note>The language and culture of ancient Babylonia</note> names, the Latins corrupted Greek names, and finally everyone, along with the Arabs, corrupted Egyptian names, so that what should be thought regarding their first origin is scarcely distinguishable.

Thus, when I had frequently weighed this confusion of historians within myself, I remained utterly perplexed; since on one hand it is most difficult and full [of...]

<summary>In this preface, Athanasius Kircher introduces his study by lamenting the loss of ancient records and the confusing, often contradictory, accounts of history found in surviving Eastern and Egyptian texts.</summary>
<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, Egyptian history, Chronology, Linguistics, Historical corruption, Ancient authors, Obelisks</keywords>

HEADER: BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN
<meta>Catchword: po-</meta>

<margin>What the author has achieved in this work.</margin>
*This risky undertaking, which I approached to untangle so many complexities, inspired in me not just fear, but almost despair. On the other hand, certain brilliant clues of hidden truth—which I sensed within such a vast forest of authors despite the differing opinions of various men—spurred me on to dare something. At last, a stubborn consistency of mind and a great desire to unearth these Egyptian monuments overcame my fear and all difficulties. Therefore, disregarding every hardship and labor with great courage, after first conducting a precise investigation of the timelines and an examination of ambiguities, I decided I must focus solely on the natural character of the Egyptians, the reasoning and methods of the doctrines established by them, and the idioms of their native language, which I recently restored in the Treasury of the Coptic Language <note>original: "Thesauro linguae Coptae," referring to Kircher's own 1643 work on Coptic</note>. Finally, through the knowledge of these things and by properly combining each part, we have arrived, with God as our guide, at the knowledge of certain truths desired until now. These I have treated extensively in the Oedipus <note>Kircher's "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," his massive study of Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, but here, according to the requirements of this work, I have decided to share them more briefly with the curious reader.*

## CHAPTER I.

->*On the primeval origin of letters, and their first inventors.*<-

<margin>The use of letters and writing before the flood.</margin>
<margin>Suidas.</margin>
<margin>Adam, the author of all arts and sciences.</margin>

It was not only after the flood, but even before it, that the use of scripture and letters existed. This is shown first by the unanimous consensus of almost all Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, Arab, Samaritan, Ethiopian, and Egyptian writers. To proceed in this work with greater sincerity, integrity, and candor, I will provide the words of each in the language and script in which they were written. To begin with the First-Formed <term>Protoplasto; a term for Adam, the first created human</term>, Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek scholar and encyclopedist</note> most clearly reports that he was both the inventor of letters and a writer of books in these words: "His are the arts and letters; his the sciences, both rational and irrational. To this the Hebrews agree, who, commenting on this passage of Genesis—*The book of the generations of Adam*—mostly interpret it as a book dictated to Adam by God. The Rabboth <note>referring to Midrash Rabbah, a collection of ancient rabbinic commentaries</note> states: "And our Rabbis of blessed memory say that Adam our father, of blessed memory, composed the book of all the commandments that God delivered to them" <note>original Hebrew: ואמרו זל רבותינו שאדם אבינו זל מחבר את ספר כל מצות שמסרו אלהם</note>.
