### CHAPTER I. BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

<margin>
Josephus, Book 1 of Antiquities.

The sons of Seth entrust the science of the stars to columns.
</margin>
He proves that these writings were falsely attributed to the <term>Gnostic Sethians</term> <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic sect who revered Seth as a divine figure</note> and the <term>Archontics</term> <note>Another Gnostic group believing the world was created by "Archons" or lesser powers</note>; however, they seem to have taken the occasion for this fiction from the fact that, as Josephus reports in Book 1 of his *Antiquities*, the sons of Seth devised the science of the stars for the knowledge of heavenly things. Since they knew that Adam had predicted two universal destructions of things—one by fire and the other by a flood—and fearing lest their discoveries perish before they could be known, they erected two columns and inscribed their findings on both. Thus, if it happened that the brick pillar was destroyed by the flood, the stone one would survive to provide mankind with the means of learning; and if the stone pillar perished by fire, the brick one would remain. Josephus reports that these pillars still existed in Asia in his own time.

<margin>
The Writing of Seth concerning the Star to appear at the birth of the Messiah.
</margin>
The author of the <term>Incomplete Work on Matthew</term> <note>An ancient commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, formerly attributed to St. John Chrysostom</note>, explaining that passage, *we have seen his Star in the East*, mentions a certain Writing of Seth concerning the Star that was to appear at the birth of the Messiah in these words:
> I have heard some reporting of a certain writing of a certain nation situated at the very beginning of the East near the Ocean, among whom was circulated a writing inscribed with the name of Seth concerning the Star that would appear at the birth of the Messiah, which was passed down through generations of studious men, as fathers related it to their sons.

<margin>
Cassian.

The impious Ham converts piously handed-down things to profane use.
</margin>
Cassian, in the 8th *Collation*, chapter 21, introduces the most ancient author, Abbot Serenus, saying:
> Receiving the knowledge of all natures through the succession of generations, the seed of Seth maintained it from the paternal tradition even from Adam himself, until it remained divided from the sacrilegious lineage of Ham; just as he had been holily commanded, so he also practiced it for the utility of common life. But when it was permitted to the impious generation, Ham diverted those things which he had piously learned toward profane and harmful things by a certain instinct of demons, and from this he boldly established the curious arts of sorceries, illusions, and magical superstitions, teaching his descendants that—having abandoned that sacred worship of the divine name—they should venerate and worship either these elements, or fire, or the demons of the air. <note>original: "Scientiam omnium naturarum... venerarentur, & colerent."</note>

<margin>
How the books before the flood were passed down to posterity after the flood.
</margin>
I think it should be briefly touched upon how this knowledge of "curious things" did not perish in the flood and became known to succeeding centuries. As far as ancient traditions go, <term>Ham</term> <note>Referenced here as "Cham"</note>, the son of Noah, who was infected with those superstitions and sacrilegious arts, knew that he could bring no book on these matters into the Ark, which he was about to enter with his righteous father and holy brothers. Therefore, he engraved these wicked arts and profane commentaries upon plates of various metals—which would not be corrupted by the damage of the waters—and upon very hard stones. After the flood was over, searching for them with the same curiosity with which he had hidden them, he transmitted this nursery of sacrilege and perpetual wickedness to posterity.

<margin>
St. Augustine, Book 18 of The City of God.

Peter Comestor. 14 columns erected by Ham, in which he displayed the handed-down doctrine.

Epiphanius in the Panarion. A book titled "The Revelation of Adam."
</margin>
In this way, the common opinion—in which they believe that angels handed down sorcery to men—is fulfilled in truth; thus he says. In agreement with this are the things which St. Augustine, in Book 18 of *The City of God*, and <term>Peter Comestor</term> <note>A 12th-century French scholar known for his "Histories of the Bible"</note> recount regarding fourteen columns—seven of bronze and as many of brick—marked with the rules of the arts and sciences, erected by Ham, the son of Noah. Epiphanius, in his *Panarion* <note>A famous catalog of heresies</note>, also makes mention of a certain book titled *The Revelation of Adam*, concerning the time when God cast a deep sleep upon him; and as Augustine mentions in *Against Faustus*, there is a certain book of the *Genealogy of the Sons of Adam*, as well as the *Penitence of Adam*, which were nonetheless declared apocryphal by Pope Gelasius. ### CHAPTER III. OF LETTERS AND OBELISKS.

<margin>Thomas Torquemada in his *Hexameron*.</margin>
...[Torque]mada, in his *Hexameron* <note>A commentary on the six days of Creation</note>, cites St. Thomas Aquinas in the book *On Being and Essence* and mentions another volume composed by <term>Adam</term> <note>The "Protoplast" or first-formed human</note> himself. This book was said to be written in the Hebrew language and concerned each and every virtue of worldly things. For the First-Formed man, foreseeing that the world would perish in a flood, and fearing lest the arts and sciences should perish along with the human race, is said to have enclosed stone plates engraved with these secrets inside a brick chest to protect them against the force of the waters. Once found and opened, his descendants would have the means to be instructed. He further reports that <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, often conflated with Thoth</note> eventually found that volume in his own time, and from it drew that wonderful knowledge of all things which we see shining forth like sparks even now in his works. Indeed, he reports that St. Thomas saw and read these books, and performed many wonders through the use of that volume.

However, although I have searched with the greatest diligence in the Library of St. Thomas in Naples—where a copy of *On Being and Essence* was said to be, which supposedly treated these and similar matters—I could find nothing of the sort there. Therefore, justly convinced by many reasons, I have judged these stories to be the empty and vain inventions of astrologers and superstitious men. For if St. Thomas did read them, one must ask: in what language? Or in what kind of characters were they written? It is well known that the aforementioned Saint, besides Latin, had hardly any singular knowledge of any other scholarly language. 

Whatever the case may be, even if the cited books are widely considered <term>apocryphal</term> <note>Works of unknown or doubtful authorship</note>, it is nevertheless probable that these first Fathers left to posterity some monuments of their discoveries, recorded on whatever material was available. These, however, were lost over the course of time, leaving nothing to posterity but rumor and tradition. In their place, curious writers—wishing to gain authority for their own works by claiming such ancient scriptural origins—later substituted these false apocryphal works we have cited. 

Certainly, among the Arabs, there is a constant <margin>The Arabs often cite the books of the sons of Seth.</margin> tradition regarding the books of Seth, the son of Adam, and of Jared, and they mention them everywhere. Jalal al-Din in his universal history, Salmas Abulhassan <note>Likely the historian Al-Mas'udi</note>, and others—whom we shall cite in their proper order—testify to this. Jalal al-Din writes thus at the beginning of his history:

<margin>Jalal al-Din, Manuscript, at the beginning of his history.</margin>
-> Verily, Adam (peace be upon him) gave his testament to his son Seth, and in him and his offspring was the gift of prophecy. And God sent down to him twenty-nine scrolls. He was succeeded by his son Cainan, and Cainan was succeeded by his son Mahalaleel, and Mahalaleel by his son Jared, to whom he handed the charge and taught him all the sciences, and informed him of what would happen in the world. He observed the stars according to the book that was sent down to Adam. <-

<margin>Adam instructed his son Seth, and...</margin>
*Adam instructed his son Seth, and in him and in his sons was prophecy, and God brought down upon him twenty-nine pages, and his son Kainan succeeded him, and Kainan was succeeded by Mahalalel, and Mahalalel by his son <margin>The Book of Seth and Cainan.</margin> Jared, and he received instruction from him, and he taught him all the sciences and the histories of what was to come in the world, and he practiced Astronomy, which he learned from the books which his father Adam delivered to him, peace be upon him.* Following these are the Samaritans, who boast that they have received many things from the books of Seth and Enoch; as can be seen in a certain ancient Samaritan fragment in the Vatican by Sephonias <margin>Sephonias in a Samaritan Manuscript in the Vatican Library.</margin> the Monk of Gaza, in which these things are recorded:

# BOOK I. ON ORIGINS
## CHAPTER I.

<margin>
The Ethiopians boast that they possess the books of Seth and Enoch.
</margin>
Adam instructed his son Seth; Seth then recorded his father's commands and institutions in books, which he handed down to his children and descendants. The nation of the Ethiopians also takes great pride in possessing the books of Seth and <term>Enoch</term> <note>A biblical patriarch said to have "walked with God" and been taken to heaven without dying; he is a central figure in ancient mystical traditions</note>; regarding these, see more recent writers on Abyssinian <note>Ethiopian</note> affairs. Indeed, it is so probable that Enoch wrote books that I consider it the height of presumption and recklessness to doubt it. This is especially true since St. Jude makes mention of him in his Canonical Epistle, and indeed St. Augustine, in the 15th book of *The City of God*, openly acknowledges it. His words are: *“We cannot deny that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, indeed wrote some divine things”* <note>original: "Scripsisse quidem nonnulla divina Enoch illum septimum ab Adamo, negare non possumus."</note>. And elsewhere: *“Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is declared to have prophesied in the Canonical [Epistle] of the Apostle Jude; his writings were not held in authority among the Jews or among us because of their extreme antiquity, which made them seem suspect, lest false things be presented for true. For some things are brought forward which are said to be theirs by those who believe whatever they wish according to their own sensibilities; but the purity of the Canon did not receive them, not because the authority of those men who pleased God is rejected, but because these works are not believed to be their own.”* These are the words of St. Augustine.

<margin>
What St. Augustine thinks about the books of Enoch.
</margin>
<margin>
Tertullian’s judgment on the books of Enoch.
</margin>
<term>Tertullian</term> <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD)</note>, in his book *On the Apparel of Women*, addresses those who say that if this book was written before the flood, it could not have been preserved: *“I know,”* he says, *“that the Scripture of Enoch, which has now assigned an order to the Angels, is not received by some because it is not admitted into the Jewish chest [the archive of sacred scriptures]. I suppose they did not think that a work published before the Cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>—that destroyer of all things in the fallen world—could have survived. If that is the reasoning, let them remember that the great-grandson of Enoch himself, Noah, was a survivor of the Cataclysm; he certainly, by family name and hereditary tradition, had heard of and remembered his great-grandfather’s grace before God and all his prophecies; for Enoch commanded nothing else to his son Methuselah except that he should hand down the knowledge of them to his descendants. Therefore, Noah could undoubtedly have succeeded in the delegation of that preaching, or because he otherwise would not have been silent, both concerning the arrangement of God his preserver and the glory of his own house. Even if he did not have it so readily at hand, this other point would defend the assertion of that Scripture: it could have been restored again in the spirit after being destroyed by the violence of the Cataclysm, just as it is well known that after Jerusalem was destroyed in the Babylonian conquest, every instrument of Jewish literature was restored through Ezra <note>The biblical scribe credited with reconstructing the Hebrew scriptures after the Babylonian Exile</note>. But since the same Scripture of Enoch also prophesied concerning the Lord, we must certainly keep back nothing at all that pertains to us. And we read that ‘every Scripture suitable for edification is divinely inspired,’ though it may later seem to have been rejected by the Jews, just like almost everything else that sounds of Christ. Nor is this at all surprising, if they did not receive some Scriptures speaking of Him, whom they were not going to receive even when He spoke to them in person.”* For this reason, it happens that Enoch possesses a testimony within the Apostle Jude.

Why the Hebrews do not receive the books of Enoch.
</margin>

The author suggests he suppressed texts that supported Christian doctrines like the Trinity.</note> rejected works that more openly confessed the Most Holy Trinity. # LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>What the books of Enoch contained.</margin>
They say these books contained many prophecies, specifically regarding what was to happen to the sons and grandsons of the Patriarchs, the future crimes and punishments of the Hebrews, the Savior of the world who would be killed by them, and their own overthrow, captivity, and perpetual dispersion among the nations. <margin>Annius, the false Berosus.</margin> Annius, in his commentaries on the apocryphal <term>Berosus</term> <note>Giovanni Nanni, known as Annius of Viterbo, was a 15th-century scholar famous for publishing forged "ancient" texts like those of Berosus the Chaldean</note>, citing Josephus, writes that in this same volume of Enoch there was a famous prophecy about the twin disasters of the whole earth, one by flood and the other by fire. <margin>Origen.</margin> Origen, as cited by Sixtus of Siena in his 28th homily on the Book of Numbers, together with Tertullian, relates that the subject matter of the Book of Enoch—besides the prophecies—concerned the number and names of the Stars and their secret powers, the descent of the sons of God to the daughters of men, the Giants born from the union of Angels, and the final judgment of God against the wicked; regarding which, the present testimony has been brought forward. Truly, all these matters are treated more extensively in the second volume of my *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, on Egyptian lore and hieroglyphs</note>, where we produce fragments of the books of Enoch in Greek and Arabic which contain marvelous things.

Furthermore, there are those who, from that passage in Genesis where Enos the son of Seth is first said to have begun to call upon the name of God, wish it to be understood that the <margin>Genesis 4, last verse.</margin> writing of the name of God flourished even then; for the Hebrew text has it thus: **אז הוחל לקרא** <margin>Onkelos in the Targum.</margin> <note>original: "Tunc cæpit invocare nomen Dei Tetragrammaton sive quatuor literarum."</note> *Then he began to call upon the name of God, the Tetragrammaton or the name of four letters:* **בשם יהוה**. Or as it is held in the <term>Chaldaic paraphrase</term> <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation and explanation of the Hebrew Bible</note>: **בכין שריאו בני אנשא לצלאה בשמא דיי** <note>original: "Tunc inceperunt filij hominum orare in nomine Dei mysterioso:"</note> *Then the sons of men began to pray in the mysterious name of God:* or even more clearly in the Chaldaic paraphrase of Jonathan: **בכין שריאו בני אנשא לצלאה ולמכתב בשמא דיהוה** <note>original: "Then the sons of men began to pray and to write in the name of the Lord."</note> <margin>A Syriac manuscript in the commentary on Genesis.</margin> with which another Syriac codex on this passage agrees:

<note>original: "Tunc cæperunt homines legere & scribere nomen Dei."</note> *Then men began to read and write the name of the Lord.* It is as if Enos laid the first foundations of divine worship, and began the ritual of honoring God with ceremonies through external signs, or through certain images or characters, by which the devotion of prayers might be stirred up; and it is likely that that ineffable name of God was inscribed or carved as a <margin>The four-letter Name of God was in great veneration before the flood.</margin> <term>mnemosynon</term> <note>A Greek term for a memorial or "memory-aid"</note> of divine benefits by the Holy Patriarchs upon the lintels of their gates and other more sacred places, as the cited codex well teaches. Added to these is the fact that Josephus, in Book 2 of his *Antiquities*, chapter 11, mentioned a certain letter written by Alexander the Great to his teacher Aristotle regarding the tomb of Cainan, son of Enos, found in a Persian city; Alexander testifies that its epitaph was written in Hebrew letters <margin>The apocryphal writing of Alexander regarding Cainan.</margin> concerning the future flood. But as these things are entirely apocryphal, and having rightly rejected them, let us move on to other matters. Yet from these adduced testimonies it is more than sufficiently clear that the invention of letters and writing was in use before the common <term>cataclysm</term> <note>The Great Flood</note> of the world, having been invented and spread by the primeval fathers. For since from Adam until the flood the world increased immensely, and almost the entire world was no different than it is now—as the narrow regions of the East were by no means able to contain such a vast and fertile offspring of the human race...

Again, since the great ambition of the mighty men of old and of the Giants <note>In the biblical and Kircherian sense, 'Giants' (Nephilim) were viewed as the powerful but corrupt leaders of the pre-Flood world who sought eternal fame</note> took hold everywhere, it is also likely that, to achieve praise, the fame of their name, and a status of divinity among posterity, they carved their deeds and discoveries into rocks and stones, as we showed just before from Josephus. ## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning the First Books and Writers after the Flood.

<margin>St. Clement.</margin>
That letters and the invention of writing were in use before the Flood has been shown more than enough, unless I am mistaken, in the preceding pages. Nor is it credible that this knowledge perished in the waters; rather, it was propagated to posterity by Noah and his sons—who were witnesses of both worlds—and it flourished at all times even after the Flood until the time of Moses (whom many, led by I know not what frivolous reasons, wrongly make out to be the first inventor of Scripture), as monuments of both Sacred and profane learning sufficiently testify.

Nor do the objections of our colleague *Juan Eusebius Nieremberg* <note>A Spanish Jesuit and mystic (1595–1658) who argued that writing was a divine gift first given to Moses</note> stand in the way; for although he strives with every argument to prove that the invention of writing did not exist before *Moses*, he is certainly forced to contradict himself in many places. Let this single demonstrative argument suffice to overturn all his arguments and the innumerable passages he cites: The *Hieroglyphic* literature of the Egyptians, by his own testimony, was already in use 400 years before *Moses*. But within the Egyptian hieroglyphs, many words of the common Egyptian *Coptic* tongue—that is, written language—are found interspersed; indeed, the Alphabet itself of the Egyptian letters, which we shall present in the third book as being constructed by *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the invention of writing and magic</note>, shows this sufficiently and clearly. Therefore, writing was in use before *Moses*. We shall demonstrate the lesser point most fully in what follows, and we have already given several specimens of it in the *Preliminary Treatise* and its *Supplement*, as well as in this present work.
<margin>Letters and the Alphabet of the Egyptian letters existed before Moses.</margin>

Furthermore, I am not unaware that various books are circulated which announce various future events, which some ascribe to the primeval Patriarchs, and others to other Holy Fathers and Prophets. # CHAPTER II. ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS.

...while expanding a vineyard, a man found a hollow within a single rock, which had no opening or crack leading into it. Inside that cavity, he discovered a book with leaves made of wood. This book was written in three languages—namely *Hebrew, Greek, and Latin*—and it spoke of the three ages of the world from *Adam* until the *Antichrist*, describing the characteristics of the people in each age. It placed the beginning of the third age in *Christ*, stating: *In the third middle age, the Son of God shall be born of the Virgin Mary, and shall suffer for the salvation of mankind.* Upon reading this, the Jew who found it was immediately baptized. It was also written there that the book was destined to be found in the time of *King Ferdinand of Castile* <note>Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452–1516), whose reign saw the end of the Reconquista and the voyage of Columbus</note>. You will find many historical monuments full of such shams, which are nevertheless immediately refuted by their own contents. For if *Seth* <note>The third son of Adam and Eve; many occult and Gnostic works were falsely attributed to him in antiquity</note> was the author of this book, how could the *Latin* and *Greek* languages have been included, when they were not yet born? Or in what kind of script was the book written? Certainly, you may find such things scattered here and there in the book titled *The Wood of Life*, in the *Cosmocritica* of *Cornelius Gemma*, in the *Theater of Human Life*, and in other works which you may consult.

I am also not unaware that many apocryphal books are circulated everywhere, such as the *Testament of the Twelve Prophets*, as well as the *Penitence of Adam* mentioned by *St. Augustine* in his work against *Faustus*. There is also the *Revelation of Adam* and the books of *Seth* condemned by *St. Epiphanius*, which the *Sethian* heretics <note>A Gnostic sect that venerated Seth as a divine figure</note> falsely substituted to gain authority for their own perfidy. I would not wish for any credit to be given to these, since anyone with sound judgment can easily detect that something adulterated and fake lies hidden within them. However, I would not want it inferred from this that no books were written immediately before or after the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>, as that would contradict the constant tradition of the most ancient authors, as has been said. But to establish this matter more solidly, let us now approach the second part of this subject, in which it falls upon us to demonstrate that books were also composed by profane <note>In this context, "profane" refers to secular or non-biblical authors from pagan antiquity</note> authors before *Moses* himself. While we do this, let us first see who those famous figures were—*Zoroaster* and *Hermes Trismegistus*—who are discussed in so many monuments of authors, and what and how they wrote. In this way, the beginnings of hieroglyphic literature may be more easily demonstrated from their very foundations and according to the order of the ages.

---

->§. I.<-
->Regarding *Zoroaster*, and who he was.<-

<margin>How many, and of what kind, the Zoroasters were.</margin>
The variety of opinions among almost all authors regarding *Zoroaster* is so great that there is hardly anyone who agrees with another. Therefore, before we proceed further, we have decided to examine this entire controversy from its foundations, so that it may be established with certainty who such a celebrated author was. *Arnobius* <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 300 AD)</note> identifies four *Zoroasters*: the first a *Chaldean*; the second a *Bactrian*; the third a *Pamphylian* (who was also called *Erus*); and the fourth an *Armenian*, the son of *Hostanes*. *Clement* [of Alexandria] says the same in the fourth book of his *Recognitions*. *Suidas* <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> adds a fifth, a *Perso-Median*, and a sixth, a *Proconnesian*, regarding whom see *Pliny* and *Lactantius* in his second book.

### CHAPTER II. 12 BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

...c. 14. Manasseh <note>Likely Manasseh ben Israel, a prominent 17th-century rabbi and scholar</note> in his political writings. Sixtus of Siena <note>A 16th-century Jewish convert to Catholicism and a noted biblical scholar</note> reports that there were two Zoroasters. The first, according to Diogenes Laertius, was a Persian and the Prince of the Magi, the true inventor of Magic. The second was a King of the Bactrians, defeated in war by Ninus <note>A legendary king of Assyria</note>, who was the first to corrupt true Magic—so says Justin. To these, Clement of Alexandria adds a third: Zoroaster Erus <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" from the end of Plato's Republic</note>, who left behind this writing about himself: *“I, Zoroaster Arimasius, of the Pamphylian race, wrote this; having died in war, I descended to the underworld and learned these things from the Gods.”* Plato mentions this Er in Book 10 <note>The source text says Book 15, but Plato's Republic consists of only 10 books; the Myth of Er is in the final book</note> of the *Republic*, chapter 12, stating that on the day he was to be buried, he revived while lying upon the funeral pyre. <margin>Goropius Becanus.</margin> Others, such as Goropius Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus, a Flemish physician known for his eccentric theories that all languages derived from Dutch</note>, maintain that no person named Zoroaster ever existed; however, since this opinion contradicts all the best authors, it is rightly to be rejected.

Furthermore, that Zoroaster mentioned by Justin has caused great confusion among authors. Indeed, Diodorus Siculus calls that King of the Bactrians defeated by Ninus "Oxyartes" rather than Zoroaster. Ligerius, cited by Francesco Patrizi <note>A Renaissance philosopher who published the "Zoroastrian Logia"</note> in his work on Zoroaster, testifies to having seen the name Oxyartes in manuscript copies of Justin as well. Leaving aside this dispute among authors regarding who that Zoroaster was, we shall make it clear once we have first offered some remarks on the etymology of the name.

<margin>The Etymology of Zoroaster.</margin>
Thus, some derive the name Zoroaster from the Greek words *zoon* and *aster* <note>original: ζῶον & ἀστὴρ</note>, as if to say "living star." Others, like Laertius, claim it comes from a Chaldean <note>Kircher often uses "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic or ancient Hebrew-related dialects</note> phrase meaning "impious sacrificer of the stars"; however, as I do not see how this could be a Chaldean phrase, I have judged its origin rightly to be rejected. Some derive it from a mixture of both languages: from the Chaldean *tsura* <note>original Hebrew: צורא</note>, which we interpret as "figure, sign, or image," and from the Greek word *aster* <note>original: ἀστὴρ</note>, which means "star"—as if to say "figure, image, or sign of the stars." Others have derived it from various other names and languages incorrectly; for these, see Goropius.

<margin>The true derivation of Zoroaster from the Chaldean language.</margin>
We say that it is a Chaldean word, derived from the word *tsura* <note>original Hebrew: צורא</note> or *iatzar* <note>original Hebrew: יצר</note>—the former meaning "figure" and the latter meaning "to form"—combined with *esh* <note>original Hebrew: אש</note> and *sether* <note>original Hebrew: סתר</note>, which signifies "hidden fire." Thus, he was called *Zairaster* <note>original: צוראסטר</note>, meaning "one who forms idols of hidden fire"; or perhaps *Tsuraster*, that is, "the sign, figure, or likeness of secret and hidden things." This agrees with the Persian etymology *Zarast* <note>original: زرست</note>. <margin>Zarast.</margin> How aptly all these things fit Zoroaster will become clear in what follows. Therefore, this name was common to all those who practiced the science of abstruse things and magic. In the same way, the name "Osiris" was common to all those who, in the earliest times, introduced and cultivated religion and the political way of life in Egypt, as will be discussed later. Consequently, just as there were several Osirises, Saturns, and Bels (which were titles for those who had served the human race in an outstanding and distinguished manner), so there were several Zoroasters. That is to say, the name applied to all those who were inventors and practitioners of the magical arts and other more secret sciences in those first centuries; as Eusebian Berosus and Xenophon (whoever he may have been) particularly note in their works on ambiguous names.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER II. ON THE ORIGIN
# OF THE CULT OF FIRE

<margin>By whom the cult of fire was instituted.</margin>
...the institution [of fire-worship] had its origin from none other than **Ham**, that most famous **Zoroaster**, the inventor and propagator of all idolatrous superstition. We have shown in the preceding pages that he was alive during this time, and profane histories record that he was eventually killed by *Ninus* <note>A mythical king of Assyria and husband of Semiramis</note>. Some claim he perished when struck by celestial fire. Whatever the case may be, since at this same time another **Zoroaster** lived—**Cush**, who was singular in the magical arts—the deeds of one could easily have been confused with those of the other by writers. It is sufficient for us to have shown here that all these **Zoroasters** were **Chaldeans** and descendants of the family of **Ham**. Indeed, I would not easily agree with those who trace **Zoroaster** from the family of **Shem** <note>Shem was the son of Noah whose lineage was traditionally seen as the "godly" line in contrast to Ham's</note>, as all the **Zoroasters** were corrupters and destroyers of that pure and divine Religion which the sons of **Shem** were accustomed to propagate with all their zeal.

<margin>Who Zoroaster the Pamphylian was.</margin>
As for the stories various authors tell—of the laughter at his birth, the complete set of teeth, the pulsing of the brain, and similar portents that shone forth in **Zoroaster**—I believe these were not said of our **Zoroaster**, but of some other celebrated magus who assumed the name of **Zoroaster**, whether he was the *Pamphylian* or the *Proconnesian* <note>Figures often mentioned in Greek myths regarding the origins of magic</note>. It is established that these men flourished in **Assyria** much later in time. Anyone who recognizes that many Greek fables have corrupted the historical record will easily see the truth of our assertion. Having therefore identified the true **Zoroaster** and the time in which he lived, we must now examine whether he wrote certain books and transmitted them to posterity.

<margin>The Books of Ham, or Zoroaster.</margin>
I say, therefore, that it is impossible that **Ham**—being most skilled in Astrology and an expert in all of nature—did not write something at the urging of his beloved children **Cush** and **Mizraim**. He would have done so partly to provide rules and precepts for operating in the magical arts for his sons’ fading memories (being occupied as they were with learning so many things about the early world), and partly to achieve fame and immortality for his name, for which he was most greedy, so that posterity would be seized with admiration for those wondrous things he had undoubtedly seen and learned from the first Fathers in the era before the flood.

<margin>Suidas</margin>
*Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist, now usually called the Suda</note> agrees with these points; indeed, he reports what he wrote in these words: <note>original Greek: Ζωροάστρης περσομήδης σοφὸς διὰ ἐν τῆ ἀστρονομίᾳ. ὃς καὶ πρῶτος ἤρξατο τὰ παρ’ αὐτοῖς πολιτευομένῳ ὀνόματι τῶν μάγων, φέρεταί τε αὐτῶ περὶ φύσεως βιβλία δ'. περὶ λίθων τιμίων ἕν, καὶ ἀστρονομικὰ ἀποτελεσματικὰ βιβλία έ.</note>
<margin>The books of Zoroaster according to Suidas.</margin>
**Zoroaster the Perso-Mede**, surpassing other Astronomers in wisdom, was also the first author of the name of the *Magi* accepted among them. There are four of his books in circulation regarding nature, one regarding precious stones, and five astrological books on the effects of stars. It does not matter that *Suidas* calls him a **Perso-Mede** while we have generally called him a **Chaldean**.

<margin>Persia named for the excellence of horses, and "Chasdim" are named after Cush, as if you said "Chusdim".</margin>
In fact, **Perso-Mede** and **Chaldean** are one and the same, as we said in the preceding pages, nor was the **Persian** language used as distinct from the **Chaldean** at that time; rather, only the regions were distinct by name. **Persia** was indeed named for the excellence of the horses produced there, while **Chaldea**, or the region of the **Chasdim**, was named after its first leader **Cush**—as if you were to say **Chusdim**—which together with Mesopota-

<margin>Pico della Mirandola on the books of Zoroaster.</margin>
**Pico della Mirandola** <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494)</note> agrees with my reasoning in a certain letter given to **Marsilio Ficino**, in which he boasts of having acquired certain Chaldean books. There is likewise a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean Theology, as well as a divine and most rich commentary on it by the Persians, Greeks, and Chaldeans.*

<margin>Hermippus, cited in Athenaeus, on the 1,200,000 verses composed by Zoroaster.</margin>
He is also said to have written on agriculture, according to the testimony of **Pliny**. That **Hermippus** <note>A Greek grammarian and philosopher</note>, whom **Athenaeus** often cites, records that he wrote, among other things, two million verses (which is, however, a manifest error that we refute elsewhere). Ethiopian authors, when they make mention of him, also cite his books on magic and demons, which we allege in another place.

<margin>Jalal al-Din the Arab on the books of Zoroaster.</margin>
**Jalal al-Din the Arab** <note>original: "Gelaldin Arabs"; likely referring to the polymath Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti</note> in his history of illustrious men, often mentions the book of **Zoroaster** <note>original: "زرست"</note>, that is, of **Zoroaster** on dreams and their interpretation. The **Armenians** also make mention of this most famous Magus in their histories. Time would fail me if every single detail written about him, or every author who cited his books, had to be brought forward here.

<margin>In what language the books of Zoroaster were written, and by whom they were translated into the Greek language.</margin>
<margin>Who Berosus properly was. Josephus.</margin>
Furthermore, since—as was said in the preceding pages—the books of **Zoroaster** were written in the Chaldean language, one may not undeservedly ask at this point: by whom were they later made Greek? Certainly, among other ancient writers, I find **Berosus** <note>A Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer and priest of Bel</note> to have acted as both a tireless researcher and an accurate interpreter of them, a view which **Josephus** <note>The Jewish historian Flavius Josephus</note> also seems to support. Moreover, who this **Berosus** was, and how he penetrated into the secrets of the Chaldeans, the same **Josephus** relates in these words from *Against Apion*:

The witness of these things is **Berosus**, a man **Chaldean** by birth, but well known to those who have studied **Chaldean** philosophy; he himself published these writings for the **Greeks**. This **Berosus**, following the most ancient records, wrote about the floods that occurred and the destruction of men within them, just as **Moses** did; and about the ark in which **Noah** <note>original: "Νῶχος" (Nochos)</note>, the founder of our race, was saved, when it was carried to the peaks of the Armenian mountains. Then, listing the descendants of **Noah** and adding their timelines...*

<margin>In what time Berosus lived, and what he wrote.</margin>

The witness of these is **Berosus**, a man indeed **Chaldean** by birth, but known to those who delight in doctrine and learning, since he himself published Greek writings concerning **Astronomy** and **Chaldean Philosophy**. Therefore **Berosus**, following the most ancient histories concerning the **Deluge** that took place and the corruption of men in it, wrote just as **Moses** did: and likewise concerning the **Ark**, in which the Prince of our race was saved, having been carried, of course, to the summit of the mountains...

<margin>The Etymology of Berosus.</margin>
The Arabs also call him **Barafa**; <note>original Arabic: "Barafa"</note> so says **Abenephi**, whom we have cited elsewhere. That **Berosus** was a Chaldean is shown by the name itself; for *Bar* in the Chaldean language signifies the same as "son." **Hosea**, moreover, is the name of his father, as if you were to say *Bar-Hosea*, the son of Hosea, just as the Arabs call **Avicenna** "the son of Sina." He was, furthermore, a Priest, because (according to the testimony of **Diodorus**, Book 3) the Chaldeans hold the same rank in their state as the Priests do in Egypt. He was also a public Scribe or Notary, because the public trust of the annals, timelines, deeds, and Kings belonged solely to the Priests, as **Metasthenes** <note>A historian whose works were often cited in antiquity, though later associated with Renaissance forgeries</note> records in his book on the judgments of time; according to Metasthenes, the Persians followed him alone during the era of the Assyrian Monarchy.

<margin>Metasthenes the Persian.</margin>
<margin>In what time Berosus flourished.</margin>
He flourished, however, long before **Alexander the Great**, which is evident from the fact that Metasthenes, a Persian Priest who makes frequent mention of Berosus in his books, flourished near the very beginning of the Greek Kingdom. According to **Pliny**, he taught the Chaldean disciplines to the Athenians in the 46th Olympiad and earned a statue with a golden tongue, placed in the public Gymnasium, on account of his remarkable skill in ancient histories and affairs; he thereby convinced the Greeks of the eternal utility of letters.

<margin>Julian the Chaldean Philosopher.</margin>
From this man, if I am not mistaken, **Julian the Chaldean Philosopher**, called the **Theurgist** <note>A "theurgist" is one who practices a type of magic intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits</note>, obtained his knowledge. Regarding him, **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says: *Julian, a Chaldean philosopher, father of the one called the Theurgist. This Julian wrote four books concerning demons; there is a protection for humans for every part of the body. Such are the Chaldean initiatory rites.* <note>original Greek: "Ἰουλιανὸς χαλδαῖος φιλόσοφος... τὰ τελεστηρικὰ χαλδαικά"</note> His son is also said to have written certain theurgical works in verse—specifically, initiatory rites, oracles, and other secrets of this science, which Suidas calls *theurgical oracles* <note>original Greek: "logia theurgika"</note>. **Proclus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> himself admits that he took his own ideas from these, as he explains them when citing the *oracles*, as will be seen in due time. He also wrote a book on *The Zones*, the nature of which will be declared in its proper place in our discussion of Chaldean Theology. **Porphyry** also brings forward **Symbolus** and a certain **Pallas**, who wrote of the affairs of the Magi in Greek. Furthermore, **Averroes** <note>The famous 12th-century Andalusian polymath</note> is the authority for the fact that the books of the Chaldeans were translated into the Arabic language.

**Philosophy among the Chaldeans was more perfect than the philosophy which existed in the time of Aristotle.** <note>original Arabic: "Wa-falsafah bi-zaman Kaldiyyun hiya akmalu min falsafah allati bi-zaman Aristutalis"</note> But all these Oracles and magical writings had no other origin except from **Zoroaster**, translated from Chaldean into Greek either by Berosus, or Julian, or someone else. I am not unaware that the *Berosus* brought forward by **Annius of Viterbo** <note>A 15th-century friar who published "recovered" ancient texts that were actually his own forgeries</note> is a counterfeit offspring and holds no authority among the learned;

...hence, whenever we speak of Berosus, we declare in this place that we speak of the true Berosus, not of the one produced by Annius <note>Annius of Viterbo was a 15th-century monk famous for forging "ancient" texts, including a version of Berosus that Kircher distinguishes from the authentic historian.</note>. Certainly, these books of Zoroaster were held in such great veneration that Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian theologian.</note> reports that those Christians who followed the heresy of Prodicus were accustomed to boast that they possessed his secret books. Furthermore, Porphyry, in his *Life of Plotinus*, relates that many Christians who had abandoned ancient philosophy became followers of Adelphius and Acylinus. He notes that they circulated many books by Alexander the Libyan, Philocomus, Demostratus of Lydia, and publicly displayed certain "revelations" of Zoroaster, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Mesos, and others of this kind, deceiving many while being deceived themselves. These individuals asserted that Plato had by no means penetrated the depth of intelligible essence. For that reason, Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism.</note> brought many arguments against them and wrote a book against those who are called Gnostics <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) as the key to salvation.</note>. Amelius, his student, also composed forty books against the book of Zostrianus, and Porphyry himself showed through many arguments that the book attributed to Zoroaster by them was a counterfeit and a recent invention, manufactured by those who were devising a heresy so that their teachings might be believed to be those of the ancient Zoroaster.

<margin>The great authority of the books of Zoroaster among the ancients.</margin>
From this passage, it appears clearly that Zoroaster was held in such high esteem that many trusted they could—either through the reasoning or the authority of those works believed to be his—overthrow the theological dogmas of Plato and either establish a new heresy in Christian theology or confirm one already established.

<margin>Syrianus on the oracles of Zoroaster.</margin>
<margin>Damascius. Iamblichus on the same.</margin>
There is, therefore, no doubt regarding the truth of the monuments of the Zoroastrians, since frequent mention of them is made by various authors cited previously many years before Christ. From their workshop, countless other monuments later emerged; of this kind seem to be the oracles of Syrianus, of whom Suidas reports that he wrote ten books on the *logia* <note>original Greek: "λογια" — meaning oracles or divine utterances.</note>, that is, on the oracles of Zoroaster. Mention is also made of Julian the Chaldean, the philosopher, upon whom Iamblichus, his student, commented in twenty-eight books; Damascius cites this twice under the title of the *Most Perfect Chaldean Theology* in these words: "as Iamblichus admits in the Chaldean [writings]" <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐν τοῖς χαλδαϊκοῖς ὁμολογούμενος ὁ Ιάμβλιχος"</note>. Psellus and Plethon followed the Oracles of this Zoroaster with extensive commentaries, which we have in our possession and which we cite frequently; these were first edited by Opsopæus in Paris in the year 1608. But let these remarks on Zoroaster, his origin, his deeds, and his written books suffice. Now let us turn our attention to explaining Trismegistus.

### CHAPTER III. BOOK I. ON ORIGINS

...Mercury, whom they called <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Greek: "Thrice-Greatest"</note> not without merit, owing to his achievements, dignity, and wisdom. With this established as the foundation of our assertions, we may proceed more safely and without error through this intricate labyrinth of antiquity.

<margin>Various Mercuries.</margin>
Antiquity counted three Mercuries. The first was considered the son of Heaven and Hemera—that is, the son of Day. The second was the son of Father Liber and Proserpine. The third was the son of Jupiter and Maia, to whom others add a fourth, born of Jupiter and Cyllene. A fifth is cited by C. Cotta the Pontiff, as recorded in Cicero; he says this one killed Argus. <margin>Who is Mercury "Argophontes"?</margin> For this reason, he is called <term>Argophontes</term> <note>Greek: "Slayer of Argus"</note>. Because of this murder committed by the command of Jupiter—so that he might free Io, the daughter of Inachus (who had been changed into a cow), from the guard of Argus, the son of Arestor—he was forced to flee Greece with Io. Macrobius interprets this fabulous narrative: *Argus*, he says, *is the sphere of the fixed stars, and Mercury is the Sun; by the Sun’s rising, Argus is "slain"—that is, the other stars vanish in its intense light.* <margin>Mercury as Lawgiver and inventor of letters.</margin> Mercury, therefore, conspicuous everywhere for his fame in astronomy, came into Egypt and was honorably received by everyone because of his great learning, his knowledge of letters, and his skill in politics. Indeed, he is said to have given laws to the Egyptians, prescribing a tranquil way of life suited to the preservation of society and human existence. He also committed the rites of the sacred mysteries to Egyptian writing and instituted colleges of priests, each of whom would worship their ancestral gods with peculiar ceremonies and offer sacrifices according to the seasons of the year. So the records of the Greeks tell us, as seen in Cicero, Clement, Arnobius, and others. <margin>Sanchoniatho of Beirut, a very ancient writer.</margin> Sanchoniatho of Beirut, who lived shortly after Moses and wrote a history of the Phoenicians (as found in Diodorus), <margin>Who is Thautus?</margin> relates that he who was called *Thauthus* among the Phoenicians was called *Thoth* among the Egyptians. Furthermore, he records that this same figure was the scribe of Saturn, was numbered among the gods, and invented letters. He was the first to observe many things concerning the honors of the gods, sacred rites, astrology, music, and nature; he discovered the wrestling-ground, the dance, and the lyre. Because of the eloquence that he taught, he was called <term>Hermēn</term> <note>Greek: "Hermes"</note> by the Greeks, which means "The Interpreter." Whether that Hermes who, as Diodorus says, was a counselor to Osiris and Isis, is the same one who killed Argus, we cannot affirm or deny by any evidence or testimony of antiquity. However, if faith is to be placed in Diodorus and others, I would say that Orpheus first, and then other Greeks, transferred things that were Egyptian to their own people (as Strabo also admits in Book 17). Consequently, I agree with Plato that the invention of letters should be attributed not to <margin>Hermes or Thautus.</margin> Mercury the slayer of Argus, but to the Egyptian *Theuth*, as we shall demonstrate at length in the following pages. <margin>Are Thautus and Trismegistus the same?</margin> Now, whether this *Theuth*, or Hermes the inventor of letters, was the same as the Mercury Trismegistus whom we are discussing, may be called into doubt. From this, it might seem clearer than light that the Hermes who served as an advisor to Isis was the same as <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Greek for "Thrice-Greatest"</note>. Yet, since Trismegistus himself confesses in his dialogues that there was another of this name before him, we certainly cannot say they are one and the same. To let the truth be known in parts, let us finally reveal what the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Syrians, Arabs, and Egyptians felt regarding the first and second Hermes.

<margin>Enoch called Adaris by the Hebrews, and Idris by the Arabs.</margin>
There is a certain old commentary here in Rome at the College of Neophytes <note>A college established for converts to Catholicism, often housing rare Eastern manuscripts</note>, named *Beit Melchizedek* (*The House of Melchizedek*). Where it treats the life, character, and origin of Melchizedek, the King of Salem, it also makes frequent mention of our Hermes. It claims he was called *Idaris* or *Adaris* and was a figure of multiple identities. Thus, it says the first Hermes, or Adris, was **Enoch**, the son of Jared. It credits him as the inventor of letters and of all things necessary for the preservation of human life. He was an exceptional practitioner of justice and piety, and the first champion of true faith in God and divine worship. Because of his virtues and works pleasing to God Almighty, he was "taken up" and "walked with God" before the time typically appointed for the mortal condition. He left behind a perpetual memory of the wonderful works he performed on earth, such that any of the descendants of Noah who appeared to do marvelous things were called "Adris." Indeed, I quote the words themselves:

Or, as the Syriac version beautifully puts it in this passage: "And he was a religious Priest of the Most High God" <note>original Syriac: "ܘܗܘܐ ܕܚܠ ܡܢ ܐܠܗܐ ܘܡܫܡܫܐ" / wa-hwa deḥel men Alaha wa-mshamshana</note>. Thus says Ahmed Ben Joseph Altiphasi, as quoted by Gelaldinus in his *History of Egyptian Affairs*, in these words:

<margin>Ahmed ben Altiphasi in the manuscript history of Gelaldinus.</margin>
> Mahalalel <note>A biblical patriarch, grandfather of Enoch</note> was succeeded by his son Jared, to whom he gave his final instructions and taught all the sciences. He informed him of what would happen in the world and observed the stars according to the book that was sent down to Adam. To Jared was born Enoch, who is Hermes—that is, the Prophet Idris (peace be upon him). At that time, the King was Methushael, son of Enoch <note>Kircher's source here follows a specific Arabic genealogical tradition</note>. God gave him the reward of his grandfather’s counsel and the sciences he possessed. He was born in Egypt (before the Flood) and departed from there to travel the whole earth. He belonged to the religion of the Sabians <note>An ancient group often associated in this era with the star-worshipers of Harran or a primordial monotheism</note>, which consists of the unity of God, purification, prayer, fasting, and other such rites of divine worship. He was the first to speak of these sciences and to bring them from potentiality into practice. He wrote a book about them in which he recorded their teachings; then he traveled to the lands of Ethiopia and Nubia, etc.

The same is reported by Kaab, as cited by Muhammad ibn Abdallah, and by Kassadi in his *Book of Sects*, in the narrative concerning Idris:

<margin>Muhammad Abdallah, in the manuscript book on sects.</margin>
> Idris (peace be upon him) was in the likeness of Seth (peace be upon him), and he was the first to write with a pen after the Prophet Seth. He was always devoted to divine worship, etc.

Vaab, the Arab Chronicler, also relates the following through Al-Lazzar:

<margin>Vaab the Chronicler in the manuscript of Al-Lazzar.</margin>
> Idris was the first to take up arms and strive in the way of the Lord, fighting against the sons of Cain. He was also the first to wear sewn garments, whereas before that men wore nothing but animal skins. He was the first to utilize weights and measures, and he taught the science of the stars.

But most clearly of all, Al-Kindi—an Arab author—writes in the chapter on the Sages of Egypt in the works of Gelaldinus:

<margin>Al-Kindi in the manuscript of Gelaldinus.</margin>
> In the time of Abraham, there was a Hermes in Egypt, who is Idris the Second (peace be upon him). He is called the "Triple" <note>Trismegistus</note> because he was a Prophet, a King, and a Sage. He is the one who transformed lead into gold and copper, and he was present there and for him...

Among the sciences are the art of alchemy, the stars, magic, the science of spirits, talismans for protection, and the secrets of nature; and from him <note>Referring to Hermes/Idris</note> learned Pythagoras, Empedocles, and Archelaus, the associates of the priests, as well as Socrates the master of the word on wisdom, Plato the master of politics, laws, and discourse on cities, and Aristotle the master of logic. <note>original Arabic: "من العلوم صنعة الكيميا والنجوم والسحر..."</note>

<margin>I</margin>
In the time of Abraham, Hermes himself—the second Idris—lived in Egypt. He was called Trismegistus <term>Trismegistus: "Thrice-Great," a title referring to his mastery as a Prophet, a King, and a Sage.</term> because he was a Prophet, a King, and a Sage (or Philosopher). He was the one who taught the science of metals, practical alchemy, astrology, magic, the science of spirits, and the apotelesmatic <term>Apotelesmatic: The art of casting horoscopes or creating talismans based on the positions of the stars.</term> or amulet-making art, and the secrets of nature. From him, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Archelaus the Priest, Socrates the Orator, Plato the Philosopher and Statesman, and Aristotle the Metaphysician eventually took their teachings, as did the rest of the astrologers.

Similar things are presented by Salamas the Arab in the book he calls *The Garden of the Wonders of the World*, which we will cite extensively elsewhere. Thus, Enoch was called the first Idris; but the first after the flood was Hermes, or the second after Enoch, who wisely proclaimed many things about God. Mori Isaac <note>A Syriac author whose manuscript Kircher claims to own.</note> in his *Syriac Philosophy* manuscript, which I have in my possession, identifies Hermes—whom he calls Iouanithun <note>original Syriac: "ܝܘܢܝܬܘܢ" / Iouanithun. ### CHAPTER III. 26 BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

...that they might know the ways and the paths, which were often buried in sand and gravel, leading from place to place, from city to city, and from region to region. This was especially difficult when the wind blew, piling the sands into great heaps. Furthermore, because the location was intensely hot due to the burning of the Sun by day, and because that land was a place of confusion, those traveling from place to place—unable to endure the violence of the Sun and not knowing the way—learned to navigate by night by the stars. They set a sign for themselves and, according to that sign, they proceeded toward their destination. From this constant scrutiny of the stars, they eventually arrived at an understanding of the changes of the seasons and began to recognize the movements of the stars from the laws of their rising. Thus, little by little, through continuous investigation and study, they learned all the laws of the stars and the signs of the Zodiac. Finally, after this rudimentary knowledge of the Stars, there came Hermes, whom he also calls *Jonithon* <note>original Latin: "Iouanithon". In some traditions, Jonithon is considered a fourth son of Noah born after the Flood, often associated with the origins of wisdom and astronomy.</note>, who retreated into the desert so that he might commit the precisely observed laws of the Stars to writing for posterity. But let us hear the words of the Author:

> There was in that Eastern region a man from the descendants of the sons of Noah who was called Jonithon. He was uniquely distinguished in knowledge and chose for himself a place removed from all human society. He went into a vast and terrible desert, far from the voices and the sight of men; there, with diligence and perseverance, he gazed upon the firmament of heaven and explored the stars, the luminaries, and the order of the seasons. He especially studied the greater luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, praising their most wise Creator. Because of the silence, solitude, and the purity of his heart—free from the tumults and disturbances of men—the meditation of his heart upon the study of the stars was granted the wisdom of the ministry and knowledge of all the groups of the signs of the Zodiac and the things that were born in them. These are the records of all the laws of the stars and of every individual thing from the desert of the East, without which the laws of the Persians and the Indians would not exist.

There was, moreover, in that Eastern Region a man from the children of the sons of Noah, who was called *Junithon*, or Hermes. He was famous for his Science and chose for himself a place removed from all human fellowship and familiarity. He went away into a vast and immense desert, immune from the voices and eyes of men, where he was constantly intent upon the firmament of the heavens. He explored the stars, the luminaries, and the custom of the seasons, and especially the greater luminaries, praising their most wise Creator. And so, through quiet, solitude, and his own self-restraint—free from the tumults and noises of men—by the perpetual intention of his heart in the contemplation of the stars, he was given the grace of the knowledge of the stars and the Zodiac. All of these things are confirmed by the Authors cited above; for the ordering of such great learning could not be perfected without great care and anxiety, except by a man withdrawn from all human custom.

### ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER III.

The commentary cited shortly before fits very closely, which also calls Enoch "Hermes," or even "Adris," which is as if to say "Asiris" <note>original: "Asiris," likely a variation of Osiris</note>. Among the Persians, I also find Osiris called ادرش *Adras*. Thus, from the records of all Eastern peoples, the knowledge of Osiris is firmly established. Certainly, whatever we have deduced in this place from the records of the Arabs fits the traditions of Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> perfectly, as will be explained in the first volume of *Oedipus*, and all these points are learnedly confirmed by Johann Swicard in his commentary on the *History of the Kings of Persia*.

These things having been properly established, I say first that all the Wisdom of the Egyptians had its beginning from <term>Enoch</term> <note>The biblical patriarch said to have walked with God and been taken up to heaven without dying</note> before the flood; for he was the one who, before all others before the flood, was instructed by the <term>Protoplast</term> <note>The "First-Formed" man, Adam</note> himself, had drawn true knowledge of divine things, and had passed it on to his descendants. He was held in such high regard not only for his admirable Wisdom and his invention of things necessary for the human race, but also because of his impenetrable removal from this world <note>Referring to the biblical "rapture" of Enoch</note>, so that many of his descendants proposed him to be worshiped as a kind of Deity.

<margin>Ham, the disciple of Methuselah the son of Enoch, spread the sacred doctrine after the flood.</margin>
Hence it is likely, as the Arabs report, that <term>Ham</term> <note>The son of Noah</note> learned not only the wicked arts regarding exotic and most curious things from the <term>Cainites</term> <note>The descendants of Cain, often associated with forbidden knowledge in hermetic traditions</note> before the flood (as was also proved above); but he also received the Sciences concerning God and the Angels—and finally the secrets of nature—from Methuselah himself, the son of Enoch and heir to his father's traditions. However, by mixing permitted arts with forbidden ones, Ham established a law that completely degenerated from the paternal tradition.

<margin>Trismegistus Hermes and the second Adras drew many things from Ham.</margin>
Afterward, a certain <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Thrice-Greatest</note> from the Canaanite lineage of Ham—by separating the permitted from the forbidden—restored this knowledge into a better form, more conforming to divine Religion, as far as was possible for a pagan Philosopher supported only by the light of nature amidst such a great depravity of things. It will be proved below that this individual was indeed that true "Second Hermes Trismegistus" so highly celebrated by authors.

<margin>Why Enoch was called Thrice-Greatest.</margin>
It is likely that Hermes was called <term>Trismegistus</term> because of a similarity and certain analogy to the works of the first Hermes Trismegistus, whom the Arabs call *Idris* and the Hebrews call *Hanoch* [Enoch]. The cited Arabs call him "Thrice-Greatest" because of three remarkable prerogatives. First, because he was a Priest of God, and was the first to show the righteous ways of the Lord to perverted mortals. Second, because of his supreme skill in natural things, through which he sought to assist the needs of human life in every way by his inventions, as he knew no Republic could long endure without laws and regulations. Third, he was called "Greatest" also for the cultivation of civil life and the establishment of laws, which are like a necessary salt for preserving human society. Furthermore, the Egyptians and Arabs maintain that Enoch—or that first Hermes—was the first after the sons of Seth to cultivate Astronomy and teach the reckoning of time and years. From his records left to the world after him, our "Second Adras" or Hermes derived his own principles regarding the division of time and passed them to posterity. For the more secret Astrologers of the Egyptians hold for certain that the Egyptian civil year was divided into as many days as the first...

### CHAPTER III. BOOK I. ON ORIGINS

<margin>Enoch lived as many years as there are days in the year.</margin>
...Adris lived among men. For Holy Scripture expressly states that he lived three hundred and sixty-five years, which is the same number of days as the Egyptian civil year. Indeed, verse 23 of Genesis chapter 5 says: <note>original Hebrew: ויהי כל ימי חנוך חמש ושישים שנה ושלש מאות שנה</note> "And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years"; <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐγένοντο πᾶσαι αἱ ἡμέραι Ἐνὼχ ἔτη τριακόσια ἑξήκοντα πέντε</note> "And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years."

And so all the days of Enoch were made three hundred and sixty-five years, etc. Since Adris taught this same method of dividing the year to the later Egyptians—as we have shown at length in our *Astronomy of the Egyptians*—it is likely that he possessed these records from the monuments of the first Hermes, which were communicated to the later world through <term>Ham</term> <note>The son of Noah, often associated in Hermetic literature with the preservation of antediluvian knowledge</note>. Since the Egyptians recognized that these years of Adris's life were by no means devoid of mystery, it is probable that from this source emerged that secret Egyptian <term>hieromancy</term> <note>Divination or sacred knowledge derived from holy objects or signs</note> concerning the revolution of the world. Specifically, they believed that the celestial Gods change their stations in the "Great Citadel" every hundred years, and that after a circuit of 36,500 years is completed, all things are restored to their original state. It is certain that Plato also caught the scent of this when he defined the cycle of <term>palingenesia</term> <note>original: παλιγγενεσίας; meaning "rebirth" or "regeneration"</note>—which to this day we call the "Platonic Year"—by a number of years nearly identical to that stated. For when they observed that the firmament completes one minute in the great circle (that is, the Zodiac) nearly every hundred years, 100 multiplied by 360 will give 36,000. If to this you add the 5 <term>epagomenal</term> <note>original: ἐπαγομένους; these were the "added" or intercalary days used to round out the Egyptian calendar year to 365</note> days multiplied by 100 years, you will have the number of 36,500 years. This is the fulfillment of all things, the number of the Great Jubilee, and the return of the <term>monad</term> <note>The "One" or the ultimate source of all being</note> passing into multiplicity and back into the monad. That is to say, it is the return to the original state of all things, as Plato, thus instructed by the Egyptians, believed; they, in turn, speculated this from the mystical number of the years of the life of Idris. Some more recent authors have followed him regarding the revolution of the firmament, but see the curious details we have provided on these matters in our *Hieroglyphic Astronomy*.

<margin>The descendants of Hermes also sought the name of Osiris and Adris.</margin>
Since, therefore, Enoch was such a man and of such greatness, it is likely that his descendants, moved by his example and seeking fame through the magnitude of their works, vied for the name of Osiris or Idris "Thrice-Greatest"—that is, the name of the highest Sages. Among the rest, Ham, infected by the stain of ambition more than all the other sons of Noah, triumphed under the title of so distinguished a name. Certainly, there is no lack of very clear traces of this assertion. Therefore, I dare to infer fearlessly that the first of all, and the most ancient Trismegistus, was Enoch, as the Arabs believe. However, Ham—whom we have also identified with Zoroaster—being boastful of both names, claimed that ambitious title of Adris for himself through pride or extreme insolence.

<margin>The second Adris was Hermes Trismegistus.</margin>
But <term>Tautus</term> <note>The Egyptian god Thoth</note>, coming from the lineage of Ham, was the one truly thought by the common consensus of all to be that second Hermes (or Adris), the Mercury Trismegistus of whom we are treating. This is despite the ambitious Ham triumphing and acting insolently with the title of this name. But lest I seem to assert anything by the conjecture of my own wit, I have decided that the reasons for my assertion must be proven by the testimony of approved authors themselves.

<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
First, Diodorus in Book 1 of his *Library* expressly relates that Mercury was a Scribe and Notary...

### OF LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER III.

<meta>catchword: Phi</meta>

...of the Sacred Rites, or the Counselor of Osiris: <note>original Greek: καὶ τοὺς ἕλληνας διδάξαι τε τὸν τὰ περὶ τὴν Ἑρμηνείαν ὑπὲρ ὧν Ἑρμῆν αὐτὸν ὠνομάσθαι· Καθόλου τε τοὺς περὶ τὸν Ὅσιριν τὸν ἔχοντας ἱερογραμματεία ἅπαντ' αὐτῷ προκοινωνεῖσθαι, καὶ μάλιστα χρῆσθαι τῇ τούτου συμβουλίᾳ.</note> "and that he taught the Greeks those things pertaining to interpretation, for which reason he was named Hermes. Generally, those around Osiris who held the office of <term>hierogrammatist</term> <note>A sacred scribe or keeper of holy records</note> shared everything with him, and especially utilized his counsel." Whence Hermes, *that is, "the interpreter and messenger," is so named; he was, in short, the Sacred Notary of Osiris, with whom Osiris communicated everything, and whose advice he especially followed.* All these things are confirmed by the *Sacred Discourse* of Hermes and by Sanchoniatho, who says he was the 

<margin>Mercurius Trismegistus, Scribe of Saturn.</margin>

Scribe of Saturn. Now, Saturn was the father of Idris (or Osiris), and as shown previously from various chronologies, he was <term>Chamephes</term> <note>A Hellenized form of a name identifying Ham as a divine figure</note> or Mizraim the son of Ham (as we shall show later), who was called "Saturn the Younger." For this reason, it is written in the Epitaph of Isis: <note>original Greek: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ τε νεοτάτη κρόνου θεοῦ θυγάτηρ πρεσβυτάτη.</note> *“I am the eldest daughter of the god Saturn the Younger.”* Indeed, the very name *Camephes*, which Hermes uses in the *Sacred Discourse*, seems to demonstrate this very thing; for he says: <note>original Greek: πρόσεχε τέκνον ὧρε, κρυπτῆς γάρ ἐπακούης θεωρίας, ἧς ὁ μὲν κάμηφις ἔτυχεν ἐπακοῦσαι παρὰ Ἑρμοῦ τοῦ πάντων ἔργων ὑπομνηματογράφου, παρὰ δὲ πάντων προγεννήτορος καμήφεως.</note> *“Pay attention, my son Horus, for you are listening to a secret contemplation, which the grandfather Camephes happened to hear from Hermes, the recorder of all works, and from Camephes, the forefather of all.”* 

Now let us examine the individual parts of this context, so that the truth of our assertion may finally shine forth. It is known from previous sections that Horus is the son of Osiris; and Osiris (or Mizraim) is the son of Ham—that is, the son of Camephes. Note here that the word *Camephes* is a corruption; in its place, as we have shown more extensively elsewhere and in the supplement to *The Restoration of the Egyptian Language*, we should place the Coptic **ⲭⲁⲙⲉⲫϯ** (*Camephta*), as if to say, "Ham the God." For this same reason, the ancient Copts called that city which the Greeks named Hermopolis by the name **ⲭⲉⲙⲛⲟⲩϯ** (*Chemnouti*), that is, "Ham our God" (concerning which, see our *Supplement to the Prodromus*). 

Therefore, Ham was the great-grandfather of Horus, and Chamephes (or Mizraim) was the progenitor of Horus. Thus, Noah or Ham (for authors often confuse these names) would be "Saturn the Elder," from whom Chamepht (or Mizraim), that is, the son of Ham and "Saturn the Younger," received the discourses, sciences, and arts. These had been handed down from the first "Thrice-Greatest" Idris-Enoch through Methuselah (with whom he lived for nearly 800 years). It is probable that from him, another man of great talent from the lineage of Ham participated in these matters and, by separating true doctrine from the false, handed them down to his son Tat (or Thoth). All these things are made known from the cited *Sacred Discourse*: <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἦν αὐτῷ διάδοχος ὁ Τὰτ υἱὸς ὁμοῦ καὶ παραλήπτωρ τῶν μαθημάτων τούτων οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν δὲ καὶ ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς ὁ Ἰμούθης σπάνιος καὶ ἡφαιστόβελος ἄλλοί τε.</note> *“But his successor was Tat, namely Thoth, his son and likewise the receiver of these teachings; and not long after, Asclepius-Imouthes, a rare man, and Hiphestobulus, and others.”* And then: <note>original Greek: Βουλῆς δ' ὁ πατὴρ πάντων καὶ καθηγητὴς ὁ Τρισμέγιστος Ἑρμῆς. Ἰατρικῆς δ' ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς ὁ Ἡφαίστου: Ἰσχύος τε καὶ ῥώμης πάλιν Ὅσιρις, μεθ' ὧν ὦ τέκνον; αὐτὸς σύ.</note> 

<margin>Trismegistus in the Pimander and Asclepius.</margin>

<note>original Greek: Φιλοσοφίας τε Ἀρνεβασκῆνις. ποιητικῆς τε πάλιν ὁ Ἡμάθης.</note> *that is, “The father and teacher of all in counsel is Hermes Trismegistus. Of medicine, truly, Asclepius the son of Vulcan. Of strength and might again, Osiris, with whom, O my son, you yourself are joined; of philosophy, Arnebaskenis; and of poetry again, Hemathes.”*

# BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>

Philosophy indeed belongs to Arnebafcenis <note>A name likely referring to an Egyptian sage or a corruption of a Hermetic title</note>. Moreover, Asclepius Imuthes <note>Imuthes is the Greek rendering of Imhotep, the Egyptian architect and physician later deified</note> is the master of Poetry. Mor Isaac <note>Likely referring to Isaac of Antioch or a similar Syriac scholar</note> records these in almost the same terms in his *Syriac Philosophy*, Discourse 1, Chapter 2, on Truth, in these words: <note>original Syriac: ܚܟܝܡܐ ܐܡܪ ܕܩܕܡܝܐ ܡܢ ܒܝܬܐ ܕܢܡܪܘܕ ܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ ܕܝܘܢܝܬܘܢ ܚܟܝܡܐ ܕܒܝܘܠܦܢܐ ܘܡܠܝ ܒܣܟܘܠܬܢܘܬܐ ܘܦܝܠܣܘܦܐ ܥܬܝܩܐ ܡܢ ܐܓܬܕܝܡܘܢ ܐܣܩܠܝܦܝܕܝܣ ܘܗܪܡܝܣ ܚܟܝܡܐ ܒܟܠܗܝܢ ܗܘܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܕܬܠܝܬܝ.</note>
> The Sages, he says, the Ancients from the house of Nimrod, and the disciples of his [son] Ioanithon, of subtle genius and much knowledge, and the ancient philosophers descended from <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>A "Good Spirit" or divine teacher in the Hermetic tradition</note>, Asclepiades (that is, the son of Asclepius), and Hermes, who was the sage in all things, the *Thrice-Greatest*. Where, as you can see, the names mentioned are everywhere confused.

From all these things duly compared, it clearly appears that Isis, Hermes, and Asclepius were <term>synchronos</term> <note>original: Synchronos; meaning contemporaries</note>, having passed from this life at the time of the younger Asclepius and Hermes. If these men bore the names of their grandfathers, why is it surprising that the son of the first Hermes was named Tat? And that the son of the second Hermes—who was the grandson of the first through Tat—was also named Tat? For in the same family, among both Romans and Greeks, and other nations even in our own time, sons are named after fathers, and grandsons after grandfathers and great-grandfathers. Therefore, it is not surprising if the same thing occurred in the same ancestral line among the ancient Egyptians.

<margin>When Hermes Trismegistus lived</margin>

What Thoth actually signifies in the Egyptian language, we shall declare elsewhere in this work.

Furthermore, authors provide uncertain accounts of what time after the flood our Mercury lived. Certain more recent writers testify that he flourished 21 years before the Law was given to Moses in the desert; thus, they wrongly think Hermes was a contemporary of Moses. For it is accepted among the ancients that this Mercury is called "Thrice-Greatest" because, according to the ancient customs of the Egyptians, he was called to the Priesthood by the greatest Philosopher, then summoned to be King by the greatest Priest, and consequently obtained dominion over the Egyptians; and it is established that among them he discovered the first principles of letters or writing.

<margin>Acts 7.</margin>

However, he could not be the author of letters unless he preceded the times of Moses. For Moses was imbued with all the learning of the Egyptians from his infancy, as scripture testifies <note>Acts 7:22: "And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians"</note>, which is difficult to believe happened without letters. Nor could he have obtained the Egyptian empire after Moses, since he lived properly under the "Dynasty of the Gods," which far preceded the dynasty of the Pharaohs and the Shepherds <note>The Hyksos rulers</note>, as will be said shortly. Furthermore, since others ruling the Egyptians before and after Moses are enumerated in histories, it appears necessary that *Trismegistus* held the kingdom before then. For otherwise, he would not be Mercury—as proved above—the son and scribe of Saturn, as he professes himself to be in Chapter 10.

<margin>Trismegistus flourished in the time of Abraham</margin>

It must therefore be said that he flourished in the time of Abraham; for <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> records that he lived before Pharaoh himself. Moreover, Suidas mentions that this Pharaoh was the King of Egypt who gave his name to those following; nor could he be one of the Pharaohs generally, as almost all monuments of writers contradict this, nor [could Hermes live] after them, unless we wish to assert he was younger than Moses, which also goes against common tradition. It remains, therefore, that he...
