->### ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER III.<-

[He] existed before the Pharaohs, and consequently at the time of Abraham, when the first foundations of the Pharaonic empire were laid, as we shall show more extensively in our *Chronology* in the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher’s own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to solve the "riddles" of Egypt</note>. The traditions of the Eastern peoples favor this opinion of ours; they commonly confuse him with Mizraim, the son of Ham <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt; in genealogy, he is the son of Ham and grandson of Noah</note>. This is recorded both by the Arabs, whom we cited above, and by Al-Kindi and Al-Tifashi as quoted in Jalal ad-Din <note>Jalal ad-Din al-Suyuti, a prolific Egyptian scholar and polymath</note> in these words: <insert>ادرس هو مصر بن ديمطر بن جم بن نوح</insert> *Idris is Mizraim himself, the son of Berther, the son of Ham, the son of Noah.* <note>original Arabic: "Idris is Misr [Egypt] son of Demeter (?) son of Ham son of Noah"</note> And above, the same author explains the matter more clearly: *In the time of Abraham there was* <insert>بزمان ابراهيم ع م كان بمصر هرميس وهو ادريس الثاني</insert> *in Egypt Hermes, who was Idris the Second*, and the rest that follows. This confusion arose from the fact that individual descendants of Ham assumed such ambitious titles for themselves. If some, following Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History"</note>, place him slightly before Moses, I would not easily contradict a man of such great authority; for it could have happened that at this time there was another man of this name, Hermes, or as the Hebrews suggest in the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, the Kabbalah</note>, Jethro the father-in-law of Moses, a man illustrious in wisdom. However, I can hardly be induced to believe that he [Jethro] was that true, first Trismegistus, the founder of Egyptian science, since we show elsewhere that this science flourished in Egypt long before the time of Moses.

<margin>Hermes: grandson, great-grandson, and great-great-grandson of Canaan and Ham.</margin>
Our Hermes, therefore, the first founder of Egyptian wisdom, could not have lived at any time other than that which we have shown. For it is probable that at this same time Ham, Cush, Canaan, Mizraim, and the rest of the progeny of Zoroaster lived. Our Hermes was the grandson, great-grandson, or great-great-grandson of all of them (namely, during the time of the "reign of the Gods," among whom he himself was numbered). We embrace this as truer than all other opinions and more in accord with all histories. We show that he is the same person who was called Thoth, Theutus, Idris, or Hermes in Egypt, and Zoroaster in Chaldea, Babylonia, and Persia. Thus, the one and the same Ham and Mizraim were called Thoth, Idris, and Saturn in Egypt and Phoenicia; in Babylonia and Chaldea they were called Zoroaster. From him, everyone thereafter who was distinguished for knowledge of celestial things and famous for the glory of their inventions was called Zoroaster in Chaldea, and Thoth, Idris, Saturn, or Mercury in Egypt and Phoenicia. And this single variety of ambiguous names and their sheer number was the sole cause of such great controversies among historians and chronologists. Regarding the years in which our Hermes lived, I find no less controversy among authors. There are those who wish for him to have associated with Noah and claim he came to Italy with him as his leader; so says the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>Also known as the *Chronicon Paschale*, a 7th-century Christian chronicle of the world</note>. All those who wish for Noah to have died in the fiftieth year from the birth of Abraham subscribe to this opinion. Although we, following better chronologists, place the death of Noah thirty years before the birth of Abraham, either opinion can maintain its authority alongside what we hand down concerning Trismegistus. I suppose, therefore, that those first Patriarchs, the sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and their progeny, were of very long life, so much so that [the life of] some, according to the Sacred Scriptures, reached even to the times of Joseph...

can be shown to have arrived; that our Hermes lived close to that century is clearly demonstrated by his deeds. Some think he lived 180 years, such as **Rosselius** <note>Hannibal Rosseli, a 16th-century commentator on the Hermetic corpus</note> in his commentary on Trismegistus; but **Boissard** <note>Jean-Jacques Boissard, a French antiquary</note> in his *Mercurius Trismegistus* believes he lived 190 years. Some, confusing Trismegistus with **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often linked to Hermes in Renaissance occult thought</note>, claim he lived for 100 years in the desert devoted to the contemplation of things, and survived another 100 years for the instruction of the human race; so says **Xanthus the Lydian** <note>An ancient historian of Lydia</note>. Others believe he lived as many years as that earlier Hermes before the flood, whom we called **Enoch** <note>The biblical patriarch said to have been "taken by God"</note>, namely 365 days <note>Kircher likely means 365 years, matching the solar cycle and Enoch’s biblical lifespan</note>; so says **Ibn Wahshiyya** <note>An Arabic author famous for works on agriculture and "ancient alphabets"</note> in his *On the Agriculture of the Egyptians*:

And the days of the years of Hermes—he is the second Idris—were three hundred and sixty-five years, the duration of his life; he equaled the years and time of Enoch, who is the first Idris. <note>original Arabic: "وكان جميع الايام هرميس هو ادريس التثنيه ثلثمائه وخمس وستين سنه..." and original Latin: "Et fuerunt anni dies Hermis..."</note>

The Egyptians more readily accepted this opinion because it was supported by mystical reasons; they superstitiously believed that the soul of the first Hermes (that is, Enoch) had passed into this Hermes of ours <term>according to the doctrine of metempsychosis <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν μετεμψύχωσιν; the transmigration of a soul into a new body</note></term>. We support the opinion of those who record that Hermes reached 190 years; for relying on this, whether we say he was born before or after **Abraham**, we will always show a remarkable harmony between his deeds, as we have reported them, and the assigned times. **Noah** died 350 years after the flood; **Abraham** was born 383 years after the flood according to our calculation; according to others, 292 years. Thus, Noah would have died 58 years after the birth of Abraham; or, what is the same, Abraham would have lived while Noah was still surviving for 58 years. According to our own view, however, as is clear from our *Chronology*, the death of Noah would have preceded the birth of Abraham by 313 years. Whatever the case, whichever opinion we hold, we shall always trace the 190-year lifespan of our Mercury down to the times of **Isaac** and the growth of his children. Since all these matters are clearly shown in our *Chronology* prefixed to this work, we refer the reader there. Having therefore discussed the time and nature of **Mercury Trismegistus**, the moment now requires that we also say something of his books in equal measure, lest we seem to have intentionally passed over the monuments of such a divine Author.

### On the Books of Mercury Trismegistus.

<margin>
The books of Mercury Trismegistus according to Seleucus and Manetho in Iamblichus.
</margin>

**Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians* reports that this Mercury Trismegistus was the Author and Prince not only of Philosophy, but of all Egyptian Wisdom, which he also handed down in the Egyptian language. He brings forward the testimony of **Seleucus** and **Manetho** <note>Ancient historians of Egypt</note>, who assert that he wrote thirty-six thousand, five hundred and twenty-nine books in the Egyptian language concerning the universal wisdom of the Egyptians. Among these, they specifically list: one hundred books on the **Empyrean Gods** <note>The highest, fiery heaven</note>; one hundred books on the **Ethereal Gods**; one thousand books on the **Celestial Gods**, most of which were translated from the [Egyptian] language...

->ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. 33 CHAPTER III.<-

<margin>Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian of the 2nd century who wrote extensively on the relationship between Greek philosophy and Egyptian religion.</note></margin>
<margin>The books of Hermes surviving in his time.</margin>
<margin>How the 36,000 books written by Hermes are to be understood.</margin>
The Egyptian writings were translated into Greek by men well-versed in philosophy. Clement writes in the 6th book of his *Stromata* <note>The "Miscellanies," one of Clement's major works.</note> that in his time, the following books still existed among the Egyptians—that is, thirty-six books concerning the universal philosophy of the Egyptians. There were six books on Medicine; ten on Sacerdotal <note>Relating to the duties and rituals of priests.</note> matters; and four on Astrology. However, I would not want anyone to think at this point that Trismegistus wrote thirty-six thousand full volumes. Rather, by "books" of this kind, one should properly understand the term <term>ni-khom</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲓⲭⲱⲙ</note> in the Egyptian language. This refers to certain **Hieroglyphic Systems** by which he indicated various arts and sciences, as will be shown in the course of this work. Or, <term>ni-khom</term> are occasionally understood as specific scientific **Conclusions**, or as <term>gnomes</term> <note>From the Greek *gnomai*, meaning short, pithy ethical maxims or "sayings of wisdom."</note> and sciences proposed on any given subject. It is in this sense that we should understand those thirty-six thousand books reported by authors. From the more choice propositions or theses among them, some later provided the material for separate, more extensive treatments, which served as commentaries.

<margin>The invention of common letters belongs to Mercury and flourished before Moses.</margin>
From this, it is also clearly false—indeed, even reckless—to say that the Egyptians had no other letters besides hieroglyphs before the time of Moses. For as we have shown, the unanimous opinion and tradition of all Eastern scholars was that Trismegistus wrote those books we have cited on papyrus in the common language (that is, Egyptian), and inscribed the more secret matters upon Columns. Since we have demonstrated that Trismegistus lived before Moses, and it is certain that Moses himself was imbued with all the wisdom of the Egyptians handed down by that same Trismegistus, it is surely so certain that he both wrote and inscribed them on stone that no one should doubt it any longer. Indeed, Hermes himself testifies to this in a sacred book, where the ancestor Hermes is introduced speaking thus:

> "These shall recognize the secrets," says Hermes, "of all my writings, and they shall discern them; some they shall keep for themselves, but those things which tend toward the benefit of mortals—that is, those things wisely instituted with the help of <term>Genii</term> <note>Spiritual intermediaries or guardian spirits in ancient thought.</note> to avoid evils and acquire good things—they shall carve upon Columns and Obelisks." <note>original Greek: "Οὗτοι τε κρυπτά, φησιν Ἑρμῆς, τῶν ἐμῶν ἐπιγνώσονται γραμμάτων πάντων, καὶ διακρινῶσι καὶ τινὰ μὲν αὐτοὶ κατεχόασιν: ἅ δὴ καὶ πρὸς εὐεργεσίας Θνητῶν φθάνει, στήλαις καὶ ὀβελίσκοις χαράξουσιν."</note>

And in the same cited book, he speaks of his own books in this way:

> "O sacred books of incorruptible things, you who have received from me gifts less than the medicine of immortality, remain unfading through all time; stay incorruptible, unseen, and undiscovered by everyone who shall pass by this learning." <note>original Greek: "Ὦ ἱεραὶ βίβλοι τῶν ἀφθάρτων, αἵ τετεύχατε ἀπὸ μὲ χείρονας τῆς ἀφθαρσίας φαρμάκων χορηγίας, ἐπικρατῶ ἀσαπεῖς διὰ παντός αἰῶνος καὶ ἄφθαρται διαμείνατε χρόνῳ καὶ ἀθεώρητοι ἀνεξεύρητοι γινόμεναι παντὶ τῷ ταύτῃ παροδεύειν μέλλοντι παιδείᾳ:"</note>

<margin>What kind of doctrine was carved into the stones.</margin>
By these words, he hints that the subject matter the books treat is so sublime that no one can grasp it by intellect unless they have followed the precepts for living handed down in the sacred discourse with absolute precision. From these things, it is abundantly clear that immediately after the confusion <note>The Confusion of Tongues at the Tower of Babel.</note>, the Egyptian language held a leading role among languages. It was the first language after the doctrinal Hebrew in which the monuments of all arts and sciences were recorded. This will be made more clearly evident partly from what has been said and partly from what follows. Indeed, it was for this reason that Greek philosophers [sought out] both kinds of books...

<header>CHAPTER III. BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN</header>

<margin>Whether the books of Trismegistus still survive.</margin>
Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*.</note> teaches that those who traveled to Egypt drank deeply of their knowledge. Furthermore, one might rightly wonder whether manuscripts of the ancients in the old Egyptian language still survive to this day. We saw just before that they certainly existed in the time of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian.</note>; thus, the question concerns modern times. Truly, nothing has held me in such doubt and perplexity as this very point, and I remember investigating nothing with greater care and diligence. From this, I believe I have achieved a result such that I now feel confident I can bring something certain to light. For through a mutual exchange established with learned Egyptians, I have finally understood that some such manuscripts written in the old language still survive. I have decided to repeat here the catalog of these works sent to me by Michael Schaia <note>A Coptic priest and scholar who provided Kircher with linguistic information.</note>, a Copt, which was printed in the *Supplement to the Coptic Prodromus* <note>Kircher's *Prodromus Coptus* (1636), one of the first European works to study the Coptic language.</note>.

<note>Original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲉⲣⲫⲱⲉⲓ ⲛⲧⲉⲛⲓϣϣⲏⲛ ⲛⲉⲉⲛⲓⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ ⲛⲉⲙⲡⲓⲥⲣⲏⲣⲓ. The Latin translation is "De Plantis, Floribus, Fructibus, eorumque usibus in sacris."</note>

*XIV.* **Concerning every kind of women, grains, stones, spices, and their uses in Sacred rites** ☩
<note>Original Coptic: ⲫⲉⲛⲛⲓⲭⲣⲟⲥ ⲛⲉⲉⲛⲓⲥϩⲓⲙⲓ ⲛⲟⲩϣⲓ ⲛⲉⲉⲛⲓⲧⲣⲁⲭⲟⲥ. The Latin translates "ⲛⲓⲥϩⲓⲙⲓ" as "fœminum" (women). In the context of grains and spices, this may refer to a classification of plants or materials as "feminine" according to ancient botanical traditions.</note>

And these are the titles of the books which are said to still survive in Egypt; but whether these are truly the works of Hermes, or of some other author, I have nothing to say, since all were transmitted to me without the author's name.

Certainly, the first five "smell" of something Hermetic <note>Kircher means they have the character or style of works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. Whatever the case may be, it is clearly evident from this small specimen that books repeatedly transcribed in the ancient language are still preserved. Regarding these, see what we have discussed more at length in the *Coptic Prodromus* <note>Kircher's 1636 introductory work on the Coptic language.</note> and its Supplement, annexed to the *Treasury of the Restored Egyptian Language*. But before I conclude this Chapter, I could not omit subjecting the unjust censure of certain people—who treat the Hermetic books as if they were forgeries—to an examination in this place, so that once the truth is known, it may be clear what should finally be believed.

## DIGRESSION.

->*Whether the Poemander and Asclepius are the true works of Hermes Trismegistus? Or are they forged offspring?*<-
<note>The *Poemander* and *Asclepius* are the most famous texts of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts.</note>

<margin>Those who call everything into doubt are ruinous to the Republic of Letters.</margin>
It is so arranged by nature in certain minds that they expend their effort on erasing, weakening, and utterly abolishing those things which have been held in prize and estimation by all the most learned authors through a long succession of ages, and which have sustained their authority through the most solid doctrine until now without violence. In this, they seem to have no other goal than to completely abolish the reputation earned by so many distinguished and weighty men. By this means, they sell themselves to the world with an insolent and intolerable ostentation, as if all writers of past times were blind, and they alone were <term>Aristarchs</term> <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a celebrated grammarian and rigorous critic of Homer; Kircher uses the name here to describe overly harsh or arrogant critics.</note> who anxiously seek after that <term>ἀνυπεύθυνον</term> <note>Original Greek: "anyperthynon," meaning "not subject to account" or "unaccountable power." Kircher is criticizing those who claim a supreme, unquestionable authority to judge the past.</note>. Indeed, these efforts, besides exceeding the limits of modesty and proving an arrogant and reckless spirit, bring a remarkably heavy loss to the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>A phrase used to describe the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>; for in this way, there is almost nothing—whether you look at sacred or profane monuments—that is not [left] with the greatest confusion of minds and inextricable perplexity...

### CHAPTER III. BOOK I. CONCERNING THE ORIGIN

...that it cannot be called into doubt; and that it is not permitted to tear it away or remove it from our midst. Whence I have always deemed that path to be the safest which has been worn by long time, by the enduring study of the Ancients, by the persistent labor of the most learned men, and by the diligent investigation of the wisest Fathers. If anyone should audaciously presume to prefer himself above them, as if they were blind or as if he possessed a superior knowledge of ancient things, I would rank him among those whom Plutarch, in his dialogues, describes with these words:

> Whom do you think oversees the elegant world, the one who sees all things?
> <gloss>Battus, the hater of wisdom</gloss>
<note>original Greek: Μισόσοφον Βᾶττον. Kircher uses this classical reference to insult critics who reject ancient wisdom as being as foolish as the legendary Battus.</note>

Just as this preposterous judgment and violent itch for contradiction is noticed everywhere in various arguments of great importance in this "critical" age, so it shines forth most especially in the calling into doubt of those most celebrated books, the *Poimandres* and the *Asclepius*—books approved as the genuine works of **Mercurius Trismegistus** by the consensus of almost all the most learned men of every age. How falsely, how unjustly, and how ignorantly such <term>Philologasters</term> <note>A derogatory term for "pretender philosophers" or those who focus on trivial linguistic details while missing the spiritual truth.</note> argue that the said books are spurious offspring, I have judged it to be my duty to show in this place.

<margin>
Objections of the Adversaries.
</margin>
The hinge of the contradiction turns chiefly upon these points: that many things occur here and there in the aforementioned volumes which savor of the doctrine of later centuries; that he disputes too openly concerning the **Holy Trinity** and the **Divine Word**; and that he reasons more clearly regarding the mysteries of our faith than could be expected from a Heathen philosopher. Finally, they object that the books make mention of the **Greeks**, who could not yet have existed at the time when Hermes was writing these things. Therefore, so that the dispute may be decided by the best method:

I suppose, **First**, from what has been extensively cited previously, that **Mercurius Trismegistus** flourished in the times of Abraham, and that he was most devoted to the study and investigation of the secrets of divinity. **Second**, that he did not consign his monuments to posterity in the Greek language, but in his own **Egyptian tongue**. **Third**, that he received much concerning the nature of **GOD**, and the benefits bestowed (and to be bestowed) upon the human race, from the primeval Patriarchs, with whose descendants he had associated; thus, it is not strange that he touched so closely upon the Sacraments of Orthodox Theology. These things being supposed,

<margin>
It is shown from the authorities of the Holy Fathers that the Hermetic books are legitimate.
</margin>
I say **First**, that these books are the proper and genuine offspring of **Hermes Trismegistus**; of which the witness is **St. Justin Martyr**, the oldest of all the Orthodox philosophers. He was born into the world shortly after the death of St. Ignatius, and in the year 150 after Christ (by his own testimony) he wrote his *Apology against the Pagans*. Here, at the end of his *Exhortation*, he says these things concerning the volumes of Trismegistus; for after he had exhorted them to studiously pore over the Sibylline and Prophetic monuments, he finally concludes his exhortation with these words:

<margin>
St. Justin Martyr and Philosopher.
</margin>
> "But if anyone should think that he has learned the doctrine concerning the Gods from those whom they call the most ancient philosophers, let him hear **Akmon** and **Hermes**. **Akmon**, in his discourses about Him, calls God 'entirely hidden.' **Hermes** clearly and openly says that to understand God is difficult, and to speak of Him is impossible. Even for one who can understand... from everywhere, therefore, it is fitting to know that in no other way concerning God..."
<note>original Greek quote from Justin Martyr’s *Cohortatio ad Graecos*. Akmon was often identified in Hermetic circles as a progenitor of the gods or an early sage.</note>

...or to learn of right piety. For instance, from the prophets alone, who teach you through divine inspiration. <gloss>that is:</gloss> *But if anyone prefers to learn about his own nature from the most ancient Philosophers, let him hear Acmon, <gloss>(read Ammon)</gloss> and Mercury; Ammon, who in his discourses calls God "most hidden," and Mercury, who clearly says it is difficult to understand God, and truly impossible to speak of Him even for one who can understand. Therefore, one must be certainly persuaded that the right worship of God can be perceived from no other source than from the Prophets alone, who teach us by the authority of the divine Spirit.* <note>Kircher is quoting Justin Martyr’s "Exhortation to the Greeks." Justin was a 2nd-century Christian apologist who often looked for "seeds of truth" in pagan philosophy.</note> All these things, as Saint Justin cites them, are found in Chapter 8 of the *Poimandres*, and in the *Asclepius* in various places. Since, therefore, Justin calls Mercury "most ancient," and brings forward the *Poimandres* and the *Asclepius* to conclude the unity of the divine nature against the Gentiles;

<margin>The Hermetic books could not have been forged after Christ.</margin>
It is certain that they could by no means have been written after Christ—as the Adversaries <note>The "Adversaries" primarily refers to Isaac Casaubon, who in 1614 used linguistic analysis to argue the Hermetic texts were actually written in the 2nd or 3rd century AD.</note> contend—and much less by the Heretics flourishing at that time. For we know that in Justin’s time, in the first century after Christ, besides Simon Magus, Hermogenes, Cerinthus, Ebion, Marcion, Basilides, Carpocrates, and the Gnostics, there were no other Heretics who possessed such great talent that they could have composed books of equal sublimity and learning. Furthermore, the said Heretics were destroyers rather than supporters of those things which Mercury—wisely in his writings and as far as the light of nature permitted—correctly said and felt concerning the Father, the Word, and the Spirit-Creator. Justin was followed by Origen, who also brought forward the aforementioned writings of Mercury and concluded thus:

<margin>Origen, Homily 13 on Genesis, Chapter 26.</margin>
> *For philosophy is neither contrary to the law of God in all things, nor in harmony with it in all things; for many of the ancient Philosophers, that is Mercury and Plato, said that there is one God who created all things, and in this they agree with the law. Some, however, add this: that God made and rules all things through His Word, and that it is the Word of God by which all things are governed; in this they write things in harmony not only with the law, but also with the Gospels.*

I will not speak here of Tertullian, Clement, and others, whom we shall cite more opportunely in their proper place; certainly Lactantius Firmianus, about a century later than these, speaks so openly of the mentioned works of Mercury that his authority alone could be sufficient to wipe away the stain branded upon them. For he speaks thus in Book I, Chapter 6:

<margin>Lactantius Firmianus, On True Religion.</margin>
> *Now let us pass to the divine testimonies; but first I shall bring forward one which is like the divine, both because of its great antiquity and because he whom we name was recorded among the Gods from among men. In Cicero, C. Cotta the Pontiff, disputing against the Stoics concerning Religions and the variety of opinions that usually exist about them—so that in the manner of the Academics he might make all things uncertain—says there were five Mercuries. Having enumerated four in order, he says the fifth was he by whom Argus was killed, and for that reason he fled into Egypt and handed down laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoth, from whom the first month of their year, namely September, received its name. He also founded the town which even now is called Hermopolis <note>"City of Hermes."</note>, and the Saitae preserve and worship him religiously. Although he was a most ancient man, he was nevertheless so well-instructed in every kind of learning that they gave him the surname Trismegistus <note>"Thrice-Greatest."</note> because of his knowledge of many subjects and arts. He wrote books, and indeed many...*

...[these works] are recognized as pertaining to the knowledge of divine matters, in which he asserts the majesty of the supreme and singular God, calling Him by the same names we use for God and Father. Lest anyone should seek His specific name, he called Him <term>anōnymon</term> <note>original: "ἀνώνυμος"; nameless or without a name</note>, that is, being without a name, for the reason that He has no need of a proper name because of His very unity. His words are: *But God is one, and he who is one does not require a name, for He is "He who is," the nameless.* <note>Kircher is quoting a Hermetic fragment here, identifying God as the essential "Being" (the "I Am") who transcends specific labels.</note> And a little later, [he notes] that the "Thrice-Greatest Mercury," whom I mentioned above, called God not only <term>amētora</term> <note>original: "ἀμήτορα"; motherless</note> but also <term>apatora</term> <note>original: "ἀπάτορα"; fatherless</note>. The words he cites here from Trismegistus are taken from the *Asclepius*; therefore, no sensible philosopher can or should suspect that a deception has been introduced. 

<margin>St. Augustine, Book 8 of the *City of God*.</margin>
St. Augustine, in Book 8 of the *City of God*, chapters 23, 25, and 26, cites this same book, the *Asclepius*, at such length that they are too extensive to be copied out in this brief time; I refer the reader to those chapters.

It is therefore evident that these two books of Mercury, the *Poimandres* and the *Asclepius*, were always held in the highest esteem—not only by secular authors but also by the Holy Fathers. Supported by the authority of these texts as being among the most ancient, the Fathers strove by every means to establish their own views on the Triune and One God against the Gentiles. They would not have performed this with such great zeal if they had not known that these works were the most ancient, true, and genuine offspring of Hermes, and were held in the highest value by all the philosophers of that time—indeed, they were sufficient to convince the nations of the error of their polytheism. And this is that Theutus, 

<margin>Plato in the *Phaedrus*.</margin>
the celebrated inventor of letters, whose books and studies Plato mentions in the *Phaedrus*. Speaking through the persona of Thamus, the King of Egypt, Plato calls him <term>euthytechnikōtaton</term> <note>original: "εὐθυτεχνικώτατον"; the most skilled of artisans</note>, Theuth the greatest craftsman, and the <term>patera tōn grammatōn</term> <note>original: "πατέρα τῶν γραμμάτων"; Father of Letters</note>. Plato says that Theuth showed his books, written in the new letters he had invented, to Thamus. Thamus, being ignorant of the more subtle matters contained within them, rebuked him, saying that by his invented characters he would bring about forgetfulness rather than a true perception and understanding of those things which are better planted in the minds of men through private and oral instruction. But let us hear the words of Plato:

> I heard that in the region of Naucratis in Egypt, there was one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom the bird called the Ibis was sacred. The name of the divinity himself was Theuth. He was the first to discover number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, as well as games of checkers and dice, and also letters. At that time, Thamus was king of all Egypt, residing in the great city of the upper region which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and its god they call Ammon. Theuth went to this king and demonstrated his arts, saying that they ought to be distributed to the rest of the Egyptians.

<note>Kircher provides the Greek text from Plato's *Phaedrus* 274c-d, followed by his own Latin translation below.</note>

> I have heard that near Naucratis in Egypt there existed a certain one of the ancient indigenous gods, to whom was dedicated the bird they call the Ibis. The name of the divinity itself was Theuth; he first invented number, and the computation of number, and Geometry, and Astronomy, and games of dice and games of hazard, and letters. At that time Thamus (or Osiris, for thus the Hebrews and Chaldeans call Osiris and Adonis) was King of all Egypt, and lived in the most ample City which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes; and the god who was the guardian of that City was Ammon. Theuth, proceeding to this King, demonstrated his arts, and declared that they should henceforth be distributed to the other Egyptians.

### ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER III.
<page-num>39</page-num>

<margin>They were not planted by any heretic.</margin>
It is clear, therefore, that the Hermetic books *Poimandres* and *Asclepius* should by no means be considered forgeries, nor could they have been planted by any of the heretics who flourished in the first century after Christ. Even then, due to their extreme antiquity, they were held in the highest esteem by everyone. Furthermore, as far as can be gathered through diligent investigation, no trace of the heresies of those times can be found within them. On the contrary, they treat of God, of the artisan Mind <note>original: "Mente opifice"; referring to the Demiurge or Divine Intellect</note>, and of its influence upon the corporeal world. They discuss drawing near to God and the spirits through a chaste life fruitful in holy works, and they contain reasoning established according to the light of nature. They are so far from being in harmony with the most shameful sects of the first century—which were contaminated by the hidden operations of demons—that they should instead be judged as entirely dissonant with them. I do not deny, however, that many things in them are contrary to Orthodox Religion; but this must be forgiven in a Pagan <note>original: "Ethnico"</note> philosopher who lacked the supernatural light of faith.

<margin>Who the translator of the Hermetic books was.</margin>
Thus, many years before Christ, they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek. Whoever their translator may have been, St. Cyril certainly mentions fifteen books of Hermes treating of the nature of God, which he asserts were translated into Greek by a certain Athenian. If these things are true, it is not at all unlikely that the *Poimandres* and *Asclepius* were among them; the latter of these was eventually brought into the Latin language <note>original: "latini juris fecit"; literally "made subject to Latin law," meaning translated</note> by Apuleius, who was nearly a contemporary of Justin. Plato was so pleased to incorporate the works of Zoroaster and Hermes into his own that anyone who diligently compares their writings will find they are almost the same, whether you look at the phrasing and manner of speaking, or the mystical reasoning—all of which we deduce most extensively in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers here to his massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. Indeed, Psellus and Plethon, in their commentaries on the *Zoroastrian Oracles*, after discussing many things about GOD and the Intelligences, about the Ideas existing in the divine mind, and about the choirs and various classes of Spirits <term>Genii</term> and Demons contained in the said oracles, finally conclude their whole discourse with these words:

<margin>Psellus on the Oracles of Zoroaster.</margin>
> *And indeed Plato and Aristotle received many of the enumerated opinions. But Plotinus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, and Proclus followed them in all things, and accepted these as divine voices without further argument.* <note>original Greek: "τούτων δὲ δόγμα τῶν τὰ πάλαι καὶ Αριστοτέλης καὶ πλάτων ἐδέξαντο. οἱ δὲ περὶ Πλωτῖνον καὶ Ἰάμβλιχον, Πορφύριόν τε καὶ Πρόκλον πᾶσι κατηκολούθησαν, καὶ ὡς Θείας φωνὰς ἀσυλλογίστως ταῦτα ἐδέξαντο."</note>

Rabbi Simeon Ben Iochai followed these same views; in the *Zohar*, while disputing most deeply about the divine attributes, he makes frequent mention of the Hermetic books in these words:

<margin>Ben Iochai in the *Zohar*.</margin>
> *As we read in the books of Hermes, whom the foreigners call Marcolis* <note>original Hebrew: "כמו נקרא בספרי הרמיס שבלעז מרקליס"</note>

<margin>Marcolis is the same as Mercury.</margin>
This "Marcolis" is the same as Mercury. To this agree Akiba, Saadias, and others of the <term>Mecubalim</term> <note>the Kabbalists, or "those who receive" tradition</note> of no small renown, whom we shall cite in their proper place. What the Arabs thought of Hermes and his books you will find extensively cited in the preceding pages. However, as for the objection raised here by adversaries—that because these books speak quite openly of the Sacred Trinity and the divine Word, and even approach certain Gospel truths, it is therefore difficult [to believe they are ancient]...

### CHAPTER III. BOOK I. ON ORIGINS
<page-num>40</page-num>

To those who respond that these books do not seem to have been composed by any philosopher before Christ: we reply that for this very same reason, Plato and Philo would have to be rejected, since both of them so frequently touch upon certain Evangelical truths that they might be seen as Christian Doctors. Indeed, some later writers have even dared to assemble "Evangelical Centos" <note>A "cento" is a poem or text composed of fragments from other authors; here, it refers to Christian texts patched together from Platonic writings.</note> from the books of the Platonists themselves. Regarding the harmony of the Platonists with Christian dogmas, we shall treat this extensively in the fifth book of this work.

<margin>Plato and Philo wrote as Christians.</margin>
<margin>Philo.</margin>
I have decided to bring forward certain points here regarding Philo the Jew, who in his *Hexameron* <note>Philo's commentary on the six days of creation.</note> calls "God the most generative, and the second the Word of God" <note>original: "τὸν Θεὸν γενικώτατον καὶ δεύτερον τὸν Θεοῦ λόγον"</note>. All of these things harmonize with the words of Hermes in the *Poimandres*: "God, most full of the fecundity of both sexes, generated a second Artisan Mind." Philo calls the "Sun the divine Word" <note>original: "ἥλιον λόγον Θεῖον"</note>; the *Poimandres* also says this: "the Sun is the Son of God" <note>original: "ἥλιον τὸν Θεῦ"</note>, and in the Gospel, Truth itself says: *I am the light of the World*; and the Church says: *Christ our God is the Sun of Justice.*

Furthermore, Philo, following Plato, calls the Word the "Image of God and the Angel of his Word, the first-born Word" <note>original: "Θεῦ εἰκόνα καὶ ἄγγελον αὐτῦ λόγον, λόγον πρωτόγονον"</note>. St. Paul calls Christ by these same names: *The Splendor of the Father, and the figure of His Substance, the first-born son of the Father, and the Angel of Great Counsel.* This is found in Holy Scripture in another place; and lest anyone should say they spoke only figuratively, let them hear what Philo 

<margin>Philo, On Dreams.</margin>
says in his book *On Dreams* regarding this Word: "For the lower world has as its presiding ruler the Artisan Word, the Lord of all, who after Him is the first uncreated, infinite Power, springing clearly from Him; he hangs over and rules those things made by him, and he is the elder and fruitful, legitimate son" <note>original: "ἔχει γὰρ ἄρχοντα ἐπὶ κ' ἡμενον τὸν δημιουργὸν λόγον τὲ πάντος δεσπότην..."</note>. All of these things are so much in harmony with the Gospel of St. John that they might seem to have been composed by a Christian of a later century. Therefore, the argument of those who think the cited books of Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> are forgeries simply because they touch too openly upon the mysteries of our faith is futile. Let them know that just as the Almighty God once spoke through Balaam's donkey <note>original: "Asinam Baal"; a reference to the biblical story in Numbers 22 where a donkey speaks divine truth.</note>, so too has He spoken at times through philosophers of a more sublime genius, having mingled Himself with their intellects and operations in some ineffable way.

<margin>God, by some supernatural way, mingles Himself with the natural operations of man.</margin>
For just as nothing is more worthy of the human intellect than to know those things which pertain to the divine nature and the benefits bestowed upon the human race—for whose sake the world and all things in it were founded—so also God willed that the highest mysteries of all should shine forth at all times, like sparks in the midst of the darkness of infidelity and pagan errors, to demonstrate the riches of His glory and goodness. For what else do Clement, Origen, Arnobius, Lactantius, Augustine, and Eusebius <note>These are early Church Fathers who often used pagan philosophy to argue for Christian truths.</note> strive for in the whole of their books of "Evangelical Demonstration," if not to conclude the mysteries of our faith from the monuments of the Pythagoreans, the Platonists, and the rest of the Greek philosophers against the pagans? For just as God spoke through the Sibylline books and oracles, saying much concerning the incarnate Word of God and the Sacraments...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher argues that the Hermetic texts are not forgeries, noting that many pre-Christian thinkers like Plato and Philo Judaeus expressed ideas strikingly similar to the Gospel. He suggests that God granted "sparks" of divine truth to high-minded pagans to prepare the way for Christianity.</summary>

### ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER III.

Just as He <note>Referring to God</note> foretold the death and passion of Christ and the final judgment through the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by early Christians to have predicted the coming of Jesus</note>, so too—out of His own infinite goodness—He was pleased to scatter certain supernatural seeds of divine mysteries into the natural contemplations of the ancient philosophers, eventually leading them toward a harvest of most fertile fruit. 

When I say this, let no one think that I believe or assert that Pythagoras, Plato, and their followers drew the divine mysteries they uttered from a direct revelation or a supernatural act of faith from God. Rather, I say that Plato spoke many things concerning God and the "Artisan Word" <note>The Logos or Divine Reason that shaped the universe</note> based on the authority of the oldest Egyptian writers—most notably Hermes Trismegistus and his followers—which had generated a deep conviction in his mind.

<margin>Who the teachers of the Greek philosophers were in Egypt.</margin>
Indeed, for many years Plato was a student of the Egyptian priest Secnuphis. When he observed the most hidden secrets being brought forth from the books of Hermes (for all Egyptian priests possessed the books of Hermes, as Clement of Alexandria testifies, holding them in exactly the same regard as Orthodox priests now hold the monuments of the Holy Scriptures), he embraced these ideas as the most suitable material for his own genius. He then passed them down to posterity, adding many things from his own intellect. 

Francesco Patrizi <note>A 16th-century Italian philosopher and proponent of Hermeticism</note> demonstrates all of this in his book titled *The Mystical Plato and Aristotle*, using the following words from Strabo, Clement, Eusebius, Plutarch, and others:

> Although that knowledge of divine things was entrusted and preserved in secret by the Hierophants <note>High priests of the mysteries</note> alone, they eventually communicated it even to foreigners when overcome by their service and time. Thus, many centuries earlier, these things were communicated to Orpheus by the priest Ethimunis; to Aglaophemus by Ochlaphus; to Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker</note> by Sonchis and Psenophis; to Pythagoras by Perenites; and finally to Plato by Sachoniatis and Secnuphis. These things were recorded partly by Clement and partly by Plutarch. Plato, therefore, obtained from these teachers not only the revelation of their mystical dogmas by living voice, but he was even shown the books of Hermes. It appears he took his dogmas from these books, but he also learned to keep them secret, just as the Hierophants preserved them in secret; thus, he later made it a habit either not to write them down at all, or to write them only in enigmas <note>Riddles or symbolic language</note>.

It is so true that the dogmas Plato wrote about were those of the Egyptians, that he himself admits it in the preface to the *Mystical Theology* (published under Aristotle’s name but reflecting the mind of the Egyptians), where he openly says:

> He wished to contemplate the world according to the mind of those who taught through the marks of figures <note>original: "per notas figurarũ", referring to hieroglyphs</note>, which are so hidden that no one else can reach the secrets of this kind of science.

<margin>Why the Greeks did not mention the name Trismegistus</margin>
But some will say that the name of "Trismegistus" <note>Thrice-Greatest</note> was not in use in Plato’s time—let alone cited by anyone—and consequently, the name seems to have been invented by later authors. I respond that it is one thing for a name to be in use, and another for it to be cited. It is possible that although the name was in use among the Greeks and other nations, the Greeks (who were then flourishing in wisdom) did not cite him by this name. They did this so as not to seem to obscure their own glory—which they sought above all else—by crediting it to a foreign philosopher with such a magnificent title. By doing so, they would have had to confess they learned these things from a foreigner, whereas they preferred to be considered the inventors by posterity. Indeed, just as the character of the Greeks was ambitious and greedy for glory beyond what can be said, so it is certain that they...

### BOOK I. ON ORIGINS. CHAPTER III.

<margin>The crime of plagiarism among certain authors of this time.</margin>
...several, indeed most things were received from the Egyptians and Chaldeans, yet the Greeks suppressed the names of those from whom they had drawn, claiming the ideas as their own rights and inventions. This is so clear that no one, unless they are ignorant of Platonic Theology, could deny it. Indeed, the most sharp-eyed Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile all schools of thought</note> demonstrates this openly in his examination of Pagan Philosophy. We ourselves shall reveal their actions at length in our work *Oedipus* <note>Kircher is referring to his massive study on Egyptian hieroglyphs, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, God willing, when it is published in its own time. It is not surprising, therefore, that Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle so sparingly cite the names of the masters from whom they drew all their knowledge. This backwards way of acting has, even in our own time, so besieged the spiteful and arrogant minds of some, that they are led only with great difficulty to honorably name those authors—or even cite them by name at all—from whom they have copied many things during the gathering of literary arguments. They do this for no other reason than to avoid appearing to grant the glory earned from a beautiful argument to another by the honorable mention of their name.

<margin>The name Trismegistus was used in ancient times.</margin>
Everyone sees that this is a case of the highest injustice and the crime of plagiarism, which is utterly loathsome to sincere and noble minds. Thus, although some Greeks did not think they should use that name, it is certain that the Chaldeans, Hebrews, Arabs, and both the earlier and later Greeks used it very frequently, as the fair-minded reader will be able to judge from the preceding Chaldean, Syrian, Arabic, and Greek citations. Seleucus, a very ancient author, was the first to call him "Hermes Trismegistus" <note>original Greek: Ἑρμὴν Τρισμέγιστον</note>, as found in the works of Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi, a philosopher who championed the Hermetic texts</note>. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> also reports that he was called this because he was the first to assert three virtues in one God, as we shall cite elsewhere. The Arabs call him "Trismegistus" because of his three offices as King, Priest, and Sage, using the name *Idris the Threefold* <note>original Arabic: ادريس مثلث or "Idris Muthallath"</note>. The Syrians and Chaldeans also call him "Triple Greatness" <note>original Syriac: ܬܠܝܬܝ ܪܒܘܬܐ or "Thluthi Robuothi"</note> for the same reason, as we have shown elsewhere. The Egyptians, truly, always considered him threefold because of these three duties, which is why they placed a three-headed statue of him in Hermopolis <note>The "City of Hermes," an ancient Egyptian cult center for the god Thoth</note> to be worshiped. Therefore, the name *Trismegistus* <note>meaning "Thrice-Greatest"</note> was used from the beginning down to these most recent times through the sequence of all ages, although they also titled him by other names: the Egyptians called him *Thoth* and *Hermanabis*; the Phoenicians called him *Taut*; and Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, also called him by the Egyptian name *Theuth*, as we showed above.

<margin>The name of the Greeks flourished since the time of Moses.</margin>
Finally, my adversaries object, among other things, that the name of the "Greeks" was not yet in use during the time of Hermes. This argument is truly as childish as it is unworthy of being refuted. However, lest we seem to have said nothing on this matter, we shall destroy it by highlighting the futility of the argument. It is certain that the Greek nation was already powerful and abounding in illustrious men in the time of Abraham, as is clear from chronologies. For in the times of Abraham and Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Assyria</note>, the kingdom of the Sicyonians was already flourishing under its first king, Cecrops (or as others say, Aegialus, from whom the Peloponnese was called Aegialia). Truly, in the time of Israel <note>referring to the era of the Patriarchs or the Exodus</note>, when Hermes lived, the Kingdom of the Argives flourished under its first king, Inachus, who also founded Argos. This is proved by the unanimous agreement of chronologers following Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian who synchronized the timelines of different ancient civilizations</note>. Furthermore, Cecrops was the first...

Furthermore, nothing remains but for us to discuss what kind of things the obelisks were, and who were their first inventors and builders.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the origin of Obelisks, and who was their first Author.

<margin>Definition of Obelisks.</margin>
Those hieroglyphic stones of the Egyptians, whose four-sided flanks converge to a point from a base in the shape of very sharp pyramids near the summit—their sides inclining somewhat with an uninterrupted path—were first called *obeloi* <note>original: "ὀβηλοὶ"</note> or "spits" <note>This refers to the Greek word for a roasting spit or a sharp skewer</note> by the Greeks because of the similarity to the skewers they resemble. Later, using a diminutive term introduced through a common misapplication <note>original: "κατα την καταχρησιν"</note>, they were called *obeliskoi* <note>original: "ὀβελίσκοι"</note> or "little obelisks," a name that the Latins retain to this day, borrowed from the Greeks. The Italians, however, because of their needle-like shape—in which they come together at a single point from a wide base as the sides gradually thin out in a set proportion—call these same things *Aguglia* <note>"Aguglia" is an archaic Italian word for "needle," related to the modern Italian "guglia" (spire)</note>. By a not dissimilar etymology, the Arabs call them <margin>Obelisks are called Pharaoh's Needles by the Arabs.</margin> *messalet pharaun* <note>original Arabic: مسلة فرعون</note>, that is, the "Needle of Pharaoh," because they were specifically the invention of the Pharaohs, the first Kings of Egypt. Finally, the Egyptian priests call them by a name that is indeed most appropriate for indicating the mysteries hidden beneath them—as is the case with all their other terms—*PITEBPERE* <note>original Coptic/Greek characters: ΠΙΤΕΒΠΗΡΗ</note>, which is to say, "Fingers of the Sun." You will see the <margin>Obelisks are called Fingers of the Sun by the Egyptians.</margin> reason for this etymology assigned throughout this work. To describe obelisks in a few words: they are nothing other than *four-sided hieroglyphic columns gradually thinning toward the summit, and then truncated into a small pyramid*. As we are about to discuss these and their mysteries and hidden secrets throughout this entire work, we shall begin the starting point of our discussion there, where the first cradles of this institution were found. It is asked, therefore: who was the first author of these obelisks?

Certainly, the school of the Arab historians teaches that pyramids existed before the flood, and that the deeds of the first men were carved upon them. <margin>Jalal al-Din in the *History of Egypt* <note>Kircher refers to the scholar Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, a prolific Egyptian writer (c. 1445–1505)</note></margin>

### CHAPTER IV. BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

<margin>Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Greek Hermes</note> corrects the corrupted doctrine of Ham and engraved it on stones.</margin>
...had brought over filthy and impious superstitions; following him came a most wise man born from the Canaanite lineage—the true Hermes, I say, after the Flood. Driven by a zeal for religion, he checked the perverse doctrine of Ham <note>In the biblical tradition used by Kircher, Ham, the son of Noah, was often blamed for introducing idolatry and magic into the post-Flood world</note> which was creeping far and wide and corrupting the minds of mortals with a most wretched stain of superstition. According to the greatness of the talent given to him by God, he strove in every way to restore the sincere doctrine handed down from the first Patriarchs and, once restored, to propagate it to posterity. However, even he did not pass it on with the same purity with which it had flowed from the original sources, but it remained subject to its own blemishes. From this, he established new characters and a new method of writing common to all, so that the common doctrine—committed to books and established for the shaping of morals—might produce the intended fruits in the minds of capable men. But for that knowledge which contained more divine and recondite <note>Hidden or obscure</note> meanings—a Philosophy and Theology removed from the understanding of the profane and the uneducated—he established another type of character with supreme genius. These were engraved on columns and obelisks as a perennial defense against all the injuries of time, to be preserved and propagated only by the priests, philosophers, and prophets, whose ranks, orders, and offices he himself established.

<margin>Hermes obtained divine honors because of his inventions.</margin>
He also invented many things most useful to the human race, for which he attained such great honors among the people of his age that they accepted him not only as a Priest, but as a King. Later, because of his miraculous wisdom and all-encompassing learning, and the works he performed which were memorable to all posterity, they decreed divine honors for him, as was shown in the preceding pages. And this is that Hermes, truly "Trismegistus" <note>Meaning "Thrice-Great"</note>, the source and origin of all Egyptian wisdom, the first teacher of hieroglyphic literature, and the inventor and builder of obelisks. From him, all subsequent Kings and priests were instructed to propagate the doctrine handed down by the most wise Hermes and applied themselves to carving it into stone columns or obelisks. This first establishment occurred a little before the death of Abraham and lasted until the age of Jacob, as was shown in the preceding sections.

<margin>The Wisdom of the Egyptians before Moses</margin>
Furthermore, since the said wisdom of the Egyptians—as is clear from Holy Scripture—preceded Moses by a long time, and the worship of divine and sacred things already flourished in Egypt in the time of Joseph, it is obvious that it could have originated from no other time than the one mentioned. Nevertheless, as usually happens, this wisdom was eventually corrupted in succeeding times by the priests and declined into a manifest nursery of all superstitions, as will be discussed in what follows.

However, so that no one may suspect me of using mere conjectures, I bring forward the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>A 7th-century Byzantine world chronicle that attempts to synchronize secular and biblical history</note> for the confirmation of these assertions, which speaks of our Mercury Trismegistus thus:

<margin>The Alexandrian Chronicle.</margin>
> *Mercury, or Fannus <note>Faunus</note>, son of Picus Jove, succeeded Mizraim <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt, personified here as a ruler</note> in the empire. He was descended from the line of Ham, and his inauguration happened in the following manner. When Picus (or Jove) died (says the Chronicle), his son Fannus, of the lineage of Janus—who is also Mercury—administered the Kingdom of Italy for thirty-five years. He was a sagacious, shrewd man and a mathematician, who first [used] gold...*

### ON LETTERS AND OBELISKS. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Trismegistus lived in Italy for some time with the Janigenae <note>A legendary early Italian people said to be descended from the god Janus</note>.</margin>
...he discovered the metal gold in the West and the method of smelting it. However, when he realized that he was burning with the great envy of his brothers—born of his father Jupiter Picus by various mistresses—who had formed a plan to kill him, he departed from Italy with a vast weight of gold. He betook himself to Egypt, to the lineage descended from his uncle Ham, the son of Noah, by whom he was received with great honor. While he resided there, he surpassed everyone in his abilities; dressed in a golden cloak, he practiced philosophy among the Egyptians. He predicted many things that would come to pass, for he was by nature exceptionally gifted. The Egyptians, therefore, worshipping him, proclaimed him the god Mercury, as one who foretold the future and brought them oracles and responses from God concerning future events as an intermediary. Because he supplied them with gold, they called him the "Bestower of Riches" and the "Golden God." 

According to the *Chronicle* <note>Likely referring to the Chronicon of Eusebius or a similar Byzantine historical compilation</note>, when Mercury arrived in Egypt, *at that time Mestrem <note>original Greek: Μεστρὲμ, referring to Misraim</note>, of the lineage of Ham, ruled the Egyptians; upon his death, the Egyptians made Hermes king, and he ruled the Egyptians for thirty-nine years with great splendor.* 

The text says that when Mercury arrived in Egypt, a certain man from the line of Ham named Mesrem <margin>Mercury Trismegistus, King of Egypt</margin> (or Misraim, which is the same) was reigning. When he passed away, the Egyptians appointed Mercury as King in his place, and he reigned most magnificently for thirty-nine years. It is said that he was the inventor of various things, that he organized words into order, and gave <margin>The Inventions of Mercury Trismegistus.</margin> names to many things. He was also the discoverer of letters and established the honors, sacred rites, and which gods should be worshipped. He also discovered the motions of the stars and the method of dividing the year. For this reason, he was held in the highest honor by Osiris (or Misraim) and served as the counselor to Isis (or Rhea), the wife of Misraim, during her husband's absence, as Diodorus Siculus records at length in Book 1, Chapter 2, whom you may consult. 

By these accounts, our previously stated opinion is so firmly established that one can scarcely doubt it further; but let us finally return to our intended goal after a discourse perhaps longer than was proper. We said a little earlier that the first Patriarchs of the human race after the Flood followed the Patriarchs of the prior age by inscribing the monuments of their discoveries on pyramids. However, when Hermes saw that pyramids did not accommodate <margin>Why Hermes carved his works on Obelisks.</margin> writing very conveniently due to the excessive slant of their sides, he designed another type of pyramid better suited for mystical writing, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote 'On the Egyptian Mysteries'</note> testifies: namely, those columns of Obelisks, which are called the "Columns of Mercury" by the author. Concerning their mysterious shape, see the end of this book. 

At that time, as has been shown, the Egyptian Kingdom was ruled by Misraim—a most curious investigator of exotic things also known as Saturn the Younger—who, having been <margin>Mercury lived with Misraim, serving as both his Scribe and Counselor.</margin> instructed by his Scribe and Counselor Mercury regarding the new construction of columns, was the first of all to apply his mind to erecting them. He did this not only to achieve fame for his name among posterity with the greatest magnificence, but also to engrave upon them that new system of Philosophy and Theology discovered by Hermes. However, being prevented by death, he could not carry out the execution as he had conceived it. Pliny teaches that this is so; he identifies the first inventor of Obelisks as Mitres or Mesphres <margin>Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of 'Natural History'</note>.</margin> (corrupted names), for in the manuscripts of Pliny surviving today in the Vatican Library...

### CHAPTER IV: BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

<margin>Mizraim, called Mizra, Mestres.</margin> ...in those passages where the printed editions of Pliny have "Mitres," "Mephres," or "Mesphees," the manuscript uses the truly clear term **Mestres**. This is the same as **Mizraim**, whom we have shown in the preceding pages was also called *Mesres*, *Mesra*, and *Mithras*. However, when he was taken by death, his son succeeded to his father’s place. This son was known partly by his father’s name and partly by a different one. Josephus, in the first book of *Against Apion*, calls him by the corrupted name "Mephramuthosis"; Saint Theophilus, in his third book *To Autolycus*, calls him "Methramuthosis"; and finally, Eusebius calls him "Mispharmuthosis." These variations stem from the corruption of the three previous names: Mephres, Mitres, and Mephres.

<margin>Who Mesramuthisis was, and why he was so named.</margin> Through the restoration of the Egyptian language, we have determined his name to be more truly *Metramuthisis* <note>original Greek: μετρα-μ-υ-θ-ι-ς</note>, which is to say, **Mesramuthisis**—specifically, from *Mesra* and his Mother *Isis*. We have shown elsewhere at length that Mesra was also called Osiris. In the Egyptian language, *metr* <note>Kircher is likely connecting this to the Greek word 'meter' or an imagined Coptic root</note> signifies "mother," and *Isis* <note>original: ι-σ-ι-ς</note> denotes Isis; thus, it is as if you were to say he was the offspring of Mesra (or Osiris) and Mother Isis.

And here, having carried on the work of erecting an obelisk that had been hindered by his father’s death, he gave the first example of the erection of obelisks at Heliopolis—which was formerly called **On** and **Bethshemesh** <note>Hebrew for "House of the Sun"</note>—where he held his residence. This is attested by Pliny. He was a most eager follower of the Hermetic and paternal arts and sciences. While he lived in On, or Bethshemesh, or Heliopolis, in the constant company of the priests, he believed (according to Pliny) that his father had been warned in a dream by some unknown deity about erecting obelisks. Out of obedience to the deity, the son wished to fulfill his father’s vows.

<margin>Mesramuthisis warned in a dream about erecting obelisks.</margin> However, it is more likely that he ambitiously claimed for himself this conversation with the gods through a fabricated dream; he likely invented such things so that the work he was engineering would be received with greater admiration and veneration by his subjects and posterity.

But someone might object at this point: how can Mesramuthisis immediately follow Mizraim, when we established a little earlier that Mercury (Hermes) was his successor? I answer that upon the death of Mizraim, Mesramuthisis was of a very tender age and incapable of ruling. In his place, Mercury administered the kingdom for thirty-nine years.

<margin>At what time Hermes Trismegistus reigned.</margin> It was during this very time that the hieroglyphic doctrine became most famous throughout all of Egypt. When Mercury passed away, the now-adult Mesramuthisis succeeded him. As has been said, because he was most curious about his father’s sciences, he increased and promoted the new hieroglyphic doctrine invented by Hermes in wonderful ways. We have shown all of this at length in our *Chronology of the Kings of Egypt*, inserted in the first volume of the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's own work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. His dominion falls in the time when the progeny of the Patriarch Jacob, son of Isaac, was considered illustrious throughout the East. This was the year 2279 from the creation of the world; 623 from the Flood; 240 from the birth of Abraham; and 65 years after his death, according to the more probable calculation of chronologists. It falls nearly in the year 1774 before Christ. These details agree perfectly with the tradition of Eusebius, who places the reign of Mesramuthisis around this same time; see the *Chronography* prefixed to this work. Let these remarks suffice concerning the first origin of the obelisks; now let us proceed to a detailed description of all of them.

# CHAPTER V.

## On the Material of Obelisks.

<margin>The type of marble from which they made the Obelisks was distinguished by mystical reasons.</margin>
So that no mystery might be lacking from the arcane construction of the Obelisks, those first inventors of hieroglyphic literature chose a stone material consistent with the mysteries they contained. This was a certain type of marble, sprinkled as if with drops of various colors, with a hardness that is nearly indomitable and in no way inferior to Porphyry. The Greeks call it *fire-variegated* <note>original Greek: πυεϱπίκιλον</note>, the Latins call it *Thebaic Stone* <note>original Latin: Petram Thebaicam</note>, and the Italians call it *red granite* <note>original Italian: Granito rosso</note>. The quarry for this stone is near Thebes—once the most celebrated royal city of the Egyptians—near the mountains that look toward Ethiopia and the cataracts of the Nile, turning toward the South. And although Egypt lacks no kind of marble, the <term>Hieromystae</term> <note>A term for priests who presided over sacred mysteries</note> seem to have chosen this one above all others because of some mysterious mechanism of nature hidden within it.

<margin>All Obelisks are made from pyritic marble, and why.</margin>
For until now, no Obelisk in the world has been seen by anyone to be made by the Egyptians from any other material besides this marble (which is not without its own mystery). It is also a wonder that this marble seems to enjoy no other soil but the Egyptian; though some contend that because of the columns in the Church of St. Catherine on Mount Sinai, the said mountain must possess such quarries, I would not easily deny it. It is well known—as we have shown at length in our *Description of Egypt* <note>original Latin: Chorographia Aegypti; a reference to Kircher's own geographical writings</note>—that the folds of Mount Sinai are continuous with the Egyptian hills through subterranean chains of mineral veins.

I am not unaware that in Lake Garda <note>original: Lacu Benaco</note> and Lake Como, as well as on Elba and other mountains of Italy, and even in Sweden, a similar kind of stone is found; however, when you look at either the hardness or the variety of spots, it is in no way comparable to the Egyptian variety.

<margin>Egypt abounds in every kind of marble.</margin>
Furthermore, the suggestion made by some that the Egyptians used this kind of marble only because they lacked others is false; for as we said a little before, Egypt abounds in every kind of marble. Egypt possesses marble of a grey or ash color, not unequal in hardness to the aforementioned stone, such as the columns on which the vestibule of the Pantheon here in Rome rests. Such a great abundance of both types is found everywhere here in Rome that there is almost no Church, no monument of antiquity, and finally no corner of the City of Rome where it does not occur. This is a clear sign that these marbles were held in the highest value by the Roman Princes at all times, and they therefore transported them from Egypt to Rome at the greatest expense. Egypt also possesses alabaster, and Parian marble, and porphyry; it has opal of a yellowish color, and <term>chrysites</term> <note>A golden-colored stone or "gold-stone"</note>, all of which served for making various statues of the Gods and vessels for sacrifices. Only the Obelisks were fashioned from this variegated "pyrite" <note>Kircher uses 'pyrite' here to describe the speckled, fire-like appearance of granite, not the modern mineral iron pyrite</note> of ours, for certain mystical reasons which we shall indicate shortly.

<margin>Why the Egyptians used no other marble besides pyritic marble for Obelisks.</margin>
At this point, some will object that the Egyptians used no other marble for Obelisks besides this one because no other marble was equal to it in hardness, toughness, and...

I reply: why did they not choose porphyry <note>original Latin: porphyriten</note>, which Egypt abounds in, rather than pyrite, as it is both more solid and more durable? They will answer that the veins of this porphyry did not provide stones of the size they desired. a fourfold composition of mixture implanted in it by nature; the substance of the principal stone shines with a red color, in which now crystalline or Amethystine, then ash-colored or blue, and sometimes black particles of Pharian marble are seen mixed here and there throughout the whole substance of the stone. When the Egyptians beheld this mixture of things, they chose it as a material truly worthy and most suitable for representing their mysteries.

<margin>Obelisks in the Egyptian language are called 'Digits of the Sun'.</margin>

Consult the last chapter of this book on these matters, where you will find everything explained more extensively. Do you see, therefore, with what great ingenuity the Egyptians labored in choosing suitable materials for their structures, and how they assumed nothing that was not mystical for the ingenious representation of their ideas? It is clear, then, from what has been said, why they used only this variegated pyrite for Obelisks; certainly, if Obelisks of another color appear anywhere, let it be a most certain sign to you that they were by no means made in Egypt, but by foreign rivals of the Egyptians, or in later times when hieroglyphic literature had already fallen into disuse.

## CHAPTER VI.

### On the differences and dimensions of Obelisks, and on their transfer from Egypt to the City.

### §. I.

### *On the difference of Obelisks.*

<margin>Various differences of Obelisks. I.</margin>
I have observed a fourfold difference among the Obelisks surviving here in Rome; for they differ either in size, proportion, sculpture, or smoothness. First, if you look at the size, there are very small Obelisks, there are medium ones, and there are very large ones. I hear that many are still seen in Egypt that do not exceed ten or twelve feet; there are some here in Rome of twenty or thirty feet; there are others of seventy and eighty; and finally, there are those of one hundred and forty feet in height, as will be seen in the text of the work.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, they differ in proportion. Some are equal-sided <note>original Latin: Isaëdri</note>, or of equal sides; others are of unequal sides. Just as the bases of the first kind of Obelisks form a square, so the bases of these others form a Parallelogram—that is, any two opposite sides, compared to the remaining two opposite sides, have a notable difference in width. For what purpose the Egyptian Hieroglyphs <note>Kircher likely refers here to the Egyptian priests or the scholars of the sacred scripts.</note> did this is hardly certain. Various people bring forward various reasons; there are those who wish the matter not to lack mysteries; others think they established this difference so that those inscribed to a Deity would be recognized by equal sides, while those inscribed to Kings who had attained divinity would be recognized by unequal sides; however, that this is false will be demonstrated at length elsewhere.

<margin>Why in certain Obelisks two opposite sides are unequal to the other two.</margin>
And so I say that there was no other reason for this difference except the defective constitution of the mineral veins from which they were cut, or a certain degradation born from ruptures, cracks, and other flaws of the stone in those already cut, by which they were forced to accommodate themselves as best they could to the condition of the mass either cut or to be cut. And since, if they had wished to make the entire mass equal according to a square base, much of the intended mass of the huge stone would have been lost. Hence, out of a desire to preserve the intended height of the stone mass, by an ingenious error, a little was taken away from the side. I said by "ingenious labor" because through this very defect, they discovered a truly remarkable mystery—as will be explained in the Chapter on the mysterious shape of the Obelisks—according to the usual Egyptian custom.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, Obelisks differ in that some are distinguished by characters, and others are without...

The fourth difference of Obelisks consists in the diversity of their characters <note>In this context, "characters" refers to the hieroglyphic inscriptions.</note>; some are marked with a completely similar form and order of characters, while others are marked with a completely different style, which indeed is better known than needs to be said, as proven by the diversity of their subject matter. ### §. I I.

->On the proportion of Obelisks.<-

<margin>An Obelisk is nothing other than a truncated Pyramid</margin>
We have said in the preceding sections that an Obelisk is nothing other than a truncated pyramid; this truncation was established by the Egyptian Sages primarily for these reasons. First, so that the sides meeting at the final point of a Pyramid would not result in a shapeless mass of monstrous height, rendered unsuitable for handling and erection due to the danger of breaking. Second, because under such an enormous height of mass, the hieroglyphic symbols inscribed on the upper region of the Pyramid would vanish from sight, escaping both the eyes and the mind. Third, because the mass of a Pyramid could easily be overturned by the winds due to excessive height. Fourth and finally, because of the abundance of mystical reasons, which they found to be greater in Obelisks than in a Pyramid, as will be discussed later. Led by these reasons, they truncated Pyramids into Obelisks, yet preserved that proportion which would both evoke the highest beauty of the structure and, as will be said in its proper place, in no way lack the mysteries which they chiefly intended.

<margin>The proportion of Obelisks in regard to height.</margin>
For they applied this proportion in almost all Obelisks, as far as could be observed with the greatest diligence: they established the height of the Obelisk, which is measured from the lowest base to the base of the truncated mass, in a <term>decuple proportion</term> <note>A 10:1 ratio.</note> to the side of the lower square base. Thus, if an Obelisk were made whose base side was one <term>palm</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the width of a human hand.</note>, the height between the lower base and the upper truncated base would be ten palms; likewise, if the side of the base of any Obelisk were 4 palms, the mentioned height would be 40 palms; and if any Obelisk had a lower base side of 10 palms, its height would be reckoned at 100 palms; and so on for the rest. This proportion is not only convenient and easy, but also ingenious, involving great mysteries within itself, as will later be made clear.

<margin>The proportion of the base of Obelisks to the truncated area.</margin>
Furthermore, they established the proportion as <term>subsesquialter</term> <note>A 2:3 ratio; literally "one and a half" in reverse.</note>; that is, from the lower side divided into three equal parts, they took 2 parts for the side of the upper base. The <term>Pyramidion</term> <note>The small, pyramid-shaped capstone at the very top of an obelisk.</note> which terminates the Obelisk equaled in its height the lower width, or the side of the lowest base of the Obelisk. In Obelisks with unequal sides, that palm's length which for the most part was removed from the narrower side was added to the height, although they did not follow this quite so mathematically in all cases—

...they followed a proportion, so that they did not deviate more or less from the true proportion. Indeed, observe the declared proportions in the following diagram.

<image-desc>A vertical diagram of a tapering obelisk structure. At the very top is a pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk.</note> with vertex labeled A and base labeled D E. Below the pyramidion, the main shaft of the obelisk is divided into ten segments, numbered 1 at the bottom through 10 at the top along a central vertical axis. Let the Obelisk be A B C, of which the side of the lowest base is B C; and the side of the truncated top is D E. Let the Pyramidion be D E A. Suppose the base B C is 10 <term>palms</term> <note>A "palm" (palmus) was a common measurement, roughly the width of a hand. Kircher is using a 1:10 ratio here for width to height.</note>. If, therefore, you multiply each of these 10 palms of width by 10 other palms and extend them into length, you will have the 100-foot height of the truncated Obelisk D E B C that was sought. The upper side D E is in a <term>subsesquialter proportion</term> <note>original: "proportione subsesquialtera." In classical mathematics, this refers to a ratio of 3:2 (or 2/3). Here, the top is 2/3 the width of the bottom.</note> to the lower side B C; that is, the side D E will constitute 2/3 of the lower base at the point where the truncation occurred. Furthermore, one side of the pyramidion, D A or E A, equals the side B C of the lower base of the Obelisk. And this is the proportion which the Egyptians for the most part applied in the construction of Obelisks, though they did not insist upon it with such rigor that they would not occasionally add something more, depending on the varying intention of the Architects or the condition of the mass. But so that everything may become more obvious to the reader’s understanding, let us now approach the measurement of these objects using the order and method common to Mathematicians.
