according to the 6th proposition of the 6th book of *Euclid's Elements*, as side AH is to side HC, so side AE is to side EG; since three of these are known here, namely CH, which is the height EF of the Obelisk at 108 <term>palms</term> <note>A "palm" (palmus) is a Roman unit of measure, approximately 22.3 cm or 8.8 inches.</note>; and AE, which is half of the lowest base at 6 palms (for we have found the entire base AB to be 12 palms); and finally AH at 2 palms; for since the upper base CD is 8 palms, its half CF will be 4, and consequently CH, being parallel to EF, will cut 2 palms from the half-base AE (which is 6 palms). Therefore, with AH, AE, and EF being known, the axis EG of the whole Pyramid will be known. If it is done as AH (2) is to HC (108), so is AE (6) to EG; for after performing the operation according to the rule of proportions, EG will come out as the height of the Obelisk if it had gradually vanished into a Pyramid, namely the sought height of 324 palms. Therefore, if the Obelisk had run out into a Pyramid in a continuous flow, it was to be 324 palms, as was said. Moreover, you will have the height of the <term>truncated Pyramid</term> <note>A pyramid with its top cut off; the main shaft of most obelisks.</note> FG if you subtract the height of the Obelisk EF from the total height—that is, 108 from 324. The remainder will give 216 palms, the sought height of the truncated Pyramid. In this manner, we found that our <term>Pamphylian Obelisk</term> <note>Also known as the Agonalis or the Obelisk of Domitian, which stands atop Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers.</note>, if it had run out to a final apex, would have been (given the stated conditions) a Pyramid of 133 palms; you shall proceed in the same way in the dimensioning of all other Obelisks.

### Problem III.

->*To investigate the volume of Obelisks.*<-

<margin>Measurement of the volume of the Obelisk, if it had continued into a Pyramid.</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a tall, tapering pyramid (A B D) enclosed within a rectangular prism (A C). Once the height of the Obelisk is known—if it were to have continued into a full Pyramid according to Problem I—its unknown prism cannot remain hidden. For the third part of this prism will give the **Volume** <note>original: "Soliditatem"</note> of our Pyramid A B G proposed in the first Problem. Once the "excess" (the part by which the Pyramid surpasses the Obelisk) is known, both the prism of that excess and consequently the third part of it (the quantity of the Pyramid exceeding the Obelisk) will be obtained. But let us demonstrate the matter through geometric reasoning. Let us therefore imagine two Pyramids in the present figure, the first of which is A B D, and the second N E D. Let the side of the first base A V be 12 palms, which, when multiplied by itself, will constitute the base of the whole, A B, of 144 square palms. Let the side of the upper base N I be 8 palms, which, multiplied by itself, will give the square surface of the base N E of 64 square palms. Let a prism A C also be circumscribed around the base of the Pyramid A B D, and another prism N G around the base N E. This being done, multiply the square of the base, 144 palms, by the height of the Pyramid, which we found in the 1st Problem to be 324 palms; and the calculation of volume <note>original: "cubicatione"</note> being completed, there will be a prism A C of 46,656 cubic, or solid, palms. The third part of this, 15,552, will give the total Volume of the Pyramid A B D in cubic palms, if the Obelisk had continued to its point.

But since the Obelisk is a **truncated pyramid** <term>pyramis truncata</term> <note>A pyramid with its top cut off, forming the main shaft of the obelisk.</note>, you will find its Volume in this way: Multiply the square of the base N E by the height of its own [smaller] Pyramid, and a prism will be produced, whose third part reveals the quantity of the truncated [top] Pyramid. This again being subtracted from the whole Pyramid, the Obelisk's...

...will leave the sought **volume** <note>original: "soliditatem"</note> of the obelisk. But let us demonstrate this with an example. Let there be a truncated pyramid N E D; let its base N E be a square of 64 square palms, which, when multiplied by the height of the said pyramid (which we found in the first Problem to be 216 palms), will produce a **prism** <note>In this context, the author refers to a rectangular block that would enclose the pyramid.</note> N G of 13,824 cubic palms. Indeed, you will find the volume of the <insert>smaller top</insert> pyramid this way: since the side of the pyramid is 8 palms and its height is 12, multiply 8 by 12 cubically <note>This likely refers to the calculation for a prism base multiplied by height.</note>, and the result for its prism will be 768; a third part of this, 256 cubic palms, will give the volume of the <insert>top</insert> pyramid. When this is joined with the volume of the obelisk, it constitutes 10,688 cubic palms, the sought volume of the entire structure.

### Problem IV.

->*To find the gravity, or weight, of Obelisks.*<-

<margin>What is the weight of the Obelisk?</margin>
First, from the same stone or material as the Obelisk, let a **palmar cube** <note>term: "cubus palmaris" — a cube measuring one palm (roughly 9 inches or 22 cm) on each side.</note> be made, squared as accurately as possible. Then, you shall weigh the cube prepared in this manner on a most exact scale. In this way, following the **Archimedean method** <note>Refers to Archimedes' principles of buoyancy and density to determine the properties of materials.</note> and applying every diligence, we found the weight of such a palmar cube to be nearly 87 pounds. Having obtained the weight of one cubic palm, you will arrive at the knowledge of the total weight by a very easy process in this manner: Since we found just before that the obelisk’s volume was 10,688 cubic palms, you will have the weight of the entire Obelisk if you multiply 87 by 10,688. The sum, 929,856, will give the pounds which the entire Obelisk weighs. If, however, you desire to know the weight of the entire pyramid A B D <note>referring to the theoretical full pyramid if it weren't truncated</note>, multiply 87 pounds by the volume of the said whole pyramid, which we found above to be 15,552 cubic palms: the product, 1,353,024, will give the sought weight in pounds of the whole pyramid as if it had not been truncated. By this industry, you will investigate the weight of all other Obelisks with infallible reasoning.

### CHAPTER VII. 58 BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

...such as the Vatican, Lateran, Flaminian, Campus Martius, and one still underground. In total, as I have said, there are twelve, which must be dealt with in order.

<margin>The Mahutean Obelisk</margin>
The *Mahutean* obelisk is so called because it was erected in front of the Church of St. Mahutus—that is, St. Bartholomew (for St. Bartholomew is called by this name borrowed from the Arabs <note>original: "hoc enim nomine ab Arabibus mutuato vocatur S. Bartholomæus"</note>)—belonging to the Bergamasque nation, in the area of the new Church of St. Ignatius of the Society of JESUS.

<margin>The Medicean Obelisk</margin>
The *Medicean* obelisk is named after the gardens of the Medici, or the Grand Duke of Tuscany, in which it was erected. This garden is most delightful and is situated on the Pincian Hill, in the place where the hanging gardens of Sallust were once seen; it is visited by a great crowd of foreigners.

<margin>The Scauro-Caelian Obelisk</margin>
The *Scauro-Caelian* is so called because it is seen erected in the Mattei gardens between the Slope of Scaurus <note>original: "Cliuum Scauri"</note> and the Caelian Hill; its upper part is remarkable for its hieroglyphics, while the lower part remains smooth <note>original: "rasa," meaning it lacks carvings</note>.

<margin>The Obelisk of the Roman College</margin>
Another is near the Roman College of the Society of JESUS, seen before its gates facing the Roman Corso; its main base is still standing, while the other two parts have been inserted into the corners of neighboring houses to serve as supports.

<margin>The Pamphilian Obelisk</margin>
Furthermore, among those of medium size is, first, our *Pamphilian* obelisk, the history of which you may see prefixed to this book.

<margin>The Veranian Obelisk</margin>
The *Veranus* obelisk, which we also called the Barberini obelisk in the *Prodromus* <note>Referring to Kircher's earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus* (1636)</note>; it was discovered by Cardinal Barberini in the Veranian field outside the walls, and now lies nearby his palace on the Quirinal Hill, broken into three parts and cast down.

<margin>The Esquiline Obelisk</margin>
The *Esquiline* is so named from the Esquiline Hill, where it is seen erected by Pope Sixtus V at the Liberian Basilica, called St. Mary Major; it is smooth and marked by no hieroglyphics.

<margin>The Sallustian Obelisk</margin>
The *Sallustian* is so called from the gardens of Sallust, in which it was once seen erected; today the most magnificent Ludovisi Villa is in that same place, in which the obelisk still lies prostrate, broken into two parts by the injury of time.

<margin>The Vatican Obelisk</margin>
Furthermore, among the largest obelisks, the first we encounter is the *Vatican*, in the Vatican Field, where it was erected.

<margin>The Flaminian Obelisk</margin>
The *Flaminian* is named from the Flaminian Way or Gate, where it is seen raised next to the house of St. Mary, commonly called *del Popolo*.

<margin>The Campus Martius Obelisk</margin>
Finally, the *Campus Martius* obelisk is so called from the Field of Mars, in which it serves the foundations of neighboring palaces, buried under the earth. One side of it, remarkable for its hieroglyphic writing, offers itself to view from a certain cellar of a private house; it is intact, and in its size it almost equals the Flaminian.

And these are the twelve obelisks that remain in the City, still visible in the open. Besides these, I have no doubt that many others still lie hidden here and there in the ruins underground; this is clearly evident from the work of Publius Victor on the *Regions of the City*, who records that after the Emperor Caligula, 44 obelisks were brought to Rome from Egypt.

<margin>Publius Victor on the Regions of the City. 44 Obelisks transferred to Rome.</margin>
But besides the two erected in the Mausoleum of Augustus and in the gardens of Sallust, neither Publius Victor nor any other of the writers on the City of Rome recounts by whom or where the rest were erected.

<margin>The Obelisk on the Tiber Island and its remains.</margin>
As for what Pomponius Laetus and others hand down concerning an obelisk on the Tiber Island, and two others in the *Agonali* <note>The Circus Agonalis, now Piazza Navona</note>, and then others erected in the Flaminian and other circuses, some think these should be considered conjectures rather than historical accounts, since they do not so much describe what was done, as what—by the logic of the mystic nature of the circuses...

# AND THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS. CHAPTER VII.

<margin>It represented the mast on a ship.</margin>
...though others have reported on how the construction of these things ought to have been done, I am nonetheless moved by strong evidence to assert that an Obelisk was erected on the Tiber Island. A fragment of it still remains today before the Church of St. Bartholomew; among five other fragments, it serves as a barrier for those entering the Temple. It is notable for its carvings of hawks and fish, which we also display in our *Oedipus* <note>original: "Oedipo"; referring to Kircher’s own work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to decode hieroglyphs</note>. Since it is recorded that the Tiber Island was built in the shape of a ship, it is highly probable that the Obelisk erected in the center of the Island was intended to represent the form of a mast in the middle of a ship.

<margin>Circuses represented the world, the Obelisk in the center represented the Sun.</margin>
Furthermore, since Circuses represented the world, according to the witness Cassiodorus <note>A 6th-century Roman statesman and writer</note>, an Obelisk placed in the center of the Circuses allegorically signified the Sun, to whose honor they were dedicated, acting as a kind of "soul of the world." Following the Egyptians in the display of mysteries, it is probable that obelisks were erected in every circus; however, we shall discuss these more extensively in the following sections.

<margin>Roman Emperors erected only the larger Obelisks.</margin>
Now, I will briefly state my opinion regarding the 44 Obelisks reported by Publius Victor <note>A 4th-century chronicler of Rome's landmarks</note>. First, I assume that the Emperors, as befitted their magnificence, ignored the rest and brought only the second and third-class Obelisks from Egypt to the City. These were conspicuous for their mass beyond all others, possessing a certain majesty worthy of admiration and suited to the lofty thoughts of Emperors. They sought such massive stones with such ambition that the one who erected a larger Obelisk was judged to have achieved something more significant and worthy than the rest.

<margin>The source of such a large supply of Egyptian monuments in the City.</margin>
Seeing this rivalry among the Emperors, other Roman elites followed their lead. For their gardens and the decoration of private buildings, they procured stones, idols, statues, and smaller Obelisks from Egypt. They took advantage of the <term>nautical cradle</term> <note>original: "cratis nauticæ"; a specialized wooden framework or raft used to transport heavy monoliths</note> on which the larger ones were carried to Rome. It was easy, and even beneficial for the ship's stability, to carry smaller Obelisks placed on the cradle—as well as the many columns of pyrite <note>likely referring to speckled granite or hard volcanic stone</note> surviving here in Rome, along with a nearly innumerable quantity of fragments found everywhere in every corner—since all these smaller masses could serve as <term>ballast</term> <note>original: "Saburra"</note> and a means of leveling the vessel.

<margin>Obelisk at the Ara Coeli and the Palace of Cardinal Sacchetti.</margin>
Publius Victor himself says that most of the 44 Obelisks brought to Rome were very small. Two of this kind are seen here in Rome to this day: one at the Church known as the <term>Ara Coeli</term> <note>Altar of Heaven</note>, and the other in the Palace of Cardinal Sacchetti. Both were discovered in Rome during the time of Pope Paul III and do not exceed 15 palms <note>about 11 feet or 3.3 meters</note> in height. Why the others do not appear is easy to guess: since they were smaller, they could easily be moved elsewhere, or even broken and scattered. Therefore, it should not seem strange that no trace of them remains to those who well know the vicissitudes of time, the changes of regimes, and the unfair fate of the Emperors. They were toppled in that general slaughter of Obelisks and the devastation of the City by the Goths, and in the course of time were either buried deep in the earth, inserted into the foundations of buildings, or their parts scattered, or even thrown into the river.

<margin>Bartholomew Marlianus in the Topography of the City.</margin>
Marlianus, in his *Topography of the City*, reports another Obelisk in the Verano field near the Church of St. Lawrence, which in the year 1630, Francesco Cardinal [Barberini]...

# CHAPTER VII. 60 BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

Cardinal Barberini <note>Francesco Barberini (1597–1679), a major patron of the arts and Kircher’s contemporary</note> moved a fragment from the Vineyard of Curtius Saccocia to the courtyard of the Barberini Palace on the Quirinal Hill, where it still lies today, broken into three pieces; you may find its most mysterious teachings explained in my work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* <note>Kircher’s massive four-volume attempt to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs, published 1652–1654</note>.

<margin>M. Fabius Calvus</margin>
I believe a similar fate befell the Obelisk that Marco Fabio Calvo <note>A 16th-century author known for his reconstruction of ancient Rome</note> describes in his *Description of Ancient Rome* as lying prostrate in the Circus of Flora (the ruins of which are still visible today in the valley between the Sallustian Gardens and the Viminal Hill). I suspect this is the same one currently standing in the Medici Gardens. But let these remarks suffice regarding the Roman Obelisks of which some knowledge could be obtained.

<margin>Surviving Obelisks in Egypt</margin>
That many obelisks still remain in Egypt is certain from Arabic records. Most travelers returning from Egypt assert that many fragments of Obelisks are still found scattered among the ruins near Cairo. Indeed, Father Joseph Marcellana of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits)</note>, who explored a large part of Egypt while journeying to Ethiopia, says that in the city of Esna—which I have shown above to be near ancient Thebes—many are still to be seen, some standing and others fallen; these were also noted by Pigafetta <note>Filippo Pigafetta, an explorer and historian</note> in his travel journals. Various religious brothers from different Orders who live there for the purpose of spreading the Faith write the same to me, especially regarding Cairo and the areas near Alexandria; more extensive material on these will be given in the *Oedipus*. Among others, the most noble and famous Mr. Mathias Balbiski—noted for his lively intellect and knowledge of antiquities—observed traces of certain Obelisks in a lake near Matarea <note>Ancient Heliopolis</note> and in Alexandria. We shall present the drawings made by this gentleman in the *Oedipus*. All this is confirmed by Father Marcus de Luca, of the Order of St. Francis of the Observance, who, returning from Egypt while I am writing this (having lived there for eleven years), asserts that besides the two surviving in Alexandria, various fragments of the same are found in Cairo. He notes that the largest of all is seen standing in a lake at Matarea, remarkable for its hieroglyphics; however, it can only be reached at certain times of the year when the waters from the Nile's inundation, which collect in said lake, have dried up. Furthermore, he asserts that fragments of many Obelisks are visible at Thebes. He also reported many things about the inscriptions in hieroglyphics at the "Red Monastery" (which the Arabs call *Deirelachmur* <note>original: "Deirelachmur"; likely Deir el-Ahmar</note>), as well as a palace famous for enchantments and incantations situated on the bank of the Nile and its hieroglyphics. He even spoke of a "shell of love" <note>original: "conchae amoris"; possibly a reference to a specific oval monument or sarcophagus</note> surviving in Cairo, shaped in an oval figure and full of hieroglyphics. All these things will be produced in their proper time, if God grants me life.

<margin>The Nubian Geographer</margin>
The Nubian Geographer <note>A reference to the famous 12th-century Arab cartographer Al-Idrisi</note>, in his geographical work, reports that two obelisks of remarkable size still remain in Alexandria, in these words:

> And in Alexandria are the two needles of Pharaoh; they are two stones, square along their length, and their tops are narrower than their bases. The height of one of them is five *qim* <note>original: "قيم"; a unit of measurement</note>, and the width of their bases on each of their sides is ten spans, the total circumference being forty spans. The author of the *Book of Wonders* related that they were carved from Mount Darim in the western land of Egypt, and on them is written: "I, Dagmar son of Sharran, built this city." <note>This is a translation of the Arabic text provided in the source; the inscription mentioned is a legendary attribution common in medieval Arabic texts.</note>

In Alexandria, there are two "needles of Pharaoh" <note>Now famously known as Cleopatra’s Needles; one stands in London and the other in New York City</note>; these "needles" are stones that are square along their entire length, and their height becomes narrower than their lower parts. As for the fact that the measurements given by the Arabs do not match in every respect, this occurred because they only measured the larger part that projected out of the ground, while the rest was hidden within the earth; this was reported by Mathias Balbiski, whom we cited above.

However, you may see the chorography <note>The descriptive mapping of a region</note> of all these places in our *Egyptian Oedipus*. ## CHAPTER VIII.

### *On the Erectors of Obelisks in Particular, and which Obelisks were erected by individual Kings of Egypt.*

**B**efore we determine the first erection of the Obelisks, we have thought it necessary to assume a few things in this place; so that our discourse might be rendered more solid, and the reasoning of our project might be supported by firmer arguments.

<margin>The long life of the first Patriarchs of the world after the flood.</margin>
I suppose, therefore, first, that the sons of Ham—Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan—as well as the sons of Shem, were of such long-lived life that some lasted until the very times of Jacob and Joseph, as we have said in the preceding pages. Indeed, the sacred scriptures openly testify in Genesis chapter 11 that Shem himself, the brother of Ham, lived for five hundred years after the flood. For as was also shown above from the teachings of the Arabs, since Egypt could not contain such a prolific progeny, each of the sons chose a Province for himself, which was consequently distributed into various dominions. And since all were held by an ambition for ruling, each claimed the title of King for himself and adopted names smelling of some sort of divinity. From this was later born in Egypt that famous

<margin>The Kingdom of the Gods in Egypt: what and of what kind was it?</margin>
Kingdom of the Gods, which we describe at length in the cited part of *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. I clearly demonstrate, from the tradition of Oriental writers, that **Misraim** <note>original: מצרים Misraim</note> (from whom Egypt was also called *Misraim*) ruled over various parts of Egypt and the neighboring regions up until the time of Joseph himself. Indeed, since Misraim was supreme in authority, power, and intellect, he first reduced Egypt into the form of a Kingdom and established himself as King. He achieved many things for which he received divine honors from posterity out of widespread admiration; sometimes he was called the **Sun**, at other times **Osiris**, then **Mithras** or **Mitres**, now **Saturn**, **Apis**, and by other names used by various nations. He was the first Pharaoh of Egypt.

Therefore, we establish Misraim as the first King and Pharaoh of Egypt. Others, as was shown above, corruptly call him *Mitres*, some *Mithres*, some *Mesphees* or *Mesphres*, and some even confuse him with *Osiris, Apis, the Sun, Sothis, Caelus, Saturn,* and *Menas*. In the preceding Chapter 4, we showed at length how he, under the guidance of **Mercury** <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian god Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus with the Roman Mercury.</note>, set his mind to erecting Obelisks, and how this work was interrupted by his death, but then put into execution by his son **Horus** under the instruction of the same Mercury. We have restored Horus’s name from the Egyptian idiom as **Mesramuthisis** (which others corruptly call *Mephramuthisin*), as if to say "born from Misra (or Osiris) and the mother Isis."

As to which those Obelisks were, although it cannot be determined with certainty, we are led by no small conjecture to believe they were by no means among the larger ones. As usually happens, the first beginnings of things take their origin from small starts rather than great ones. In succeeding times, as the pride and magnificence of the Kings grew, they erected larger and larger ones—not so much for the sake of displaying the **Hieroglyphic** <term>Hieroglyphic: "sacred carvings," the symbolic writing system of ancient Egypt</term> teachings, as out of an ambition to acquire glory among posterity through the magnitude of insolent masses of stone. It seems likely, therefore, that the first Obelisks were from those we place in the lower class, such as the **Macuteo**, the **Medicean**, the **Matteiano** <note>original: Mahutæus, Mediceus, Monticælius. These are smaller obelisks brought to Rome from Egypt.</note>, and others like these surviving in Rome. For the identity of the characters, the similarity of the doctrine hidden beneath them, and the likeness of the characters themselves clearly demonstrate that all these were made at the same time; they seem to have been like a set of multiple copies of a first, new doctrine. Since the substance of the stone was extremely hard, and in those early times arts had not yet reached such perfection, it was difficult to work...

# CHAPTER VIII. BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

It seems likely that they began with small obelisks; until the art of sculpture, advanced by frequent practice, finally stimulated the magnificent Kings to quarry ever larger and larger stones. Pliny records that Misraim—or what is the same, Mitres or Mesres—was the first author of this undertaking: (*Near Syene in the Thebaid is found the Syenite stone, which they used to call "pyropæcilon" <note>original: "pyropæcilon" - a Greek term for red-spotted granite</note>. Kings once vied with one another to make beams from it, calling them Obelisks, and they were consecrated to the Divinity of the Sun. The physical form of the obelisk represents the Sun's rays, and this is signified by its Egyptian name. The first of all to institute this was Mesres* (for so the Vatican manuscript has it) *who reigned in the City of the Sun, being commanded by a dream; and this very fact is inscribed upon it.*) This is consistent with what I find among the Arabian historians concerning the first institution of Obelisks; for they say, as was clear from the citations above, that Mesram was the first who erected Obelisks, which his son Mesramuthisis, whom they call Nacraus, advanced with wondrous works. For thus speaks Salamas Ben Kamdaathi, in the book which he calls the *Garden of the Wonders of the World*:

<margin>Misraim was the first erector of Obelisks.</margin>
<margin>Pliny, book 36, chapter 8.</margin>

<note>original Arabic: "وقال الاول جبار ابن مصر ملك اسمه ذفراوس..."</note>
*King Mesra, whose name was Nekraus; he lived in the land with the natives of his Kingdom; and in the place of Agabak <note>likely a corruption of a geographical name</note> Mesra built a City, which he called Mesra after the name of his father, and he inhabited it, placing various artistic things within it; he also erected Columns, upon which he carved every beautiful Science.* Which City of the Sun this was, which City was Mesra, and at what time these were founded, will be declared more fully in their proper places. It suffices for us to have shown in this place that Misraim and his son Mesramuthisin, under the instruction of Mercury <note>The author identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Roman Mercury</note>, were the first erectors of Obelisks; and the Obelisks which they erected were among the smaller ones, such as are seen today in Rome, equal in both size and the style of their characters; of which kind are those we have designated as the Mahutean, Medicean, and Monticelian.

Following their example, thereafter not only Kings but also Priests everywhere applied their minds to similar Obelisks, adorned with a similar form of mystic characters: inasmuch as these served not only for the knowledge of secret matters, but also in the place of amulets to fortify the fatherland against the incursions of evil, as is shown more fully in its own place. However, the antiquity of those times has begrudged us the knowledge of who these Kings were; until finally, after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, when the whole Kingdom was shaken and as if destroyed by the calamitous death of the Egyptians in the Red Sea, the later Kings, anxious to restore the Kingdom to its pristine splendor and magnificence, labored by every means to restore the religion, sacrifices, and letters handed down by Mesra and Mercury; with the Priests, who had preserved the secret method of writing until then, diligently bringing their help to this task.
<margin>The Priests also erected some of the smaller Obelisks.</margin>

<header>CHAPTER VIII.</header>

## ON THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS.
### SECTION I.
*Concerning the Obelisks erected by Sothis and his son Ramesses.*

The first King, therefore, after the death of Moses—who, once Egypt had been restored to its former magnificence, ruled over the whole with the highest power—was Menuphtha. Eusebius calls him Amenophis, Josephus calls him Menophis, Africanus calls him Amenophten, and the Arabs call him Omer. We, more truly according to the Egyptian language, call him Menuphtha or Monupta, as if you were to say "God of Memphis." <note>The author is attempting to etymologize the royal name Merneptah using Coptic or reconstructed Egyptian roots.</note> He was a man of great spirit and a most fierce defender of ancestral traditions. After a reign of 40 years, he departed this life and left the governance of the Kingdom to his son Sothis, so named after Mercury, whom the Egyptians call Sothis or Sothis. <note>original: "Sothis vel Sothis"</note> Now, *Sothis* is a celestial star which we call the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note>; we have shown more extensively elsewhere that Mercury was admitted into heaven under the title of this name on account of his sagacity and the variety of his inventions necessary to the human race.

Therefore, the son of Menuphtha, named Sothis after this deity, was in no way inferior to his father in greatness of soul. He entered into his reign approximately two hundred years after the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, according to Eusebius, specifically during the time of Ehud and Othniel, the Judges of the people of Israel. <note>The author is synchronizing Egyptian dynasties with Biblical chronology from the Book of Judges.</note> Eusebius also corruptly calls him Zethus or Zethos, a word which differs little from Sothis. Thus, equipped with knowledge, authority, and power, and with the help of the Priests, he revived the hieroglyphic learning handed down by his predecessor Sothis (or Mercury-Mesra) by engraving it upon eight obelisks, which he erected in On, or the City of the Sun <note>Heliopolis</note>, together with his son Ramesses.

Pliny calls the King who erected these obelisks *Sothis*, though it appears as *Sothis* <note>original: "Sothis" vs "Sothis" - likely a note on a specific spelling variant like 'Sothis' vs 'Sothis' or 'Sothis' vs 'Sothis' in the Latin manuscript tradition</note> due to a fault of the transcribers, who could easily change the letter. However, since I doubted this, I thought it necessary to consult the manuscript copies of Pliny preserved in the Vatican Library. In these, I detected a manifest error; for in that place, instead of *Sothis*, I clearly found the name *Sothis*, which I remember Mercatus also observed later. And these are the obelisks, two of which were brought to Rome, while the remaining two stayed in Alexandria in Egypt. His son Ramesses was the coadjutor of the Kingdom, as we have demonstrated in the history of this obelisk; Theophilus calls him Sethossos, Josephus calls him Sethosis, but we more truly call him Ramesses <unclear>son of</unclear> Sothis, which according to the Egyptian language signifies nothing other than "son of Sothis." <note>The author is conflating the names Seti and Ramesses, interpreting the suffix as a patronymic.</note> He is recorded to have erected the aforementioned obelisks together with his father, as Pliny testifies in Book 36, Chapter 8.

But concerning the labor of both Kings, let us hear the words of Pliny: *Afterward,* he says, *other Kings also in the aforementioned City [erected them]: Sothis, four in number, forty-eight cubits in length; and Ramesses, under whom Troy was captured, [erected] forty cubits: namely, four others.* Thus we have here eight obelisks: four by Sothis, and just as many by Ramesses Sothisos—that is, the son of Sothis. What sort of obelisks these were, however, can be determined by no means except through the material and the theme they contain, and by the measure which...

# CHAPTER VIII.
### BOOK I. ON THE ORIGIN

Authors provide a measurement appropriate to each. Thus, Sothis, together with Ramesses, completed 8 Obelisks, some of which had a height of 48 cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm; Kircher is calculating its conversion here.</note>. When these are broken down into palms—assuming one cubit equals two palms—the height for each of Sothis's Obelisks is 96 palms. However, since some are said by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist and author.</note> to have reached a height of forty cubits, these, when converted into palms, will give a length of nearly 80 palms each, if you subtract a few. Although Pliny attributes 4 to Sothis and 4 to Ramesses, we nevertheless find that all were erected by both through a common and shared administration. Let us see, therefore, whether we can find the builders of each through the consistency of the measurements.

Certainly, to begin the matter sagaciously, I first took the exact measurement in palms of all the Roman Obelisks. And I found indeed that the **Pamphilian Obelisk** <margin>The Pamphilian Obelisk was erected by Sothis.</margin>—for the sake of which we are undertaking this entire Work—reaches a height of nearly 74 palms. To this, the **Barberini** <margin>Barberini.</margin>—that one, I say, which Cardinal Francesco Barberini <note>A powerful patron of the arts and sciences in 17th-century Rome.</note> redeemed for a certain sum of money from Curtius Saccoccia, in whose vineyard it was hidden after being dug up from the Circus of Aurelian in the Verano field—corresponds most closely in length compared to the others, if not exactly equal; although the base, consumed by the greed of time <note>A poetic way of saying the base was eroded or weathered away.</note>, prevented me from finding an exact measurement. Since, therefore, I have found no other among the Roman Obelisks of this measurement, I assert, convinced by a not improbable conjecture, that these are two among the remaining eight which Sothis once erected with Ramesses.

But as the measurement reported by Authors is uncertain, I would not wish anyone to trust it too much. For Authors have handed it down only from the reports of others, which is shown to be true by the measurements of the Roman Obelisks reported by Pliny; these least correspond to the measurements found by me with the greatest diligence (as will be said later), as most people measure the height of Obelisks either by eye, or including the pedestals or the ornaments placed on the peak. Nor have I found the tenfold proportion <note>The classical architectural rule that an obelisk's height should be ten times its width.</note> to be exact in all of them, with the proportion in various cases falling short of or exceeding the truth. 

But to the point: the remaining two either stayed in Egypt or, buried in the earth by the length of time, have escaped the notice of posterity. That these are almost similar, both in size and in the learning <note>Referring to the "hieroglyphic wisdom" or inscriptions.</note> they contain, will be seen when we begin the explanation of each. Of the remaining Obelisks, I show that two were brought to Rome and the rest remained in Alexandria in this way: There were some Obelisks, according to Pliny, forty-eight cubits long, which, as has been said, when converted into feet <note>original: "pedes", though he previously used palms; he likely uses the terms interchangeably for units of measure here.</note>, make ninety-six palms. Since, indeed, two of nearly this size remain among the others, we conjecture that they are the same ones Sothis once erected in Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in Egypt, a major center for obelisks.</note>, as no others of this size are seen in Rome—unless the proportion of the base to the height has deceived me, which is not so accurate in all of them. 

For the former, the **Campus Martius Obelisk** <margin>The Campus Martius Obelisk was erected by Sothis.</margin>, still lies hidden under the ground and serves as the foundation for neighboring buildings; however, one can reach a view of it through the underground cellar of a certain carpenter, which, together with the inscription...

Regarding the remaining two still surviving in Alexandria, an Arabic Geography taught me in the following words:
<margin>Others claim the Sallustian Obelisk is 60 palms; we found this by proportion.</margin>
<note>original Arabic: "الذي ولهت..." This passage describes two square stones in Alexandria, tapering at the top, with specific measurements in rods and spans.</note>
"There are in Alexandria two obelisks, namely square stones, whose higher parts are *narrower* than the lower ones, and their *length* is five *reeds* <note>original: perticarum</note>: the base indeed on every side or face is ten *palms*, and the *circuit* is forty *palms*." For thus the Arabs determine this measure: a *Kim* is a reed consisting of 20 *palms* <margin>Kim: a measure used by the Arabs of 20 palms.</margin>; therefore, 5 multiplied by 20 makes exactly one hundred *palms*, the height of the two obelisks which are still found surviving in Alexandria. These, above all others, harmonize with the proportion of the base to the height suggested above, where we said that the side of the base in almost all obelisks is a tenth part of the height; which is clearly evident in these two mentioned obelisks. For since the sides of each are ten *cubits* <note>The author likely means palms here to maintain his math.</note>, their height will necessarily be one hundred *palms*; which the five *reeds* or canes show, each of which is 20 *palms*. Since, therefore, Pliny says that Sothis <note>Seti I</note> with Rameses <note>Ramesses II</note> made four obelisks out of eight, each of forty-eight *cubits*—that is, ninety-six *palms*—the two Roman ones will be shorter than the two Alexandrian ones by not a few *palms*. Since this discrepancy kept me perplexed for a long time, I finally noted that the Egyptians established the mass of the whole obelisk from the base to the tip of the pyramidion as one hundred *palms* long, but we, in the Sallustian and Campus Martius obelisks, computed only 96 *palms* from the base to the pyramidion: since the pyramidion in said obelisks is four *palms*, those added to 96 will constitute exactly a height of 100 *palms*. And thus those four Sothisian obelisks will all have, as it were, the same height of 100 *palms*; since no others are found more equal to these, these are to be judged by probable conjecture to be those obelisks which, according to Pliny, Sothis erected in the City of the Sun <note>Heliopolis</note>; but more on these at length in the history of the Pamphilian Obelisk.

Diodorus narrates that they were erected by him <note>Referring to Sesostris, a legendary king of Egypt</note> in these words: *He added moreover two Obelisks of hard stone, each 120 cubits high, upon which he described both the magnitude of his empire and the multitude of his revenues, as well as the nations he had subdued.* Pliny, however, asserts that one of these was moved to Rome by Augustus and set up in the Campus Martius <note>The "Field of Mars," a public area in ancient Rome</note>, being 116 palms high. Since, therefore, the Obelisks of Diodorus said to be erected by Sesostris are 120 cubits, these, when converted into palms, would give a height of 222 feet—namely, one hundred and twelve palms longer than those reported by Pliny. From this, it must be concluded either that a significant error has occurred, or that Pliny’s Obelisk is by no means the one that Sesostris erected. Furthermore, Diodorus asserts his were erected in Thebes, while Pliny asserts his were in Heliopolis. *Moreover, the one which Pliny asserts was erected by Augustus in the Campus Martius as being 116 palms, I have found to be only one hundred palms; tossed about by various conjectures, I finally concluded that I consider that subterranean Obelisk in the Campus Martius, whose remains are still visible from a certain wine cellar, to belong by no means to Sesostris, but to Sothis, as I have shown at length a little earlier from its dimensions.* I believe Pliny, or rather the scribe before him, was deceived by the similarity of the names Sochis and Sesostris and wrote one for the other. That the Obelisks of Sesostris remained among the ruins of Thebes, and were not moved at all—whether due to the magnitude of their mass or other causes—I gather from the description of the Arabs. For the author of the *Garden of the Wonders of the World* says that two columns of immense magnitude are seen in that same place, the first of which stands one hundred cubits from the base to the summit; the other is of such vast magnitude that, being impossible to move from its place, it has hitherto defied all human labor. ...they say, of which one is recorded to have a height of 100 cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note>, and a circumference of 40 palms: which number perfectly fits the proportions of Egyptian Columns alone, <margin>they were-</margin> but not likewise those of Obelisks, whose height we have shown above to be ten times the side of the base. To this is added that Diodorus asserts there was described upon them the magnitude of the Empire of Sesostris, and the multitude of tributes, and similar things regarding his achievements; which can or should by no means be said of Obelisks, as we shall show at length in the following pages; since on Obelisks only the greatest secrets, known only to the Priests and the leaders of the Kingdom, were accustomed to be engraved; whereas on Columns alone the public affairs and the deeds of Kings were inscribed in a language and characters known to all. It is indeed clearly evident that those Obelisks reported by Diodorus were by no means Obelisks, but Columns; and it has already been shown in the preceding pages that the Obelisk erected by Augustus in the Campus Martius was not the work of Sesostris, but of Sothis or some other, whatever Mercatus <note>Michele Mercati, author of a 1589 treatise on obelisks.</note> may say; unless perhaps we say that Sesostris, besides Columns, also erected Obelisks, which, as it is not inconsistent with the greatness of his spirit, I would not easily deny.

->§. V.<-
### Concerning the Obelisks erected by Pharaoh *Momphercur*.

After Sesostris followed Pharaoh Momphercur, whom Herodotus calls Pheron; Eusebius, Amenophis; others wish him to be the son of Sesostris. Following his father's example, he erected the largest Obelisk of all after the Ramessaean one, although it is smooth and destitute of hieroglyphics; this is the one which Sixtus V <note>Pope Sixtus V, who relocated several obelisks in Rome in the 1580s.</note> moved from the Vatican Circus, where Gaius Caligula and Nero had placed it, and erected in the Vatican Field before the Church of St. Peter, in an undertaking to be remembered in all ages. The name of the first builder was Momphercur, that is, "ruler of Memphis," which is indeed the same as Amenophis, or Monuphtha, that is, <margin>Memphis.</margin> the Deity of Memphis. For *Non*, or even *Mes*, or *Monph* in the <margin>Egyptian-</margin> Egyptian language signifies *Memphis*, as we have taught in the *Chronography of Egypt*; while *hercur*, <margin>begin-</margin> as is evident from our *Egyptian Dictionary*, signifies *ruler*. Hence <margin>ing</margin> Eusebius corruptly rendered this name as *Nephercheres*, which, with a few letters changed, is brought back to its genuine origin in this way: *Mephercher*, or *Monphercur*, as if it were said *Mephercheres*. Pliny calls him *Nonconius*, also a corruption, as are all similar names; yet it is not so remote from our etymology of the name *Monphercur* that it cannot be traced back to it.

First, it reads: *Out of all of them, one was made in imitation of that which Noncorius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*

Second, thus: *Out of all of them, it was laid down in imitation of that which Nuncoius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*

Third, thus: *Out of all of them, one was broken in imitation of that which Noncorius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*

Fourth: *Out of all of them, it was broken in its softness, which Noncorius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*

Fifth: *Out of all of them, it was broken during the construction of that which Nuncoius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*

Sixth: *Out of all of them, one was completely broken during the construction, which Noncorius, son of Sesofidis, had made.*
<margin>Various readings regarding the erection of the Obelisk by Noncorius.</margin>

If the true meaning is that of the first manuscript, it follows that Pliny’s report is false—namely, that this Obelisk was not erected by Noncorius, but by someone else. The meaning of the second manuscript is as difficult to grasp as it is rightly to be rejected as a fabrication. The third manuscript suggests that several Obelisks erected by Noncorius were broken during the business of erection, which contradicts Pliny. The fourth shows that the Obelisk was of a brittle material and therefore broken, which can be said for no logical reason. The fifth and sixth openly assert that it was shattered during the work of erection itself, an opinion which we accept as more probable. For that this Obelisk was broken in its upper part is clearly shown not only by the signs of a manifest rupture but also by the very proportions of the Obelisk; since its length is by no means ten times the side of the base, as is found in all other Obelisks. Indeed, if there is any most brilliant proof, it is that of a rupture made in the upper part of the Obelisk. For since the base of the said Obelisk is found to be 12 palms, its height—according to the tenfold proportion which the lowest width of Obelisks has to their height—should be 120 feet. Since its height is now found to be only 108, according to the proportion common to all Obelisks, the broken part was necessarily 12 palms high. That it was broken during its first erection is clear from the words of Pliny: *broken during the construction*; since no...

## CHAP. VIII.
None of the other remaining Kings' obelisks suffered a fracture during their erection except for this one of Noncorius <note>likely a variation of Menkaure or Nuncoreus</note>; which he seems to report as a matter worthy of record. For it was shown above, regarding the obelisk of Rameses, with what great diligence the Kings acted in the erection of obelisks; for it is said (according to the testimony of Pliny) that so the architects might act more cautiously and the work might rise uncorrupted, the King bound his own son to the summit, so that the imminent danger to the Royal Offspring might ensure the integrity of the obelisk. As for the fact that Herodotus and Diodorus assert that the obelisks erected by Noncorius were one hundred cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm</term> high, this is either an error or must be understood such that the hundred cubits are counted from the lowest base of the obelisk (which they usually made proportional to the height) all the way to the apex. However, as with many other things, I judge this passage in the aforementioned authors to be corrupt.
<margin>Momphercur: when he erected the obelisks.</margin>
Furthermore, from the beginning of the reign of Sothis until the beginning of the reign of this King Monphercur <note>original: "Monphercur"</note> there are 154 years; 99 years from the beginning of the reign of Rameses; and 33 from that of his father Sesostris. These times fall roughly in the year 1237 after the Flood, and nearly the 34th or 45th year after the destruction of the City of Troy. And this Noncorius was the first who was an erector of a smooth <note>original: "rasi", meaning unpolished or blank</note> obelisk, whereas all preceding Kings erected "lettered" <note>inscribed with hieroglyphs</note> obelisks. This might seem strange to some, since at that time hieroglyphic learning flourished greatly, and the most powerful Kings excited the minds of the Priests toward the promotion of studies with the greatest promises. However, concerning smooth obelisks and their mysteries, we shall speak at length in the following sections.

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER VIII.</header>

## ON THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS.

Anyone who has examined the chronologies of the ancients more precisely will see that these claims can in no way be consistent. For most authorities establish Amasis <note>Amasis II, a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty who reigned shortly before the Persian conquest.</note> as the last King, and maintain that he reigned in such a turbulent time that he could not have applied his mind to thinking about obelisks, let alone erecting them. Added to this is the fact that at that time the hieroglyphic doctrine, being as it were near its end, had lost much of its ancient dignity and no longer flourished; indeed, there were very few even among the Priests who understood it exactly. This was due to the outrages of the foreign Ethiopian Kings who ruled Egypt, during whose Dynasty the Monarchy of the Egyptians was transferred to the Persians, and the Wisdom handed down by the Ancients almost perished. How, therefore, Senneferteus, the last of the Kings, could have erected this Obelisk in such a short time and amidst such great disturbance of affairs, I do not see.

When I saw that the aforementioned things could not agree with this narrative of Pliny, and that I could not avoid inextricable difficulties, I was tossed about by this tide of doubt. Finally, having consulted all of antiquity, I discovered that this Obelisk was erected not by the last King Senneferteus, but by King Plammirtaos. Furthermore, I knew that the nature of the names given to Egyptian Kings was such that they were mostly composite—as is evident in the names Mesramuthifis, Sothofis, Manuphra, Monphercur, Simendes, and others, as will be shown from the origin of the Egyptian language in our *Egyptian Chronography*. I finally grasped that "Senneferteus"—for so it is read in the Vatican manuscript of Pliny—was a name composed of "Plammos" and "Amirteus," as if you were to say "Plammirteus"; and thereafter it was corrupted, as are all other names of Kings, into "Senneferteus" or "Semmiferteus." Certainly, Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian from the 5th century BCE.</note> openly calls the third King of the 23rd Dynasty "Amirteus."

According to our Egyptian Chronology, this King lived about 1527 years after the Flood, around the beginning of the Olympiads and the founding of the City <note>Rome, traditionally founded in 753 BCE.</note>; and about 340 years from the reign of Sesostris. And this Plammirtaos, or Semmiferteus, at that very time when the hieroglyphic disciplines were flourishing most highly in Egypt, erected that Obelisk in Heliopolis. Augustus later moved it from there and erected it in the Circus Maximus. After its second fall, it was dug out from there and Sixtus V <note>Pope Sixtus V (r. 1585–1590), famous for re-erecting several ancient obelisks in Rome.</note> erected it before the Flaminian Gate, or the Church of the Blessed Virgin, commonly called *del Popolo*, where it stands as a remarkable sight 110 palms high.

Hence I wonder what came into Pliny's mind when he asserted its height to be 120 feet; if that were true, it would already surpass the Ramesseum Obelisk. But anyone who reads Pliny attentively will find that he has failed in many similar matters. All these things will be demonstrated by us at length from the fragments of Oriental Writers; therefore, it will suffice to have merely indicated these points. What truly should be thought concerning the interpretation of this Obelisk made by Hermapion and cited by Ammianus Marcellinus will be decided specifically in its own place in the following sections.

### SECTION VII.
#### Concerning the Obelisks erected by Simarres, Aphries, and Nectabis.

<image-desc>Large initial capital H</image-desc> Following this Nuncoreus <note>original: "Nuncorium"; likely referring to a legendary Pharaoh, sometimes identified with Amenemhat or a successor of Sesostris</note>, other Kings followed much later in time: Simarres and Apries (or more correctly Vaphrius) likewise erected smooth <note>original: "rasos"; meaning unpolished or lacking inscriptions</note> obelisks. Thus
<margin>Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 9.</margin> Pliny says: *There are also two others, one placed by Simarres, the other by Eraphius (read Vaphrius or Aphries), without inscriptions, forty-eight cubits high. According to Strabo, one of these was placed at the Mausoleum by Claudius; later, Sixtus V had it moved to the Esquiline Hill and erected before the Church of the Blessed Virgin, conspicuous for its lack of inscriptions, while the other remains buried beneath the Church of St. Roch.* There was also another smooth one erected by King Nectabis,
<margin>The other in the ruins of the said Mausoleum, Pliny, cited location.</margin> about which Pliny writes: *At Alexandria, one of 80 cubits was set up by Ptolemy Philadelphus, which King Nectabis had cut out plain; it was a much greater task in the transporting and setting up than in the cutting.* Some record that it was brought down on a raft by the architect Satyrus. And a little later: *Six such were cut in the same mountain, and the craftsman was gifted fifty talents.* This obelisk, however, was placed in Arsinoe by the aforementioned King as a gift of love for his wife (who was also his sister), Arsinoe. From there, a certain Maximus, Prefect of Egypt, because it was an inconvenience to the shipyards, transferred it to the forum after cutting off the tip, intending to add a gilded peak, which he later abandoned. Truly, who
<margin>That Aphries was also a King.</margin> these three Kings—Marres, Eraphius, and Nectabis—the erectors of the smooth obelisks, were, is a matter of great controversy among chronologists. Leaving each to his own opinion, we say that Smarres was the same as Simarres the Ethiopian, whom we place first in the 26th Dynasty, making him nearly a contemporary of Manasseh, King of Israel, and Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome</note>. For since he was a foreigner and not skilled in hieroglyphics, he nevertheless wished to erect an obelisk so as not to be inferior to his predecessors, but did so without inscriptions. Eraphius, however—whom we, following Eusebius, call Apries, and others more correctly Vaphrius—was the second King of the same Ethiopian Dynasty and erected another obelisk without inscriptions; according to our chronology, this falls in the time of the Prophet Daniel. Nectanabus, whom Herodotus calls Necho and we, following Eusebius, call Nectao, was the third King of the Ethiopian Dynasty,
<margin>Why the Ethiopian Kings erected smooth obelisks.</margin> by whom Jehoahaz, King of Israel, was killed in the 746th year after the founding of Rome. It is therefore clear that all the erectors of smooth obelisks, except for Nuncoreus, were of Ethiopian origin. This is evidenced by the fact that they erected obelisks without inscriptions; it appears either that the Priests considered that their secret literature should not be revealed to foreign Kings (for reasons we shall disclose elsewhere), or that the Kings neglected it as something they were incapable of understanding, being content with only the silent, mysterious form of the obelisk. There are those who say that King Vaphrius, cited shortly before, lived in the time of Solomon; letters are circulated by Pineda and Salianus from Solomon to Vaphrius, and from the latter to Solomon, which I have thought should be included here.

## King Solomon to Vaphrius <note>Also known as Pharaoh Hophra or Apries</note>, King of Egypt and friend of his father, Greetings.

**Y**ou know that by the benefit of the highest Divinity I have received the Kingdom from my father David, by whom I was commanded to build a Temple to God, the Maker of heaven and earth; at the same time, I ask you by letter to send to me men and craftsmen from your Kingdom who may devote their labor to me until, as is fitting, I have accurately completed all things as I was commanded.

## The Response of King Vaphrius to the letter of Solomon.

**A**s soon as I read your letter, I both took great joy in my soul and celebrated a festive day with my entire army and people, because you have received the Kingdom from the best of men and one most approved by such great Divinity. Moreover, because you request men and craftsmen from us, I have sent eighty thousand of them to you, whose native soil I am also pleased to indicate to you. 10,000 are counted from the district of Sebrubide, 10,000 from Mendes and Sebennytos, 10,000 from Busiris, Leontopolis, and Athribis; you shall see to it that they are abundantly supplied with whatever things are necessary, partly so that no disturbances are stirred up among them, and partly so that, the building being finished, they may return safe and sound to their own people. But these things are *incidental* <note>original Greek: παρέργως (parergos), meaning a secondary matter or digression</note>.

**F**inally, we embrace the view that Vaphrius, the erector of the Obelisk, flourished in later times, as is more consistent with the histories.
<margin>The multitude of Obelisks in Egypt.</margin>
The reader has thus seen up to this point how the Hieroglyphic discipline, promoted by Misraim <note>The biblical name for Egypt, here personified as a founder</note> under the authorship of Mercury <note>The god Thoth, often identified with Hermes/Mercury as the inventor of writing</note>, and the custom of erecting Obelisks was promoted at all times; not only by Kings, who applied their minds only to erecting the larger ones, leaving the care of erecting the smaller ones to the Priests and other men conspicuous in dignity. It is established that this custom grew so strong that there was scarcely any place in Egypt so small that it was not adorned with Obelisks. And these are the things which we thought should be put forward concerning the first Erectors of Obelisks, so that the series of times might correspond in every way to the propagation of the Hieroglyphic discipline. From these things it will be clear that the Erectors of the rare <note>or "few remaining"</note> Obelisks were from the final 26th Dynasty of the Ethiopians, the last of the Egyptians, as the Priestly disciplines gradually verged toward ruin, and the magnificence of Kings and the ardor for promoting sacred letters was extinguished. Having seen the first Erectors of Obelisks, the logic of order now seems to require that we also treat the second Erectors, who were the Emperors of the Romans, so that we may proceed *methodically* <note>original Greek: ἐμμεθόδως (emmethodos)</note> in our work.

§. I.
->Concerning the Obelisks of Augustus erected at Rome.<-

<margin>Cambyses occupies Egypt and destroys everything.</margin>
In the year 189 from the founding of the City <note>original: "ab V.C." (ab Urbe Condita), referring to the traditional founding of Rome in 753 BCE; however, the author's chronology here likely refers to a different era or contains a printing error regarding the specific date of the Persian conquest.</note>, Cambyses, King of the Persians, having seized Egypt by the violence of arms, turned everything upside down. First, raging against the monuments of Religion, he set fire to the temples, overturned the altars, and slew the Priests. He scorched the Obelisks with fire and flame so severely that even now they bear the scars of the glassy flames as traces of the committed cruelty and savagery. This immense slaughter of Egypt was soon followed by the almost total destruction of the priestly disciplines; and this miserable face of devastation endured <margin>Augustus occupies Egypt and erects Obelisks brought from Egypt in Rome.</margin> until the times of Octavian Augustus. In the eighteenth year of his Empire, after Egypt had been reduced under the power of the Roman people, Augustus—having heard various reports from many men concerning the magnificent works and monuments of the ancient Egyptians, and being himself a man of exalted mind and ardently desiring to imitate the deeds of the ancients—took care to bring two of the larger obelisks which were found intact from Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in Egypt.</note> via the Nile first to Alexandria, and then here to Rome, so that he might bring both novelty and ornament to the Eternal City. The first of these, formerly erected in Heliopolis by King Psammetichus (corruptly called Senneferteus), he erected again in the *Circus Maximus*, and, emulating the ancients, dedicated it to the Sun. The other he established in the *Campus Martius* <note>The "Field of Mars" in Rome.</note>; it had first been erected in Heliopolis by King Sothis (whom some call Zethus, or as others will have it, Sesostris), and its traces still appear through a certain chamber or subterranean crypt. And this is that most celebrated Obelisk which served as a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> to show the hours by shadows upon a vast area inscribed with bronze lines and laid out by Manilius the Mathematician.

<margin>Pliny.</margin>
But let us hear the very words of Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 10: *And to the Obelisk which is in the Campus <margin>The Campus Martius Obelisk designates the hours.</margin> Martius, the Divine Augustus added a marvelous use for detecting the magnitudes of days and nights by the shadows of the Sun. A stone pavement was laid out according to the magnitude of the Obelisk, so that the shadow would be equal to it at the sixth hour of the day at Rome, and would decrease and increase again day by day through rules (which are enclosed in bronze); a thing worthy of knowledge and secondary to genius. Manilius the Mathematician added a gilded ball to the apex, so that the shadow would be collected into itself at the summit, whereas the apex otherwise would cast scattered increments; the reasoning, as they say, was understood from the shadow of a human head.* *This observation for nearly thirty years now <margin>The Obelisk no longer shows the time correctly 30 years after its erection.</margin> has not been in agreement, whether because the course of the Sun itself is discordant and the heaven changed by some reasoning, or because the entire Earth has shifted somewhat from its center (as I hear is detected in other places), or by tremors of the city having twisted the gnomon in that place only, or by floods of the Tiber having caused a settling of the mass, although the foundations are said to have been cast into the earth to a depth equal to the height of the object.*

And since many have for a long time requested an account of this work, I shall lead into it a little more extensively for the sake of the curious. And before all else, three types of hours must be demonstrated by us in this sundial <note>original: "horologio" - while it can mean clock, in this context it refers to the massive solar sundial of Augustus</note>. Second, the length of the shadow considered according to the reckoning of different seasons and hours. Third, the actual form of the sundial. The type of sundial was undoubtedly that ancient one which all the ancients used; which divides each day and night of the entire year into twelve equal hours, whether they be long or short; this is called by moderns the sundial of unequal hours <note>also known as "temporal hours," where the length of an "hour" changes depending on the season</note>, not because the hours compared to a single day are unequal, but because the hours of this shadow-measuring device <term>Sciaterici: a Greek-derived term for an instrument that tells time by shadows</term> compared to different days of the year are unequal. For here in Rome, the shortest daylight arc of nine hours was formerly divided into twelve equal hours; and the longest daylight arc of fifteen hours was likewise divided into twelve equal hours; hence it happened that the twelve hours of the shortest daylight arc were, as it were, twice as small as the twelve hours of the longest daylight arc. Hence the individual hours of the Southern daylight arcs were all smaller than the individual twelve hours into which the Northern arcs were divided, until at last they were equalized at the equinox; and in this consisted the inequality of the ancient hours; which must also be understood regarding the nights. But the sixth hour, of which Pliny's text speaks, always showed the midday hour, at which moment the shadow of that day was at its minimum, which, as in other sundials, grew continuously from sunrise until noon, then decreased toward sunset by the same proportion by which it had grown. How much shadow it would cast at individual hours, you will learn from the following table, in which you will find the quantity of the shadow with the Sun positioned in Cancer, Aries, or Libra, and Capricorn. <margin>Description of the Sundial in the Campus Martius; its pointer was an Obelisk.</margin> Therefore, the Obelisk in the Campus Martius was erected by Augustus for this reason: so that what he had dedicated to the Sun might be assigned to exhibiting the Sun's operations; this, from the demonstration of the authorities above, gave the length of the gnomon or Pointer from the horizontal plane up to the highest point of the Sphere, which the astronomer Manilius (celebrated at that time for his knowledge of mathematics) placed upon the summit; the Obelisk itself, or the ray, contained—as was evident above—a length of nearly one hundred palms, to which if one adds the height of the pedestal <note>original: "abaci"</note> upon which it was founded, which in the time of Pope Julius II was uncovered in the Campus Martius and found to have a height of seven feet. According to Mercatus, an eyewitness, these when resolved into palms give nearly twelve palms, to which if the three-palm Sphere is added, the whole Obelisk from the horizontal plane to the final limit of the gilded Sphere will give 115 palms, and this is the total length of the Obelisk, or gnomon, by which the hours were shown for each day; which having been exactly explored, we will necessarily also have the form of the entire sundial. Consequently, the twelfth hour could not be determined on this sundial. Therefore, the first hour of this sundial was Hour I, and the last of the day was Hour II <note>The author likely refers to the 11th hour here, as the 12th is sunset</note>, which, when the Sun was positioned in Cancer <note>The Summer Solstice</note>, had an Obelisk shadow of 61 parts and 44 minutes—based on the Obelisk itself being 12 parts. If the equinoctial shadow of the 1st and 11th hours is doubled, you will have 1072 palms, the required length of the sundial. The meridian width, however, will be 212 palms. All of these things we have deduced by mathematical reasoning from the previously known size of the gnomon, so that no one may doubt the truth of the matter further. <margin>The shadow on the sundial at sunrise or sunset was infinite.</margin>

The Sundial in the Field of Mars was therefore necessarily seen in the following form: its meridian line F E, contained between the tropics A F B and C L D, was 222 palms; while G H, the length of the sundial, extended to a space of 1072 palms. The numbers contained within the spaces A C and B D indicated the lengths of the days and nights which those curved arcs displayed. For the shadow of the Obelisk, falling upon one of those seven arcs, showed on the sides that the day or night was as many hours long as the number assigned to it indicated. For example: the shadow falling precisely on the arc A F B noted that at Rome the day was fifteen hours and the night nearly nine. If, however, it fell on the equinoctial line G H, it indicated a day of twelve hours, equal to the night, and so on for the rest. The lines intersecting the arcs demonstrated the position and order of the "ancient hours" <note>Unequal hours where the day is always divided into 12 parts regardless of season</note> which the ancients used (as shown above, and as we have treated most fully in the *Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>A reference to Kircher's own famous work, "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae"</note>). These lines, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note>, who had observed it accurately, were made of bronze strips embedded in the horizontal floor, providing a beautiful spectacle for those looking down from a higher place. # ON THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS. CHAPTER IX.

§. I. I.
### *Concerning the Obelisks of Gaius Caligula Caesar.*

<margin>The Obelisk in the Vatican Circus erected by C. Caligula.</margin>
Gaius Caligula Caesar the Magnificent, following the example of Augustus's daring, set his mind toward achieving immortality through a similar feat of magnificence. Thus, after various monuments of grandeur—circuses and gates—he decided to erect an obelisk greater than all those that had been seen in Rome at that time. Skilled architects were therefore dispatched to Egypt, and they selected the largest obelisk they could find to serve as an ornament for the City of Rome. This one was deemed more worthy than the rest, having been originally erected by Momphercur <note>Also known as Amenophis or Rameses</note>, otherwise known as King Sesostrides of Egypt; a subject treated at length in the preceding pages. Having placed this upon a ship of marvelous architecture constructed at Alexandria for this purpose (which will be discussed more fully in the following), he brought it to Ostia. There, the ship—as if having properly fulfilled its duty—was submerged to lay the foundations of the harbor, with a tower built over it. This obelisk, through the laborious hauling of many men, was brought into his Vatican Circus (which he had begun to build not long before) in the year of our salvation 42, in the third year of Gaius's reign. He erected and dedicated it in honor of Augustus, his grandfather, as a testimony of his grateful spirit, as the inscription testifies, which reads as follows:

> TO THE DIVINE CAESAR AUGUSTUS, SON OF THE DIVINE JULIUS,
> AND TO TIBERIUS CAESAR AUGUSTUS, SON OF THE DIVINE AUGUSTUS,
> CONSECRATED.

<margin>Measurements of the Vatican Obelisk.</margin>
The first pedestal <term>Abacus: a flat slab or pedestal base</term> placed upon the foundation was of white marble, 4¼ palms high; this was followed by a support made of Thebaic pyrite—or as it is commonly called, red granite—4¼ palms high, which was placed beneath another pedestal thirteen palms high, surrounded by a molding <term>cimatio: a decorative architectural molding</term> of four palms of the same pyrite; this finally supported a last pedestal of eleven palms. Above this, resting upon four astragals <term>astragalos: small supporting blocks or moldings, here likely the bronze lions</term> of gilded bronze 1¼ palms high, the obelisk was finally erected, measuring 113½ palms. Thus, the entire obelisk from the horizontal plane to the summit, which a gilded ball adorned, was 152 palms high. In the general destruction of Roman monuments brought about by the Barbarians, this one was spared above all others—whether out of reverence for its mass, the resistance of its solid structure, or for other reasons. Later, Pope Sixtus V had it moved from its original station and erected in the Vatican Field before the portico of the Basilica of St. Peter the Apostle, dedicating it to the Holy Cross; where, even to this day, it offers itself to be seen, not without the admiration of all, as a model <note>original Greek: τυπωμα (typoma) - a form, model, or impression</note> of ancient magnificence.

## §. III.

### ->*Concerning the Obelisk of the Emperor Claudius.*<-

<margin>The Claudian Obelisks erected at the Mausoleum of Augustus.</margin>
After the death of Gaius Caligula, the helm of government was held by Claudius, a kinsman of Augustus, a magnificent man intent on perpetuating the memory of his predecessors and relatives. When he saw that extraordinary Mausoleum <note>The massive circular tomb of Augustus, still visible in Rome today.</note>, constructed with unheard-of magnificence by Augustus in the Campus Martius <note>The "Field of Mars," a public area of ancient Rome.</note> to serve as a burial place for himself and his descendants, he judged that it should be adorned—among many other ornaments—with two obelisks, even though they were plain <note>original: "rafis," meaning smooth or without carvings.</note>. He did this to demonstrate his gratitude toward his ancestor and to perpetuate the memory of his parents through these monuments. And although nothing is found among the historians regarding this effort by Claudius, it is clearly evident that no one else besides him erected them. This is because <margin>Strabo, Book V.</margin> Strabo, a contemporary of Augustus, described the Mausoleum of Augustus with the greatest exactitude but made no mention of obelisks. <margin>Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII.</margin> Ammianus Marcellinus, however, expressly says they were erected after the time of Augustus. Let us hear his words: > *Succeeding ages transported others, of which one was erected in the Vatican, another in the gardens of Sallust, and two in the monument of Augustus.* <note>original: "Secutaque ætates alios tranftulerunt..."</note> This Mausoleum of Augustus was erected in the Campus Martius near the bank of the Tiber, next to the Flaminian Way, in that place where now the illustrious church of St. Roch <note>San Rocco</note>, built from its ruins, is seen. The obelisks were plain and without any hieroglyphic sculpture. The first of these, dug out from the subterranean ruins, was moved by Sixtus V to the Esquiline Hill and erected in front of the Liberian Basilica (or St. Mary Major) facing the Montalto gardens. The other remains to this day among the ruins. Furthermore, both obelisks—without the supports, pedestals, and without the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk.</note> which was six palms in length—measured 60 palms. Including the supports and pedestals (or what is the same, from the horizontal plane up to the pyramidion), the entire mass rose to a height of 96 palms. <margin>The Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> Another obelisk, remarkable for its hieroglyphics, is thought to have been transported from Egypt by this same Emperor Claudius and erected in the gardens of Sallust <note>Horti Sallustiani</note> as an ornament for that most pleasant of places, which was decorated with magnificent buildings and trees of every kind most pleasing to the sight. <margin>Measurement of the Ludovisi Obelisk.</margin> At the present time, this lies broken into two parts in the Ludovisi gardens. We found its total length to be 66 palms, excluding the pyramidion (which, being buried in the earth, denied us an exact measurement); its width at the base was 6 ½ palms. We conjecture elsewhere that the entire mass, including the pedestals and moldings <term>astragals: decorative curved moldings</term>, was 81 palms. Whatever the case, the measurements of the obelisks reported by the ancients do not correspond to ours at all, whether because many took the height only by eye, or because they considered them together with the pedestals and moldings; I leave this for others to consider. Hence, let the curious reader be persuaded that the argument by which we stated above that the Pamphilian, Veranian, Campus Martius, and Sallustian obelisks are of Sothis <note>Referring to a specific Egyptian astronomical or royal lineage theory held by the author.</note> is drawn not so much from the measurements, which are uncertain among authors, and least of all from my measurements...

### §. IV.

*Concerning the Obelisk of the Emperor Antoninus Caracalla, and the forty-four other Obelisks brought to Rome.*

Regarding the Obelisk of the Emperor Caracalla <note>The "Pamphilian Obelisk," now located in the Piazza Navona</note>, formerly in the Hippodrome and recently erected by Innocent X in the Circus Agonalis <note>Now known as Piazza Navona</note>, which we have titled the "Pamphilian," since we have provided a particular account in the history, we shall not dwell longer upon it here. Regarding these, however, he remains silent; we believe that these were all of the lowest class, transported from Egypt by Emperors or private persons whenever the opportunity arose to ship larger ones, serving as ballast for the ships. For since we see so many columns, <term>abaci</term> <note>The flat slab on top of a column capital</note>, and <term>cippi</term> <note>Small pillars used as landmarks or funerary monuments</note> brought from the Thebaid <note>The region of Thebes in Upper Egypt</note>, it is probable that those small, lettered <note>inscribed with hieroglyphs</note> obelisks were sought out and selected above all else for the adornment of the City of Rome. But since we have dealt more extensively with these and other similar obelisks above, lest we create nausea in the reader by tedious repetition, let us move on to other matters.

### §. V.

*Concerning the Obelisk of Constantine the Great and the Emperor Constantius.*

Constantine the Great, intending to make Byzantium (which was thereafter called Constantinople after his name) equal to Roman magnificence, while erecting temples, circuses, and amphitheaters, also turned his mind to the erection of obelisks in the Circus constructed at Byzantium, lest he should seem to have yielded in greatness of soul to his predecessors Augustus, Caius <note>Caligula</note>, and Caracalla.

Architects having been dispatched to Egypt to find an obelisk worthy of the greatness of soul of so great an Emperor, while surveying everything, they finally discovered at Thebes the largest of all that had ever been made in Egypt. It had been left behind by predecessors, whether out of reverence for the sacred pledge or out of despair at the mass to be moved from the site. This they tore away from its place at enormous expense and, having placed it upon beams, soon brought it down the Nile to Alexandria. But as the labors of men are uncertain, so the death of Constantine followed and utterly interrupted this arduous undertaking. Meanwhile, the Empire having been divided among his three sons, Constans, Constantine, and Constantius, Constantius finally, having entered into peace with the King of Persia, intended this one thing: that with his enemies subjected and his brothers now deceased, he might acquire the whole Roman Empire, which had been divided among many, as subjugated to himself...
