## CHAPTER IX.

Constantius <note>Constantius II, son of Constantine the Great, reigned 337–361 AD</note> acquired [the empire], but at last, after Magnentius was conquered and slain by his successful arms, he stood supreme.
<margin>He applies his mind to erecting an Obelisk</margin>
And so, with affairs succeeding according to his wishes, Constantius, through victories and triumphs, entered Rome—which he had never seen before. When he had thoroughly contemplated that incomparable magnificence of his predecessors, shining forth in the most exquisite structure of buildings, in the wonderful architecture of the Amphitheaters, and in the mysterious construction of the Circuses, he was seized by a desire to perpetuate his own memory among posterity by some not dissimilar monument, and to hand down his Name. > And since the fawning flatterers, according to their custom, were noisily dinning into Constantius's ears that when Octavianus Augustus had transferred two Egyptian obelisks from the city of Heliopolis—one of which was placed in the Circus Maximus and the other in the Campus Martius—he [Augustus] had not dared to touch or move this recently brought one, terrified by the difficulty of its magnitude; let those who are ignorant learn that the ancient prince [Augustus], though he moved some, passed over this one untouched for this reason: because it was dedicated to the Sun God as a special gift, and fixed within the shrines of a magnificent temple which could not be touched, it stood out like the peak of all things. From these it is clearly evident that the Obelisk was first erected in Egypt by Ramesses, and finally torn away from Thebes by Constantine the Great. It was moved to Alexandria with the intention that it should serve as an ornament for the New Rome, Constantinople. However, due to the death of Constantine, it remained at Alexandria until the twenty-second year of the reign of Emperor Constantius. He, famous for his victories, finally had the same moved to Rome and erected it in the Circus Maximus as a symbol of Caesarean magnificence and power. Later, Sixtus V dedicated it to the Holy Cross, as has been said, after it had been buried by the injuries of time and excavated in the Lateran Field.

## ->CHAPTER X.<-
*Concerning the mechanical powers by which the Obelisks were first erected in Egypt, and then moved to Rome and erected in the same place.*

Although I have found almost no clear account of this mechanics among the ancient historians, nevertheless, because some not-obscure traces of such a great undertaking remain among the Arabs, as well as in Pliny, Marcellinus, Diodorus, and Herodotus, I trust that we shall finally attain the truth of them by following the scent.

<margin>Instruments and machines by which the Obelisks were erected.</margin>
Two things, therefore, must be considered in this place: First, the nature of the instruments with which the Ancients used to erect their Obelisks; Second, the nature of the ships they used to transfer them to the appointed place. Both matters must be discussed in this final chapter of this book.

And first, indeed, I suppose that from the beginning of the world there has always been some kind of knowledge of Mechanics, which I teach most extensively and by profession in my *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. For mechanics is, as it were, innate to us, so that we can perform hardly anything in our natural and locomotive functions without it.

<margin>The mechanical art is innate to us.</margin>
And we rightly assert that the lever <note>original: "vectem"</note>, as the simplest of all mechanical instruments, has been in use at all times; for who does not know that when we wish to break something, we apply the thing to be broken by a certain natural instinct either to our knees or to another resisting object as a <term>hypomochlion</term> <note>The fulcrum or pivot point of a lever</note>, and then...

...we know that if we take hold of both ends and bend it, a break naturally follows. Or when we wish to lift a weight, we do not attempt it by the service of hands alone, but we accomplish the mechanical operation by placing wood or iron underneath <note>The author is describing the principle of the lever</note>. Indeed, since certain weights could not be moved by the help of a single lever alone due to violent resistance, the multiplication of the lever—either through screws or pulleys—was introduced, so that this multiplication might in some way equal the strength of a multitude of men.
<margin>A column erected by Semiramis 152 feet high.</margin>
I suppose, secondly, from histories that approximately two hundred years immediately after the Flood, men turned their minds toward most magnificent works. For they devised both the Tower of Babel and performed other works which, if similar things were to be performed today, would cast even the most enlightened and skilled architects of this age into despair. Who would not marvel at that column which, according to Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>, was cut from the mountains of Armenia and erected in Babylon by Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Babylon</note>, being 152 feet high and 24 feet wide? Who does not know of the other arduous labors of this woman performed in Babylon? In Egypt, truly, it is certain that the erection of the Pyramids, built not long after, has deservedly drawn all posterity into admiration. Yet these could by no means have been finished without great mechanical skill. Also, the remarkable multitude of Obelisks which they erected can only be understood by one who has some knowledge of this faculty, showing how much mechanical knowledge they possessed from the frequent exercise of these works and long-standing experience. Herodotus writes that an entire temple was cut from the rock by the Egyptians, conveyed down the Nile, and erected at Heliopolis. He says the Egyptian Labyrinth was constructed with such architecture that he himself, seeing things so unusual and greater than human genius, remained suspended in *infinite admiration*—these are the author's own words. Indeed, the machines which the Egyptians used in constructing the Pyramids are described at length by the cited Herodotus in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>; these I gladly omit for the sake of brevity. Let one also read the wonders concerning the Temple of Jupiter and the monuments of Babylon, which far exceed all industry of human genius, as related at length in *Clio* <note>The first book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>.
<margin>Herodotus: An entire temple from the rock.</margin>
From these things it is clearly evident that the ancients not only possessed a most exact knowledge of the machines they used in erecting such unheard-of works, but also, incited by the ambition for marvelous works and relying on daily experience, they devised new ones. Thus, I would dare to say that we in these centuries have not yet reached such great industry of genius. Certainly, whatever wonders Archimedes performed in moving ships from the shore, it is so clear he drew them from the Egyptians that he himself admits it; indeed, he learned many things from the custom and conversation of Egyptian architects, whose cultivation was held in such esteem among posterity that nothing seemed denied to his genius.
<margin>Archimedes learned mechanics from the Egyptians.</margin>

# CHAPTER X. BOOK I. ON ORIGINS
<page-num>88</page-num>

Since the direct application of force to erect even the largest obelisk can scarcely accommodate a hundred men; indeed, such a great multitude would be more of a hindrance than a help. Therefore, these tasks were accomplished with the aid of ingeniously devised machines, through which the multitude was distributed into various groups by means of ropes and cords proportioned to the work, now lifting the immense weights after they were drawn together, now lowering them once raised. The Arabs <note>The author likely refers to medieval Arabic traditions or commentaries on Egyptian ruins</note> assert that they were raised by instruments equipped with a multiplication of wheels and cords, which Herodotus also affirms. However, as for Pliny’s statement that the Ramesside Obelisk <note>original: "Obeliscû Ramelleum"</note> was erected with the help of twenty thousand men, I do not think it should be understood as if all of them applied themselves to this one obelisk at once; but rather that so many men were occupied at different times and places—partly in cutting it from the veins of the cliffs, partly in shaping it, moving it to the designated location, and finally in erecting it. It is probable, therefore, that they chiefly used <term>capstans</term> <note>original: "Ergatis," a vertical-axle winding machine</note> and <term>pulleys</term> <note>original: "Trochleis"</note>, which the history of the Arabs seems to confirm. A capstan is nothing other than a <term>wheel-on-axle</term> <note>original: "peritrochium"</note> turned on its axis, by the multiplication of which the mechanical power was increased almost to infinity.

<margin>Mechanical methods for building the Pyramids.</margin>

In raising the huge stones of the Pyramids, Herodotus writes that they proceeded with this ingenuity: they employed a bifurcated wooden machine, to which a pulley was attached at the upper part to wind the ropes; outside the base of the Pyramid another machine was applied—which I interpret as a capstan—around which the other end of the cord was wound. This machine, rotated by the labor of men or animals, gradually placed the stone in its designated spot. They moved the first bifurcated wooden machine to each individual step of the Pyramids, and thus completed the work step by step, so that there were as many machines as there were steps of the Pyramids. But let us hear the words of Herodotus himself from Book 2, where he discusses the Pyramid of Cheops as follows: *"This Pyramid was built in the form of steps, which some call 'altars' and others 'little stairs.' After they had first made it in this fashion, they lifted the remaining stones with short machines made of wood, raising them from the ground to the first row of steps; when the stone was upon this step, it was placed on another machine which stood on that first step, for from there it was then drawn to the next row upon another machine. For there were as many machines as there were rows of steps; or perhaps there was only one machine, which, being easy to carry, they transferred to each row whenever they moved a stone."*

<margin>The method of transporting excavated obelisks to their designated location.</margin>

Furthermore, the architect of the obelisk which Ptolemy Philadelphus set up at Alexandria—which was 80 cubits long and had been cut from the Theban rock by King Nectanebo—was Satyros, as Pliny reports. The method by which they placed it on a ship and transported it to Alexandria was this: first, they dug a very deep canal, which began beneath the obelisk itself and extended all the way to the Nile. When this was subsequently filled with the waters of the Nile, it resembled not so much a canal as a great river. In this canal (or rather river), according to the testimony of Callixenus the Phoenician in Pliny's writings, they arranged two very large ships, which they loaded with stones to such an extent that the weight of the stones was twice as great as the weight of the obelisk. This having been done, the ships...

<header>AND THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS.</header>

# AND THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS.

## CHAPTER X.

...they would drive ships, firmly lashed together, with their ends hanging over both banks, beneath the Obelisk itself. Once the ships were brought under the Obelisk by this ingenious method, <margin>By what ingenuity the Obelisk was brought to Alexandria.</margin> they gradually lightened the vessels by unloading stones until they took up the hanging weight of the Obelisk. Having received it in this manner, they would lead it through a canal into the Nile, and then to Alexandria, just as is clear from Figure 2 of Diagram 1 inserted here, from which you will easily perceive the *logic* of the entire machine. But to confirm what has been said, let us bring forth the words of *Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 9.* <margin>Pliny, Book 36.</margin> *At Alexandria*, he says, *Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II, a Greek King of Egypt (3rd century BCE).</note> set up one of 80 cubits, which King Nectabis <note>Likely Nectanebo I or II, the last native Egyptian pharaohs.</note> had cut clean; it was a much greater task in the transporting and setting up than in the cutting. Some report it was brought on a raft by the architect Satyrus; Callixenus says it was brought from the Nile by a canal dug all the way to where the Obelisk lay. Two broad ships, loaded with foot-long blocks of the same stone—doubled in proportion to twice the measure of the weight—were placed so that they went under the Obelisk as it hung by its ends on both banks; afterwards, the ships, lightened by the removal of the small blocks, took up the weight of the monument. Six such were cut in the same mountain, and the craftsman was gifted fifty talents. Thus says Pliny.* By similar industry, undoubtedly received from their ancestors through tradition, others among their descendants used these methods in transferring great masses. Some maintain that the Obelisks were moved to their designated places at the time when the inundation of the Nile in *Egypt* was at its height; <margin>At the time of the Nile's flood to reach the location.</margin> for with the waters rising high above the lands, nothing was easier than to carry the load outside the channel of the Nile to any flatter place in *Egypt*. If, however, necessity required it, they rolled the Obelisk to the place of erection placed upon *Chamulci* <note>A type of heavy sled or low carriage used for moving massive weights.</note> or Cylinders. Once placed there, first upon a solid foundation—which for the most part was a rock or native stone—they finally erected the Obelisk with the help of capstans and pulleys, protected against all violence by beams, wooden planks, and padding made of wool, hay, and straw; consult *Oedipus* <note>Refers to the author's own work, "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," a massive study of Egyptian lore.</note> for a more exact treatment of all these matters.

As for which ships the *Roman* Emperors used for bringing Obelisks from Alexandria to Rome, *Pliny and Ammianus Marcellinus* report. The ship of *Augustus Caesar*, by which his larger Obelisk had been brought, was preserved at *Puteoli* <note>Modern Pozzuoli, a major Roman port.</note> as a kind of miracle for a perpetual memory of the feat, but it finally perished in a fire by some accident. <margin>The ship that brought the Obelisk of Augustus perished in a fire at Puteoli.</margin> Indeed, the ship by which *Gaius Caligula* had brought that obelisk of *Nuncoreus* <note>A legendary Egyptian king mentioned by Herodotus and Pliny.</note>—more wonderful than any ever seen on the sea—stopped at *Ostia*, where it was submerged by *Claudius*, the successor of *Gaius*, <margin>The ship that brought the Obelisk of Nuncoreus was submerged at the mouth of the Tiber in Ostia to serve as a tower.</margin> to serve as the foundation for a tower built over it in the harbor, which lasts to this day; so says *Suetonius in the Life of Claudius, and Pliny* in the place cited.

The ship, however, by which the *Ramesside* Obelisk was brought by the *Emperor Constantine*, was a raft constructed of beams and huge trees, equipped with three hundred oars according to the testimony of *Marcellinus*. The main mast, besides others on which the sails were spread, was of such thickness that two men could not put their arms around it. Indeed, the form of the ship—as far as can be perceived from the acts of the Emperor *Constantius*, *Ammianus Marcellinus*, and other histories—was of the form which we show here in *Illustration 1, Figure 1.*

<page-num>91</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER X.</header>

### ON THE ERECTION OF OBELISKS.

Authors mention three ships by which Obelisks were carried from Egypt to the City <note>Rome</note>: Pliny mentions two, and Ammianus one. They all testify that these ships were of a truly great and prodigious size. Regarding the ship in which Augustus brought his own Obelisk into the City, it was dedicated at the permanent shipyards of Puteoli <note>modern Pozzuoli</note> as a marvel, though it was later consumed by fire, as was mentioned shortly before. Concerning the ship in which Gaius Caligula transported his Obelisk to Rome, Pliny reports the following among other details: *The fir tree used in the ship was of particular admiration; this ship, by the order of the Emperor Gaius, brought the Obelisk now standing in the Vatican Circus, along with four blocks of the same stone to support it. It is certain that nothing more wonderful than this ship has ever been seen on the sea.*
<margin>Pliny, Book 16, Chapter 40.</margin>
*One hundred and twenty thousand measures of lentils served as ballast. Its length took up a great part of the side of the port of Ostia; for it was sunk there by the Emperor Claudius, with three moles <note>massive stone piers</note> as high as towers built upon it using Puteolan dust <note>volcanic ash or pozzolana, used to make hydraulic concrete</note> which had been brought there.* Indeed, in Book 36, Chapter 9, he writes: *The Divine Claudius, having preserved for some years that ship which Gaius Caesar had used for the import—the most wonderful of all that had ever been seen on the sea—sunk it at Ostia for the sake of the harbor, after towers made of Puteolan dust had been constructed upon it.* These accounts agree with the report of Suetonius in his "Life of Claudius": *He constructed the harbor at Ostia,* he says, *by drawing out an arm on the right and the left, and by placing a mole at the entrance where the sea was already deep. To make the foundation of this mole more stable, he first sank the ship in which the great Obelisk had been brought from Egypt; he then piled rocks upon it and placed a very high tower on top, modeled after the Pharos of Alexandria, so that ships might direct their course by its fires at night.* It is likely that the Emperor Constantius constructed his own ship—which we have shown here as described above by Ammianus Marcellinus—according to this same standard. The aforementioned authors indicate in express words that it was of the type of ships they call "Rafts" or "Crates" <note>original: "Rates, sive Crates"</note>.

Finally, if anyone desires to know the method observed in the Obelisks erected by Sixtus V, let him consult the machines employed by the architect Domenico Fontana, which have been most elegantly engraved in copper and described at length by Mercati, Bargaeo, and others.

And these are the matters concerning the history of Obelisks which I thought should be presented first, so that the sequence and order of our interpretation may rest upon a more solid
->foundation.<-

# AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

## C H A P T E R I.
### Concerning the first founder of Hieroglyphics, and their construction.

<image-desc>Large ornate initial capital 'A' with foliage design.</image-desc> **A**round the three-hundredth year after the Flood <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>, there came forth from the lineage of Canaan a certain man, most highly adorned with all the gifts of Nature. It seemed that Nature had fashioned him for the investigation of the secrets of arts and sciences and the invention of new things, while God had given him to the world’s empire so that the human race might be instructed through his help. The Arabs name him *Idris*, from the Hebrew *Hadores* <note>original: "Hadores"</note>, which denotes a distinguished disputant; the Phoenicians, according to *Eusebius* (Book 1, Chapter 7), call him *Tautus*; the Egyptians call him *Thoth*—corruptly, for more truly it is *Phthath*, that is, the God of Gods; and the Greeks call him *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>Thrice-Greatest Hermes, a legendary figure credited with ancient wisdom</note>. For he was a man of the sharpest intellect, of admirable subtlety, and a tireless searcher of nature. Having been instructed in the state, customs, institutions, and disciplines of the primeval world through constant conversation with both Noah and his sons and grandsons, he made it his sole aim to cultivate the disciplines handed down by the primeval Patriarchs and, once cultivated, to consign them to posterity. Since he was a most curious investigator of all things that could be grasped by human intellect, he traveled through various places of the world, spurred by a curiosity for investigating things, so that he might confirm his acquired store of knowledge through varied use and experience.

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>This Trismegistus was the instructor of hieroglyphic literature.</margin>

Meanwhile, as the human race increased immensely in the East, Noah—or *Janus* himself <note>The author identifies the biblical Noah with the Roman god Janus</note>—departed to the Western regions of the world to found new colonies for his family. Joining himself as a companion to these "Janigenae" <note>descendants of Janus/Noah</note>, he [Hermes] arrived in a short time at such a great knowledge of things that he was held in admiration by all as if he were a divinity. Thus, when quarrels and wars arose among the natives in the Hesperian kingdom (which was afterwards called *Italy*), he himself, having acquired a vast amount of gold, traveled to Egypt. There, *Misraim* <note>The biblical name for Egypt, here treated as a person</note>, the second son of the lineage of Ham, was ruling far and wide. Since Misraim was also a most curious investigator of things and kept his mind perpetually intent on great and arduous matters, it happened quite opportunely that he was supported by the help of one who was his equal in greatness of soul, but who surpassed him in science and the light of intellect as much as the Sun surpasses the stars. Therefore, that Prince should rightly be judged fortunate who, while desiring great and grand things, is joined by such a man who both desires and is able to achieve grand things; for who does not see that great and arduous things are born from such a union? To this King *Misraim*, therefore, *Idris* was joined as his supreme Scribe and Counselor. When he discovered that the science handed down from the Fathers had been defiled by various superstitions and was degenerating into manifest idolatry, he thought seriously within himself how he might oppose such an evil of idolatry. And because he saw that it was by no means advisable to reveal so many and such deep mysteries of divinity and Nature to that people—whom he knew to be both most addicted to superstitions and incapable of the said sacred mysteries, and who would undoubtedly turn them into various abuses—he recognized...

# BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION

<page-num>94</page-num>

From this point, he directed his mind toward the construction of more recondite Symbols <note>original: "Symbolorum"; here meaning sacred signs or hieroglyphs</note>, through which he displayed the mysteries of divinity and Nature in such a way that they were manifest only to the wise and those of clear understanding. To the common people and the unlearned <note>original: "Idiotis"; used in the classical sense of private or uneducated persons</note>, he left nothing accessible to their grasp beyond mere wonder, having protected his work from the reading of the profane by his supreme genius. Yet, lest he should seem to have reserved the secret of such a great undertaking for himself alone, and so that the ingenious architecture of these Characters might be passed down to posterity, he established an order of Priests. These were most select men, excellent in talent and skill in sublime matters, who alone had hope of access to the Kingdom. To them, he delivered the rule of the hidden arts and sciences he had prescribed, and he bound them by an oath never to communicate these things to anyone outside their own Order. He also prescribed the rule for sacred rites, sacrifices, and whatever pertained to the worship of GOD, so that by this means the delivered doctrine might be carried out by a uniform institution throughout the entire Kingdom.

And because he saw that books composed of fragile and corruptible material—such as papyrus, bark, and the leaves of palm trees—could by no means escape the greed of time, and those made from metal plates could easily be moved elsewhere to the detriment of the Kingdom or be lost; lest the doctrine delivered by him slip from memory, he adapted the hardest Stones, remarkably fortified against all injuries of time, into mysterious shapes. Thus, by a wonderful method of his own invention, he engraved them so that they might stand for eternity. Because of these things so nobly performed, he was held in such great admiration by all that they revered and worshiped him not as a man, but as a certain Deity <note>original: "Numen"</note> fallen to earth. They called him now Taut, Thoth, or Thoyth; sometimes Hermanubis, and now Marcorptha—that is, the GOD of hidden inquiry.

And this is that first Mercury Thrice-Greatest <note>original: "Mercurius termaximus"</note>, most celebrated in all the monuments of writers: a most consummate Theologian, Philosopher, Physician, Magician, and Mathematician. He was the first inventor—or perhaps the restorer of those things existing before the flood—of Letters; not only the common ones used for everyday letters and the writing of books, but also the doctrinal and symbolic ones, as will be seen in the course of this Work.

But, lest anyone be able to say that the things I have narrated thus far with such confidence are either fabricated by my own wit or entangled in false conjectures, one thing remains: that everything we have asserted be confirmed and established by the all-encompassing doctrine of Writers. This we promise to do in this place, with the assistance of God's grace.

It has already been shown from the preceding pages that this Mercury flourished about three hundred and thirty years after the flood—that is, in the times of Abraham—conspicuous for all science and a perfect knowledge of things, and that he traveled through various places of the world. The Hebrews first assert this; thus in the book entitled *The House of Melchizedek* <note>original Hebrew: "Beit Melchizedek"</note>, of which we made mention previously, which among many other things besides those cited elsewhere, has these words:

*And there went out from the house of Canaan a man, he was a great sage, whose name was Hermes <note>original: "Arash Shebe-la'ach Hadamash," a phonetic rendering of Hermes</note>, and he was the first who established the houses of study, and he was the first who found the things of divinity.*

However, the way the *Chronicle* calls him Sesostris <margin>Mercury, Sesostris, or Osiris.</margin> kept me anxious and perplexed for a long time, until at last I found in a Vatican manuscript that he was called not Sesostris, but *Siosiris*, which in the Egyptian language signifies the same as "the son of Osiris." Now Mercury, as was shown above, was sometimes taken for Osiris himself, sometimes for his son, and sometimes for his Scribe and Counselor. # CHAPTER I. BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION

> <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον μὲν οὖν..."</note> First, then, it happened that Manetho of Sebennytos, being a high priest of the idols in the Heliopolitan district for Ptolemy Philadelphus, and being skilled in the sacred dialect in which things were written, and the hieroglyphic letters which were in the inner sanctuaries of the temples, interpreted them for Ptolemy Philadelphus, both for the King and for the world, just as you have given to me to describe the first sacred books written by the high priest Hermes Trismegistus. Be favorable to me, O Lord King.

From the writings of *Manetho* of Sebennytos, who in the time of *Ptolemy Philadelphus* was the *High Priest* of the Idols which are in *Egypt*, we learn that he was taught by the oracle of the images lying in the *Syradic* land <note>A legendary land where the pillars of Hermes were said to be hidden</note>, inscribed in the sacred dialect and engraved with Sacred letters by *Thoth*, the first *Hermes*. These were interpreted after the *Deluge* <note>original: Cataclysmum</note> from the sacred Dialect into the *Greek* language with hieroglyphic letters, and *Agathodaemon*, the second *Hermes* and father of *Tat*, placed them in books in the inner sanctuaries of the *Egyptian* temples. He announced these to King *Philadelphus*, the second *Ptolemy*, who writes thus in the book *Sothis*:

> To the great and venerable King *Ptolemy Philadelphus*, *Manetho*, Scribe of the Sacred sanctuaries of *Egypt*, by race a *Sebennyte* and an *Heliopolitan*, to my *Lord, Greetings*. *It is necessary for us to discourse, Greatest King, concerning all things which you examine; to you inquiring, therefore, about those things which are to happen to the world, those things shall be manifested which I have learned from the *Sacred Books* written by your forefather *Hermes Trismegistus*. *Farewell, my Lord King*.

From these things it is first evident that before the flood there was a Hermes who engraved letters and arts upon stones, which harmonizes beautifully with the tradition of the Arabs; for they say that *Enoch* was the first *Mercury Trismegistus*, the inventor of letters and arts. The second, however, was after the flood—namely, this one of ours—who delivered to posterity the mysteries of the arts which had been handed down by the first *Hermes* and engraved on stones, now veiled by the new invention of hieroglyphic literature. For thus says *Amed ben Joseph Altiphasi* in the works of *Gelaldinus*:

<margin>Amed Ben Joseph Altiphasi in Gelaldinus.</margin>

> <note>original Arabic: "وولد ليرد حنوخ..."</note>
which is: *And to Jared was born Enoch, he is Hermes, he is Idris*; and the rest, which we have cited at length from the doctrine of the Arabs on page 10. And a little later:

> <note>original Arabic: "ودرمان ابراهيم..."</note>
And in the days of Abraham there was in Egypt Hermes, who was *Idris* the second: and he was *Trismegistus*, for he was a Prophet, King, and Philosopher. Furthermore, *Philo of Byblos* teaches in these words, from the fragments of *Sanchoniathon*, a most ancient *Phoenician writer*, that *Tautus* (or *Thoth*, or *Mercury*), having been instructed in the true Religion by the first Patriarchs of the World who inhabited *Chaldea* and *Phoenicia*, organized the fabulous doctrine of the *Egyptians*—which was leaning toward manifest idolatry—and corrected it according to the rule of science:

<margin>Sanchoniathon according to Eusebius.</margin>

> <note>original Greek: "Τάαυτος, ὃν Αἰγύπτιοι..."</note>
*Tautus*, however, whom the *Egyptians* call *Thoth*, distinguished for the *Wisdom of the Phoenicians*, was the first to reduce the religion of the *Gods* from the ignorance of the *Chydaeans* (perhaps *Chaldeans*) into a scientific dignity of doctrine. *Eusebius* relates these things in almost as many words from *Philo* in Book 1 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 7.

<margin>Hermes corrects the superstitious primary doctrine of the nations.</margin>

Therefore, it is *clearly* evident from the cited sources that *Hermes Trismegistus* was none other than the one we have described: the first *Lawgiver* in *Egypt* after the flood, and the first inventor of *Egyptian characters* and hieroglyphics...

## CHAPTER II.

->On the propagation of *hieroglyphic doctrine*, and the length of time it endured.<-

After Hermes, having well deserved the gratitude of the human race, had imbued Mizraim <note>original: "Mesram"; the biblical grandson of Noah, identified here as the progenitor of the Egyptians</note> and his son Mizraim-uthisin in the disciplines of sacred things; and after he had taught them the mystical method for carving those things upon Obelisks, as was proven extensively above; the invention was first propagated by them to posterity. Posterity, stimulated by such admirable doctrine, promoted it at all times as a unique patrimony and a rich inheritance they had received. And so it happened, that whoever possessed a distinguished knowledge of these matters was an object of admiration to all; they were called "Hermes" after Hermes himself, as well as Priests and Prophets, being closest to divinity. And lest the Divine invention handed down by their predecessors become known to many, and to common men, they bound themselves by an oath that it should be communicated to no one except men of the Priestly Order, of singular talent, and those fit for the Kingdom. For they trusted that in this way both the disciplines and the Priests skilled in them would be held in greater value and estimation by all. Hence the Priests, applying themselves with the greatest zeal to the handed-down doctrine, not only propagated it, but building upon the foundation already laid, they devised more and more mystical Symbols according to the Hermetic rule, right down to Potiphar, the Priest of Heliopolis, whose daughter was given in marriage to Joseph. This man, according to the testimony of Rabbi Eliezer, was one of the Priests of Egypt who had established their seat in Heliopolis; he was uniquely devoted to philosophy and sacred disciplines, and was a man of great wisdom and the Overseer of letters. The words of Eliezer are: <margin>Priests bound by oath to suppress the doctrine in silence.</margin> <margin>Potiphar, Priest of Heliopolis, overseer of letters.</margin>

<note>original Hebrew: וְהוּא חָכָם גָּדוֹל וּבַעַל סְפָרִים מְרֻבִּים וְחָכְמָה שֶׁמֶשׁ</note>
And he was a great sage, and a master of many books, and of the wisdom of the Sun.

A great Philosopher, and Overseer of letters, and of the worship of the Sun: for Heliopolis was properly the Seat of the Priests, and the unique training ground for hieroglyphic Wisdom, which was propagated by successors after him until the time of Moses. But, as usually happens, while they were more desirous of vain glory than was proper, they led the Symbols handed down by Hermes concerning divine mysteries and the secrets of Nature into manifest superstition. From this soon arose that monstrous mythology of the Gods, the worship of brutes, and the ridiculous ceremonies of sacrifices; these things, which had been instituted by Hermes for the mysteries of divinity, emerged from them as if from a certain Trojan horse and gradually infected the whole world. To this was added the base profit of the Priests, which they obtained from the people, whom they persuaded of everything other than what had been prefigured. Hence the utterly ridiculous cult of ceremonies, hence the wailing and lamentations, hence the fables concerning Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon. <margin>Sacred doctrine handed down by Hermes turns into superstition.</margin>

## CHAPTER II.
Through Typhon and Serapis <note>Typhon was the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set; Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity</note>, demons secretly insinuated themselves into their operations, from which emerged diabolical Magic, the impiety of Oracles, the manufacture of likenesses and idols, and many other things which we have most extensively prosecuted in the first volume of our *Oedipus* <note>A reference to the author's work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>; and so it happened that *Egypt* became a public 
<margin>Egypt: a nursery of superstition.</margin> theater of superstition and the damned arts. And first indeed there emerged from there that famous sect of the Zabians, or more truly the Sabaeans, who had 
<margin>The sect of the Sabaeans: its nature and origin.</margin> their origin from a certain person of the lineage of Cush, the brother of Mizraim <note>Biblical figures associated with the settlement of Africa and the Near East</note>, who made great progress in Chaldea, where Nimrod, the son of Cush, and Ninus then ruled far and wide. From here came the worship of the fire of the sun, the moon, and the seven wandering stars <note>The seven classical planets</note>; from here the vanities of Astrology and the stars; the most fierce promoter of all these was Nahor. Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses Maimonides</note> pursues all these matters at length in the *Guide for the Perplexed*, and we have pursued this sect of the Zabians or Sabaeans at length in the first part of *Oedipus*, to which we refer the reader. These things are so true that even the sacred scriptures themselves deplore such 
<margin>Why the Hebrews instituted sacrifices contrary to the Egyptians.</margin> superstitions; and lest the Hebrews be contaminated by them, many of the better-known Hebrew Masters maintain that those precepts in *Leviticus* and *Deuteronomy* placed by Moses concerning animals and ceremonies were for no other reason than to avoid the customs and impieties of the *Egyptians*, as we have shown elsewhere. 
<margin>The worship of the Ox and other animals flourished in Egypt before Moses.</margin> For the sacred text teaches in clear words that the worship of the Ox and other animals existed before Moses; as is evident from Exodus 8: where, when Pharaoh urged that offerings and sacrifices be made in *Egypt*, [Moses] responded that it could by no means be done in these words:
> *Behold, if we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?* <note>original Hebrew: הַנּוֹבֵחַ אֶת הַתּוֹבֵחַ מִצְרִים לְעֵינֵיהֶם וְלֹא יִסְקְלוּהוּ</note>

> *Behold, if we sacrifice the animal which they themselves worship while they are watching, will they not stone us?* <note>original Aramaic: הַאֵין נִזְבַּח בְּעֵינֵינוּ אֶת תּוֹעֲבַת מִצְרַיִם לֵאלֹהֵינוּ וְלֹא יִסְקְלוּנוּ</note>
For this same reason, all *Egyptians* abominate shepherds of 
<margin>Egyptian animals consecrated to the Gods.</margin> sheep, as is said in the last verse of the 46th chapter of *Genesis*. For the Egyptians worshipped with the highest honor the *Ram*, the *Ox*, and the *Goat*—in the Ram, Hammon (or Jupiter Ammon); in the Calf, Apis; in the Goat, Priapus—as the living habitations of Divinities. Not only was it unlawful to kill or sacrifice them, but they even punished those who killed them with death, according to the testimony of Eusebius 
<margin>Rambam in the Moreh Nevukhim.</margin> Pamphilus; moreover, they lamented the dead animals with the greatest grief and wailing. To destroy this impious ceremonial worship, Moses decided it should be performed in no other way than through contrary laws and ceremonies; hence the rams, calves, and goats which the *Egyptians* worshipped, the *Hebrews* destined for death through sacrifices. Rambam describes all these things beautifully and eruditely in the book called *Moreh Nevukhim*, or the *Guide for the Perplexed*. Therefore, I shall bring forth his words at length. Each and every one according to his own providence. And he said that the Torah has already stated, according to the translation of Onkelos <note>Onkelos was a famous 2nd-century convert and scholar known for his authoritative Aramaic translation of the Pentateuch</note>, that their tradition was to worship the sign of the Ram <note>The zodiacal sign of Aries</note>. Because of this, the people of India are found to this day never slaughtering cattle at all, even in lands where they might slaughter wild goats for demons. They considered these to be abominations of fire <note>or "false abominations"</note> which are not true, as they intended in these investigations of theirs.

> *...contemplation, and music in its entirety through the use of instruments and the theories found in the arts and the paths handed down by logic. The Greeks taught the rest of the general curriculum, while others taught the sacred letters and the Chaldean science of the Hebrews; this and all mathematics he received from the Egyptians.* <note>original Greek: "θεωρίαν, καὶ μεσικὴν... μαθηματικὴν." > *Teachers*, *he says*, were immediately available to him from various places, some arriving voluntarily from neighboring peoples and the *Egyptian Districts* <note>original: "Nomis," the administrative divisions of ancient Egypt</note>, others summoned from *Greece* with great rewards. He surpassed their abilities in a short time, for with his natural brilliance he mastered things so easily that it seemed not like learning, but like *recollection* <note>A reference to the Platonic idea that learning is remembering innate knowledge</note>; and he ingeniously devised many things that were obscure even to his own teachers. *Numbers* indeed, and *Geometry*, and the whole of *Music*—*Rhythmic*, *harmonic*, and *metric*—whether *contemplative* <note>theoretical</note> or performed through voices and instruments, he received in various ways from *Egyptian Teachers*. But most especially he learned the hidden *Philosophy* described, *as they call it*, in *hieroglyphic* letters—that is, by the marks of *animals*, which they themselves worship as *Divinities*. The *Greeks* taught the other *general education* <note>original: "encycliam doctrinam," the 'circle of arts' or liberal arts</note>; from neighboring places he learned *Assyrian letters* and the *Science of the Chaldeans* regarding the heavens; but *Mathematics* he received from the *Egyptians*. *Thus says Philo.*

<margin>Mathematical disciplines were common in Egypt before Moses.</margin>
*Justin, Philosopher* and *Martyr*, disagreeing somewhat with *Philo*, asserts in his book of questions posed by the gentiles:
> *Moses*, setting aside the study of all *Mathematics*, which were then common and lowly in *Egypt*, applied his mind only to the *hieroglyphic disciplines*, which alone were then held in honor and value among them. These were not handed down to just anyone, but secretly in hidden places to the most eminent and proven men. When *Moses* had learned these, he nevertheless never said or did anything according to them that was contrary to the *worship of the one true GOD*. Nor should it be believed that *Moses*, powerful in deed and word, performed miracles by the use of *Egyptian Wisdom*, but rather that he performed his wondrous works solely by the *power of the true GOD*. *Clement* however,

<margin>Clement, Book 5 of the Miscellanies.</margin>
> in the 5th book of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromat." or Stromata</note>, *says* that *Moses*, following this custom of *hieroglyphic teaching*, secretly handed down many precepts of the *moral life* under tropical <note>figurative</note> and mystical *Symbols of animals*, accessible only to lovers of the *divine law*. Such are those rules: that one must not eat pig, nor eagle, hawk, or raven; how these are to be understood was shown a little earlier from *Rambam* <note>Maimonides, the medieval Jewish philosopher</note>. *Iamblichus*, moreover, shows in plain words that there was no other Author of all *Egyptian Wisdom*, especially the *hieroglyphic*, except *Hermes Trismegistus*; he addresses all subsequent *Philosophers* in his chapter on the mysteries. There, by the *Columns*, he indicates nothing other than the *Obelisks*, upon which that more sublime doctrine was accustomed to be engraved, which all the *Arabs* also testify to by common consent, as has been proven elsewhere.

<margin>Hieroglyphic disciplines existed before Moses.</margin>
And from these things, unless I am mistaken, it clearly stands that the *hieroglyphic disciplines* flourished long before *Moses*, namely from the times of *Mizraim* and *Abraham*, with whom their founder *Hermes* was *Contemporary*. From these men, the name of the *Pharaohs*, the *Sacerdotal Order*, and the origin of both common and scholarly letters took their beginning. Therefore, those who think that *Moses* himself was *Hermes Trismegistus*, or *Jethro*, are greatly hallucinating.

### AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

Some wish for Jethro <note>The father-in-law of Moses in the Bible</note> to be his father-in-law; those also hold a mistaken view who assert that those [hieroglyphics] were discovered by others named Trismegistus <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note> after the time of Moses. Since these claims conflict with both chronology and history, they must be rejected as inconsistent. We have, therefore, the propagation of the hieroglyphic discipline up to the time of Moses; it remains for us to continue its advancement after him. After the departure <margin>The first propagator of hieroglyphic writing after Moses.</margin> of the children of Israel from Egypt, and after Pharaoh with all his leaders and lords was swallowed in the Red Sea, the Kingdom incurred a massive disaster; thus, the passion for this discipline was somewhat interrupted until the time of Amenophis, or Menuphra. He was the first, as was shown above, <margin>Menuphra, the first promoter of hieroglyphic doctrine after Moses.</margin> who not only restored the Kingdom to its former splendor, but also endeavored to promote the sacred disciplines with the greatest zeal and fervor. This man, pondering great things in his mind, called together the Priests—in whose hands alone the knowledge of hieroglyphics and mathematics remained—and entered into a council concerning the restoration of the rites and ceremonies that had been somewhat neglected, and the erection of Temples, Obelisks, and pyramids. And when nothing remained but the execution of these decisions, he was taken by death and left the governance of the Kingdom to his son, Sothis. This man, <margin>Sothis the son follows his father's plan.</margin> mindful of his father’s great undertakings, was the first of the Kings after Moses to apply his mind to carving the traditional disciplines upon Obelisks. What he actually achieved regarding these, and which Obelisks he erected, has been discussed above in specific chapters; therefore, I judge it superfluous to repeat those things here. Upon his death, his son Ramesses succeeded him, who not only <margin>Ramesses, son of Sothis, erects Obelisks.</margin> propagated the traditional arts with remarkable study, but also erected a magnificent Obelisk, the greatest in hieroglyphic literature of all that have ever been seen. The Priests followed him, each according to his own ability remarkably promoting the Royal efforts; so much so that at no time was the study of hieroglyphics in greater bloom or value than in this century. Next succeeded, as is clear from the Chronography <note>A reference to historical timelines or king-lists</note>, King Sesostris. Because of the immense greatness of his soul, just as <margin>Sesostris, otherwise Sesostris, promotes the erection of Obelisks.</margin> he subjugated a great part of the world to his empire, so he also wonderfully propagated this study; this is evident from the Columns <note>referring to obelisks or monumental pillars</note> which we described previously, the largest of all that have ever been seen in the world. His son Momphercur, or corruptly Noncorius, followed him; he also applied his mind to the cultivation of hieroglyphics and <margin>Momphencur the son erects a massive Obelisk.</margin> labored upon an Obelisk even more massive than the others—namely, the one which we look upon with admiration surviving to this day in the Vatican Field <note>The Vatican Obelisk in St. Peter's Square, Rome</note>. Following him later were Psammirtao (or as Pliny corruptly calls him, Sennaferteus), Aphries, Psammus, and Necho, and other Kings, who themselves testified to posterity how much they valued the ancestral doctrine by the Obelisks they erected. Truly, what these Kings achieved, and concerning their Obelisks, since we have shown it most extensively in the preceding sections, I have thought it necessary to repeat them here only as a summary <note>original: "anacephalæoticas"</note>, so that the order, time, and method of the hieroglyphic propagation might be better known. This study lasted, by the propagation described, until the time of Cambyses, King of the Persians, who, having finally occupied Egypt by force, [overthrew]...

### CHAPTER III.

*Whether in succeeding ages the hieroglyphic doctrine was utterly destroyed, and whether Orpheus, Linus, Pythagoras, Plato, and other writers had knowledge of such doctrine?*

<margin>Orpheus
Linus.</margin>
It is certain that from the disaster brought upon Egypt by Cambyses, the entire hieroglyphic doctrine did not collapse so suddenly that some traces of it did not remain. For besides the fact that Orpheus, Linus, and Amphion (who were the first philosophers of the Greeks, living in Egypt two centuries after the passing of Moses, at the time when the aforementioned arts and sciences flourished most greatly) learned it perfectly through frequent conversation with the Priests and transferred it to the Greeks; it is also entirely probable that the exiled Priests communicated it to the neighboring nations of the Arabs, Phoenicians, and Greeks. This is evident from the fact that

<margin>Orpheus, a disciple of the Egyptians, was imbued with and propagated hieroglyphic literature.</margin>
the hymns of Orpheus "smell" of something Egyptian <note>A Latin idiom meaning they have the character or essence of Egypt.</note>; indeed, they exhibit the hieroglyphic doctrine so exactly through their mysterious allegories that they seem to have been composed not by a Greek, but by an Egyptian Priest. Following these men much later,

<margin>Pythagoras promoted and propagated hieroglyphic literature.</margin>
around the year of the first Olympiad <note>The first recorded Olympic Games, traditionally 776 BCE.</note>, about four years before the arrival of Cambyses in Egypt, came Pythagoras, who made the entire symbolic doctrine of the Egyptians his own by "plucking its flowers." Following him, Plato, Democritus, Thales of Miletus, Eudoxus, and Aristotle each had Priests as their masters by whom they were instructed in the Egyptian mysteries, as will be seen later. Regarding Orpheus, Diodorus reports thus:
> *Orpheus, he says, a Thracian by birth, the son of Oeagrus, surpassed all whose memory survives in learning, melody, and poetry; for he produced a marvelous poem, and being famous above others for the sweetness of his song, his fame grew so great that he was said to draw wild beasts and trees to hear him by his melody. Devoted to learning, when he had applied himself to the study of Theology, he traveled to Egypt, and having perceived the knowledge of many things there, he was considered the most learned of the Greeks, both in the ceremonies of the Gods, in Theology, and in poetic songs.*
Regarding himself, he testifies in the *Argonautica* that he was in Memphis, Egypt. Furthermore, that Pythagoras lived for a long time in Egypt with the Priests and fully drank in their symbolic doctrine is clearly shown by Eusebius, Clement of Alexandria, Diodorus, Laertius, and Malchus <note>Also known as Porphyry.</note> in his biography. <header>CHAPTER III.</header>

## AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

Claiming that all discoveries were made by *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurio"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, they inscribed their books to *Mercury*. *Mercury* presides over *wisdom* and *eloquence*; *Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus*, and many others went to the *Egyptian Priests*. The *doctrines* of this book are of the *Assyrians* and *Egyptians*, and are *from the columns of Mercury*. *Pythagoras* and *Plato* learned *Philosophy* *from the columns of Mercury in Egypt*; the *Columns of Mercury* are full of *teachings*. <margin>From the Columns of Mercury, the Philosophers of Greece drew their own ideas.</margin>

From these things it is clearly evident that all the learning of the Greeks, and especially that which is symbolic, was transferred from the *Egyptians* to the Greeks, as *Eusebius, Clement*, and others show at great length. For since *Pythagoras* and *Plato* drew their hidden philosophy from obelisks, as *Iamblichus* testifies, it is likely that the hieroglyphic doctrine still flourished at that time among the surviving priests, and that the aforementioned most curious philosophers drew a full knowledge of it from their instruction. And regarding *Pythagoras* indeed there is no doubt; since he lived with the *Priests* for many years before the arrival of *Cambyses* <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note>, during the time of the last King of *Egypt, Amasis*, and his books, full of mysteries, sufficiently indicate this; the difficulty concerns only the philosophers after *Cambyses*. But we say that even then the symbolic doctrine of the *Egyptians* did not cease, but the priests communicated it orally, in secret, to those whom they wished and judged it appropriate. <margin>After Cambyses, the sacred doctrine still flourished.</margin> Certainly, his books indicate that *Plato* was imbued with these things above all others, as will be demonstrated elsewhere. Indeed, his sublime discourses—hidden through numbers, lines, sounds, and allegories, as well as his concepts or ideas of universal things—seem to suggest nothing other than an unfolding of hieroglyphic schemes. Moreover, *Eusebius* records in Book 10, Chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel* that *Plato* flourished near the end of the *Persian Kingdom* in *Egypt*, a little before *Alexander the Macedonian*, four hundred years or a little more before *Augustus Caesar*. Furthermore, *Malchus* <note>Porphyry</note> testifies in the *Life of Pythagoras* that in *Egypt, Pythagoras* obtained as his *Master* the *Priest Oenuphis of Heliopolis*; *Eudoxus* obtained *Conuphis of Memphis*, and *Solon* obtained *Sonchis the Saite*; so that whatever secret and hidden thing occurs regarding the notion of the *Gods*, whatever is allegorical in the mysteries of their rites, ceremonies, and the worship of the *Gods*, must be judged to have flowed from the hieroglyphic doctrine (as we demonstrate most extensively from all the doctrine of the *Orientals* in the *Hieroglyphic Mystagogy* in the following book). <margin>Who the Masters in Egypt were for Pythagoras, Eudoxus, and Solon.</margin> Since these things are so, it must necessarily be asserted that the hieroglyphic doctrine carved upon the *Obelisks* always survived in the monuments of neighboring nations; not indeed displayed by the signs and sculpted figures themselves, but adorned with symbolic discourses and the wrappings of fables. For what else are those *Pythagorean* *riddles* <note>original: "gryphi"; refers to intellectual puzzles or enigmas</note> and most hidden parables, if not hieroglyphic maxims <note>original: "gnomæ"</note>, fashioned according to the *Egyptian* rule and precision? What is expressed by that life of *Pythagoras*, conspicuous for its abstinence, restraint, and silence, other than the life of the *Egyptian Priests*? What did *Plato* himself express throughout all his dialogues by his ideas, other than the theological and political ideas of the *Egyptians*? <margin>Hieroglyphic literature did not perish, but remained scattered here and there in the monuments of the Greeks.</margin>

<margin>How the Author unearthed literature that was as if lost.</margin> There is need only for labor and industry, so that through the various scrutiny of the Reader and of the Oriental languages—by whose help alone the inner shrines of the Oriental Writers and monuments are opened to us—we may penetrate them. Then, at last, like a busy bee, from all the excerpts that pertain to the matter, and having rightly compared them among themselves through the combinatory art, we may in this way restore to its wholeness the mystical body of Osiris, which was scattered by the Typhon <note>In Egyptian myth, the god Set (Typhon) dismembered Osiris; Kircher uses this as a metaphor for reconstructing lost knowledge.</note> of the injury of time. <margin>2. Wise men of the Order: <term>Asaphim</term> (Physicians/Enchanters).</margin>

<margin>The Sabaeans were expelled from Egypt.</margin> Imbued with superstitions, and having been expelled like heretics by Hermes <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-king of Egypt</note> who was then powerful in Egypt, they occupied those parts of Arabia Felix <note>The fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula</note> which face toward Chaldea. <margin>Hermes having been expelled from Egypt.</margin> These people carried about with them books in which they boasted of the more advanced doctrine of Hermes. <margin>These people were treated as heretics.</margin> They treated of Astrology, of the hidden influences of the Stars, of the making and consecration of Statues, of the institution of Oracles—or rather, the construction of speaking images—and of the powers of herbs, fruits, wood, trees, and animals, all of which they believed to be the living dwelling-places of the Gods. In these matters, if the doctrine of hieroglyphics is indeed base, it is certainly explained here most fully according to its genuine principles, even though it has been corrupted by innumerable superstitions.

Philo of Byblos <note>original: "Philo Biblius"; a Greek-speaking historian of the 1st-2nd century AD</note>, who was not a Hebrew, translated the entire description of this matter from the language of the Phoenicians into the Latin language <note>The author likely means Greek, as Philo wrote in Greek; he may be referring to the Latin translation he is currently using</note>; of whom Porphyry also makes honorable mention in the fourth book which he wrote against us <note>referring to Porphyry's "Against the Christians"</note>. <margin>Porphyry against the Christians concerning Sanchuniathon.</margin>

<note>The following Greek passage is translated below in the main body text as provided by the author's own Latin version.</note>
"Sanchuniathon, a lover of truth, collected the most ancient history of the Phoenicians, partly from the individual annals of the Cities, and partly from the writings preserved in the temples, *with a skillful and diligent wit*. He lived around the time of Semiramis, Queen of the Assyrians, and is described as having existed before the Trojan War <note>original: "Iliacum bellum"</note>, *or around that very time*. *These writings of Sanchuniathon were indeed turned into the Greek language by Philo of Byblos*, who, *dividing the entire history of Sanchuniathon into nine books*, *prefaces it immediately in the first description of the introduction*. These things being so, Sanchuniathon, a man *both most eager for knowledge and distinguished by his dexterity in handling affairs*, *since he seems to have been ignorant of none of those things which were done from the beginning that are worthy of memory*, *appears to have examined and investigated most curiously above all others the writings and inventions of Tautus*. *For he saw that Tautus was the first of all mortals under the Sun to devise the invention of letters*; *and he was the first who dared to commit memorable things to eternal memory; whom the Egyptians call Thoth, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks call Hermes*." 

<margin>The praise of Sanchuniathon.</margin>
<margin>He investigates the writings of Tautus.</margin>

Thus far Porphyry. Moreover, this Sanchuniathon wrote, according to the testimony of Philo of Byblos, the following books: *The History of the Phoenicians, in which he treats the Origin of the world; the principles of natural things; the Theology of the Phoenicians and Egyptians. Concerning the wonders of Tautus, or Mercury; concerning the inventions brought forth by him for the good of the world; concerning the institution of sacred sculptures <note>hieroglyphs</note>; and concerning the worship of the Gods.* 

<margin>The books of Sanchuniathon.</margin>

Of these, only certain few fragments have reached us; some of which I understood not long ago still remain in the Library of the Grand Duke of Tuscany <note>original: "Hetruiae"</note>. There is also in my possession a fragment of only a few pages by this Author in the Aramaic language—that is, the Phoenician language, which is almost the same as Chaldean and Syriac—or rather, translated from Philo of Byblos into the Aramaic language. It treats the institutions of the Egyptians, and touches especially upon the mysteries of Mercury <note>Hermes/Thoth</note>, in which, however, nothing so singular occurs that other Authors have not already handed down. Indeed, the great man Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc <note>original: "Nicolaus Peresius"; a famous 17th-century scholar and patron of science</note> had received this fragment through the industry of friends from the Library of Damascus, commonly called *Schàm*, most celebrated in all the East. Out of his zeal for the promotion of good literature, he wished to transmit it to me in Rome in the year 1637—namely, the last year of his life—to be interpreted.

This author is called Sanchuniathon <note>original: "Sanchuniotho"</note> <unclear>ܠܠܠܠܠܠܠ</unclear> by the Syrians, which in the said dialect signifies the same as *wonders support me*. Among the Arabs after the time of Christ, there were Salamas, Jelal ad-Din, Al-Sa’ig, and above all Abenephius <note>Likely referring to Ibn Wahshiyya or a similar Arabic hermetic source</note> and Abenuachsia <note>Ibn Wahshiyya</note>, who, by making the writings of all their predecessors their own, accurately and successfully touched upon several parts of Egyptian philosophy. By following the foundations they handed down, and sensing the first true meaning of the primeval doctrine—as if led by Ariadne’s thread <note>A classical metaphor for a guiding clue through a maze</note>—I confess I have made no small progress. For Abenuachsia, whom Rambam <note>Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher</note> often cites, was the first to translate Egyptian books into the Arabic language; by a singular providence of God, I discovered his Arabic work in Malta among the spoils of the Turks. Furthermore, after the coming of Salvation <note>The birth of Christ</note>, there flourished in Greece Plotinus, Porphyrius, his disciple Iamblichus, Dionysius the Areopagite, Justin, Origen, Tertullian, Clement, Eusebius, and Irenaeus. These men, weighing the writings of the ancients more precisely, exhibited the Egyptian doctrine—albeit in scattered fragments—with such clarity that they seem to have explained the hieroglyphic symbols themselves through the very context of their words. Various historians and philologists, as well as many of the Holy Fathers—Athanasius, Epiphanius, Lactantius Firmianus, Augustine, and Jerome—and among the Pagans, Ammianus Marcellinus, Martianus Capella, Pliny, Aelian, Solinus, Macrobius, and countless others, provided such evidence of this Egyptian wisdom in their monuments (even if sporadically) that it has greatly profited my undertaking.

<margin>The Arabs after Christ.</margin>

After these, following a long interval of centuries, came Pierio Valeriano and our own Caussin, who indeed published vast commentaries on Horapollo <note>A 5th-century author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>. However, neither of them gave a specimen of truly hieroglyphic interpretation; instead, they produced a discourse on emblems patched together from the histories of all times, rather than the actual hieroglyphic doctrine of the ancients. Finally, after these followed Lorenzo Pignoria, a man of great genius, who attempted an interpretation of the Bembine Table <note>The Mensa Isiaca, an elaborate bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs</note>; he did not entirely miss the mark, but he touched upon it so briefly that he scarcely reached the bare husk of the symbols. Herwart also published a book on the same table, in which he thinks he has unraveled the "Nautical Science of the Egyptians" recorded under the hieroglyphics of the said Bembine Table; but how far he wandered from the mark will appear shortly, when, in refuting his interpretation, I shall clearly show that it cannot possibly be consistent with the intention of the ancient Egyptians. Having followed these men only so far, the present work will testify to what I myself have achieved.

<margin>What is a Symbol?</margin>The word "Symbol" takes on the meanings of various things, according to the testimony of Stephanus <note>Likely referring to the lexicographer Henri Estienne (Stephanus).</note>; for insofar as it is derived from *to bring together* and *to join* <note>original: "τὸ συνάβειν & συνάβειν" [sic - likely intended συνάγειν/συμβάλλειν]</note>, it is the same as to collect, to unite, or to intermingle; or, what is the same, it signifies a certain collation or
<margin>Athenaeus.</margin>contribution. It can also mean a sign which men of old, according to Athenaeus, used to contribute while feasting together; the "symbol" was named from the share which each person gave toward preparing the banquet. Hence Terence, alluding to this in *The Girl from Andros*, Act 2,
<margin>Terence.</margin>says, "He gave his symbol <note>In this context, a 'symbol' was a 'scot' or a share of the cost for a communal meal.</note> and dined." Those who were admitted for free to a banquet without a contributing share were called "Asymboli," according to Giraldus in his book *On the Symbols of Pythagoras*. Furthermore, the Greeks called a ring a "Symbol," and the Latins called it a "Sign," which they used to impress upon vessels and letters to indicate that another's property should not be opened; from this, it seems that seals <note>term: *sigilla* (little seals or signets)</note> took their origin, a custom of the ancients brought down even to our own times. <margin>Plutarch on the symbol of Romulus.</margin>In the same way, Plutarch, in the *Life of Romulus*, called the sign that Romulus gave to the Romans a "symbol"; it was a sign that the opportunity for undertaking an action was at hand, when, rising up, he would gather his purple robe into his lap and then unfold the gathered cloth again. Moreover, in olden times, a Symbol was accepted for every indication, conjecture, and argument by whose aid we arrive at the knowledge of something unknown to us; thus, in the past, a ring was an indication of marriage. That is, *the nature of a symbol is to lead our mind, by means of a certain definite similarity, to the understanding of some thing that differs greatly from the things offered to our external senses; its property is to be concealed and hidden under the veil of an obscure saying.* From this comes **symbolic Theology** <note>original: "συμβολικὴ Θεολογία"</note>, whether **initiatory** <note>original: "τἀλεσιὴ"</note> or **mystical** <note>original: "μυσικὴ"</note>, which teaches the hidden meanings of Scripture and explains mysteries; of this kind also are the **Pythagorean symbols** <note>original: "τὰ σύμβολα Πυθαγορικὰ"</note> mentioned in Plato’s 8th Symposium and in Caelius Rhodiginus, book 10 of *Ancient Readings*, in the chapter where the symbolic additions to statues are described.
<margin>Mystical Theology.</margin>

Furthermore, the ancients used symbols in two ways, according to Giraldus in his book *On Symbols*. Some were explained by certain words, others were not; the Egyptians used both of these especially to explain the mysteries of Religion and Theological discipline, judging them to be worthy, and the majesty of such great mysteries to be unsuitable

if they were understood by any common person. Hence their priests indicated divine mysteries under some covered sign and the shadowy appearance of an allegorical figure, by which discipline only the priests, the wise, and those educated in philosophy were instructed. Among the Greeks, Pythagoras, a true pupil of Egyptian wisdom, especially tried to emulate these; he so covered the sentiments and teachings he wished to give under obscure meanders of words and the circuit of metaphorical speech, that he seemed to suggest his meaning only to the wise, while leaving the common Philosophers without even a suspicion of the conceived mysteries. Hence Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, speaking thus, says: *But Pythagoras especially, as it appears, being held in admiration and having wondered at those priests, imitated their method and way of proposing through ambiguities, and wove his opinions in wrappings; whence all those who either established new religions, or founded cities and laws, used this obscure and enigmatic way of speaking.* So (to say nothing for now of Zoroaster, Zamolxis, Seleucus, Dardanus, Charondas, Numa Pompilius, and other ancient Pagan philosophers) did that great Moses, the Leader and governor of the Israelite people, do among the first. <header>CHAPTER V.</header>

# AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

->He states<- that no one can deny that obscure similarities of things elevate our minds more than other matters, and therefore *they ought to be hidden from the unrefined as being dangerous to them.* <note>The author argues that complex truths are simplified or hidden to prevent misunderstanding by those without proper training.</note> Hence we see that almost all Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy is full of verbal signs and coverings for things; and Pythagoras and Plato themselves, as we said before, are believed to have been the first to translate this method of teaching from the Hebrews and Egyptians to the Greeks. For the *Egyptians were accustomed, as we shall soon* explain, to communicate sacred matters among the Priests through certain artificial letters, so that they might be kept secret from the common people, whereby they would be held in longer admiration and grasped more attentively. Whence those colossi, statues, altars, arches, and bronzes publicly engraved with the sacred letters of the Egyptians stood out as things to be looked at by everyone, but were understood only by the initiates and those schooled in hieroglyphics <term>hieroglyphics: "sacred carvings," used here to mean symbolic wisdom</term>, as Chaeremon, Horus, and many of the Egyptians have written about them. Thus Pythagoras did not think it the mark of a wise man *to display his lyre constantly, or to receive mysteries in such a way as a pig receives a trumpet, or a beetle receives a lute and ointments.* <note>A proverbial way of saying that holy things should not be given to those who cannot appreciate them.</note> Therefore he imposed silence upon his disciples, lest they reveal the secrets of divine things to the vulgar, which were to be apprehended more easily by meditation than by speaking. Whence, having embraced all parts of philosophy in three volumes—the physical, the instructional, and the political—he is said, when dying, to have commanded his daughter in his will not to publish them outside the family, or rather, not to make them public at all.

<margin>The care of the Egyptians in hiding mysteries.</margin>
<margin>In what the Pythagorean silence consisted.</margin>

But while he lived, he clearly demonstrated all that was contained therein—especially mathematics—by living voice, using no covering, only to those worthy and few in number; the rest he gave to others in parables. Therefore, speaking one way and thinking another, the same Wise man always imparted his doctrine to his followers through certain symbols, as if by memory-aids, so that in imitation of the ancients, one thing was said and another understanding was conveyed. For by him, to start from the first principles, the infinite and the "one" are put for God; numbers for incorporeal things; figures for corporeal things; harmony for mixed things; unpruned vines for filth and sins; and flour for that which is purest in life. A white rooster is the sign of one dedicated to GOD; a seat designates humility; turning around signifies prudence; and these pertain to divine matters. The following look toward private affairs and virtues: the balance scale is a symbol of justice; salt notes moderation; the public way signifies the errors of the common people. The Sun is placed in the stead of the manifest and open; a sharp sword signifies dangers; a thong, immodesty; singing, pleasure; bait, the torment of the heart; the lyre, harmony; bed coverings, sleeplessness. A fluted ring signifies grief; a boiling pot, the eruption of anger; hooked claws, robbery; a *choenix* <term>choenix: an ancient Greek dry measure, roughly a quart</term>, nourishment; sinking things, fortune; boundaries, fate. These pertain to a man regarding himself. That which follows concerns his behavior toward another. The right hand notes friendship; a black tail, false brothers; nails and hair are symbols of kinsmen; swallows signify talkative people and those who are ungratefully excessive. Bread is a symbol of true friendship; Oil, of flattery; fire, of wrath; a sword, of exasperation. A burden suggests trouble. Thus far mostly private matters: now concerning the Republic. A crown is a sign of law and governance; wood on the road, the affairs of the community; a bean demonstrates ambition; all things are symbolic, all things are figurative.

He explains it himself in this way: "Turn your eyes away from me, for they have given me wings," <note>original: "auerte oculos tuos à me, nam ipfi alas mihi addiderunt"</note> as if he wished to **insinuate the aforementioned symbol** regarding our proposal; **indeed, in many places in Holy Scripture, we see mention made of the wings of GOD, most notably in Psalms 16 and 35: "Under the shadow of your wings," and "under the cover of your wings they shall hope."** <note>original: "Sub umbra alarum tuarum, & fub tegmine alarum tuarum fperabunt."</note> Therefore, when <margin>St. Gregory.</margin> St. Gregory says that Holy Scripture, dictated by the Holy Spirit, attributes wings to GOD *metaphorically* <note>original: "ἀποττεικῶς" (apotteikos) - likely a Greek-derived term for figurative or winged representation.</note>; it was fitting that to the soul, created in the image and likeness of GOD, wings should also be added. Thus, the image might better correspond in all things to the one imagined, and the likeness to its own model and exemplar.

<margin>Abenephi.</margin> Hence, as Abenephi <note>An Arabic author often cited in early modern works on Egyptology.</note> relates, the ancient priests and philosophers—the first founders of Egyptian theology—alluding to the same symbol, placed in their symbolic and mysterious figures many such images which represented animals with human faces and winged bodies. Many of these occur in the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs, popular in the Renaissance for studying hieroglyphs.</note>, which, God willing, will be explained in their own time.

->Three winged figures. From left to right: a winged lion with a human head (sphinx-like), a human figure with bird wings and legs, and a human figure with bird wings, bird legs, and an Egyptian crown/headdress.<-

These images and figures, although they were fashioned by the ancients for no other reason than to indicate the highest mysteries; nevertheless, the unrefined and ignorant common people foolishly and unwisely worshipped them as something divine. It remains, therefore, for us to declare what a Hieroglyphic properly is.

<margin>What a hieroglyphic properly is, and its definition.</margin> A Hieroglyphic, therefore, properly derived *from "sacred" and "to carve"* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἱερᾶς καὶ γλύφω" (apo tēs hieras kai glyphō)</note> as if "by carving sacred things," is nothing other, according to the testimony of Goropius Becanus <note>A 16th-century Dutch physician and linguist.</note> in Book 2 of *Hieroglyphics*, **than a symbol of a sacred thing, carved into some material**; from which the difference between a Symbol and a Hieroglyphic appears: for all hieroglyphics are Symbols, but not the reverse. For a hieroglyphic is only a sign of a sacred thing carved into some material. Secondly, a hieroglyphic is not properly formed by speech, but is expressed only by marks, characters, and figures. For as has already been said often, the Egyptians used to compose and form their symbols with images and figures, expressing their concepts under a hidden significance and through the properties of those things. Furthermore, insofar as they were obscure and far removed from the senses of the uninitiated, <margin>The symbols of the Egyptians are similar to those of the Hebrews.</margin> the symbols and enigmas of the Egyptians were not unlike the Kabbalah of the Hebrews. Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian who wrote on the relationship between Greek philosophy and Christianity.</note> clearly supports this in Book 5 of the *Stromata*, Chapter 3, with these words: **"As far as concealment is concerned, the things of the Egyptians are similar to the Hebrew [mysteries]."**
