Thus, fashioning them from precious material, they would attach eyes and golden ears to the Gods to indicate the immensity of God, who sees and hears all things. To them, the Lion signified strength and fortitude; the Horse a noble spirit, and a man great in both virtue and liberty. The Sphinx, with the face of a human and the rest a Lion, indicated a powerful and robust intellect. Finally, the Human figure among other characters and shapes signified intellect, prudence, reason, fortitude, power, art, and industry. The Egyptians were also accustomed during certain solemnities to carry around four gilded statues of the Gods, which they called *nomasias* <note>original: "νομασιας" - likely a variant of "Comasias," referring to ritual processions</note>; two of these shone with the figure of Dogs, the second <insert>third</insert> with a Hawk, and the third <insert>fourth</insert> with an Ibis. By the two Dogs, they understood the two Hemispheres; by the Hawk, the Sun, on account of this bird’s extreme heat and its strength for killing and seizing; by the Ibis, they indicated the Moon, because its two-colored feathers, mixed of white and black, represent the face of the Moon. Others, however, wish to suggest the two Tropics by the Dogs; which are like certain dogs appointed by nature to watch and guard, preventing the further elongation of the Sun toward the South and the North; by the Hawk they show the equinoctial, and finally by the Ibis, the Zodiac.

<margin>The solemnity of the Comasias and the hieroglyphic images usually carried around.</margin>
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that nothing else was indicated by the solemnity of the Comasias than the deeds and acts of Osiris and Isis, which explanation seems more conformable to history and to the Authors; so indeed, that we may understand Osiris by the hawk, the symbol of the Sun (as will be more fully explained below), Isis by the Ibis, and by the two Dogs, Anubis and Macedon, the former of whom bore a dog and the latter a wolf on his arms <note>heraldic devices or standards</note>, according to the testimony of Diodorus. Moreover, the wolf and the dog are so similar in form and figure that many say the wolf is nothing other than a wild dog. But let us hear Diodorus speaking of these things, for he says thus in Book 1, Chapter 2:
> Osiris had two offspring unequal in virtue, Anubis and Macedon; both used distinguished arms, featuring some animal not dissimilar to their own nature; for Anubis bore a Dog as his coat of arms, and Macedon a Wolf. Because of this fact, the Egyptians hold these animals in the highest honor, and they are worshiped among the Egyptians in the forms of these living creatures.
We say, therefore, that by the procession of the Egyptians and the display of the Comasias, according to the historical sense, nothing else was indicated than the wandering of Osiris, which we described above in Section 3. For as Diodorus Siculus well notes, once the kingdom was committed to Isis, Osiris—accompanied by his sons Anubis and Macedon, and also by Hercules, Apollo, Triptolemus, and others—traveled through the whole world, in memory of which the festivity of the Comasias seems to have been instituted. Secondly, through this representation of the Comasias, it can be not incongruously understood that Osiris was destroyed and dispersed by Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set</note>, Isis seeking and gathering him again through the hawk, and through the Ibis; and through the dog, Mercury, who is also called Hermes interchangeably. For the aforementioned Diodorus testifies that Mercury was the counselor to Isis in these words:
> They relate, moreover, that Osiris, King of Egypt, having established the kingdom and permitted the care of all things to his wife Isis, gave to her Mercury, whose counsel she should use, since he seemed to excel among his friends in prudence.

<margin>Mercury is depicted as a dog-headed baboon.</margin> Among the Egyptians, the Dog-headed Baboon <note>original: "Cynocephalus"</note> was used to indicate sharpness of intellect, as he was greatly valued for his skill in both counsel and the discovery of new things. Furthermore, the fact that two dogs are carried about in procession signifies the twofold search of Isis, which history records as having first occurred through the counsel and help of the dog-headed Mercury <note>The author identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Roman Mercury</note>; first, when she sought the lost Osiris, and second, when she sought Horus, who had been submerged by Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set</note>. In memory of these deeds, the Egyptians were accustomed to honor the *Comasias* <note>A Greek term for a festive procession or "revel"</note> with solemn festivities. Whatever the case may be, the solemnity of the *Comasias* signifies the particular worship of the four principal men whom they cultivated, concerning whom I shall speak expressly in the fifth book of this work. But to finally return to the point from which we digressed: the Egyptians possessed many other symbols which they used in concealing their mysteries. Among others cited by Cornelius Tacitus in Book 14, Strabo in Book 17, Diodorus at the beginning of Book 4, Pliny, Clement, and others: through the image of the hawk <margin>What does the hawk represent?</margin> they understood the nature of the universe, or the spirit of the world, concerning which Eusebius, Horus <note>Likely referring to Horapollo, author of a famous treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, Ammianus Marcellinus, and others have written much. Through the eagle and the falcon <margin>Eagle and Falcon.</margin> they represented a thing of the greatest speed, on account of the extreme swiftness of these birds. Through bees <margin>Bees.</margin> they represented a king, distinguished by justice and clemency, who possesses a sting joined with honey. Through a dragon or a snake biting its own tail <margin>Snake biting its tail, Wolf, Dog, Lion.</margin> they represented the year. Through the head of a wolf, they represented past time, because the wolf is a most forgetful animal; through the head of a lion, the present time, on account of its strength and power; and finally, through the head of a dog, the future time, because it always invites us to itself with hope, fawning upon us in the manner of dogs. Through the ox <margin>Ox</margin>, an animal of much labor, they indicated the earth or agriculture. Through the stork <margin>Stork</margin>, because it supports its parents when they are advanced in age in recognition of the benefit of the nourishment it received, they indicated justice and piety. Through the eel <margin>Eel</margin>, they indicated an envious person, because the eel seems to have no commerce with other fish. Through the right hand <margin>Right hand</margin> and extended fingers, they indicated a liberal and sincere man. Through the crocodile <margin>Crocodile.</margin>, a harmful animal, they indicated a malignant man. Through an open eye, a good man and a keeper of justice; through hearing, memory; through a hare <margin>Hare</margin> with upright ears, a man endowed with the greatest memory. Through statues of judges lacking hands and with eyes cast down toward the ground—as Plutarch testifies in his book *On Osiris and Isis*—they signified incorruptible justice. Finally, the Egyptians employed many symbols devised after the pattern of nature for the purpose of establishing their sacred rites, concerning which Iamblichus <margin>Iamblichus</margin> writes in his *On the Mysteries* in these words: *"The Egyptians, imitating the nature of the universe itself and the fabricator of the Gods, also display certain images of mystical and hidden notions in the creation of their symbols, just as they express the hidden reasons of nature in apparent forms as if through symbols, and the Gods explain the truth of ideas through manifest images. Since, therefore, they perceived that the higher beings are delighted by the likeness of all lower things, and moreover desire that lower things be filled with goodness from the higher, insofar as they can be imitated, they rightly offer a mode of acting suitable to the celestial beings according to their strength; when they introduce hidden mysteries into manifest symbols; in the interpretation of which, leave behind the words and receive the meanings."* Therefore, when they name or introduce "mud" in the sacred rites, <margin>What is mud?</margin> this is understood to be the body of the world and the material and generative power...

...to this uncertain, and as if equally agitated and flowing, or even the principal cause, placed like a foundation for the elements and the things composed of elements. Since this is so, *GOD* <note>original: "DEVS"</note> himself is the cause of generation and of all the powers of nature which are in the elements; inasmuch as he is above these material things, indivisible, immovable, and unbegotten, entirely from himself and entirely within himself. Whence the Egyptians represent *GOD* sitting upon a *Lotus* <note>original: "Loton"</note>, which is an aquatic tree, by which it is signified that *GOD* in his sovereignty transcends the worldly mud, and does not touch it in his governing, but exercises a sovereignty that is entirely intellectual and empyrean <note>The "empyrean" refers to the highest heaven, the realm of pure fire and light.</note>. For all things in the *Lotus* are round, both the fruit and the leaves, by which is signified the circular action of the mind through the same things and in the same manner. *GOD* himself, therefore, exists in himself above this very action, surpassing such sovereignty, holy and venerable, and resting entirely within himself, which is indeed signified by the act of sitting. Furthermore, where they introduce *GOD* as the pilot of a ship, they signify his sovereignty as the governor of the world. For just as a pilot, separated from the ship and the rudder by a certain unity, moves, rules, and directs the ship from every side in an easy moment, so *GOD* himself directs the world from above, namely from the first principles of nature, exhibiting the principal causes of ideas. But since all parts of the heaven, and the celestial animals <note>Likely referring to the constellations of the Zodiac.</note>, and the entire motion of the universe, and time itself according to which the world is moved—in short, all things contained in the whole—receive powers descending from the *Sun* <note>original: "Sole"</note>, therefore the symbolic mode of signaling also introduces these things, designating in words that they are figured according to the celestial animals, and that they change their forms in turn through the seasons. Meanwhile, however, it demonstrates his immutable and simultaneous transmission through the whole world; and as these things, according to the diversity of their natures and motions, receive multiform powers from the *Sun*, so the symbolic tradition intends that through a multitude of *Gods* <note>original: "Deorum"</note> there is one *GOD* among them, and through multiform powers there is one power of *GOD* present. *Thus far Iamblichus.* <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians."</note> <margin>What God sitting on the Lotus signifies</margin> <margin>Description of the Lotus.</margin>

## §. I.

### *On the Letters and Alphabet of the Egyptians.*

The Venerable *Bede* <note>An English monk and scholar (d. 735 AD) known as the "Father of English History."</note> rightly teaches in his book *On the Nature of Things* that the ancients did not only write or speak with words as we do, but also transferred whatever the world contains and can be comprehended by us into a certain industrious method for signifying things; whence, he adds, there is such a great diversity of Alphabets, such a difference of letters and characters, whose strokes, figures, and crossings <note>original: "chiasmata"</note> likely gave origin to letters either from the likeness of material things, or the gait of beasts, or the flight of birds and fowl, or some other similar occasion; thus they say that *Cadmus* <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who introduced the alphabet to the Greeks.</note> first brought the use of sixteen letters found by a similar occasion into Greece, to which *Palamedes* the *Soothsayer* <note>original: "Aruspex"</note> added four others at the time of the *Trojan* war; *Plutarch* however, and after him *Volaterranus*, with many others... <margin>The bringing of 16 letters into Greece by Phoenix and Cadmus.</margin> <margin>Palamedes, inventor of 4 letters.</margin>

# CHAPTER VI. BOOK II. ON THE INSTRUCTION <note>The header refers to the "Institution" or "Instruction" of the subject of the book, likely Titus.</note>

<margin>Hermes, the first inventor of letters.</margin>
The Egyptians, according to others cited by Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), a Venetian scholar known as the "Varro of his age."</note>, claim that after the Hebrews, the Egyptians were the first to hand down the use of letters, which were invented by Mercury <note>The author identifies the Egyptian Thoth with the Roman Mercury/Greek Hermes.</note>. However, regarding what kind of letters these were, there is great disagreement among various authors in untying this knot. Abenephi <note>An Arabic author, likely Ibn Wahshiyya, often cited in early modern studies of hieroglyphs.</note>, whom we have decided to follow in this matter, says that the Egyptians used a fourfold kind of letters or characters. The first was the common kind, which the unlearned and the common folk used. The second was fictitious and devised by the Sages for concealing the mysteries of nature. The third was mixed, consisting of characters and symbols. The fourth was called "sacred," by which they carved any sublime mysteries and hidden sacraments concerning GOD, Angels (or spirits), demons, the world, man, and other secrets of nature—comprehending them as if in certain symbols—upon obelisks, pyramids, temple doors, halls, altars, and tablets, to commend them to eternity; whence they later earned the name "hieroglyphics." His words are these:

<margin>A fourfold kind of letters used by the Egyptians.</margin>

<margin>Abenephi.</margin>
<note>original Arabic: "ولم يعلمون اربع انواع الحروف..."</note>
And they knew four types of letters: the first was used by the illiterate; the second was used for philosophy; the third was a mixture of letters and images; and the fourth was for the manifestation of letters by which they intended the divine secrets.
---

There were, then, four kinds of letters among the Egyptians: the first was in use among the people and the unlearned; the second among the philosophers and the wise; the third was mixed from letters and symbols or images; the fourth was employed by the Priests, and these were the "letters of birds" (for so the Arabs call hieroglyphics) by which they indicated the sacraments of divinity. These things which are so beautifully discussed here regarding Egyptian letters agree perfectly with those which Clement of Alexandria mentions in the 5th book of his *Stromata* <note>Clement's "Miscellanies," a key source for early Christian understanding of Egyptian writing.</note> concerning the characters of the Egyptians; for he says thus: that they first teach the way and method of certain characters which they call *epistolographic* <note>original Greek: ἐπιςολογραφικὴν</note>, that is, suitable for writing letters; the second is the *Sacerdotal* <note>Priestly or Hieratic</note> kind, which the *sacred scribes* <note>original Greek: ἱερογραμματῇ</note> use, those who wrote about sacred matters. The last is the *hieroglyphic* <note>original Greek: ἰεογλυφικὴν</note>, that is, sacred writing, which is carved; one type of this is *cyriologic* <note>original Greek: κυριολογικὴν</note> through the first elements, that is, speaking properly; the other is *symbolic*, that is, signifying through signs. Of the symbolic type, one speaks properly through imitation, another is written as if tropically <note>metaphorically</note>, and another is taken openly as an allegory through certain enigmas: those who paint the Sun make a circle; for the Moon, they make a figure showing the form of a curved Moon, according to that form which is properly named.

<margin>A triple kind of letters recounted by Clement of Alexandria.</margin>

The letters of the first kind were undoubtedly those "epistolographic" ones—that is, those which they used in writing letters and manifesting their thoughts through writing. In earlier times, the elements of these letters were fewer, but in succeeding times, they borrowed so much from neighboring nations here and there...

...letters, they increased until they reached thirty-two, as I have clearly shown in the *Supplement to the Prodromus*, where you may examine the Alphabet. Regarding how many those first characters actually were, the opinions of authors vary. Demetrius Phalereus <margin>Demetrius Phalereus</margin> <note>A Greek statesman and scholar (c. 350–280 BCE) who helped establish the Library of Alexandria.</note>, the keeper of the most celebrated Library of Alexandria—which was later burned to the great detriment of posterity—says that they had seven vocal letters dedicated to seven Gods; his words are: <margin>Demetrius Phalereus on the letters of the Egyptians.</margin>
> In Egypt, he says, the priests celebrate the Gods with seven vowels, sounding them in succession; and instead of the flute and the lyre, the sound of their letters is heard for the sweetness of the voice. <note>original Greek: "Εν Αιγύπτω δέ φησι τῷ Θεῷ τῷ τάδε φωνήεντα..."</note>

These things are indeed correct; but how he says they had those seven vowels, I do not understand, since nature has ordained only five for the proper pronunciation of things: A, E, I, O, U. Perhaps they joined two marks of aspiration <note>Breathing sounds or "h" sounds.</note> together with these vowels. Pierius <margin>Pierius.</margin> <note>Pierio Valeriano (1477–1558), a famous Renaissance scholar of hieroglyphics.</note> thinks there were fifteen in total, figured from the likeness of some animal or limb, of which he assigns only four. For the first, A, he places the Ibis; for the second, B, the *Otem* <note>Likely referring to a specific Egyptian creature or symbol mentioned in Renaissance sources.</note>; for the third, he places a sickle in place of G; for the fourth, D. And while almost all authors cited up to this point report them as being taken from animals, they remain silent as to which ones they actually were. Hence, we, sparing no effort so that we might arrive at some knowledge of this matter, finally discovered that the first of the Egyptian letters <insert>the fish</insert> <note>original Greek: "τὸν ἰχθύν"</note> was fashioned out of fourteen letters, as <margin>14 Letters of the Egyptians taken from the forms of animals.</margin> Clemens, Eusebius, and others also correctly hand down; taken from the form and gait of created animals and the positions of other body parts. So also the author of the *Great Coptic Scale of Egypt*, or the *Coptic Dictionary*, says in the Beginning:
> Egypt took its first characters from the shapes of animals. <note>original Coptic: "χηλ ει τιχι ποτκερπες..."</note>

How, however, this first institution of the elements was carried out remains to be explained. The ancient writers of Egyptian affairs relate that the lower part of Egypt was once covered by the sea; but Osiris, the first King of Egypt, when he perceived this gulf of the sea was bringing forth something like land—formed from a vast accumulation of mud and sands brought down from Ethiopia by the flow of the Nile—led the waters of the Nile into channels. He rendered the intervening land, separated from the waters, not only fit for inhabitants but even pleasant. However, because a great abundance of serpents born from the putrefied mud rendered the place continuously dangerous <margin>The Ibis in opposition to serpents.</margin>, and since many died daily from the habits of the serpents (among whom was Canopus, the Pilot of Osiris), Osiris sent a great force of Ibises into these places. By devouring the serpents, they quickly purged the place and rendered it immune from dangers. Thus, as the Ibises multiplied, and as posterity noted that said birds transformed themselves into various shapes according to the different positions of the body; and with many other benefits received from the Ibis being added, the Egyptians—calling it a Spirit, or *Agathodaemon* <margin>Why the Ibis was called Agathodaemon.</margin> <note>Greek for "Good Spirit."</note>, from the figure it expressed with its feet—recorded it in the sacred register of animals, and called the place itself by the name Agathodaemon; which Ptolemy records in these words...

### CHAPTER VI.
## BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION

teaches in these words: <note>original: "Δίλτα μέγισον ὀνομάζεται..."</note> *The Great Delta is so named, near which the river is divided;* <note>original: "διζύγιον Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων"</note> *the double-yoked Good Spirit.*
<margin>The first letter of the Egyptians.</margin>
The Ibis, therefore, with its legs spread wide and its beak placed across them, means the same as the <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit" or "Noble Serpent," a protective deity in Hellenistic Egypt.</note>: so Plutarch says in *Symposiacs*, Book 5: <note>original: "ἰβις ἐπὶ τῶν πόδων..."</note> *The Ibis, by the spreading of its feet among themselves and in comparison with its beak, renders an equilateral triangle.*
<margin>The 2nd letter of the Arabs and Egyptians.</margin>
And in Book 9, *Symposiacs* 9.3: <note>original: "Ἑρμῆς λέγεται Θεῶν..."</note> *Hermes is said to be the first of the Gods in Egypt to write letters after the manner of the Ibis.*
It is handed down that Mercury was the first of the Gods in Egypt to discover letters, and therefore the Egyptians make the Ibis the first letter, as it is fitting for Mercury, namely the Agathodaemon.

<margin>The second Egyptian letter is taken from the neck and beak.</margin>
The second letter was taken from the neck of the Ibis with the beak held crosswise, which, because it resembles a square <note>A "norma" or carpenter's square.</note>, they called *GEEE*. For it signifies, as is evident from our Coptic Dictionary, that *GEEE* is nothing other than a square or a rule fit for performing measurements. Since Mercury was the author of Geometry as well as of letters, he aptly established the second letter as the Geometric square, taken from the neck and beak of the Ibis; Clement of Alexandria suggests this in plain words in the 5th book of the *Stromata*: <note>original: "ἀειθμὸς γὰρ ἐπνοίας..."</note> *For the Ibis seems to have provided the Egyptians with the greatest number for invention and measure among living things, as if from oblique circles.*

<margin>The third Egyptian letter taken from the Ibis.</margin>
The third letter was taken from the spreading of the Ibis's feet, with the insertion of the beak omitted: for in this way, it exactly expressed a *Delta* against the level ground. Consequently, the Egyptians designated this region near the sea by no other name than the "Delta"; and posterity has retained this name even to our own times. For the Egyptians believed that Mercury, under the form of an Ibis, handed down various forms of letters to the human race, and among other things taught through the form of the Δ <note>The Greek letter Delta.</note> how the Nile was to be divided, so that the land submerged by waters and marshes might be rendered fruitful and fit for human habitation.
<margin>What the letter A signifies.</margin>
From this, perhaps, the name *DELTA* was imposed on this letter, because I find that in Coptic it signifies nothing other than "good field." Certainly, Pausanias (cited in Pierius, Book 17) teaches that the Delta was taken from the Ibis in these words: *There is also another reason,* he says, *why the Egyptians signified the Ibis hieroglyphically: namely, since that region was called the Delta and by the figure Δ, it has a similarity with the Ibises, because otherwise they seem to mark the letter by that gait of their feet, with the interval drawn out to the equal lines of a triangle; and the opened beak signifies the same.* And in Book 47, concerning the seven letters: *He reports,* he says, *that Mercury, who first communicated letters to the Egyptians, wished the Ibis to be the first letter; if indeed by its gait it presents a triangular image, with the legs so disposed as has been said in its place; and that which is the first letter among us and the Greeks is adapted to the face of an Isosceles triangle.*

<margin>4th Letter.</margin>
The fourth letter was V, taken from the opening of the Ibis's beak, and it resembled our Y; for from the beaks of birds, figures and characters were taken...

<header>CHAPTER VI.</header>

## AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

<margin>Theogenes.</margin>
Theogenes, in his hymn to the Sun, bears witness with these words: *ὃς ἐδίδαξε γραμμὰς ἐν τῇ ῥίγῃ τῷ ὄρνιθι* <note>original Greek: "Who taught lines by the beak of the bird."</note>. He who taught lines and letters from the beak of birds. Indeed, the Ibis, by the wide opening of its beak, first taught the Egyptians the use of the compass, which among them was a symbol of the measurement of things and the process of nature from the interior to the superior parts, as will be taught at length in what follows.

<margin>The fifth letter</margin>
<margin>D+S</margin>
The fifth letter among them was O, and it corresponded to the Greek *omicron*. For they observed this animal, either purging itself with a clyster <note>A reference to the ancient belief that the Ibis performed self-enemas using its long beak</note> or arranging its spread feathers, with its neck twisted into a circle, expressing that figure which they, referring it to the number of letters, called D+S, as the author of our Dictionary mentions (which we shall cite later); although others wish this letter also to have been taken from the shape of the Sun. We have, therefore, five different figures represented in a single Ibis, which they referred to the number of letters; so that henceforth no one should wonder why this animal was held in such great honor among the Egyptians. For first, it is probable that it indicated the whole of Geometry and the progression of quantity to the Egyptians: lines indeed by the various stretching of the neck and the longer feet; the angles by the spreading of the beak and feet; rectilinear triangles through the two legs, which, when spread while they insert the beak across them, create an equilateral triangle; and by the ratio of triangular quantity, they perfectly express the perfection achieved; these are the first foundations of both speculative and practical Geometry. Concerning the other mysteries of this bird, we shall deal with them at length in their proper places.

<margin>The sixth letter</margin>
<margin>λ and ℨ ℨ</margin>
The sixth letter was Λ, which corresponds to the Greek *lambda*, and it was expressed by the spread feet of the Ibis, whence it was also called λ and ℨ ℨ, which in Egyptian signifies "progress." For the Ibis, when walking, reflected this character, whence also came the invention of the Egyptian (or Ibiac) cubit <note>term: cubit - a traditional unit of length based on the forearm</note>; for from the tracks of this animal left in the mud of the riverbank, they took the measure of the cubit, as will be said in its proper places; and it is placed in opposition to the preceding letter V, from the conjunction of which is born X, another letter frequent on our obelisk, by which they indicated the process of the Soul of the World toward the lower things and again to the higher; but these things, as I have said, will be treated specifically in their proper places.

And from this it is clear why Plutarch, Clement, and others called the Ibis the "first letter," for it will be said elsewhere that from this they learned not only letters, but the secret logic of the hieroglyphics. For among them, a "letter" is taken not for a simple figure of some character, but for an entire hieroglyphic system, which although it was one, the Ibis exhibited in its various and greatest forms. Hence they dedicated it to Mercury alone, as to a God and the inventor of the greatest things. But concerning the Ibis, see what we have discussed in its own hierogrammatism <note>term: hierogrammatism - the sacred study or writing of symbols</note> in Book I, Chapter 5 of this Work; the other letters, however, are handed down as having been found in this manner.

It is established from all the monuments of Authors that the Ox was worshipped with divine honors by the Egyptians on account of its signal benefits, so much so that Osiris, under the form of an ox, taught men various things necessary for sustaining human life...

Plutarch asserts this to be the case in Book 9 of his *Table Talk* <note>original: "Sympol. q. 3."</note>, in these words:
> They say that Cadmus placed Alpha as the first letter because among the Phoenicians it is the name for an ox, which they considered not the second or third most necessary thing, as Hesiod did, but the first. <note>original Greek: "Καδμὸν φασι, τὸ ἄλφα πρῶτον..."</note>

<margin>What kind of letters the Hawk gave.</margin>
The third sacred animal among the Egyptians was the hawk, from which we read that both common and symbolic characters were similarly borrowed. And indeed, the head with the beak gave the letter which they called *Scima* in the Alphabet, that is, "vision"; because through the head of the hawk, which expressed this character,
<margin>Scima, the 9th letter.</margin>

<margin>Oseles and allegory.</margin>

<margin>10th Letter: What letters the Dog gave.</margin>
The fourth animal was the dog, under which although they displayed great mysteries, as will be seen in the interpretation of the obelisk, it has not yet been possible to find whether, and what kind of common letter, they derived from it. And these were those four
<margin>4 Sacred Animals.</margin>
most celebrated animals, which they called "letters" because they had assigned the principal letters to them, and they used to carry them about in the solemnities of the *Comasiae* <note>A Greek term for festive processions or revelries</note>. > Now in those things which are called by others the Processions of the Gods, they carry about golden images of the Gods: two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis; and they call those four images the "four letters." <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δὲ δὴ τῶν κατὰ κομασίας..."</note> This was evidently in honor of Mercury <note>The Roman equivalent of Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing</note>, who had ingeniously extracted the first elements of letters, filled with mystical reasons, from their forms.

<margin>Ten letters extracted from 4 animals.</margin>
We have, therefore, ten letters derived from the four said animals. The remaining letters they derived from other living creatures, or even from the likeness of instruments. From the horned head of the ram, which they called *Amun*, or the dwelling place of Jupiter Ammon,
<margin>11th Letter taken from the horns of a Ram.</margin>
they derived the letter which they called *Amun*, and it corresponded to our B, the sound and pronunciation of which letter they learned from the voice of that same animal. Certainly, it is likely that the interpreter of the etymologies had this in mind when he sings thus:

Like a stupid beast, he walks saying "Be, Be."
Hence Pierius also asserts that this was the second letter of the Egyptians.

<header>AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS.</header>

### CHAPTER VII.
## CHAPTER VII.
### *Concerning the second, third, and fourth types of letters used by the Wise.*

Beyond the marks of common wisdom, the *Egyptians* employed another class of characters; many of these, however, do not appear among the remains of the obelisks and other monuments. We call this type, not inappropriately, Gnomic or parabolic; it consisted of certain maxims and <margin>What Gnomic symbolic letters are.</margin> political teachings, which they expressed through a clever arrangement of symbols. Of this kind are those which Horapollo <note>A 5th-century author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, which influenced Renaissance scholars despite being largely allegorical.</note> left to posterity. To this class are also referred those symbols which we read that Pythagoras used, which were discussed in the preceding sections. Clement of Alexandria also pursues these at length in the 6th book of his *Stromata* <note>original: "stfomatum" (misprint for Stromatum), meaning "Miscellanies."</note>. Thus, Horapollo indicates a man who has no care or concern for himself by means of an Oyster and a Crab; <margin>What Horapollo indicated by the oyster, the crab, and the wrasse fish.</margin> but when signifying a man suffering from gluttony, they would paint a wrasse fish <note>original: "scarum piscem"</note>, on account of the extreme voracity of this fish; and so with the rest, which you may see in the cited Author.

In this manner, King Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt often identified with Ramses II.</note> caused female genitalia to be carved upon columns erected in the Regions which he occupied with no resistance offered to him; by these symbols, he silently signified the <margin>Why Sesostris carved female parts on stones.</margin> small and effeminate spirit of the inhabitants. Such are the things that Herodotus relates concerning Pheron, the son of Sesostris: that on account of sacrilege against the Nile <margin>Pheron, sacrilegious against the Nile, is struck with blindness.</margin> (against whose waves he had cast a spear), he incurred a divine vengeance of many years of blindness. He could not be freed from this until he received an oracle from Buto stating that he must wash his eyes with the urine of a woman. When he had first attempted this experiment with his own wife, and <margin>The urine of a Gardener's wife as a remedy for blindness.</margin> then with many other women, and it had profited him nothing, he finally made trial of the matter with the wife of a certain gardener and was immediately restored to health. All those women who had contributed no help to his recovery he gathered into a place called "Red Earth" <note>original: "gleba rubra"</note> and burned them all to a woman, except for the Gardener's wife, whom he took for his own wife. The Priests did not understand this history literally, as with all other things, but denoted by this allegory the very wicked life of this King. For he was so proud that he cared nothing for the GODS, nor the sacred rites, nor the Priests who were their ministers; he despised the ancestral rituals and did many other unworthy things, on account of which he incurred a total blindness of mind. By the "woman's urine" prescribed by the oracle, it was indicated that he had been urged away from a luxurious life by the frequent admonitions of the Priests; but when these profited nothing, finally the "urine of the Gardener's wife," applied to the King, restored his sight. By the "Gardener's wife," they denoted the Earth <note>original: "Tellurem"</note>, which brings forth fruit only when studiously cultivated (which labor they noted by the "gardener"). By the said "urine," they denoted the herbs, plants, and similar things which the Priests used on account of their extreme temperance, which are, as it were, the "excrements of the earth" born from the copious irrigation of waters. Thus, by abstaining from immoderate luxury, while [leading] a frugal and temperate life...

established, he gradually regained the light of his mind, so that the more hostile he had previously been toward God and His sacred rites, the more devoted in spirit and more ardent in zeal he became after receiving that mental illumination. I could bring forward innumerable examples of this argument drawn from the lives of the Kings of Egypt, but since we have explained those in our *Oedipus* <note>referring to Kircher’s own work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, we did not think time should be wasted here by repeating them.

<margin>The third kind of literature.</margin> Furthermore, the third kind of literature was composed partly of simple letters and partly of symbols. For it is certain that the Egyptians not only mixed common characters with symbolic ones, but also intermingled entire words of the Coptic language, as will be seen shortly.

<margin>What is the 4th genus of letters?</margin> The fourth genus of letters used among the Egyptians consisted of pure symbols, mystically expressed through animals, men, birds, instruments, herbs, parts of the human body, and figures of every kind. Concerning these, Lucan writes in Book 3:
->Memphis had not yet learned to weave the papyrus<-
->By the river, and only birds and wild beasts<-
->Were carved on stones, and animals preserved magical tongues.<-
<note>original: "Nondum flumine... magicas animalia linguas."</note>

Alexander ab Alexandro supports this, recording that the Egyptians and Phoenicians first fashioned the secrets of their thoughts and the perceptions of their minds through various figures of different animals carved on stones in place of letters. Diodorus Siculus says more clearly in Book 4: "The letters of the Egyptians are like various living creatures, and the extremities of men and instruments, but especially those of craftsmen; for their system does not consist of syllables, but of the form of images, their significance, and use, handed down by human memory." And a little later: "In the same way, the figures of other parts of the body and instruments denoted something certain, which people, through long use and meditation, observed and distinguished by the trace of what they expressed."

<margin>Petrus Crinitus.</margin> Petrus Crinitus also writes in Book 7, Chapter 2, that this was the method of writing among the Egyptians. Regarding the letters of the Egyptians, which are called hieroglyphics—of which mention is made among ancient authors—this can still be observed on the obelisks, in which those figures and effigies of diverse animals, herbs, rivers, and trees are carved, designating the philosophy of that nation. For on the Obelisks of Kings Sesostris and Psammetichus <note>original: "Pfamifertao"</note>, which were brought into the city from Egypt, the interpretation of the nature of things was noted through such symbols and hieroglyphic marks. For thus the philosophy of the Egyptians is believed to have been first illustrated. Among other effigies, they were accustomed to note scarabs, bees, rivers, oxen, vultures, and others of that kind. Furthermore, the symbol of a King was signified by the effigy of a bee, because in undergoing the duties of life, he ought to have no less the sting of justice than the sweet clemency of honey. In the vulture, they indicated the genius and majesty of nature, because among these, only females are said to be found. Apuleius subscribes to this in his *Metamorphoses*, saying: "They had those ancient books marked with unknowable letters, partly suggesting the condensed words of spoken language through figures of animals of this kind, and partly protected from the curious reading of the profane by knotted characters, twisted like a wheel and crowded together like vine-tendrils."

<margin>Chaæremon and Horapollo.</margin> Chaæremon and Horapollo agree with this, who in their monuments [recorded] some of these letters still...

...they have left traces even to this day. *Ammianus Marcellinus* <note>A 4th-century Roman historian.</note> also, cited by *Caelius Rhodiginus* <note>Ludovico Ricchieri, a Renaissance humanist.</note> in Book 29 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 26, says: That letters of this kind consisted of the figures of animals and other such bodies and signs. By partridges, they seem to show the abusive <note>original: "contumeliosos"</note> (as *Caelius* says), because birds of this kind, when worn out by old age, inflict abuse upon themselves; just as the eel seems to signify envy, which is as hostile to all good things as the eel is to other fish, whose society and community it flees. <margin>Symbols of the Hippopotamus.</margin> The *hooves of the Hippopotamus* turned downwards signify the impious, the unjust, and the ungrateful. But the *River Horse* <note>The literal translation of the Greek 'hippopotamos'.</note>, as soon as his age permits, tests his strength against his father; if he overcomes him in a fight and notices him yielding his place, he mates with his mother, and the father's life is spared. But if the defeated father refuses to permit him to lie with the mother, then the son, relying on his might and strength, kills the father and forces the mother. <margin>Two hooves of the Hippopotamus.</margin> Therefore, not without reason, these same *Egyptians* also paint two hooves of the same *Hippopotamus* at the bottom [of a composition], so that men, looking upon this and reflecting on what is said of such a beast, might be more prompt in returning gratitude. From this doctrine it also seems to be derived that on the scepters of Kings they used to figure a stork at the top, but a hippopotamus at the bottom, by which they hinted at the power of sparing justice, since the hippopotamus is a most unjust animal. <margin>What the stork-catcher of the Egyptians signifies.</margin> Moreover, there was such a great itch for this writing through symbolic animals that it made almost all nations its own. *Caelius Rhodiginus*, following *Ammianus Marcellinus* and *Heliodorus*, says: That the *Egyptians* first transferred the use of these letters—the gnawing <note>original: "rosum," likely a typo for "usum" (use) or "rosam" (arrangement)</note> of these symbolic characters—to the *Ethiopians*; which *Diodorus* also hints at in Book 3, chapter 1, and *Volateranus* <note>Raffaele Maffei, a humanist scholar.</note> says thus of the *Egyptian* in Book 12: <margin>Volateranus.</margin> They also have a double kind of writing: one which they commonly call [demotic]; the other which they call Sacred letters, which only the Priests touch, handed down by hand from their parents, which they first received from the *Ethiopians*, namely from *Cush*, the son of *Ham*, the first colonist of *Ethiopia*. Others assert that they learned that kind of writing from the wise men of the Indians; such as *Arrianus*, who says that the *Indians* formerly knew no other use of letters except that which is through diverse animals; <margin>Arrianus says characters were transferred to the Indians from animals.</margin> which is also testified by more recent writers of Indian affairs, *Maffei* and *Jarric*, who assert that characters of this kind are still seen in many places in the Indies. <margin>Theseus Ambrosius.</margin> *Theseus Ambrosius* <note>An Italian scholar of Oriental languages.</note> asserts in his appendix on various letters that he saw in the hands of a certain *Canon Paleoti* of *Bologna* a book brought from *India* covered in *Tiger* skin, in which various figures of men and other things and animals were only depicted. Of such a kind are those books brought from *Mexico*, variously transformed with figures of men and animals, which are even now preserved in the *Vatican*. From these things it appears that this use of letters was common to all the more ancient wise men, and they employed it chiefly to excite admiration for the excellence of their wisdom among posterity. <margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> *Marsilio Ficino* in his *Commentary on Plato’s Philebus*, chapter 29, says: That the use of such letters, according to *Plato* and *Pliny*, was eternal; nevertheless, proper and particular characters and forms of writing were invented and introduced by different men; thus he says: *Zoroaster* and his Priests [had] one particular method of writing;

# CHAPTER VII 136 BOOK II. ON EDUCATION

<margin>The spread of Egyptian letters</margin>
They possessed a method greatly differing from the common one. By using characters formed from the figures of celestial signs, stars, and other heavenly bodies, they concealed the mysteries of their wisdom. Hermes Trismegistus <note>literally "Thrice-Greatest Hermes," a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the invention of writing and magic</note>, taught by the example of Zoroaster regarding the necessity of not manifesting the more sublime mysteries of wisdom rashly to just anyone, expanded upon Zoroaster's invention. He devised new *living images* <note>original: "ζωοα λοα βδον" (zoa loa bdon) - likely a corruption of Greek for "living images" or "animal figures"</note>, that is, an alphabet composed of various kinds of animals and plants. He commanded that the priests alone use this for hiding the secrets of the mind. This opinion certainly agrees well with what we said above, when we proved that the Egyptians first received their wisdom from the Hebrews—that is, handed down by Zoroaster or Ham—then to the Phoenicians, and from here to the Greeks, and finally from the Greeks it poured forth through the whole world. For, to remain silent for now regarding those things which Olaus Magnus the Goth <note>A 16th-century Swedish ecclesiastic and writer</note>
<margin>Olaus Magnus the Goth</margin>
relates in his *Northern History* concerning various letters and characters (which are seen to this day carved into the stones and cliffs of the mountains of Angermannia <note>Ångermanland, Sweden</note> under the figures of different animals), certainly the coins and various currencies of the ancients show this most clearly. On these, they were accustomed to stamp temples, conquered cities, caducei <note>the staff of Hermes/Mercury</note>, right hands joined together, two-faced and four-faced Januses, ships,
<margin>Medals of the ancients honored with symbols in the likeness of the Egyptians</margin>
bundles of grain, cornucopias, the goats of Amalthea, two-horse chariots, Mother Cybele, wild boars, dogs, stags, does, bulls, lions, dolphins, hippopotamuses, snakes, felt caps with daggers, scales, elephants, lynxes, tigers, little Mercuries wearing winged hats, she-wolves nursing twins, the sun, the moon, Rome reclining on a couch, the club of Hercules, Cerberus, the lyre, Marsyas flayed alive, tripods, cupids, crocodiles, lambs, pegasi, and other almost infinite things. Guillaume du Choul, Brassicanus, Hulsius, and other Antiquarians <note>scholars of ancient artifacts</note> have written copiously about these, which are truly nothing other than certain hieroglyphics which the Romans, having been taught by the Egyptians, once used.

<margin>Cicero's hieroglyphic writing.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the characters which Cicero used in his more secret letters, and which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a famous Renaissance cryptographer</note> says were similar to the Egyptian ones, I show that it cannot and should not be said so; for the individual marks of Cicero corresponded to individual words and names, which happens in a very different way in the hieroglyphics among the Egyptian sages. In those, individual marks have their own proper and mystical concepts, which would not happen if individual hieroglyphics corresponded to individual words. Added to this is the fact that the labor of reading anything written with such marks was so great that even those who had devised them could scarcely extricate the meaning even once, due to the almost infinite multitude of characters. The Egyptians, however, did not have a multitude of characters, but rather a multitude of things signified through a few characters. Whether this custom of writing was first received by the Hebrews from them, or they from the Hebrews, has been debated elsewhere; it is certain that Moses presented many things mystically in the sacred scriptures. And first
<margin>Moses relates almost all his things mystically under symbols.</margin>
indeed, if we consider the physical exposition of things, we will see that the mystical senses of scripture transfer here to the universality of nature, or to the powers and works of all nature—that is, to the matter, form, and parts of this sensible world—while he inquires in the divine utterances into the motion, order, and ornament of the spheres...

The celestial spheres, the qualities of the elements, the properties of metals, the virtues of plants, and the behaviors of living creatures; indeed, certain distinguished commentators on Exodus and Leviticus among the Hebrews have entered upon this way of explaining: they have explained the natures of almost all things in the interpretation of these volumes; discussing how Moses, according to the harmony of the triple world <note>The "triple world" refers to the Renaissance conception of the universe divided into the Elemental (Earth), Celestial (Stars), and Intellectual (Angelic) realms.</note> and the universal nature of things, ordered the ark, the tabernacle, the vessels, the garments, the rites, the sacrifices, and the remaining mysteries to appease God and the celestial powers, and to purify man, who is the image of these things. An example of this explanation, collected from Philo, Josephus, and Jerome regarding the tabernacle of Moses, and especially from Clement of Alexandria, is as follows:

If anyone contemplates the structure of the Mosaic tabernacle and those things which are in it, and considers each part not idly but prudently, he will find that Moses, a divine man, represented in all these things in some way the nature of the entire universe. For it was necessary that he, who had intended to build a man-made tabernacle for GOD, the Author of the whole World, should take the likeness of those things from which the world was established by GOD. First, therefore, for this reason, he divided the admirable structure of his tabernacle into three parts, namely into the vestibule, the hall, and the inner sanctum; or into the courtyard, the hall, and the sanctuary; which would represent to us the universality of the divine workmanship distinct in three parts, or three worlds; that is, in this sublunary world which we inhabit, in the celestial world closest to this, and in that supreme world of all, the ultra-mundane; which Theologians call the angelic and Philosophers the intellectual world, which has been celebrated by no one according to its dignity, as Plato says.

The first part of the tabernacle, therefore, which is called the courtyard and the vestibule, <margin>Explanation of the parts of the mystical tabernacle.</margin> displayed the image of this sublunary world: in whose likeness <margin>The first part: the vestibule.</margin> it was placed under the open sky, protected by no roof or shade, but always exposed to rains, the heat of the Sun, and the cold; and in it there moved about indiscriminately not only clean and unclean men, sacred and profane, but also animals of every kind; and in it, on account of the sacrifices and perpetual offerings, there was a constant vicissitude of life and death.

The second part, or the hall, which was called the Holy Place, occupying the middle place between the vestibule and the inner sanctum, and shining entirely with the splendor of gold, prefigured that celestial world which is the medium between the super-celestial and the sub-celestial. For there was in its southern region a golden lampstand, distinguished by seven burning lamps: which signified the movements of the seven wandering lights <note>The "wandering lights" are the seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. For the Sun and the Moon, along with the other planets, deviating far from the Northern regions, are observed more in the southern parts of the world; moreover, among these lamps, that which occupied the middle summit of the lampstand, having three lamps on each side, bore the likeness of the solar star. For the Sun, possessing the fourth orb equally from the highest and the lowest heaven, and shining in the middle among the other six wandering stars, tempers that musical and truly divine instrument of the celestial spheres.

## CHAPTER VII

<margin>The third part: The Holy of Holies.</margin>
The third part of the tabernacle, truly the most sacred and secret of all, which was called the inner sanctum, the shrine, and the **Holy of Holies**, expressed the figure of the super-celestial and angelic world, which is the dwelling place of the Angels and of God the Best and Greatest. For just as that secret shrine of the Mosaic tabernacle was invisible and inaccessible to mortals, nor could anyone enter into it except the high priest, who bore that ineffable name, the *tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> **Jehovah**, upon his forehead; so into that super-celestial and divine world it is lawful for no one to enter, nor to look upon the things within it which are invisible and incomprehensible, nor to grasp them exactly with the mind, except for him alone who is foreshadowed by the high priest of sacred things, displaying on his forehead the unspeakable name **Jehovah**, which is interpreted as: *He who is, and who is to be, and who causes to be.* This, moreover, is the supreme moderator of all things, **GOD**, alone bearing the ineffable name **Jehovah**, that is, always existing, and granting the power of being to all others, and alone most fully embracing the incomprehensible things of the super-celestial world by that same <margin>Mystery.</margin> wisdom with which He comprehends Himself. Also the **Ark**, which was hidden in the shrines of the tabernacle, <margin>What the Ark in the tabernacle signified.</margin> signified divine providence and governance toward the world. For just as the ark had been destined for preserving the tablets of the divine law, and the rod of Aaron, and the manna; so in the storehouses of divine providence are contained all the laws of wisdom by which the entire universe of creatures is governed, the rod and scepter of the ruling power by which it is directed, and the manna of most liberal bounty by which it is quickened and fed. Truly the **Cherubim**, surrounding the ark with the curves of their wings, <margin>What the Cherubim denote.</margin> denote those celestial minds and those blessed spirits who surround and attend the divine majesty with the services of most ready speed, as if by a winged and swift ministry. But enough on these matters for now. It remains, therefore, for us to say that **Hieroglyphic characters** were nothing other than certain brief symbols by which they indicated many things in a few words, as was most extensively proven from various authors in the preceding chapter; and will be clearly shown below in the practical explanation itself. And in these things, **Clement of Alexandria**, a man learned in all antiquity, most fully proves in the 5th book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "stromatum"</note> that they were imitators of the Hebrews; <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin> his words are:
> *It would be a long task to follow all the prophetic and legal matters by asserting those things which were spoken through enigmas. For now, the concealment is established, which in the ancient temple of seven circuits—which looked toward something—among the Hebrews was a Relation; and that composition which was in the robe reaching to the ankles through various symbols, which refer to those things that are apparent, signifies the composition which reaches from Heaven even unto the earth. And the covering and the veil were varied with hyacinth <note>A deep blue or violet color.</note> and purple, and scarlet and fine linen;* <margin>Mystical explanation of the divisions according to Clement.</margin> *it signified, moreover, that the nature of the elements possesses the revelation of GOD; for the purple is from the water, the fine linen from the earth; and the hyacinth is likened to the air, since it is dark and obscure, just as the scarlet is to fire. In the middle of the covering and the veil, where it was permitted for the Priests to enter, was placed the censer, a symbol of the earth, which is placed in this middle of the world, from which exhalations arise; that middle place also, which is within the veil, into which it was permitted for the high priest alone to enter on appointed days, and the outer court, which was open to all, the Hebrews say is the midpoint of Heaven and Earth, others say it is a symbol of the world, which is perceived by the intel—*

The Greeks, however, do the opposite. From which we perceive that they had a great affinity with the customs of the Hebrews, the names of the Prophets, circumcision, and the institutions of writing; yet it must rather be thought that the Egyptians borrowed these things from them while they lived together at various times.

## CHAPTER VIII.
->Concerning the Coptic or Pharaonic language.<-

The Copts have thirty-two letters in total, whose shapes, names, and powers you may contemplate prefixed at the front of the Coptic Onomasticon <note>A vocabulary or dictionary</note>; and from these they compose their Alphabet, which indeed was shown in the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher's earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus*</note> to be the same as the alphabet of the ancient Egyptians, if you remove a few letters. Truly, just as the ancient Hebrews were accustomed to arrange their alphabet so that the letters themselves consisted of their own mystical significance, and the elements of the letters showed the elements of all things—as will be explained at length in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note> regarding the Cabala of the Hebrews—so the ancient Egyptians, though otherwise degenerate from the true lineage of the Hebrews, yet like apes of their ancestors from whom they had descended, arranged their letters in such an order that there were indeed shapes of letters and characters; but the meaning was in all things entirely analogous to the secrets of the Hebrews. # BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION
## CHAPTER VIII.

The Copts <note>The native Egyptian Christians</note>, who retained the Alphabet of the ancients, by a certain parallel reasoning, have hidden many things concerning the most holy mysteries of our faith under these types of letter-forms, numbers, and mystical significations. In doing so, they hinted that they affected that ancient hierophantic <note>The wisdom of the "hierophants" or high priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> wisdom in all things. This is also indicated by that Great Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher</note> in his mystical books *On the Divine Names*, chapter 9, where he is entirely, if it is permitted to speak thus, **manifesting God** <note>original: *θεοφανίζων* (theophanizōn)</note>, and
<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin> indicates this everywhere with **hierarchical** <note>original: *hicæ* (likely a fragment of *hierarchicæ*)</note> and similar words; *seeking the souls in a bodily manner, and the head as the mind, the hand as the opinion, the chest as the spirit, and the belly as the nature that examines.* *Namely, that the Mind corresponds to the head, opinion to the neck, the soul to the chest, desire to the belly, while the legs and feet denote nature.* All of these things, spoken according to the mind of the Egyptian hierophants in the sacred writing concerning the hieroglyphic symbols of the parts of the human body, we shall show at length.

What else does that Tauric staff <note>A staff shaped like the Greek letter Tau (T)</note> in the hands of Saint Anthony, formed in the likeness
<margin>The Tauric Staff of St. Anthony.</margin> of the letter T, denote, if not that handled cross of Serapis <note>The Ankh, often called the *crux ansata* or "cross with a handle"</note>, the rule of salvation, the symbol of rectitude, and a mystical token, as it were, of the future life? Concerning these things, consult the *Prodromus* <note>Likely Kircher's own earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus*</note> which treats them more extensively. Indeed, when those first Fathers of the Egyptians, equipped with a remarkable knowledge of divine matters, considered these mystical characters of the Ancients, they discovered they had a great affinity with the mysteries of our faith; they converted them also to a use suitable for their own sacred studies, to which they were uniquely devoted. And that this is so is demonstrated more than sufficiently by certain letters
<margin>The Symbolic Letter of St. Pachomius and Theodore.</margin> of Saint Pachomius and his disciple Theodore, mentioned by Gennadius of Marseilles, a very ancient writer. These letters, written to various Monasteries of Egypt, were recently discovered and communicated to me—out of his affection for the Republic of Letters <note>The international community of scholars</note>—by the distinguished Lucas Holstenius, a most famous philologist and expert in all antiquity. In these, he seems to observe entirely the ancient method of writing, while he describes—now the secrets of the hidden divinity, now the occult connection of souls with GOD, now the method of establishing a holy and blessed life—by truly most abstruse metaphors and most intricate parables. Sometimes he draws from the form and figure of the letters, now from the numbers lying hidden beneath them, and frequently from the very signification of the letters, so aptly that you would say you were reading an Egyptian Hierophant, or some Pythagoras of Samos, belching forth his symbols. Saint Cyril mentions this secret
<margin>St. Cyril and Sozomen.</margin> method of writing in a certain letter to Saint Pope Leo, as does Sozomen in Book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 2 and 3, where he says that on the tablet of Pachomius, which he is said to have received from an Angel, it was written: *And having divided the whole community into twenty-four orders, he joined three peculiarities to each order. And so that the position of each order might have the proportion of its withdrawal, he thus established it to be in the place of Zeta, Xi, and other proportions.* <note>original Greek: *Πᾶσαν δὲ τὴν συνοικίαν εἰς ἑκοσιτέσσαρα τὴν τάγματα διελὼν...*</note> *Indeed, he divided all into 24 orders, and joined three properties to each order. # AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

In the life of Saint Pachomius <note>Pachomius (c. 292–348 AD) was the founder of Christian cenobitic monasticism—communal living for monks.</note> we read the following: *It was also commanded that, according to the number of the elements and the Greek letters, twenty-four groups of monks should be established, so that to each group the names of individual letters were assigned, that is, from Alpha and so on until Omega. Thus, when someone asked the Archimandrite <note>A title for the head of a monastery or a group of monasteries.</note> about someone in such a great multitude, he would recognize them by a simple response. For example, when he said Iota or Epsilon; and again Lambda, or Sigma, or Phi, he would express the character of the group by a specific sign of the letter's name. To the simpler and more innocent, he assigned the letter Iota. To the more difficult and crooked, he appropriately assigned letters suited to them, so that according to the manner of their conduct and the rule, they would fit the elements of the letters to each group; only the spiritual fathers themselves were able to know what these things signified.* But so that the reader may see at least some specimen of this hidden writing and its solution, it seemed appropriate to propose a single paradigm here, which we have gathered from the first letter of Saint Pachomius. For thus Pachomius writes in a certain letter to Cornelius, the Archimandrite of the Monastery of Mochanza:

> *Perform the work of 12821 <note>original: "ι" or Iota, represented here by numerical/symbolic placeholders in the transcription</note> and place 28λ2λ <note>original: "Δ" or Delta</note> before your eyes, so that it may be well with your soul. Sing "ko," lest perhaps the world sing "to" to you; and do not forget the Kalends <note>The first day of the month.</note>; etc. Are not the Kalends "to," "totl" Easter; and so on for the others, which we interpret with the help of the Coptic language as follows.*

<margin>Explanation of the mystical letters of St. Pachomius.</margin>

Therefore, when Abbot Pachomius says in his letters, *Perform the work of Iota,* the Holy man understands nothing else except that for him who is called to the eminent state of Religious life, all things must be carried out in simplicity and sincerity with a right intention, without any regard for personal convenience or utility. For just as the number one is among numbers, so is Iota among the Egyptian letters <note>The author is likely conflating Greek letters used in Egypt with hieroglyphic concepts.</note>, from which, as the smallest of all, all other letters are composed; so a sincere and right intention, and a humble way of life before GOD, is like the first foundation of all other actions and the highest operations to be employed in the spiritual edifice, composing all other things. Whence not undeservedly the holy man applied this to children, who, being unpolluted by this world, have as yet tasted nothing of the false allurements of worldly things, and are accustomed to perform all things by the pure instinct of nature, without any deceit, pretense, or the craftiness of a perverse intention; since, moreover, in the Egyptian language Iota denotes nothing other than a "little one," does it not aptly allude to that exclamation of the heavenly Teacher:

> *Unless you become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven?* <note>Matthew 18:3</note> And this is the first point, which I leave to others to explain more fully.

<margin>Interpretation of the Character.</margin>
<margin>What the letter Iota signifies.</margin>

Furthermore, when he says in the same letter:
> *Place Delta before your eyes, so that it may be well with your soul,*

it seems to denote nothing else but the perfect imitation of divine virtues, according to that saying:
> *Be perfect, as your heavenly father is perfect;* <note>Matthew 5:48</note>

which happens through that union and conformity of our intellect and will with the divine. For since, as Plato testifies, Delta <note>Represented as a triangle Δ.</note> is the first of all figures, because it composes all remaining figures—that is, the perfections of all beings, which are like certain numbers and figures—and into which all things are resolved...

<header>CHAPTER VIII</header>

## AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

...whether or not it proceeded from the Egyptians? Certainly, it is clear from Herodotus in his books *Terpsichore* and *Clio* that letters were first transferred from the Egyptians to the Greeks by Cadmus; and for that reason they are called *Phoenician letters* <note>original: "Φοινικια γραμματα"</note> or *Cadmean* <note>original: "καδμεια"</note>. <margin>Cadmus the inventor of these letters</margin> Whence also that most ancient consensus of all Greece sufficiently proves that the Greeks received letters from Cadmus; nor is there any reason why we should either deny so manifest a thing, or agree with Tzetzes <note>Johannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian</note> who denies it. He strives to prove by a double argument that the Greeks had earlier letters before Cadmus: first, because an oracle was given to Cadmus: *Do not seek the Phoenician [letters], Cadmus, but the voice of the mind* <note>original: "Φοινιξα μηδον αδηνοεος εκδον καδμοι"</note>. The second argument is that Bellerophon, who was older than Cadmus, brought written tablets concerning his own death. Both arguments are futile, and both were invented by the Poets. For why were they called "Cadmean letters" if they are not attributed to Cadmus as their author? And if Cadmus is the author, or at least the first teacher and indicator of them in Greece, how did the Greeks have letters before Cadmus, since older ones are nowhere found than those called *Cadmean letters* <note>original: "καδμεια γραμματα"</note>? <margin>Cadmean letters</margin> To all of which Clement of Alexandria subscribes in the first book of his *Miscellanies*: <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> *Cadmus the Phoenician was the discoverer of letters among the Greeks, as Ephorus says* <note>original: "καδμος δε φοινιξ εσιν, ο των γραμματων εν ελλησιν ευρετης, ως φησιν ευορος"</note>. Whence also Herodotus writes that the letters were called Phoenician. However, Cadmus and Phoenix, together with their brother Phoenix, had set out from Egyptian Thebes (where they originated) into Syria; so that it is probable that in the time of Othniel <note>A Biblical Judge of Israel</note> he came from Phoenicia into Greece, and there, in memory of Egyptian Thebes, he founded Boeotian Thebes, leaving Phoenicia to his brother Phoenix, from whom it obtained its name. <margin>Cadmus and Phoenix were Egyptian by origin</margin> Moreover, Egyptian men could not hand down any letters other than those they had learned from childhood in Egypt. Therefore, there should be no doubt that Cadmus was that first man who perfectly imbued the Greeks with Egyptian letters.

However, that there was some seed or some rudiment of these letters in Greece before Cadmus, and that there were already at that time most learned men in Greece, was clear from Philo in the preceding pages. He reports in the *Life of Moses* that the most learned men were called from Greece with great promises for his instruction; therefore, they either had their own letters at that time, or they received them from Cecrops, the first King of the Athenians, out of Egypt, or they were introduced by Inachus before him. Whence it is probable that the fable later emerged (that the Greeks had letters before Cadmus); for Cecrops himself was an Egyptian, nearly a century older than Cadmus, and a *contemporary* <note>original: "συγχρονος"</note> of Moses, according to Eusebius. <margin>Why Cecrops, King of the Athenians, was called "two-natured"</margin> Therefore, according to Tzetzes, he was called *two-natured* <note>original: "διφνης" - often interpreted as half-man, half-serpent, but here explained as bilingual</note> because he was equally skilled in the Greek and Egyptian languages. Pausanias is the authority that he also transferred the *office of the council* <note>original: "Βυλαρχαν"</note> from Egypt into Greece, along with other ceremonies; concerning which Tzetzes also sings thus:

->*Cecrops was the first King of all Attica,*<-
->*The first who was called "two-natured,"*<-
->*Having the stature of two great men in length,*<-
->*Or because he was learned in the Greek and Egyptian tongues.*<-

Cecrops was the first King of all Attica, and the first who was called *two-natured*, for the reason that he had the size of *two men* in length, and because he was skilled in the Greek and Egyptian languages. <margin>Letters</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII
## BOOK II. ON INSTRUCTION

It is clear from what has been said that Greek letters first originated from the Egyptians, concerning which I have written most extensively in my *Oedipus* <note>referring to Kircher’s work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. However, whether the Greek language also proceeded from the Egyptian, someone might rightly doubt; in my *Prodromus* <note>referring to his *Prodromus Coptus*</note> in **chapter four, I asserted the affirmative**. But, eventually becoming better informed by daily experience, I have found that the Egyptian language is one of the mother tongues, **self-grown** <note>original: *αὐτοφυῆ*</note>, having no affinity with any other, at least as far as can be gathered from its idiom, conjugation, and the inflection of nouns. Nor should we be moved by words savoring of **peculiarity** <note>original: *ἰδιωτισμὸν*</note> or Greek terms occurring here and there in the Lexicon. Indeed, I teach at length elsewhere that the mixing of such words with Coptic terms first happened during the times of Alexander the Great and the other Kings descending from the Ptolemaic **lineage** who held power in Egypt. This occurred through the frequent commerce that took place between them and the Greeks traveling back and forth over a space of three hundred years and more; and the Coptic authorities consulted by me on this matter affirm the very same thing.

Therefore, I would not wish my words in the *Coptic Prodromus* to be understood in the sense that I was asserting that the Greek language stands in the same relation to the Egyptian as, for example, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language does to Hebrew, or Italian to Latin, as some have thought. No one, unless unskilled in the said languages, will deny that the latter is the daughter of the Latin language, and the former of the Hebrew. For I do not feel that Greek drew its origin immediately from Egyptian; much less would I think the Egyptian language should be called a corrupted Greek. Rather, anyone who compares one with the other **without prejudice** <note>original: *ἀνειξίθιεπς* (likely a typo for *ἀνεξετάστως* or similar, meaning without careful examination, though Kircher uses it to mean impartial comparison)</note> will know that the entire similarity of each to the other happened from a mixing of words, as I have said. For some languages can use the same words used by another language, even if they themselves differ in substance by "the whole span of heaven," as they say. Thus German intersperses many Latin, Italian, and French words; Latin also willingly adopts Greek words, yet each remains very different from those languages from which it borrows, which you will find treated more fully elsewhere.

<margin>Whether the Egyptian language proceeded from the Greek, or the opposite.</margin>
<margin>The mixture of foreign languages occurring in Coptic.</margin>

But as the priests and the Egyptian rites gradually failed, so too this language gradually failed, until it seemed that scarcely a trace of it remained. This continued until, after the soul-saving advent of Christ, the Egyptian Gentiles, illuminated by the light of the Holy Gospel, collected the remaining fragments—the "planks," so to speak—of their native tongue. They attempted to restore it into a whole as best they could, so that the primeval language, marked by so many and such great signs of wisdom, would not perish entirely. Recording it in the register of learned idioms, they used it in the writing of sacred and ecclesiastical books. As for why they reserved only Coptic <note>The author refers to the Coptic language as the direct descendant of ancient Egyptian.</note>, and not Arabic or Greek, for sacred use, the reason was partly a natural affection for their native idiom, and partly so that by this native language, the Egyptian Church might be distinguished from the other Eastern Churches by a certain mark. Furthermore, it seemed wise to deliberately hide the mysteries of the Christian faith under their own language, lest they be contaminated by infidels. That the Maronite Syrians do this to this day with their own character (<insert>Karshuni</insert> <note>A method of writing Arabic using the Syriac alphabet.</note>) is more well-known than needs to be stated.

## DIGRESSION.

->*Whether the Egyptians occasionally interspersed characters and names of the common language, written in Egyptian characters, among their Hieroglyphic Symbols.*<-

Truly, we propose a great doubt to the curious reader at this point, to the dissolving of which I have applied myself with many years of study and investigation. It is remarkable how much it has tormented my mind; yet, from the continuous combination of hieroglyphic characters with one another, I believe I have finally achieved that by which I trust I can cut this Gordian knot.

I say, therefore, first: that the Egyptians did not use sacred and zoomorphic <note>animal-shaped</note> characters in such a way that they did not occasionally intersperse letters of the common alphabet and names among the hieroglyphic signs. Thus, hieroglyphic literature did not consist only of mystical and abstruse characters, but was composed also of common ones. I show this as follows: First, it has been clearly shown from the preceding pages that the Egyptian Alphabet was constructed by Mercury <note>The author identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Roman Mercury.</note> not by chance, but by a certain mystical reason, with letters derived from the limbs, position, gait, and actions of sacred animals. Indeed, the obelisks, tablets <note>original: "abaci"</note>, and almost all fragments found thus far testify that most hieroglyphics were transformed into these same letters.
