# CHAPTER VIII, BOOK II. ON THE INSTRUCTION OF THE ATTE <note>The "Atte" likely refers to a specific class of Egyptian symbolic or priestly knowledge discussed in the preceding chapters.</note>

Near the standing <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>A dog-headed baboon, often associated with the god Thoth.</note>, who is equipped with a <term>sistrum</term> <note>A sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual to ward off evil spirits.</note>, these words are placed: *Stipsichi*, which is to say, *the soul comes*. Below these, however, are the words; — *ti SD* — that is; *ti eeoi*, *the life of the water*. This is beautifully declared by the Nilotic vessel <note>A vessel used to measure or hold the sacred waters of the Nile.</note> placed separately; and indeed the Cynocephalus denotes the rising Moon, while the sistrum denotes the cutting away of malignant power—as if to say, let the soul come, or rather the Spirit of the sacred moisture, and let it dispel every harmful force; for in this way the waters will acquire their due life.

-> [A circular diagram containing various symbols. At the top, the text "EMΦΣΙ+". At the left, "IVE ΦM+". At the right, "IΦB". At the bottom, "ΦIC". In the center, there is a stylized face, a crescent moon, and a square symbol resembling a table or altar. Around the inner edge of the circle are several small, stylized animal figures, including what appear to be cats and birds.] <-

A fifth example is found in a certain <term>Phylactery</term> <note>An amulet or charm worn for protection.</note>, which the man of immortal memory, Lord Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc <note>A famous 17th-century French scholar and antiquarian.</note>, once sent to me to be interpreted. In its center, the Sun and Moon are seen enclosed within a gate, which refers to <unclear>pi</unclear> Coptos <note>Likely referring to the city of Coptos or a specific Coptic linguistic root.</note>; this gate is surrounded on four sides by four hieroglyphic statues of the kind commonly met with on all obelisks. To each of these, Egyptian names are attached as follows: *eeph d t*, *p eeph t*, and *ph ic*, which are the names of the four cardinal quarters of the world. Finally, a serpent biting its own tail <note>The Ouroboros.</note> encompasses the entire arrangement of the diagrams. By this, they signify nothing other than the Sun and the Moon; the character is <term>monogrammos</term> <note>original: "μονοσεαμμος" - a single-letter or linear character</note>, and it signifies the same as the word *pac*, that is, *Lord*. Through the symbolic *pi* they intimate the gate of the worldly house; through the *O* the Sun, and through the *C* the Moon, according to the testimony of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who wrote on Egyptian symbols.</note> in the 5th book of the *Stromata*, following the script—namely that used by the Egyptians—appropriated to things or <term>kyriological</term> <note>original: "κυριολοχικω" - speaking or writing in a literal or primary sense.</note>. By the serpent biting its tail and formed into a circle, according to the testimony of Horapollo <note>An author of a treatise on hieroglyphs.</note>, they denote the mundane spirit surrounding all things, the Author of years and times, or of the age. By these things they have cleverly indicated that the lords of this worldly house and of time have been established by the supreme Spirit of the world—that is, the presiding Sun and Moon placed in the center—so that all parts of the world might participate in these kindly influences. Hence the *pi* is open below, to signify that the influence and emanation happen from the higher to the lower, and not the reverse. The *ph t*, however, together with the hieroglyphic statues assigned to each quarter, indicates the Spirits <note>Genii</note> presiding over those quarters, as the Egyptian names assigned to them clearly teach. But consider this diagram more fully explained in the supplement to the *Prodromus Coptus*, page 529.

Yet someone might rightly doubt at this point why, in phylacteries, tablets, coins, and hieroglyphic statues, these names are only occasionally found inserted, yet no name of this kind is ever seen on obelisks except through the most abstruse transformation. I answer: since the obelisks were the work of priests alone, they recorded in them whatever most profound mysteries would be a source of admiration for posterity; as these were intended for a religious understanding, away from the intellect of the profane...

<page-num>149</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IX.</header>

# AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

Just as they were bound by oath to keep the readings hidden, they also forbade, with the greatest care, that anything common or accessible to the unlearned masses should be placed within them. However, since not only priests but also commoners applied themselves to the making of statues, tablets, and amulets, it is not surprising that in these objects, pure Egyptian names are occasionally found interspersed with hieroglyphics.

It is clear, therefore, from this discourse, that the Egyptians did not mix the common language with hieroglyphics—not because they lacked characters other than hieroglyphics (as some wrongly claim), but lest they should seem to diminish their sublime concepts, expressed through mysterious hieroglyphic literature, by using common elements. But since we shall deal with these matters formally in our work *Oedipus* <note>A reference to Kircher’s major work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, God willing, it suffices here to have indicated them in a few words.

## CHAPTER IX.

*What Hermapion achieved in the interpretation of the Obelisk of Psammetichus, and whether he reached the true sense of the Egyptian Priests.*

After so many centuries, we read of only one man who attempted the interpretation of the Obelisks; and that was Hermapion. The obelisk which he undertook to interpret for the sake of Augustus, during whose time he lived, was the one Pliny calls the "Sennefertean," erected by King Psammetichus. This is the same one formerly placed in the Circus Maximus by Augustus, and which is now seen, most richly adorned with hieroglyphics, before the church of the Blessed Virgin, commonly called *del Popolo* on the Via Flaminia. Ammianus Marcellinus cites the interpretation of this in his book of histories; but, so that we may form a more solid judgment concerning such an interpretation, we shall first present his translation in this place.

The words of the aforementioned Ammianus are these: *Later ages transferred others, one of which was erected in the Vatican, another in the gardens of Sallust, and two at the monument of Augustus. Regarding the text of the marks on the Obelisk, we have set it down below in Greek letters, following the book of Hermapion.*

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus.</margin>
<margin>Hermapion, interpreter of the Sennefertean Obelisk.</margin>

And this is the interpretation of Hermapion; which, when we examined it with a more exact scale against the hieroglyphics carved on the Flaminian Obelisk, we found only that which we had long suspected: that this interpretation can stand by no reasoning whatsoever. And lest we do an injustice to an Author celebrated by the monuments of so many writers, we shall place the beginning of the four sides of the said Obelisk before the eyes of the curious Reader, so that—when the words are compared with the figures—it may be revealed to lovers of truth how ineptly they agree, how with difficulty they cohere, and finally how poorly everything stands <unclear>as a heap of dust</unclear>. Hence, I strongly suspect that Hermapion, in place of an interpretation of the Obelisk, substituted some other inscription—acting all the more boldly because there were so few, indeed scarcely anyone, who could accuse him of imposture.
<margin>Hermapion's interpretation is false, and why.</margin>

In the Obelisk, therefore, four things must be considered: first is the Argument or theme of the Obelisk; second, the figures; third, the four sides; fourth, the order and placement of the figures. We show by these reasons that Hermapion touched upon none of these. And first, indeed, it has been said extensively in various preceding places that the Argument of Obelisks by no means contains the praises, victories, triumphs, and extraordinary deeds of Kings; for since the hieroglyphic teaching was obscure, enigmatic, and mysterious, far removed from the understanding of the profane—

# CHAPTER IX. BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION
<note>The header "INSTITVTIONB" in the original is likely a truncation of "INSTITVTIONIBVS" (Institutions) or "INSTITVTIONE" (Instruction/Education).</note>

...those to whom the care of sacred things was committed were skilled: and they were forbidden to hold these matters in anything but the greatest silence, or to disclose them to any other person outside their own order under penalty of death. Certainly, the obelisks could not contain the mere deeds of Kings. Therefore, in the opinion of all, a man would be reckless—not to say foolish—who, intending to hand down the magnificent deeds of some Prince or King to posterity (either for imitation or to excite admiration of virtue in descendants and preserve their memory), would use an impenetrable kind of writing for things that, by their very nature, seek the light. We can form a similar judgment regarding the Egyptians if their monuments contained the praises and deeds of Kings. 

<margin>Herodotus's argument regarding the obelisks</margin> Whenever, therefore, Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Pliny, and others say that the monuments of the Kings contained their deeds, the expenses incurred for various buildings and expeditions undertaken throughout the world, and even the costs spent on garlic and onions <note>A reference to the famous passage in Herodotus regarding the food supplies for the pyramid builders</note>, they by no means understand this to refer to the obelisks. Rather, they understood it to refer to the pyramids, or the columns, or the tablets and stones inserted into the walls of the temples. For upon columns and similar structures, they were accustomed to carve famous deeds and histories in the common character used by the Egyptians, which we call Coptic <note>The author identifies the "vulgar" or demotic script with Coptic, the final stage of the Egyptian language</note>. You may see many of this kind in Herodotus and Diodorus. But on the Obelisks, they exhibited only ideal and intellectual matters that are difficult to grasp, and these under the darkest veils of figures, as will appear in what follows. 

Since, therefore, Hermapion <note>An ancient translator whose Greek version of an obelisk inscription was preserved by Ammianus Marcellinus</note> describes nothing other than the praises and glory of King Rameses on the said obelisk, 

<margin>The praises of King Rameses cannot be contained on Hermapion's Obelisk.</margin> it immediately appears from this very heading that the interpretation cannot correspond in the least to the mind of the Egyptian priests. But let us come to the figures. Where you see at the beginning of the obelisk, human figures are placed, signifying the actions of those sacrificing by their position and gestures; as these correspond to the four parts of the world, each is seen equipped with different things. 

There follow afterward on each side three hawks <note>original: "accipitres"</note>, distinguished by headdresses <note>original: "tutulis"</note>, as appears here in the figure; for it suffices to have placed the figures of one side here. These are followed by as many oxen, and afterward four extended arms; so much so that on each side, three rows and series or columns are contained. Since these contain the mysteries and secrets of the twelve geniuses <note>Spiritual beings or protective deities</note> of the world indicated through the four sides of the Obelisk, let anyone who possesses even a tiny grain of judgment see now how the interpretation of Hermapion can be adapted to them. 

<margin>Another error in the interpretation.</margin> For since there are twelve hawks and as many Oxen carved in the circuit, which undoubtedly signify one and the same thing differing only in various effects, he ought to have named the same thing twelve times; since he did not do this, and not even a trace of these things shines through, his interpretation will deservedly be judged false. 

Added to this is that while there are four sides on the Obelisk, he [Hermapion] posits six; it is impossible for the interpretation to agree with the facts; but if anyone should say...

<header>CHAPTER IX</header>

# AND THE STRUCTURE OF THE HIEROGLYPHICS.

<note>The author is discussing the physical layout of an obelisk and why previous translations do not match the visual evidence.</note>
...indicates that he described three rows contained on only one or two sides, yet even so the difficulty is not resolved, since even then the words do not match the figures. And indeed, on the first side which faces the southern region, he describes not three but five rows; while on the side facing the East, he describes only one row, as is evident in the context of the interpretation—how these can be made to agree, I do not see. Therefore, the entire sequence of the interpretation is confused and *uneven*. Furthermore, the words of the interpretation attached to the individual rows are so abhorrent to the style and character of the hieroglyphics that it appears at first glance that it cannot be true, being so dissonant and remote from the teachings of the <term>Hieromystae</term> <note>Priests or initiates who guarded the secrets of sacred symbols</note>. For what figures could possibly show King Ramesses? What figures could show such glorious epithets or such a beautiful construction of words? It is impossible to find them. For what does Ramesses, or Apollo, or Vulcan, or the son of Heron have in common with the rites of the sacrificers, with hawks, oxen, and the rest? I do not see it. Added to this is the fact that those words, by which Hermapion explains the individual hieroglyphic rows, are far too few to signify such great matters as were governed under the hieroglyphics. For I would dare to solemnly affirm that such a great mass of hidden knowledge is contained in each of the twelve rows of the obelisk that I will not say a page, but not even an entire volume could sufficiently explain it according to its dignity. All of this will be more than sufficiently proven in the interpretation of the Sannefertean obelisk <note>Likely referring to the Lateran Obelisk</note>, which we have reserved for our *Oedipus* <note>A reference to the author's major work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. From this entire discourse, therefore, unless I am mistaken, it is clearly evident that the interpretation of Hermapion produced by Ammianus Marcellinus can stand by no reasoning. This is what we had undertaken to prove at the beginning. Whether Hermapion copied this description from some other Egyptian monument, which was later falsely attributed to this obelisk, let him who wishes believe it; our task was to demonstrate in these few words that this cited interpretation of Hermapion by no means fits or can be adapted to the hieroglyphics of the obelisk. Thus, if detractors should hurl this interpretation at us, it would be known what should be decided concerning it. Similar interpretations are found in the apocryphal Berosus of Annius of Viterbo <note>A famous 15th-century literary forgery</note>, but since those were fabricated by the author himself, I judge them unworthy of wasting time and paper in citing them. Of this same sort is Volaterranus’s interpretation of the discovered Etruscan letters, which appeared not long ago. Another "Egyptian Oedipus" in later times was Herwart, who, having attempted the interpretation of the *Bombine* tablet <note>The Mensa Isiaca or Bembine Tablet</note>, managed the business so unhappily that I greatly wonder what came into the mind of that distinguished man, that he should have devised an interpretation so discordant with the intention of the Egyptians. The title of the book is: *The Admirable Mysteries of Ethnic Theology Disclosed*. There, the author [claims] that the Loadstone <note>The Magnet</note> was worshipped as a GOD everywhere by the most ancient nations, and that the art by which navigations were established by means of the Magnet throughout the entire World was hidden by the ancient Egyptian priests under the coverings of Gods and Goddesses, and under the bark of other similar fables, with the greatest zeal...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book II, Chapter IX regarding the history of the magnet and its supposed use in antiquity. The author is specifically addressing the theories of Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg.</meta>

# CHAPTER IX. BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION

<margin>The Bembine Tablet does not contain the mysteries of the magnet nor the art of navigation</margin>He endeavors to demonstrate with all his might that [the magnetic art] was hidden. And first, indeed, through that Bembine Tablet <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs once owned by Cardinal Bembo</note>—celebrated throughout the whole world for its hieroglyphics—he suggests that the ancient Egyptians indicated nothing other than navigation throughout the entire world, performed by the help of the magnetic compass and the aid of a nautical or hydrographic chart. He goes so far as to claim that by the characters of that hieroglyphic tablet, they intended to signify nothing else but the regions of the world and the winds. To prove this, however, it is a wonder how he exhausts himself in twisting the entire history of antiquity to his purpose, and how distortedly and forcedly he labors to apply anything and everything—whether they fit or not—to his subject matter. I am greatly amazed that a man otherwise wise, most skilled in antiquity, and of such varied reading, could even conceive of these things in his mind.

From this, he thinks the *Iynges* <note>original: "λυγγας" - magical spinning wheels or charms</note> of Zoroaster are the Rhombs <note>compass roses or directional lines</note> of the winds, just as he thinks those famous *apsides* <note>original: "αψινας"</note>—the "path of the traveler" <note>original: "δὸν τὲ ἠρεψινος" - likely a corruption of a Greek phrase for a celestial or terrestrial path</note> derived from the Pythagoreans—are the four principal regions of the world. Furthermore, he believes the mysteries of magnetic navigation were indicated symbolically through Ormuzd and Ahriman <note>original: "Orimafium & Arimanium" - the dualistic deities of Zoroastrianism</note>, the Zoroastrian deities; as well as through the handled cross of Serapis <note>The Ankh</note>; and even through that health-bringing *Tau*. He opines that this magnetic navigation was prefigured in the rites of Orpheus, the mysteries of Isis and Osiris, the sacrifices of Mithras, the Zoroastrian stone *Mnizurus*, the bones of Europa enclosed in Ellotia, the chariot of Jupiter and Neptune, the Bulls of Erynnis and Aeëtes, the doe of Hercules, the eagle of Jupiter, the dragons of Medea and Triptolemus, the caves and grottoes of the Nymphas, the labyrinths, and the pyramids of the Egyptians—in a word, in every single fable.

Certainly, when I first examined this new interpretation of the Bembine Tablet, I was not a little astonished. Since it is the specialty of my profession to restore the abstruse hieroglyphic discipline of the ancient Egyptians from Oriental books with all my strength (according to the measure of my talent), and since I recognize that the Egyptians had other ends in mind for establishing such symbols than the "potential" <note>original: "δυναμικῶς" - dynamically or potentially</note> magnetic art, I could not help but disapprove of this interpretation of the tablet, which wanders so far from the truth. Although I have decided to refute it in its proper places, the occasion and the subject matter itself seemed to demand, as if by its own right, that it be refuted here in a few words.

<margin>Refutation of Herwart's interpretation.</margin>I show by four reasons that the use of the magnet in nautical business was never known to the ancient Egyptians and other Orientals. First, if the nautical compass <note>original: "nautica pyxis"</note> had been known to the Egyptians, some traces of it would undoubtedly be found among the hieroglyphic symbols. But in the entire scope of hieroglyphics—as will be clear to anyone examining my *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's own work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>—absolutely no ship appears except for the *Baris* alone (which is a certain sacred type of vessel in which they record that Isis crossed the Nile, and which for that reason alone found a place among the sacred symbols). It is more certain that no other symbol appears which could represent a nautical compass or the rhombs of the winds than it is that it should be said. Why, then, if it had been known to them, would they not have placed it among their sacred symbols, as they did many other things of lesser importance? Second, the Egyptians were not even greatly intent upon navigation...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher refutes the theory of Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, who claimed that ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs and myths were secret codes for magnetic navigation. Kircher argues that the Bembine Tablet and other antiquities have religious meanings rather than technological ones.</summary>

# CHAPTER IX.

->AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS.<-

<margin>The Egyptians were not given to navigation.</margin>
...that they were [contented]; from this it is argued, that being satisfied with a most abundant land and accustomed to the worship of their ancestral Gods, they looked down upon almost all other regions outside of Egypt as rude, uncultivated, and unfit for their inhabitants. For this reason, according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD), a Greek philosopher and biographer.</note>, they established a law by which all travel outside of Egypt was forbidden; the causes and reasons for the passage of this law we explain elsewhere. Added to this is the fact that the Egyptians, led by a certain religious feeling, abhorred the sea, as Plutarch beautifully teaches in his book *On Isis and Osiris*. Hence Pythagoras, having been taught by the Egyptians, calls the sea "the tear of Saturn" <note>original: "Saturni lachrymam"</note>; for the Egyptians believe, according to Xenophon, that the face of the world is in that part where the Sun rises, the right hand is where the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note> blows, and the left where the South Wind <note>original: "Notus"</note> blows. 

<margin>The Sea is the tear of Saturn.</margin>
From this, the Egyptians say—not incorrectly—of the Nile, that it rises from the left and perishes on the right. For the Nile, flowing from the South (the left part of the world), is absorbed in the North as it mixes with the sea. Therefore, the priests shun the sea, which they also call "the foam of Typhon" <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and storms.</note>, just as they call salt its offspring; for this same reason, they are not accustomed to place salt on the table. 

<margin>Which parts are the right and left of the world according to the Egyptians.</margin>
Indeed, for the same reason, they shun seafaring and maritime men as if they were inhuman, cruel, and fierce sons of Typhon, sustaining their lives from the sea and from onions (which they abominated as being contrary to their goddess Isis, as Lucian <note>original: "Lutianus"</note> notes). They also hate fish so much that, according to Clement of Alexandria in the 5th book of the *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromat." referring to the *Stromata*.</note>, it was adopted by them as the hieroglyphic for hatred itself. It is therefore sufficiently clear from what has been said that the Egyptians, prohibited by a certain religious scruple, were not as devoted to navigation as the previously cited Author thinks.

Thirdly, since the Egyptians were the first in the world to flourish with the praise of wisdom, and invited all other nations to themselves—indeed, they alone hid the sacraments of recondite wisdom concerning GOD, Angels, Demons, Spirits <note>original: "Genijs"</note>, Heroes, and their attraction, concerning the nature of things and the world, Medicine, Astrology, sacrifices, and other similar matters under abstruse hieroglyphic characters of this kind—these were known to no others except the Leaders of the kingdom conspicuous for wisdom and age. Of these secrets, and indeed of the entire hieroglyphic literature, the Bembine Tablet <note>The *Tabula Bembina* or Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian mysteries, once owned by Cardinal Bembo.</note> is a kind of compendium. 

<margin>The nature of the nautical art.</margin>
Who does not see now that the mysteries of the Magnetic nautical art <note>A reference to the use of the magnetic compass in navigation.</note> hidden under symbols of this kind are repugnant not only to the genius of the Egyptians but also to their historical monuments? Indeed, so far is this from being asserted, that the contrary must rather be held. For either the nautical art at that time was public or private: if the latter, then it is false that a journey of the entire world was accomplished by its aid, since modern voyages teach more than enough that such navigation could not be done except at public and vast expense. If it was public, what necessity compelled the Egyptians to veil an art so public—which, among the Mathematical arts in Egypt at that time (according to Clement), was almost common and in the hands of vile men of the lowest sort, such as Sailors are—and which was even abominable to them, as was said a little before? Why would they shroud a necessary and common art, serving only public utility, in so many abstruse symbols devised with such great genius? Therefore, other [mysteries lie] under these...

<margin>Why the Egyptians displayed their knowledge on obelisks.</margin>
Hence the wise men of the Egyptians, so that they might leave behind an admiration of themselves among posterity, carved upon those huge stones of prodigious size the hidden mysteries of nature, the commentaries of astrological predictions, the ravings and vanities of the divining arts, and the rest of the sacred rites of their magical wisdom. They fashioned these stones in such a way that the containing object itself, by its mysterious shape, would immediately indicate how many mysteries lay hidden within the content.

<margin>The origin of obelisks.</margin>
Among other stones, they chiefly chose those which, by their shape and color, appropriately imitated the solar rays, such as the masses of obelisks or pyramids made from *mesomphalos* stone <note>original: "μεσομϕάλῳ" — likely referring to a central or "omphalos" stone, often associated with the center of the world or specific granite types from Syene</note>. Truly, since the Egyptians placed a great part of their recondite philosophy in the shape of the obelisk, it seemed best to first explain what that shape is and what mysteries they represented through it, so that the mysteries may be more clearly revealed through these introductory explanations.

Therefore, having invoked the Principle of Principles, and having appeased God, the giver of arts, science, and all good things, and having called upon the favor of the most holy Mother of God, the thrice-venerable Mother, and the other inhabitants of Heaven, we begin our explanation.

## DISTINCTION I.
### The hieroglyphic mysteries of the Pyramid or Obelisk.

<margin>Definition of an Obelisk.</margin>
In the first book, we stated that our hieroglyphic pyramid or obelisk—according to the definer Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 17—is nothing other than *a certain very hard stone, gradually rising to a great height in the shape of a turning-post <term>meta: a conical goal post used in Roman circuses</term>, lofty and thinning out little by little to imitate a ray of light; it is square in appearance, extended to a point at the top, smoothed by the hand of a craftsman, and distinguished by innumerable marks of forms, devised by the authority of the ancients to demonstrate the beginnings of wisdom then emerging.* If we bring this description back to the mathematical anvil, we shall find that an obelisk is nothing other than that pyramid which the Greeks call a *four-sided obelisk* <note>original: "τετράεδρον ὀβελίσκον"</note> and the Latins call an acute pyramid; and that it is four-sided and truncated, lest it be raised more than is proper by its own extension.

<margin>The logic of Pyramids.</margin>
According to the definition of the moderns, this is nothing other than a solid figure contained by planes, established from one plane to a single point. It is clear, moreover, that all the planes by which a pyramid is contained are triangles, since they all tend toward a single point—except for the plane opposite to that point toward which they all tend. For nothing prevents this base plane from being a triangle, a quadrangle, or a pentagon, from which the entire pyramid takes its name: for any pyramid contains as many triangles as the said plane contains angles or sides. From these things it is clearly evident that the figure of the obelisk in the school of Mathematicians...

<page-num>161</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER ON THE SAME SUBJECT.</header>

### AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

...that they admit no difference from the figure of a pyramid; as is also clearly shown in the following figure. For if the sides of an obelisk were extended to their furthest limit, you would produce a four-sided *acute-angled* <note>original: "ὀξυγώνιον"</note> pyramid, which is in no way distinct from any other pyramid of equal base, being founded upon the same base, except that the latter is obtuse-angled and the former acute-angled. Between an obelisk and an acute-angled quadrilateral pyramid, however, there is only this difference: that the latter possesses the figure of a whole and complete pyramid, while the former possesses that of a truncated one. Hence, I would wish for greater skill in mathematics among those authors who establish a specific difference between these mentioned figures. 

<margin>Why the Egyptians used truncated pyramids.</margin>
Now, as to why the wise men of the Egyptians used obelisks, or truncated acute-angled pyramids, three principal reasons are usually brought forward. The first and most important is that this structure, with its pointed peak rising gradually in the manner of a spit <note>The author refers to an "obelus," a roasting spit or needle.</note>, might more exactly and elegantly imitate the rays of the Sun (in whose honor it was erected). 

The second reason is taken from optics: an obtuse pyramid would be unsuitable for distinctly representing hieroglyphic writing to those looking from a distance. This is because the sides, which by their steeper slope gradually meet at a point, would be too far removed from the perpendicular line of sight; not falling correctly into the view, the things inscribed there could only be discerned with difficulty according to the laws of optics. This defect and inconvenience was repaired by the sides of the acute-angled pyramids, which fall closer to the perpendicular of the visual line and thus present themselves more correctly to the eye. 

The third reason was that they found this figure, among all solid shapes, to be both the primary and the most mystical, as we shall show at length in what follows. Furthermore, this truncated pyramid is called an obelisk. 

<margin>Etymology of Obelisk.</margin>
The word *obeliskos* <note>original: "ὀβελίσκος"</note> refers to an iron instrument which is thick in its first part and gradually diminishes until it ends in a sharp point. It is therefore not inappropriately called *Aguglia* <note>Italian for "needle."</note> by the Italians, as if you were to say a needle like a spit, on which meat is customarily roasted over a fire; "and we shall roast the fatty innards on hazel-wood spits" <note>A reference to Virgil's Georgics.</note>. In likeness to this, the Sabines also called the weapon they used in wars a *veru* (spit). *The Sabines fight with both the dagger and the spit.* <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid: "Et tereti pugnant mucrone veruque Sabelli."</note> 

It is called by the diminutive name *obeliskos* <note>small spit</note>, not *obelos* <note>large spit</note>, after the Greek custom; just as they call the little stars, bars, or wheels—which they consider little gods or Pans—*obelisks, little baskets, or amulets* <note>original: "ὀβελίσκοι, καλαθίσκοι, βασκάνιοι"</note>. 

<margin>The purpose of obelisks.</margin>
Finally, the principal end which the Egyptians had in the erection of obelisks was to worship Osiris and Isis—that is, the Sun and the Moon—in these figures, as if by a certain mystical representation of rays, silently suggesting by this honor the magnitude of the benefits received through the rays of these secondary Gods. 

<margin>Why they chose such hard stone.</margin>
Furthermore, so that the color of the mystical figure would not be inconsistent, they did not choose just any stone. To signify the perpetuity of the Sun, they chose the hardest stone, endowed with a certain adamantine strength and power, incorruptible by any injury of air or fire—as appears from the nearly innumerable fragments of this kind to be seen in Rome. They chose that stone which they called *pyroeidēlon* <note>original: "πυροειδῆλον"</note>, that is, of a certain fiery color.

That most obelisks were dedicated to the Sun is so well-worn a fact from Herodotus, Diodorus, Pliny, and other authors everywhere, that I consider it superfluous to say anything further on it here. However, I would not want this to be understood only regarding that material, sensible Sun; but also regarding that supramundane, archetypal, insensible, and immaterial Sun. Hence I said *most* obelisks, since many were also dedicated to the supreme, triform Deity; as will be clear regarding this *Pamphilian* <note>Referring to the Pamphili Obelisk now in the Piazza Navona</note> obelisk of ours from what follows. Regarding their first inventor, there is greater disagreement and controversy among authors. To reconcile these, it must be known (as was also stated in the first book) that some make the first inventor of obelisks Mercury, surnamed *Thrice-Greatest* <note>original Greek: "Τρισμέγιστον" (Trismegiston)</note>; others say Sesostris, Psammeticus, or other Kings of the Egyptians. 

<margin>Genebrard on Columns, folio 6.</margin> Diodorus Siculus, in Book 3, attributes the first erection of pyramidal columns to Semiramis, and says that a huge stone 150 feet long and 24 feet wide was extracted from the mountains of Armenia and placed by Semiramis in the principal square of Babylon, as a testimony of the power and strength of the first age flourishing again after the Flood <note>original: "Cataclysmum"</note>. Moreover, Josephus testifies in Book 7 of the *Antiquities of the Jews* that in the first ages of the world, there was a custom of carving deeds upon stones, which he attributes to the descendants of Seth <note>The text says "Sem" (Shem), but Josephus refers to the children of Seth</note>. These are his words: 

*When Adam had foretold to his sons the destruction of all things—one to come by the power of fire, the other by the force and multitude of waters—they, fearing lest the discipline of Celestial things which they had first discovered should slip away from men or perish before it came to notice, made two columns: one of brick, the other of stone. On both they inscribed what they had discovered, so that if the one built of brick were ruined by storms, the stone one would remain, the traces of which are still preserved in Syria. If, however, the stone column were consumed by fire, the brick one would remain.*

<margin>The ancients carved their arts on columns before the flood.</margin> All of which is confirmed by Berosus the Babylonian in Book 1 of his *Antiquities*, Chapter 4. *Then,* he says, *many preached and carved into stones that destruction of the world which was to come.* And in Book 3: *When the ground was dried and the earth parched, Noah with his family descended from Mount Gordyaeus into the underlying plain full of corpses, which to this day they call Myriadam—that is, of the eviscerated men—and he inscribed the event upon a monument.* Joseph Ben Gorion agrees with this in Book 1 of his *Antiquities* with these words:

# CHAPTER X. BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION
# [OF HIEROGLYPHICS]

As to the person they establish, it is easily seen that Mythra can be none other than Misraim <note>The biblical Mizraim, son of Ham, considered the progenitor of the Egyptians</note>, whom Holy Scripture testifies was the first possessor of Egypt. We would have to assume he abdicated his kingdom to another, which is unlikely for a man consumed by an uncontrollable desire for glory and rule. But let us hear Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century bishop and historian</note>, who seems to confirm our opinion in clear words when he says in Book 1 of his *History*: *The firstborn of Ham was Cush; he was the master of the entire magic art under the devil's instruction and the first inventor of idolatry. He was the first to set up a small statue to be worshipped, and he falsely claimed by magic arts that stars and fire fell from heaven. When he passed over to the Persians, he was called Zoroaster by them, which they interpret as "Living Star."* Gregory drew this opinion from the fourth book of the *Recognitions of Saint Clement* <note>An early Christian romance/theological work attributed to Clement of Rome</note>; namely, that the Persians trace their lineage from one of the sons of Ham called Misraim, whom they called Zoroaster (meaning "Living Star") after his death. Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of Greek philosophers</note> also notes in Book 1 that this Zoroaster signifies one who sacrifices to the stars.

<margin>Author of the *Scholastic History*</margin>
The author of the *Scholastic History* <note>Peter Comestor, a famous medieval theologian</note> also calls Ninus <note>A legendary king of Assyria</note> "Ham" in his commentary on Genesis chapter 39. He claims Ham was still living and reigning and was called Zoroaster, the inventor of the magic art. He allegedly wrote this art, along with the seven liberal arts, upon fourteen columns—seven of bronze and seven of brick—to protect them against the double destruction of the world by water and fire which he feared was coming.

<margin>St. Chrysostom</margin>
Chrysostom also says in his *Borysthenic Oration* that Zoroaster lived in the time of Ninus and Abraham, when the sacred pages testify that the cult of fire flourished most strongly. There is, therefore, a great diversity among authors concerning Zoroaster, Ninus, Belus, Cush, and Misraim; because they confound one with another and mix individual details, they have rendered historical texts almost inextricable. Therefore, so that something certain may be established in this great confusion of names, we say briefly (as was shown in Book 1, Chapter 2):

<margin>1. Zoroaster as Ham</margin>
Zoroaster, who first taught the Persians magic and the cult of fire, was Ham <note>The son of Noah</note>. He was also called Belus and Saturn. From him, his son Misraim was instructed in all the arts and magical superstitions. Because of the wondrous enchantments Misraim performed with these arts, he was called by the Egyptians "the other Zoroaster" and "the Egyptian Saturn."

<margin>2. Misraim</margin>
Misraim, son of Ham, was the first author and origin of Egyptian superstition. Because he appeared to bring down the sun and stars to earth through magical superstitions, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, translator of the Vulgate</note> (in Book 2 *Against Jovinianus*) testifies that he was said to be transformed into the Sun by the mere heat of his lust. They called him the "Living Star," and in the Egyptian language, they called him Osiris—that is, <term>polyophthalmon</term> <note>original Greek: πολυόφθαλμον, meaning "many-eyed"</note> or "the one with many eyes."

<margin>Misraim or Mythras is confused with Osiris</margin>
Therefore, among the Egyptians, Zoroaster, Misraim, Mythra, Osiris, and Vulcan all signify one and the same thing. He was called Zoroaster after the name of his father, Ham; in the Chaldean language, this sounds the same as "the hidden image of a star": <gloss>Tzurath Ash Sethar</gloss> <note>original: צורת אש סתר</note>, that is, "the figure of hidden fire," as is demonstrated at length in Book 1, Chapter 2, where we said that Zoroaster was the leader of the Perso-Medes.

<margin>Also called Vulcan</margin>
He was called Mythra or Mesra from a corruption of the name Misraim; Osiris because of the Sun into which they believed he was transformed; and Vulcan because of his discovery of the use of fire.

<margin>Osiris the "many-named"</margin>
Regarding this, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> says in Book 1, Chapter 1:

> Just as the same Osiris, because of his various effects, is called by the Greeks various names: Jupiter, Bacchus, Mercury, Hercules...

...is called. And this was that Mythras, who delivered to the Egyptians the first foundations of the sciences—such as Astrology, Magic, and other profane arts—inscribed upon stones. He did so under the guidance and counsel of Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure conflated with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with inventing writing and all sciences</note>, who was remarkably still alive at that time when:

> *Memphis did not yet know how to weave the river-reeds into books;*
> *only on stones did birds, wild beasts,*
> *and carved animals preserve magical tongues.*
<note>original: "Nondum flumineas Memphis contexere biblos / Nouerat, & in ſaxis tantum volucreſque feraſque / Sculptaque ſeruabant magicas animalia linguas." — A quote from the Roman poet Lucan’s Pharsalia, describing a time before papyrus was invented.</note>

<margin>Mercury Trismegistus, the author of hieroglyphic literature.</margin>
The Priests and Philosophers who followed them gradually built upon the foundations of the arts they had laid, eventually bringing them to such perfection that, seizing the whole world in admiration of them, they easily drew others toward what they believed to be the true method of philosophizing. For since the depth of the sciences flourishing in Egypt was no less than their power, it is no wonder that among such a great multitude of people as was there—whether due to the natural fertility, goodness, and pleasantness of the soil, or because of the immense commerce they conducted not only with those nearby but also with foreigners—there were those who practiced the invention of arts and other things necessary for human life.

<margin>Praise of Egypt in the invention of things and the tradition of the arts.</margin>
Therefore, as the records of historians testify, the invention of various arts was attributed to no other nation in the same way. For besides the mechanical arts—sculpture, painting, molding, and architecture—they also cultivated those we call the "liberal arts": arithmetic, astrology, music, and geometry. Furthermore, they practiced magic, medicine, and finally the whole of theoretical and practical philosophy. We read that after the Egyptians, no other nation either knew or practiced these things to such an extent.

<margin>Arithmetic. Geometry. Astrology. Music. Medicine. Theology.</margin>
And indeed, **Arithmetic** was born because of their unique commerce with foreigners; **Geometry** emerged because of the annual and new measurement of field boundaries, which were obscured by the silt of the flooding Nile that buried them <note>Because the Nile flood erased property lines every year, the Egyptians had to "re-measure" the earth, hence the Greek name "Geo-metry"</note>; **Astrology** because of the perpetually clear face of the Egyptian sky, which was most suitable for observing the movements of the stars; **Music** because of the harmonic course of the heavens and the great and abundant supply of reeds <note>papyrus or Arundo donax</note> suitable for musical modulations; **Medicine** from the continuous scrutiny of the virtues of natural things; and **Theology**, having finally arisen from the order of things flowing from one source and returning to one principle of all things—the "unmoved mover" <note>An Aristotelian concept of God as the primary cause of all motion who is not Himself moved</note> as the cause of causes—made the greatest progress. All these sciences, organized into a proper method, reached posterity through that most celebrated Mercury Trismegistus.

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> himself testifies in clear words that Mercury also devised hieroglyphic symbols to hide a more sublime philosophy from the reading of the profane. He states: *Egyptian writers, believing all things to have been invented by Mercury, inscribed their works to him. Mercury presides over wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others went to the priests of the Egyptians; the dogmas of this book are of the Assyrians and Egyptians and come from the columns of Mercury; Pythagoras and Plato learned philosophy from the columns of Mercury in Egypt; the columns of Mercury are full of doctrines.* These things are so clear that no one can doubt them any longer. ## SECTION II.

### Concerning the mysteries of the Pyramid and the Obelisk

<margin>Among the Egyptians all things are full of mysteries.</margin>
Since, as Clement testifies in Book 6 of the *Stromata* <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian writer who documented Egyptian customs</note>, nothing was done among the Egyptians that was not filled with mystery—to such an extent, indeed, that even the houses, temples, tools, and garments which they wore in solemn processions for the worship of the Gods or in performing sacrifices, and even the nods and gestures they made, were something mystical signifying the highest matters. Certainly, we shall not think that it was by chance or without reason, or for the sake of decoration alone (as many wrongly feel), that they used obelisks <margin>The figure of the Obelisk is mysterious</margin> to represent their hieroglyphic wisdom to posterity. Rather, we believe that with the greatest zeal and a remarkable investigation of the mind, they wished to provide for themselves a figure which, being itself filled with mysteries, would correspond in every way to the mystical context of the symbols. That a four-sided pyramid is such a shape will be shown copiously in the following pages. 

For whatever the hierophants <note>The priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> noted down through the description of particular things expressed under symbols, they represented all of this universally on the exterior face of the Obelisk or Pyramid as if in a summary, or in the first principles of a stone inscription, summarized <note>original Greek: ἀνακεφαλαιωτικῶς (anakephalaiōtikōs) — meaning "recapitulated" or "summed up"</note>. So much so, that nothing is so hidden in the depths of nature that it does not seem prefigured here. And these are those greatest columns of which Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> speaks, in which—as if inside a Silenus <note>A "Silenus" refers to a statue that is rough or plain on the outside but contains beautiful, golden images of the gods within</note>—the greatest mysteries of astrology, geometry, music, arithmetic, theology, and the more recondite philosophy lie hidden. And from these columns, Pythagoras, Plato, and other philosophers among the Greeks learned their doctrine and the true method of philosophizing, as mentioned a little before...

For just as a pyramid, beginning from its highest peak as if from a point, proceeds through lines into surfaces and a body, gradually expanding in all directions, so the nature of all things proceeds from a single principle and fountain that cannot be divided—namely, from GOD the Supreme Architect. It then takes on various forms and spreads into various genera and species, yet it joins everything back to that apex and point from which all things flow and stream forth. By this, the original beginning of the world seems most excellently represented, by which all parts of the world were shaped and produced that appearance which we now see. For the world was once formless and muddy, not yet having attained the integrity of its form through the distinct marks of things; for neither had the earth established its center as the foundation of all things, nor was the perpetual motion of the heavens revolved in a certain seat, but all things lay motionless without the use of the Sun, languishing, weighed down by a sad silence. <margin>The world as a raw and unordered mass.</margin> Nothing else existed but the sluggishness of formless, diffused matter, before that principle from which all things are produced and established—bringing forth the healthy motion of life—gave the world back to the world, and distinguished the heaven from the earth, and the sea from the mainland. At which time the four first elements of things, from which as from a root and a principle of their kind everything is born, received their own order and proper form, represented by the square base of the pyramid. <margin>The four elements indicated by the four sides of the obelisk.</margin> Agazaël the Arab <note>Likely referring to the philosopher Al-Ghazali</note> gives another reason for the pyramid in his first book on *Judicial Astrology*, namely an astronomical one: For they say, he says, that in that celestial machine there is a circle under which the Sun and the rest of the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> complete their courses and circuits, and in which the life of all living things and the birth and death of natural things are placed, <margin>Agazaël the Arab.</margin> so much so that even Aristotle, in his book *On Generation and Corruption*, says that the cause of generation and corruption, and of all change or growth, is the approach and retreat of the Sun in that oblique circle, which astronomers have called the *zodiac* <note>original Greek: ζωδιακὸν, meaning "circle of animals"</note>, because the life of living things depends upon it. This circle, then, to which alone among the celestial circles he attributes width, is divided into twelve parts, or

### BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION
#### CHAPTER X.

<margin>
The distribution of the Zodiac and the individual parts of the Gods.

Iamblichus.

The distribution of the Zodiac and the Gods presiding over it.
</margin>

The Egyptians divide the **twelve-fold divisions** <note>original Greek: δωδεκαμόρια (*dodekamoria*); these are the twelve 30-degree segments of the Zodiac</note>, which they call "mansions," and they place over each of them individual angels or spirits, which they call "lesser gods." They say that all lower things are divided along with them, so much so that whatever is contained under one of these divisions, all the way down to the center of the earth, is said to be subject to that twelve-fold sign and its presiding Angel. They intended this sign or division to be like a certain pyramid, whose base is in the Zodiac and whose apex is at the center of the earth. Regarding these, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian theology</note> writes thus in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*:

*Dividing the heaven,* he says, *into two, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six parts, or doubles of these, or in any other way whatsoever, they also place rulers over these, whether fewer or more. Again, they place one leader over these, and thus the Egyptian treatises on principles are like a pyramid which, proceeding from the base—that is, from the multitude—towards the one, descends from the one into the multitude. This multitude is clearly governed by the One, and by GOD from every side, an indefinite nature being held together under a certain defined limit by His command. This is especially true of the Unitary Cause, the highest of all. God produced Matter from materiality—that is, derived from essentiality—which the Creator, taking as a unity, made into simple and impassive spheres; but finally, he used it for the making of generative and corruptible bodies.*

<margin>
The 12 signs of the Zodiac with their Gods.

Who is Pantomorphos?

Who are the Usiarchs?
</margin>

Since all things happen within these pyramids, and the approach of the Sun causes the birth of things while its retreat causes their death, they certainly represented the nature of all things through the pyramid in a way that was not at all unfitting. Indeed, Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom</note> is the authority in Chapter 8 *To Aesculapius*, which begins: *For indeed, there are choruses of spirits* <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ δαίμονον χοροὶ</note>, and so on, stating that they placed twelve Horoscopes <note>In ancient astrology, "Horoscopes" could refer to the presiding spirits of the rising signs</note>, decans <note>The 36 ten-degree subdivisions of the Zodiac</note>, and <term>Isiarchs|Rulers associated with the goddess Isis or the governance of sacred timing</term> over each of these twelve pyramids of the twelve-fold divisions. He says:

*Around him are very many companies of spirits, to be joined with various forces; they are familiars, existing not far from the immortals, and having been allotted this region, they act as Overseers of human affairs. They proceed to execute what is commanded by the Gods through whirlwinds, storms, fire-blasts, changes of fire, and earthquakes; moreover, they punish impiety by the fury of wars.* And a little later: *But the Sun is the preserver and educator of every kind.* 

And the rest that follows, by which words he insinuates nothing other than the diversity of effects produced by the mixture of different stars existing in different twelve-fold divisions. And these are those twelve Horoscope Gods, over whom he says **Pantomorphos** <note>Literally "The All-Formed" or "Multiform One"</note> presides with the seven **Usiarchs** <note>Rulers of substance or essence, often identified with the seven planets</note>, about whom Trismegistus says much in the cited chapter. These are indeed nothing other than the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which those people called the twelve lesser Gods, and the seven Planets, which they called the **Usiarchs**, or the greater Gods and Spirits. From this, the words of Artephius are:

Artephius.

...the corruptions of evils, the hidden harmonies and discords of things; likewise, they believed that the mixture of spirit and matter coming together into a single composite does not occur except through a certain pyramidal progression. This is so much the case that those beings which are furthest removed from any association with corruption—founding the base of their pyramid in the **supramundane Zodiac** <note>A spiritual realm of the stars existing above the physical world</note> above the paths of the Sun and Moon—do not touch the orbit of corporeal things with their downward-turned apex except at a single point. Conversely, those things which are seen in the elementary world, clothed in the shroud of earthly mixture, have the base of their pyramid founded in the opposite position at the center of corruption; with their apex turned upward, they touch the orbit of immortal things only at the tiniest point.

<margin>How the pyramid of light and darkness is to be understood.</margin>
For this reason, they called the pyramid **ABC** the pyramid of light, and **DEF** the pyramid of darkness. They believed that the more the pyramid of light was mixed with earthly things, the more it suffered a loss of its own brilliance, the closer it approached the lower and earthly realms.

<margin>Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Moses Maimonides, the medieval Jewish philosopher</note> page 32.</margin>
On the other hand, the further it ascended away from corruptible things, and the more it was freed from earthly and corrupting qualities, the more light and splendor it acquired, until it was absorbed into the immensity of light like a drop in the sea, as is evident in the accompanying figure. From this, they compared the soul to the pyramid of light and the body to the pyramid of darkness. For they called a soul that was immersed in corporeal pleasures and filthy delights "heavy, sluggish, and dark." But that soul which followed the guidance of right reason and raised itself to the contemplation of incorruptible and heavenly things, they called "bright, heavenly, and angelic." In this they were taught, if I am not mistaken, by **Zoroaster** <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often cited in the Renaissance as a source of "ancient theology"</note>, who said that the soul was winged, but lost its wings when it yielded to corporeal desires and vices, only to recover them when, with the wings growing back, it sought heavenly things. For this reason, they fashioned winged sphinxes as <gloss>hieroglyphs</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἱερογλύφους (*hieroglyphous*)</note>; but we have treated these matters more extensively in the preceding sections.

<margin>What the Egyptians indicate by the Pyramids.</margin>
But they also seem to have wished to represent the human soul—being of a fiery nature—under the form of a pyramid, insofar as it adheres to the body just as a pyramid adheres to its base, or like a flame to its fuel. Thus, they constructed the magnificent tombs of Kings and Heroes as immense pyramids to testify that, although the body is dissolved and corrupted, the soul survives.

<margin>What is the Great Hermetic Year?</margin>
And when it seemed fit to the Supreme Architect—that is, at the completion of that **Hermetic Circle of 36,500 years** <note>The "Great Year," a cycle after which the stars were thought to return to their original positions</note>—the soul would choose to enter another body. This follows the principle known to geometricians: that a pyramid, while its vertex remains unmoved, describes a circle if its base is rotated, and its entire body describes a cone. Thus, the circle signifies that cycle of years, and the cone signifies the body which is perfected within that cycle. For it was the opinion of the Egyptians that all things would be restored to the same state in the space of 36,500 years. **Plato** testifies that he received this from them when he says in the *Timaeus* that the soul was made by GOD in such a way that he received one portion from the Universe, which...

### CHAPTER X. BOOK II. ON THE FOUNDATION

Without a doubt, unity is signified by that point which sits at the summit of the pyramid. The second part is double the first; the third is one-and-a-half times <note>Latin: sesquialteram, a 3:2 ratio</note> the second and triple the first; the fourth is double the second; the fifth is triple the third; the sixth is eight times the first; and finally, the seventh exceeds the first by twenty-six parts. After this, he filled the double and triple intervals, by which numbers he certainly signifies nothing other than the expansion of those lines which, drawn from a point to the base, create angles and, through their intervals, the very surfaces enclosed by lines. From this it appears that he also received these concepts from the Egyptians. The Egyptians placed all these things excellently before our eyes through the allegorical <gloss>conception</gloss> <note>original Greek: epinoian</note> of two Gods, Arimanius and Orimazes. This concept was received from Zoroaster and inserted into their own fables and mystical narratives, as they did with many other things.

<margin>
Allegory of Orimazes and Arimanius.
</margin>
Plutarch relates the matter in the following words: *Indeed, they also tell many fabulous things about them, such as what he reports in these words: They say Orimazes was born from the purest light, and Arimanius from gloom, and that they wage war against each other. Orimazes created six GODS. The first of Benevolence; the second of Truth; the third of Equity; the fourth of Wisdom; the fifth of Wealth; the sixth of Pleasure. Arimanius created the same number of contrary GODS. Then Orimazes tripled himself, and removed himself from the sun by as great an interval as the Sun is distant from the earth, and decorated the Heaven with stars, and established one before all others, Sirius, as a guardian and Watchman; furthermore, he created twenty-four other GODS and placed them in an egg. But an equal number made by Arimanius pierced that egg, and from this, evils have been mixed with goods.*

What Zoroaster intended to suggest through this allegorical way of speaking has certainly tormented the minds of many. We explain these things according to the mind of the Egyptians as follows:

<margin>
Interpretation of the allegory of Orimazes and Arimanius.
</margin>
That Arimanius and Orimazes, denoting contrary principles among the Egyptians, were nothing other than Osiris and Typhon. The former, Osiris, represents

everything that is good, consisting of equality and in harmony with nature (as Synesius testifies in his book *On Providence*). <margin>
Orimazes is Osiris and Arimanius is Typhon, noting the contrary principles of nature.
</margin>
Typhon-Arimanius and Osiris-Orimazes is due to the consensus and disagreement of nature, which composes all things from contrary and fighting principles, whereby:

> Cold things fight with hot, moist things with dry,
> Soft things with hard, and things having weight with the weightless.

Empedocles.

Against these, Typhon Arimanus <note>Arimanus is the Latinized form of Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of darkness and chaos</note> opposed just as many contrary gods; that is, for each of the Beneficial gods, he set another contrary and malevolent one, whose wicked gaze might hinder them in their actions. But let us hear the words of Iamblichus. *The first God*, he says, *is before Being and is the sole father of the first GOD, whom he brings forth while remaining in his own solitary unity. This is "super-intelligible" <note>Meaning a reality that exists beyond the capacity of human thought or intellect</note> and is the very exemplar of himself. He is called his own father, his own son, the "one-father," and the GOD who is truly good. For he is the greatest and the first, the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, the Ideas. From this "One," the self-sufficient GOD unfolded himself, and thus he is called the self-sufficient father of himself, and his own prince. For he is the beginning, the GOD of Gods, a unity from the One before essence, the beginning of essence, for from him essence comes; therefore he is named the father of essence. For he himself is Being in a pre-eminent way, the principle of all things that can be understood. These are the most ancient principles of all, which Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," here referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note> presents to the Ethereal, Empyrean, and Celestial Gods, composing one hundred books on the empyrean (that is, the fiery), just as many on the aerial, and a thousand on the celestial. According to another order, however, he presents the GOD Emeph to the Celestial Gods as a Leader, whom he says is the intellect understanding himself, and turning his own thoughts back into himself. Before this one, he places a single indivisible thing, which he calls the first exemplar, or the expression or image, which he calls Icthon, in whom is the first understanding and the first thing understood, which is worshipped only with silence. Beyond these, however, other Leaders preside over the creation of visible things. For the craftsman-intellect, who is also the master of truth and wisdom—insofar as he proceeds into the hidden work of generation and brings the power of latent reasons into the light—is called Amun in the Egyptian language. Insofar as he accomplishes all things without falsehood, he is named Phta; and insofar as he acts with artistic skill alongside truth, he is called Phta or, what is the same, Vulcan. Insofar as he is the bringer of good things, he is called Osiris, and he has other names because of his differing powers and actions. There is also another lordship among them over all the elements placed in the process of generation, and over their power, which they attribute to the Sun. Likewise, another lordship over all nature involved in generation is attributed to the Moon.* And thus far Iamblichus. From these words it appears that the Egyptians viewed all these things according to an analogy in three [different worlds]...

# BOOK II. ON THE CONSTRUCTION [OF HIEROGLYPHICS]. 174 CHAP. X.

<margin>
3. The dependency of the worlds.
</margin>
...considered that light shines forth in different worlds: the super-mundane <term>super-mundane: The "Archetypal" realm beyond the physical universe, often associated with pure divine ideas.</term>, the celestial, and the elementary. Indeed, Orimazes <note>original: "Orimazes", the Greek name for the Persian Ahura Mazda.</note> with his six Gods—whom we said he created above him, or, which is the same thing, his attendant Gods: Emeph, Ichthon, Phtha, Vulcan, Amun, and Osiris—is the same in the super-celestial or Archetypal world as the Sun is in the celestial world with the six remaining planets. Similarly, in the Elementary world, this corresponds to the four elements acting upon the three grades of corruptible things: the Entitative, the Vegetative, and the Sensitive. By this, he ingeniously wished to suggest the dependency of these three worlds upon one another, so much so that the Elementary world cannot act without the Celestial, nor the Celestial without the special influence of the super-mundane world.

<margin>
How is Mithras a mediator between Orimazes and Arimanius?
</margin>
Furthermore, Plutarch says that Arimanius, the "adversary" <note>original Greek: ἀντίθεον (antitheon)</note>, opposed the six Gods of Orimazes with six others of his own. Between these two was Mithras, whom the Persians call the *Mesytes* <term>Mesytes: From the Greek for "mediator" or "middle-man."</term>. This signifies that the beneficial power of the planets is represented through Orimazes-Osiris, while the malicious power is shown through Arimanius-Typhon. Mithras, however, represents Horus or Apollo—who here, as in many other places, is identified with Osiris—the Author of all harmony. By mixing hot things with cold, moist with dry, and good with evil, he tempers them through the generations, corruptions, births, and deaths of things. Just as on a seven-stringed instrument <note>original: "Heptachordo"</note> one tempers deep tones with sharp, sharp with middle, and middle with the lowest, he excites a most pleasing harmony in the world according to the saying:

> The power of the Apolline mind moves these Muses from every side.
<note>original Latin: "Mentis Apollineæ vis has mouet undique Musas."</note>

Therefore, evils are mixed with good things so that the good may be strengthened in their goodness and rendered more powerful. But so that all these things may be made more clear, we have chosen to place here a certain paradigm of the antithesis of the rival Gods.

### Mithras or the Mediator, Horus, Apollo; that is, the Author of Harmony.

Now, Horus is the son of Osiris, or the power of the Sun, and a certain tempering of the surrounding air, which preserves and nourishes all things.

<margin>The power of Typhon-Ahriman in:</margin>

| Planets | In the Greater World (Macrocosm) | In the Lesser World (Microcosm) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Saturn** ♄: Extinguishes with excessive cold. | The harmful force of snow, hail, and ice. | Melancholic complexion <note>original: ἄκρατος (*akratos*), meaning "extreme" or "unmixed."</note> |

| **Moon** ☾: Exceeding the limits of both heat and moisture. | Deluges and earthquakes; the origin of all corruption. | Intemperance of humors and the cause of all infirmities. |

Lest that violent force of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian Set, a god of chaos and storms.</note> utterly overwhelm Osiris, behold Mithras in the midst of them—that Horus-Apollo of things, the father of all health and medicine. He provides middle ground against those malignant incursions of rays by producing herbs, shrubs, trees, animals, gems, and stones. By these, we are rendered safe and secure from every violence of cold, heat, dryness, and moisture; and even from the dangers of lightning, hail, flood, sterility, famine, and similar evils. Plutarch confirms all this in these words:

> *Zoroaster placed Mithras in the middle between Orimazes <note>Ahura Mazda, the god of light.</note> and Arimanius <note>Ahriman, the spirit of darkness and destruction.</note>; for this reason the Persians call him the **Mediator** <note>original Greek: μεσίτην (*mesitēn*)</note>, that is, the intermediary. He taught him the manner and reasoning for placating the gods and for the sacrificial victims to be offered to him. Hence, prophylactic measures were instituted for the sake of averting evil. For, pounding a certain herb called **omomi** <note>Likely referring to *Haoma*, a sacred plant in Zoroastrianism.</note> in a mortar, they invoke Hades <note>original: Ditem</note> and the darkness; then, having mixed in the blood of a slaughtered wolf, they carry it out and cast it away into a place (namely, into the receptacle of the Typhon-Ahriman) where the rays of the Sun do not reach—believing this to be a kind of amulet against that Ahrimanic Typhon. <margin>What the herb *Omomi* provides.</margin> For they judge similarly concerning plants: some belong to the good spirit, and some to the evil spirit. Of animals, they assign some to the good, such as dogs, birds, and land hedgehogs; others they assign to the evil, such as aquatic creatures (as if born from the stock of Typhon). Therefore, they declare that man to be most blessed who has slain the most of the evil creatures.*

# BOOK II. ON THE EDUCATION 176 CHAP. X.

From this, as if from a certain source, the delusion of all Egyptian superstition concerning the attraction of good and evil **Genii** <note>The "Genii" or "daemons" were believed to be spiritual intermediaries that could be summoned or influenced by specific rituals.</note> flowed forth; as will be seen everywhere in this whole treatise.

<margin>Ormuzd established 24 Gods in an egg; Ahriman did the same.</margin>
Furthermore, Plutarch says that **Ormuzd** <note>original: "Orimazen." The chief deity of Zoroastrianism, representing light and goodness.</note> tripled himself—that is, he communicated his power to the three-fold world: the super-mundane, the celestial, and the elementary. He raised himself as far above the Sun as the Sun is distant from the Earth, reaching the orbit of the fixed stars (which the ancients believed was as far above the Sun as the Sun was above the Earth). He also decorated the stars—that is, he communicated his light to them—placing them above other natural things primarily because of the clarity of the light they shared so abundantly. Once these things were done, he established twenty-four Gods and placed them in an egg. These were the twenty-four stars which were to be the judges and dispensers of worldly affairs. He established them in the "egg"—that is, the world—which the Egyptians (according to the testimony of Eusebius, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and others, as will be proven extensively in the following pages) compared to an egg. Against him, **Ahriman** <note>original: "Arimanius." The Zoroastrian spirit of darkness and destruction.</note> opposed an equal number of <term>δαίμον' ἀντίτεχνον</term> <note>original Greek: "daimona antitechnon," meaning "rival-crafting spirits" or "opposing artisans."</note> established in the same egg. That is, he placed an equal number of opposing stars in the northern region; their malignant rays, mixed with the rays of the Beneficent ones, became the cause of the mixture of good and evil. To understand these things more clearly:

<margin>48 constellations established by the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>The Nile is the outflow of Osiris.</margin>
<margin>The foam of the sea is called Typhon.</margin>
Note that the Egyptians observed forty-eight constellations in the Heavens, which Aratus and Hyginus recount according to their tradition. They placed twenty-four of these in the region of the Southern Hemisphere, which they themselves (according to Plutarch) called the **Urn of Light**, the **Kingdom of Osiris**, the **right side of the world**, and a **healthy benefit**. They placed an equal number in the Northern part, which they called the **left side of the world**, the **malignant**, the **poisonous**, the **feminine**, the **origin of darkness**, and the **kingdom of Ahriman or Typhon**. For this same reason, they considered the **Nile** something divine and the "outflow of Osiris," because it drew its origin from the Southern region, the kingdom of Osiris or Ormuzd. Conversely, they abhorred the **Sea**, which was to the North of Egypt, calling it the "foam of Typhon" as if it were something most foul; for in it the Nile, the giver of all good things and the outflow or "secondary tear" of Osiris, would be swallowed up, becoming the cause of the mixing of good and evil.

And from this also, according to Plutarch, they signify through the snares and tyranny of Typhon the drying force of the humors, by which the Nile is increased and born. The **Queen of Ethiopia**, who is said in fables to have assisted Typhon, denotes the Southern winds from Egypt; if these defeat the **Etesian winds** <note>Seasonal Mediterranean winds that blow from the North, helping to push rain-clouds toward the source of the Nile.</note> (by which clouds are driven toward Ethiopia, preventing the rains from falling which increase the Nile), then the prevailing Typhon burns with heat. Thus, utterly overpowering the Nile—which flows into a different part because of its weakness—he drives it into the sea through a hollow and low-lying channel. This is from Plutarch.

From these things it is clear that these twenty-four <term>ἀντιθέους</term> <note>original Greek: "antitheous," meaning "opposing gods" or "rival deities."</note> are nothing other than the twenty-four Southern constellations and the same number of Northern ones, about which the philosopher speaks in Bulengerus regarding the Gods of the Chaldeans:
> Beyond the circle of the Zodiac, he says, they define another twenty-four stars. One part of which [is directed] toward the

## On the mystic Numbers contained under the figures of Obelisks.

<margin>Moses was imbued with the wisdom of the Egyptians.</margin>
Now, furthermore, let us see by what reasoning they expressed the aforementioned mysteries of nature through the mystic numbers contained within the shape of the Obelisks. For Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> clearly states that Pythagoras and Plato learned all their more recondite philosophy from the columns or pyramids of Mercury <note>The "Columns of Hermes/mercury" were legendary pillars said to contain the sum of all ancient knowledge.</note>. Most of this philosophy was delivered to their disciples under a great vow of silence, concealed behind the veils of geometric figures, numbers, and harmonic proportions. Philo, in his *Life of Moses*, also testifies that Moses applied himself to this same study while being educated in Pharaoh's Court, and was imbued with Arithmetic, Music, and all the rest of the wisdom of the Egyptians. It is therefore manifest that they applied themselves with the highest and most singular zeal to rightly perceiving those mystic proportions of numbers and Music that shine forth in the majesty of nature. They shadowed forth the greatest mysteries hidden beneath these forms, as will become clear from what we shall now say.

### Unity in the Obelisk.

<margin>What the apex in the obelisk indicates.</margin>
Therefore, in the pyramid, the apex is the point, the unity, the fountain and origin of all numbers. By this, the Egyptians hinted at the genuine archetype of the divine origin of creatures and the eternal principle: that one and supreme summit of things, from which, and through which, and toward which all things are, are ordered, remain, are contained, and are filled. This is, of course, that Hermetic Circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere <note>A famous philosophical definition of God used frequently in the Renaissance.</note>. For just as the apex is the beginning of the pyramid, from which—as if from unity—all the remaining numbers of the pyramid flow out through radiant lines and surfaces, so too the unity of that supreme Architect of things (the origin of every creature) begot and brought forth the multitude of beings. This was a movement, as it were, proceeding from an undivided unity into a chorus of numbers. And this is that Pythagorean Apollo <note>Apollo’s name was often etymologized by ancient philosophers as "a-pollo," meaning "not-many," i.e., the One.</note>, or that first architect-intellect; here, according to Iamblichus, is that Hermetic "All-Formed" <note>original: "Pantomorphus."</note> one, and the Egyptian Proteus transforming himself into all shapes, of whom we spoke previously. Among the Hebrew Kabbalists <note>original: "Macubalim," a Latinization of Mequballim.</note>, this is well represented by the *Ein Sof* <note>original: "אֵין סוֹף" (Ensuph), the Infinite or Boundless God in Kabbalah.</note>, that great
<margin>What is the Ein Sof among the Kabbalists?</margin>
sacrament in the Tree of the *Sefirot* <note>original: "Zephiroth," the ten attributes or emanations of God.</note>, which is the vein and fountain of life, in the first and highest...
