# AND THE FABRICATION OF HIEROGLYPHICS. 179 CH. XI.

...from the first principles, and from there applied to the physical elements through a certain analogy. Unity, therefore, is properly called Proteus <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape; here he represents the "First Principle" that takes on many forms.</note>, because it holds the *primacy* <note>original: "$\pi \rho \omega \tau \epsilon \tilde{\iota} \alpha$" (proteia), meaning first place or excellence.</note> in all things. However, because things in that "one" do not differ from each other, but all are one—as the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, specifically referring to the dialogue *Parmenides*.</note> demonstrate from *Parmenides*—it came to be said of the "one" that all things are made; and just as all things are in the one, so the one becomes all things; not otherwise than how every diversity of numbers grows out of the number one.

<margin>A description of Unity.</margin>
Unity is therefore transformed into various species; nevertheless, in all of them, that Protean unity holds the first place. From the "one," then, first proceeds *The All* <note>original: "$\pi \tilde{\alpha} \nu$" (pan), meaning the whole or the universe.</note>, that is, Being, by which the one is drawn into actual existence. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the essence of all things.</note>, taught by the Egyptians, demonstrate it thus: The "one" therefore in the beginning gives birth to the "two," losing its infinite power in this act; in the same way, matter (corresponding to the "one") possesses infinite potential and is transformed into all kinds of things—which are represented in the pyramid through points, lines, surfaces, and bodies. For this same reason, it is called "The All" by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note>, for the same reason that the ancient philosophers named it Proteus.

<margin>What is Proteus?</margin>
Just as all things proceed from the "one" as from the first and most general principle, intrinsic to all things and woven into the very peak of substance; so too do all bodies depend on matter as their first principle. And by this analogy, Proteus was called the father of Idothea <note>In Homer's *Odyssey*, Idothea is the daughter of Proteus.</note> by Homer, just as the "one" is the father with respect to the "two" or to Being. Furthermore, he who seeks the first principle of a house descends to the foundations; so he who seeks the first principle of all bodies descends to *prime matter* <note>The fundamental, formless substance from which all physical things are made.</note>. But let us now proceed to the Binary.

->The Dyad in the Pyramid.<-

<margin>The significance of the Binary number.</margin>
The *Dyad* <note>original: "$\delta \acute{\upsilon} \alpha \varsigma$" (dyas), referring to the number two or duality.</note> is indicated in the pyramid by the flow of any two of the side lines. Since this is the principle of diversity, inequality, and dissimilarity, and the first distinction from unity—the first "fall" from the one—it is not undeservedly considered the number of "dissection" in every discipline. By this number, the Egyptians indicated the distribution of opposites, and the shifts of clashing qualities in nature. This was represented not incongruously by the Persian Magi under the allegory of Ahriman and Ahura Mazda <note>The Zoroastrian deities of darkness/evil and light/good.</note>, or by the Egyptians under the history of Osiris and Typhon. Hence the Pythagoreans, as Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian myths.</note> testifies, assign different names to each principle. To the **Good**, they assign: unity, the finite, the resting, the straight, the odd, the square, the equal, the right-handed, and the splendid. To the **Evil**, they point with the names: the binary, the infinite, the moving, the curved, the even, the oblong <note>literally "longer in the other dimension."</note>, the unequal, the left-handed, and the dark; and they establish these as the principles of the origin of things. Hence Osiris is said to be everything that is beneficial, as mentioned above and as Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and bishop who wrote *On Providence*.</note> testifies in Book 1. Typhon, however, to speak with Synesius, is the "workshop of all evils," whom the Egyptians also call Seth, Bebon, and Smy; <margin>The names of Typhon.</margin> by which words they indicate a certain violent inhibition, contrariety, and overthrowing, without which Horus—or that sensible world—could not be preserved...

# INSTITUTION AND FABRICATION OF HIEROGLYPHICS. 180 CH. XI. BOOK II.

...it can by no means; and accordingly, the Egyptians correctly—as is read in the works of Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 120 AD) was a Greek philosopher whose work *On Isis and Osiris* is a primary source for Egyptian mythology.</note> citing Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek in the 3rd century BC.</note>—called the bones of Horus <note>The Egyptian god of kingship and the sky, representing order and light.</note> the magnet, and those of Typhon <note>Also known as Set, the god of chaos, storms, and disorder.</note> iron.
<margin>The bones of Horus are the magnet; those of Typhon are iron.</margin>
For just as iron in a magnet experiences different motions of attraction and repulsion, so the healthy, good, and rationally consistent motion of the world somehow revolves, draws to itself, and makes more compliant that harsh and Typhonian force. Hence they tell the myth, according to Plutarch, that Mercury 
<margin>Mercury animated the nerves of Typhon, cut out for a Lyre.</margin>
cut out the nerves of Typhon and used them for strings to harmonize the universe, rendering it consonant from dissonance. Meanwhile, the force of the world was not abolished, but fulfilled; from this it happens that this [force], weak and languid, clings to bodies in this world of varied changes and affections. Indeed, in the earth it causes concussions and tremors; in the air, heat and unseasonable winds, as well as fiery whirlwinds and lightning; it also infects the waters and the spirits with the plague of pestilence, and rushes even as far as the Moon, often raising itself up to darken the bright air. 

These two principles of things are well denoted in the pyramid through the flow of two lines from a single point—although others twist this binary <term>binarius</term> <note>The number two or the concept of duality.</note> toward the production of forms. For just as the binary arises from the one, so by maintaining the ratio of similarity, "form" is first drawn out from the potential of matter. For that reason, it was named by Homer not *eidos* <note>original: εἶδος (form or appearance)</note>, but *eidyllia* <note>original: εἰδυλλία; a term likely used here to suggest a "Goddess of forms" or "little forms."</note>, that is, the Goddess of forms. 

This, therefore, was the consideration of the ancients, who deduced all things from the "one" by a certain perpetual and continuous chain through all levels of existence, and by the same steps referred them back to the one. Since, therefore, matter is the final result in the process of resolution <note>The process of breaking a complex thing down into its basic parts.</note>, it will necessarily be the first in the composition of bodies. This is clearly evident through the apex of the pyramid: while it expands into lines, surfaces, and a body, and returns from these back into itself, it beautifully teaches this process. For that reason, matter is rightly called Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek myth, used here to represent matter's ability to take any shape.</note> in physics, just as "the one" was called Proteus in the "first wisdom" <note>Metaphysics.</note>. And because form is the penultimate step in resolution, it becomes the second in composition, and thus takes on the nature of the binary, which for the Pythagoreans is feminine. Therefore those ancients—whether Sages, Magi, or even Priests—following the order of nature in composing and resolving things, called matter "Protean," and established God as the second form, hence His daughter, just as duality is born of unity. The Egyptians also suggested this through Oceanus the Father and Tethys the Mother; but enough of such things for now.

### *The Hieroglyphic Triad in the Obelisk.*

Furthermore, from the binary and unity is born the *triad*, which is signified in the pyramid by $\Delta$ <note>The Greek letter Delta, which is triangular in shape.</note>. It takes its beginning from the point or monad of the pyramid, and is extended through any two sides into the base, by which the triangle is constituted. 
<margin>Praise of the number three.</margin>
That sacred triad, celebrated in so many writings of the ancients; that archetype of Horus, the true Platonic model of the triple world and of the Idea; that true scale of Pythagorean justice reduced to the middle of two vices on either side; the principle of all numbers, the triangle of divine nature, the mistress of all imperfection and...

# AND THE FABRICATION OF HIEROGLYPHICS. CH. XI. 181

...is the fulfillment of a crippled nature, the unique center of the desire for forms flourishing in Proteus <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape; here he represents the ever-changing nature of prime matter.</note>, the foundation of the mystical pyramid, and the source and origin of bodies—than which nothing is more abundant for mystical meanings and the hidden explanations of things. For just as the first even number, namely duality, represents division, the first diversity, and (as we have said) the first fall from the One, so the ternary [the number three] is the first odd number, acting as a return to the One and to the beginning. It is more perfect than the even number because it encompasses the even, rather than being encompassed by it. Thus, it is the most fitting number for justice; for in even numbers, justice is almost dissolved because there is no midpoint—as Plato correctly warns in Book 1 of *The Laws*—nor does it have any hinge upon which to lean. But in the odd number itself, above the One itself, there is a midpoint acting as a center and a Divine presence, by which equal distribution is made, and toward which everything is directed as if toward an end. An odd number is also its own bond because of its midpoint, as Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century AD and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> correctly says: it possesses its own bond within itself, exists because of its circular center, and, because of the comparison of the extremes to the middle, it is the principle of the universal order; for in the ternary there is a beginning, a middle, and an end. Whence also "all things are three" <note>original: "τὰ τρεία πάντα"</note> and ancient theologians, to designate that the beginning, middle, and end should be referred back to GOD, offered three things in sacrifices.

<margin>Rites performed by the number three.</margin>
Hence the Egyptians also, according to Plutarch, performed their incense burnings three times—in the morning, at noon, and in the evening. That this number, full of mysteries, was always held in the highest veneration is attested by so many triangular species and forms of things—namely, so many pyramids, tripods, and triangles—as well as various figures that appear everywhere, both on Obelisks and especially in the diagrams of the Bembine Table <note>The Bembine Table, or Mensa Isiaca, is a famous bronze tablet decorated with Egyptian motifs that was studied extensively by Renaissance scholars.</note>, which we will interpret at length in their proper place. Most importantly, however, through the triangles represented in a pyramid, they intended to suggest nothing else (according to Plutarch) but the nature of the universe and a certain idea of Osiris, Isis, and Horus, represented through three operations and effects. For that cruel Typhon—whom we previously represented through the binary [the number two]—by tearing apart the body of Osiris and scattering it into many parts, proceeding from the one to the many, from the perfect to the imperfect, from the whole to the parts, and from the good (which consists in an entire cause) to the evil (which arises from any defect), sowed many dissensions and dangerous enmities in the nature of things, signified by the binary. Wishing to prevent these, Isis—the provident part of nature—diligently searched for the scattered parts of Osiris and, by adapting the found parts to parts and limbs to limbs, restored Osiris to wholeness. From their subsequent union was born Horus, that sensible <note>Meaning the physical, perceptible world that can be experienced through the senses.</note> part of the world, which is especially expressed by this triangle of ours;

# CHAPTER XI. 182 BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION 
<meta>catchword: and three</meta>

...but let us hear Plutarch, speaking of these things as if from a tripod:

> "Now," he says, "a more excellent and divine nature consists of three parts: that which is perceived by the mind, the matter, and that which is composed of these two, which the Greeks call *kosmos* <note>original: κóσμος; meaning the 'world' or 'ordered universe'.</note>, that is, the world. Plato indeed calls that first part the idea, the exemplar, and the father. Matter he denotes by the names of mother, nurse, seat, and the region capable of births; that which consists of both, he is accustomed to call the offspring and the birth. It is probable that the Egyptians compared the nature of the universe especially to the most beautiful of Triangles; a comparison which Plato also seems to have used in the *Republic*, where he composes the 'nuptial figure' <note>original: γᾶμος γονιμòν; referring to a mathematical ratio used by Plato to describe the generation of better or worse offspring.</note>. This Triangle consists of three sides, of which the base is 4; the side forming a right angle to it is 3; and the side subtending this angle [the hypotenuse] is 5 units long; it has as much power as the sides forming it <note>This is an early description of the Pythagorean theorem ($3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$, or $9 + 16 = 25$).</note>. It must be understood that by the line standing at a right angle to the other, the male is represented; by the base, the female; and by the hypotenuse, the offspring of both. Thus, Osiris is the principle, Isis the receptacle, and Horus the effect. For the Ternary [the number three] is the first odd and perfect number."

Thus speaks Plutarch. From these words it is clearly evident that nothing else is being described to us here than that most celebrated Pythagorean *Hecatombe* <note>A 'sacrifice of a hundred oxen'; historically used to refer to Pythagoras’s celebration upon discovering his famous geometric theorem.</note>, famous for so many mysteries and of such infinite use in mathematical work. I strongly suspect that Pythagoras first received such a great geometric secret from the Egyptians and afterwards made it his own right and invention. For if you multiply the line of the triangle subtending the angle—which is 5 units—by itself, it produces 25, a square; and the squares of the surrounding sides of 4 and 3 units make 16 and 9. These surely hinted at the greatest mysteries in nature; but of these elsewhere. From this it is clear with what genius and with what great mysteries they displayed their wisdom through a triangle of this kind. But I trust the sign annexed here.

### The Tetrad, or the Quaternary in the Obelisk.

**T**hey exhibited the Tetrad, or the number four, on Obelisks through the four sides, but in a different manner: First, in the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone at the top of an obelisk.</note>, as a triangular quaternary; then, in the remaining trunk of the Obelisk, as a quadrilateral quaternary. Through the former, they secretly hinted at the angelic world, insofar as from the center of divinity—which is aptly judged by the apex of the obelisk—the immediate seal of the divine nature is spread into the generative nature, marked with the triangular character of divinity. Through the four sides, they represented the protection of the fourfold world distributed into the twelve citadels of the world, which the three numbers of the four triangular surfaces aptly denote; for 3 multiplied by 4 makes 12. Again, just as 3 joined to 4 constitutes 7, so they judge it to be the sacrament of all natural perfection of the generative world. Moreover, the four triangular sides joined to the four quadrangular sides constitute 8, a most fitting symbol of the influx of the angelic nature into the corporeal world. If the base of the pyramid is added to these, they beautifully indicated the mystical Ennead <note>The number nine.</note>, a symbol of the angelic and corporeal world, which the 9 solid angles considered in any obelisk also noted. Finally, if the apex of the pyramid were added to these, then 10 was constituted—the perfection of all nature...

...and they signaled the completion of the three worlds: the archetypal, the angelic, and the corporeal world. This total was implicitly contained in that *tetras* <note>original: tetras; the number four or the quaternary.</note>, or the number four. For if you join the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 in their proper order, that mystic *decas* <note>original: decas; the number ten.</note> will come forth—the *tetractys* <note>original: tetractys; a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, sacred to the Pythagoreans as a symbol of the organization of the universe.</note> celebrated with such silence by the Pythagoreans and shrouded in such great mysteries. They beautifully indicated these through two groups of five. The first group aptly suggested the influence of the divine nature into the Angelic world, flowing from the apex <note>The pointed top of an obelisk.</note> into the fourfold angelic world. The other group suggested the womb of creatures, or the corporeal world, rising from the quadrangular base upward toward the center with a continuous narrowing of the sides. Furthermore, the formal unity <note>The number one, representing the singular source or God.</note> hidden in the heart of the Divinity—indicated by the apex—

<image-desc>A schematic diagram of numerical relationships. The numbers 1 through 10 are arranged in a horizontal row. establishes 10 whenever you add it to any order of things. This number 10 is the completion of all things, the type and exemplar of Divine perfection. For if you add 1 to the 9 of the tripartite angelic triad, you establish 10, the number that exhausts all things and the type of the Divinity that embraces all. If you add 8 to 2 (in which a doubled unity resides), you will have the influx of the Angelic nature through formal unity into the lower world—namely, the sensible world—which is aptly suggested by the cubic number 8. If again you add 3 (that Triad which is the exemplar of all perfection) to 7 (the symbol of worldly perfection), you will have 10 again. Finally, if you add the quaternary <note>The number 4.</note>, or that *tetractys* so celebrated by Pythagoras, to 6 (the symbol of the number of worldly operations), 10 will result once more. Lastly, if you double 5—that is, join two fives together—the same number ten will emanate. You see, therefore, how the orders of the worldly constitutions, joined to one another, always produce 10. That is to say, the formal unity involved in each class, when added to the other numbers which are symbols of created things, always establishes 10: a fitting hieroglyph of the entire universe with its Author. Furthermore, 1 joined to 2 gives the triad [3] again; this joined to the triad generates the tetrad [4], and this again joined to the tetrad generates the pentad [5]; and thus, with each number continued in its natural order, that addition generates the hexad [6], heptad [7], octad [8], ennead [9], and decad [10]—the completion of all, beyond which no other number is given except by repetition. The ancients opportunely displayed this mystic philosophy through the figure of obelisks. But since we are treating this philosophy through arithmetic in our work *Oedipus* <note>original: Oedipo; referring to Kircher's major work, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, where he explores Egyptian lore and mathematical mysticism.</note>, we did not wish to be more expansive here. With these things duly explained, let us now move to the third book of this work. From it, it will clearly appear how the ancient Greeks emulated these mystic Egyptian principles in the architecture of the Gods and in their other fabulous narrations, in order to indicate the secrets of divinity and the nature of things with singular zeal, presenting them under mystic coverings of symbols removed from the understanding of the profane.

## P R E F A T I O.

> Having laid the foundations of the Egyptian **Adytum** <note>The innermost, most sacred part of a temple, usually off-limits to all but priests.</note> in the preceding book—that is, having demonstrated the origin, construction, order, and symbols of the hieroglyphic doctrine in general <note>original Greek: καθ’ ὅλως</note>—it seemed that nothing further remained except that we, entering more deeply into the secret recesses of the hidden Mysteries, should reveal what they finally intended through such a great apparatus of symbols and what they properly wished to signify. We trust that we shall provide this in this third book, God willing. In this volume, we shall accurately <note>original Greek: ἀκριβῶς</note> demonstrate the method not only of the reasoning observed by the Egyptians in their sacred disciplines, but also of the mystical doctrine of the Greeks, which is parallel to the Egyptian. We shall provide specimens of the interpretation of both kinds of wisdom, which are variously hidden within the coverings of fables <note>Kircher refers to myths and allegories as "coverings" (involucris) that hide deeper truths.</note>. From these, unless I am mistaken, it will be more than clear to the kind Reader that hieroglyphic wisdom—both that of the Egyptians and the Greek doctrine parallel to it—looked toward the mysteries of four principal faculties: namely, **Theology**, **Magic**, **Physics** <note>In the 17th century, "Physics" referred to the study of the natural world and the laws of nature.</note>, and **Politics**.

# CHAPTER I.
## On the Mystical Interpretation of Fables.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure seated amidst elaborate botanical scrollwork.</image-desc>

<margin>What the Egyptians intended through that allegorical mode of speaking.</margin>
Since the Priest-Philosophers and the other Egyptian **Hierogrammatists** <note>original: "Hierogrammatiſtis"—sacred scribes or writers of hieroglyphs</note> possessed keen and subtle intellects, and were continually occupied in the study of seeking truth through a certain profound contemplation of the mind, it was altogether difficult to persuade them of the truth of those things told everywhere about Osiris, Isis, and the various metamorphoses of other deities, which seemed most remote from the truth. For since, supported by the dictates of right reason and the light of nature, they recognized no other besides one supreme, eternal, infinite, and unchangeable Divinity—from whom everything that exists flowed as if from an ideal source—nor knew that any other could be known; and since they moreover beheld that admirable majesty of nature shining in all things, that most orderly harmony of the heavens, and their power diffused into the lower world, as well as the connection of the elements and that most excellent <term>well-balanced mixture</term> <note>original Greek: ἐυκρασίαν (eukrasian)—referring to the perfect 'temperament' or blending of the four elements in living things</note> in all mixed things, and also the consensus and dissent of properties hidden in things—they were seriously persuaded that these things existed neither by themselves nor by some other fatal necessity, but were thus intended, ordered, existing, and preserved by that one ineffable Divinity of Divinities.

<margin>How they arrived at the knowledge of one Divinity from the order of things in the world.</margin>
Therefore, intent on higher contemplations, they transferred those fables and histories of the Gods—which were either invented or wrongly understood through false narratives, and which the unrefined people, prone to believing anything, understood literally—as things unsuited and incongruous to reality, by means of a certain allegorical and symbolic method of interpretation. For this purpose, they devised certain symbols and letters, which by a secret similarity were conformable to the things to be signified, transferring them both to moral conduct and to the mystical meanings of nature, and finally to the archetype of all things itself, so that they might hide these things from the unlearned masses. They carved these upon pyramids, obelisks, pillars, temples, and marbles to excite the admiration of posterity for themselves.

<margin>Palaephatus on fabulous narrations.</margin>
The very ancient writer **Palaephatus** suggests these things in his book <term>On Unbelievable Tales</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν ἀπίστων ἱστοριῶν (peri ton apiston historion)</note>; or concerning fabulous narrations not to be believed.

<summary>Kircher argues that Egyptian priests were monotheists who used complex symbols and allegorical fables to hide divine truths from the common people while recording them for posterity on monuments. He asserts that the Greeks merely imitated these Egyptian methods.</summary>

*Some people,* he says, *and especially those who are furthest removed from all wisdom and learning, are accustomed to give faith and persuasion to everything that is told. However, others, who are by nature more prudent and curious, and who are experienced in many matters and affairs, cannot be brought to fully believe everything that is handed down as having actually happened.*

<margin>Poets amplified matters so that they might seize posterity with admiration.</margin>
*To me, however, it seems that everything that has been said did indeed happen: for it should not be thought that these were merely names; otherwise, no discourse concerning them would exist. Instead, the events existed first, and only then was the story layered upon them. <margin>The fable of Prometheus.</margin>
else does **Prometheus**, the first molder of men, indicate to us, except that he was the first who formed men—previously barbarian and brutal—into a political way of living through laws established holily and piously? One must feel no differently about the remaining fabulous narrations, such as the two-formed **Sphinx**, the horses of **Ganymede** <note>The text likely means the man-eating horses of Diomedes, though it names Ganymede.</note> devouring men; **Daedalus** and **Icarus**, **Aeolus**, the statues of Daedalus, the triple-bodied **Geryon**; **Orpheus**, **Pandora**, **Cerberus**, **Medea**, and the innumerable other fictions handed down by the poets. For the cited Palæphatus and **Fulgentius** <note>A Latin mythographer of late antiquity.</note> (whom you may consult in his *Mythologies*) teach that all fables of this kind drew their origin either from misunderstood proverbs of men, or from names conforming to things, or from the ambiguity of names and deeds, or finally from diverse things differing in appearance being fused into one.

<summary>This page explains the "Euhemeristic" or rationalizing approach to mythology, arguing that fantastic fables like Centaurs, the Minotaur, and Hercules' golden apples were actually based on misunderstood historical facts and linguistic puns.</summary>

## CHAPTER II.

### On the mystical significance of the Gods.

<margin>The ancients believed the powers of things were Genii.</margin>
St. Augustine in *The City of God*, Lactantius Firmianus, Eusebius, and others whom we shall cite in what follows, testify that the powers of visible things were called Gods or **Genii** <note>In ancient Roman religion, a 'Genius' was a protective spirit or divine nature inherent in every person, place, or thing.</note>. For the ancients, observing the power of the heavens, the essences of the Elements, the potent operations of the stars, and finally the hidden harmony of things, believed the whole world to be a kind of vast living animal crowded with innumerable spirits, which they assigned to each individual thing in the universe. Concerning these, Marcus Cicero <margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2.</margin> wrote much in his second book *On the Nature of the Gods*, following the opinion of the Stoics. Among other systems of <term>polytheism</term> <note>original: "πολυθεΐας", the worship of many gods.</note>, that system which is called **physical** was established. From this, a great multitude of Gods flowed forth, who, being presented in human form, supplied fables for the Poets—if not for the Historians—and filled the lives of men with every kind of superstition. This ancient opinion indeed overwhelmed not only Greece, but our own people, and finally the entire world. <margin>Where did the multitude of Gods come from?</margin> Dionysius of Halicarnassus <margin>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</margin> writes in the second book of his *Roman Antiquities* that the ancient Romans forbade those legendary fictions of the Poets as the seeds of all superstition—specifically those in which the Gods are imagined to be fighting among themselves, distrusting one another, and mixing adulteries with murders; things which could not even be said of honorable men, let alone the Gods themselves. Eusebius confirms these statements with these words: <margin>Eusebius.</margin>

> Do you see, therefore, how from physical things well and usefully discovered, a system was drawn toward fictitious Gods? This matter generated false opinions, turbulent errors, and superstitions almost like old wives' tales. For the forms of the Gods are known to us, as well as their ages, clothes, and ornaments, etc.

To which he adds: Moreover, Varro says that the ancients fashioned images, insignias, and ornaments of the Gods so that those who had approached the mysteries of the doctrine—having observed these with their eyes—might be able to see the soul of the world and its parts, that is, the true spirits, with their mind. The Hebrews certainly seem to have attributed these Genii to created things after the Egyptians, ahead of other nations. For as was shown in the previous volume, they thought the whole world was full of Genii or certain "forms." Among others, they numbered seventy such spirits, of whom Rabbi Joseph Ben Carnitol—a celebrated master in the Cabalistic art—makes mention in his commentary on Exodus 14 with these <margin>The Hebrews introduce 70 spirits.</margin> <margin>Rabbi Joseph Ben Carnitol.</margin> words: **ונמסרו כל אומות מסורות ביד שבעים שרים** <note>original: "Ve-nimseru kol umot mesurot be-yad shiv’im sarim"</note>, that is: *And all the nations were left, handed over into the hands of 70 Presidents or Genii.* Some read here instead of **שרים** (*Scharim*, "Princes") the word **שדים** (*Sedim*), meaning "Demons"; either way works well. What kind of beings these are, what their duties are, and from where they derived their names, we shall say (God willing) in the third part of our *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher’s monumental work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, where we have treated this story more extensively. Others, agreeing with what has been said, assert that there is no herb on earth which does not have some star or Demon presiding over it; thus Rambam <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> says in the *Guide for the Perplexed*: <margin>Rambam in *Moreh Nebuchim*.</margin> **אין לך כל עשב מלמטה שאין לו מזל ברקיע שמכה אותו ואומר לו גדל** <note>original: "Ein lekha kol esev mi-lemata she-ein lo mazal ba-rakia she-makeh oto ve-omer lo gedal"</note> *There is not, he says, any herb or plant below for you, which does not have a star in the firmament that strikes it and says to it: "Grow."*

Whence they say that if anyone should drink even a tiny bit of water in that moment, he could not escape <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: *hydropisis*, an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid, now called edema</note> or some other grave infirmity. ### CHAPTER II. BOOK III. ON THE GUIDANCE OF MYSTERIES

<margin>Genesis 2.</margin>
...completing that work by the conception of his own power, according to the following words: <margin>Hebrew: "And the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."</margin> <note>original: וייצר יהוה אלהים את האדם עפר מן האדמה ויפח באפיו נשמת חיים ויהי האדם לנפש חיה</note> *And the Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.* The remaining details regarding the labors of Epimetheus <note>In Greek myth, Epimetheus ("afterthought") was the brother of Prometheus; the author here uses him to represent the "afterthought" or the weary state of humanity after the Fall.</note> and the cares of man, which he incurred after the Fall, are consistent with this. From all of this it is clear that many of the fables of the pagans drew their origin from the context of Sacred History. Because of the sublimity of that history, they either did not understand it, or if they did, they nevertheless veiled it with their own allegorical fictions so that they seemed more like myths than sacred history; or, they certainly applied these truths to natural things.

<margin>Empedocles of Agrigentum.</margin>
<margin>Origen and Simplicius.</margin>
Hence, Empedocles of Agrigentum wished the four natures <note>The four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> from which he believed all things were composed to be Divine; and from this same source arose those most diverse opinions of the philosophers concerning the principles of things. Origen says that Empedocles established Strife, Enmity, and Fire as the principles of the universe. Simplicius mixed both views—that is, the four elements along with Strife and Harmony. From this, some earned the name of Atheists, such as Theodorus and Protagoras of Abdera, because they judged the Gods to be nothing other than the powers of natural things.

<margin>Xenocrates of Chalcedon.</margin>
<margin>Speusippus. Alcmaeon of Croton.</margin>
<margin>Marcus Varro.</margin>
<margin>All worldly spaces are full of Spirits and souls.</margin>
Xenocrates of Chalcedon put forward eight Gods: five in the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>, one composed of all the fixed stars, the seventh being the Sun, and the eighth the Moon. Speusippus, born of Plato's sister, determined that a natural force is God. Alcmaeon of Croton attributed divinity to the Sun, the Moon, and the remaining stars, as well as to the soul; he, as Cicero says, did not realize he was giving immortality to mortal things. Marcus Terentius Varro says that he believes God is the "soul of the world" <note>term: *anima mundi* — the idea that the universe itself is a living being with a rational soul.</note> and that the world itself is God. He soon adds that the world is divided into two parts, that is, into heaven and earth. Heaven is also divided twofold, into the ethereal and the aerial regions. The earth is divided into water and soil. He claims all these parts are full of souls—the ethereal and aerial regions being full of immortal ones. From the highest circuit of heaven down to the circle of the Moon, the ethereal souls are the planets and stars; these are not only understood to be celestial Gods, but are also seen. Between the orbit of the Moon and the peaks of the clouds and winds, there are aerial souls; but these are seen by the mind, not the eyes, and are called Heroes, and Larvae <note>Ghosts or malevolent spirits.</note>, and Genii <note>term: *Genius* — a guardian spirit or the inherent power within a person or place.</note>, or the virtues of things. Thus, fragile and toiling mortality divided these into parts, mindful of its own weakness, so that each person might worship that portion which they most lacked.

<margin>The Panegyrist's Address to GOD</margin>
Thus we find different names for different nations, and innumerable Deities among them, so much so that the Panegyrist <note>An orator delivering a formal speech of praise, likely referring to the *Panegyrici Latini*.</note> sings with good reason, as if complaining about the hidden nature of God:

> *You, he says, the supreme sower of all things, whose names are as many as the languages of the nations you wished to exist, we cannot know what you wish to call yourself. Whether there is in you some divine force and mind that, infused throughout the whole world, is mixed with all elements and moves by itself without any external impulse; or whether there is some power above all heaven that looks down upon this entire work from a higher citadel of nature: you, I say, we pray to, etc.*

It is gathered, therefore, from what has been handed down so far, that the innumerable forms of things contained in this universe and their hidden, imperceptible virtues provided the origin for the fabrication of countless Gods and Goddesses, concerning which...

# CHAPTER III.
## *That among the Egyptian Priests, nothing was without mystical meaning.*

<margin>Plato in his book *The Republic*.</margin> That the road to Wisdom is very long, and the journey is most full of every kind of difficulty, is demonstrated more than enough by the labors undertaken by the ancients to acquire it. This is attested by their journeys across land and sea, full of dangers; and finally, by their diligent avoidance of all things that could in any way hold them back from its pursuit. Plato records in his book *The Republic* that the Egyptians, more than any other mortals, applied themselves most intensely to the pursuit of this wisdom. For, as they believed that the happiness of the Supreme Deity consisted primarily in the knowledge of all the best and most beautiful things, and since they rightly attributed immortality to Him because He understands not only the present but also the future and the past, they abstained from everything that could in any way hinder that pursuit. <margin>The ancients abstained from all things to acquire wisdom more easily.</margin> For we see that whichever mortals pant after divinity—those especially seized by the love of wisdom and truth—embrace chastity and the worship of sacred things in order to attain it more easily. <margin>Isis is mystically Wisdom; Typhon is ignorance.</margin> The Greeks expressed this most aptly when they mystically called the Egyptian Goddess ISIS <note>original: ISIM</note> "knowledge," and her enemy Typhon "ignorance." For this reason, they celebrate the sacred rites of this Goddess with a meager diet and abstinence from certain foods and other pleasures—most especially the restraint of <term>Venereal acts</term> <note>Sexual intercourse, named after Venus.</note>. Through all these practices, purity of mind and sharpness of intellect were sought for the sake of knowledge. Hence, they called her sanctuary the ISÆUM <note>The Isaeum was a temple dedicated to Isis.</note>, that is, the "abode of knowledge." For the same reason, some said she was born of Mercury, others of Prometheus; the latter was made famous by the invention of wisdom and foresight, the former by the invention of Grammar and Music. They did not clothe themselves in woolen garments, but performed the Isiac rites dressed in linen garments and with shaved heads. By these signs, they suggested that one must abstain from everything impure, such as hides, wool, hair, nails, and the remains of food. They rejoiced only in linen, which produces a flower most similar to ethereal splendor, born from the immortal earth, and not prone to breeding any small vermin. <margin>They abstained from salt because it made them thirstier; and from Nile water because it made them fatter.</margin> Indeed, they abstained from all those things that might hinder the focused study of wisdom, to the point that they would not even use salt, because it made them more inclined to eating and drinking. For the same reason, they never used the water of the Nile, because it makes bodies more obese; for they thought it better for the soul to be enclosed in a light and agile body, lest its divinity be oppressed. For, as <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> rightly perceived, a soul suffocated by fat and blood cannot foresee anything heavenly. <margin>The saying of Iarchas, King of the Indians, to Apollonius.</note> To this also alludes the excellent saying of Iarchas, the King and philosopher of the Indians, with which he addressed Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD.</note>...

<summary>This page discusses the extreme asceticism and intellectual discipline of the Egyptian priests, framing their worship of Isis as a pursuit of "Wisdom" and their physical purity as a means to prevent the soul from being stifled by the body.</summary>

## ON MYSTAGOGY
<note>Mystagogy refers to the process of being initiated into sacred mysteries or religious secrets.</note>

...addressed him with these words: "I do not wonder, Apollonius, that you have attained all knowledge of divination, since you keep so much of the ether in your heart." <note>original Greek: "ἐ μὴ θαυμάζω Ἀπολλώνιε ὅτι πᾶσαν τὴν μαντικὴν γνῶσιν τετυχηκὼς εἴης, τοσούτῳ αἰθέρος ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σοῦ συνέχεις." Indeed, even their Kings, according to the institution of the sacred writings, drank only <margin>Hecataeus</margin> moderate amounts of wine, as Hecataeus records, because they had been initiated into the dignity of the Priesthood. <margin>They abstained from fish.</margin> Most of them also abstained from fish, viewing them as symbols of sadness and evil—the products of the Nile and the "black sea," a mournful and mixed element, and a catch-basin for all impurity. Furthermore, onions were kept away from Sacred Rites because of their ill-mannered odor; for the same reason, the eating of garlic seems to have been forbidden to those entering the temple of the Great Mother, as Athenaeus relates.

Hesiod.
</margin>
Diodorus relates that a column was placed in the temple at Thebes by Technatis, the father of Bocchoris, containing curses against King Menides, who was the first of all to lead the Egyptians away from a needy and frugal life toward the use of money. Thus, Hesiod rightly said that foolish men—those driven sideways by an excessive appetite for pleasure—do not know how much utility exists in simple mallow and asphodel. The Persian Magi also testified to this; to better practice philosophy, they rejected all seasonings of food and lived on watercress alone.

<margin>
Many Philosophers migrate from Greece to Egypt.
</margin>
When the report of this admirable zeal for wisdom spread through Greece, the wisest of the Greeks were lured by the desire to taste it: namely Solon, Thales, Plato, Eudoxus, Pythagoras, and Lycurgus. They traveled to Egypt to establish an acquaintance with the Priests.

<margin>
Who were the teachers of the Greek philosophers in Egypt?
</margin>
Eudoxus is said to have heard Conuphis of Memphis; Solon heard Sonchis of Sais. Pythagoras heard Oenuphis of Heliopolis, who is said to have most highly approved of that man’s way of philosophizing; this is evidenced by the hidden philosophy Pythagoras handed down regarding things, which did not differ much from the study of <term>hieroglyphics</term><note>Kircher views hieroglyphs not just as writing, but as a system of symbolic, mystical philosophy.</note>.

<margin>
Great mysteries under the "bark" of fables.
</margin>
Therefore, whatever "monsters" Egypt worshipped, or whatever fables it handed down concerning its Gods—Osiris, Isis, Typhon, Horus, and others—one must by no means think that the wisest Priests actually believed them, or were led by some dull and foolish persuasion to adore statues as if they were Divinities (as the common people did). For everyone knows that such a thing is utterly foreign to a wise mind. Rather, as we shall say in what follows, these things signified great mysteries. They were not without reason, but had certain causes introduced either by history or by nature, hidden within those symbols.

<margin>What the Egyptians signify by the dog.</margin>
...they have clearly confessed in such multiform ways. For they did not truly believe Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium." The author refers to the Egyptian god Anubis, whom the Greeks and Romans identified with Hermes/Mercury as "Hermanubis."</note> was a dog, but rather they attributed a guardian and ever-watchful nature to this most perceptive of the Gods—a nature that distinguishes a guest from an enemy; as Plato says, related through Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the scholar who translated Plato's works into Latin during the Renaissance.</note>. Nor do they only think an infant was recently born from the Lotus <margin>What is meant by the Lotus.</margin>, but they also interpret it as the rising of the Sun and its elevation from the moist elements. Similarly, they call the most cruel Persian King, Ochus <note>Artaxerxes III Ochus, who conquered Egypt and reportedly slaughtered the sacred Apis bull to mock the local religion.</note>—who was not only a murderer of his own kin but also the killer of the Apis bull itself, which he served as a meal to himself and his companions—the "Sword" <note>original: "Machæra," from the Greek word for a short sword or dagger.</note> even to this day. By this, they did not express the literal nature of the man, but his character through the instrument, which they likened to an act of parricide. <margin>Why the history of the Egyptians is so varied.</margin> Since various people spoke in various ways about the Egyptian Gods, interpreting their deeds differently—some literally, some morally, others according to nature, and some even drawing them toward the ineffable mysteries of God—it is truly no wonder that the history of the Egyptians is so varied and diverse as we find it among various authors. It is impossible that a variety of opinions does not greatly hinder the understanding of historical events and their circumstances. Lest the aforementioned variety place some obstacle in the way of explaining the hieroglyphics, it seemed appropriate in this place to deal with the various senses of Egyptian Theology and Philosophy, so that this variety of things, collected into one, might appear more clearly through this distinction:

# CHAPTER V.
## On the Fourfold *Theology* of the Egyptians founded upon the history of *Osiris* and *Isis*.

<margin>A fourfold method of interpretation used by the Egyptians.</margin>
From four types of men, a fourfold Theology of the Egyptians arose. The first class of men comprised the unrefined and illiterate, or the common folk, who understood the history of their Gods and the other fables connected to them only literally; from these came those detestable and unheard-of superstitions of all ages, which were discussed above. Under the second class were included those who applied their minds to the study of wisdom; these, gradually leaving behind fables and awkward fictions, joined the literal sense with a mystical meaning, transferring history to the secrets of nature; hence arose Natural Theology or Philosophy. The third class was made up of those called by the name of Sages; these translated the stories of the Gods partly to nature and partly to morals <term>τροπικῶς</term> <note>original Greek: "tropikos," meaning figuratively or metaphorically.</note>; hence Moral or Ethical Theology. Finally, the last class, placed in the highest rank of dignity above the others, was represented by the Priests. Being already sufficiently instructed in the science of nature and morals, they raised their minds to higher things. They turned the history of the Gods toward that Archetypal and intelligible world through a certain sublime and anagogical <note>A method of spiritual interpretation that "leads upward" from literal stories to divine truths.</note> method of interpretation, under an obscure but ingenious representation of symbols deliberately devised to cover the mysteries. From this, that mysterious [theology] of the Egyptians...

->### CHAPTER V.<-

->*On the History of Osiris, Isis, Typhon, and Horus.*<-

The Egyptians say, according to the testimony of Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is a primary source for Egyptian mythology.</note>, that Rhea <note>The Egyptian goddess Nut.</note> came secretly into the embrace of Saturn <note>The Egyptian god Geb.</note>, and soon after had relations with the Sun; but having been cursed by this pregnancy, she found neither a month nor a year in which she might give birth. Mercury <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, god of wisdom and writing.</note>, also captured by love for her, lay with her; subsequently, while playing a game of knuckle-bones <note>original: "Astragalis," a game similar to dice using the heel bones of sheep.</note> with the Moon, he won the seventieth part of each day. From these parts, he composed five days and joined them to the three hundred and sixty days of the year. These the Egyptians now call <term>epagomenas</term> <note>original: "ἐπαγομένας," meaning "added" or "intercalary" days.</note>, that is, "brought-in days"; they also call these the birthdays of the Gods. For on the first day, they say Osiris was born; at whose birth, according to Diodorus Siculus, a voice was heard declaring that the lord of all things had come forth into the light. Others celebrate a certain woman named Pamyle. They say that as she was leaving the temple of Jupiter <note>Amun-Ra.</note> at Thebes to draw water, she heard a voice commanding her to proclaim the birth of the great King and Benefactor, Osiris. Because she raised Osiris, she later established the festival of the Pammylia in his memory, about which we have written extensively elsewhere. On the second day, they say Arueris was born, whom some call Apollo and others the Elder Horus. On the third day, they devise that Typhon <note>The god Set, often associated with chaos and storms.</note> was born—not at the right time nor in the right place, but that he leaped out through a wound driven into his mother's side. On the fourth day, Isis was born in the <term>Panygris</term> <note>original: "παnygris," referring to a place of public assembly or a general festival.</note>, that is, during public gatherings. On the fifth day, Nephthys was born, whom some suspect to be Death, others Venus <note>Aphrodite/Hathor.</note>, and some even Victory.

While Osiris was traveling abroad, Typhon attempted no new schemes, as Isis was keeping a very careful watch against his machinations. But upon Osiris's return, now famous throughout the world for the glory of his deeds, Typhon was spurred by envy and set a trap for him. There were 72 conspirators with him, along with help from Aso, the Queen of the Ethiopians, as Mnaseas <note>Mnaseas of Patara, a Greek geographer of the 3rd century BC.</note> reports. When the Titans conspired, as follows presently, Typhon secretly measured Osiris's body and constructed a chest <note>original: "arca," the chest or sarcophagus that becomes Osiris's coffin.</note> to his size. This chest, crafted with wondrous skill and decoration, was brought to a banquet by Typhon and, as is known, seized everyone's admiration. Then, as a joke, Typhon promised he would give it as a gift to the one whose body it seemed to fit. All the guests made the attempt, but since it fit no one, they say that at last Osiris entered it. As soon as he did, all the conspirators rushed forward, threw on the lid, and having violently forced it shut, they even poured molten lead over it. Then, having carried it to the river, they cast it into the sea through the Tanitic mouth <note>One of the ancient navigable branches of the Nile delta.</note>, which even now is called a hateful and detestable opening; and these things are recorded to have happened on the 17th day.

<margin>The month of Athyr.</margin>
In the month of Athyr <note>original: "Ἀθὺρ," the third month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly corresponding to November.</note>, when the Sun was passing through Scorpio, and Osiris was now in the 28th year of his reign; when indeed the Panes and Satyrs, who dwell around Chemmis <note>An ancient city in Upper Egypt, modern Akhmim.</note>, were the first of all to find out what had happened, they suddenly raised great crowds and great uproars, which up to this time are called "Panics." <note>original: "Panici," referring to sudden, irrational fear attributed to the god Pan.</note>

When Isis heard this, she immediately cut her hair and put on a robe of mourning; from this, the name of the City of Coptos still remains. Although others signify "privation" through this name, derived from *kopēn* <note>original: "κοπὴν," Greek for "cutting," referring to the cutting of hair in mourning.</note>. From that time on, it has been suspected that a power of foretelling resides in children, and people observe their divination while they play and babble in the temples, whatever comes to mind without distinction.

Out of fear of Typhon, she is said to have cast out the child before its full term rather than having given birth; and thus he was added as a guardian to the Gods, just as dogs are assigned to mortals.

Thus, having set out for Byblos, and dissolving into tears without speaking to anyone, she sat down by the edge of a fountain. Her beauty, helpfulness, and wisdom being noticed, she was summoned by the Queen of Byblos to be the nurse for the royal infant; she therefore nourished the boy, using her finger instead of a breast...

# CHAPTER VI.

## The history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon translated into physical meanings.

<margin>Physical interpretation.</margin>
Archemachus of Euboea, an ancient Greek writer, after having spoken much regarding the ancient names of the Gods, finally attempts to translate the entire history of Osiris into the laws of nature; for he says that just as among the Greeks, Saturn is nothing other than time, Juno is air, and the birth of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here representing the elemental change of air into heat.</note> is the change of air into fire; so among the Egyptians, Serapis is no other than Pluto <note>The god of the underworld.</note>, nor is Isis anyone other than Proserpina <note>The queen of the underworld.</note>. Osiris, moreover, is nothing other than the Nile, and Isis nothing other than the earth, with which the river "lies" <note>An allegorical way of describing the flooding of the fields.</note>: Typhon is the sea, into which the Nile, discharging itself, is consumed and destroyed. Indeed, as much of the earth as admits the Nile and is mixed with it is commended for its fertility.

<margin>Macrobius. The sea is called the tear of Saturn.</margin>
Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial administrator and writer.</note> agrees with this, saying that on account of Saturn (for so they call the sea) mourning is renewed every year; Pythagoras also, for that reason, calls the sea the "tear of Saturn."

<margin>According to Xenophon.</margin>
For the Egyptians believe, as Xenophon <note>Presumably referring to a lost or pseudo-Xenophontic work often cited in Renaissance scholarship.</note> testifies, that the "face" of the world is in that part where the Sun rises, the right side is where the North wind blows, and the left where the South wind blows. Whence the Egyptians say not inappropriately of the Nile that it rises from the left and perishes on the right. For the Nile, flowing forth from the south, mixing itself with the sea in the northern region on the left part of the world, is absorbed; and for this reason the Priests loathe the sea, and the salt born from it,

<margin>The sea is the foam of Typhon.</margin>
calling it the "foam of Typhon," and for the same reason they are not accustomed to place it [salt] on the table; moreover, they even loathe seafaring men as if they sustain life from the sea, regarding them as inhuman, cruel, wild, and "sons of Typhon."

<margin>They hold sailors and fish in hatred.</margin>
Indeed, they hated fish to such an extent that it was adopted by them as a hieroglyphic for "hatred," as Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian customs.</note> testifies.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, Book 5 of the *Stromata*. Pythagoras.</margin>
Pythagoras, who was most deeply trained in Egyptian rites, suggests something similar when he commands that one must abstain from fish. For the Egyptian priests, as has been said, called the sea "ruin," because although it received the benefits of its entire nourishment from the Nile, they noticed that it was corrupted as soon as it was mixed with the sea; and thus they said that the sea vitiates and corrupts that which is most useful to the human race.

<margin>Clement, cited above.</margin>
Clement, cited a little before, reports that in the Saitic vestibule of the temple dedicated to Pallas <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian goddess Neith, the patroness of Sais.</note>, symbols of this kind are seen carved: an Infant, an Old Man, a Hawk, a Fish, and finally a Hippopotamus. The child and the old man seem to indicate the condition of human nature verging from childhood to old age, and then becoming like a child again. The Hawk showed both the love of God and that which is divine within us, and life itself as vital. The Fish [showed] hatred as well as death, which they called destruction and ruin. The river-horse <note>original: "equus fluuiatilis," a literal translation of hippopotamus.</note> noted impudent violence, as one who would not even spare his own father, and would kill him so that he might enjoy the marriage of his mother. Truly these symbols

# CHAPTER VI. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>Hieroglyphic symbols carved into the vestibule.</margin>
<margin>All moist force is called Osiris.</margin>
<margin>Typhon is whatever is squalid.</margin>
<margin>Egyptians associate with pale people with difficulty.</margin>
-> [Image: An engraving of an Egyptian obelisk featuring five symbolic figures stacked vertically. From top to bottom: the head of an infant (**We are born**), the head of an elderly man (**We grow old**), a hawk (**We live**), a fish (**We die**), and a hippopotamus (**Through the discord of nature**).] <-

The following are read: **We are born, We grow old, We live, We die, Through the discord of nature.** And let these things be said by us only in passing and "through the lattice" <note>original: "per transennam"; a Latin idiom meaning to view something briefly or glancingly.</note>. Furthermore, those among the Priests who excel in wisdom call Osiris not only the Nile, and Typhon the sea, but they say Osiris is every moistening power, and in this they confuse him with Dionysus <note>The Greek god of wine and vegetation, often associated with life-giving fluids.</note>, whom they called the primordial cause of generation and ripening. Typhon, on the other hand, they say is whatever is squalid, fiery, or parched, which resists moisture; or more clearly, they called Typhon everything that tends to harm the fertile moisture of the Nile by its drying and scorching power, such as the Northern winds. For this reason, they also fable that Typhon was born with a red body and affirm that he is pale; nor do they think it very pleasant or auspicious to associate with people of this kind. They hand down, again, that Osiris was of a black color; because such is the nature of water that it blackens the earth, clothes, clouds, and other things with which it is mixed, or perhaps because the element of moisture seems imbued with a dark color.

<margin>Why the Mnevis Bull is black</margin>
And for this same reason, the Mnevis Bull <note>original: "Bos Neuis"; the sacred bull of Heliopolis, a precursor or counterpart to the Apis bull.</note> worshipped by the Heliopolitans was imbued with a black color. But Egypt itself—which on account of its fertility and the richness of its soil we can call <term>melanchroon</term> <gloss>original: "μελάγχροον"; meaning black-skinned or dark-colored</gloss>, that is, a black vessel—they call <margin>Egypt is called Chemia.</margin> <term>Chemia</term> <gloss>original: "χμίαν"; the ancient name for Egypt, likely the root of the word "chemistry"</gloss>, which Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46 – 120 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian myths.</note> nevertheless interprets as the pupil of the eye, for just as the pupil represents the forms of things, so does Egypt; others also signify the "heart" by it. For Egypt is hot and moist, and situated in the southern parts of the world, which we said above is the left side of the world, just as the hot and moist heart occupies the left side in a human being. <margin>Eusebius</margin> Likewise, according to the testimony of Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop.</note>, they think the Sun and Moon are carried about not in chariots, but in ships, believing their nourishment and generation to come from moisture. Hence Giraldus <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), a Renaissance scholar of mythology.</note> reports <margin>Giraldus.</margin> that Homer and Thales <note>An early Greek philosopher who famously proposed that water is the primary substance of all matter.</note>, having been taught by the disciplines of the Egyptians, perceived water to be the beginning of all things. For the Greeks also called the effusion of seed <term>apousia</term> <gloss>original: "ἀπουσίαν"; literally "absence," but here used as a play on words for "emission"</gloss>, as if an absence; and its commingling <term>synousia</term> <gloss>original: "συνουσίαν"; meaning communion or sexual intercourse</gloss>; and they called the son <term>Aion</term> <gloss>original: "αἰῶν"; meaning an age or eternal life</gloss>; and they called Dionysus or Osiris <term>Hyen</term> <gloss>original: "ὕην"; meaning the "Moist One"</gloss>, as if the master of moist things, <term>from water</term> <gloss>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕδατος"</gloss> and <term>from rain</term> <gloss>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑετοῦ"</gloss>. They also used this to denote the King, and to signify the southern region. But they also say that the *phallophoria* <note>A ritual procession in which a representation of the phallus was carried to celebrate fertility and the life-giving power of moisture.</note> took its origin from the *thrium*; hence also the myth of Osiris’s private parts being cast into the sea by Typhon. <margin>Apep, brother of the Sun.</margin> Furthermore, the Egyptians say that Apep <note>original: "Apopin"</note> was the brother of the Sun and took up arms against Jupiter <note>referring to the Egyptian Amun, often equated with the Greek Zeus or Roman Jupiter.</note>; but when Osiris, bringing aid to Jupiter, had put the enemy to flight, he was adopted as a son by Jupiter and called Dionysus. They relate this myth to nature in this way: Jupiter is the spirit, to whom the fiery power is most hostile—a power which is not the Sun itself, but has a kinship with the sun. But moisture destroys the parched and dry exhalation by increasing and compressing it; moreover, the wind blows forth once formed from the exhalation. Other details can be seen in Hermaeus, Mnaseas, Anticlides, and in <margin>Eusebius, book 3, chapter 2. Plutarch, [On Isis and Osiris] 10 and 11. But so that all these things may be more accurately clarified, it must be known: moisture, or Osiris, can do nothing by itself unless joined with the earth, and therefore they fashioned Isis as the earth; <margin>Isis is the earth, from whose union Horus is born.</margin> from whose union they say Horus was born. Horus, moreover, is nothing other than a certain spirit, nourishing and preserving all things by its power; whom we have not inappropriately called Apollo above. He is the very tempering of the air, tempered by the heating power of the Sun. They say this Horus was raised near Buto in the marshes, and indeed it is so; for the marshy earth, overflowing with water, nourishes the exhalations that destroy aridity and drought. 

Indeed, the shore which the sea licks with its alluvial flow is called Nephthys; <margin>The Nile, as Osiris, is joined with Nephthys.</margin> but when the overflowing and flooding Nile spreads itself further, Osiris is said to be joined with Nephthys. Nephthys is also said to have been sterile when first joined to Typhon; <margin>What Nephthys is.</margin> so that it may be understood that from the beginning the earth stood unfruitful and sterile. Indeed, the impotence and tyranny of Typhon was nothing other than the prevailing force of squalor <note>The parched, infertile state of the land during a drought.</note> and the choking of the generative nature of moisture. 

<margin>What the impotence of Typhon is. What the Queen of the Ethiopians is.</margin> The Queen of the Ethiopians, of whom mention was made above, being called to help, represents the southern winds blowing from Ethiopia, which drive the clouds that the Etesian winds <note>Annual Mediterranean winds that blow from the north in summer, pushing clouds toward the Ethiopian highlands to create the Nile floods.</note> bring toward Ethiopia, from which the Nile takes its increase. But that ghastly Typhon, conqueror of the moist nature, constricts the thinned Nile and forces it to descend into the sea, greatly weakened and reduced. <margin>The thrusting of Osiris into the chest.</margin> And this is that casting and locking of Osiris into a chest, that is, the death and concealment of the water itself. 

Accordingly, they say Osiris died in the month of Athyr <note>An Egyptian month corresponding to late autumn, when the Nile's waters receded.</note>; at which time, the Etesian winds clearly failing, the Nile returns to its bed and the earth is uncovered. Then again, with the night increasing, the light is thinned by the darkness. The priests then perform other rituals, such as dressing an ox in a somber garment—specifically one made of fine linen <margin>An ox dressed in a somber garment. Four causes of Isiac grief and mourning.</margin>—and showing it to the mourning Goddess, [representing] Osiris to Isis; all of which they solemnly perform for four days starting after the 16th of the month of Athyr. For four causes of grief occur: namely, the receding Nile; the force of Typhon’s northern blasts; the shortness of the days; and finally the stripping of the earth and the sad death of the trees and shrubs.

<margin>The mystical image of the Moon.</margin>
On the nineteenth day at night, the robed priests go down to the sea and bring out a sacred chest containing a small golden box, into which they pour potable water. Meanwhile, a great shout arises from those standing by, crying that Osiris has been found. Soon they mix a clod of earth with the water, and adding spices and precious incense, they fashion an image in the likeness of the Moon; they then adorn this with a robe and bring it forward. In this way, they signify Isis receiving Osiris. And through Horus, they suggest that while Typhon <note>The personification of drought, chaos, and destruction.</note> was indeed conquered by mists and vapors, he was not however slain.

<margin>Why Typhon was not entirely killed.</margin>
For the Mistress of the Earth <note>Isis, representing the receptive nature of the world.</note> did not permit the nature opposite to moisture to perish entirely, wishing a balance of temperament to remain forever. Since the complete adornment and assembly of the world could in no way exist if the fiery power were to perish utterly.

And we have mostly taken these accounts from Plutarch. However, others interpreting it differently say that Osiris is nothing other than the seminal or generative power, and therefore they used to depict him in human form with an elevated genital organ. They said that Isis, moreover, was that feminine power of nature and the recipient of all generation; for which reason she was called by Plato <term>the Nurse</term> <note>original: "τιθήνη"</note> and <term>the receiver of all</term> <note>original: "πανδεχής"</note>. By Plutarch, she was called <term>she of a myriad names</term> <note>original: "μυριόνυμος"</note>; for she admits all ideas and images, having an innate love toward that which is first and highest among all things, which is indeed the Good itself. Toward this she is drawn, this she desires, this she follows; but that which is evil, she flees and turns away from. Hence, not without reason do they testify that the soul of Osiris is incorruptible and eternal, but his body was torn apart by Typhon, and that Isis seeks it and restores it into limbs. For that which is perpetual is much more excellent than that which is shifting and changeable; and the impressions she takes from the changeable image neither endure nor are always the same, but like seals in wax, the impressions and traces are wiped away.

<margin>What Horus represents.</margin>
When she therefore admits and borrows these things beyond reason, she is then said to join hands against Horus, whom Isis brought forth as the sensible image of the intelligible world. Furthermore, what else does that wondrous conception of Apollo (or Horus) from Isis and Osiris indicate, except the first and still imperfect generation made before the visible condition of the world? And what else is meant by Horus being blind in his eyes from birth, except a certain raw and unpolished likeness of the nascent world? Later, the now more perfect and adult Horus is said to have broken the attempts of Typhon; and therefore in Coptos, the image of Horus is depicted holding the genitals of Typhon in one hand. They also say that Mercury <note>The god Thoth, often associated with wisdom and the invention of music.</note>, having plucked out the nerves of Typhon, uses them for lyre strings; thus suggesting that the craftsman Reason <note>The Logos or creative principle.</note>, fitting this universe together, made a harmony out of discordant things. He did not destroy the wasting power, but repressed and blunted it. Nevertheless, it still—though greatly disjointed—disturbs, changes, and entangles things, bringing wondrous vicissitudes to the affairs of the world; and exciting dry motions, it shakes the earth; in the air, summoning troublesome spirits, it hurls whirlwinds and lightning; it even infects the waters, and subverts everything below the Moon, defiling whatever is most beautiful and bright. For the rest, the better part consists of three things: the Intelligible, Matter, and that which coalesces from both, which we call the world, and the Greeks call the <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "κόσμος"</note>.

<margin>Names of Isis: Mut, Athyr, Methyer</margin>
To this it is alluded that they call Horus *Coemin*, which means "visible"; for the world is perceptible and subject to our sight. They name Isis sometimes *Mut*, sometimes *Athyr*, and sometimes *Methyer*. The first of these names means "mother"; the second, the "mundane house of Horus," which Plato called the region and receptacle of generation; and the third signifies a name composed of "multitude" and "cause." <margin>The mixing of Poverty with Plenty.</margin> Socrates also seems to have alluded to this in Plato’s *Symposium*, when he devises the idea that Love was born from the mixing of **Penia** <note>Poverty</note> and **Porus** <note>Plenty or Resource</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>The eternal outpourings of God in the heavens.</margin>
For the goddess **Isis** is like matter, whom we call *Penia* <note>Poverty</note>, who is always intent upon the love and desire for **Osiris**. She is said to mourn and lament when she encounters extremes or experiences devastation, and she is said to sometimes gather the remains and fragments of Osiris, and sometimes to cover them with a robe, so that she might later show him restored and reconstituted in his limbs. For in the heavens and the stars, we see the species and eternal outpourings of God, but on the earth and in the sea—as in plants and other living things—we see them dissipated and hidden when they are brought into being. For this reason, the myth relates that **Typhon** <note>The principle of chaos and drought.</note> and **Nephthys** <note>The sister of Isis, often representing the desert or the end of things.</note> come together, and that Osiris practiced secret intercourse; this is because the destructive and decaying power greatly infests the outermost parts of matter, which they call *Nephthys* and *Teleutē* <note>Greek for "the end".</note>. However, the generative and moistening power is driven away by Typhon, and from it only that survives which Isis has taken up and received into her protection. For this reason, they call Isis *from going* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἴεσθαι [apo tou iesthai]</note>, that is, from the prudent progress of nature. Conversely, they call Typhon *Seth*, *Bebon*, and *Smy*, by which names they indicate a certain force made for prohibiting, resisting, and subverting. <margin>Typhon is Seth, Bebon, Smy. ## CHAPTER VII.
### *Concerning the Sun and Moon signified by Osiris and Isis.*

<margin>Osiris as Sun, Isis as Moon.</margin>
Although these meanings have been dealt with elsewhere, it seemed appropriate to treat them more abundantly and specifically in this place, since most explanations of hieroglyphs rest upon this as a foundation. Thus the Egyptians, just as other nations, interpreted Osiris as the Sun and Isis as the Moon, because the whole of nature is sustained by the dominion and influence of these stars; the myth of Hercules expresses this aptly, who, added as a companion to the Sun, traverses the celestial circuits with him. To the Moon, however, they add Mercury <note>The god Thoth, often associated with the moon and wisdom.</note>; for they compare those things which pertain to the Moon to philosophy and reason, and those which look toward the Sun to strength and supreme activity. But this place seems to require that we also adapt the myth cited above to the Sun and the Moon. 

Thus they tell the myth that Osiris perished on the 17th day of the month of Athyr <note>An Egyptian month roughly corresponding to October/November.</note>, by which number the elongation of the Moon from the Sun is shown, which the Greeks call the "full moon" <note>original Greek: παυσέληνον [pauselenon]</note>; the Pythagoreans call it "obstruction" <note>original Greek: ἀντίφραξιν [antiphraxin]</note>, that is, the inter-segment, and they utterly loathe this number. For while 16 is a "tetragon" <note>A square number ($4 \times 4$).</note>, that is, a square number, 18 is "longer on one side" <note>An oblong number ($3 \times 6$).</note>, or a parallelogram—which are the only numbers whose areas happen to have the same value as their perimeters <note>A 4x4 square has an area of 16 and a perimeter of 16; a 3x6 rectangle has an area of 18 and a perimeter of 18. This was a significant observation in Pythagorean geometry.</note>. The number 17, occurring between them, cuts through both and distinguishes the "sesquioctave" <note>original Greek: ἐπόγδοον [epogdoon], the 9:8 ratio, which forms the whole tone in music.</note> proportion; therefore they loathe this number as both imperfect and unfortunate. 

Moreover, the number of years they say Osiris reigned—namely 28—they refer to the days in which the Moon completes its paths, or to the monthly span <margin>What is the mystical meaning of Osiris reigning 28 years?</margin>; and accordingly they decorate the tombs of Osiris with various things imitating the figure of the Moon, because the Moon, approaching the Sun, ceases to shine and is taken from our eyes. <margin>Osiris cut into 14 parts</margin> Indeed, Osiris being torn into 14 parts seems to designate nothing other than the interval of days of the Moon between conjunction and opposition <note>The time between a new moon and a full moon.</note>. Whence, on the day when the Moon withdraws itself from the rays of the Sun, they call it the "perfect good," according to the testimony of Manetho <margin>Manetho</margin> <note>A famous Egyptian priest and historian of the 3rd century BCE.</note>. They then interpret Osiris as the benefactor, robust and powerful; indeed, they also call another name of the God "Omphin" (more correctly "Momphta"), which means "benefactor" <note>original Greek: εὐεργέτην [euergetēn]</note>...

<margin>Columella, Book 1 on Rural Affairs.</margin>
...[she] taught men to commit seeds to the earth at the certain and opportune time, to cut timber suitable for building, and to labor in other works of agriculture; for which reason Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a prominent Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD.</note> testifies in Book 1 *On Gardening* that the arts necessary for life and human use arose from her. Moreover, Isis is called Juno because of her feminine virtue, which she continuously flows into the air through her moistening power. She is called Venus because of the reproductive appetite by which all lower creatures are inclined toward the procreation of their like; and also because of the supreme fertility she possesses in producing things, which is why she is not wrongly imagined by the Poets to have been born from the genitals of Saturn <note>A reference to the myth of Venus/Aphrodite born from the sea foam created by the castration of Uranus, who was often syncretized or confused with Saturn in later allegorical traditions.</note> when they were cut off and thrown into the sea. Finally, she is called Proserpina <note>The Roman name for Persephone, queen of the underworld, whose myth explains the seasonal cycle of grain.</note> because of her dominion over the "children of the earth"—I mean plants, trees, seeds, and other fruits: for by communicating her moist influences to the earth, joined with the power of the Sun, she causes plants, shrubs, leaves, and seeds to grow, or rather to prosper. Finally, Horus represents all those effects which are generated on the earth by the power of the Sun and the Moon.

<margin>Why is Horus depicted as an infant?</margin>
->HORUS | WORLD<-
<image-desc>A circular woodcut emblem depicts a standing nude infant, identified as Horus. He holds a cornucopia filled with produce in his right hand and a leafy branch in his left.
