Hence he is depicted as an infant because of the tenderness of young plants, and with a cornucopia to indicate the abundance of things produced. Typhon, however, seems to represent nothing else than either excessive moisture, by which Horus is submerged as if cast into the sea, or the "Saturnine rays" <note>In ancient astrology, rays from the planet Saturn were often considered cold, dry, or destructive to life.</note> or a certain scorching force, by which Horus is forced to die violently through a lack of moisture, as if killed by Typhon.
<margin>What is Typhon?</margin>
For nothing is so harmful to plants, fruits, or flowers as excessive humidity, by which they are choked and rot; or excessive dryness, by which they are necessarily forced to waste away as their roots dry up, unless they are soon sought out by Isis—that is, restored to life by the kindly gaze of the Moon’s rays. And from all these things it is clear with how much ingenuity and erudition the ancient Egyptian sages represented that fertile spirit of Nature under this symbolic history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon. But the sequence now requires us to say by what method they eventually applied these things to morals.

Hence, Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop.</note> in a truly beautiful discourse shows that this history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon is a certain mirror of moral discipline set before everyone,

For just as in the greater world (the macrocosm), all lower things are ruled and sustained by the unhindered conjunction and operation of the Sun and Moon, so in the political world, by a certain analogy, there is a given Sun and Moon, by whose unanimous consent the entire remaining political body is nourished and sustained. Indeed, we say that this Sun and Moon in moral philosophy are nothing other than
<margin>What are the Sun and Moon in Ethics?</margin>
the concord of the **intellect** and the **will**, represented by **Osiris** and **Isis**. Just as Osiris, or the Sun, by illuminating and warming, makes both the Moon and the rest of the lower world fit for generations, so the intellect, by illuminating the will (or Isis), and inciting it to love through the representation of the true good, makes it capable of producing good works.
<margin>Horus is concord and peace in the political world.</margin>
From their mutual concord is born **Horus**, that true **Apollo**, the inventor of music and harmonic proportions. When he plays in harmony, the highest things respond to the lowest, the lowest to the highest, and finally the lowest and highest to the middle, with the greatest proportion everywhere; that is, the exterior powers are subjected to the interior ones, the sensitive appetite is conformed to the rational, the will is subjected to the intellect, and the remaining powers consent as if into one, being unanimously intent on the good. They are found to produce a certain admirable peace of mind, not poorly shadowed forth by the attribute of Apollo’s cornucopia and flowers. 

However, since all things in human affairs are mixed, and good is tempered with evil—and as Homer wrote, there are two jars at the threshold of Jove <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, where Zeus dispenses blessings from one jar and miseries from another.</note>, of which it is right to believe there is not just one dispenser or manager, but that they are paid out by two contrary principles and opposing powers, of which one is carried straight to the right, while the other is carried obliquely to the left—it happens that the harmony of that microcosm is repeatedly disturbed: **Osiris** is killed by **Typhon** and thrown, scattered, into the sea. **Isis** mourns, and by a simulated discovery of his body, she restores his limbs in a certain deceptive figment of a statue.
<margin>When Osiris is killed.</margin>
That is to say, the rational power is overcome by the sensitive and brutal appetite (the true symbol of Typhon), and is clouded over, the splendor of its light being extinguished in the darkness of brutal passions. For Osiris is truly said to be killed by Typhon when the intellect, enticed by vain concupiscence and conquered by brutal appetite, judges that what must be done is diametrically contrary to the law of nature or the dictates of right reason. Isis is said to mourn and seek Osiris when, with the intellect clouded and prostrate, the will seeking the good cannot find it because of the defect of the one who should lead and propose the truth. She fashions a "false Osiris" with deceptive art when she thinks she must rest content in an apparent and false good. Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius ter-maximus"</note> and Zoroaster once aptly shadowed this discord with their symbolic fictions, placing the said rational and sensitive appetites, so contrary to each other, under...

By the name of these gods—of whom he called the former the creator of good and the latter the creator of evil—he designated the better one Horomazes <note>Ahura Mazda</note> and the worse Arimanius <note>Ahriman</note>. He likened the former to light and the latter to darkness and gloom; but between these two, he placed Mithras <note>The Persian god of the sun and covenants, acting here as a mediator.</note> as a middle point. He established that the former should be entreated with constant prayers and sacrifices, while to the other, averting amulets and funereal sacrifices ought to be offered, accompanied by curses. Among other things, they also crush a certain herb
<margin>The herb Omomum.</margin>
by the name of Omomum <note>Likely referring to Haoma, a sacred plant in Zoroastrian ritual.</note> in a mortar, invoking Hades <note>original: "Ditem"</note> and Darkness <note>original: "Scotum"</note>—that is, the deity of the shadows—and mixing in the blood of a wolf, they carry it to a dark place and cast it away. By this description, he intends to suggest nothing other than the ceremonies by which the Egyptians treated Osiris and Typhon: the former as the "Greatest Genius" through sacrifices, incense, and countless other rites; the latter as an unfortunate demon to be driven away with curses and the mournful clatter of sistrums <note>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument used in rituals to ward off evil.</note>. In doing so, they intended to signify obscurely what ought to be done regarding the discord of powers in domestic disputes, and finally, in the tumults and seditions of Republics. For as we said above, moral philosophy is considered in three ways: as it concerns private persons, as it concerns the **Economy** <term>Oeconomy|From the Greek 'oikos' (house) and 'nomos' (law), referring to the management of a household or family unit.</term>, or finally, as it concerns the Republic or State.
<margin>Parallel comparisons</margin>
For what that rebellious and traitorous Typhon is between Osiris and Isis in the rational soul, such is distrust, jealousy, and suspicion between a husband and wife in the Household. In the political world, it is war, tumult, seditions, and contempt for healthy laws between a Magistrate or Prince and rebellious, disparaging subjects. To begin with the first: if the better part of a human being—that is, the superior—is subjugated by the inferior, then Osiris is killed by Typhon, and the entire harmony of the soul perishes. Likewise, if in a household the spouses are distrustful, jealous, and suspicious, having no confidence in one another, Osiris is killed by Typhon and his body is cast away, torn into various parts. That is to say, those who ought to be as "two in one flesh" are instead distracted into many parts, stained by adultery and a wandering lust for fornication in various and diverse mixtures. Isis mourns; that is, she is consumed by fear, suspicions, grief, and other accidents proper to such spouses. Therefore, Typhon must be put to flight by sistrums, curses, and other means customary to the Egyptians. Finally, if the Magistrate, King, or Prince is in discord with his subjects, or if the laws established for the common good are held in contempt, Osiris is killed by Typhon. This means the master-building intellect of the lawmaker becomes deformed in the minds of the subject recipients; and through various and wicked interpretations of the laws, Osiris is torn apart. From this arise wars, civil seditions, inhuman slaughters, and other "Iliads of woes" <note>A classical idiom for a vast series of evils or troubles.</note> which usually accompany this discrepancy like a shadow follows a body. On these matters, see the excellent discourses of

Finally, a life is lived free of all pain and evils; everyone, having at last attained the intense and long-desired tranquility and peace, enjoys them happily and without weariness. # CHAPTER IX.

### *Concerning the anagogical interpretation of the history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon, or concerning the sublime wisdom of the Egyptians indicated through this.*

<note>Anagogical interpretation refers to the "sublime" or spiritual level of meaning, seeking to find hidden truths about the divine nature and the afterlife within a text or myth.</note>

<margin>Cicero.</margin> Since all good things ought to be sought from the immortal Gods, says Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, then that wisdom which consists of knowledge of the gods themselves ought to be sought above all. Imbued with this, that great King of the Macedonians, Alexander, used to say that it was much more pleasant for him to think rightly about the Gods than even to rule over many nations. For he judged rightly and wisely that nothing greater could be given by the Gods, nor could anything more noble and worthy be received by man, than that truth and wisdom which consists in the knowledge of that highest and incomprehensible Good. <margin>Fabulous narrations transformed into Divine mysteries.</margin> Hence the wise men of the Egyptians, subtle in intellect and most fit for the scrutiny of sublime things, looked upon that abominable and plainly ridiculous system of the superstitious common folk in the worship of the Gods; yet they saw that they could not take away the already deep-rooted custom of idolatry, nor the opinion once absorbed by the stubborn crowd concerning their ridiculous Gods. Under these figments of fables, they attempted to express the greatest mysteries concerning GOD, the world, Angels, and Demons—as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> testifies—by fleeing to anagogical methods of explanation. ### CHAPTER IX. 208 BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>The ancient sages did not believe in <term>polytheism</term> <note>the belief in many gods; original: πολυθέαν</note></margin>
It was never the intention of the ancient sages to attribute the nature of the Divinity—which is the best, most noble, and most excellent thing the intellect can conceive—to things subject to corruption or the wicked affections of the mind, such as lust, envy, and fear. Nor did they truly apply it to those things which are furthest removed from both reason and the senses, such as that deceptive Apis or the Mnevis Bull, the Goat of the Mendesians, the monstrous crocodile, the unfeeling and lifeless Nile, garden herbs treated as deities, the fodder of beasts, and similar portents of gods. Such things did not merely turn sacred matters into objects of laughter and contempt (which would be the least of the harms), but through sheer and intolerable superstition and the various deceptions of demons, they entangled the minds of some, while dragging others into a beast-like and shameful impiety and an outright license for sinning. For who is so ignorant of philosophical discipline that he would believe <term>hawk-formed</term> <note>original: ἱερακόμορφον</note>, <term>dog-headed</term> <note>original: κυνοκέφαλον</note>, and similar <term>many-formed</term> <note>original: πολύμορφα</note> idols to be actual Gods? Furthermore, the idea that the Gods, as the Egyptians supposedly thought, transformed themselves into various shapes—now an Ibis or a dog, now taking on the bodies of hawks or cows—out of fear of the power of Typhon <note>the chaotic spirit of destruction in Egyptian myth</note>, exceeds all fables and portents. Therefore, it must by no means be thought that the wisest Priests of the Egyptians either attributed anything to these things or, being persuaded by some false opinion, felt that there was anything of Divinity within them. Rather, they used these fables as a kind of symbol <note>original: symbolis</note> for the sacraments of sublime things, to be hidden from the unworthy, indicating a deeper philosophy. For they were so empowered by the light of nature that they believed that being which we call GOD could not possibly be finite, corruptible, changeable, or manifold.

<margin>Zoroaster. Trismegistus.</margin>
<margin>One God.</margin>
And indeed, they first gathered the infinity of GOD by the natural reasoning of the mind—as is apparent from Zoroaster, Trismegistus, and others—from the preservation of all things and the essential dependence of created things upon GOD; for it is impossible for this to belong to a finite and changeable being. Hence Orpheus wisely says in the hymn of Saturn: *“You who inhabit all parts of the world, void of birth”* <note>original: Qui omnes mundi partes habitas, generationis expers</note>; following him, Parmenides the Pythagorean said that God is the One, immobile, and infinite being. Furthermore, Trismegistus confesses that God is not mixed with anything: He is the private Leader of no one, but exists as the common Leader of all. If He is common, then a common duty belongs to Him; and if His "being" is common to all things, then wherever "being" may be, it depends upon Him.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
<margin>Trismegistus, dialogue 12.</margin>
Touching upon this mystically, Zoroaster says: *“All things were generated by a single fire”* <note>original: Omnia esse vno igne genita</note>; and Orpheus calls God "Necessity" for this reason, asserting that Necessity dominates everywhere. But let us hear Trismegistus treating more clearly the infinity of God in Dialogue 12: *“God,”* he says, *“is around all things at once and through all things; for He is the act and power of all, and there is nothing in the whole world that is not God himself. Thus, neither magnitude, nor place, nor quality, nor figure, nor time exist around God, for He is everything.”* Following him, Plato, Pythagoras, Plotinus, and other students of Egyptian wisdom reported similar things regarding the aforementioned points (to say nothing of Aristotle for the moment).

<margin>The nerve in an animal which, when moved, causes everything in the animal to move.</margin>
It has been discovered in animals that there is a certain nerve around the <term>Nucha</term> <note>the spinal cord or nape of the neck</note>, which, when pulled, moves all the limbs of the living creature simultaneously, so that each part is stirred by its own proper motions; and thus the Egyptians...

### EGYPTIAN MATTERS. CHAPTER IX.
### Dd

[Egyp]tians, and after them Aristotle in his book *On the Universe*; they taught that the members of the world are moved by God, the "cause of causes." Since they therefore called the one God a necessary being, infinite, and immobile—that eternal and immense circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere <note>This famous definition of God was often attributed in the Renaissance to Hermes Trismegistus</note>; from whom and into whom whatever exists, proceeding, returns; they consequently considered it impossible for a plurality of Gods to exist. This is because, taught and led by the light of nature, they judged it <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον (*adynaton*)</note> for there to be more than one first principle. For in any category of things, they knew that which is the highest must be only one. They recognized that if there were several Gods, one would necessarily lack the perfection of the other, and consequently be liable to some defect—which is repugnant to the Divine nature. Therefore, they confessed one God, <term>nature naturing</term> <note>original: *natura naturans*; a philosophical term referring to God as the creative force that brings forth the natural world</note>, or the essence of essences, the beginning and the end of all things. Furthermore, the motion and order of such a vast and complex machine, remaining so steady through so many ages, taught them that the Governor was tireless, and possessed a certain infinite power.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 4 of the *Physics*.</margin>
For as Aristotle rightly teaches, a finite power cannot continue motion indefinitely, whether in a finite or infinite time, without fatigue. But to finally come to the point: the Egyptian sages wished to obscurely indicate to us this God—whose multiple virtues and perfections they represented—through Osiris, Isis, and Horus.

<margin>The ancients expressed the Deity through Osiris, Isis, Typhon, and Horus.</margin>
They established Him as the principle and author of all things, while representing His wisdom through Isis (whom we noted above from Plutarch, by the force of her name, signifies nothing other than the "prudent progress of nature") governing and disposing all things. Finally, through Horus, they intended to signify that external and sensible fabric of the world, produced by God with the highest wisdom. And Iamblichus, treating *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, testifies that this is indeed the case. For when his disciples asked what he judged the first cause to be—whether it was an intellect, or something above the intellect? Whether it was one single thing, or one together with others? Whether it was corporeal or incorporeal? Whether it was the same as the Creator of the world, or superior to Him?—and similar questions concerning the first principle.

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*.</margin>
Iamblichus is said to have responded with these words:

> I will first tell you, he says, the reason why the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians thought various things about these matters, and furthermore, why the sages of this age do not speak of them in the same way. Since there are many essences in the universe, and since they differ among themselves in many ways, it is rightly handed down that many of them have principles of different orders. From some priests, certain principles are handed down as total and universal, as Seleucus relates; Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-king of Egypt</note> himself handed them down in 20,000 volumes, or as Manetho <note>original: *Maneth*; the 3rd-century BC Egyptian priest and historian</note> records, 36,000, and also 6,526, and in these he perfectly demonstrated all things.

<margin>Mercury [Hermes] wrote 20,000 accounts of the principles. Seleucus. Manetho.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, to briefly declare the truth about all these things, and first, regarding what you initially ask. The First God, existing before being and alone, is the father of the first God, whom he begets while remaining in his solitary unity. This is something "above the intelligible," and is the exemplar of that which is called "father of itself," "son of itself," "father to the one," and "truly good God." For he is greater and first, and the source of all and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, of the Ideas. From this one, the self-sufficient God unfolded himself, and therefore he is called...

*Since therefore, as Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Renaissance humanist and philosopher</note> testifies in his commentary on the cited passage of Iamblichus, those manifold Gods of the Egyptians signify nothing other than the different force and power of the one God, and consequently Phta, Amun, Emepht, Ichthon, and Osiris are nothing else but the creative intellect, the closest Leader of the world's creators, arranging all things; we shall say most excellently that Osiris is that supreme Archetypal Intellect of all things. Isis, however, is his providence and love, by whose virtue Horus Apollo was born—that sensible world, and that admirable concord and harmony of all things, which was mystically indicated by the ancients under the fable in which they imagined Harmony to be the daughter of Apollo, born of Mars and Venus. Similarly, they imagined Harmony was born from Mars and Venus because of the agreement of similar things with dissimilar ones, and because of the consensus and dissent of hidden things, in which alone the beauty and music of the world consists. Moreover, that Osiris is the Archetypal Intellect is shown by his very name, which they say beautifully signifies "many-eyed" <note>original Greek: πολυόφθαλμον (polyophthalmon)</note>; that is, having many eyes, doubtless because of the manifold virtues and operations he performs, and the all-penetrating power of his divine rays.*

### EGYPTIAN MATTERS. CHAPTER IX. 211

It is everywhere, and cannot be divided into parts, nor can it be confined anywhere, nor truly separated from its source; and although it is present, it is not permitted to be mixed with the air. In the same way, the light of GOD is entirely indivisible and is deeply present to the whole world, even though it imparts its power especially to certain parts adapted to it. Meanwhile, however, it fills all things in a certain way, because of its perfect power and its utterly immense dominion over all things. Hence it perfects all things and unites the furthest extremes with one another, encompassing all things within itself through intermediary means, reflecting itself back upon itself, and thus remains entirely united to itself. This is the very function that the world imitates through its circular motion and the connection and reconciliation of its parts into a unity, as the elements turn into elements in succession, and the power of the higher things is sent down to the lower.

<margin>Isis is Love and Providence.</margin>
Furthermore, what has been said concerning the light of the Sun or <term>Osiris</term> <note>In this context, Osiris represents the primary Divine Intellect or the Sun</note> may also be said of <term>Isis</term> or the Moon. For Isis is nothing other, as has been said, than that Wisdom, love, and providence of the <term>Archetypal Intellect</term> <note>The original blueprint or divine mind of the Creator</note>, by which the world, or <term>Horus</term> <note>Representing the physical universe or the "offspring" of the divine principles</note>, is born and preserved. These are indeed always inseparably connected; for he who sees the light of the Moon also sees the light of the Sun, indistinguishable from the Moon’s light, since the light of the Moon is nothing other than the light of the Sun reflected toward us.

<margin>St. Dionysius</margin>
Thus, therefore, he who sees the Wisdom, providence, and love of GOD shining forth in this world, sees GOD himself; for according to the testimony of <term>St. Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist theologian</note>, all created things are nothing other than certain mirrors reflecting the rays of Divine Wisdom to us.

<margin>From providence, etc. <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς προνοίας</note></margin>
Hence the Egyptian sages fashioned a story that Osiris, having entrusted the care of affairs to Isis, traveled through the whole unknown world. What else is signified by this but the invisible power of GOD penetrating the innermost parts of everything? For Isis, or the Wisdom and providence of GOD, appears in all things; but the intellect from which she proceeds—that is, Osiris, who moves all things invisibly—appears only through his image expressed in Isis.

<margin>Plotinus, book on the 3 Hypostases.</margin>
But let us hear the opinion of the most enlightened <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism</note> regarding these matters; for thus he says in his book on the *Three Hypostases*: *If anyone admires this sensible world,* he says, *considering its magnitude, beauty, and the perpetual order of its motion, and the Gods within it—some visible, others invisible—and the spirits, animals, plants, and all other things, let them ascend in mind to the primary exemplar, and there let them contemplate all intellectual things, and the eternal mind and wisdom presiding over them all.* And a little later: *Who then begot this? Surely that simple one, who is before this in order, who is the cause of its existence, and of its greatness, and who created number. For number is not first; for before duality there is the One; then duality is born from the One.* And a little later: *Everything loves that which it begot, especially when the generator and the generated are alone. When that which he begot is also the best, it is necessarily with him, so that it is separated only by the fact that it is another.*

<margin>Plato.</margin>
For this reason, **Plato** also says that all three things are around the King:

<margin>All three things around the King.</margin>

### CHAPTER IX. 212 BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>
God produces all things through His wisdom.

The Kabbalists in the Tree of the <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>.

Pallas born from the brain of Jove.

Numenius cites Zoroaster as saying that God produced all things through His Wisdom and His Love. This is supported by the Jerusalem Targum, which, in the place of the Hebrew phrase <note>original: "Berēšît bārā’ ’Ĕlōhîm ’ēt haššāmayim"</note> *In the beginning God created the heavens*, uses the Aramaic phrase <note>original: "Be-ḥokmthā’ bĕrā’ ’Ĕlāhā’ yāt šĕmayyā’"</note> *In Wisdom God created the heaven and the earth.* Hence, in the Tree of the Sephiroth among the Kabbalists, three "measures" or three properties are attributed to GOD, by which they record that GOD made all things; these are <note>original: "Keter, Chokmah, Binah"</note> *Crown, Wisdom, and Intelligence.* These are what Rabbi Abraham, in the *Yetzirah* <note>The "Book of Formation," an early foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note>, calls <note>original: "Sopher, Sephar, and Sippur"</note> *the counter, the number, and the counted*. These three correspond exactly to the three names cited above from Iamblichus: Amun, Phtha, and Emepht. For just as the Hebrews establish that <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>The Infinite or Boundless Godhead before emanation.</note> is <note>original: "bli techilah harashit ab sebat hassebot"</note> *without beginning, the first Father and cause of causes*, so too the Egyptians consider *Emepht* to be the first intellect and the Creator, whom they also prefigure in the second series of sensible causes through Osiris, or the Sun. Again, just as the Hebrews say that *Chokmah* or Wisdom is the creator of the world, so the Egyptians call the Wisdom of the first intellect *Phtha*. By this name they refer to Mercury, the counselor of Isis, and indeed to Isis herself, who is the full image and archetype of the intellect of the first Osiris; for this reason, Orpheus not inappropriately called her Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena, associated with wisdom.</note>, and the ancients also imagined her to have been born from the brain of Jove.

*Amun*, however, responding to the *Binah* or "Intelligence" of the Hebrews, is the active power of both directed outward, by which the world—*HORUS*—is produced. From this arise the various patterns of hieroglyphic equipment by which the priests of the sacred mysteries everywhere expressed Horus. For instance: the staff known as the <term>kekumophoros</term> <note>original: κηκυμόφος</note>, which is distinguished by the head of a hoopoe bird; also the <term>lituus</term> <note>A curved wand used by augurs or priests.</note> and the <term>gnomon</term> <note>A carpenter's square or an instrument for measuring shadows.</note>; and from the back, a triangle to which a circle is attached. These indicate nothing other than the world produced by God through His wisdom, with the wonderful variety of things signified by the head of the hoopoe. The highest harmony shines forth through the staff, and finally, a fitting order is indicated by the square. Truly, since we discuss this hieroglyphic pattern more extensively in other places, we refer the reader there; let us resume our mystical reflections. Thus Horus, produced from *Emepht* through *Phtha* and *Amun*, is described by Plato—a studious disciple of the Egyptians—in these words: when he asserts that this sensible world flowed from that Archetypal Triangle, he demonstrates it. This is also clearly indicated by that Triangle with the globe attached among the other symbols of Horus, and it is expressed quite beautifully and elegantly in the following Diagram.

These things indeed correspond perfectly to the eternal Wisdom of GOD; moreover, they signify the supreme generating Wisdom through a beautiful hieroglyphic on the **Bembine Tablet** <note>Also known as the *Mensa Isiaca*, this is a famous bronze tablet of Roman origin depicting Egyptian deities, which Kircher believed held the keys to ancient Egyptian theology.</note>. He sits upon a variegated seat to demonstrate his authority over all things of the lower worlds. You may see the explanation of these things established by various authorities in what follows.

<margin>Interpretation of the symbols of Horus.</margin>
Horus, however, is depicted as a boy, to show that the world was *produced* by the Wisdom of GOD in time, like a small infant. He is represented with a cornucopia to indicate the variety, abundance, and fullness of created things in the world; he stands upon a cube to indicate the stability and solidity of the world. A triangle with a globe inscribed upon the cube signifies that HORUS flowed forth from the archetypal triangle; a staff marked with the head of a Hoopoe <note>The Hoopoe was often associated with gratitude or filial piety in Renaissance symbol books, though here Kircher links it to the support of the world's variety.</note> indicates that the world is, as it were, propped up and sustained by the variety of things. The *lituus* <note>A curved wand used by Roman augurs, here symbolizing cosmic harmony.</note> signifies the harmony of the universe. The *gnomon* <note>An instrument used for measuring shadows or an architect's square, symbolizing order.</note> designates the order and admirable arrangement of things. Finally, Horus presses his lips and suggests silence with his finger to indicate the ineffability of the mysteries.

From the preceding inscriptions, therefore, all those things which we have said thus far concerning the secret Theology of the Egyptians—signified through *Osiris, Isis, and Horus*—are clearly demonstrated.

<margin>What is the killing of Osiris in Egyptian Theology?</margin>
Furthermore, that they imagine Osiris torn into parts by Typhon <note>Typhon, or Set, represents the principle of chaos and destruction in this theological framework.</note> and enclosed in a chest is by no means without meaning. By this they wish to indicate nothing other than the ignorance and darkness of the human intellect. Since the human mind cannot grasp that ineffable and most simple essence of God by its own natural powers, it uses analogies and similarities of created things—which are, to speak with **Horace**, "breaths of the divine particle" <note>original Latin: *Diuinæ particulæ auræ*. A reference to Horace’s *Satires* 2.2.79, suggesting the soul is a spark of the divine.</note>—and by confusing Him with corruptible and imperfect corporeal things, the mind seems to tear Him, as it were, into parts. For according to the testimony of **Porphyry**, it was a custom among the Egyptians to compare that supreme Deity with whichever animal in which some exceptional power or property shone forth.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>

<margin>God has the head of a falcon.</margin>

### EGYPTIACA. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>What are the multiform Gods of the Egyptians?</margin>
The multiform images of the Gods denote nothing other than the manifold power of God, shadowed forth by the diverse properties of animals. Osiris is, therefore, torn into parts when, through ignorance and the darkness of the intellect, people confuse God with created things. By applying to Him things that are corporeal—which does not and cannot befit Him—they, as it were, tear the whole into parts. Indeed, **Plato** rightly says that plurality by no means befits God; for all things that imply a multitude, by receding from unity, are more imperfect and worse the further they recede from it. Osiris is shut in an ark by **Typhon** <note>In Egyptian myth, Typhon (Set) trapped Osiris in a chest; Kircher interprets Typhon here as a symbol of carnal desire or ignorance.</note> when the intellect of men is darkened by the desire for earthly and fleshly things. By dismissing the love and contemplation of heavenly and divine things, man places an obstacle before himself and makes himself incapable of perceiving the divine rays of Osiris.

<margin>How is Osiris to be restored?</margin>
However, the lost Osiris is sought by **Isis**, and once found and having been mutilated, he is restored to wholeness. This is achieved through true wisdom and love, accompanied by <term>sistrums</term> <note>The sistrum was a metallic rattle used in Egyptian religious ceremonies.</note>—that is, by frequent songs of praise. Thus, having been recollected from where he was scattered in creations (as if through certain parts) and adored in true faith, he is restored to his own unity. When this is done, a great joy soon arises in the mind, which is fittingly represented in the Egyptian ceremonies by that celebrated *finding of Osiris* <note>original Greek: τῆς Οσείδος εὐρέσει (tēs Oseidos heuresei)</note>.

<margin>Application to the mysteries of our faith</margin>
And from this discourse, it is clear how harmoniously these things can be adapted to the mysteries of our faith. For what else does **Osiris** indicate but that eternal Sun, the first archetypal intellect, the first and most fruitful life, that Father of immense majesty? He, by understanding Himself and all things in Himself, conceives in Himself a perfect notion of His whole being and all perfections. He produces an equal, full, perfect, and <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Of the same substance or essence; a key theological term for the Trinity.</note> image and life of Himself—an idea indistinct in nature, which is the **Word of the Father** and eternal **Wisdom**, represented by **Isis**. By the consubstantial power of both, **Horus** is produced—that is, that admirable machine of the world, an absolute exemplar of the most eminent beauty and perfection.

<margin>How the Hebrew Theologians express the holy Triad. Pico della Mirandola in the *Heptaplus* near the end.</margin>
The more secret Theologians of the Hebrews confirm this in the first chapter of Genesis, asserting that through $\beth$ (*Beth*), that is, through *Aleph* acting by *Beth*, He created the world—which is to say, the *Father* through the *Son*. **Pico della Mirandola** explains this more clearly in his *Heptaplus* <note>A work by the Renaissance philosopher Pico della Mirandola that provides a seven-fold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis.</note> regarding the word *Bereshit* <note>The first word of the Hebrew Bible: "In the beginning."</note>. Through a certain "metathetic" <note>A method of rearranging letters to find hidden meanings.</note> method of the Kabbalistic discipline, he produces this sense:

-> אב בבר ראשית שבת ברא ראש אש שת רב איש ברית תוב <-

which is: *The Father, in the Son, the beginning, the rest, the end; created the head, the fire, the foundation of the Great Man* (understand here the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," usually referring to man as a reflection of the universe.</note>) *by a good covenant*. By these things, nothing else is suggested but that admirable order, disposition, and most absolute harmony of the three worlds—the Angelic, the Great, and the Small—corresponding to one another in a beautiful analogy: a most similar exemplar of the Divine Triad.

<margin>The world made in the image of the Holy Trinity.</margin>

In the Greater World (the universe), there are three spaces: the elementary, the sidereal, and the empyrean, distinct by three qualities: figure, light, and motion. In any composite or mixed thing, there is matter, form, and a measure of virtues in all things, a nu-

...measure and weight; furthermore, a beginning, a middle, and an end. In the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a common Renaissance term for the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>—that is, in yourself—you find memory, the power of understanding, and the will. In the sciences, you find the natural, rational, and moral faculties. In every series of Triads, the first is the power of God represented by Osiris; the second is wisdom represented by Isis; and the third is love—namely, that spirit <note>original Hebrew: מרחפת על פני המים (*merachephet al penei hamayim*)</note> "hovering over the face of the waters" <note>Genesis 1:2.</note>, called *Amun* in the Egyptian tongue. With that fruitful breath of His Divinity, He adorns and brings life to the world, demonstrating the power of both, through which *Horus* <note>In Kircher's system, Horus often represents the created world or the restored soul.</note> was produced. *For the invisible things of God are seen through those things which are made.* <note>Romans 1:20.</note>

Therefore, the Eternal Father, shining with His Son in eternal wisdom and ineffable majesty of glory, produced the greater world and introduced the lesser world—man, the microcosm—created in His image and likeness. Man was equipped with all the talents of grace and nature to act as its ruler. But behold Typhon! <note>Kircher associates the Egyptian god Typhon/Set with the fallen angel Lucifer.</note> Having already been deprived of all grace and the splendor of light due to his rebellion against God, and having been cast into the abyss along with his followers and the confederated Titans, he was full of envy, rancor, and indignation. Driven by a sting for revenge, he began to attempt the overthrow of Osiris's glory by every possible machination.

<margin>The Figure of Typhon.</margin>
> *As Apollodorus writes, Typhon was terrifying even to look upon, the very image of horror. He appeared in an unusual form of human stature, so tall that he seemed higher than the peaks of all the mountains. His head frequently reached the stars; one of his hands stretched to the West and the other to the East. From these hands, a hundred dragon heads emerged. His legs consisted of a thousand massive coils of vipers, whose winding lengths extended all the way up to his crown.*

Such was Typhon, the enemy of the human race, who went out against Osiris and the supreme Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>. He is depicted by these symbols of malevolence, envy, malice, and extreme perversity, hurling glowing stones toward heaven with a poisonous hissing and a horrible bellowing, vomiting a great storm of fire from his mouth. Although he provoked the supreme deity in vain, he used a certain fraudulent and clever invention to trap Osiris in an ark <note>A chest or coffin.</note> and later

<margin>Allegorical description of Typhon.</margin>
tore him into pieces. Having done this, he vented his anger upon the son, *Horus*, as well, killing him and throwing him into the sea. But let us see what these things mean. Osiris was hidden in the ark when our first parents, led by the persuasion of the malignant Typhon, transgressed the Divine law. When this happened, as St. Augustine testifies, they were turned from children of light into children of darkness. The human intellect, which used to sparkle with a certain wonderful radiance of grace, fell into extreme ignorance, blindness, and a fog of errors. As if intoxicated by a cup from the river Lethe <note>In mythology, the river of forgetfulness.</note>, man incurred forgetfulness of both God and all heavenly things. Furthermore, Typhon's cruelty did not stop there. He took the hidden body of Osiris, tore it into parts, and threw it into the river; he also killed Horus. By this, nothing other than idolatry is signified. Through the suggestion of the malignant spirit, the human race was infected and turned away from the true knowledge and worship of God. It happened that the most simple entity of God—His nature or essence—was attributed to many things, as if being pulled apart into pieces. Hence, some worshipped the Sun, others the Moon, and others of the stars...

Others, finally, worshipped and appeased with sacred rites whatever a malignant spirit suggested, or a foolish fantasy persuaded each one, in the name of God. Whence the diverse rites and ceremonies of the nations, abominable sacrifices and thoroughly ridiculous superstitions, by which the world—as if entangled in certain serpentine coils of Typhon <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian Set/Typhon with the serpent of Eden and the fallen angel Lucifer.</note>—was miserably detained, and struggled in vain under the tyranny and dominion of a powerful enemy, flowed forth as if from a Trojan horse. Subjected to innumerable labors and persecutions, she gathered again the parts of Osiris—that is, she gathered the nations who were disagreeing in the worship of various gods and brought them to the knowledge of the one true God, and into the distinguished profession of one God, one faith, and one law. By this Divine calling, it happened that the dispersed parts coalesced again into one body, as if mystical. She also recalled Horus, who had been slain by Typhon, to immortality; that is, calling the world submerged in sins back to life by the word of her power, she restored it to its former splendor, with Typhon coerced and extinguished. When all these things were completed, having chosen twelve Apostles as Priests, to whom she prescribed certain laws to be observed concerning the worship of the restored God Osiris, she returned to heaven from where she had come, alongside Osiris the eternal Father, to reign eternally. And these are the things which I thought should be said briefly regarding the <term>mystagogy</term> <note>The interpretation of sacred mysteries or the guidance of initiates into religious truths.</note> of the Egyptians. Now let us return to their disciples—that is, those of the Greeks and Hebrews—and let us discuss what mysteries lie hidden under that manifold mythology of Gods and Goddesses: for I trust that no small increase and benefit to our <term>apparatus</term> <note>Kircher's term for his scholarly system or collection of evidence.</note> will come from these.

### CHAPTER X. 218 BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

# CHAPTER X.

### *On the mystical significance of the Gods: Heaven, Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Neptune, and Pluto.*

<margin>Tertullian.</margin> Tertullian rightly noted that the Pagans, when they grew ashamed of the fables they had invented about the Gods, fled to the interpretation of natural things, so that the disgrace of the fables might be overshadowed by the clever games of the intellect. <margin>Lactantius.</margin> Wherefore Lactantius Firmianus records that this was a cunning invention of Satan—who transforms himself into an Angel of light—designed to blind the minds of mortals. For when he saw that the authority of the Poets was by no means sufficient for learned men to approve the false opinions regarding the Gods, he provided an opportunity for them to dwell upon and exercise their intellects regarding moral and physical interpretations. He did this so that, on this pretext at least, they might not condemn those empty delusions which ancient superstition had fashioned to deceive people of the lowest class. Certainly, as we said above, <margin>Athenagoras.</margin> Athenagoras records that Empedocles adapted the natures of the Gods to the powers and nature of the universe. <margin>On Unbelievable Tales.</margin> <margin>Palæphatus.</margin> Palæphatus, in his book *On Histories* <note>Original Greek: "περὶ τῶν ἱστοριῶν". Palæphatus is best known for his work "On Unbelievable Tales," which is noted in the margin as "ἀπίστων".</note>, notes that they learned this from no other source than the Egyptians, for whom nothing was so vile or contemptible that they would not reduce it to mystical reasons. <margin>The Greeks as imitators of the Egyptians.</margin> Thus the Greeks, prone to every kind of superstition and taught by the Egyptians, also fashioned similar disciplines by which they might more easily defend that monstrous *theogony* <note>theogony: the genealogy or origin of a group of gods.</note> under the guise of mystical reasoning. In order that all these things might be shown *according to the method*, we shall begin with the first of all the Gods, Heaven and Saturn, so that it may be revealed what they expressed mystically through them and their progeny.

<margin>Cicero. Lactantius. Phornutus. Uranus or Heaven.</margin> SATURN is the son of Heaven, as Marcus Cicero records, along with Lactantius and Servius. Moreover, HEAVEN is called *Ouranos* in Greek; according to Phornutus, he is named as if he were *phyros*, that is, the preserver of all things that are above, and *horizon*, that is, the limiter and boundary of all nature. This Heaven, I say, begat Saturn, who is the author of time, or rather time itself; for according to Aristotle, time is nothing other than "the number of motion of heaven according to before and after." <note>A famous definition from Aristotle's *Physics*.</note> Whence he is also called *Chronos*, because he contains the course and revolution of spaces and times. He is said to have eaten his own children because all time is said to consume whatever it brings forth. Furthermore, as Fulgentius says, he carries a scythe, either because all time turns back upon itself like the curves of a scythe, or because of the harvest; hence he is also said to be castrated, because it is necessary that all the powers of fruitfulness, once cut off and cast into the moisture of the entrails as if into the sea, should beget lust, just as they begot Venus there. They depict a snake joined to him, devouring its own tail <note>The Ouroboros.</note>, a symbol of the year, which is the child of time. Furthermore, because some say he was born from Alcmone, they obscurely signified *the unceasing nature of the rotation*, that is, the incorruptible or indefatigable turning and revolution of the sky. <margin>Macrobius.</margin> Macrobius also thinks the name is derived *from the phallus*, because time is the author of all corruption and generation.

Others, among whom is Apollophanes in his Epic poem, wish Saturn to be so named as if he were "showing" <gloss>original: φαίνων, phainōn</gloss> the sacred, or as a creator of "wisdom" <gloss>original: φρόνησιν, phronēsin</gloss>, acting as the sense and mind that creates, because all reason, sense, and an educated spirit are acquired through time. <margin>From where is Saturn named?</margin> That Saturn is indeed time, and nothing else—which destroys all things and produces all things—is indicated by that line of Orpheus in the hymn to Saturn:
<margin>Orpheus in the hymn to Saturn.</margin>

> *You who consume all things and in turn increase them yourself.* <note>original: "Ὃς δαπανᾷς μὲν ἅπαντα καὶ αὔξεις ἔμπαλιν αὐτός."</note>
> *You who bring forth all things, consume them, and bring them forth again.* <note>original: "Omnia qui profers, consumis, & omnia rursus."</note>

Nor is it surprising, when we say that Saturn is Time, that he was considered a God, since Sophocles in *Electra* openly called Time a God:

> *For Time is a gentle God.* <note>original: "Χρόνος γὰρ εὐμαρὴς Θεός."</note>
> *Time is truly a God, most easy-going.* <note>original: "Deus profectò tempus est, facillimus."</note>

<margin>Sophocles.</margin>
For since the Sun declines now to the North, now to the South, traversing as it were all places of the world with its motion—now creating days, now nights, now winters, now summers—and according to the changes of the seasons, all things born on land and sea receive their beginnings and causes of birth from it, he was rightly called Saturn by Orpheus, "father of both men and gods." Those who also attributed a sickle to him seem to have intended nothing other than Time itself, by which all things are cut down, laid low, and brought to ruin. <margin>Mystical symbols of Saturn.</margin> Furthermore, the rank of the Platonists, since they thought that Heaven (of whom Saturn was the son) was a God, did they not imply that sublime body which contains all things, and that Divine Mind which embraces the rest? They call this sometimes Jupiter, sometimes Venus, sometimes Saturn, or the virtue of the mind proceeding from heaven and diffused into all bodies. For when that Divine Mind is understood as governing in the ethereal region, it is called Jupiter; but when it descends to the lower bodies to stir them toward generation, it is then called Venus. From this it happens that Saturn is sometimes understood as the supernal mind, in which resides the universal light of all things and the providence which pertains to the order, <margin>The Divine mind is variously understood.</margin> life, and changes of all fortunes. Others, however, have said that the soul belongs to that sphere which is called "fixed" <gloss>original: ἀπλανὴς, aplanēs</gloss>; but they called the lower sphere Saturn, which order is thereafter preserved in the others. Hence there are those who twist the entire fable of Saturn toward astronomical matters, which you may see in Natalis Comes <note>Noël Conti (1520–1582), a celebrated Italian mythographer whose "Mythologiae" was a standard reference for interpreting classical fables.</note>, Book 2 of his *Mythology*. The Chemists <note>In this context, "Chemists" (Chymistæ) refers to Alchemists.</note> have also twisted this to their own art. <margin>The fable of Saturn drawn toward astronomical matters.</margin> For they say it was a fiction of the ancients that Jupiter cut off Saturn’s genitals with a sharp sickle and threw them into the sea, from which and from the foam Venus was born. This is because Saturn is a certain salt, the father of prepared Jupiter <note>In alchemy, Saturn often represents Lead and Jupiter represents Tin, but here they are being used to describe the chemical behavior of salts.</note> (namely, of prepared salt), and who is made from that prepared thing. But because when Jupiter exists in a glass vessel, he is dissolved into very sharp and thin water due to the force of <margin>Chemical interpretation.</margin> fire (which is also taken from Jupiter himself), as he brings the masculine parts with him, cutting and separating the innermost sulfur lying hidden in the salt, which falls back into the vessel placed to receive it: for this reason they say the masculine parts were cut from Saturn; and since the salt falls into water as if into the sea, Venus is born from that salt and sulfur.

### CHAPTER X. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>Saturn, [as] Osiris King of Egypt.</margin>
Certain of the ancient writers, confusing Saturn with Osiris, say that Saturn reigned in Egypt and took his sister Rhea in marriage; from them were born Jupiter and Juno, who, on account of their virtue and the most excellent ornaments of their souls, ruled over the entire circle of the lands. From these were born five children: Osiris, Isis, Typhon, Apollo, and Nephthys (otherwise known as Venus), concerning whom you may read in Plutarch’s previously cited book *On Osiris and Isis*. The Greeks, however, varying in this account, assert that Saturn fathered only Jupiter, Juno, Neptune, and Pluto; concerning whom we must now speak further.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
**JUPITER**. Just as the "microcosm" <gloss>the "little world" of the human being</gloss> has a soul by which it is governed, so the "macrocosm" <gloss>the "great world" of the universe</gloss> also has a soul, which Plato calls the Universal Soul. The poets call it Jupiter, and the Hebrews call it *Mitraton* <note>Metatron, a high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition often regarded as the celestial mediator or governor of the world</note>; and this is the Jupiter called the son of Saturn, either because he provides life and being to all living things, or because through him all things stand and are preserved. The ancient Greek theologian Orpheus, as quoted in Eusebius, beautifully expressed Jupiter's power, force, and supreme dominion over the world in the following verses:

<margin>Orpheus in the hymn to Jupiter.</margin>

Albricus the Philosopher <note>likely Albricus of London, a medieval author who wrote on the visual iconography of the gods</note>, writing on the images of the Gods, describes him as being painted on an ivory throne, placed in his seat of majesty, holding a royal scepter in his hand (specifically the left); from the other hand (the right), he sends lightning bolts to the inhabitants of the underworld, and keeps the giants crushed by the lightning beneath his feet, possessing dominion over heaven and earth. Others represent Jupiter sitting upon clouds and half-naked. For, as Porphyry explains (reported by Eusebius in book 3 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*), he was believed to be the providential and life-giving force of things. He was depicted sitting so that his immutable stability might be expressed; the upper parts were made naked because that same power is conspicuous to the intellectual and celestial parts. The lower parts were covered to indicate that he is hidden from mortals dwelling upon the ground. Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> brings forward this same exposition under the word <unclear>Zeus</unclear> <note>original: "ζευς"</note>, as does George Kedrenos in his book *On the Origin of Constantinople*. Nevertheless, Jupiter was not only considered the creative power and mind of things, but sometimes the sky or the air: and as Seneca testifies above all in book 4 of *Natural Questions*, chapter 45, every name was suitable to him by which the reason or governance of the universe was hinted at, just as was said regarding Osiris in the preceding pages. Hence we read concerning Jupiter in Saint Augustine's *City of God*, book 7, chapter 9: "God," they say, "is the one having power over the causes by which anything happens in the world," whence he is called by Orpheus:

->*All-generating origin of all, and of all the end.*<-

### EGYPTIACA. 221 CHAPTER X.

<margin>
Martianus Capella: Another description of Jupiter.
</margin>
Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century Latin author known for his encyclopedic work on the seven liberal arts</note>, in Book 1 of *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, depicted Jupiter in the Senate of the Gods. He says that Jupiter wore a flaming crown on his head, and over it a reddish veil fashioned by the hands of Minerva. He was dressed in a white garment and adorned with a glass-like cloak that was interspersed with frequent markings resembling stars. In his right hand, he held out two orbs: one made of gold, the other of electrum <note>A natural alloy of gold and silver</note>.

<margin>
Porphyry.
</margin>
Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who often interpreted myths as allegories for natural forces</note> testifies that by this round shape, he signifies a "provident and life-giving power." Jupiter seemed to lean his left hand upon a nine-stringed lyre and wore green shoes upon his feet, pressing down upon a support with them. By this hieroglyphic image, Martianus seems to have signified that Jupiter is the presiding ruler of all nature. Furthermore, it is observed that the name of Jupiter is uttered by the Greeks in more than ten monosyllables: *Zeus, Zen, Deus, Bdeus, Zan, Zes, Dis, Den, Dan,* and *s' Zeus*. All of these were assigned to him by the Greeks because of the multitude of effects he performs in the world, in addition to a hodgepodge of other names that can be read in Lilius Giraldus's first *Syntagma*.

<margin>
Lilius Giraldus.
</margin>
In this matter, the Greeks followed the Egyptians, whose custom it was to decorate their Egyptian Jupiter—that famous Osiris—with ever-newly invented names, as if he were the nature of the universe itself.

<margin>
Jupiter as the nature of the universe.
</margin>
That Jupiter is the nature of the universe was made clear from the previously cited hymn of Orpheus, and it will be even clearer from what follows. For the aforementioned Orpheus, while saying that all things are full of Jupiter and while finding within him earth, water, air, fire, day, and night, does nothing other than represent the image of the entire universe. Jupiter's head, shimmering with a yellow crown, represents the bright sky adorned with shining stars. Moreover, his radiating eyes designate the Sun and Moon, the breadth of his chest the air, and his spacious shoulders—standing out with a great "oarage" of wings—designate the speed of the winds and the readiness of God in his operations. This image expressed by Orpheus is nearly the same as the image by which the Greeks formerly depicted Pan, and not without reason.

<margin>
Jupiter is called Pan because he is all things.
</margin>
For Jupiter was called <term>pan</term> <note>original: πᾶν, meaning "all" or "everything" in Greek</note> for no other reason than his dominion over the universe; the symbols demonstrate this sufficiently. Horns (according to Boccaccio) were placed on him to signify the rays of the Sun and Moon and the other stars. His face, ruddy and inflamed, signified the ethereal fire. His long beard signified the masculine elements, and his spotted skin represented the sphere of the fixed stars. His curved staff represented the dominion he holds over things, and most especially over the year as it recurs upon itself. Finally, the seven-piped flute in his hand denoted the celestial harmony which shines forth most clearly in the movements of the planets.

<margin>
The image of Pan or Lycian Jupiter.
</margin>
Furthermore, just as the lower parts, being hairy and rough with goat's feet, signified nothing other than the hard, rough, and uneven earth covered with trees and every variety of herbs and plants; so too his genitals and goat's foot mystically hinted at nothing other than the fertility which he bestows upon the world. For the Satyr is a lewd and lustful animal, wonderfully desiring of generation. Hence, the Egyptians and Greeks, not without reason, represented the "Lycian Jupiter" or Pan in the form of a goat, specifically on account of the lustfulness and desire for generation which he was believed to confer upon things. But regarding these hieroglyphs, see what we have handed down in the section on the "hierogrammatism of the ram." However, so that you may better understand the mysteries of Jupiter-Pan, it seemed appropriate to present here his entirely hieroglyphic image, just as it was described by Orpheus and others.

### The Hieroglyphic Representation of Jove or Pan.

---

**A** A reddish face, signifying the power of heat in the world. <note>original: "Facies rubicunda, caloris vis in Mundo"</note>
**B** The influence of celestial rays upon sublunary things. <note>original: "Radiorum cœlestiu̅ in sublunaria virtus." Sublunary refers to the region below the moon, meaning the Earthly realm subject to change.</note>
**C** The masculine elements. <note>In ancient philosophy, active elements like fire and air were often classified as masculine.</note>
**D** Authority over the year and all its revolutions.
**E** By his power, all things are supported.
**F** Dominion over the firmament, or the sphere of the fixed stars. <note>original: "Dominium in firmamentu̅, seu fixarum Stellarum Sphæram"</note>
**G** The Earth (a feminine element), bristling with plants, sown crops, and trees. <note>original: "Terra (elementum fœm.)"</note>
**H** The source of water and liquid (a feminine element), making the earth fertile through irrigation.
**I** Fields, grain crops, and other vegetation.
**K** The harmony of the seven planets. <note>Refers to the "Music of the Spheres," the mathematical and musical harmony believed to govern planetary motion.</note>
**L** Rough and uneven features indicate mountains.
**M** The power of fertility. <note>original: "Vis fæcundatiua"</note>
**N** A stable foundation.
**O** The power of the winds and swiftness in action.

# EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS. 223 CHAPTER X.

Thus the ancients imagined Pan as the son of Jupiter. They depict him as hairy in his lower part, resembling a goat, which signifies the roughness of the earth. In his upper part, however, he is a man. For the ether, because reason is situated within it, holds command over the entire world. They imagine him as lewd and lustful due to the many causes of procreation and the blendings that arise from them.

<margin>
A precise description of Pan and an explanation of the symbols.
</margin>
They say he dwells in deserted places to indicate his unity, for the world is one and "only-begotten" <note>original: *unigenitus*</note>. He pursues Nymphs because he delights in the exhalations that come from moisture, without which it is impossible for the world to appear. He is said to be clothed in a fawn-skin or leopard's hide, both because of the beautiful variety of all things and because of the colors seen in the world; Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD known for allegorical interpretations of myths</note> describes him with these symbols.

<margin>
Pan and Jupiter are distinguished.
</margin>
From these things, it is clear that Pan is indeed the same as Jupiter, yet they are distinguished; for Pan is the same as this corporeal world, while Jupiter is, as it were, its mind and governor. Frequently, however, they are confounded, just as all other deities are with one another. See the things we treat more copiously elsewhere regarding this; for the massive size of the work does not permit me to touch upon everything here. Let us proceed to Juno.

JUNO, at once both the sister and wife of Jupiter, is Juno, who denotes the air: for she is immediately joined to Jupiter and clings to him, raised from the earth. For when he unites with her, the essence itself, flowing into the thinnest parts, constitutes fire and air.

<margin>
Rhea, mother of Juno. Phornutus.
</margin>
For this reason, they mythologized Rhea as the mother of these gods and Saturn as their father—either because these things occur by a fixed revolution of time, or because (as Phornutus <note>A variant spelling of Cornutus</note> says) the distinction between the elements is produced by the mixing and "boiling over" of matter. Furthermore, for this reason the ancients said that Neptune was the son of Saturn and Rhea; they named him Poseidon <note>original: *ποσειδῶνα*</note> because they established him as the third element, that of water. This is as if to say "maker of images" <note>original: *ποιεῖν τὰ εἴδη*; the author connects the Greek name to the way water reflects shapes</note>, which we express in Latin as "the one making an image," because this element alone forms images of those looking into it.

<margin>
The image of Neptune.
</margin>
They depict a trident in his hands because the nature of water performs a triple function: liquid, fertile, and drinkable. Amphitrite is associated with this Neptune—that is, "from 'around' and 'third'" <note>original: *ἀπὸ τῶ ἀμφὶ καὶ τρίτη*; a Greek etymological wordplay</note>—because this element is enclosed by the other three and is found in the sky, the air, the clouds, and the earth.

<margin>
Pluto. Fulgentius. Pluto, the subterranean Demon.
</margin>
Finally comes Pluto, their brother, whom we call, along with Fulgentius <note>A late antique mythographer</note>, the Ruler of the lands, or the earth itself. For *ploutos* <note>original: *πλοῦτος*</note>, or wealth, is assigned to the earth alone. Through the darkness to which they imagined him bound, they obscurely hinted at the matter of the earth, which is darker than all else, or perhaps "prime matter," which philosophers call *hyle* <note>original: *ὕλην*</note>. Or finally, they did so because all things subject to corruption are eventually resolved back into it. Others will have Pluto be the Sun of the underworld. But before we proceed further, it seemed fit at this point to examine the mysteries of the rape of Proserpina, so greatly celebrated among the mythologists.

CHAPTER X. 224 BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

### *The mystical significance of the abduction of Proserpina: See the first figure of the following diagram.*

**A**lthough various authors have interpreted this fable in various ways, we briefly explain it in this manner: Pluto is the abductor; Ceres is the mother searching anxiously with torches; Hercules precedes Pluto’s four-horse chariot; and Jupiter sits upon the clouds.

**PLUTO** riding in a chariot is nothing other than that solar power implanted in the earth, which penetrates its innermost depths. Impregnated by this power, the earth produces various crops for the use and benefit of sustaining human life, just as Claudian aptly says of Pluto:

> *You who rule over life and death. For whatever matter*
> *produces everywhere, it is created by your gift*
> *and is owed to you through the fixed cycles of time.*
> <note>original: "Qui vitam lethumque regis... certis ambagibus ævi."</note>

<margin>Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book 1, Ch. 29.</margin>
<margin>Cornutus.</margin>
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
<margin>What Proserpina properly is</margin>
<margin>What is Pluto?</margin>
<margin>What is Ceres?</margin>
<margin>Cornutus.</margin>
<margin>Arnobius.</margin>
<margin>Cornutus.</margin>
<margin>Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 2.</margin>
Macrobius also supports this in the *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter 29. He says, *"The name 'The Lower One' <note>original: Inferi</note> is given to the Sun when it performs its course in the lower hemisphere, that is, through the winter signs. 'The Upper One' <note>original: Superi</note> when it travels the summer part of the Zodiac."* Thus, the winter sun is said to have snatched Proserpina, as Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher who interpreted myths as physical allegories</note> rightly notes, because in the winter months the seeds lie hidden beneath the earth and are nurtured by the Solar power so that they may burst forth into stalks at the proper time. For Proserpina—whom they said was either the crops themselves or the vital power of the dry seeds—was then said to be led back to the light to see her mother again. To this agrees the statement of Porphyry reported by Eusebius: *"Because,"* he says, *"there is a certain power in the seeds cast upon the ground, the Sun, running beneath the hemisphere in the winter time, draws that power away."* Proserpina is indeed that power of the seeds, while Pluto is the Sun entering the earth and running through its hidden orbit and the winter solstice; therefore, they say Proserpina was snatched by him, and Ceres searches for her while she lies hidden under the earth. Nor is Cornutus far off when he says: <term>it is told in myth that Hades snatched the daughter of Demeter</term> <note>original: ἁρπάσαι δ᾽ ὁ ᾅδης τὴν θυγατέρα τῆς δήμητρος ἐμυθεύθη</note>, etc. Pluto is said to have snatched the daughter of Ceres because the seeds of the crops are hidden by the earth for a certain time. Arnobius also subscribes to this with these words: *"He who says Proserpina was snatched by Dis <note>Another name for Pluto</note> does not mean, as you might think, that she was snatched into a pit of shameful lust, but because we hide seeds in the soil, he signifies that the God has gone beneath the earth"* ❦ *"to arrange the treaties of procreation with Orcus <note>The Underworld</note>."* Although Cornutus wishes to suggest that Pluto represents the thick air near the earth, he does not accept this unless that air is prepared by the solar power to generate crops, as Cicero says well in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book 2: *"All earthly power and nature is dedicated to Father Dis."* Hence Orpheus, in his hymn to Pluto, says:

<margin>Orpheus, Hymn to Pluto.</margin>
<term>Bestowing wealth upon the human race with the yearly fruits.</term> <note>original: Πλετοδοτῶν γενεὴν βροτέην κάρποις ἐνιαυτῶν.</note>
->Bestowing riches upon the human race with annual fruits.<-

<margin>What is the Helmet?</margin>
By the helmet attributed to Pluto, nothing else is signified but the winter Sun, withdrawn from our sight by frequent mists and clouds. Thus he "snatched" Proserpina, or <term>Persephone</term>, which is either the seed of the crops, or as others say, Proserpi-

<margin>Augustine, The City of God, Book 7, Ch. 20.</margin>
For whether the crop, before it springs forth into the light, was called <term>Hecate</term> <note>original: "ἐκάτη"</note> by the Greeks because a crop brings forth a hundredfold fruit, as witnessed by Fulgentius in his *Mythologies*, Book 1, and Saint Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 7, Chapter 20.

<margin>What are Minerva and Diana?</margin>
Furthermore, Minerva and Diana are remembered as the companions of Proserpina, which is nothing other than the solar power joined with the lunar power to produce crops and fruits; for Eusebius, in *The Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, Chapter 2, testifies that Minerva and Diana are understood as the Moon: <note>original Greek: "ὅπερ σὲ Ἀπόλλων ἐν ἡλίῳ, τοῦτο ἀθηνᾶ ἐν σελήνῃ."</note> "As Apollo is in the sun, so is Athena in the moon." <margin>Diogenianus in the Proverbs.</margin> Diogenianus, indeed, says in his *Proverbs* that Minerva, Diana, Hecate, or Proserpina are one and the same. Thus, Minerva is nothing other than lunar heat; Diana is the moist power, which they said delighted in springs. Proserpina, meanwhile, is the lunar virtue mixed with the earth, suited for bringing forth crops. Why Ceres seeks her with torches is taught by Fulgentius in these words: <margin>Fulgentius.</margin> <margin>Torches.</margin> "This Proserpina," he says, "is said to be sought by her mother with torches; hence the 'Day of Torches' is dedicated to Ceres; for this reason: that at this time, with torches—that is, with the heat of the Sun—the crop is joyfully sought for harvesting." They also imagine that Jupiter and Hercules were present at the abduction; <margin>Hercules.</margin> by Jupiter, they wished to indicate nothing other than the <term>generative power</term> <note>original: "vim feminalem"—the text likely intends "seminalem" (seed-power), as it refers to Jupiter as the active father fecundating the earth.</note> which Jupiter, the lord of heaven, is thought to send down into the Great Mother, according to that famous passage by Virgil:
<margin>Virgil.</margin>
> Then the almighty father, the Sky, descends with fertile rains
> into the lap of his joyful bride, and, great himself, 
> mingling with her great body, nourishes all her offspring.

<margin>Palladius.</margin>
Through Hercules, one can conveniently understand the labor and industry necessary for agriculture. For, as Palladius well says in Book 1, the method of good cultivation consists of four things: air, water, earth, and industry—that is, Pluto, Proserpina, Jupiter, and Hercules, because of the labors to which the latter was always subjected in life. But so that all these things may be more easily understood, it seemed best to place here before your eyes the hieroglyphic diagram of the abducted Proserpina from the solar tablets of Hieronymus Alexander.

### EGYPTIAN TOPICS. CHAPTER X.

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
That time is further indicated through Hercules is sufficiently clear from Orpheus, who in his hymns calls Hercules *all-devouring and all-begetting* <note>original: "πάμφαγον παγγενέτορα" (pamphagon pangenetora)</note>, as he consumes all things and brings all things forth; nor did the "voracity" of Hercules, so often sung of, look to anything else. Indeed, it is pleasing to record here what Athenagoras, in his *Apology for the Christians*, handed down from Orpheus concerning Hercules representing Time and the beginnings of things:

<margin>Athenagoras.</margin>
*For water was, according to his opinion, the principle of all things; from the water, mud was established, and from both was born a living creature, a dragon having a lion’s head growing upon it, and in the middle of them the face of a God named Hercules and Time.* <note>original: "ἦ γὰρ ὕδωρ ἀρχὴ τῷ αὐτῷ τοῖς ὅλοις ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ὕδατος ἰλὺς κατέστη ἐκ δὲ ἑκατέρου ἐγεννήθη ζῶον δράκων προσπεφυκυῖαν ἔχων κεφαλὴν λέοντος, διὰ μέσου δὲ αὐτῶν Θεוῦ πρόσωπον ὄνομα Ἡρακλῆς, καὶ χρόνος."</note> Water was, in his view, the principle of all things; from the water, mud arose; and from both was produced a creature, a dragon, to which a lion's head was attached; but between these two they contained the face of a God, whose name was Hercules and Time. Orpheus said all these things concerning the Egyptian Hercules, as we shall prove elsewhere. But let these remarks on the abduction of Proserpina suffice. Now let us proceed to show the remaining significations of the Gods.

<margin>Saturn.</margin>
**SATURN**, therefore, is imagined to have descended from heaven so that he might be mingled with the earth; and that Jupiter castrated him and restrained his violence. For Jupiter, having ejected him from his kingdom, sent him to the underworld <note>original: "tartara"</note>; and by this obscure placement of fables, they signify the order of universal generation—namely, that the abundant flow of Osiris, which had hitherto occurred upon the earth, was contracted when he made the exhalations more subtle. But the nature of the world, pouring in its influence—which we have said is Jupiter—restrained the abundant impulse through change and tempered it perfectly with vegetable moisture and heat.

<margin>What is meant by Venus being born from the genitals of the Heavens?</margin>
Furthermore, by the story that **VENUS** was born from the severed genitals of the Heavens <note>referring to Uranus/Caelus</note> cast into the sea, they wished to signify that feminine and generative power of Heaven, derived from Jupiter (the world-virtue disposing all things), into the sea. By this, the sea was rendered fertile and fit for generation. Venus is seen to be born from the sea because every generation requires motion and moisture, and it is unknown to no one that the sea excels in both. For the Goddess called Venus by the Latins, and *Aphrodite* <note>original: "ἀφροδίτη"</note> by the Greeks, was believed by the nations to be the Goddess of generation, pleasure, and beauty. She is called Venus either because she "comes to all" <note>original: "veniat"</note> or because "through her all things come forth" <note>original: "proveniant"</note>; so says Cicero.

<margin>From where is Venus named?</margin>
Varro, however, says: *The poets say that a fiery seed fell from heaven into the sea, and Venus was born from the foam through the conjunction of fire and moisture which they possessed, signifying the power of Venus; from which power the life given to those born is named, according to that line of Lucilius:*

> ->Life is force, you see, which compels us to do all things.<-
> <note>original: "Vis est vita vides, quæ nos facere omnia cogit."</note>

Moreover, she is called *Aphrodite* because the seeds of living creatures are "foamy" <note>original: "spumosa"; a reference to the Greek 'aphros' meaning foam</note>, or as Euripides devises, because those raving for Venus are *aphrones*—that is, "mindless" or lacking control of their intellect.

<margin>Love and Cupid.</margin>
Furthermore, from Venus was born **LOVE**, or **CUPID**, which is nothing other than that natural appetite in all things for procreating something similar to oneself.

<margin>The image of Cupid.</margin>
He is depicted in the likeness of a winged boy with a quiver, arrows, and a torch, because lovers are of an "imperfect mind," as Phornutus <note>The Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, often called Phornutus in older texts</note> says, or because of the unsatiated appetite for natural things.

<margin>Phornutus.</margin>
<margin>Explanation of symbols.</margin>
The arrows indicate that those captured by love are struck from afar by the sight of it, as if by a wound; or conversely, that from the sight of beauty, the desire...

### CHAPTER X. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

...so that they are wounded; he carries wings, because nothing is found to be lighter or more changeable than those in love, as <margin>Servius Honoratus.</margin> Servius Honoratus <note>A 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note> proves abundantly in his commentary on the first book of the *Aeneid* regarding Dido herself. He carries a torch because of the fiery power of love and the heat of passion by which people are, as it were, consumed; Propertius beautifully describes these symbols of Cupid.

<margin>Propertius, Book 3, Elegy.</margin>
> *Whoever it was that painted Love as a boy,*
> *Do you not think he had wondrous hands?*
> *He first saw that lovers live without sense,*
> *And that great blessings perish through trivial cares;*
> *Not in vain did he also add windy wings,*
> *And made the God fly over the human heart,*
> *Precisely because we are tossed on a shifting wave,*
> *And our breeze never stays long in one place,*
