> *Since he strikes before we see the enemy in safety,*
> *And no one ever walks away healthy from that wound.*

But these things are mentioned only in passing <note>original: "παρέργως" (parergōs)</note>; let us now return to the main goal. Since neither Saturn, nor Jupiter, nor Venus, nor Love are of any benefit unless they are applied through industry and the invention of the mechanical arts; <margin>Vulcan and Minerva.</margin> the ancients imagined Vulcan and Minerva to be the offspring of Jupiter. Of these, Minerva denotes Wisdom and industry born from the brain of Jupiter, by which we are made capable of devising all kinds of things necessary for life. Vulcan is the cultivator of labors, insofar as he demonstrates the use of fire to the whole world and fashions every kind of tool necessary for man; for no element is more necessary to man than fire, as Aristotle testifies in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*. <margin>Aristotle. The mysteries of Vulcan.</margin> And for this reason, Vulcan is called "the fire-kindler" <note>original: "πυραύσος" (pyrausos)</note> from the act of setting things ablaze. Hence some have said he was born of Juno, whom we previously identified as the Air. For thicker and richer flames take their substance, in a way, from the very air being set on fire. Moreover, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> suggests why he was cast down from heaven by Jupiter: because fire was first discovered from the burning strike of a lightning bolt.

<margin>Grace and Venus joined to him.</margin> Furthermore, they imagine Venus and one of the Graces joined to him in marriage, by which they seem to mean that the mechanical arts find "grace" (favor) among all people, because no one can do without them; or perhaps because of the intense power of heat that exerts itself in the act of Love. MINERVA, however, born from the brain of Jupiter, signifies nothing other than the intellect of Jupiter himself—the principal part of the soul and the seat of Wisdom, by which alone man is distinguished from the beasts. This was given to him both for the sake of knowing and loving GOD his creator, and for devising the things necessary for his own life.

Again, so that the human race, provided with all necessary things, might live in greater peace and tranquility, and might more easily defend itself from the injury of enemies who <margin>Bellona.</margin> occasionally bring war upon it, *Mars* and *Bellona* were fashioned from Jupiter, who—

### EGYPTIAN MATTERS. CHAPTER X.

...of whom that God of war invented the art of waging war, for which reason he is also called *Agis* <note>original: "Agis". This is likely an etymological play on the Greek verb for "leading" or "acting," or a specific epithet for Mars as a driver of battle.</note> from the taking away of the cruelty of enemies and the breaking of their defiance by the opposing of arms, and this occurs in the political world. In the sublunary <note>The realm of the earth below the moon, which in ancient cosmology was the region of change and decay.</note> world, however, <margin>Mars.</margin> *Mars* is nothing other than that active force fitting things together, from which the ancients—not without reason—fabled that Harmony was born of him. *Bellona*, <note>The Roman goddess of war, often associated with Mars.</note> meanwhile, is fortitude itself, both necessary for martial men in war and representing that strength by which things are sustained in the world. But since Republics are disturbed in a wondrous manner by the inconveniences of wars, fields are devastated, and sciences and arts are handed over to oblivion: <margin>The 9 Muses.</margin> they imagined the nine Muses to be the offspring of Jove. By their aid, the soul, broken by cares and sorrows, might be refreshed; the lands and locations of estates might finally be justly distributed among men; and the minds of mortals, made more savage by the rigor and brutality of wars, might once again be tamed and civilized through the cultivation of the more humane Muses.

But more on these matters in what follows. Finally, lest men—as the golden ages return—should forget virtue and plunge headlong into every kind of pleasure, <margin>The Fates.</margin> the wise said that the three *Fates* <note>original: "Parcae"</note> were born of Jove. These are nothing other than the brevity of this life, the inconstancy of human affairs, and inevitable death; by the consideration of these things, men might be restrained in the continuous exercise of virtue, as if by certain leashes, as Seneca says. The Fates, moreover, are named "antiphrastically" <note>original: "ἀντιφραστικῶς" (antiphrastikōs). A rhetorical term for naming something by its opposite quality—in this case, naming the "Sparers" (Parcae) because they spare no one.</note> because they spare no one; so says Servius. They imagined three of them: one speaking, another writing, and the third drawing out the threads; and therefore Martianus Capella, <note>A 5th-century writer known for his encyclopedic work on the liberal arts.</note> in *The Marriage of Philology*, calls them the librarians or scribes of the gods and the guardians of the Archive. They are called <margin>Clotho. Lachesis. Atropos.</margin> *Clotho*, *Lachesis*, and *Atropos*; or, what is the same, Evocation, Lot, and "without order." By this they wished to imply that the first is the Evocation of Birth; the second is the Lot of life; and the third is the condition of death, which comes without law. Others derive the first, Clotho, from the Greek "to spin together," <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ συνκλώθω" (apo tou synklōthō)</note> because she revolves and draws all things together. *Lachesis* is from "to obtain by lot," <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λαγχάνειν" (apo tou lanchanein)</note> that is, she allots fate. *Atropos*, however, they explain as "invertible" or "unchangeable." There are others who interpret the Fates in this way: by *Clotho*, the seven Planets; by *Lachesis*, sublunary things; and by *Atropos*, they denote the "Aplanes" or the sphere of the fixed stars. There are some, like Aristotle, who assign Clotho to the present time, Lachesis to the future, and Atropos to the past. The poets commonly establish them such that one holds the distaff, the second the spindle, and the third breaks the thread, according to that verse:

> *Clotho holds the distaff, Lachesis spins, and Atropos cuts.*

<margin>Hesiod. Lycophron.</margin>
Hesiod says the Fates <note>original: "μοίρας" (moiras)</note> were born of Night and Erebus, because of the hidden and concealed power of future things; Lycophron called them girls of the sea, because of the wild and pitiless law of the fates. Do you see, therefore, how great a connection exists between the Gods and Goddesses and the progress of natural and moral things? Certainly, that the ancients fashioned nothing without mystical reasons is evident, clearer than the midday light, even from what has been said.

# CHAPTER XI.

## *Concerning the Mystical Significance of Apollo, Bacchus, Hercules, and Mercury.*

Phornutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who specialized in the allegorical interpretation of Greek myths.</note>, Fulgentius, Apollodorus, and, among the more recent writers, Girolamo Aleandro in his *Heliac Tables* <note>original: "tabulis Heliacis"; these were scholarly tables relating to the sun and solar worship</note>, all testify that these four gods, though distinguished by various names, are nothing other than the diverse effects of a single thing: the Sun. In this view, they follow Macrobius and other ancient authors who reduced all divine powers to the one Sun. We shall follow them, beginning our study with Apollo.

APOLLO, whom Themistius in his 16th Oration calls "the sun, the progenitor of Apollo," <note>original: "ἥλιον τὸν πρόγονον τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος"</note> was depicted as a youth with uncut hair, distinguished by golden locks, and equipped with a lyre, bow, and arrows. At his side was placed a tripod, a crow or swan, and a basket overflowing with flowers and fruits. We have chosen to display his image here, as seen in figure 2 of the preceding diagram on page 226.

A, The rays of the Sun.
B, The youthful appearance, representing the Sun’s daily rebirth.
C, The golden hair, signifying the Sun's splendor.
D, The bow and arrows, representing the power of the Sun shooting its rays.
E, The Harmony of the World, which he creates through his motion.
F, Time: present, past, and future.

<column-break/>

G, The crow, a symbol of the black night.
H, The crops, which he produces through his heat.
I, The white swan, a symbol of the day.
K, The shepherd’s clothing, indicating the preservation of livestock through the grasses he makes grow.
L, The clouds, which he draws up and designates for rain.
M, The physician’s clothing, indicating the medicinal power implanted in herbs.

---

What else does the representation of youthful age indicate but the vigor, beauty, and power of heat of the Sun, reborn every single day? From this, all things draw life and are preserved in their being, as the Poet <note>Likely referring to a classical poet such as Ovid or Virgil.</note> beautifully shows:

> The Sun, forever young, who divides the swift axis of the sky.

<margin>Fulgentius.</margin>
<margin>The Radiant Sun.</margin>
<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin>
<margin>Fulgentius.</margin>
<margin>Lucian.</margin>
<margin>Explanation of symbols.</margin>
And Fulgentius in book 1 of his *Mythologies* says: "By always being reborn, he is younger." <note>original: "Renascendo semper est iunior."</note> Martianus Capella, in his first book on the *Marriage of Philology*, explains what the uncut head, radiating with golden hair, signifies: "The Sun," he says, "imitates a golden head of ruddy hair with his majestic head, drenched and encircled by flaming rays." Macrobius shows that the bow and arrows likewise represent nothing else, supported by Fulgentius in these words: "They also define the bow and arrows because his rays leap out from his circle in the manner of arrows." <note>original: "Arcum quoque sagittasq; circumscribunt..."</note> Lucian, in his work *On Astrology*, agrees with this, suggesting that "the Sun's javelins are nothing other than the casting of its rays." This agrees with Phornutus’s interpretation of Diana (the Moon) for the same reason—I mean the long casting of rays—attributing arrows to them as well.

...tation; <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing the word "agitation" or "vibration."</note> whence the rays are called "the weapons of the day" by Ausonius, "darts" by Prudentius, and by the Chaldeans *Salkin* <note>original: סלקין; a term denoting ascending or vibrating movement</note> from their vibration. Although some understand the allegory <note>original: τὴν ἀλληγορίαν</note> through the rays to mean the enlightenment of the human mind in divinations and prophecies, over which Apollo is imagined to preside. By the addition of the Tripod, according to the testimony of Fulgentius, nothing else is signified but the triple difference of time—present, past, and future—which is an effect of the Sun’s motion; or as Martianus and Suidas wish, *prophesying in three ways the three times: the present, the past, and the future* <note>original: τριπῶς καὶ τὰς τρεῖς χρόνους μαντεύομενος ἐν ἑστῶτα παραλελυθότα καὶ μέλλοντα</note>. Apollo is also depicted and introduced in the form of a Musician or Lyre-player to show, as Suidas testifies, that the Sun is the harmony of the universe; Phornutus gives the reason for this in the following words: *“Because the Sun,” he says, “strikes and rules all parts of the world with due measure, and ensures that the world is harmonious everywhere in a mutual concert, with no dissonance appearing.”* He is imagined as a Physician because the Sun, through the most temperate influence of his power and his perfectly proportioned heat, is considered the preserver of all living things by promoting the vigor of the heart and fostering natural color. He is imagined as a Shepherd because, by producing fruits, herbs, grasses, and shrubs, the Sun is considered to feed the cattle. The Crow and the Swan, which are usually dedicated to him, are nothing other than the effects of the Sun, as well as the alternations of night and day—the latter being signified by the white swan and the former by the black crow. These are essentially the things attributed to Apollo by the Poets; now let us proceed to Hercules.

<margin>What is Hercules?</margin>
<margin>The Symbols of Hercules and their mysteries.</margin>
<margin>Plutarch, Proclus, Porphyry.</margin>
<margin>The 12 Labors.</margin>
HERCULES is the reason <term>ratio: here used as the animating logic or "organizing principle"</term> inherent in all things, by which nature is strong and vigorous according to Phornutus. We say that Hercules is nothing other than the strengthening and invigorating power of the Sun over all things in which he holds dominion. Just as we said Apollo is that power which consists in the illumination and efficacy of diffused rays, this is most clear from the instruments and dress with which he is depicted. For what else does that Lion skin signify, if not the force and efficacy which he impresses upon lower things by his fiery power? Aelian says that the Egyptians placed the Lion at the domicile of the Sun precisely because it is a strong, effective, hot, and fiery animal; a view supported by Horapollo, Plutarch, and Proclus. Why he is equipped with a club is beautifully explained by Porphyry: *“They assign to him the club and the lion skin,” he says, “the one to indicate the inequality of his motion; the other because he shows his strength especially in Leo [the Lion].”* Do not those twelve labors, in the exhausting of which Hercules is remembered by the Poets to have proven his strength, correspond perfectly to the effects of the Sun, which he works by running through the twelve houses of heaven [the Zodiac] every year? Indeed, that Orpheus once looked to this is clear from the following:

> *Who carries the dawn and the blackness of night with strength,*
> *Performing twelve contests from the setting to the rising.*
> <note>original Greek: Ὅς περὶ κραππορᾶς ἠῶ καὶ νύκτα μέλαιναν / Δώδεκ' ἀπ' ἀντολιῶν ἄχρι δυσμῶν ἆθλα διέρπων.</note>

# CHAPTER XI. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

The <margin>Garden of the Hesperides</margin>
is nothing other than the "glory of the air" <note>original: ἡρας κλέος (*hēras kleos*), a common etymological play on the name Hercules (Heracles)</note>, namely, its illumination; and perhaps the fable alludes to this when they imagine that Hercules traveled the whole world, penetrated almost to the underworld, and despoiled the Garden of the Hesperides of its golden apples. For it is better known than is necessary to state that the Sun, by his own power, influences the whole world; further, what else is the descent into the underworld but the setting of the Sun? And what else is the plundering of the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides but the rising of the Sun? Once this occurs, the sky—which is like a kind of celestial paradise—seems to be deprived of its stars, which are denoted by the golden apples. Indeed, because some call him a Physician <margin>Plutarch, Hesychius.</margin> and a Musician or "leader of the Muses" <note>original: μεσηγέτης (*mesēgetēs*)</note>, as do Plutarch, Hesychius, Macrobius, and others, they signify that he is one and the same as Apollo or the Sun; for the health of all things and the harmony of the universe depend upon the Sun. Just as Apollo was called the Archer, the Physician, and the Leader of the Muses because of the aforementioned effects of the Sun, Hercules was distinguished by these same names for the same reasons. And just as they signified the changes of days and nights through the crow and the swan, they did so through Hercules's crown woven from the poplar (whose leaves are blackish on one side and white on the other, or because this tree, according to Dioscorides, turns its leaves after the summer solstice). The only difference made between them is that Apollo, as I have said, is the illuminating and penetrating power; while Hercules is the consolidating or strengthening power of the Sun, or that generative solar force which is not incongruously represented by the <margin>He compressed 50 women. Apollodorus, Library, Book 2.</margin> fable where they attribute a numerous offspring to Hercules from the compression of fifty women in a single night. Plutarch in *On Fraternal Love*, and Apollodorus. Finally, the twelve victories or twelve Labors of Hercules can be quite well adapted to the effects of the Sun which it exerts in the twelve houses <note>The twelve "houses" refer to the signs of the Zodiac.</note> through the twelve months, although others transfer them to moral conduct in this way:

BACCHUS, whom ingenious antiquity imagined to preside over wine, is considered to be nothing other than the moistening and <term>maturing power</term> of the Sun, by which all things created by the Author of Nature for the benefit of mankind achieve their due perfection. Trees, vines, and plants are filled with sap, and swelling fruits are brought to ripeness by this <term>peptic power</term> <note>original: *pepticâ*; from the Greek *peptikos*, meaning to cook, digest, or ripen through heat.</note> of the Sun—especially wine, because of its nature similar to the Sun, which the symbols attributed to him demonstrate more than sufficiently. Therefore, without ivy, clusters, vines, grapes, apples, and other...

The reason he is depicted as a **Young Man**, luxurious, lustful <note>original: *salax*; the OCR reads "falax" (deceitful), but the context of fertility and Priapus indicates *salax* (lustful/fertile)</note>, raging, with golden horns, and crowned in ivy, is to show that he is not distinct from Apollo and Hercules. He is depicted as a young man because of the sun being reborn daily; he is luxurious and lustful because of the abundance of wine and other fruits which he produces by the influence of his power, and because he causes men, enticed by the sweetness of the things produced, to be poured out into every kind of joy. Hence also, because the Sun is the giver of fertility, they imagined Bacchus to be lustful and the father of Priapus <note>a minor deity of fertility</note>, and they added satyrs to his company because he possesses a great abundance of natural seed; for this reason, the <term>phallus</term> <note>a representation of the male generative organ used in religious processions</note> was carried about in his sacred rites. Furthermore, the golden horns attached to him express the rays of the Sun quite well through metaphor. That tigers, lynxes, and panthers—animals that are very swift and very hot-blooded—are consecrated to him, indicates the swiftness of the Sun and the force of its fiery nature. The fawn skin <note>original: *nebris* (misprinted as *Hebridis* in the source)</note> attributed to him by Diodorus denotes nothing other than either the diversity of the stars, of which the Sun is the presiding officer and governor (according to Martianus), or the variety of things produced in the sublunary world by his power. Orpheus confirms the former in his hymns with these words:

<margin>Orpheus</margin>
->Star, mimic of the skillfully wrought and sacred firmament.<-

Bacchus is imagined to have descended to the underworld to indicate the setting Sun; he is said to have traveled the world to demonstrate the power of the Sun mentioned above. That he conquered the Indians designates the immense heat of the Sun under the Torrid Zone; the story they tell of Bacchus emerging from his mother’s womb by the work of fire also seems to allude to this. Whence an ancient poet elegantly wrote:

->Thus Apollo, and thus Liber <note>another name for Bacchus</note> the Lawgiver appear,<-
->Both are created from flames and born from fire,<-
->Both bestow heat from their hair, and both bestow rays;<-
->This one breaks the shadows of night, that one the shadows of the heart.<-

But let these remarks on Bacchus suffice.

# MERCURY, called *Hermes* by the Greeks and *Thoth* by the Egyptians, was believed by the ancients to be the God of Speech.

Mercury is so named as if he were "the runner between" <note>original: *medicurrius*, an etymology suggesting he runs in the middle (*medius*) between speakers</note>, because speech is the intermediary between men. By us, he is said to be nothing other than the attractive power of the Sun; for the rest, he is not distinguished from Apollo, Bacchus, Hercules, etc. This is proven by the insignia attributed to him in the third figure of the preceding diagram. I have extracted this from the collection of antiquities of the most renowned Lord Claude Menedrius, in which the symbols of nearly all the gods occur. In the rays of the head, he possesses Apollo; in the horns, Ammon; in the ivy crown, Bacchus; in the lion skin, Hercules; in the serpents, Aesculapius; in the quiver and arrows, Diana; in the helmet, Pallas; and finally, Mercury in his winged feet and shoulders. Furthermore, in other diagrams, wings are attached to his head and feet, and he takes the form of a beardless statue. He is depicted with a seven-stringed psaltery <note>a type of harp or lyre</note>, a helmet partly black and partly white, a three-colored rod, and similar things which poetic chatter has attached to him. His youthful form was discussed previously; that the swiftness of the Sun, which reveals unknown and secret things, is signified by the wings attached to him is testified by Artemidorus in his second book, with these words: *for he brings all things to light and makes them easily seen*, or better...

...more so because by his attractive power, lifting up vapors and exhalations, he makes them fly into the heights; and for this reason, the mythologists fable him to be a thief, because the Sun, by drawing lower things to himself, seems as if stealing them.

<margin>Macrobius.</margin>
Cleanthes, cited in Macrobius, confirms this opinion; he says that Mercury is called *Lycium* <note>original: *Lycium*, from the Greek *lykos* (wolf). This is a common ancient etymological play connecting the "snatching" nature of a wolf to the "snatching" of moisture by the Sun's heat</note> because, like a wolf snatching cattle, he snatches and sucks out moisture. For Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, rightly perceives that all earthly things return into him when they are snatched away by the heat he sends in.

<margin>Explanation of the fables regarding Mercury.</margin>
Furthermore, the lyre or "seven-stringed" <note>original Greek: *ἑπτάχορδον*</note> psaltery signifies nothing other than the orbits of the seven planets, of which the Sun is the leader and moderator; the "black dog-skin" helmet <note>original Greek: *κυνέη μέλαινα*. This helmet, often associated with Hades or invisibility, is here interpreted as the darkness of night</note> demonstrates the successions of day and night. But what else is suggested by the fable of the "many-eyed" <note>original Greek: *πολυοφθάλμῳ*</note> Argus killed by Mercury, if not the rising of the Sun depriving the star-bearing heaven of its eyes (for stars are nothing else but the eyes, as it were, of the greater world) and meanwhile killing the very face of the sky? They also assert that Mercury discovered music, medicine, and the three-stringed tortoise-shell—or rather, the three voices of the strings: the high, the low, and the middle—

<margin>Mercury’s six-stringed instrument.</margin>
which indicate the harmony hidden in the world, caused by the power of the Sun.

<margin>The Rooster is sacred to him.</margin>
The rooster is dedicated to him because of the twilight or the dawn which the Sun shapes, and the rooster announces with his song. Lucius Apuleius writes of him thus:

<margin>Lucius Apuleius. The image of Mercury.</margin>
> *A boy, he says, radiant, except that he covered his left shoulder with a youth's cloak, conspicuous for his golden hair: among his locks, golden feathers joined together stood out, along with the herald's staff [caduceus] and a small wand;*

This description does not differ from the one we brought forward above regarding Apollo; for each detail signifies the rays of the Sun. Concerning the wand and the caduceus, various things are handed down by various authors; we say that Mercury’s wand was a symbol

<margin>Mercury’s Caduceus.</margin>
of the union of Jupiter and Rhea (or Ceres), from which Proserpina was born; since it is handed down that this was performed under the form of dragons, which designates the conjunction of the Aether and the Earth for the procreation of crops, and no one is ignorant that this pertains to the power of the Sun.

<margin>The Reed Wand.</margin>
Furthermore, it was a reed wand, from which arrows—a symbol of the Sun's rays—were once made. It was also tricolored—namely of gold, blue-grey, and black—to indicate the celestial, aerial, and terrestrial places where the solar power exerts itself: although Fulgentius, Phornutus, Albricus, and Apollodorus trace these sayings to the power of eloquence; which will be best understood if we consider eloquence as a kind of mystic Sun.

Finally, the Hieropolitans, who are people of Assyria, reduced all the effects and virtues of the Sun to the appearance of a single bearded statue; a statue of this kind is shown in the figure for Scheme III, figure IV on page 226, and calling him Apollo, they worshipped him. His face was fashioned with a long beard tapering to a point, with a <term>Calathus</term> <note>a basket-shaped crown, often representing fertility or the abundance of the earth</note> standing out above his head; the statue was protected by a breastplate, and in its right hand it held an upright spear, with a small sign of Victory standing over it; in its left hand, it held out the appearance of a flower; from the tops of the shoulders, a Gorgon-like covering, encircled with snakes, covered the shoulder blades. Then an eagle was seen flying.

<margin>Description of the Deity of the Hieropolitans.</margin>
Before its feet was a female image, from whose right and left were icons of women, which a Dragon encircled in a winding coil. The theologians taught that the rays being cast from above onto the earth were signified by the hanging beard. The rising golden basket...

You see, therefore, how appropriately in this figure the Apollonian power <note>original: *Apollinea vis*</note> of the Sun—summery, radiant, healing, and fruit-bearing—is displayed through the youthful form of the radiant head, through the quiver and arrows, and through the cluster <note>original: *corymbum*</note> conspicuous with every kind of fruit and flower, with which he honors the whole year. You may also recognize the Herculean virtue of the Sun—that is, the power that solidifies all things—shown in the club clothed in the aegis <note>original: *ægide vestita*; here the "aegis" refers to the protective lion-skin associated with Hercules, symbolizing the Sun's concentrated strength in the cold of winter</note>, namely, the winter power. So too, you see in the vine-leafed vessel the Bacchic autumnal power of the Sun, which ripens all things; and in the Mercurial heaps <note>original: *aceruis Mercurialibus*; these are the "herms" or piles of stones at the base of the diagram</note> and the caducei <note>The winged staffs of Mercury, symbolizing peace and the flourishing of life</note>, the power of the Sun brought forth <unclear>displayed</unclear> in the springtime. Let us therefore proceed to other matters.

**Apollo** <note>The Greek and Roman god of the Sun, medicine, and music.</note>, **Sol** <note>The Sun personified.</note>, **Hercules** <note>The hero of immense strength, representing the Sun's "solidifying" power in winter.</note>, **Bacchus** <note>The god of wine and the harvest, representing the Sun's ripening power in autumn.</note>, **Mercurius** <note>Mercury, the messenger god, representing the Sun's life-giving movement in spring.</note>, **Hieroglyphic Figure** <note>original: *Typus Hieroglyphicus*; a symbolic diagram intended to reveal hidden spiritual truths.</note>

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS. 237 CHAPTER 11.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut illustration featuring a central human figure with four arms, appearing behind a plinth labeled "Solmiisticus" (The Mystic Sun). Each arm holds a symbolic object: a spear pointed upwards labeled "Ignis" (Fire), a chalice labeled "Aqua" (Water), a caduceus labeled "Aer" (Air), and a club labeled "Terra" (Earth).</image-desc>

In the year 1626, a certain coin or medal was unearthed in Trier, upon which was seen an image not unlike the one we have just displayed.

It consisted of a head supported by four arms, of which the first was seen equipped with a spear, the second with a cup, the third with a caduceus, and the fourth with a club, as appears here in the figure. Through this <term>hieroglyphic: a symbolic image used to convey sacred or hidden meanings</term> I believe nothing else is signified than the fourfold power of the Sun, represented under the four symbols mystically attributed to the said Gods: so that by the spear, Apollo, or the illuminating power of the Sun, is indicated; by the cup, Bacchus, or the moistening and ripening <note>original: *decoctiua*—literally "cooking," referring to the Sun’s role in maturing crops</note> power of the Sun; by the caduceus, Mercury, or its attractive power; and finally by the club, Hercules, or the solidifying property of the Sun. Although the aforementioned four symbols can also be suitably adapted to the four Elements: so that by the spear we represent the penetrating power of fire, and to speak with the philosopher Porphyry: "the vibration of the rays" <note>original: *πάλσιν πῶν ἀκτίνων*</note>, which the ancients, on account of a certain similarity of heat and splendor, called the Sun. The caduceus of Mercury, however, is nothing other than the fluid air, permeable to winged things, reaching no less to the higher regions than the lower. For the air, joining the highest things to the lowest, intervenes everywhere in the middle, as Seneca well says in book 2 of his *Natural Questions*; and for that reason, Mercury is observed by the writer Arnobius as if he were "Medicurrius" <note>original: *Medicurrius*—a wordplay suggesting Mercury is the one who "runs in the middle" (*medium currens*)</note>. The cup, which was once attributed to Bacchus, seems to represent Water most excellently, because of his power over moist things, and for which reason Plutarch calls him "the lord and author of every moist nature" <note>original: *πάσης ὑγρᾶς φύσεως κύριον, καὶ ἀρχηγὸν*</note>. Finally, the club designates nothing else but Hercules and the strengthening power of the Sun, or the Earth: for, according to the testimony of Apollonius of Rhodes in book 4, the club of Hercules was made of olive wood, which has a great affinity with the earth, as Theophrastus and Pliny relate; these things are confirmed by the carving of an ancient gem, displaying the symbols of the four elements, taken from the treasury of Abraham Gorlaeus by Alcandrus.

<image-desc>A circular diagram containing four symbolic illustrations arranged around the central word "ERYX". At the top (A) is a winged lightning bolt; on the left (B) is a dolphin; at the bottom (C) is a caduceus; and on the right (D) is a gnarled dry tree trunk.</image-desc>

It signified fire through the lightning bolt **A**; water through the Dolphin **B**; air through the caduceus **C**; and finally earth through the dry trunk **D**. But to return to our purpose: the table placed above can certainly be very well adapted to the four seasons of the year, which the Sun brings about by its motion. If by Mercury we understand Spring; by Bacchus or the cup, Autumn; by Hercules, Winter; and finally by Apollo, Summer. And to begin with the latter: what else does that radiant Apollo, equipped with such a manifold supply of arrows, intend for himself but the supreme power which he exerts in the summertime? And as <margin>Hesiod.</margin> Hesiod says, "the strength of the sharp sun" <note>original: *μένος ὀξέος ἠελίοιο*</note>, drying up all rot and harmful humors? To which perhaps "Python," meaning rot <note>original: *πύθω*—to rot or decay</note>, or the Dragon slain by Apollo, seems to allude; indeed, through the laurel and the crow...

# CHAPTER 11. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGIA

<margin>
Philostratus, *Imagines*.
Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book 1.

</margin>
...things which are hottest by nature, such as the union of *Apollo* or *Summer*, as Albricus <note>Albricus (likely Alexander Neckam or a similar mythographer) was a medieval author known for describing the images of the gods.</note> testifies; so too the *Phaethontic* fire <note>A reference to the myth of Phaethon, who nearly destroyed the earth by driving the Sun's chariot too close to it.</note> according to *Philostratus*, *Cassiodorus*, and *Lucan*. Indeed, that common saying (that one is struck by the disk of *Apollo*) sufficiently demonstrates that *Apollo* denotes the summer. By *Bacchus*, however, nothing else is represented than *Autumn*, as shown by the wine, cornucopias, clusters of grapes, vines, trees, and plants that were attributed to him—as well as that *Encarpus* <term>Encarpus: a classic architectural or decorative motif consisting of a festoon of fruit and flowers</term>, or cluster filled with every variety of fruit, seen in the preceding illustration, of which *Virgil* wrote:

<margin>Virgil, *Georgics*, Book 2.</margin>
> . . . for you the field flourishes, pregnant with vine-leafed Autumn,
> the vintage foams with full brims.

*Phornutus* <note>Also known as Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> also records that for this reason Bacchus was called the guardian and God of trees, with *Athenaeus* in agreement. *Demarchus* notes that in the Dionysiac contests, virgins used to carry golden baskets filled with the first fruits of all produce as the festival of *Bacchus* approached. To this also pertains what is recorded in the words of *Porphyry* <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3.</margin> found in *Eusebius*: *The power of tree-fruits, and generally of all that is planted, is named Dionysus.* <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἀκροδρύων, καὶ ὅλως τῶν φυτευτικῶν ἡ δύναμις διόνυσος ὀνομάσεται."</note> The fact that *Autumn* follows summer is indicated by the fable of *Bacchus* being extracted from his mother's burning womb <note>Bacchus/Dionysus was saved from the womb of Semele after she was consumed by the fire of Zeus's true form.</note>. Furthermore, the various metamorphoses of *Bacchus* represented by the ancients reflected the inconstancy, variety, and the shifting nature of the autumnal air.

Moreover, that *Hercules* denoted *Winter* is shown by his shaggy beard, animal skins, and club, according to *Phornutus*. For winter is nothing other than a certain old age of the year, in which—as the fields stiffen and grow white with frost—all trees are deprived of their greenness and bloom; but the greatest remedy for defending oneself against the cold is <margin>Callimachus, *Hymn to Artemis*</margin> skins. *Hercules*, or *Winter*, is called *Boethagos* <note>original: "Βοϑάγος" meaning "ox-eater" or "ox-driver"</note> because he consumes the labors of the oxen, as *Athenaeus* and *Callimachus* record. Furthermore, *Hercules* was an adversary to *Juno* <note>In mythology, Juno (Hera) was the stepmother and persecutor of Hercules; here, Juno represents the air/atmosphere which becomes harsh in winter.</note>, because winter disturbs the air with clouds, snow, and rain, making it unpleasant. *Hercules* was called the "Averter of Evils" because he is accustomed to drive away autumn, the most disease-ridden part of the year, with his cold.

Finally, *Remigius the Monk* (cited in *Alcander*) records that **MERCURY** himself denotes the time of spring; this is because he is said to preside over the seeds of the sea and the earth. Hence he is associated with *Favonius* <note>The West Wind, which heralds the beginning of spring.</note>, who is said by *Philostratus* to be winged and is called "beautiful in form." The "union" of *Mercury* seems to intimate nothing else than that lustful time of spring, in which all things are excited toward *Venus*, according to that passage of *Lucretius*:

> For as soon as the vernal face of day is laid open,
> And the birth-giving breeze of the West Wind is unlocked and thrives,
> First the birds of the air, O Goddess, signal your arrival,
> Struck to their hearts by your power.

And *Columella* in his *On Agriculture*:

> Now love hastens to union; now the spirit of the world
> Revels for Venus, and driven by the stings of desire,
> It loves its own parts and fills them with offspring.
> From this the seas, from this the mountains, from this finally the whole world
> Enacts Spring; from this comes the lust of men, of cattle, and of birds.

# CHAPTER XII.

## *On the mystical significance of the Muses and Apollo.*

There are diverse opinions among authors regarding the Muses; some posit only three, the daughters of heaven and earth, because of the "three-stringed" harmony <note>Original Greek: *trichordum*</note> discovered by them, which contained the *hypate*, *mese*, and *nete*—that is, the lowest, middle, and highest notes. By this, nothing else is indicated but the triple world: the elemental, the ethereal, and the super-celestial, as Plato teaches. Others have written that there are nine Muses, born of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> and Mnemosyne <note>The goddess of Memory</note>, concerning whom Ovid writes in the 5th book of the *Metamorphoses*, calling them the "Mnemosydas" after their mother:
> For he had recognized the daughters of Memory; "Stand still," he said.

Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian known for his universal history.</note> truly interpreted them most famously, describing the specific duties of each according to those things which pertain to the art of music. Homer also honored them with incredible renown. They were called Muses because they teach good and useful things to men laboring under ignorance. For since, as was said above, Jove is nothing other than the father and soul of the world, while the remaining stars or planets, and even the elements, are considered his sons and daughters—and Apollo, the first-born son of Jove, is surely the Sun, the ruler, leader, and governor of those children (the stars and elements)—the ancient sages, under this obscure shroud of a fable about the Muses born of Jove and taught by Apollo, wished to suggest the marriage of all nature and its admirable harmony.

<margin>The Arts.</margin>
From the frequent contemplation and curious investigation of nature, the arts or "Muses" finally emerged, such as Astronomy, Geometry, Arithmetic, Music, Rhetoric, Dialectic, and so on. These are, as it were, the daughters of memory and imagination. For when men grasped the constant laws of the heavens with the greatest admiration, applying frequent observations and firmly impressing those motions upon the intellect through the imagination, Astronomy finally arose. But since they could not investigate such manifold motions without <margin>Astrology.</margin> a knowledge of quantity—both continuous and discrete <note>The author refers to the classical division of mathematics: Geometry (continuous quantity) and Arithmetic (discrete quantity).</note>—for hypotheses and phenomena could in no way be demonstrated without geometric reasoning, nor the number of motions without arithmetic, Geometry and Arithmetic <margin>Geometry Arithmetic</margin> drew their origin from that occasion. Truly, when they observed that admirable mutual connection and harmonious order of such diverse things and natures, differing across the whole sky—the highest things joined with the lowest, and finally the highest and lowest joined with the middle—highest...

### CHAPTER XII. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>Music.</margin>
...observing things corresponding everywhere in proportion, they believed that harmonic ratios were inherent in all things, from which **Music** was born. But because they could not discuss these matters firmly and distinctly, they established a method to be followed in reasoning through certain rules, giving rise to **Dialectic** <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth.</note> and **Rhetoric** <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing.</note>.
<margin>Dialectic. Rhetoric.</margin>
Behold the lineage of the Muses. Furthermore, others imagine them derived from the head of Apollo, according to that line of the Poet:

->The power of the Apolline mind moves these Muses from every direction.<-

This does not differ from our own opinion, if those things which we said above regarding the identity of Jupiter and Apollo are rightly considered. Anaximander of Lampsacus <note>A Greek philosopher often associated with early scientific inquiry.</note> and Xenophanes of Heracleopolis interpreted the Muses differently in their books; as others, such as Pisander the Natural Philosopher and Euximenes in his book 
<margin>Pisander. Euximenes.</margin>
<margin>They denote the instruments of the human voice.</margin>
<term>Theological Discourses</term> <note>Original Greek: *theologoumenon*</note>, seem to confirm. For they compare the Muses in order to the necessary instruments of the human voice. For the voice is formed by four teeth <note>Likely referring to the incisors used in articulation.</note> positioned opposite each other, against which the tongue strikes. They assign one of the Muses to the two upper teeth, and another to the lower, because when either of them is missing, a hiss is produced rather than a voice, as they were accustomed to say. Likewise, they assign two of the Muses to the two lips, which are like cymbals suited for the modulation of words. They apply another to the tongue, which, by striking frequently, forms a certain vocal spirit. They also dedicated one of the Muses to the palate, whose cavity carries the sound; they derive another Muse from the pipe of the throat, which provides a spiritual passage through a smooth and round path. Again, they assign one to the lungs, which, like an aerial bellows, returns and recalls the conceived voice. The ninth they assigned to rest and silence. For if any of these nine instruments of truth 
<margin>Fulgentius.</margin>
are missing, the voice will not be perfect. Fulgentius <note>A Latin writer of the late 5th/6th century known for allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> indeed, in the second book of his <term>Mythologies</term> <note>Original Greek: *mythologikon*</note>, said that the nine Muses represent the modes of 
<margin>They denote the reasons of Wisdom.</margin>
learning and wisdom; hence, according to the laws of allegory, they are placed in this order:

In the first place is <term>Urania</term> <note>Meaning "Heavenly."</note>, that is, the loftiness of human intelligence. Second, <term>Polyhymnia</term> <note>Meaning "Many Hymns."</note>, that is, the capacity of memory. Third, <term>Euterpe</term> <note>Meaning "Well-pleasing."</note>, that is, the delight of the will; for intelligence is joined to memory and the will. Fourth is placed <term>Erato</term> <note>Meaning "Lovely."</note>; that is, the "amiable," for the will is delighted by nothing more than the comparison of similar things; however, this cannot happen without profound thought, therefore <term>Melpomene</term> <note>Meaning "Songstress."</note> follows. To her is associated <term>Terpsichore</term> <note>Meaning "Delighting in the dance."</note>, as if the delight of the arts; for perfection of thought cannot be achieved without the perfection of disciplines. From all these is born the beauty of all human speech, which is called <term>Calliope</term> <note>Meaning "Beautiful-voiced."</note>; from there is born <term>Clio</term> <note>Meaning "Fame" or "Glory."</note>, that is, good reputation, under which <term>Thalia</term> <note>Meaning "Blooming."</note> is placed in the final position, that is, the budding of virtues. For every virtue exists through the beautiful reputation of desire and glory, and is therefore lifted up by a white bird—that is, a swan—and is soon set down in pools, because the seeds <note>The Latin text reads *femina* (woman), but contextually *semina* (seeds) is much more likely, as they are "sown" (*disseminantur*).</note> of glory and good fame, having been raised high and sublime, are then scattered and spread across the ground—that is, among mortals and the mouths of men. According to Fulgentius’s consideration, just as knowledge and disciplines are sought out through the gift of the Muses, so too are the acts of willing, delighting, persisting, grasping, remembering, and inventing...

...be recognized to indicate, choose, pronounce, and fit together successively and necessarily. It is also not unworthy of consideration what the

<margin>Macrobius, Book 1 of the Saturnalia.</margin>
Macrobius writes in Book 1 of the *Saturnalia* that Apollo's lyre had seven strings, through which he allows us to understand the movements of as many celestial spheres. 
<margin>Diodorus. Three-stringed.</margin>
Diodorus, however, says that Mercury was the inventor of the lyre and that he established it with three strings, like the three seasons of the year; likewise, three voices were chosen: the low from winter, the high from summer, and the middle from spring—to the great injury of autumn, which, though burdened with fruit, is unjustly exiled from here.
<margin>Orpheus. Four-stringed.</margin>
Others report that Orpheus established a lyre with four strings, either for those same seasons of the year—so that autumn, having been treated unjustly, might be restored to its rightful dignity by a return to status—or to denote the four elements, as others have written.
<margin>Ten-stringed</margin>
Others attribute a ten-stringed lyre to Apollo; our minds are indeed so fertile whenever they cannot extricate themselves from extreme difficulties. To say in a single word, then, what I think of this variety of opinions:
<margin>Triple world.</margin>
By the "three-stringed" attribute of Apollo mentioned by Diodorus, the triple world (discussed above) is signified, or the triple dominion of Jupiter over the celestial, terrestrial, and infernal realms, as Orpheus expressly demonstrates in the hymn to Jupiter cited above.
<margin>Orpheus in the hymn. 4 Elements, and 4 seasons of the year. 7 Planetary orbits.</margin>
Indeed, all authors who have treated this subject testify that Orpheus’s "four-stringed" lyre was a symbol of the four elements and the four seasons; those who attribute a "seven-stringed" one to him are separately suggesting the orbits of the seven planets. If the heaven of the fixed stars is added to this, an "eight-stringed" instrument is created. Finally, those who attach a "nine-stringed" instrument to him include the Earth in the eight-stringed count, as Glareanus <note>Heinrich Glarean, a famous 16th-century music theorist.</note> does, which they express through the names of the nine Muses: thus, different many-stringed instruments are attached to the orders of different things.

<margin>Musical Tones.</margin>
So they say that **Thalia** has no harmony, and thus they assigned her to silence and the Earth, which they compare to the three-headed Cerberus prostrate at Apollo's feet. **Clio** moves with the Moon in the Hypodorian mode and the *proslambanomenos* string <note>The "added note," the lowest in the ancient Greek musical system.</note>. **Calliope** and Mercury possess the Hypophrygian mode and the *hypate hypaton* string <note>The "lowest of the low" string.</note>. **Terpsichore** with Venus contain the Hypolydian and the *parhypate hypaton* <note>The "next-to-lowest of the low."</note>. **Melpomene** with the Sun fit the Dorian and the *lichanos hypaton* <note>The "index finger" note of the lowest tetrachord.</note>. **Erato** with Mars keep the Phrygian with the *hypate meson* <note>The "lowest of the middle" strings.</note>. **Euterpe** and Jupiter are suited by the Lydian and the *parhypate meson* <note>The "next-to-lowest of the middle."</note>. **Polyhymnia** and Saturn preserve the Mixolydian and the *lichanos meson* <note>The "index finger" of the middle tetrachord.</note>. To **Urania** and the Starry Heaven, the *nete* strings <note>The "highest" strings.</note> are ascribed. By all these things, they seem to demonstrate nothing other than the harmony of the whole universe. For that highest course of the starry heaven, whose rotation—when it becomes more rapid—is moved with a sharp and excited sound, while the lunar and lowest is moved with the deepest, of which Cicero makes mention in these words:
<margin>Cicero, Book 6 of the Republic. Musical course of the Planets.</margin>
*For the earth, remaining motionless, always stays in the lowest seat, embracing the middle place of the world; but those eight courses, in which the power of two modes—those of Mercury and Venus—is the same, produce seven distinct [sounds]...*
<note>From the "Dream of Scipio" in Cicero's De Re Publica.</note>

</margin>
And the common saying of musicians agrees: *The same judgment holds for octaves*; although, to say what I truly think, Cicero’s passage is undoubtedly corrupted in this place, and Macrobius did not understand it exactly, even though he wrote four very long chapters upon it. Theodorus Gaza, a man of exceptional erudition, when he translated that passage into the Greek language, himself omitted certain things which are found in the common manuscripts of Cicero, such as these words: *of the measures of Mercury and Venus*. Others he translated differently, such as *a double power belongs to them* <note>original Greek: ἐν διπλῇ αὐτοῖς προσεῖ δύναμις</note>, which is frequently read this way in certain common Latin manuscripts. However, those eight orbits, in which there is the "same power of measures," is a reading far different from the words of Theodorus. Some think that in these words of Cicero—*seven produce sounds distinguished by intervals*—the word "seven" should be joined to the ablative "intervals," in this sense: these eight orbits produce sounds distinguished by seven intervals. But this is undoubtedly forced, and far removed from Cicero’s phrasing and judgment. I judge that this passage of Cicero should be read as follows: *Those eight orbits, however, in which the same power of the extremes exists, produce seven intervals with distinct sounds*; or as the more learned musicians put it, seven **species**, which is the measure of nearly all things. If these words are read in this way, they appear both uttered according to nature and will be in agreement with the tradition of musicians.

<margin>
VII.
Species of the Octave.
</margin>
For nature holds it so: that with eight pitches or voices, arranged according to musical ratio and measured by a certain type of modulation, the eighth is of the same nature as the first. And although there are eight pitches, there are nevertheless only seven intervals, which, when varied seven times in any kind of modulation, produce the seven species of the **octave** <note>original Greek: διαπασῶν (diapason). These species refer to the different arrangements of tones and semitones within an eight-note scale, similar to modern musical modes.</note>, of which the books of authors very frequently make mention. Since I have seen most learned men struggle so many times in untying the difficulty of this passage, I did not wish to pass it over here.

<margin>
Doctrines of the Hebrews.
</margin>
The wise men of the Hebrews also, when they beheld that multiform shape of the world and the "discordant concord" of things, believed it to be governed by certain presiding Angels. It is certain that both the "Intelligences" of Aristotle and the fables of the Nine Muses flowed from this source. But so that you may better perceive the context of history and the progression of disciplines from the Hebrews to the Egyptians, and from them to the Greeks and others, it seemed fit to add here the entire opinion and tradition of the Hebrews regarding the harmony of the world.

<margin>
The Hebrew doctrine on the Harmony of the World.
The Triple World.
</margin>
Thus the Hebrews, in order to properly distinguish the differences and grades of all things, figure three worlds (just as we read that Plato did). The first is the "supramundane" world, which the philosophers call the **archetypal** <note>original Greek: ἀρχέτυπον (archetypon)</note> or "intellectual" world; the Hebrews call it the **World of Angels** <note>original Hebrew: עולם המלאכים (Olam Ha-Malakhim)</note>. In this world, creatures are clothed in no covering of earthly mixture; they are enumerated through the letters **A, B, G, D, H, etc.** <note>Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He</note> in the mystical alphabet, signified up to the letter **Iod**. The world next to this they call the **Celestial World** <note>original Hebrew: עולם הגלגלים (Olam Ha-Galgalim) – "World of the Spheres"</note>, which they represent through the letters from **Kaph** <note>כ</note> onwards...

> The powers of the Apollonian mind move the Muses from every side.

<margin>Apollo, Leader of the Muses, accompanied by the three Graces.</margin>

By the **lyre**, they signified nothing other than the harmony of the world, as has already been said. By the **heliotrope**, they signified the connection of lower things with higher things. The three Graces signified the splendor, the liberality, and the fecundity of Apollo in this universe; the first is signified by **Aglaia**, the second by **Euphrosyne**, and the third by **Thalia**. The **serpent** represented the generative power of Apollo diffused through the entire world; indeed, the **three heads** resting on the earth signify the triple power by which he makes the earth fertile: the powers of moistening, heating, and seeding. All other philosophers, besides Aristotle, testify that these three powers concur in every generation. And from all these things, it is brilliantly clear how beautifully the different inventions of different people agree on the same matter. But so that all things which have been said thus far may be more easily perceived, it has pleased me to place here a diagram of the entire discourse before your eyes.

### EGYPTIAN STUDIES 245 CHAPTER 12

<margin>The number nine.</margin>
But one difficulty remains for us to solve, which that ninefold number of the Muses thrusts upon us. For here, the number nine signifies the imperfection and diminution of things and works. I say, therefore, that this sensible world <note>The "sensible world" refers to the physical universe perceivable by the senses, as opposed to the "intelligible" or spiritual world.</note> is completed by the Ennead <note>original: "Nouenario"; the number nine.</note>. First is the Firmament, which the Ancients believed to be the greatest and highest of sensible bodies; next follows the sevenfold number of the Planets; and below the moon there remain the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Although these elements are heterogeneous and different from one another, they are recognized as distinct from the ethereal and celestial substance by one simple logic: they are perishable, mutually transmutable, continuous, and are the "nurseries" of all sensible things. Thus, we embrace them under a single name and call them the **elementary body**. In this way, this entire sensible world is comprised of two bodies—namely, the elementary and the celestial—and we call that whole which is held enclosed from the center to the connected surface of the firmament the "sensible world," the body of the entire sensible world, and whatever is perceivable by the senses.

<margin>Pythagorean mysteries in number.</margin>
Now let us prove that these things were demonstrated by the Pythagoreans. You should know, then, that the Pythagoreans noted this property in numbers: that in all **perfect numbers** <note>In mathematics, a perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its positive divisors, excluding the number itself (e.g., 6, 28, 496).</note> containing a multiple proportion to their parts, as many times as unity <note>The number one.</note> is taken away, a plurality of nines is left behind. For if you add the digits of the number 28, you will fashion a ten from the 2 and 8, from which unity subtracted leaves 9. By the same logic, the digits of 496 (the third of the perfect numbers) collected together constitute 19, from which unity withdrawn leaves 18: a double plurality of nine. By this arithmetic mystery, they wished to signify nothing other than that no substance of a perfect number exists unless unity is coupled to the nine; thus, the nine are so dependent on the one in order to be perfect. Similarly, the 9 orders of Angels cannot flow forth at all without that Unity which they call <term>אין סוף</term> <gloss>Ein Suph, that is, the Infinite</gloss>, nor can the Muses perform anything without Apollo (or the Soul of the World). Likewise, we know that the celestial spheres represented by the Muses can effect nothing without <term>Mitatron</term> <note>Metatron; in mystical tradition, the highest archangel or the "Prince of the Countenance" who governs the movements of the heavens.</note>, or the *Primum Mobile* <note>The "First Moved" sphere that imparts motion to all other spheres.</note>, by whose power all other things are moved. To prove this, we turn to the 10 Categories, or the 10 primary types of things, divided into **substance** and **accident**, about which it is often said:

> ->Great Aristotle, weighing the peaks of reality,<-
> ->Divided into two whatever existed in the World.<-
<note>original: "Magnus Aristoteles, trutinando cacumina rerum, / In duo diuisit, quicquid in Orbe fuit."</note>

For **Substance** is one predicament <note>A "predicament" is another term for a Category in Aristotelian logic.</note>, and the remaining 9 are **Accidents**. Substance, being absolute in all numbers, exists through itself; it can be considered and perceived by the mind as separate from all accidents. The nine accidents, however, are so affected that they can never exist through themselves, but must always exist in a subject, which is substance. For Logicians say that "to be in a subject" means that while something is in another, it cannot exist without it, and yet it is not a part of it. From these things it is clear that the nine Muses can do nothing without the complement of Apollo, nor can the harmony of the world be perfect, unless

### CHAPTER 13. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

...is completed by the ten <note>original: "denario"; referring to the number ten or the Decad.</note>. For the two, the seven, and the nine are found to be discordant in music. Indeed, the second and the seventh intervals, etc., are the most dissonant; but since the octave, the most perfect of all harmonies, returns to the

<margin>
Harmonic property.

first, the ninth will be similar to the second, and therefore also discordant. Concerning this, Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile Platonism, Aristotelianism, and the Kabbalah.</note> says in his *Conclusions*:

<margin>
Pico, Kabbalistic Conclusion 8.

<margin>

in this way—1, 2, 3, 4—you will see these numbers joined together constitute the ten, which contains all things <note>This is the "Tetractys," a triangular figure of ten points used by Pythagoreans to symbolize the organization of the universe.</note>. For the order of the elements—earth, water, air, and fire—fitting to each, appears clearly in these numbers. All harmonic proportions become manifest here, such as: the Unison, the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, and the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. Thus, 1 to 1 refers to the Unison; 1 and 2 to the Octave (the double proportion); 3 and 2 to the Fifth (the sesquialter proportion); and finally 4 and 3 to the Fourth (the sesquitertian proportion). The Octave with the Fifth is 3 to 1; and finally the Double Octave <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note> is the 4 to 1 ratio, namely the quadruple proportion. However, because I have treated these and similar matters more copiously in my *Musurgia Universalis* <note>Kircher’s massive 1650 work on music theory and acoustics.</note>, I have judged it unnecessary to dwell on them any longer, for it is not my purpose at this time to scrutinize all these details minutely. It will be enough for the Reader to have perceived from what has been said my mind regarding this hieroglyphic arrangement of the nine Muses and Apollo.

### C A P V T XIII.

->*All Gods are reduced to the one Sun, and all Goddesses to the Moon.*<-

Human nature is so constituted that, having Bewohnered those things which are inaccessible to the senses, it pursues with all affection those objects which are pleasing, useful, and beneficial. It seemed very troublesome to many to investigate GOD by the intellect alone, and not also to perceive Him by sight. Therefore, since nothing more beautiful or useful than the Sun presented itself to their view, they judged the Sun itself to be God. They saw that even if it did not occupy everything with the magnitude of its body, it nevertheless brought health and life to the lands and plants, imparted light to the rest of the stars, and made the heavens themselves visible. Pliny.

# EGYPTIAN MATTERS. 247 CAP. XIII

He now mocks the belief concerning the Gods. He seems to doubt whether there is any God besides the Sun. There are some who, for this reason, would have the word *Helios* <note>original: "ἥλιος"; the Greek word for the Sun.</note> derived perhaps from the Hebrew *El* <note>original: "אל"; a primary Hebrew name for God.</note>, which signifies God. 

<margin>Macrobius</margin>
Certainly, Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (c. 385 – 430 AD), a Roman provincial writer whose *Saturnalia* argued that all pagan gods were ultimately masks for the Sun.</note> contends more than others, using many arguments, to prove that all the Gods are referred back to the Sun, and that this is the one Divinity whom the nations worship under various names. But in order to discuss all these matters more profoundly, it seemed best to begin the matter from a slightly higher point.

In the first centuries after the flood, because men could only with difficulty grasp that supreme Lord of the whole universe, the unapproachable light <note>original: "φῶς οἰκεῖτα ἀπρόσιτον"; a reference to 1 Timothy 6:16, "dwelling in light unapproachable."</note>, they looked with religious awe upon the command the celestial bodies held over all the comforts of life—as was said a little earlier. Being impious, they did not distinguish the Creator from that which is pure and proper to the Supreme alone. Measuring Divinity rashly by their senses, they acknowledged no other God besides the one who dispensed the successions and seasons of light and darkness, motion and silence, and the fateful cycles of nights, days, and years. They were driven by the guidance of natural reason and yet seduced, as the sacred words we have quoted say. 

For this reason, even the Chaldeans <note>Ancient people of Mesopotamia, famous for their early advancements in astronomy and astrology.</note> in the first times after the deluge, having cast off the worship of the true GOD, embraced this very philosophy, as was said in the 1st and 2nd books.

<margin>Rambam</margin>
And Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher.</note>, cited above, teaches this at length. Moreover, they esteemed the Sun as the greatest Divinity of all (whom the Phoenician theologians also called the "only God" <note>original: "μόνον θεὸν Θεὸν".</note>). They judged the planets and the other stars to be observing his will, just as the ancient Egyptians viewed the arrangements <gloss>arrangements</gloss> of the zodiac: the Counselor Gods <note>original: "Θεοὶ βυλαῖοι".</note>; while the Planets were considered the "rod-bearers" <note>original: "ῥαβδοφόροι"; in Roman terms, *lictors* or officers who cleared the way for a magistrate.</note>, who stand as attendants in the consistory of the kindled Sun.

Indeed, I do not think this error of impiety first invaded men only after the flood, but they drank it in not many centuries after the very beginning of things. This is how I understand that passage of Moses in Genesis 4, the last verse: "then it was begun <note>original: "אז הוחל לקרא בשם יהוה" (*az huchal likro b'shem Yehovah*). The author highlights a linguistic ambiguity in the Hebrew root *CH-L-L*.</note> to profane the name of the Lord." For the word *huchal* is interpreted as both "to begin" and "to profane," according to that passage in Leviticus 19: "You shall not profane the name of the Lord your God." <note>original: "לא תחלל שם אלהיך".</note> Furthermore, it is consistent with those Hebrew interpretations: "Then it was profaned in the calling upon the name of Jehovah"; which is likewise admitted by Onkelos, and the other Chaldean Paraphrast, known as Uzielides under the name of Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targums, ancient Aramaic translations and commentaries on the Hebrew Bible.</note>, as well as Rashi, Radak <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note>, and others, who understand Moses in that place to be speaking about the origins of new Divinities. 

To be "profaned in calling upon the name of Jehovah" is the same as if he had said that the most holy name, which designates the Creator and Lord of the whole Universe, was impiously attributed to created things. Flavius Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> indicates this best when he writes that for seven generations, men perceived that the one Great and Good GOD was the master of all things <note>original: "δεσπότην εἶναι τῶν ὅλων".</note>. But thereafter, they degenerated from the ancestral customs <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν πατρῴων ἐθισμῶν".</note>; that is, they worshipped created things or celestial bodies.

From here came the first inventions of the Egyptians in manufacturing Gods; all of whom were indeed reduced to Osiris and Isis, that is, to the Sun and the Moon. Their powers were indicated mystically through various forms of living creatures: thus, through the hawk, the fiery power of the Sun or Moon; through the goat, the power of fertility...

# CHAPTER XIII. BOOK III. MYSTAGOGIA

...the moist force through the Crocodile; through the ibis, the power that consumes harmful things; through oxen, the power over all crops; and so with the others, about which there is extensive discussion throughout this whole work. In a similar way, the symbol of the Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated with early astronomy and astrology.</note> was fire; of the Persians, Mithras; of the Babylonians, Bel; the Hebrews had Thammuz; the Phoenicians, Adonis, etc. These people, who were the foremost practitioners of the type of Theology we are discussing, regarded these figures as an outflow <note>original: "ἀποῤῥοὴ" (aporrhoē); an emanation or discharge from a divine source.</note>, a deputy, or a sign of the Sun, the king of the heavens. Since, because of the distance of the celestial bodies, sacred rites could not be performed for them as conveniently as desired, they judged it right to consecrate symbols of this kind, which seemed especially fitting, in their honor.

Nor should you think that the Dragon of the Philistines <note>likely referring to Dagon, who was often depicted as part-man, part-fish, though the author uses the word "Draco" (dragon or serpent) here.</note>, with its form mixed of human and marine features, denoted anything other than Neptune, Amphitrite, Salacia, Ocean, or Thetis <note>These are all Greco-Roman deities associated with the sea.</note>, or all of these—that is, the sea itself. In that simpler age, it was used as a symbol of the Divinity, just as in a great assembly of the leaders of nature. Both sexes were attributed to each God, as we have shown in many places.

For the mystery of the figure does not allow it to have been merely a statue of a deceased person; the same must be said of the fish sacred to him. They were worshiped because they were symbols of the sea, just as heifers were among the Egyptians,

<margin>The origin of polytheism</margin>
which were received with the highest and even divine honor because of the benefit of their milk—first as symbols of Mother Earth and the Nurse, and later of Isis or the Moon (for they recognized that nourishment was chiefly due to the benign powers of the Earth and the Moon); similarly, the marked Bulls were symbols of the Sun. In the first centuries, they worshiped only the beneficial powers of nature. However, with the addition of the cult of demons <note>The author uses "demonia" to refer to intermediary spirits or fallen angels that Christians believed took up residence in pagan idols.</note>, following various superstitious beliefs, and with demons under the names of the dead, the Sun, the Moon, and the remaining stars (conspicuous above all for their light), as well as the sea and Earth and the remaining dispensers of nature, were all celebrated together with the same rites at the same statues and pillars. Thus, error eventually proceeded into infinity. The impious could not distinguish the dead from the demons, nor either of these from the natural powers of the machine of the universe. 

Hence, the Moon, Venus, and the Earth were combined in the figure of Astarte. The Moon, Venus, and the Sea were in the figure of Dagon; and all of these in Isis. The Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn were in Baal, and Moloch in Osiris. Furthermore, for every idol, a demonic name or a Hero was frequently invoked, and they were confounded in inextricable hallucination. From this came the ancestral Gods and innumerable geniuses <note>original: "genii"; guardian spirits or protective deities of a person or place.</note>, about which we will speak in the following pages. From this also came almost as many Moons, Venuses, Suns, Jupiters, and Saturns; and hence those innumerable statues placed everywhere among the nations, dedicated to Gods fabricated by antiquity, which, taking on individual local names, differed in almost no other way. For diversity in sacred rites does not mean the deities themselves differ in reality. 

And thus among the ancients, polytheism <note>original: "πολυθεία" (polytheia).</note> emanated from the multiform worship of a single deity, about which we have spoken thus far. Following the Egyptians, Hebrews, Chaldeans, Babylonians, and Phoenicians, the Greeks brought all these things to completion by weaving together innumerable genealogies of the Gods; however, they derive all of them entirely from the lineage of the one Sun or Moon. So it is that, on the testimony of Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer who argued that all gods were ultimately the Sun.</note> and others cited shortly before, Saturn, Jupiter, Pluto,

### EGYPTIAN MATTERS. CHAPTER XIII.

Pluto, Apollo, Bacchus, Mercury, Hercules, Aesculapius, Neptune, Vulcan, Mars, Pan, and Aeolus were nothing other than the various powers of the one Sun.

For the Sun, insofar as it regulates the seasons and the year by its motion, is called Saturn; as the Lord of the celestial bodies and the entire world, it is called Jupiter; and as it illuminates and penetrates all things with its rays, it is called Apollo. It is called Mercury insofar as it is the cause of all <term>meteors</term> <note>In this historical context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> through its attractive force. It is called Neptune because of its dominion over the sea and rivers, and Pluto because of its dominion over the subterranean regions. It is called Bacchus because it presides over wine and other liquids, without which nothing can reach maturity; however, insofar as it prevails with a strengthening power, it is called Hercules. Vulcan takes his name from the fiery power of the Sun, just as Mars does from the heat which it excites in living creatures—from which come rage, madness, wars, homicides, and similar works of Mars. It is called Aesculapius because of the healing power emanating from the substance of the Sun that aids the souls and bodies of mortals, and Pan because of the fecundity <note>fertility or life-giving power</note> that penetrates all things. Finally, it is named Aeolus insofar as it causes winds and storms by drawing up a great abundance of exhalations.

However, when they found these various virtues in other stars and planets as well—especially when they found that stars impregnated with solar light produced similar effects when aided by the light of the Sun—they called them by similar names. Furthermore, just as they called the Sun the active principle of all things, being one in substance but manifold in power; so they established that the Moon was one in reality, but manifold in the power of her name alone, acting as the passive principle of things and the spouse of the Sun. They also called her the Great Mother of the Gods, because all that pertains to the Goddesses may be traced back to her. 

Thus, the Moon is first called *Rhea* because she stands under the influence of the Sun like a wife to a husband, and is, as it were, the mother of the generation of things. She is called Ceres insofar as she presides over the crops; *Lucina*, because after the nocturnal shadows are dispelled, she fertilizes the lower parts of the world with her benevolent light; and *Venus* because of the fertile female power and the appetite for the generation of things—and since this power consists of moisture, she is said to be born from the foam of the sea. She is named *Juno*, or *Hera* <note>original Greek: "Ἥρα"</note> from the air over which she presides; she is called *Proserpina* from the seeds and plants of the earth which she causes to prosper; and *Flora* from the flowers and grasses. She is called *Diana* from the moistening power of the Moon, which acts strongly upon wooded and brush-filled places. *Minerva*, however, earned her name from lunar heat (as we said above), which is of great benefit to the intellect. *Hecate* is the low and subterranean Moon, named for the hundreds of kinds of things she produces in underground places. She is called *Tethys* from the sea and rivers, which she stirs by her influence. Finally, she is called *Bellona* from the heat she produces in bodies by multiplying the bile, the types of which you may see in what follows. 

But lest we seem to assert these extensively discussed points with only our own words, I thought they should be confirmed by a single testimony from Eusebius.

<margin>Eusebius, Book 3, Chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*.</margin>
> *Here, he says, pay close attention: they call the power of fire Vulcan, and they fashion a statue for him in the form of a man, on whose head is a blue cap, a symbol of the celestial revolution where the pure and unmixed fire is found. For the fire that has fallen from heaven to earth, since it is weaker and requires matter to burn, is depicted as limping; this power they place in the Sun.*
