### BOOK III. MYSTAGOGY

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
They called him Apollo, evidently from the motion of his rays, since *pallein* <note>original: πάλλειν</note> in Greek means "to move." Furthermore, nine Muses sing in harmony around Apollo: namely, the seven orbs of the planets, the eighth sphere <note>The "fixed stars" or firmament in the Ptolemaic system.</note>, and this last one, which is the Moon. They dedicated the laurel tree to him because this tree is of a fiery nature, for which reason it is held in the greatest hatred by demons; and because if it is burned, it crackles loudly, which signifies the power of prophecy. This same solar power they call Hercules because he heals the sick and drives away diseases, and they attribute twelve labors to him because he passes through the twelve signs of the zodiac. They assign him a club and a lion’s skin: the former to signify the inequality of his motion, and the latter because he shows his powers most strongly in the constellation of Leo. 

Aesculapius designates his healing power, to whom a staff is given as a support for the sick. A serpent is entwined around it as a healthy sign for both soul and body; for among natural things, they say other reptiles are of a coarser and more earthy substance, but they say the serpent is a most keen-sighted animal. It sheds the weakness of its body <note>By sloughing its skin, representing rejuvenation.</note> and seems most perceptive toward medicine. For it is handed down that the serpent discovered an herb for sharpening the sight and knows of a certain herb for reviving the dead. 

The fiery power of the Sun, by which it ripens fruit, is named Dionysius <note>Also known as Bacchus.</note>; but when it completes the seasons of the year by revolving, it is called Horus. Its power by which we receive the fruits of agriculture—being the giver of wealth—is asserted to be Pluto. Since this power also contains a corruptive <note>The decay necessary for new growth.</note> quality, he is said to dwell together with Serapis. They say Cerberus is threefold because there are three regions of the Sun above: Sunrise, Sunset, and Midday. 

They also named the Moon Diana; although she is a virgin, she is nonetheless Lucina <note>The goddess of light and childbirth.</note>, since the power of the new moon contributes not a little to the act of giving birth. Furthermore, what Apollo is in the Sun, Minerva is in the Moon, by which wisdom is designated. Again, the Moon is called Hecate because of the various shapes of its body, which it appears to take based on its distance from the Sun. For its power is threefold. They signify the power of the new moon with white and golden garments and a burning torch. A <term>cista</term> <note>A sacred basket used in ancient mystery cults to hold ritual objects.</note> is designated when it is at the midpoint, since as its light grows, it ripens the crops. They denoted the power of the full moon with a rust color; a golden branch is attributed to it because it becomes fiery from the Sun. The poppy is assigned to it because of fertility and the multitude of souls that inhabit the Moon as if in a city—for the poppy is a symbol of a city. She carries a bow like Diana because the pains of childbirth are sharp. They also say the generative power of fruits, which they call Ceres, dwells with the Moon to increase its power; for the "Good Goddess" <note>Bona Dea, a Roman deity of fertility and healing.</note> is contained within the lunar power. They also attribute Dionysius to the Moon, partly because of the production of "horns" <note>The crescent shapes of the moon.</note> and partly because of the region of the clouds, which lies beneath the Moon. 

Regarding the power of Saturn: because they saw it was a slow and cold power, they attributed the power of Time to it. They depict him as an older man because all things grow old with time. Indeed, we attribute the four seasons of the year partly to the Sun, which is said to open the gates of the air, and partly to Ceres. They carry two baskets: one of flowers, by which spring is signified, and the other of grain-ears, by which summer is signified. 

The power of Mars, because it is fiery and bloody, they set over wars. They say Venus possesses the power of generating, being the cause of seed and desire; she is said to be from the sea because that element is moist and warm, and by frequent motion, it casts out foam—which is a symbol of the generative seed. The power of speech and interpretation they called Mercury, who is fashioned as outstretched and upright because of the vigor of speech, although he also carries the seminal...

-> ### EGYPTIAN STUDIES, CHAPTER XIII <-

And from these diagrams, it is clearly evident that those multiple Gods and Goddesses devised by the mythologists are nothing other than the various virtues <note>In this context, 'virtues' refers to the specific powers, influences, or active properties exerted by a celestial body.</note> of the one Sun or Moon. These powers, produced from the mutual mixing of rays, are diffused into the whole of nature as if drawn from a central point. For by these, whatever this sensible world <note>The physical world that can be perceived through the five senses.</note> contains is supported and sustained. From these comes the distinction of years, months, and other divisions of time. Upon these, all vegetable and sentient life depends. All the theology of the heathens alludes to this Sun and his spouse, the Moon. Indeed, as we have already often mentioned, they learned this from the Egyptians, who were the first of mortals to devise this "architecture of the Gods." They reduced all things to the Sun and the Moon—calling him Osiris and her Isis. Following them, the Chaldaeans established Saturn and Rhea as parallels to Osiris and Isis, attributing all things to them. The Hebrews, imitating these, also established Baal and Ashtoreth <note>original: "Astaroth"</note> side-by-side <note>original Greek: "παραλλήλως" (parallēlōs)</note>. The Phoenicians established Adonis (or Tammuz) and Venus; the Persians, Mithras <note>original: "Mythram"</note> and Anahita <note>original: "Annaitidem"</note>; the Canaanites, Moloch and the aforementioned Venus; the Moabites, Chemosh <note>original: "Chamos"</note> and Baal-Peor <note>original: "Beelphegor"</note>; and the Philistines, Dagon and Atargatis.

However, so that the reader may recognize the differences within such a vast variety of Gods and Goddesses worshiped among diverse nations, it seemed appropriate to attach in this place a certain "parallel representation" of the said deities. This is so that the specific power by which each is distinguished from another, or the points where they agree, may be brought to light. For although—as was seen a little earlier—all Gods and Goddesses may be traced back to one thing (namely, the Sun or the Moon) and are materially one with the Sun, they are nonetheless "Gods" and "Goddesses" because they represent the Sun's various powers and operations. Since these powers provide distinct concepts in our intellect—owing to the specific "formalities" <note>A philosophical term referring to the distinct qualities or aspects of an object that allow it to be categorized in different ways.</note> by which one virtue is distinguished from another—reason certainly dictates that they should by no means be confused. Therefore, lest any confusion arise for the reader, we shall trace all the Gods of the other heathens back to the Egyptian Deities from whom they flowed; we shall do the same for the Goddesses, so that the logic of our dissertation may be more clearly revealed.

# THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK
## BOOK IV.
### HIEROGRAMMATIC IDEAS

-> All things contained in the Pamphilian Obelisk, <-
-> explained separately, and demonstrated from <-
-> every kind of learning. <-

-> P R E F A C E. <-

We call a **Hieroglyphic Idea** the sublime conceptual argument of some great thing. However, a **Symbol**, through which this kind of concept is indicated; if it is simple, we call it a <term>Hierogram <note>From the Greek 'hieros' (sacred) and 'gramma' (letter or character). A single sacred sign.</note></term>; if it is composed of many, we call it a <term>Hierogrammatism <note>A complex arrangement or "sentence" of sacred symbols that conveys a complete doctrine.</note></term>.

Since, therefore, each individual symbol contains hidden doctrines and dogmas founded upon the books of the most obscure writers, it would be difficult for the continuous context of an <term>Ideal Reading <note>original: "Idealis Lectio." A reading based on the underlying philosophical concepts (Ideas) rather than just phonetic sounds.</note></term> of the hieroglyphs to maintain its consistency among such a vast multitude of cited subjects. For this reason, it seemed best to explain those individual **Hierogrammatisms** of greater importance separately. That is, to interpret the "idea" of the doctrine that the ancients signified through each such sacred composition individually, and to prove that interpretation with the most extensive testimonies drawn from every branch of learning. 

We did this with the intention that the reader, while following the literal interpretation of the Obelisk, would not be confused by having the thread of the narrative broken by the sheer number and variety of authorities cited, which might cause the beautiful context of the symbols to be lost. Instead, within the main body of the interpretation, the more long-winded citations have been omitted. The reader is instead referred to these **hierogrammatisms** as if to specific side-paths <note>original: "diverticula," referring to places where one turns aside from a main road for rest or deeper exploration.</note> in which all the underlying reasons for the things explained remain hidden, established by the authority of ancient monuments. In this way, I trusted that the interpretation would be both clearer and more satisfying to the reader. But so that with greater <meta>catchword: method</meta>

BOOK IV. IDEAS

To proceed with a clear method, we shall divide this book as follows: first, we will explain the <term>hierogrammatisms <note>Complex arrangements of sacred symbols conveying a complete doctrine.</note></term> of four-legged animals; second, of birds; third, of insects; fourth, of plants; and fifth, of various figures and instruments. Let us therefore begin from Alpha—that is, from the **Ox**.

# IDEA
### or
## HIEROGRAMMATISM I.
### Regarding the Ox and its hieroglyphic significance.

<margin>Divinity diffused through all things.</margin>
The doctrine of the Egyptian <term>Hieromants <note>Sacred interpreters or priests of the mysteries.</note></term> was handed down by the ancient Patriarchs. Because they recognized that divinity was diffused through all things, they made it their sole business to detect the effects of that divinity which lay hidden in every level and order of natural things and beings. Once detected, they would properly display these effects through suitable symbols drawn from the nature of things. For this reason, they applied their minds to investigating the powers and properties of every living creature. Furthermore, since they were of the opinion that specific <term>Genii <note>In this context, "Genii" refers to guardian spirits or tutelary deities assigned to protect specific places or species.</note></term> were deputed by God to all individual things, they acted with the greatest zeal to learn which Genius's protection governed each class of natural substance. Once this was known, they were certain that they could make that spirit favorable through appropriate symbols, sacrifices, hymns, rites, ceremonies, and purity of life. Once the spirit was won over, they promised themselves every happiness drawn toward them; they believed all evils would be turned away; and they trusted that, by its help, they would obtain a blessed state after the course of this life.

<margin>The purpose of Hieroglyphic doctrine and the worship of living creatures.</margin>
<margin>The Genii of one region are contrary to those of another.</margin>
<margin>Why the Egyptians applied such care to rites and ceremonies.</margin>
And this was the sum and the goal hidden beneath the arcane mysteries of hieroglyphic literature, which they concealed with such zeal and care that they believed it a wicked crime, expiable only by death, to reveal it. For they feared that if they revealed these secrets, the spirits could easily be turned away by rivals <note>original: "Antagonistis"</note> using other contrary rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices. Since they also knew that certain Genii preside over certain regions, under whose protection everything in that region falls, and they believed these were opposed to the presiding spirits of other regions, they only adopted the living creatures of the Egyptian land for the use of sacred magic. They feared that by adopting animals from another region—whose nature they did not know—they might commit an error in appeasing the Genii and invite their indignation rather than their goodwill. They considered it of such importance to be occupied with the greatest care and most exact industry in sacrifices, rites, and ceremonies, that they believed if even a single circumstance were omitted, their entire intention would be rendered void. Instructed by this, the ancient Romans concealed the name of their tutelary genius with such zeal that they considered revealing it a crime to be punished by death. But these things having been briefly introduced, let us now see how each animal of Egypt...

<meta>This page follows the introduction to Book IV, where the author began his specific analysis of animal symbols. Having established that the Egyptians sought the divine in the natural world, he now turns to the most prominent symbol in their system: the Ox.</meta>

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>HIEROGLYPHICS.</header>

Let us see what symbols they expressed, with what icons they adorned them, and what they signified through each individual mark, beginning with the Ox. They call this creature now *Alpha*, now <image-desc>hieroglyphic symbol of a bull's head (aleph)</image-desc> <note>original: "Aleph"</note>, which in the Coptic language means the same as "great"—that is, the Ox—representing the greatest of the Gods and the very beginning of things.

<margin>Why did the Ox hold the first place among living creatures?</margin>
Since, according to the testimony of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop.</note>, the Egyptians worshipped it with the greatest veneration of all, it was from the Ox that the greatest benefits flowed to them. Those benefits consisted of an unfailing supply of the things necessary for sustaining life and living well and happily. Since agriculture provided all these things, and agriculture could not be accomplished without the Ox, ancient antiquity adopted the Ox as a symbol of the beneficent Deity <note>original: "benefici Numinis"</note>. This was done to such an extent that they established the Ox as the first of all things, dedicating the first letter of the alphabet to it and naming it *Alpha* after its name.

<margin>Why was the Ox called Alpha?</margin>
Thus Plutarch writes in Book 9 of his *Table Talk*, Question 3: <note>original: "Καδμὸν φασὶ τὸ ἄλφα πάντων προτάξαι διὰ τὸ τοὺς Φοίνικας οὕτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν, οὐ δεύτερον, οὔτε τρίτον (ὥσπερ Ἡσίοδος) ἀλλὰ πρῶτον τῶν ἀναγκαίων"</note> "They say that Cadmus placed Alpha first of all because the Phoenicians call the ox by this name; they consider it not the second or third of necessary things (as Hesiod did), but the very first." The Phoenician term is <term>Bôc <note>A phonetic rendering of a Phoenician or Semitic word for cattle.</note></term>.

<margin>From where did the Greeks get Alpha as their first letter?</margin>
For, as the Chaldean dictionary <note>original: "onomasticon"</note> of Masius <note>Andreas Masius, a 16th-century scholar of Near Eastern languages.</note> rightly teaches, the word <term>אלוף <gloss>Aluph</gloss></term> signifies not only a teacher, master, leader, or prince, but also an Ox; from this, the Greeks later borrowed <term>Alpha</term> as the first letter of their alphabet.

<margin>The Deity appears to men in the form of an Ox and instructs them.</margin>
Furthermore, since they held by tradition that Divinity manifested singular effects in individual living creatures, and since divine benefits shone forth most greatly in the Ox—being granted for the sustenance of human life through the cultivation of the fields—they believed that God appeared to men under the form of an Ox. They believed He taught them the proper method of cultivating the fields and handed down other things necessary for sustaining life.

For this reason, they observed its natural dispositions and inclinations with the greatest study, calling these the "nods and wonders of God." Yet they did not grant this honor to every ox indiscriminately, but only to those distinguished by peculiar marks, signs, color, and wonders, which served as messengers of the hidden Divinity.

<margin>How many and what were the signs of the Ox worshipped with divine honors?</margin>
They observed a total of twenty-nine signs. First, if the cow was conceived by a flash of light <note>An ancient belief that the sacred Apis bull was conceived by a bolt of lightning or lunar light.</note>. Second, if it was moved by the praises and hymns of children. Third, if a gift of prophecy followed from the aforementioned praises among the children. Fourth, if it portended dire or prosperous events by whether it took food from the hand of those offering it or turned away. Fifth, if during the seven days of the birth of <term>Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, a physical manifestation of the god Ptah or Osiris.</note></term> no one was touched by crocodiles. Sixth, if it expressed a shape near its horns like the crescent of the Moon. Seventh, if it had a knot under its tongue, which they called a "scarab" or "beetle" <note>This "cantharus" or knot under the tongue was a primary identifying mark of the Apis bull.</note>. Eighth, if it had bright, round eyes emitting the form of rays. Ninth, if it had a white spot on its right side. Tenth, if it had the figure of an eagle on its back. Eleventh, if its entire body was otherwise black. Twelfth, if it had a square-shaped spot on its forehead. Thirteenth, if it had double hairs on its tail. Fourteenth, if it had very large testicles, swollen and full of seed. Fifteenth, if its mouth was frequently turned toward the rising or setting [sun]...

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...should he move with his mouth gaping. Sixteenth, if he could predict the future. Seventeenth, if he possessed a tail and a whole body with hairs slanting in the opposite direction from how they grow on other oxen. Finally, if he were marked across the rest of his body with a notable distinction of twelve spots; for through these they denoted the powers of the stars, and they assigned each one to one of the twelve greater Spirits <term>Genii: in this context, protective or guiding deities presiding over the world</term> of the universe. Thus, it was necessary that he consist of twenty-nine signs in total, which is exactly the number of days the Moon spends completing its cycle through the Zodiac. But lest we seem to have fabricated anything on our own authority, it is now time to bring forward the testimony of individual authors.

<margin>Plutarch</margin>
First, Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and historian (c. 46 – 120 AD) famous for his "Parallel Lives" and "Moralia."</note> describes at length in his book *On Isis and Osiris*—which the reader can consult, as it is frequently cited in various places of this work—that Osiris and Isis, whom the Egyptians say are eternal Gods and equate with the Sun and Moon, were worshipped under the form of a Bull and a Cow respectively, because of the benefit they brought to agriculture. They believed the gods appeared to the first humans in these forms.

<margin>Aelian</margin>
Furthermore, Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author and teacher of rhetoric known for his works on natural history.</note> teaches that the Ox was distinguished by various signs as indications of a hidden divinity, using these words:

<margin>Who was Apis, and why was he worshipped in the form of an Ox?</margin>
"Apis," he says, "is believed by the Egyptians to be a most powerful God. He is born from a cow that conceived when struck by lightning. The Greeks call him Epaphus, and tracing back the ancient lineage of this race, they testify that Io of Argos, daughter of Inachus, was his mother." But the Egyptians reject this story as a lie, citing the vast span of time as witness;

<margin>Herodotus and Aristagoras</margin>
"For they say Epaphus lived many centuries later. But they say Apis first came among men many thousands of years ago." Herodotus and Aristagoras explain his remarkable markings. "However, the Egyptians do not agree with them, but teach that there are twenty-nine marks suitable and appropriate for this sacred Bull. What these are, how they are scattered across the body, and how he is adorned by them as if by flowers, must be understood from other sources." The Egyptians declare more than sufficiently which nature of the stars each mark signifies through these signs. "For they say one mark signifies the rising of the Nile; and that other marks have meanings for other things, which are certainly not easy to understand for the uninitiated <note>original: "prophanis"</note> and those unskilled in Divine history." And a little later: "Now, it would be a long task to explore what processions and sacrifices the Egyptians perform, celebrating both the arrival of the new flood and the rising of the God, as well as what dances they perform then, what assemblies they hold, and how all the cities and men rejoice immortally."

<margin>The quality of the ox to be worshipped</margin>
"That man, from whose herd this divine beast arose, is considered blessed and held in the highest admiration by the Egyptians." This Ox possesses the power of foreknowledge. Even children, stirred by a divine inspiration while playing outside and dancing together in rhythm, predict future events to those who consult them. Thus says Aelian.

<margin>Pliny</margin>
Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the monumental "Natural History" in the 1st century AD.</note> in Book 8, Chapter 46, agrees with these points in these words: "The Ox," he says, "is even worshipped in place of a Deity in Egypt. They call him Apis."

<margin>The spots of the Ox</margin>
"His mark is a white spot on the right side, shaped like the horns of the moon when it begins to wax. There is a knot under his tongue, which they call a *cantharus* <note>original: "cantharum," referring to a beetle or a cup; here describing a specific physical growth under the tongue.</note>. And a little later: He has twin shrines, which they call chambers <note>original: "thalamos"</note>, which serve as omens for the people; to have entered one is joyful, but in the other he portends dire things; he gives answers to private individuals by taking food from the hands of those consulting him."

<margin>When Apis turned away from the hand of Germanicus Caesar, what did it portend?</margin>
"He turned away from the hand of Germanicus Caesar <note>A beloved Roman general and nephew of Emperor Tiberius.</note>, who died not long afterward. Furthermore, when he rushes out from his seclusion into the crowds, he walks with a flock of attendants..."

### HIEROGLYPHICA.

...and is accompanied by the song of boys singing in his honor, which he seems to understand and desires to be adored. These herds, suddenly seized by a divine frenzy <note>original: "lymphati"—often implying a state of prophetic madness or inspiration</note>, predict future events. During the seven days of Apis’s birth, they submerge a golden and a silver bowl in the place called the *phiala* <note>A Greek term for a shallow bowl or, in this context, a specific sacred pool or vessel</note>. It is a marvel that during these days no one is touched by crocodiles, but on the eighth day, after the sixth hour, the ferocity of the beasts returns. <margin>Porphyry.</margin> These things are consistent with what is read in Porphyry, in his book *On Abstinence*. "Furthermore," he says, "the Egyptians dedicated a bull to the Moon, which they call Apis, which is blacker than others and carries signs of the Sun and Moon; moreover, the Moon borrows light from the Sun. The blackness of the color is a symbol of the Sun, for the Sun’s heat makes human bodies darker; and the beetle <note>The scarab beetle</note> which is under his tongue represents the division of the Moon’s color." <margin>St. Augustine.</margin> How so many and such great signs could be found in an ox is beautifully shown by Saint Augustine in Book 18 of *The City of God*, Chapter 5, in these words: "That bull, however, which a deceived Egypt nourished in the midst of flowing luxuries in his honor, because they worshipped him alive without a sarcophagus, was called Apis, not Serapis. <margin>How it happened that the ox was distinguished by so many marks.</margin> When that ox died, because a calf of the same color was sought and found—that is, marked similarly with certain white spots—they believed it to be a marvelous thing and divinely provided. For it was no great thing for Demons, in order to deceive them, to show a phantasm of such a bull to a cow at the moment of conception and while pregnant, so that the mother’s desire might attract that which would then appear physically in her offspring. This is just as Jacob brought about with the variegated rods, so that sheep and goats would be born speckled; for what men can do with real colors and bodies, Demons can easily exhibit to conceiving animals by means of fabricated images." Thus far Saint Augustine. Now, let us reveal what the Egyptians indicated through the hieroglyphic Ox.

---

<margin>The Hieroglyphs of the Ox and their meaning.</margin>
Since it was not possible to denote the beneficial generosity of the divine Power and its inaccessible and invisible essence by any physical thing, they sketched it through the image of the "sensible God"—for so they called the Sun—just as they represented the power of the lunar Deity through a cow marked with similar spots. <margin>The ox spotted with different marks denotes the different effects of the Sun.</margin> Since they furthermore found various properties of the Sun in the ox through certain hidden signs, they treated the ox as a living receptacle of the solar Deity, in which the deity might teach men through the signs appropriated to itself and instruct them in the use of necessary things. Certainly, through the individual signs narrated a little while ago, they denoted nothing other than the various effects of the Sun upon the earth—that is, upon Isis. What else are the horns but the rays of the Sun? <margin>The image of Osiris.</margin> What is the beetle under the tongue but the solar Deity, and to speak with Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Greek historian and bishop</note>, "the living animal is the image of Osiris" <note>original Greek: ζῶον τὸ Ὀσείριδος ἄγαλμα</note>? That it lies hidden under the tongue, what else does it mean but that the said Deity teaches various things necessary to the human race, as if conversing with men? What is the figure of the eagle on the back (or as I, following the mind of the Egyptians, would more truly interpret it, a hawk with outstretched wings shadowing the back of the ox) but that penetrative power of the universal Deity, the nourisher of all animals? As will be discussed later in the hierogram of the hawk. <margin>Interpretation of the symbols of the ox.</margin> What is that blackness mixed with whiteness, by which the whole body of the ox is varied, but the alternation of days and nights, without which the generation of things cannot be completed? What are the hairs of two colors in the tail, but the "posterior parts" of the Deity—that is, the sensible effects which the said solar Deity displays to the world? What, finally...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Apis bull’s physical markings and their supernatural significance. ### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>
The origin of the Egyptians' divinatory science.
</margin>
...and what are those white spots flashing out from the black, if not the principal powers of the stars in the firmament? These powers the Sun exerts while it traverses the twelve dwellings of the sensible Gods <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>. What is the reason for presaging in the ox, if not the mantic or divinatory power in the Sun? Through the powers of the Divinity acting within the bull, they clearly foretold the events of future things: namely, the future rising of the Nile, the fertility or sterility of the year, and similar occurrences and signs portending prosperity or doom. From this proceeded that famous Egyptian *manteia* <note>original Greek: μαντεία; meaning divination</note> or divinatory science and *oneiromancy* <note>The interpretation of dreams</note>.

<margin>
What the bull licking the cloak of Eudoxus portended.
</margin>
Hence, if the bull with an open mouth looked toward Boreas <note>The North Wind</note>, the left part of the world, they interpreted it as a doubtful outcome for affairs. Conversely, they interpreted the kind reception of offered fodder as the favor of a benevolent Divinity; on the other hand, the refusal of the same was a sign of an angry Divinity. Because of this, when a bull is said to have licked the cloak of the philosopher Eudoxus, the Egyptians reckoned he would be a great man. Laertius shows this in the following epigram:

<margin>
Laertius.
</margin>
> From a horned bull to predict his own fate,
> Fame says Eudoxus once did in the city of Memphis:
> But because nature denied speech to the calf,
> It said nothing; licking his robe, it did what it wished. <note>Suggesting the bull communicated its prophecy through the gesture since it could not speak.</note>

<margin>
From where the name Serapis is derived.
</margin>
Furthermore, from this source the ridiculous rites and ceremonies used in the sacrifices of the bulls and the Mithraic mysteries <note>Ancient mystery cult centered on the god Mithras, often involving bull sacrifice</note>—instituted for the appeasement of an angry Divinity—found their first origin. For a copious treatment of these, consult Herodotus in *Euterpe* <note>Book II of Herodotus's Histories</note>. From this comes that solemn allegory of the Egyptians concerning Osiris being cast into a chest, whom after this event they called Serapis. *Sorapis* <note>original: σωραπις</note>, that is, Serapis. For, as we have interpreted in our Coptic Dictionary, *Sora* is the same as "chest," and *pios* is truly the same as "lord," as if you were to say, "Lord of the Chest." St. Augustine beautifully teaches this in Book 18 of *The City of God*, Chapter 5. ...if a line were to cross through the eyes, it expressed the figure of a Cross; moreover, the horns twisted into a circle perfectly expressed that "handled" Cross <note>original: *anſatam illam Crucem*; also known as the Ankh</note>, or the Tautic character. This is what Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher for Egyptian lore</note> suggests. However, this character was not found except on an Apis bull marked with twenty-nine signs, among which the said character was the sole indicator of the hidden divinity. It was seen impressed upon the forehead of the Deity to show that it is the most mysterious of all characters and, with the Deity as the teacher, a most perfect prophylactic <note>A protective charm or preventative measure</note> against the ferocity of all evils. But more on this sacred symbol <note>original: *hierogrammate*</note> at length in its proper place.

<margin><image-desc>A marginal symbol of the "ansated cross" or Tautic character, consisting of a 'T' shape topped with a circular loop.</image-desc></margin>

<margin>Two bulls were worshipped by the Egyptians: one consecrated to the Sun, the other to the Moon. Plutarch, Eusebius, Strabo, Ammianus Marcellinus.</margin>
With these matters thus duly set forth, we shall now introduce the hieroglyphics by which the Priests of the Mysteries <note>original: *Hieromyſtæ*</note> represented the sacred Bull; for from these, everything said thus far will become clearer. The Egyptians worshipped two bulls with special honor above all other living creatures. The first of these they consecrated to Osiris, or the Solar Deity; the second to Isis, that is, the lunar Deity. So says Plutarch in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, Eusebius in Book 3, Chapter 3, Strabo in Book 17, and Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 22. Since we have treated these elsewhere, as well as at length in the third book, we refer the Reader there. The first bull, prefigured by various signs and symbols, they displayed in this engraving <note>original: *ectypo*</note>.

->*Figure of Apis according to the signs by which the Ancient Writers described him.*<-

The Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet from antiquity depicting Egyptian motifs, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note> shows both bulls adorned with these symbols; there you see two asps <note>Egyptian cobras or *uraei*</note> enclosed in a circle placed between the horns, to indicate the power of the fiery Deity poured into the Sun and the Earth. The bull is a symbol of both, indicating the presence of the Deity working in secret, and for that reason, he was also called Osiris.

The other bull was consecrated to the Moon, or to Isis, and was black-and-white <note>original: *μελανόλευκος*</note>, or marked with black and white patches, by which the variation of light and shadows on the Moon was indicated. The horns, meeting to form a circle with a small flame rising in the middle, denote a certain hidden fiery power in the Moon, by which the lower things <note>The terrestrial or earthly realm</note> are most highly fertilized. This is quite aptly indicated by the "witnesses" <note>original: *testes*; Kircher is likely following Plutarch’s reference to the generative organs as symbols of fertility</note> hanging from the neck which are, according to the testimony of Plutarch, the "hot and moist witnesses of Osiris"—that is, of a Solar-Lunar nature. Through these, Isis (or the Moon, or the Earth) is rendered wonderfully fruitful and fertile.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

### Explanation of the Bull

A. The ray of the Sun represented by the horns.
B. The year represented by the square spot.
C. The beneficial power of the Solar Deity represented by the scarab <note>The dung beetle, a symbol of the sun and self-creation</note> under the tongue, through which He teaches men things that lead to their well-being.
D. The power of the Lunar-Solar influence received through the Ibis, which is transformed with the wings of a hawk.
E. The fertilizing power represented by the testicles.
F. The alternation of days and nights represented by the white and bright hairs.

<column-break/>

G. The contrary movement of the Sun represented by the opposing direction of the hairs; the twelve Deities who preside over as many stars are represented by the twelve white spots shining out from the black background.
Indeed, the entire Bull denotes the Earth, upon which the Sun exerts its power.

---

And you will find him described with almost these same symbols on the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous Roman-era bronze tablet with Egyptian motifs, also known as the Mensa Isiaca, which Kircher studied extensively</note>. We reserve its full interpretation for other sections. All the things the Greeks imagined about this Bull agree with this, for they borrowed everything from the Egyptians. You may see the story fully described in Ovid: Jupiter, pining for Io, the daughter of the Argive King Inachus, because of her elegant beauty, detained and overwhelmed her as she was returning from the river Inachus. Juno, however, driven by her husband's jealousy, when she saw the darkness from on high, descended to the earth and dissolved the shadows. <margin>Physical explanation of the fable of the girl transformed into a cow by Juno <note>The original Latin text attributes the transformation to Juno in this margin note, though the narrative correctly identifies Jupiter as the one who changed Io to hide his crime.</note></margin> Jupiter, sensing this, so that the crime might not be revealed, granted the girl—now transformed into a Cow—to Juno; she handed her over to the hundred-eyed Argus to be guarded. Mercury, sent by Jupiter, killed the sleeping Argus. Juno, grieving, sent a gadfly <note>original: *oestrum*</note> to the Cow, by which she was driven through many places, eventually coming to Egypt. There, restored to her original form and called Isis by the Egyptians, she married King Osiris and attained divine honors.

In this mythical narrative, whether the Egyptians or the Greeks had the nature of physical things in mind, I show it thus: From Plutarch and other cited authors, it is clear that Io—whether she signifies Isis, the daughter of Inachus, or Neptune—sometimes signified the Moon, and sometimes the Earth; for to those standing far off, the Earth seems to rise gradually from the waves. Jupiter embraced her in a cloud—that is, the ethereal Sun drawing up and generating vapors. He changed Io into a cow, an animal devoted to the fertility of the earth, whose entire industry is spent in cultivating fields for the sake of the earth's own abundance. Jupiter granted the cow to Juno—that is, to the milder heat of the air—since the earth becomes fertile neither through excessive heat nor intense cold. Juno gave the cow to Argus to guard. What else is the hundred-eyed Argus but the starry sky? By its influence, it cherishes the earth and uniquely promotes fertility. Of these stars, or "eyes," one part sleeps while the other watches. The lower hemisphere watches, bright with twinkling stars like open eyes; the upper part sleeps, with the stars covered and obscured by the brilliance of the Sun. But why did Jupiter command Mercury to kill Argus? Because, clearly, reason <note>Represented here by Mercury, the god of intellect and communication</note> is of the greatest power in Agriculture. For this cow is said to have been liberated after Argus was slain, and to have traveled the whole world and swam across all the seas, because the prudence and industry of Farmers seems to overcome even the goodness of the air or for-

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>The origin of agriculture.</margin>
...fortune overcomes malice, since the earth becomes most fertile through the industry of farmers. This same principle of agriculture, spread to all lands, finally reached Egypt. Because that land, through its fruitfulness and goodness, most clearly reveals the power of nature and its abundance, it was called the "Cow," and there it recovered its former shape. 

<margin>Relating to the fable of the Moon.</margin>
They applied this fable to the Moon in this way: they say Isis, the daughter of Neptune, is the same as the Moon, moistening all things with the dampness of nighttime light. She is "compressed" by Jupiter in a cloud because, during the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, mists and clouds are usually generated. Soon Io is changed into a Cow, since the Moon almost always emerges "horned" <note>Referring to the crescent moon</note> on the third day after the conjunction, mimicking the horns of a Cow; indeed, it was said that unless she freed herself from the clouds and stood in the open air before the fourth day, she would portend rain for the entire month. Juno receives her after she emerges from the clouds after the conjunction and hands her over to be guarded by Argus, because the Moon is lower than all the other stars, by which she is looked down upon. Argus is killed by Jupiter's command, and the Cow is freed from Argus, because when the Sun imparts light and strength to the Moon, she overcomes the powers of all the stars through the influences she exerts on human bodies while she waxes. She traverses the circle of the earth, returning now to the Northern region of Scythia, now to the Southern region of Egypt, to demonstrate the Moon’s monthly motion between the tropics. But since I have interpreted these things more extensively in the *Mystagogic* <note>Original: "Mystagogico," referring to the "Mystagogia Hieroglyphica," a section of Kircher's work where he leads the reader through the "mysteries" of symbols</note> section of the third book, I have judged it unnecessary to dwell on them any longer.

<margin>Ethical exposition of the fable.</margin>
Furthermore, the said fable can be transferred to moral behavior through the same analogy. Indeed, they explain the secrets of Divinity hidden under this hieroglyphic in this way: By the Bull, they denoted the earthly and material body. By the horns shaped into a circle, between which an asp <note>The uraeus or sacred cobra, symbol of sovereignty</note> raises its head—as appears on the Bembine Tablet—they denoted the eternal and hidden divinity permeating all things by the virtue and efficacy of its rays. By the "Tautic" character <note>A symbol resembling the letter T or a cross, which Kircher associated with the Egyptian Thoth/Mercury and the concept of "right reason"</note>, the mark on the forehead of Mercury, they denoted the dictates of right reason impressed upon man, with which he might arm himself against all incursions of evil, while a hidden Deity confers various necessary aids for the use of human life. By the figure of the hawk spread across the back, they denoted the impulse of the divine mind surveying all things, and the presence and protection of providence over all, indicated by the expansion of the wings. By the scarab hiding under the tongue, they denoted the operations of the Solar Deity which he carries out for the benefit of men in the earthly world, marked by a certain hidden speech impressed upon the things of nature through the tongue under which the scarab hides. By the black and white, they beautifully designate the presence of divinity in things—partly obscure, partly manifest in its effects, just like the "back parts" of God <note>A biblical reference to Exodus 33:23, implying that man can only see the effects of God's presence, not His face</note>. 

<margin>Exposition of the spots of Apis.</margin>
This is also shown through the tail of the bull which is *blackened* <note>original: αποµελασιν (apomelasin), meaning to turn black or be marked with black</note>, that is, distinguished by black and white hairs. By the white spots, they signaled the twelve principal rays of the supreme Deity, which are like the messengers of divinity—whom they called Geniuses <note>Spiritual beings or guiding spirits</note>—dispersed throughout the entire mass of the earthly world to perpetually bedew, nourish, and preserve it with their influences.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

...Indeed, they did not only fashion this ideal concept of divinity under the form of the sacred bull, but they also solicited that Numen <note>original: *Numen* — a Latin term for a divine power or presiding spirit</note> to be drawn to them—whether by words or by analogous sacrifices—through a type of prayer formula established according to the analogy of these signs. They called these formulas "ancient hymns," and believed them to be of such efficacy that, merely by reciting them, they could obtain whatever they sought. They believed they could make the Numen present and familiar to themselves through this kind of magical incitement. We shall present hymns composed from such hieroglyphs elsewhere. And although the ancient philosophers, thinking rightly about the divine essence, judged that nothing of material things could be attributed to it, they nevertheless used sensible symbols of this kind to exhibit the virtues and mysteries of God shining forth in their effects through perceptible signs. To this end, that oracle of Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster was the legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many mystical "Oracles" were attributed in the Renaissance</note> appears to look toward this, as found in the works of Psellus and Phlegon:

<margin>The Oracle of Zoroaster.</margin>
*Do not call the sun a visible image of nature, for the form of nature is not entirely intelligible,* <note>original: *Μὴ φύσεως καλέσης αὐτόπτον ἄγαλμα τὸ ☉ τῆς φύσεως μόρφωμα, ἐκ ἔστ' παντάπασι νοητὸν*</note> that is, *Do not call it the image of nature, which is to say, do not seek to gaze upon the image of nature, for the form of nature is not everywhere knowable,* as Phlegon explains, but is something placed beyond human sight. For those things used by those performing sacred rites—such as fire, lightning, or anything else of this kind—you should safely believe to be only bare symbols, not the nature of God. But later generations, because they 

<margin>Whence the idolatry of the Bull, and how was it spread?</margin>
could not reach the lofty description of divinity with their intellect, fell back upon sensible things and lapsed into manifest idolatry. Hence that celebrated "bull-worship" <note>original: *βυλατρεία* (bulatreia)</note> among the Egyptians, or rather, the madness of the bovine cult, took on such great increases in a short time that, unable to be contained within the borders of Egypt, it first invaded the minds of the Hebrews in the desert, then in the course of time Palestine and the minds of the Kings of Israel, and also Greece and the western part of the world, Rome, and finally the whole world. Thus, even to this day, the foolishness of the bovine or cow cult is found to endure in almost the whole of India. Since this has been demonstrated most extensively in my *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher’s own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, we refer the reader there.

The Egyptians were also accustomed to signify a mas-

<margin>Another meaning of the Bull.</margin>
culine mind, prudent and moderate, through the bare figure of a bull. Thus Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> says in Book 1, Hieroglyph 46: *To indicate courage joined with temperance, they paint a Bull endowed with a healthy constitution.* <note>original: *Ἀνδρεῖον δὲ μετὰ σωφροσύνης δηλῶντες, ταῦρον ὑγιᾶ φύσιν ἔχοντα ζωογραφᾶσι.*</note> And a little later: *Moreover, it is temperate, because it never mounts the female after she has conceived.* <note>original: *ἀλλὰ καὶ σώφρων ἐστὶ, διὰ τὸ μηδέποτε τῷ θήλεος ἐπιβαίνειν τὴν σύλληψιν.*</note> Furthermore, they indicated specific powers through different members of the bull; 

<margin>What the individual members of the Bull signify.</margin>
through the head, they signified the descent of the Solar Numen <note>The divine power of the Sun</note> onto the earth with a strengthening power that solidifies it; through the feet, however, they signified the movement of the Solar Numen through all parts of the earth. Thus says Abenephi: <note>Abenephi is the name Kircher used for Ibn Wahshiyya, an Arabic author he believed held the secrets of ancient Egypt</note>

> ودر اس الثور كان يدلون النزول الملك الشمس ودر حركة الهيوجه بكل جزو الارض

*And they were signifying through the head the downward flow of the solar Genius upon the earth; through the feet, movement and agitation through all parts of the earth.* When denoting an effect or a work performed, Horus testifies: *The drawing of a horn of a male bull signifies work,* <note>original: *Βοὸς ἄῤῥενος κέρας γραφόμενον, ἔργον σημαίνει*</note> in Book 2, Hieroglyph 17. Abenephi adds, moreover, that through the Bull they secretly signified royal offspring.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

Through the *figure of the Bull*, they also designated—<note>original Arabic: بصورة الثور كان يدلّون النسل الملوكي — "In the form of the bull, they used to signify royal offspring"</note>—royal progeny. How this is to be understood remains to be explained, so that the skill of the wise in constructing sacred symbols <term>hierogrammatis (sacred symbols)</term> may be apparent. <margin>Bees are born from the Bull</margin> The Egyptians observed, therefore, I know not what hidden sympathy between bees and oxen; they noted that the bee has its origin from no other source than from cattle. Archelaus also beautifully indicates this in an epigram with these words: *Children created from a dead bull* <note>original Greek: *Βοὸς φθιμένης πεποιημένα τέκνα*</note>, that is, *bees are the offspring of a putrefied bull*. On the testimony of Varro, Pliny, and Virgil, it is well-established that bees are born not only from bovine dung, but also from its decaying body. They say that in Egypt there are certain places where, if a bull is buried so that only the horns project above the ground and are then sawn off, bees will fly out; for the bull is changed by rot into that little animal. Hence they are called *Bull-children* and *Bull-born* <note>original Greek: *Βουπαῖδες Βουγενεῖς*</note> by the Greeks; indeed, Phyletas (as cited in Antigonus) calls bees "Bull-born."

->You approached the bull-born bees from afar, having spoken thus.<-

Ovid also describes their origin <term>Genesis (origin/birth)</term> quite elegantly in these words:
<margin>Metamorphoses, Book 15</margin>
> Do you not see that whatever bodies rot
> From time and fluid heat, are turned into small animals?
> Go, bury also chosen slaughtered bulls
> (A thing known by sight); from the rotting viscera everywhere
> Flower-gathering bees are born, which in the manner of their parents
> Dwell in the countryside, favor work, and labor in hope.

<margin>As bulls produce bees, so bees generate something bovine</margin> Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, likely Ibn Wahshiyya or a similar Hermetic source</note> adds that there is not only a remarkable sympathy between the bull and the bee, but even as bulls generate bees from themselves, so bees bring forth something bovine. I first understood this when I happened upon that wonderful history of bees by Bernardino Gomez <note>Bernardino Gómez Miedes (c. 1515–1589), a Spanish historian and cleric</note>, whose words I shall place here. <margin>A rare story</margin>
> While I was spending time near the beehives in Saguntum <note>A city in Spain</note> for the sake of recreation, I greatly marveled at their singular works—especially the obedience and kindness of the drones, and the nursery of bees enclosed within them, which alone led me into great admiration. For I shall relate a new thing, unheard of and unseen until now, nor recorded by any writer to my knowledge. For when a drone captured by me was pressed between my fingers and middle nail, to see if perhaps it might emit something in place of a sting, behold—its viscera being ruptured and the skin of its posterior part broken—the white or saffron-colored head of a Bull suddenly emerged, skillfully formed with outspread and twisting horns and a hooked snout. Those who were present marveled greatly at this; and because they demanded to try it again for themselves, five other drones were subsequently pressed by me, and just as many bull heads erupted at once. Nature—in whom, rightly, the greatest care resides—exercises in this portent the seminal logic of the bees and a certain friendship with bulls.

Thus far Bernardino Gomez. Certainly, when I had read these things, stimulated by the desire for a most curious experiment, I too made a trial with drones; and what I at first marveled at as a paradox, I finally knew to be most certain. For I found I know not what bovine thing generated within the viscera of the drone; which all [students] of natural things...

### HIEROGLYPHICS.

I would like it to be noted by researchers that since this was by no means hidden from the first Egyptian sages, they quite beautifully and ingeniously—on the testimony of Abenephius—indicated royal progeny by depicting a bull. <margin>Horapollo.</margin> Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a famous 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> in Book 1, chapter 62, confirms this with his own assessment: *To show a people obedient to a king, they draw a bee; for alone among all other living creatures, these have a King, whom the rest of the multitude of bees follows, just as men obey a King. They also suggest obscurely, both from the remarkable utility of the honey and from the power the creature has in its sting, that a King should be both beneficial and powerful in his actions and governance.* <note>original Greek: λαὸν πρὸς βασιλέα πειθήνιον δηλοῦντες μέλισσαν ζωγραφοῦσι... (“indicating a people obedient to a king, they paint a bee...”)</note> <margin>Symbols placed between the bovine horns of Isis</margin> Therefore, a bull with a bee painted between its horns beautifully designates royal progeny. From this, I believe, arose that hieroglyphic by which they denote that Isis was of the royal family: through bovine horns between which we learn from the <term>Bembine Tablet (an elaborate bronze altar-top featuring Egyptian-style motifs)</term> that sometimes a scarab, sometimes a bee, sometimes a Phallus, and sometimes a star or similar object is placed, all of which will be demonstrated precisely in their proper place.

It is thus clear that the bovine species was always held in great honor because of its <margin>The Bull as a symbol of agriculture.</margin> utility and the benefits providing for the human race. The bull was also a common symbol not only of agriculture or the things that successfully arise from it—such as the abundance of grain and offspring—but even of the Great Mother Earth herself, the nurse of all living things. The Greeks call her blessed and propitious cultivation <term>bebaion (firm or steady)</term> <note>original Greek: βέβαιον</note> after the bull, and they are accustomed to signify this with the figure of a fat bull, whose tail did not end in hair, but in ears of grain. Such a likeness is found in that image common throughout Rome: the figure of a Bull upon whose back the Unconquered Sun Mithras, the God of the Persians (for so Dionysus was called there), sits prostrate and pierces the chest with a dagger. <margin>Physical interpretation of the imagery.</margin> By this <term>anagoge (a spiritual or mystical interpretation)</term>, they seem to indicate that when the Sun climbs into the sign of Taurus in the month of April, it opens the swelling earth and brings its genital seeds into the open by the rays of its heat for the procreation and nourishment of all living things. When the Sun again declines and passes into Scorpio in the month of October, it hides these same seeds, their strength lost, back in the inner chambers of the earth because of the cold. This is demonstrated by the Scorpion clasping the Bull's testicles. Now, the two animals—namely the Serpent and the Dog—which lick the drops of blood flowing from the Bull’s wound, signify that both aquatic and terrestrial creatures sustain their lives through the nutrients born of the earth. Thus, following the Egyptians beautifully and with their remarkable hieroglyphic <margin>The utility of the Bull</margin> interpretation, the Persians designated the power and efficacy of the Sun working upon the earth. Consequently, among all nations thereafter, the bull was assumed as a symbol of the fertile earth and of agriculture, two things which promote and sustain life. No more proper or fitting paradigm could be applied here; for the bull, as was shown a little earlier, once its living body is extinguished, not only provides nourishment but even in its death generates many thousands of lives, as Ovid elegantly sings from the oracle of Proteus:

# HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>What does the bull with a human face signify?</margin>
<margin>A political explanation of the symbols of the Bull.</margin>
From this, the ancient Romans, instructed by the Egyptians, marked their coins with a bull graced with an elderly human face, with spreading and short horns, and a countenance moreover displaying something of a Jovian <note>Like Jupiter, signifying majesty and authority.</note> quality. By this they wished to imply the praised state of their City and Republic, whose "head"—as if it were a certain council and Senate of reason—was not accustomed to refuse the yoke of justice; while the rest of the "body," the people who are strong for work, did not labor for themselves so much as for the Republic, being devoted to peace and agriculture. The Ancients usually added certain <term>pererga</term> <note>original: "pererga"; decorative or subordinate additions to a work of art.</note> belonging to the same argument; as can be seen on the coin of the Cellenoi described by Winandus Pighius <note>Stephanus Winandus Pighius (1520–1604) was a Dutch antiquarian famous for his studies of Roman coins and history.</note>, in which a lyre is placed above the bull, signifying the equity of the laws and the harmony of the social orders. On the side, the head of the unshorn Apollo stands out, his hair flowing gracefully down his neck under a laurel; such as Orpheus calls <term>Akersekomēn</term> <note>Greek: Α'κερσε-κόμην; "with unshorn hair," a common epithet for Apollo signifying eternal youth.</note> and Pindar calls <term>akeirekomēn kai eutomon</term> <note>Greek: ἀκειρεκόμην καὶ εὔτομον; "unshorn and well-trimmed."</note>, as if he were maned without a haircut. By these epithets, those leaders of the poets most elegantly described the radiance and rays of the Sun, which temper the elements and promote all the fruits of the earth with a vital spark; they also wished to signify the agitation and fiery motion of the divine light that illuminates human minds and propels them toward the works of reason. They named him Apollo, or <term>Phœbus</term> <note>Greek: Φοῖβον; "The Radiant One."</note>, who was so called <margin>The etymology of Phœbus.</margin> <term>from light and life</term> <note>Greek: παρὰ τὸ φῶς καὶ βίος (para to phos kai bios); an ancient etymological theory linking the name Phœbus to the Greek words for light and life.</note>, because he seems to bestow light to minds and life to all living things, for which reason he was called the <term>life-giver</term> <note>Greek: βιοδότης (biodotēs).</note> in sacred hymns. This is why the shepherd <term>Nomius</term> <note>Latin: "Nomius"; a title for Apollo as a god of pastures and shepherds.</note>, mentioned in Virgil, is imagined to pasture the bulls while, by striking his lyre, he leads the dances of the Muses, tempers the movement of the heavens with rhythmic harmony, and adapts the elements for generation.

And from all these things it appears brilliantly with how much study the ancients cultivated the Bull, and with what ingenious hieroglyphics they adorned it. Since these things are so, nothing else remains but that we turn our pen to the sacred hierograms of other animals.

## HIEROGRAMMATISM II.
### Concerning the Ram and its hieroglyphic significance.

The Egyptians held that divinity was diffused through all things, a tradition passed down from their ancestors. Just as they related its individual virtues in the lower world through various Deities or Spirits [Genii], so they also adorned its various ministries, by which it labored for the good of the world, with various allegorical coverings.

They fashioned these [spirits] as if they were certain assessors and executors of the supreme Deity for the things established for the good of the world. These spirits, entering the paths of the world and its secret inner places, urged all things toward the preservation of that same world through various effects. And so that it might be clear to men who they were, they believed that each spirit assumed for itself that animal appropriate to its virtues and operations, so that they might instruct and inform the human race through the hidden characters of divinity lurking within the animals. For as it is correctly—

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>Psellus on the oracles of Zoroaster.</margin>
Zoroaster, according to Psellus <note>Michael Psellus was an 11th-century Byzantine scholar who preserved many ancient "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to the Persian sage Zoroaster.</note> in the oracles, says: "The paternal mind sowed symbols into souls" <note>original Greek: Σύμβολα πατρικὸς νόος ἔσπειρε ψυχαῖς</note>; that is, the paternal mind implanted signs and marks of its own unique property into souls. For not only were souls produced from these paternal seeds, but all the superior orders of being also took their origin from there. In those incorporeal substances, some signs are likewise incorporeal and harmonious; but in the various worlds <note>Meaning the different levels of the cosmos, from the celestial to the earthly.</note>, there are signs and symbols of the unutterable qualities and properties of God. Because this secret was not hidden from the Egyptians, <margin>What the Egyptians signified by the Ram</margin> they would depict a ram to represent that hidden Divinity which expressed the principle of "moist heat" in the terrestrial world. For the Ram is a hot and moist animal; and heat and moisture are the very beginnings of all generation. Thus says Abenephi <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher for Hermetic and Egyptian secrets.</note>:

When they wanted to indicate the power of heat in the world, they would look [to the Ram], etc. <note>original Arabic: فلما يريدون يدلون على الحرّ بعالم كانوا يبصروا الخ</note>

Indicating the force of heat in the world, they painted a Ram. The historical reasoning is as follows: when the Gods of Egypt were fleeing the ferocity of Typhon <note>A monstrous giant in Greek myth; the Egyptians identified him with Set, the god of chaos.</note>, it is said that they hid themselves in Egypt under the forms of various animals, as we have shown elsewhere at length using the accounts of Diodorus, Herodotus, and Eusebius. Ovid describes this event aptly:

<margin>Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*</margin>
> And that Typhoeus, sent from the lowest depths of the earth,
> Caused the inhabitants of heaven to fear, and they all turned
> Their backs in flight, until the land of Egypt received them,
> Where the Nile is divided into seven mouths;
> To this place also, they say, the earth-born Typhoeus came,
> And the high gods hid themselves in false forms:
> "The leader of the flock," he said, "became Jupiter,"
> Whence even now Libyan Ammon is formed with curved horns.

<margin>The deity Amun in the form of a Ram.</margin>
From this, the Egyptians believe that the deity whom they call *Amun* appeared in the form of a Ram. They did this so that through the nature and properties of the Ram, they might show what kind of nature the deity possessed, and what his duties and ministries were in the administration of the world. Various accounts of this deity are circulated among the Egyptians. <margin>Hecateus. What Amun signifies.</margin> Hecateus says that *Amoun* in the Egyptian language signifies the "voice of those calling upon God"; they were accustomed to use this name especially when they spoke of him as unknown and hidden. Alluding to this, Phestus <note>Possibly a reference to a poetic source or a variant of Festus.</note> used this prayer formula to Ammon: <gloss>O prophet of Libya, hear us, horn-bearing Ammon.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ζεῦ Λιβύης Ἄμμον κερατηφόρε κλυθί μάντι.</note>

<margin>What Amun meant to Iamblichus</margin>
Iamblichus, however, says it signifies a certain power of the Divinity that brings the hidden principles of latent reasons into the light; Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian.</note> agrees with this. Indeed, they said it was granted to this deity to draw out the secret and hidden powers of reality, whether they lie hidden in the sensible or the insensible world. <margin>Why the Ram holds the first place in the Zodiac.</margin> For this reason, they dedicated the first part among the twelve houses of the Zodiac and the month of *Pharmuti* (the beginning of which corresponds to the twenty-seventh day of March) to the Ram.

### HIEROGLYPHICS.

<margin>Pherecides.</margin>
For in this month <gloss>Pharmuthi</gloss> <note>The eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, falling around March/April.</note> Amun—that is, the Sun—most powerfully moves and promotes the latent forces of all seminal things with his moist heat, and finally brings them forth into the light through fertile sprouts. Whence, according to the testimony of *Pherecides* <note>An early Greek thinker from Syros, often cited in matters of ancient theology.</note>, in this month of *Pharmuthi*, the Priests used to carry around the head of a Ram, adorned with various crowns and equipped with thyrsuses <note>Staffs tipped with pinecones, usually associated with Bacchus.</note> and foliage. By these means, they demonstrated to some the benefits they enjoyed through God’s kindness, and to others they showed the dominion of the Deity as if through the offspring of the earthly world; meanwhile, they invoked God with unformed voices <gloss>in the name of Amma</gloss>, to which *Hecataeus* <note>Hecataeus of Miletus, an early Greek historian.</note>, as was mentioned a little earlier, seems to allude. This is how it happened that the Ram was established in the first place among the twelve Gods in the Zodiac, <margin>The Ram is the living dwelling of Amun.</margin> for the reason that they called the living Ram the dwelling-place of *Amun*. By his benefit, the first <gloss>elemental beginnings</gloss> <note>original Greek/Hebrew hybrid: στοיχειώσεις (stoicheioseis)</note> were stirred in the inner sanctums of the earthly world and arranged for the greatest convenience of the human race.

<margin>The Hammon of the Greeks borrowed from the Egyptians.</margin>
Certainly, it is clearly evident that the Greeks borrowed this *Amun* from the Egyptians, received him among their own, and called him *Jupiter Hammon*. For they also said that the Sun was glowing hot, and for that reason, they represented him with ram’s horns, just as the Egyptians did. They say that this God first appeared to Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus or Dionysus.</note> as he was conquering Africa with his army, in a place that posterity thereafter called <gloss>Ammodes</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἀμμούδης, meaning "sandy."</note> because of the vast amount of sand. For when, <margin>Origin of the Ammonian oracle</margin> in addition to a great lack of all things, they were being tortured by intense heat in the vast wilderness, a Ram appeared to those who did not know the way. Having followed it to that very place—which subsequently became famous for the temple and oracle of Jupiter Hammon—they report that after finding an <margin>Why the Ram was placed among the stars.</margin> abundance of water, the Ram vanished from the sight of all. Moved by this event, posterity fashioned an upright statue of *Amun*, or Jupiter *Hammon*, with ram's horns, and depicted the Ram among the stars. Thus, when the Sun enters its sign, all newly-born things are restored, which happens in the springtime; this is largely because, by the Ram's appearance, Liber restored his army.

<margin>Origin of the worship of sheep.</margin>
Furthermore, he [Liber] wished the Ram to be the leader of the twelve signs because it had proven itself to be the best guide for the army. Indeed, the Egyptians worshipped the sheep-herd with such honor at all times that they believed it a supreme sacrilege and crime to kill a ram or a sheep. It is said that *Moses* also, in order to counteract the impious laws of the Egyptians, zealously commanded the paschal lamb to be killed and eaten, so that he might free the Hebrews from this insane superstition by a contrary rite. Thus says *Rambam* <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, or Maimonides, the great medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> in *Part 3, Chapter 46* of the *Guide for the Perplexed*. I quote his words:

> The writing of the Torah says, according to what Onkelos explained, that the Egyptians used to worship the constellation of the Ram; because of this, they forbade the slaughter of sheep and held shepherds of sheep in contempt. It says: "Behold, we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians." <note>original Hebrew: ואמרה כתיבת התורה כפי מה שפירש אונקלוס שהמצרים היו עובדים מזל טלה מפני זה היו אוסרים לשחוט הצאן והיו מואסים רועי צאן אמר הנה נזבח את תועבת מצרים</note>

<margin>Rambam.</margin>
I say, however, that the law taught us—according to the explanation of <gloss>Onkelos</gloss> <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note>—that because the Egyptians worshipped the star or sign of the Ram, it was not only forbidden among them to slaughter sheep, but shepherds of sheep were held in the highest contempt and abomination. Hence *Moses* says: *Behold, we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians.* <note>Quoting Exodus 8:26. To the Egyptians, killing the sacred ram was an "abomination" or sacrilege.</note> Rabbi *Chya* in the book <margin>R. Chya in the book of the Zohar.</margin> *Zohar, column 466*, considers that the word "abomination," which is attributed to the Egyptian Gods, is also applied to the shepherds of sheep, as if they were other Gods. Whence—

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>
Ammu, the God armed with fire
</margin>
Regarding Genesis 46: **For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians.** <note>original Hebrew: כי תועבת מצרים כל רועי צאן</note> Rabbi Judah says in the Zohar, column 469: **The Egyptians used to worship the sign of the Ram, the master of fire.** <note>original Hebrew: המצריים היו עובדים מזל טלה בעל אש</note> Rabbi Levi Hadarshan also cites this in his commentary on Exodus, as does Masius in his work on the fifth chapter of Joshua; they believed that god was "armed with fire" because he would take vengeance if provoked. For the ram is a combative animal; hence, 
<margin>
Porphyry on abstinence. Why the Egyptians abstained from woolen garments.
</margin>
according to the testimony of Porphyry in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, he says the Egyptians never used woolen clothes in their sacrifices, but only linen. They believed that the God *Amun* <note>Amun was the king of the Egyptian gods, often depicted as a ram or a man with a ram's head.</note> would avenge himself because of the taking of the "clothing" of those creatures over whom he presided, and because of the shedding of blood, in which the animal's soul—and some measure of divinity—was thought to reside.

<margin>
Rabbi Moses Gerundensis.
</margin>
Furthermore, since that month was especially dedicated to the Ram, during which the Jews departed from Egypt, Rabbi Moses Gerundensis <note>Better known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note> reports that the Paschal Ram was ordered by God to be slaughtered so that the Hebrews, about to migrate to Palestine, might distance themselves from Egyptian focuses. This was to ensure that the success of their departure would not be attributed to that star <note>The constellation Aries (the Ram).</note> which held dominion in the heavens at that time; rather, they were to treat that star with "injury" by slaughtering so many rams, which shared the same form as the constellation.

It is clear, then, why the Egyptians treated the Ram with such great honor. With these 
<margin>
How the Egyptians represented Amun hieroglyphically.
</margin>
foundational points established, let us now see how the Egyptians expressed him in their sacred carvings and what they signified through him. It should be understood that the Hieromants <note>Priests who interpreted sacred mysteries or hieroglyphs.</note> frequently adopted the figure of this animal: sometimes in its whole and natural form; sometimes whole but with two ram-heads, as can be seen in the Bembine Table <note>An elaborate bronze tablet of Egyptian style, likely of Roman origin, which was a primary source for early Egyptologists.</note>; sometimes only the head of this animal, shining with two flames bursting from the skull, as on our Obelisk; or they would even transform a human torso with a ram’s head, as is evident in various hieroglyphic fragments. Through the whole figure, they signified the power of *Amun* diffused through the inner reaches of the earthly world. Thus says Abenephi: **The Egyptians who wish to express the divine power of Amun, who is the leader of the world, visualize the form of their god [as a ram].** <note>original Arabic: المصريون الذين يريدون ان يعبروا القوة الاهم امون الذي هو مقدم الدنيا يبصروا الصورة الهم</note>

<margin>
Various figures of Amun and their meanings.
</margin>
Therefore, wishing to indicate the power of the God *Amun*, the ruler of their world, they painted the figure of a Ram. As for what they indicated hieroglyphically through the <term>two-headed</term> <note>original Greek: δικέφαλον (dikephalon)</note> Ram conspicuous with two heads, it shall be discussed, God willing, in the explanation of the Bembine Table. Furthermore, through the head alone, the ruler of the vital parts, they denoted the providence of the Deity—specifically, *Amun* working for the good of the world and instructing the human race in investigating those things necessary for sustaining life, as we shall prove in the various following authorities. By the flame, divided as if into two horns upon the ram's head, they meant the effect of the diffusion of fiery power and heat latent in the earth. By the head, they also meant the "beginning" of the animal and the "beginning" of the restoration of things, which usually occurs when the Sun enters the sign of the Ram. Through the warm and moist animal, they hinted at the promotion of the generation of things, as has been said. Hence, among the hieroglyphics, one occasionally finds a human head that is <term>ram-faced</term> <note>original Greek: κριοπρόσωπον (krioprosopon)</note>—that is, conspicuous with ram’s horns—upon whose head a basket is placed, to...

# HIEROGLYPHICS

We must note that by the benefit of this God, happy outcomes arise from abundant fertility, as will be explained later. Not only did the Egyptians express him through the aforementioned hieroglyphs, but they also believed the very name **Amun**, which they invoked, possessed great power to appease the Deity through the mystical structure of its letters.

<margin>Explanation of the hieroglyphic diagram.</margin>
The hieroglyphic diagram, which Marcus Milesius—a Roman Legal Consultant—once shared with me from his own collection to be explained, shows that these things are so. The diagram is enclosed in an oval figure, in which the first place is held by a Ram's head *having the form of flaming horns* <note>original Greek: φλογοκερατόμορφον</note>, that is, distinguished by a bifurcated flame and horns, of the exact same form as our Obelisk displays. After this follow four letters *in a literal sense* <note>original Greek: κυριολογικῶς — used here to mean letters that represent concepts directly</note>, that is, taken from appropriate objects, as is clear in the diagram placed here; which we interpret thus: *Amun, the solar Deity, bringing to light the secret powers of hidden reasons. The Agathodaemon of moisture and heat, by which the generations of things in the earthly world are promoted through continuous motion and agitation.*

What is meant by the *flame-horn-shaped* ram’s head was mentioned a little earlier. There follow four characters which express the mystical name **Amun**; these characters are derived from the ingenious architecture of the Egyptian Alphabet (which was treated at length in Book 2, chapter 10); to which the characters of the Coptic alphabet ⲁ, ⲙ, ⲏ, ⲛ correspond, each of which denotes certain mysteries. 

And first, indeed, it was demonstrated in the cited place that the letter **A** signifies nothing other than the Agathodaemon. The second letter is taken *literally* from the flow of water, whence it is also called *Moi* <note>The Egyptian word for water</note> from water, and corresponds to the Coptic letter **ⲙ**. The third letter corresponds to **ⲏ**, derived from the ram’s horns, as was proved in the mystical alphabet; for the power of the heat of the earth, implanted by Amun, is beautifully denoted by flames breaking out from the terrestrial globe like horns. Finally, the fourth letter, which is **ⲛ**, corresponds to the Coptic letter, forming two angles under doubled horns, [representing] the principle of motion...

BOOK IV. IDEAS

The **above and below** <note>original Greek: ἄνω καὶ κάτω</note> of the said Deity is beautifully portrayed, as was shown both in my *Prodromus* <note>referring to Kircher’s earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus* (1636)</note> and in the place cited. From these, that sense which we have described is fashioned, and another hieroglyphic demonstrates this to be the case. This is taken from the *Hieroglyphic Theater* published by Herwart <note>Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, a scholar of ancient chronology and symbols</note>, which we displayed on the preceding page. There you see a human head that is **ram-shaped** <note>original Greek: κριόμορϕον</note>—that is, in the form of a ram—equipped with a basket <note>term: canistro, referring to the "modius," a grain-measure or basket worn on the head to symbolize abundance</note>. Beneath this is placed a triangle with the letter **ee**, exhibiting the same meaning we have described. From these things it is also clear that although the Egyptians occasionally prefigured the names of the Gods themselves with common letters, they nevertheless derived their structure from the animals dedicated to them. They believed these animal forms possessed great power in the proper administration of sacred rites and ceremonies.

Hence, they attributed immense power to names of this kind, because they consisted of a certain mystical logic known only to the Gods themselves and taught by them. They considered that these names should by no means be translated into a foreign language, as they would lose their inherent power. For this reason, Zoroaster urged that oracle found in Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar who preserved many ancient oracles</note>: **Do not ever change the barbarous names** <note>original Greek: ὀνόματα βάρβαρα μήποτ' ἀλλάξῃς</note>. For every nation has certain names delivered by the gods, which possess an incredible and ineffable power in sacred rites. The words of Psellus are: **For there are names among every nation delivered by the gods, possessing an unspeakable power in the initiations** <note>original Greek: ἐσὶ γὰρ ὀνόματα παρ' ἑκάστοις ἔθνεσι θεοπαράδοτα, δύναμιν ἐν ταῖς τελεταῖς ἄρρητον ἔχοντα</note>. These will be discussed more extensively in their proper place. Thus, from what has been said, the origin of the worship of the Ram is clear, as is the structure of the hieroglyphs by which the Egyptians sketched him. Therefore, leaving these behind, let us move on to other matters.

# HIEROGRAMMATISM III.
