### On the Goat, and its hieroglyphic significance.

<margin>The Goat as a symbol of fertility</margin>
<margin>Pan transformed into a goat</margin>
<margin>fish-formed <note>original Greek: ἰχθυόμορϕον</note></margin>
<margin>Goat-worship among the Mendesians.</margin>
Since nothing was more desirable to the Egyptians than fertility, they sought to obtain this highly valued and desired abundance by attracting the favor of that Deity who presided over the propagation of all things with zeal and diligence. This was done through the cult of that animal which was most commended by all for its reputation for fertility. Since the **Goat** surpassed all others in this praise of fertility, they uniquely venerated it at Mendes as a living habitation of **Pan** and the guardian of all fecundity. Hence, according to Hyginus <note>a Latin mythographer</note>, in that common flight of the Gods undertaken into Egypt for fear of Typhon <note>the chaotic monster of Greek myth, identified with the Egyptian Set</note>, it is said that Pan transformed himself into a goat. When he had cast himself into a river, with his lower part degenerating into a fish, **Capricorn** emerged. From there, he was translated to the stars and earned divine honors. By this allusion, they beautifully expressed the dual empire of Pan as a fertile Deity: through the head roughened with goat-horns, they expressed the fertility of terrestrial things, and through the tail of a fish, that of aquatic things. Certainly, it is established that the Mendesian Egyptians held goats in such high honor that killing them was considered an inexpiable crime. Herodotus explains the cause in his second book with these words: *Moreover, those who inhabit the temple of the Theban Jupiter, or belong to the Theban province, all...*

...abstaining from sheep, they sacrifice goats; for not all Egyptians worship the same gods in the same way, except for Isis and Osiris (whom they say is Bacchus), whom everyone worships equally. However, those who hold the temple of Mendes, or are from the Mendesian province, abstain from goats and sacrifice sheep. And a little later: furthermore, those Egyptians we mentioned do not slaughter goats or bucks for this reason; because <margin>Herodotus:</margin> <note>original Greek: τὸν Πᾶνα τῶν ὀκτὼ θεῶν...</note> the Mendesians consider Pan to be one of the eight gods. They say these eight gods existed before the twelve gods. Indeed, painters and sculptors depict the image of Pan just as the Greeks do, with a goat’s face and the legs of a buck. They do not believe he is actually like that, but rather that he is similar to the other gods. But as for the reason why they paint him in this way, it is not very pleasant for me to say. Nevertheless, all the Mendesians revere goats, and the males more than the females, and the goatherds among them receive greater honors; and out of these, one goat especially, who, when he dies, causes great mourning throughout the entire Mendesian district. Both the buck and Pan are called "Mendes" in the Egyptian language. Because, clearly, the Mendesians number Pan among the eight gods, who they say existed before the twelve gods. Moreover, the sculptors of animals and makers of idols carve the likeness of Pan—just as the Greeks do—with a goat-like face and buck-like horns; by no means thinking him to be such a thing, but rather similar to the other gods. For what reason they paint him thus, however, is not <margin>A buck is called "Mendes" in Egyptian.</margin> pleasant for me to relate. But all these people venerate both female goats and especially the bucks; and among the Mendesians, the goatherds are treated with particular honor, especially one among them, and when he dies, a huge period of mourning is declared for the entire Mendesian Province. Furthermore, the buck and Pan are called *Mendes* in Egyptian.

<margin>Diodorus.</margin> Diodorus Siculus asserts: The Egyptians deified the buck in the same way the Greeks did Priapus <note>The Greek god of fertility, often depicted with a permanent erection</note>, because of that part of the body which is the origin of all birth. At all times, such a madness for this cult possessed the souls of men that Sacred Scripture seems everywhere to confuse bucks with demons, because of the impious worship offered to them. The first authors of this <term>tragolatria</term> <note>literally "goat-worship," from the Greek "tragos" (goat) and "latreia" (worship)</note> were the <margin>Sabaean Heretics.</margin> Sabaean Heretics, the first promoters of superstitions after the flood, about whom Maimonides <note>referred to here by his acronym, Rambam (Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon), a 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> writes in Part 3, Chapter 46:

> And thus the impure sects used to worship demons, and they thought 
> they dwelt in the form of goats, and for this reason they called the demons *Seirim* <note>A Hebrew word meaning "shaggy ones" or "bucks," often used to refer to desert demons or satyrs</note>. And this 
> <margin>Why demons are called Seirim.</margin> evil spread so widely that because of it, Moses said: "they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the *Seirim*." And for this reason, those sects were forbidden from

And the Sabaean people were worshippers of demons, believing they possessed the form of bucks; and therefore the demons were called *Seirim*, that is, bucks. This opinion was so widely and deeply spread that Moses therefore said, "you shall not sacrifice to bucks," that is, to demons, and the eating of kids was forbidden to those nations. Certainly Lucian <note>A 2nd-century satirist known for mocking religion</note> seems, not without reason, to mock this Egyptian custom; <margin>Lucian.</margin> among the Egyptians, he says, the temple is indeed most beautiful on the outside, built of costly stones; but if you look for the God inside, you will find either a monkey, or a stork, or a goat or a cat.

And since this kind of <term>tragolatria</term> had taken deep root in the minds of men before Moses, the Greeks borrowed it from there, and everywhere expressed Pan under the form of a goat; see his hieroglyphic representation on page 222. And although the common people may have missed the true target of such worship, the first "Hieromants" <note>Priests or interpreters of sacred mysteries</note> nonetheless indicated the divine power hidden beneath the goat symbolically; for they ingeniously described the fertility—sometimes of the Archetypal Sun, sometimes the sidereal, and sometimes the subterranean—under the symbols of the goat.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>What is meant by the Hieroglyphic of the goat.</margin>
Therefore, to return to our purpose, the goat was a hieroglyphic: First, of divine fertility; Second, of the fertility by which the Solar Deity, acting as an analogue to the Archetypal Sun, impregnated the earth; Third, also of the fire enclosed within the bowels of the earth, which performed a substitute work for the Sun in promoting fertility. All of this is beautifully described by Pherecydes the Syrian <margin>Pherecydes.</margin> <note>A 6th-century BCE philosopher known for his early theories on the origins of the world.</note> in his hymns with this verse: *The god was the sun and the earth was very fertile.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ θεὸς ἥλιος ἦν καὶ ἡ γὴ πολυγονενὴς"</note> Fourth, when designating a fertile man, they painted a goat, according to the testimony of Horus <note>Horapollo, the traditional author of a treatise on hieroglyphics.</note>, who assigns the reason for this in these <margin>Horus.</margin> words: *To show the fertile genitals of a man, they paint a goat; but as for the bull, since it becomes pregnant and mounts through struggle. A goat, however, mates on the seventh day after its birth; though it emits an infertile and seedless sperm, it nevertheless mounts first among the other animals.* <note>original Greek: "αἰδοῖον δὲ ἀνδρὸς πολυγονὰ δηλῶντες τράγον ζωγραφῶσι..."</note>

But indeed, when showing the member of a fertile man, they do not paint a bull, but a goat; for the bull is not accustomed to mate before reaching a year, while the goat joins in intercourse immediately seven days after birth, secreting a seed that is indeed infertile and least suited for generation; yet it mates earlier and faster than other animals.

<margin>A goat's head.</margin>
Furthermore, a goat's head found among hieroglyphics always denotes that Deity who presides over fertility, just as a statue conspicuous with a goat's head does; the likeness of which may be seen everywhere on Obelisks, as will be explained in its proper place. But now it is time that we prove these things to be so from all kinds of learning.

<margin>What is Niben?</margin>
Therefore, not without reason, the Egyptian Sages <note>literally "Nilotic Sages," referring to those living by the Nile.</note> expressed their Deity—whom we said above was called *Niben*, that is, the "Cause of Causes"—by a Goat or a goat-like head as a unique symbol of fertility. For that God is endowed with a certain unique fertility, which through the nature of the immense and eternal good propagates itself in action within itself from eternity. Not only do sacred Authors teach this, and we, instructed by the Holy Mother Church of Faith, believe it, but also all the Masters of ancient Theology everywhere demonstrate it in the clearest words. For what else do that intellectual progeny of Zoroaster <note>referring to the Chaldean Oracles attributed to Zoroaster.</note>, and that fertile "Monad" (the One) of Plato, and the "Triad" (the Three) of Plotinus arising from the fertile nature of God (according to Saint Augustine) indicate?

<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
I will not speak here of other testimonies of the Platonists concerning the fertile nature of God; let Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note> stand for all, who speaks thus in the *Pimander*: 

> *But Mind, God, most full of the fertility of both sexes, being life and light, brought forth with his word another mind, the artisan; and he saw the mind stretching itself toward external things through its exuberant fertility, and forming all things according to the pattern of his divine word, and distributing to each in the air, water, and earth, its own nature according to its kind.*

Indeed, nothing is clearer than these words; nor did this escape the "stiff-necked Jews." For besides the fact that in the 1st chapter of Genesis—*In the beginning God created*— <note>original Hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים (Bereshit bara Elohim)</note> they understand through the name *Elohim* three properties, which they call *Middoth* <note>original Hebrew: מדות, meaning "measures" or "attributes."</note>, and these are Crown, Understanding, and Wisdom <note>original Hebrew: כתר בינה חכמה (Keter, Binah, Chokhmah).</note>. These they place in the highest position of the tree of the *Sephiroth* <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah.</note>, namely, Keter, Chokhmah, Binah; by which they believe the world was founded, and which Simeon Ben Jochai in the book *Zohar*, and Ludovicus Carretus <note>A 16th-century Jewish convert to Christianity who wrote on the Kabbalah.</note> in the book he titles *Of Divine Visions*, call everywhere in clear words Father, Son, and Holy Spirit <note>original Hebrew: אב בן ורוח הקדש (Av, Ben, v'Ruach HaKodesh)</note>; which also from the first...

...they gather from the words of Genesis: for where the common text has: *In the beginning God created, etc.*, Jonathan in the Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translates it as **In Wisdom God created** <note>original Aramaic: "בחכמתא ברא" (Bechochmatha bra)</note>, that is, *In Wisdom God created, etc.* Since these words are mysterious, it is pleasing to explain them here a little more fully. God therefore created the world **In Wisdom** <note>original: "Bechochmath"</note>; however, what sort of Wisdom that might be is shown by the word **Created** <note>original: "Bra"</note>, which in the Chaldean language signifies **Son** <note>original: "Bro"</note>. Moreover, they understand this Son, together with the Father and the Spirit **who was moving over the face of the waters** <note>original Hebrew: "אשר הוא מרחפת על פני המים"</note>—who, brooding over the cosmic egg to animate it with His fertility, was carried above the waters—to be shown by the three letters of the word **'Aleph'**, by which they understand **Father** <note>original: "Ab"</note>; **Son** <note>original: "Bra"</note>; and **Spirit** <note>original: "Ruah"</note>. Again, what for the Hebrews is the second property, *Chochma*—that is, *Wisdom*, through which they assert the world was created—is for the Egyptians *Isis*, whom they called the Wisdom of the First Mover, and the full image and exemplar of the first intellect, Osiris; whom Orpheus also called...

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>The three-form deity among the Egyptians.</margin> He called her Pallas <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom (Athena), whom Kircher identifies here with the Egyptian concept of divine wisdom.</note>, and for this reason the ancients feigned that she was born from the brain of Jove; among the Egyptians she is called Phta <note>Ptah, the creator god of Memphis.</note>. *Amun* indeed, corresponding to the Hebrew *Binàh* <note>The Sephirah of "Understanding" in Kabbalistic thought.</note> or intelligence, is the active power of both directed outward, by which the world Horus—the son of Osiris and Isis—is produced. And all those things which have been said thus far, the instruments show beautifully as if in a certain summary, with which we see Horus depicted on the Bembine Table <note>Also known as the Isiac Tablet, a famous bronze plaque with Egyptian-style motifs used by Kircher as a primary source.</note>, as also on our Obelisk, as will appear below: namely, the Staff marked with the head of a hoopoe, the lituus <note>A curved wand or shepherd's crook, symbolizing priestly or royal authority.</note> and the gnomon <note>A carpenter's square or an instrument for measuring shadows.</note>; from the back, however, is a triangle to which a circle is attached. This signifies nothing other than the world produced by the wisdom of God with an admirable variety of things, indicated through that reticulated <note>Net-like or woven.</note> garment; the highest harmony is indicated through the lituus; and finally, the world produced in a fitting order is indicated through the gnomon. To these things agrees the testimony of Plato, who says this sensible world flowed forth from that archetypal triangle. And we have deliberately treated these matters regarding the fertility of God at greater length, so that the mysteries of Egyptian philosophy might be more clearly revealed as parallel to Hebrew philosophy.

Since therefore the Egyptians devoted themselves to this one thing—to attach suitable symbols to the Gods—that is, to express the virtues and effects of their Gods (which they shadowed forth in this way) through a certain analogy to those animals in which similar virtues or effects shine forth as living images of them, marked with characters; <margin>Why they marked Osiris by the horns of a goat.</margin> certainly they thought Osiris, that most fertile Deity, could be shown by no more apt, better, or more congruent symbol than that of a goat's head. For the goat is the most fertile among other animals, as has been said, and is eager for generation.

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> Hence Eusebius, in Book 2, Chapter 1 of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, says that the goat was held in such honor among the Egyptians because of its desire for generation, just as Priapus <note>The Greek god of fertility and procreation.</note> was among the Greeks. I will add his words: "They say the goat was accepted into divine matters for this reason, etc." whence also wishing to show the abundance and fertility of <gloss>spring</gloss>, they suggest it through a goat, upon which sits a boy turning toward Mercury. A similar relief exists, as can be seen in Aleandro <note>Girolamo Aleandro, a scholar of antiquities.</note> in the exposition of the Heliacal Table at the end: a young boy sitting on a goat, as if the tender and fertile world were sent from the Sun, the moderator of the seasons, to Mercury, the presiding deity of Spring; it seems to signify the renewal of the year.

<margin>Pausanias.</margin> For as Pausanias rightly says in Book 2: that the club of Hercules, consecrated to Mercury, sprouted again; this should be referred to the matter we are discussing. For we said in the third book that the Herculean club denotes trees stripped of their leaves in winter time, which the Deity Mercury—that is, the power of Springtime—clothes again. Also the fable which is told of the birth of Pan—namely that he was fathered by Mercury, having turned into a goat, from Penelope—indicates that the world itself arose in Springtime, of which we have spoken. <margin>What is Pan?</margin> For Pan, in the opinion of all mythologists, is the totality of things; but we have already taught that Spring is signified by Mercury, who is said to have turned into a goat to mark the fertility of that season, since spring <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἔαρ γονιμωτάτη" (he ear gonimotate)</note> is the most <margin>Theophrastus, *On Plants*.</margin> fertile time, says Theophrastus in Book 3 of *On the Causes of Plants*. And indeed, that the goat itself was adored by the Egyptians as a sign of fertility, we have [shown]...

...as we saw before from Eusebius, and as Diodorus confirms in Book 1. Hence Suidas asserts that the Mendesians worshiped Pan *as one who has care over the generative power, and that they abstain from goats in his honor, because the animal is lustful*; likewise, that there was a temple among the Egyptians in Mendes in which there was a statue with goat legs and an erect phallus (at which point note the mistake and error of Hermolaus, who incorrectly read *Meden* as "mouse" <note>The translator notes that the scholar Hermolaus Barbarus mistakenly transcribed the place name "Mendes" as the Greek word for mouse.</note>); for the same reason, as Pausanias witnesses, the people of Phlius celebrated a bronze she-goat. Furthermore, the solemnities of the goat cult were increased not only by the fertile nature of the goat itself—for which they especially celebrated it—but also, <margin>What do the goat horns signify?</margin> because it imitated the solar rays with its horns, and the heat of the Sun with the great heat which it possesses; because by its nature it always seeks the higher slopes of mountains, and in a way affects the path of the Sun, which always holds to the higher places. Hence the Egyptians, as Herodotus witnesses in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus’s *Histories*, titled after the Muse of music.</note>; *Those who inhabit the temple of the Theban Jove, all of them abstaining from sheep, sacrifice goats; those who follow the Mendesian rites, these, abstaining from goats, sacrifice sheep.*

Therefore the Thebans, and whoever else spare sheep on their account, say that this law was established for them because Jove—when Hercules wanted to see him but he did not want to be seen—finally being persuaded, devised a plan whereby he showed himself by cutting off the head of a ram and dressing himself in the shaggy skin he had pulled from it. <margin>The fable of Jove covered in a goat skin.</margin> And for this reason, the Egyptians established the statue of Jove as ram-faced <note>original: *κριοπρόσωπον*</note>, that is, formed in the likeness of a ram; and from the Egyptians the Ammonians <note>A people of Libya known for the famous Oracle of Ammon.</note> received this, who are colonists of the Egyptians and Ethiopians and use a language between the two, and who seem for the same reason to have called themselves Ammonians, because the Egyptians called Jove "Ammon." But concerning these things, the cited Herodotus wrote more in Book 2. And from here, perhaps for the same reason, Jove was called *Aegipes* <note>Literally "Goat-footed," though here implying a connection to the goat-skin *aegis*.</note>, although the mythographers Phornutus, Apollodorus, and Hyginus would have it that he was called this because he was hidden so as not to be devoured by Saturn, and was raised by a goat in Crete and covered by the *aegis*, or goat skin, which he carried.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that both she-goats and he-goats were always in the highest honor among the Egyptians, not only because of the remarkable fertility they possess and the heat that rivals—and is in a way parallel to—the fertility and heat of the Sun, but also because they reflect a certain ectype <note>In Kircher's philosophy, an "ectype" is a physical manifestation or copy of a higher, divine "archetype."</note> of the Sun; for indeed, they might reflect the solar rays with their horns, and the movement of the Sun—which always seeks higher places—with that leaping spirit by which they are always carried toward the highest mountain slopes. Hence, according to Varinus, <margin>The nature of the goat is parallel to the effects of the Sun.</margin> they sacrificed goats to Apollo, because of the impetuous nature of this animal, its desire for high places, and because goat horns are suitable for making bows; moreover, it has already been said above and is known everywhere from the monuments of the ancients that Apollo is the "Archer" <margin>Apollo the Archer.</margin> <note>original: *τοξότην*</note>, that is, he delights in bows and arrows, which symbolically are nothing other than the rays of the Sun. For the stated reason, Pan was called "goat-footed," and by the Greeks "goat-mad" <note>original: *αἰγομανὴς*</note> and "Saint Pan" <note>original: *ἁγíπαν*</note>. Hence Propertius: 
> The goat-footed Pans will sing with the gaping reed.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

Giraldus notes that Aristophanes also mentions this *Horn-walking Pan* <note>original: "Ceratobates Panos"</note> in his play *The Frogs*, as one who, according to the Commentator, walks across the peaks of mountains as if they were horns. Or, according to Didymus, he is named from his "horns," meaning his goat-like hooves; for he says Pan has the lower parts of a goat, so that he is called "horn-walker" <note>Greek: κεροβατης (kerobates)</note> because of his feet. Furthermore, according to Herodotus, the Egyptians do not sacrifice the female goat in accordance with the Mendesian rites because the Mendesians count *Pan* among the eight gods who they say existed before the twelve later gods. For this reason, Herodotus says, the Egyptians venerate both female goats and male goats, and among the Mendesians, the goat-herders are treated with special honor, as was mentioned above. One goat in particular is held in such high esteem that when it dies, a great period of mourning occurs throughout the entire province of Mendes. In the Egyptian language, both the goat and Pan are called Mendes <note>Greek: ΜΕΝΔΗΣ</unclear></note>. In order to denote more of the mysteries of Nature, the ancient

<margin>
The image of Pan and its physical explanation.
</margin>
wise men depicted the image of Pan in this way: with a goat's face, a red color, shaggy horns, and wearing a dappled panther skin. His lower part was hairy with goat-like feet; in one hand he held a flute of seven reeds, and in the other a curved staff or crook. Through the red face they signified the ether <note>The upper, fiery atmosphere</note>; through the two horns, the Sun and Moon; and through the panther skin, they signified the variety of the celestial bodies. He was fashioned as shaggy in his lower members to indicate trees, shrubs, and wild beasts; they showed the solidity of the earth through the form of the goat's foot. Through the flute of seven reeds, they indicated the harmony of heaven, which is composed of the highly ordered movement of the seven planets, like the intervals between low and high musical sounds. Through the curved staff, they noted the year recurring into itself, which he moderated. Thus he was called *Pan*, which means "The All," <note>The Greek word *Pan* (Πάν) means "all" or "everything."</note> representing everything according to the interpretation of Eusebius, Phornutus, and Servius. We have already shown his image on page 222, along with an explanation of his individual parts, which we now repeat briefly.

<margin>
Another explanation of the image of Pan.
</margin>
According to the mind of the Egyptians, we say that the horns signify nothing other than a certain radiant and fiery power of the divine Osiris (or the Sun) and the Moon. This is also denoted by the reddish face, which nourishes everything in the world with divine heat. This power flows from the upper part—that is, from the Archetypal world—through that <term>Raqia</term> <note>Hebrew term for the firmament or "expanse" of heaven.</note> or expanse of the fixed stars (represented as a sort of spotted skin).

<margin>רקיע [Raqia] expanse.</margin>
This power is diffused through the space of the seven planetary orbits over the course of the entire year, and it animates the two lower worlds—the Elemental and the Terrestrial—which are indicated by those two shaggy goat legs (for a goat's extremities occupy the bottom of Pan). That is to say, it produces air, water, earth, trees, shrubs, plants, and animals of every kind, fertilizing them with its power as it permeates all things. This is that fertile power of God which the Egyptians dimly worshiped through the image of Pan as one of the eight Gods or Spirits. We see this power represented by a goat's head not only here, but everywhere in the designs of the *Bembina Table* <note>Also known as the *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs studied extensively by Kircher.</note>; as Herodotus testifies in his second book with these words: *And for this reason the sacred scribes and makers of idols write and carve the image of Pan in the form of a goat.* <note>Kircher provides the Greek: και διο τω. γραφουσι δη και γλυφουσι οι ζωογραφοι και οι αγαλματοποιοι το Πανος αγαλμα αιγοπροσωπον</note> For with the power in the head, as I have said above...

# HIEROGLYPHICS. 281

...as we have said, they believed that while the [generative force] resided there and diffused into the lower parts, it governed the rest of the entire body. For the same reason, they celebrated Satyrs, Sileni, Fauns, Sylvans, and similar monsters because they served an immoderate lust. Hence, Satyrs and Sileni, brandishing *thyrsi* <note>ritual staffs topped with pinecones</note> and fennel stalks, are joined as companions to Bacchus as he sits in his vine-leafed chariot, according to the testimony of Giraldus in Book 10. Strabo also asserts that the Sileni, Satyrs, Bacchic women, Nymphs, and Tityri <note>another name for satyrs or flute-playing spirits</note> were followers of Dionysus for this same reason.

<margin>
What Satyrs signify in company with Bacchus.
</margin>

Hence arises that famous boldness of Pan toward the Nymphs and his never-satisfied lust; for the world is constantly occupied in the production of new species and makes much use of moisture, which is a material especially fit and convenient for generation. For this reason, the statue of Pan was placed in forests and fields, as well as in gardens and by wells, as a protective deity. 

By the Hebrews, these creatures are also called *Scheriim* <note>original: שעירים (se'irim); literally "hairy ones" or "he-goats"</note> due to the coarseness of their hair. These are certain monsters of the desert, or lustful demons, whom we call *incubi* or *succubi* <note>demons believed to have sexual encounters with sleeping humans</note>. Indeed, that demons sometimes exercise their deceptive lust upon humans under the form of a goat is taught to us everywhere by experience in the public confessions of magicians and witches, such that we can by no means doubt it in the future. 

<margin>
What are the *Scheriim*?
</margin>

And for that reason, the Chaldean paraphrast <note>the Targum, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> on Leviticus 17 translates *Scheriim* as *Sedim* <note>original: שדים (shedim)</note>, that is, evil demons. The Arabs call them *al-Shayatin* <note>original: الشياطين; "The Devils"</note>, that is, Satan and Demons; the Persians call them *Denoni*, to which the Illyrian word *dodai* is related. For we read in the works of Hesychius and Varinus: "*dodai* are what the Satyrs are called among the Illyrians" <note>original Greek: δόδαι οἱ Σάτυροι παρὰ Ιλλυριοῖς</note>. Not dissimilar to this are the Bohemian *Diabel* and German *Teuffel*, as if from *dalai*; but let us leave this to the grammarians. 

It is enough that the ancients everywhere took such monsters as symbols of fertility because of their insatiable lust. Whoever desires more regarding Satyrs and Fauns should consult Pausanias, who treats extensively of such monsters found on a certain island of the Ocean; St. Augustine in *The City of God*; St. Athanasius in the *Life of St. Anthony*; and Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*. 

<margin>
The herb *Satyrium*.
</margin>

From the Physicians, regarding the herb *Satyrium* <note>an orchid believed to be an aphrodisiac</note> and the disease *Satyriasis* <note>excessive sexual desire in males</note> or *priapism*, one should consult Galen in his *Definitions of Diseases* and his work *On the Disease of Satyriasis*, as well as Dioscorides, the Paraphrast, Hippocrates, Pliny, and Giambattista della Porta in the sections where they treat the herb *Satyrium*. 

Plutarch says that among the Egyptian Mendesians, a goat was cared for and enclosed in a sacred temple by a college of many and most famous young women. Pausanias also observed a statue of Venus sitting upon a goat, for no other reason than the goat's wantonness. 

<margin>
Venus sitting on a goat.
</margin>

And Astrologers assigned the image of a naked woman carrying a goat on her shoulder to the twenty-second degree of the sign of Virgo, signifying by this the impurity of anyone born while that degree was rising. From all these examples, it is clear why the Egyptians expressed the fertility of the Sun—both the sensible <note>the physical, visible sun</note> and the insensible and archetypal <note>the spiritual or divine source of energy</note>—through a goat or a goat-headed figure.

BOOK IV. IDEAS

# HIEROGRAMMATISM IV.

### On the Lion and its hieroglyphic significance.

<margin>Various parts of the Lion.</margin>
**A**mong the other animals used by the Egyptians to represent divine mysteries, the image of the Lion—and the various parts that comprise it—occupies a position of no small importance. This is seen primarily on our Obelisk in various transformed states: sometimes as a complete figure resting on the earth, at other times in the likeness of an anthropomorphic <note>human-shaped</note> Sphinx, and occasionally as just a head, a haunch, or a tail. We must discuss the meaning of each of these individually. To make the origin of this *leontolatry* <note>original: λεοντολατρεία; the worship of lions</note> more clearly apparent, I have decided to first examine its earliest beginnings in this section. By doing so, I hope that the structure, reasoning, and purpose of these sacred images will become more easily understood by the curious reader. According to Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, it was the opinion of the ancient Egyptians that divinity did not pass through humanity alone, but through all living animals; for God moves through all things:

->And through the lands, the tracts of the sea, and the deep sky.<-
<note>A quote from Virgil’s *Georgics* (IV.221-222), illustrating the idea of a universal spirit or "world soul" present in all nature.</note>

<margin>A physical explanation of the Lion’s nature.</margin>
And so, they wished to suggest the kindness of the divine Power—which he communicates to the world through various effects—through the form of animals endowed with a similar analogy of traits, as was shown partly in the preceding sections and will be shown more extensively in the following. Thus, when they looked upon the Lion as a strong, robust, magnanimous, and highly vigilant animal, one that is hot and clearly of a fiery nature, they called that divine power "Leonine." This power strengthens all things, prevails with a certain fiery vigor, and rests upon every single thing with unceasing vigilance. In the Sun, a deity perceptible to the senses, they secretly shadowed this same force.

<margin>What do the Lions under the Throne of Horus mean?</margin>
<margin>Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris and Isis*.</margin>
<margin>What does Hercules dressed in a Lion skin mean?</margin>
For this reason, according to Plutarch, they placed Lions under the throne of Horus (whom they called sometimes the "World" and sometimes the "Sun") to indicate the fiery power hidden in the world by this symbol. They also depict Hercules dressed in a lion's skin for no other reason than the "Herculean" or strengthening power of the Sun. According to Macrobius <note>a 5th-century Roman writer</note>, Hercules is nothing other than the Sun, as was stated in the third book; for the Lion "drives away diseases because the solar vortex is of a fiery nature" <note>original Greek: τὰς νόσους ἐκδιώκει διὰ τὸ πυρῶδες εἶναι τὸν στρόβιλον</note>. From this, they used Osiris and Isis—whom the Hebrews and Syrians later worshipped under the names Adad and Atargatis—to signify the Sun and the Earth; Giraldus <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, a Renaissance mythographer</note> proves in his *Syntagma 4* that they placed a Lion beneath their statues.

<margin>Why is Cybele’s chariot pulled by Lions?</margin>
Lucian <note>a Syrian-Greek satirist</note> testifies that this method of representation was also used for the Syrian God by the people of Hierapolis. Pausanias <note>a Greek traveler and geographer</note> notes that the Phrygians depicted Cybele, the Mother of the Gods, with Lions pulling her chariot, in accordance with the lines of the Mantuan <note>the poet Virgil</note>:

> The Great Mother of the Gods, turreted with a grand crown,
> Who binds the Libyan lions to the yoke on Mount Ida.

<margin>Mithras, the Persian Deity, in Lion form.</margin>
However, above all others, the Persians—the first heirs of Egyptian doctrine—followed the Egyptians by depicting Mithras with a Lion’s head. Mithras, however, as shown elsewhere...

However, lest anything occur that might cause doubt in the reader, we will demonstrate everything from its source, as the saying goes. That Divinity which, through its fiery power, acts upon moisture, I found to have been called *Mophta* in the Coptic Secrets <note>original: "Coptitarum Arcanis"</note>, that is, the "Divinity of the Waters." This name is composed of the words *mu* and *phta*; of which it has been shown in my *Prodromus* and its *Supplement* (annexed to the treasury of the Egyptian language) that the former signifies "water" and the latter "God." They held by continuous tradition that this deity appeared to the first men in the form of a Lion near the banks of the Nile.

<margin>Origin of the worship of the Lion.</margin>
Hence the Egyptians, suspended in wonder and astonished by this omen, gradually received the Lion among the sacred animals and related it to the heavens; they viewed it as a living habitation of the *Mophta* <note>the water-spirit</note>, just as we showed above for the same reason that the Ram and the Bull were elevated to the heavens. This is affirmed by Abenephi <note>an Arabic author cited by Kircher</note> with these words:

> The Egyptians had another divinity, whom they called Mophta, which is to say, the God or King or Spirit of the waters. They represented it under the figure of a Lion, and it is one of the twelve signs of the Zodiac. They venerated it just like a God because, when the Sun enters the sign of Leo, Mophta their God grants an increase in the waters of the Nile, which brings fertility to the land of Egypt. For this reason, in memory of this benefit, they placed the measure of the Nile's increase among the "letters of animals" <note>hieroglyphs</note>.

The nature of that Nilometer <note>a device for measuring the Nile's height</note> placed among the hieroglyphics will be discussed elsewhere. This agrees most beautifully with what Horapollo <note>author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> describes in Book 1, Hieroglyph 21, in these words:

> When signifying the rising of the Nile—which they call *Nun* in Egyptian, which when interpreted means "new"—they sometimes draw a lion, and sometimes three large water-jars. Sometimes they draw a heart and the earth gushing forth water. They use the lion because the Sun, being in the sign of Leo, makes the rising of the Nile more abundant; for as long as the sun remains in this zodiac sign, the double portion of the new water often overflows. Whence the ancient overseers of the priestly works fashioned the gutters and the inlets of the sacred fountains in the shape of lions. Because of this, even to this day, they make the form of the lion in accordance with a prayer for an abundance of moisture.

<margin>What "Nun" means in Egyptian.</margin>
Furthermore, to signify the inundation of the Nile, which they call *Nun* in Egyptian (meaning "new"), they frequently paint a Lion, or sometimes three large water-jars, or occasionally 
<margin>Three water-jars.</margin>
the heaven and the earth gushing with a mountain of water. The Lion is used because when the Sun enters Leo, it causes a greater inundation of the Nile; for as long as the Sun stays in this sign, the water of the Nile often increases to double its size. Because of this, those who oversee the sacred works are accustomed to present the pipes and channels of the sacred fountains in the shape of a Lion. Therefore, even to the present day, when they pour out prayers for an abundant inundation, they form the sign of the Lion.

Thus, the letters "ee, n" <note>Nun</note> could easily have been substituted in that place by mistake.

<margin>
The etymology of Mophta.
Nephte
</margin>
For both the etymology itself and the name of the God *Mophta*—composed of *Mo* and *Phta*—clearly declare that it ought to be called *Mophta*. Indeed, I believe *Mophta* to be the same as the one Plutarch calls *Nephte*, one of those five Egyptian gods whose names they used to title the five *intercalary* <note>original: ἐπαγομένους; these are the five extra days added to the 360-day calendar to align with the solar year</note> or leap-year days. These days occurred at nearly the same time that the Sun enters the sign of Leo. For the letter *m* could easily be changed into *n*, which I remember observing in other similar names such as *Moph* and *Noph*, and *Moncorius* and *Noncorius*, just as in this present word I have noted the exchange of *Mon* and *Nun*.

<margin>What Mophta signifies.</margin>
By *Mophta*, they understood a Divinity: that strengthening power of the Archetype <note>the original divine pattern or world-soul</note> acting upon earthly powers, or the fiery force of the Sun. Through this force, the Sun acts upon moisture, stimulating it so that the earth—enriched as if recovering from a long period of decay—is strengthened and rendered fit and suitable for bearing fruit. For when the Sun enters Leo, being at its hottest at that time, it gathers a vast abundance of vapors drawn from rivers, lakes, and seas within the highest mountains of Ethiopia. When these gathered vapors are released into water, both the rivers and lakes, and most especially the Nile situated below Ethiopia,

The Bembine Tablet <note>a famous bronze tablet with pseudo-hieroglyphs, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note> provides us with this entire idea expressed in a beautiful hieroglyphic. The front post of this bed is a Lion's paw, joined to the head in such a way that they appear to form a single statue; the back post of the bed represents the Lion's hind leg, with the tail curved into the shape of a crescent moon <note>original: Lunæ sextilis</note>. Beneath the bed are placed three canopic jars or water vessels, the first of which is marked with a dog's face, the second with a hawk's face, and the third with a human face. This hieroglyphic scheme signifies nothing other than the descent of the tri-form Divinity (or the World Soul, indicated by the winged globe above) into Horus or the Sun; and the Sun into the Nile through the Lion-like power of Mophta, by which Anubis (the dog-headed one <note>original: κυνοκέφαλος</note>), Osiris (the hawk-formed one <note>original: ἱερακόμορφος</note>), and Kanub (or Canopus), the Guardian Spirits of the Nile, act to procure the fertility of the earth, and...

# HIEROGLYPHICS

<page-num>285</page-num>

...the abundance of subterranean waters and all good things are stirred up. Through Anubis, providence and protection are signified; through the hawk's head marked with a crescent moon <note>original: *sextili*</note>, the power of the Sun mixed with the Moon, or Osiris combined with the Earth is shown. Finally, through the Canopus <note>a deity represented as a vessel with a human head</note>, the beneficial intelligence of the element of moisture is indicated, as Plutarch testifies and as was shown in Book 3. All these things are beautifully expressed through the Lotus flower, which we see everywhere appropriately depicted alongside the figure of the Lion as a symbol of the Sun (concerning which we shall speak in its proper place). But lest anyone say we have handed these things down based on mere conjecture:

<margin>Horapollo</margin>
Let us hear Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, the legendary author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, who describes the Nile being indicated by three water jars, or Canopi, in these words: *Three jars, representing either heaven and the earth which gushes with a bounty of water; what is the jar? They make it similar to a heart having a tongue. A heart, because among them this is considered the ruling and most powerful part of the whole body, just as the Nile is established as the leader and prince of all Egypt. They call it a tongue because it delights in always being in moisture, and moreover they call it the parent and cause of the state of things. Furthermore, they paint three jars, neither more nor less, because according to their opinion there is a triple cause that effects the inundation.* <note>original Greek: "Τρία δὲ ὑδρία... τριμερὴς ὑπάρχει"</note> Do you see, therefore, how the vessels ending in a point from a wide base express the shape of a heart, and how the attached leaf of the Persea tree <note>original: *persae folium*; a sacred Egyptian tree</note> expresses the tongue? Do you also see those who, through the three different spirits explained above, assigned a triple cause for the inundation? Through three manifold jars, they also indicated the three parts of Egyptian philosophy to which this Lion-hieroglyphic can be adapted: namely, through the human face, that part of philosophy which pertains to reason; through the hawk-face in the form of the moon, that which pertains to nature; and through the canine face, that which belongs to ethics, as will be explained more extensively elsewhere.

<margin>Mithras in lion-form and its explanation.</margin>
And from here the first of the Persians, having been instructed by the Egyptians, expressed the fiery power of the Sun by representing Mithras in lion-form <note>original: *λεοντόμορφον*</note>, enclosed within a cave (by which they interpreted the universe). This cave had two parts, Northern and Southern, through which they indicated the effects of the Sun as it runs between the tropics; concerning which, see Porphyry’s beautiful discussion in *On the Cave of the Nymphs*. The Egyptians aptly denoted this idea through that hieroglyphic which can be seen on the Bembine Table <note>the *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze tablet featuring Egyptian-style motifs, likely of Roman origin</note>: namely, within a gateway stands a statue in lion-form, adorned with various symbols, all of which look toward the idea of the present subject. There you see a serpent emerging from a circle, within which a scarab is enclosed, placed like a headband <note>original: *struppi*</note> upon the lion’s head; by this, Momphta, or the solar power of the Lion-God, was indicated. While this power enters the innermost parts of the world, it animates and fertilizes all things, which are also aptly represented by the handled cross— <note>the *crucem ansatam*, known today as the Ankh</note>

# BOOK IV. THE CONCEPT

...indicated by the handled cross <note>the *Ankh*, original: *ansatam*</note> which she carries in her left hand, and by the lotus scepter. I would interpret all these things more extensively in this place, were it not that I have reserved them for other sections; and so, let us return to the subject at hand.

<margin>Hieroglyphics of the Lion</margin>
First, the Lion was the hieroglyph of the Divine Power *Mophta* <note>A Kircherian name for a solar/creative deity associated with the Nile's source</note>. Secondly, it represented the flooding of the *Nile*, which occurred when the Sun entered the sign of Leo; this was thought to be caused by the fiery power of the Sun dissolving moist vapors. They sketched this event in various ways: either through a reclining Lion, or through one with a human or *Virgin’s* face—because this flooding happens as the Sun passes from Leo into the sign of *Isis*, or the *Virgin*—or through a Lion marked with the face of a hawk and possessing wings as if attempting flight, as can be seen in the *Bembine* table <note>An ancient bronze tablet, also called the *Mensa Isiaca*, which Kircher believed held the key to hieroglyphs</note>. What they signified through such symbols in an anagogical <term>anagogical: a spiritual or mystical interpretation that points toward a higher reality</term> sense will be discussed elsewhere. Thirdly, *Horus* <note>Horapollo, the 5th-century author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> describes at length in Book 1, Hieroglyph 19, what they understood by the Lion placed before the valves and doors of temples, which we shall discuss in its proper place.

<margin>Moral explanation of the Lion's symbols</margin>
Furthermore, the figure of the Lion, depicted in various ways, demonstrated the manifold emotions and functions of man. For instance, a man endowed with virtue was represented by the Lion’s skin; for this reason, the poets say it was dedicated to *Hercules*, the tamer of monsters—that is, the subduer of the soul’s disturbances. Again, a man who offers a unique example of fortitude, a standard of magnanimity, and a model of prudence was represented by a Lion and a *Fox*, according to the testimony of *Horus*; through the former, they expressed strength and magnanimity, and through the latter, prudence. Finally, because the *Egyptians* believed that the Lion sleeps with its eyes open, or spends sleepless nights, they painted the Lion as a hieroglyph of vigilance and guardianship, as *Horus* testifies. This is the primary reason why Lions were both painted and sculpted beside the doors of temples, a custom that has persisted even to our own times.

<margin>What a Lion devouring an Ape signifies</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that the *Egyptians* indicated a person suffering from a fever by a Lion devouring an Ape (according to *Horus*) contains other mystical reasons. Since they understand the Moon by the "Ape" (as will be said later), and by "fever" they mean *Egypt* suffering from a certain febrile aridity and dryness; therefore, the Sun—or the Lion—devouring the Ape signifies nothing other than the mixing of solar light with the lunar. By this, the Sun is imbued and, as it were, saturated with fertile moisture, watering the earth and freeing it from "fever"—that is, from destructive aridity and dryness. However, most of those hieroglyphs by which the ancients designated the operations of nature can also be transferred to moral behavior "according to analogy" <note>original Greek: *κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν*</note>, which we have also provided in the third book of this work.

<margin>A gluttonous man exhibited hieroglyphically</margin>
In this manner, *Horus*, designating a gluttonous man, draws a Lion feeding on pieces of meat. For a man with a foul-smelling mouth, he paints the gaping mouth of a Lion, on account of the heavy-smelling breath of this animal. An avenger is shown by a Lion pierced with a spear, for the Lion knows its striker. An angry man is shown by a Lion's head, for this animal is "great-hearted" <note>original Greek: *μεγαλεκάρδιος*, meaning high-spirited or stout-hearted</note> and endowed with fiery pupils in its eyes. They also expressed the shameful parts of a woman through a Lioness, because that area smelled of a leonine stench, much like the herb which is for that reason called *vuluularia* <note>Likely *Stinking Goosefoot*, known for its foul odor</note>. They represented great movements of anger by a Lion whipping its cubs with its tail; and anger itself by the Lion...

Kircher relies heavily on the "hieroglyphs" of Horapollo to explain how the Lion's physical traits were translated into abstract concepts.</summary>

### HIEROGLYPHICS

...[they depicted] the Lion and flogged cubs, because it was believed that lions' bones, when struck together, emitted fire. Through the Lioness, they signified a "once-bearing" woman <note>original Greek: *monotokos*</note>, or one who brings forth young only once in a lifetime, as they believed the Lioness did not give birth twice. All these matters are described at length in the work of Horus <note>Horapollo, a 5th-century author who wrote a famous treatise on hieroglyphs</note>. However, most of the symbols in Horus are not so much hieroglyphic as they are allegorical symbols and emblems invented for the shaping of morals; for no trace of these last-mentioned images is found among the hieroglyphs visible on the Obelisks, sphinxes, canopic jars, or other tablets. For this reason, I would consider most of Horapollo’s descriptions, with a few exceptions, to be counted among allegorical proverbs <term>apophthegms: concise sayings or maxims</term> rather than true hieroglyphics.

<margin>Various symbols of Osiris.</margin>
As for what the Egyptians intended to suggest through the image of Osiris, which reflects the face of a lion or a cat, various authors have offered various conjectures. Some, persuaded by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> in Book 1, Part 2, Chapter 2, think Osiris is seen in so many different forms because Osiris, like all subsequent Egyptian Kings, used to wear the front part of a Lion, Bull, or Dragon on his head as an insignia of leadership. We, however, say they wore the head of a Lion or Bull on their own heads both for the worship of such Gods and to secure their favor and attraction. Others say this was done because, when Typhon <note>The chaotic antagonist of Osiris</note> occupied Egypt, the Gods transformed themselves into the shapes of various beasts to protect themselves from his fury and madness, so that they might be immune to his rage; we will speak of this metamorphosis later, as it is not entirely irrelevant to our purpose. Plutarch, offering the genuine reason for this leonine metamorphosis among others, says: *"They dedicate the Lion to the Sun because, among all curved-clawed quadrupeds, the Lioness alone gives birth once; because she sleeps for only a moment, and her eyes shine while she sleeps; and because they find the Leontine springs and their openings filled with new water when the Nile overflows, which happens when the Sun passes through Leo."*

<margin>Why the Lion was placed among the stars</margin>
The ancient inventors of fables imagined that after the most ferocious Nemean Lion was killed by Hercules—who was then a youth of only sixteen or eighteen years—Jupiter placed the image of this Lion as the fifth among the twelve signs in the Heavens to commemorate his valor, as a testament to Herculean strength. Moreover, that Hercules is the Sun is shown both by his club and by the lion's skin added as his badge <note>attributes representing solar rays and power</note>, but most especially by the etymology of his name. Macrobius <note>a late Roman writer</note> writes on this in Chapter 20 of Book 1 in these words: *"And indeed, that Hercules is the Sun is clear even from his name; for what else is Heracles but Hera’s glory <note>original Greek: Ἥρας κλέος</note>, that is, the glory of the air? Furthermore, what other glory is there of the air but the illumination of the Sun, at whose departure darkness and gloom rush in?"* This explanation seems to have so pleased Pontanus <note>Giovanni Gioviano Pontanus, a Renaissance humanist poet</note> in his first book *On the Stars* that he took it as suitable material for his verses:

<margin>Etymology of Hercules.</margin>
<margin>Pontanus.</margin>
> . . . . *Bearing the Herculean name, when*
> *He scatters the clouds of the air and provides light:*
> *He is the God of the air himself, a God and his own glory of Heaven.*

Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> follows another reasoning for the etymology, whose words are read in Eusebius: *"He gave the name Hercules to the Sun because of his breaking through the air <note>original Greek: ek tou klasthai auton pros ton aera</note> as he goes from the East to the West, the father of time."*

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

->He who cries out through the dawn and the black night,<-
->Dragging through twelve wretched struggles from the east to the west.<-
<note>original Greek: Ὃς περὶ κεκραγαῖς ἡῶ καὶ νύκτα μέλαιναν / Δώδεκ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἀντολῶν ἄχει δυσμῶν ἄθλια δέρπων.</note>

->*He who bears mightily the dawn and the darkening night,*<-
->*Toiling through twelve contests from the Sunrise to the Setting.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Qui valde fers auroram noctemque nigrantem / Sex bis ad occasum exanthlans certamina ad Ortum.*</note>

<margin>The 12 Labors.</margin>
By these words, truly nothing else is suggested but those twelve labors of Hercules—which poetic chatter has attributed to him—representing the Sun’s journey through the twelve signs of the Zodiac in the world. As Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher of the 3rd century</note> mentions in the works of Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note>: 
<margin>The Club of Hercules.</margin>
what the club and the lion skin signify, the cited Porphyry shows with these words: *They assign him a club and a lion skin; the former to indicate the inequality of his motion, and the latter because he displays his greatest strength specifically in the sign of Leo <note>the Lion</note>.*
<margin>Macrobius.</margin>
Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer</note> likewise, in the *Saturnalia*, book 1, chapter 21, fits the nature of the Lion to the Sun with these words: *In the Zodiac, they consecrated that animal in the part of the sky where the Sun, in its annual course, seethes with the most powerful heat. They call the sign of Leo the "house of the Lion" because that animal seems to derive its substance from the nature of the Sun. First, it surpasses other animals in force and heat, just as the Sun surpasses the stars. The Lion is strong in the front part of its body but grows weaker in its hind members; similarly, the Sun's power grows from the first part of the day toward noon, and from the first part of the year—spring—into summer, but soon it fades as it is led either toward the setting of the day or toward winter, which is seen as the lower part of the year. Furthermore, the lion is always seen with open and fiery eyes, just as the Sun looks upon the earth with an open and fiery eye in a perpetual and tireless gaze. These words are certainly so clear that they do not require a more extensive explanation.*

<margin>What do the bow and arrows mean? What do the poplar leaves signify?</margin>
Adding to the confirmation of these sayings are the bow and arrow, by which nothing else is signified but the power of the solar rays, of which mention has already been made above. The Physician <note>referring to the Sun/Apollo/Hercules as a healer</note> is said to be crowned with a wreath of poplar, because, as Porphyry testifies, the Sun drives far away the evils from these lower regions. Truly, the poplar crown with which he was wreathed shows nothing else but the cycles of night and day; for just as the leaves of the poplar are white on one side and darkened with a black-green on the other, so the Sun, by its alternating movements of rising and setting, leaves the earth either luminous or shadowy. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> also relates that Osiris, having taken Hercules as his companion, traveled the whole world; by which he certainly means nothing else but the masculine strength of the Sun subjecting all things to itself, and that fiery vigor by which this sensible world is, to some extent, nourished and sustained.

<margin>The Lion is sacred to the Sun.</margin>
Thus the Lion was sacred to the Sun because, as Macrobius says in the *Dream of Scipio*: *When souls, by sliding down, arrive from Cancer to Leo, they begin the first stage of their future condition there. Because the beginnings of birth and the first steps of human nature are in Leo, and Aquarius is opposite to Leo and sets as soon as Leo rises, therefore when the Sun holds Aquarius, sacrifices are made to the spirits of the dead <term>Manes: the deified spirits of ancestors or the dead</term>.*

In all things, therefore, the Lion represents the Sun: in its heat, light; in its mane, the rays; in the glare of its eyes, the brightness of the Sun; in its passion, the intense heat; in its sleepless vigilance, the unwearied labor of the Sun. And since the Lion is a most fervent animal (to the point that Pliny, cited above, claimed that fire could be struck from its bones as if from a flint), it was held in the highest honor due to this analogy with the Sun, in...

### HIEROGLYPHICS

...in whose honor they dedicated both cities and temples. But let us hear Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note>:
<margin>Pliny.</margin>
*For lions in Egypt,* he says, *not only is religious worship granted, but a city even took its name from them <note>Leontopolis, the "City of the Lion"</note>. It will not be out of place to explain their power and nature: they have temples consecrated to them, and spacious seats for resting, and wide spaces and courses for exercise; then, they are provided daily with beef, which is torn apart*
<margin>The ridiculous worship of the Lion.</margin>
*and stripped of its bones. While the lions eat and finish this, the Egyptians chant to them in the Egyptian tongue; the theme of this song is that they should not cast a spell <note>original: "fascinent" — to bewitch or cast an evil eye</note> upon any of the onlookers. Indeed, not only do many of them hold divinity and religious status among the Egyptians, but seats are dedicated to them. These have windows facing opposite directions; those that pertain to the rising of the Sun and those that look toward its setting are kept open to provide them with a more pleasant way of living and a more delightful home to dwell in. They also have places for exercise to maintain their health, as well as nearby wrestling grounds <note>palaestrae</note>. The Egyptians consecrate them to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, here used to represent the Egyptian Ptah</note> for this reason (for Vulcan is nothing other than a certain fiery power of the subterranean Sun, shining forth like lightning), because they are of a violently fiery nature; and thus, because of the intensity of their internal fire, they can only with great difficulty look upon an external fire.*

And from all these things it is clear that just as the Egyptians used the image of Osiris in the form of a hawk <note>the falcon-headed Horus or Osiris</note> to indicate the clear power of the Sun which penetrates all things; so, on account of his supreme strength in action and his corroborating force, they represented that same power under the form of a Lion. Hence, on the Mahuteo, Mediceo, and Caelimontana Obelisks <note>three specific Egyptian obelisks located in Rome</note>, you see placed the lion-shaped image of Mophta <note>A Kircherian term for a specific solar spirit or "genius"</note>, equipped with a Tautic character <note>A symbol related to the "Tau" cross or the Egyptian Ankh</note>; the ideal meaning of which follows:

<margin>Note, Reader: the head of this figure must be understood not as a hawk, but as a Lion.</margin>

◯ *Of the sacred or divine Osiris*

[Figure] *Or the fiery power and strength of the Sun*

♀ *By which he strengthens and preserves the World, the Heavens, and the elements, and therefore all things which are composed of them, by his own virtue.*

Furthermore, the Sun was depicted with the face of a Lion, says Lutatius Placidus <note>A 5th-century grammarian and commentator</note>, either because this God excels others by the force of his name and power, as the Lion does among other beasts, or because it is a swift animal. Minutius Felix seems to have written about this and similar idols in his *Octavius* when he says:
<margin>Lutatius Placidus.</margin>
*You speak of Gods mixed from a Goat and a man, and of Gods with the faces of Lions and Dogs.* Arnobius, in his book *Against the Heathen*, also says: *Among the Gods we see Lions with the grimmest faces, smeared with pure vermilion, and called by a "fruit-bearing" name.* And Tertullian also says: *They ought to have worshipped that two-formed Deity immediately, because they received Gods mixed from canine and leonine heads; and horned from goats and rams; and goats from the loins; and snakes from the legs; and winged from the soles of their feet or their backs.* From this, Porphyry seems to have taken the origin in his fourth book *On Abstinence*, regarding his own heresy...

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>Regarding the composition of idols, any animal was joined with a human.</margin>
...of establishing their own [ideas]; namely, that for the composition of idols, any animal was joined with a human in ancient times, such as when the face of some bird or a lion was joined to a human body. Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century Greek satirist</note> seems to have had this in mind when he recounts the "celestial lion-headed ones" <note>original Greek: λεοντοκεφάλους αἰθερίους (leontokephalous aitherious)</note>. Indeed, these things were inserted for their mystical meanings not only among the Egyptians, but among all nations and peoples everywhere, as various inscriptions testify. Simandius <note>Likely Osymandias, the name used by Greek historians for Pharaoh Ramses II</note> wished for the head of a terrifying lion to be painted on his tomb as a sign of his courage. According to Hesychius, lions are dedicated to the springs of the Alpheus river. In Sicyon, as witness accounts tell, a lion lulled in sleep is seen in the temple of Aesculapius <note>The god of healing</note>. But if you desire more on these and similar matters, consult Suidas, Herodotus, Coelius, Diodorus, Gyraldus, Pierius, and others.

<margin>What the Magi and dream-interpreters signified through the parts of the Lion. What Apollonius of Tyana noted regarding a lioness carrying 8 cubs in her womb.</margin>
For this reason, the Magi made much use of the lion in their divinations. For dream-interpreters <note>original: Oniromantæ</note> assert that a lion appearing in a dream portends leadership and dominion. They confirm this with the dream of Olympia, the wife of King Philip of Macedon, who appeared in her sleep to give birth to a lion, and shortly after she bore Alexander, the terrifying ruler of the world. Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note> also, when he had traveled not far from Babylon, found a lioness whose womb had been cut open, in which eight cubs were found. From this he conjectured that his journey to the King of the Indians would last one year and eight months. For the ancients believed that the lion possessed something above that which is merely a brute beast. From this, no doubt, comes what is read regarding a similar matter in Philostratus’s *Life of Apollonius*:

<margin>A marvelous example regarding the Lion from Philostratus's "Life of Apollonius."</margin>
> *A certain man,* he says, *led a tame lion on a leash like a dog, wherever he wished. The lion not only fawned upon the one who led him, but upon all others who met him; even entering temples, yet he touched none of the sacred sacrifices. This lion, coming to Apollonius—who by chance was then sitting in a temple—and falling down at his knees, seemed to supplicate even more humbly than men do. Seeing this, those standing by thought he did it for the sake of a reward. But Apollonius, looking at him, said: "This lion asks me to teach you that he possesses the soul of a man. This is Amasis, once King of Egypt in the district of Sais." <note>Amasis II was a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty</note> Hearing these words, the lion roared with a wondrous and mournful sound, then gnashing his teeth and undoubtedly appearing to weep, he most fittingly shed tears. Therefore, Apollonius, stroking him, said: "I judge that the lion should be sent to Leontopolis <note>The "City of the Lion" in Egypt</note> and placed there in the temple; for I judge it wrong for a King turned into a royal beast to beg like a pauper." After this, the Priests gathered together and sacrificed to Amasis, and they sent the beast, adorned with collars and ribbons, into the interior of Egypt, singing songs and hymns on flutes before him; thus far Philostratus.*

<margin>The transmigration of souls <note>original: Metempsychosis</note>.</margin>
All the Magi also believe in the transmigration of souls, suggesting a nature common to us and the rest of the animals. They call the hymn-singers or those initiated into the sacred rites "Lions," and the women initiated into the same rites "Lionesses," while those serving are called "Ravens." They call the fathers "Eagles" and "Hawks," and those who are initiated into the Leonine rites are surrounded with various figures of animals, as Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> testifies; and such is the excellence and dignity of the lion.

### AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER IV.
Oo 2
<meta>catchword: meris</meta>

<margin>John Cassian regarding Ham.</margin>
...but if he had not derived some portion of it into himself, having been instructed by the Egyptians in the aforementioned parts; hence arose that "itch" for the science of hidden things among his descendants. Who, then, among those descendants wrote about these matters, and how they were propagated down to our own times, I have seen fit to demonstrate in this place from the surviving fragments of authors of all ages; beginning with the first writer. Thus Ham, the son of Noah—the first "Zoroaster" <note>A common early modern identification of the biblical Ham with the Persian sage Zoroaster</note> after the Flood—is said to have been the first to transmit the monuments of Magic to the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Phoenicians, and Persians. Regarding him, John Cassian <note>A 5th-century Christian monk and theologian</note> speaks beautifully in his 8th *Collation*, chapter 21, the words of which were cited above on page 4, which you may consult. Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century French theologian known for his "Ecclesiastical History"</note> agrees with this in his *Ecclesiastical History*, reporting from Clement and Josephus that Ham inscribed the Magic art, Astrology, and other arts upon fourteen columns—seven made of brick and seven of bronze—to protect them against water <note>the Flood</note> and fire.

<margin>The Books of Mercury, in Clement, Book 6 of the *Stromata*.</margin>
Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth</note> followed him, being the second Zoroaster, who corrected the false doctrine of Ham, Mizraim, and the other sons, and (as was proven in the preceding pages) published a doctrine conforming to that of the ancestors. He was the author of letters, and because of his singular knowledge of natural things, he too was called Zoroaster by the Chaldeans, as we have proven above. But regarding the books of Hermes, let us hear Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> in Book 6 of the *Stromata*, page 130: "There are therefore forty-two books of *Mercury* <note>original: Mercurij</note> which are highly necessary; thirty-six of these contain the entire philosophy of the Egyptians, which those previously mentioned as the Presidents of the Sacred Rites learn by heart. The remaining six are studied by the *Pastophoroi* <note>original Greek: παστοφόροι, meaning shrine-bearers or those who carry the sacred robe</note>, which pertain to medicine: namely, on the construction of the body, on diseases, on instruments and medicines, on the eyes, and on women." Origen says in his book *Against Celsus* that fragments of these were still surviving in the libraries of Egypt in his time. Certainly, it will be seen in the course of this work that many Arabs and Chaldeans inserted excerpts from Hermes into their own monuments. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> testifies that the ancients wrote many of these things; indeed, those fragments of the Oracles, upon which Pletho and Psellus <note>Byzantine scholars</note> wrote voluminous commentaries, should be considered as belonging to no other than the said Mercury Trismegistus, the second Zoroaster, as we have proven elsewhere. Read concerning these the small work by

<margin>Johannes Opsopoeus in his work on the Oracles of Zoroaster.</margin>
Johannes Opsopoeus, printed in Paris in the year 1612. The Oracles and Wisdom of this Zoroaster also exist in the Vatican and Altemps libraries in various fragments, which will be cited in their proper time, both here and in my *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>.

<margin>Iochaiades in the Zohar.</margin>
The Chaldeans, truly, also made these things their own property, as Iochaiades <note>Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note> beautifully shows in his book filled with hidden things, which he entitles the *Zohar*; there, having been instructed by the Egyptians, he establishes five orders of Sages: namely, the *Chesdaim*, *Asaphim*, *Hartamim*, *Mecalschephim*, and *Cazarim*, which orders are also indicated in the book of Daniel, chapter 7 <note>Though the list of wise men appears in Daniel 2:2</note>.
<margin>The Five Orders of Sages.</margin>
<margin>כשדים <gloss>Chasdim</gloss>: what kind they were.</margin>
By the *Chesdaim* <note>Chaldeans</note> he designates the "Genethliaci" <note>Casters of birth-horoscopes</note>, who Pliny says had their beginning from Belus Jupiter, the father of Ninus, King of the Assyrians. These men observed the motions of the heavens most diligently and were occupied with the calculations of Astronomy and predictions.
<margin>Philo in his book on Abraham.</margin>
Philo also mentions them in his book *On Abraham* in this manner:
> "The Chaldeans, being skilled in the science of the stars, attributed all things to the motions of the stars, by which they believed the powers of the world were dispensed, which consists of num—"

It highlights the "forty-two books of Hermes" and the various classes of wise men in the ancient Near East who preserved this hidden wisdom.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV. BOOK II. ON THE INSTITUTION [OF WISDOM]

<margin>The World believed to be GOD by the ancients.</margin>
...[nu]mbers and their proportions; these men, not perceiving invisible and intelligible things through visible objects, worshipped the latter. They scrutinized only the order of those things, and thus from the circuits of the *Sun*, *Moon*, *Planets*, and *Fixed Stars*, and the shifts of the year distinct in its four seasons, and the consensus of celestial and terrestrial things, they judged the world itself to be **GOD**. By this profane opinion, they made the creature equal to the Creator. And this is the first branch derived from the *Egyptian Hermes Zoroaster* <note>Kircher frequently conflates the Persian sage Zoroaster with the Egyptian Hermes Trismegistus</note>; for while he symbolically indicated the invisible virtues of the one *GOD* through these visible substances of the world—the *Sun*, *Moon*, and *Stars*—they, looking only at the visible things and believing everything to be full of "Sensible Divinities," eventually provided the first world and its descendants with a nursery for all idolatry and superstition.

<margin>
2. The Sages of the Order of
אשפים
<term>Asaphim</term> <note>original: "Asaphim." Often translated as "enchanters" or "astrologers" in biblical contexts.</note>
</margin>
The *Asaphim*, who are called *Philosophers* by the ancient translator of the *Latin* edition <note>The Vulgate</note> and *Magi* by the *Septuagint Translators* <note>The 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, philosophized regarding the causes of all things, both divine and human. Some believe their author was *Balaam* <note>A non-Israelite prophet mentioned in the Book of Numbers</note>, who was instructed by his contemporary *Hermes*; I find that *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar, c. 184–253 AD</note> wrote this very thing in his *book against Celsus*. It was by the scripture of his prophecy that, after many centuries, the *Magi* were warned and set out from the East to Judea to adore *Christ*. However, we more truly prove that this flowed from *Zoroaster*, whom we have shown elsewhere to also be called *Balaam*; their decrees will be examined more extensively in another place.

<margin>
3. The Sages of the Order of
חרטמים
<term>Hartumim</term> <note>original: "Hartumim." Traditionally referring to Egyptian priest-magicians or diviners.</note>
</margin>
Furthermore, the *Hartumim*, who are called <gloss>enchanters</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐπαοιδοὶ (epaoidoi)</note> by the *Septuagint* and *Soothsayers* <note>original Latin: "Harioli"</note> by *St. Jerome*, were devoted to the execrations of Demons. According to the testimony of *Justin* and *Augustine*, they drew their origin from the *Egyptian Hermes Zoroaster*, the true inventor of *Magic*. This art was later corrupted by another Magus of the same name and led down into the delusions of incantations.

<margin>
4. The Sages of the Order of
מכשפים
<term>Mecaschaphim</term> <note>original: "Mecaschaphim." Usually translated as sorcerers or witches.</note>
</margin>
The *Mecaschaphim*, who are called <gloss>sorcerers</gloss> <note>original Greek: φαρμακοὶ (pharmakoi), implying the use of drugs or potions</note> by the *Septuagint Translators*, are called *poisoners* by *Jerome*. He believes them to be those who use blood and sacrificial victims, and who often touch the bodies of the dead and derive [their power] from them; concerning their rites and ceremonies, we shall treat extensively in the following sections.

<margin>
5. The Sages of the Order of
גזרים
<term>Gezarim</term> <note>original: "Gezarim." Often translated as "soothsayers" or "astrologers" who "cut" or determine fates.</note>
</margin>
The *Gazarim*, or as the *Septuagint* translates them, *Gazarenes*, are called *Haruspices* <note>Priests in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note> by *Jerome*, or those who divine by inspecting the intestines of sacrificial victims. And these were the parts of *Chaldean Wisdom*, which lasted from the times of *Ham* until the times of *Nebuchadnezzar*. We read that *Daniel* was also imbued with these in *Daniel 7* <note>Likely a reference to Daniel 1 or 2, where Daniel is trained in the wisdom of the Chaldeans</note>, and this was, as I have said, a branch propagated from the fifth part of *Egyptian Wisdom*, which they called *Magic*. From this source came the book of *Ham*, containing the elements and practice of the *Necromantic* art—a book published under the name of *Ham* by impious Magi through a certain counterfeit birth, which *Cecco d'Ascoli* <note>A 14th-century Italian encyclopedist and poet</note> also mentions in his book *on the Sphere*. For those treating these matters more extensively, consult the *Rambam* <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in his great *Talmudic Work*, and in the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More nebuchim"</note>, *Book 3, Chapter 29*.

But to return to our purpose. *Hermes* therefore composed various books, from which first the *Chaldeans* and then the *Sabaeans* made the foundations of their superstition. Now, the *Sabaeans* were from the seed of *Cush*, who [followed] the [teachings] of Zoroaster...

<meta>catchword: per- (part of "perpetuated" or "persisted")</meta>

It explains how symbolic theology devolved into idolatry, sorcery, and divination among the Chaldeans and Egyptians.</summary>
