# AND THE STRUCTURE OF HIEROGLYPHICS. 109 CH. IV.

<margin>The Sabeans expelled from Egypt by Hermes as heretics.</margin>
...steeped in superstitions, they were expelled as heretics by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-king of Egypt</note>, who held power in Egypt. They occupied those parts of Arabia Felix <note>Southern Arabia, modern-day Yemen</note> which face toward Chaldea. They carried with them books by which they boasted of the more learned doctrine of Hermes. These books dealt with Astrology, the hidden influences of the Stars, the making and consecration of Statues, the institution of Oracles—that is, the manufacture of speaking images—and the powers of herbs, fruits, seeds, trees, and animals, all of which they believed to be the living dwellings of the Gods. In these works, if anywhere, the hieroglyphic doctrine is certainly explained most closely according to its genuine principles, even if corrupted by innumerable superstitions, as will become clear in what follows. But lest I seem to have fabricated anything from my own wit, I bring forward as a witness to this matter the most celebrated author among the Hebrews, Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides (1138–1204)</note>, who says the following regarding the Sabeans in Part 3 of the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More nebuchim"</note>, Chapter 29:

<margin>Rambam in the *Guide for the Perplexed*.</margin>
> <note>Translation of the Hebrew quote:</note> It is known that Abraham our Father, peace be upon him, was raised in the faith of the Sabeans, who established that there is no God except the stars. When I point out to you in this chapter their books, which are now in our hands translated into the Arabic language, and their ancient annals, and I reveal to you their opinions and affairs from them, it will become clear to you. They say explicitly that the stars are deities and the Sun is the Great God. They also say that the other five planets are gods, but the two luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> are greater. You will find them clearly stating that the Sun is that which governs the upper and lower world in this language; and you will find these matters explained thus in the book called *Nabataean Agriculture* <note>original: "Abadat hagubti" (The Nabataean Agriculture)</note>.

*It is known that Abraham our Father was educated in the faith of the Sabeans, who established that there is no GOD except the stars; but when I shall have indicated to you in this chapter their books, which are now in our hands translated into the Arabic language, and their ancient Annals, and shall have brought forth their opinions from there, you will see them expressly say that the Stars are Gods, and the Sun is the great God; so they say also that the remaining five Planets are Gods, but the two luminaries are the greater Gods. You will also find them clearly saying that the Sun rules the upper and lower world; you will also find all these things in manifest words in the book called* <term>Abadat hagubti</term> <note>Kircher's transliteration of the Arabic title for "Nabataean Agriculture." He interprets it here as "concerning the culture of the Egyptians."</note>*, that is, "On the Culture of the Egyptians," and other books, of which more hereafter.*

<margin>The books of the ancient Egyptians according to Rambam, from which Ibn Wahshiyya and Abenephi took most of their material.</margin>
The writers of the Arabs make mention of these same books: Salamas in the book entitled *The Garden of the Marvels of the World*; Jalaluddin <note>original: "Gelaldinus"</note> in his treatise on the history of the ancient Egyptians; Abenephi, and Ibn Wahshiyya <note>original: "Aben Vachasia"</note> in *On the Culture of the Egyptians*, and in a book on the antiquity, life, customs, and letters of the ancient Egyptians—which I have in my possession—from which no small assistance has been brought to the study of hieroglyphs. Rambam expressly says that these books were written by the Sabeans long before the times of Moses. For in those centuries, the celebrity and fame of these books was so great throughout almost the entire world that while everyone attempted to interpret these books full of mysteries according to their own judgment, they were led into manifest idolatry. These are the words of Rambam:

> <note>Translation of the second Hebrew quote:</note> The great book on this subject is the *Nabataean Agriculture*, translated by Ibn Wahshiyya. This book is full of the madnesses of the idol-worshipers... matters toward which the souls of the common people incline and are bound, such as the making of talismans, the bringing down of spirits, sorcery, demons, and harmful spirits that dwell in the deserts... at which men of intellect would laugh...

<margin>
What the book on the culture of the Egyptians, which Abenvaschia translated, contains.
</margin>
...by them to justify and argue with the clear proofs which you know, with which all the people of the world asked them.
<s>Judge over all the children of the world.</s>
<note>Kircher is quoting a Hebrew passage from Maimonides’ *Guide for the Perplexed* regarding the Sabean belief that the Sun is the supreme judge of the world.</note>

*Among others, the most famous book is on the Agriculture of the Egyptians.* (The Hebrew text has חכבטי [*Chachbti*] corruptly; it ought to be חגושי [*Chgubti*], that is, *Gubti* <note>Coptic or Egyptian</note>, for so the Arabic has it) which *Abenuachsia* <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th-century scholar who claimed to translate ancient Nabataean texts</note> translated. It is a book full of madnesses and other things toward which men commonly lean and incline: namely, concerning the fabrication of speaking images, the descent of familiar spirits, illusions, and demons dwelling in deserts, such as satyrs, etc. From this, *Moses* took the occasion to organize the legal books <note>the Torah</note>, so that he might overturn the rites and ceremonies of the nations which were contrary to his laws, and free the chosen people of God—who were otherwise most prone to this sort of thing—from this pestilential plague. See the fragments of these books, drawn from the monuments of the Arabs and Chaldeans, which are to be brought forward a little later. Moreover, *Eusebius* (citing *Philo*, who in turn cites *Sanchoniathon*) testifies in these words that these were the books of *Mercury*, transcribed by the Sabeans at the command of *Tautus* <note>The Egyptian god Thoth</note>, or *Mercury* himself:

<margin>
The books of Tautus and the seven brothers.
</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ταῦτα φασὶ νεώτατοι πάντων ὑπομνηματίσαντο οἱ ἑπτὰ Συδὺκ παῖδες Κάϐοι, καὶ ὄγδοος αὐτῶν ἀδελφὸς Ἀσκλήπιος ὡς αὐτοῖς ἐνετείλατο Θεὸς Τααυτὸς.</note> *These things indeed, he says, the seven sons of Cabyus (or as another text more truly has it, Cabari, the Sabeans) and their eighth brother Asclepius, delivered to posterity as the first to record them, just as the God Tautus had commanded them.* But Tat, the son of Tautus, acting as a Mystic and Priest, first published certain mysteries to the world under analogies regarding nature and the world. The same *Philo* cited a little earlier in *Eusebius* testifies in these words: <note>original Greek: Ταῦτα πάντα ὁ Θαϐίωνος παῖς πρῶτος τῶν ἀπ᾿ αἰῶνος γεγονότων Φοινίκων ἱερομάντης ἀλληγορήσας, τοῖς τε φυσικοῖς καὶ κοσμικοῖς πάθεσιν ἀναμίξας, παρέδωκε τοῖς ὀργιῶσι καὶ τελετῶν κατάρχουσι προφήταις.</note> *All these things the son of Thabion (more truly Tation, or the son of Tatius), the first hierophant of the Phoenicians since the beginning of time, having allegorized them and mixed them with natural and cosmic forces, delivered them to the prophets who lead the orgies and initiations.* You see, therefore, how beautifully all these things are drawn by a single thread from the greatest of all antiquities.

<margin>
Who was Sanchoniathon?
</margin>
Who *Sanchoniathon* truly was—the most ancient of all writers after *Moses*, to whom he is believed to have been nearly equal—remains to be shown. *Sanchoniathon* of Beirut, or the *Phoenician Berytus*, lived many times before the *Trojan* war and wrote a History of the Phoenicians divided into nine books, parallel to those of the Egyptians;

<margin>
What and about whom he wrote.
</margin>
in which he treats the deeds of the Jews, the disciplines and institutions, and the sacred books of the Egyptians and Phoenicians, the most ancient nations of the world. He brought down to posterity the books of *Tautus*, or *Mercury*, which he had sought out and transcribed with the greatest care.

<margin>
Eusebius' testimony concerning Sanchoniathon.
</margin>

Φίλων δὲ τότε πᾶσαν τὴν συγγραφὴν ἐν ϐίϐλοις, οὐχ ὁ ἐϐραῖος μεταϐαλὼν ἀπὸ τῆς Φοινίκων γλώσσης ἐπὶ τῆς ἑλλάδα φωνὴν ἐξέδωκε; μιμῆται τέτων, ὁ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς τῶν καθ᾿ ὑμῶν πεποιημένος σκευὴν, ἐν τετάρτῳ τῆς πρὸς ὑμᾶς ὑποθέσεως, ὧδε τῷ ἀνδρὶ μαρτυρεῖ πρὸς λέξιν.</note> *Sanchoniathon, a most ancient man and, as is said, older than the Trojan times, relates these things; they testify that he wrote the history of the Phoenicians with the greatest diligence and truth. Did not Philo then—not the Hebrew Philo, but the one who translated the whole work from the Phoenician tongue into the Greek language—publish it? One of our own time who fashioned a defense against you <note>Porphyry</note>, in the fourth book of his work against you, mimics these things and testifies to the man word for word as follows:*

# HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>Explanation of the schema of Anubis.</margin>
And through the head marked **A**, he denotes nothing other than Anubis and his sagacity; through the sphere, he represents the discovery of things relating to celestial disciplines; through the snake-entwined <note>original: ὀφιο-μίγ-μορ-φον (*ophio-mig-morphon*), meaning "mixed with serpent forms"</note> caduceus **D**, he signifies the swift movement of the mind, fit for reasoning and discovery, by which eloquence and persuasion are prepared for drawing the souls of men in any direction; and the truth of things is indicated through the nudity **B**, just as the fertility of the mind is indicated by the exposed male genitals. He stands upon a crocodile **E**, to indicate the protection of Egypt, which is entrusted to the Genius <note>a protective spirit or tutelary deity</note> of the Nile, against Typhonian insults <note>attacks or disruptions from the chaotic god Typhon/Set</note>. Furthermore, the ram-faced <note>original: κριωπρόσωπον (*krioprosopon*)</note> head **G**, made formidable by the basket placed upon it, as well as the dual-formed <note>original: δίμορφον (*dimorphon*)</note> head **K**, equipped with a modius <note>a grain-measure or cylindrical head-dress symbolizing fertility and abundance</note>, denoted the attendants of Anubis. <margin>Explanation of the physical figure.</margin> Through the former, they appropriately expressed Amun, the presiding deity of the "fiery-moist" element, as explained in the preceding pages; through the latter, they expressed Serapis, the presiding deity of all earthly goods. These were the principal Egyptian spirits through whom all good things were procured. Through the two stars **F**, they designated the rising and setting of Sirius <note>original: σειρὶ (*seiri*)</note>, whose rising promised the increase of the Nile and the happiness of good things, while its setting promised the contrary fate. Happiness was indicated by the olive leaf **L**, and sterility by the palm leaf **M**; but contemplate all these things in the attached figure. These three deities are called the *Adelphi*, that is, "the brothers," because they seem to conspire with a common love, like brothers, for the common good of Egypt, which is committed to their faith and protection. By what sacrifices and ceremonies the Egyptians studied to appease them and make them favorable to themselves will be discussed at length elsewhere. I do not append authorities <note>citations</note> here, because most have been indicated in the preceding sections, and I would rather not produce boredom than pleasure for the reader by alleging the same authorities so many times.

<margin>Various forms of Anubis.</margin>
Instructed by the Egyptians, the Romans everywhere struck Anubis the "Cynocephalon" <note>dog-headed</note> on coins to establish public vows, distinguished by a sistrum <note>a sacred ritual rattle</note> and a caduceus; on the other side, they displayed Isis, likewise with a sistrum and a cup full of fruits. The meaning of these symbols harmonizes beautifully with those explained above; for through the sistrum, according to Plutarch, they noted nothing but the genius, or *Agathodaemon* <note>a "good spirit"</note>, by whose tinkling they believed Typhon the *antitheon* <note>the "adversary" or "opposing god"</note> was put to flight.

<image-desc>A circular Roman-style coin or medal. It depicts a canine-headed figure (Anubis or a Cynocephalus) standing and facing left. The figure is clothed in a tunic and holds a sistrum in the left hand and a caduceus in the right. Around the inner border of the circle, the words "VOTA PVBLICA" are inscribed in capital letters.</image-desc>

William Choux offers such a coin for our inspection from the collection of the most learned man, Lord Giovanni Battista Casali, as follows.

Thus, the hieroglyphic of the Dog is proposed to be viewed in various ways on our Obelisk: either through the dog-headed <note>original: κυνοκέφαλον (*kynokephalon*)</note> man, or through the complete figure of a sitting dog. First, they signified Anubis, the president of reason and the discovery of things; second, they signified the Sacred Scribe <note>original: Hierogrammatea</note>, the Priest and Vate <note>Prophet or Seer</note>, or the King. <margin>Horapollo.</margin> Horapollo <note>an author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics</note> agrees with these points in these words: *When they wish to represent a Sacred Scribe, or a prophet, they paint a dog; a Sacred Scribe indeed, because he who wishes to become a perfect Sacred Scribe must meditate much, and bark...* <note>original: Ἱερογραμματέα δὲ πάλιν, ἢ προφήτην βουλόμενοι γράφειν: κύνα ζωογραφῶσι; ἱερογραμματέα μὲν ἐπειδήπερ τὸν βουλόμενον ἱερογραμματέα τέλειον γίνεσθαι, χρὴ πολλὰ μελετᾶν, ὑλακτᾶν... (*Hierogrammatea de palin, e propheten boulomenoi graphein: kyna zoographousi; hierogrammatea men epeideper ton boulomenon hierogrammatea teleion genesthai, chre polla meletan, hylaktan...*)</note>

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>The Dog as a symbol of the Seer and Prophet.</margin>
<margin>Dogs gaze at the statues of the Gods with fixed eyes.</margin>
<note>original: συνειχῶς καὶ ἀπηχειῶσϑαι, μηδενὶ προſχαριζόμενον, ὥſπερ οἱ κύνες (*syneichōs kai apēcheiōsthai, mēdeni proscharizomenon, hōsper hoi kynes*)</note> "...continually and sounding out, showing favor to no one, just like dogs." Furthermore, it is added that because the dog, more than other animals, stares at the images of the Gods, it is like a Prophet. *Again*, the author says, *those wishing to write of a sacred Scribe, or a Seer, or a Prophet, depicted a dog. They depicted a sacred Scribe because anyone who wishes to perform this duty properly and perfectly must meditate much, and like a dog, bark continually at everyone and be fierce, showing favor to none—that is, sparing no one when rebuking a perversion of morals, and having respect for no person. They depicted a Seer or Prophet because the dog, contrary to the habit of other animals, gazes with intent and fixed eyes upon the statues of the Gods, just as seers are accustomed to do.* Ælian, in Book 7, Chapter 18, states: "I have heard it said that only the dogs of Memphis put their prey in the middle and live communally; of all animals, they especially gaze upon the statues of the Gods with fixed eyes."

<margin>Sothis or <image-desc>Coptic character for S</image-desc></margin>
<margin>The meaning of the sistrum in the hand of Anubis.</margin>
<margin>Thoth.</margin>
Furthermore, through the figure of a sitting dog with a <term>sistrum</term><note>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument used in religious ceremonies to ward off evil</note> or an <term>ankh</term><note>the "cross with a handle," a symbol of life</note>, they signified the <term>Genius of the Nile</term><note>the protective spirit of the river</note>, whom <term>Horus</term> calls **Arpokyona** or **Sothis** <note>the Egyptian name for the star Sirius</note>, but whom we more truly call <image-desc>glyph for Sothis</image-desc>. By this symbol, the rising of the Nile was noted, which occurred during the rising of the Dog Star when the Sun enters Leo. At this time, the fertility of Egypt was marvelously promoted. Through the sistrum, they denoted the "driving away" of <term>Typhon</term><note>the god of chaos, drought, and the desert</note>, who, according to <term>Plutarch</term>, destroys all things with his dryness and scorching power, as has been discussed more fully in its proper place. Hence, they dedicated the first month to <term>Mercury</term> or <term>Anubis</term> (after the earth, or <term>Isis</term>, had been fertilized by the benefits of the flood and enriched with the new seeds of things), whom they also called **Thoth** after his name. Concerning his institution, we have written most extensively in our **Hieroglyphic Astrology**, to which we refer the reader. Why **Sothis** is commonly confused with **Isis** and **Anubis** is certainly not without its mysteries, but that must be explained more opportunely elsewhere.

<margin>What the Wolf, the companion of Anubis, signifies.</margin>
<margin>The "wolf-killer" herb.</margin>
<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin>
They worshipped the <term>Wolf</term> as a living image of the Sun because this animal, as <term>Macrobius</term> explains, seizes all things just like the Sun, which draws everything to itself by the power of its rays. From this comes the surname of **Apollo Lyceus** <note>Apollo the Wolf-god</note>; from this also comes the Egyptian superstition of **Lycopolis**, where they followed the cult of **Apollo** and the wolf with equal devotion. For this reason, they even forbade the importation of the **Lycoctonum** <note>literally "wolf-killer," likely aconite or wolfsbane</note> herb into Egypt. <term>Plutarch</term> records that <term>Osiris</term>, returning from the underworld to protect <term>Isis</term> from the violence of <term>Typhon</term>, transformed himself into a Wolf. <term>Diodorus</term> also teaches that the Wolf was always a companion to <term>Osiris</term>. However, since nothing singular regarding the Wolf occurs on our Obelisk, I have decided not to discourse upon it at greater length here; rather, we have more prudently reserved this symbolic treatment of the Wolf for the proper treatises of the **Oedipus**.

<header>HIEROGLYPHICS.</header>

# HIEROGRAMMATISM VI.

## On the Dog-headed Ape or Long-tailed Monkey, and its hieroglyphic significance.

<margin>The malice of Typhon.</margin>
<margin>Horus as the world.</margin>
<margin>Mercury fashioned a lyre from the sinews of Typhon.</margin>
If the Sun were alone in the universe, it is certain that everything would be consumed by a ruinous heat and dryness. Therefore, the Egyptians—seeing that the Moon receives the Sun’s rays (which are more burning than is fair) and tempers them with her own moisture—believed that the beauty and grace of the entire sublunary world, and all the abundance of fertility, found its origin there. Indeed, they judged it impossible for the Sun to exist without the Moon, or the Moon without the Sun. For this reason, they considered them the principal and first-order Gods and Powers; according to Plutarch, Eusebius, and Diodorus, they called the Sun Osiris and the Moon Isis. However, they gave the name <term>Typhon</term><note>In Egyptian mythology, Set or Typhon represents chaos, storms, and the desert, often standing in opposition to the order of Osiris.</note> to whatever in the Sun is flawed, harmful, fatal, and imbued with a destructive force, as the same Plutarch testifies. Thus, if Typhon were alone, being contrary to the human race, he would destroy all things with his giant emptiness. Therefore, Osiris and Isis were necessary, whose son is Horus—that is, everything contained within the circuit of this worldly mass that grows, is nourished, is cherished, and reaches its perfection. For this reason, every single thing established under the protection of Osiris and Isis is armed with great zeal against the violent machinations of Typhon. Through these skirmishes, conflicts, and the discord of Typhon and his giant followers, the ancients seem to have intended to signify nothing other than the "dissonant harmonies" and "harmonious discords" of natural things, which they called the <term>antipathies</term><note>A historical concept in natural philosophy where certain elements or objects naturally repel or "dislike" each other.</note> of things, without which it is impossible for the world to be preserved. Appropriately, Plutarch records that Mercury cut out the sinews of Typhon and from them fashioned a lyre for himself; by this, the power of the universe—constituted from opposites and "dissonant-consonants"—is beautifully hinted at. In this way also, to return to our purpose, they adopted animals of a "Lunar-Solar" nature for the structure of their sacred writing; for by these animals, they signified the fertile union of the Sun with the Moon intended by nature for the perfecting of the generation of things. The animals of a Lunar-Solar nature are the dog, the cat (or <term>aelurus</term><note>From the Greek *ailouros*, meaning cat.</note>), and the <term>Cynocephalus</term><note>Literally "dog-head"; the ancient name for the baboon, which the Egyptians associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom and the moon.</note> (or long-tailed monkey), and with this last one we shall begin our discussion.

<margin>The Cynocephalus is frequent among hieroglyphics; what is it?</margin>
There was never any animal that could express a greater number of hieroglyphics than the Cynocephalus; indeed, by the icons of this beast delineated in various ways, they denoted almost all things celestial and terrestrial. The Cynocephalus—or as others call it, the <term>Caepus</term><note>Likely referring to a specific species of guenon or long-tailed monkey.</note>—is a species of monkey with a tail, having a face similar to a dog, but with eyes and a forehead not unlike the faces of men.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a baboon (Cynocephalus) sitting upright on its haunches, facing left, with its hands raised toward the sky in a traditional Egyptian gesture of worship or greeting the sun.</image-desc>

<margin>What is denoted by the Cynocephalus</margin>
First, by the figure of a standing Cynocephalus with hands raised to heaven, they indicated the time of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon. This represented the <term>Neomenia</term><note>The New Moon, or the festival marking the beginning of the lunar month.</note>, because they discovered that this animal has some kind of sympathy with the Moon. For at the time of the <term>Syzygy</term><note>The alignment of the Sun, Earth, and Moon; here specifically the conjunction at the New Moon.</note>, it would pass blood instead of urine, and it became sad and melancholy...

<header>BOOK IV. THE IDEA</header>

...as if he were mourning the abduction of the Goddess; for he would not eat, but always gazed at the earth, fleeing the company of men. Soon, however, once the <term>Syzygy</term><note>The alignment of two celestial bodies, specifically the Sun and Moon during a new moon.</note> was dissolved and the Moon began to wax, he would raise himself up as if awakened from a deep sleep, congratulating the Goddess. He would show his great consolation through unusual gestures and a rhythmic dance of his body, appearing as though he were about to offer strange applause. All of this is beautifully described by <term>Horapollo</term><note>The purported author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, which influenced Renaissance scholars' understanding of the script.</note> in Book 1, Hieroglyphic 14, in these words:

<margin>Horapollo.</margin>

> When the Egyptians wish to represent the Moon, the inhabited world, writing, a priest, or even anger or change, they paint a <term>Cynocephalus</term><note>Literally "dog-head," referring to the baboon, which was sacred to the god Thoth.</note>. They use it for the Moon because this animal possesses a certain sympathy for the Goddess's meeting [with the Sun]. For when the Moon, moving in conjunction with the Sun, becomes unlit and dark for a period of time, the male Cynocephalus does not look up nor does he eat; instead, he crouches toward the earth in sorrow, as if grieving the abduction of the Moon. The female, besides suffering the same loss of sight as the male, also bleeds from her private parts. For this reason, even to this day, Cynocephali are nourished in the sacred temples so that the time of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon can be known from them. <note>original: Horapollo's Greek text followed by the author's Latin translation.</note>

<margin>How they noted the world through the Cynocephalus.</margin>
Furthermore, let us see how they prefigured the inhabited world through the Cynocephalus. The Egyptians had received a tradition from the earliest Patriarchs after the Flood: that the world, after the confusion of languages, was divided into seventy-two nations. Since they observed that the Cynocephalus seemed to decline and prepare for death over the span of exactly seventy-two days—unlike other animals which die in a single day—they used it as a symbol. For, as Horus correctly states in the cited passage:

> These animals, if they are carefully nourished and tended in the sacred precincts, do not die in a single day like other creatures; rather, a certain part of them dies and withers each day and is buried by the Priests, while the rest of the body remains in its natural state. This continues for 72 days, at the end of which the animal finally perishes entirely. <note>original: Kircher provides the Greek text and a Latin translation of Horapollo (Horus).</note>

Therefore, they not inappropriately indicated the inhabited world, divided into 72 nations, through the Cynocephalus, as the aforementioned Horus shows in the same place:

> To signify the inhabited world, they paint a Cynocephalus, because they say there are seventy-two ancient regions of the world.

Secondly, because the Egyptian priests noted something divine in these animals—something more sublime than the typical behavior of beasts—they revered them as having a spark of the divine.

<margin>The Cynocephalus knows letters.</margin>
Specifically, they can write letters and studiously carry out the commands of the Priests. When they are brought into the <term>adyta</term><note>The innermost, most sacred part of a temple where only priests were allowed.</note>, the Priests set a tablet before them along with a reed pen and ink; soon, as if to...

# HIEROGLYPHICS.

...at the command of the High Priests, [the baboon] is said to take up a tablet and form letters. Hence, not without reason, it is considered the living dwelling of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>, as if he had been transformed into its body to teach men astronomy, writing, and all other things of which he was the inventor. So says Abenephius <note>Kircher's name for the Arabic author Ibn Wahshiyya, a common source for his Hermetic theories.</note>:

> <note>original Arabic: "وكان يصدقون ان ادريس هو هرميس تحت صورة القردة ويعلم الناس ان هذا الحيوان هو يعرف مجامعة الشمس مع القمر ويعرف الحروف ويعمل كل ما يامرون الكهن"</note>
> *For they firmly believed that Idris, who is Hermes, in the form of an ape, teaches men; for by its nature this animal knows the union of the Sun and the Moon, understands letters, and acts at the command of the Priests.*

<margin>The Cynocephalus avoids fish and is born without a foreskin.</margin>
Furthermore, since the Cynocephalus <note>Literally "dog-head," referring to the baboon.</note>—no differently than the <term>Hierophants</term><note>High priests or interpreters of sacred mysteries.</note> and Priests—shrinks from eating fish and is born without a foreskin, as if naturally circumcised, the Egyptians seem to have derived from it their laws regarding abstinence from fish and the circumcision of the foreskin. However, it is more likely they received this practice from the Hebrews; for so says Rabbi Tichon in Chapter 12 of Genesis:

"The Egyptian priests also circumcised the flesh of their foreskin, having been so instructed by the children of Israel because of the great benefits they believed would flow from circumcision—specifically, that they might administer sacred rites more purely." Truly, whatever has been said thus far is aptly confirmed by Horus <note>Horapollo.</note> in the following words:

> <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ δὲ καὶ τὸ ζῶον ἐπὶ Ἑρμῆ ἥκει τὸν πάντων μετέχοντα γραμμάτων..."</note>
> *Furthermore, this animal is dedicated to Mercury because it shares in the knowledge of all letters. It signifies a Priest because by nature the Cynocephalus abstains from eating fish; even if it should happen to feed on fish bread, the animal does not become sluggish or prone to torpor like the foreign Priests. Additionally, it is born circumcised, which is why the Priests take such great care to perform circumcision with the utmost devotion.*

<margin>The Cynocephalus denotes letters in hieroglyphics.</margin>
Thirdly, Horus shows in the cited passage that the Egyptians used the Cynocephalus to represent letters in their hieroglyphs:

> <note>original Greek: "Γράμματα σημαίνοντες οἱ ἱερεῖς, κυνοκέφαλον ζωγραφοῦσιν..."</note>
> *When signifying letters, the Priests paint a Cynocephalus, because there is among the Egyptians a certain kinship and race of Cynocephali that understand letters. Therefore, as soon as a Cynocephalus is first brought into the sacred temple, the priest sets a tablet before it along with a reed pen and ink, to test whether it belongs to that race of Cynocephali that knows letters and whether it can write; and indeed, it writes upon it.*

Aelian also mentions this admirable teachability in Book 6, Chapter 10, in these words: *That animals are teachable we learned in the time when the Ptolemaic Kings reigned; the Egyptian Priests taught Cynocephali writing, dancing, and the playing of flutes; and the Cynocephali would collect payment for these performances, casting the money they were given into a purse which they carried.*

<margin>The rising Moon indicated by the Cynocephalus.</margin>
Fourthly, when they wish to indicate the rising Moon, they again paint the Cynocephalus in this manner. The words of Horus are: *When they wish to write of the rising Moon, they draw a Cynocephalus standing with its hands raised toward the sky, wearing a royal crown upon its head.*

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

[He describes the animal] standing and lifting its hands to heaven, wearing a royal diadem on its head; he adds the reason: <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι ὁ κυνοκέφαλος ποιεῖται ὡς εἰπεῖν, περιευχόμενος τῇ Θεῷ, ἐπειδὴ ἀμφότεροι φωτὸς μετειλήφασι"</note> "Because the Cynocephalus <note>Literally "dog-head," the baboon.</note> joins in prayer, as it were, to the Goddess <note>The Moon, often identified with Isis.</note>, since both have partaken of the light." This clearly means that the Cynocephalus, in this posture, is seen to congratulate the Goddess because both—the Sun, I say, and the Moon—are sharers of light.

<margin>The Cynocephalus urinates twelve times a day; why?</margin>
Fifthly, the curious Egyptian investigators of nature discovered another wonderful property in Cynocephali, which also gave them an occasion for their hieroglyphic equipment; they observed, I say, that when the Sun enters Aries and Libra <note>The Spring and Autumn equinoxes.</note>, the Cynocephalus—out of a certain hidden property and sympathy it has with the Sun—discharges urine twelve times at intervals of the twelve hours, both by night and by day. Because of this, they seem to have found the opportunity for the construction of hydraulic clocks <note>Water clocks, known as clepsydrae.</note>. For, in imitation of the Cynocephali, they fashioned certain bronze vessels in the shape of seated baboons, which would discharge water poured into them through the "genital" as if through a pipe, in a strict and narrow stream, in proportion to the time that was to be measured. This water, being caught in a hollow cup, would show the current hour as it gradually rose to the hour-lines inscribed within the cup. A bronze vessel of this kind, <margin>The origin of hour-measuring clocks.</margin> shaped like an ape <note>original Greek: "πιθηκόμορφον"</note>, was brought to me while I was writing this from the collection <note>original: "gazophylacio"</note> of the most expert Francesco Angeloni, by his nephew Giovanni Pietro Bellori <note>Bellori was a famous 17th-century antiquarian and art historian.</note>; I have decided to place its figure here. Hence, to signify the two Equinoxes, they paint a seated Cynocephalus. But since Horus <note>Horapollo, the supposed author of a treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> describes the reason for this kind of hieroglyph most exactly in Book 1, Hieroglyph 6, it will suffice to quote his words without further explanation. For he says:

<note>original Greek: "Ἰσημερίας δύο πάλιν σημαινόντες..."</note>
"To signify the two equinoxes again, they paint a seated Cynocephalus. For during the two equinoxes of the year, it urinates twelve times a day, once for each hour. It does the same thing during the two nights. Therefore, not without reason, the Egyptians carve a seated Cynocephalus on their water-clocks; and they make water flow from its member, because, as I said before, it signifies the twelve hours of the equinox. But so that the water-mechanism does not become too wide—through which the water is discharged into the clock—nor again too narrow (for there is a need for both: for the wider opening, pouring out the water quickly, does not complete an even measurement of the hour, while the narrower opening, releasing the stream little by little and slowly, would stretch the hours out), they manufactured an iron piece of a specific thickness for this intended use. They chose to do this not without some reason, as with other things; and because during the equinoxes, it alone of all other animals cries out twelve times a day, once for each hour."

### HIEROGLYPHICS

...twelve [hours], as I have said, into which the days and nights are equally divided at the time of the equinox, it signifies the hours. Furthermore, so that the artificially constructed opening—through which water flows into and is discharged from the clock—is neither too wide nor too narrow (for both are of great consequence: if it is too wide, it pours out water with great speed and does not correctly achieve the measure and dimension of the hour; if it is too narrow, it releases the flow of water more gradually and slowly than is proper), they devised this remedy: shaving off the hair right down to the tail, they manufacture a certain iron pipe for use based on its thickness. This seemed to them not without some reason, just as they do in other matters; and because it is also the only one among all living creatures that, at the equinox, barks twelve times a day, once for each hour. You see, therefore, how aptly the description of the Hour matches what we said a little earlier regarding the hieroglyphic construction of the Cynocephalus <note>Literally "dog-head," the baboon.</note> and the water clock. It is clearly evident that this vessel was also of a "female-shaped" <note>original Greek: θηλυκόμορφον</note> use, for pouring water over the hands of the Priests performing sacred rites, as seen from the handle D, which in the figure placed a little earlier possesses remarkable "lion-toed" <note>original Greek: λεοντοδακτύλοις</note> features on its back part. But of this hieroglyphic water clock, more elsewhere at greater length.

->[A rectangular woodcut illustration depicting a seated Cynocephalus (baboon) in profile, facing left. The creature wears a crescent moon crown and holds a small cup or bowl. To its right, a tall lotus flower stands on a long stem with a leaf. Further right is a circular solar disc with radiating lines. The entire scene is framed within a simple border.]<-

From this, there was almost no temple in which—as Lucian, cited above, witnesses—one would not find either a goat, a stork, or an ape; these the people of Hermopolis <note>The "City of Hermes," a major cult center for Thoth.</note> held in the place of Deities on account of the cult of Hermes <note>The Greek equivalent of the Egyptian Thoth.</note>, to whom they were consecrated, as Strabo witnesses in Book 16. In the Bembine Table <note>A famous bronze tablet from antiquity depicting Egyptian deities, highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, a hieroglyphic of the same animal is shown in a seated form, crowned with a crescent moon like a diadem; it holds a vessel in its hand to indicate the moist power of the Moon, and it has fleawort <term>psyllium: a medicinal plant</term> joined to it, which herb—since its seed pods resemble the head of an ape—was appropriately joined to it in sacrifices to attract the Spirit through the similarity of things. On the other side, it has a lotus flower joined to it, to demonstrate the sympathy that the Cynocephalus has with the Sun and Moon, of which more will be said at length in the hieroglyphic of the Lotus. For with the Sun and Moon, as has been said and as Iamblichus witnesses, it maintains physical relationships, which are: to rejoice when the Moon rises and to be saddened when it wanes; now standing erect as if to congratulate the Heavenly Lights, and then, through its twelve-fold urination during the twelve equinoctial hours, to follow the works of the Sun; in a word, to show signs of a certain intellectual faculty in all things. Hence Minutius Felix reports that the Cynocephalus was accustomed to be joined to Isis; "Isis," he says, "mourns, laments, and seeks her lost son with her Cynocephalus and other Priests: soon, the little one having been found, Isis rejoices, the Priests exult, and the Cynocephalus, the discoverer, glories"—although in this passage they may understand Anubis <note>The jackal-headed god, often confused with the dog-headed baboon.</note> more truly by "Cynocephalus" than an ape.

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

These figures were not only commonly carved upon obelisks, but statues of this kind—of the same "flour" <note>An idiomatic way of saying "of the same type."</note>—are still viewed separately. I found one such figure still surviving on the Capitol <note>The Capitoline Hill in Rome, home to many ancient artifacts.</note>, in exactly the same pose as shown on the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet from antiquity depicting Egyptian deities, used extensively by scholars like Kircher to study hieroglyphics.</note> and in the position we have described. Clear evidence of this is also found on a mummy shroud sent to me from Florence. However, please examine the images and figures placed here, from which the reader will more easily understand my meaning.

<margin>A comparison of Anubis with the Cynocephalus.</margin>

![A rectangular woodcut divided into two horizontal sections. The upper section shows a seated cynocephalus (baboon-headed figure) in profile facing left, holding a small cup or vessel. Above its head is a crescent moon supporting a circular disk. To its right stands a tall papyrus or lotus plant. The lower section shows a smaller cynocephalus in profile, in a walking or crouching posture.](image)

According to Diodorus, Anubis was the "dog-faced" <note>original Greek: κυνοπρόσωπος</note> son of Osiris, and he used a dog as his emblem. It seems from this that he came to be called Cynocephalus <note>literally "Dog-Head"</note> after the canine head by which he was depicted. Plutarch makes him the son of Osiris and Nephthys, saying that Isis took him in after he was abandoned by his mother and kept him as a perpetual guardian. He adds that Anubis is the same as the "Horizon" and Saturn, and that he imitates Hecate, being a deity of both the heavens and the earth. Servius and Apuleius call him Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, identified with the Egyptian Thoth and Anubis.</note>, as do we; for according to Lucian, in his dialogue of Notus and Zephyrus, Mercury became "dog-faced" <note>original Greek: κυνοπρόσωπος</note> upon Isis’s arrival in Egypt and stood as her guardian. Thus, there were "votive offerings of Anubis" in the form of the Cynocephalus, as many ancient authors now demonstrate. Indeed, in the works of Virgil, Ovid, Propertius, Prudentius, and Ammianus, he is everywhere marked by the epithets "The Barker," "The Barking One," or "Dog-shaped." I have pursued these matters at such length so that it might be clear how the Cynocephalus Apes were distinguished from the Cynocephalus Anubis. But leaving these things behind, let us now turn to explaining the mystical reasons for the Cat.

### HIEROGRAMMATISM <term>Hierogrammatismus</term> VII.
<note>Kircher uses this term to refer to a sacred or symbolic explanation of a hieroglyphic figure.</note>

->*On the Cat, or the mystical and hieroglyphic significance of the Cat.*<-

<margin>What does the Cat on the top of the sistrum mean?</margin>

Among the Egyptians, the Cat was a primary hieroglyphic used to represent the Moon. For this reason, they placed a cat at the very top of the sistrum <note>A sacred rattle used in the worship of Isis.</note>, as will be discussed in its proper place. From this cat hung four movable bells, as it were, at equal intervals from one another. These were meant to signify that all things subject to birth and decay—generation and corruption—are placed beneath the lunar sphere, below which all changeable things are necessarily seen. Indeed, if you look at the Cat's shining and flashing eyes, it seems to possess something similar to the Lion; yet if you look at its natural inclinations, it is found to be entirely Lunar. This animal is like a lion in both form and gesture, and it carries out its hunting more by night than by day. Because of its variety, its power of acting at night, its fertility, and its moisture...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sacred animals in Egyptian symbolism. Having previously discussed the baboon-headed Cynocephalus and its lunar associations, the author now transitions to the cat (aelurus), explaining its physical and mythological connection to the Moon and the Sun.</meta>

### -> HIEROGLYPHICS. 303 <-

...and certainly, it is entirely similar to the Moon, both because of the phases of the Moon and the expansion and contraction of its eyes.

<margin>The cat imitates the phases of the Moon.</margin>
For the pupil of its eye dilates as the Moon waxes, and it constricts in the same proportion as the Moon wanes, so that it appears to mimic every single phase of the Moon. For this reason, the Egyptians imagined that just as the Lion was created by the Sun, the cat <term>aelurus</term> <note>From the Greek 'ailouros,' a common term for the domestic cat.</note> was brought forth by the Moon, according to this fable: They say that at the beginning of things, the Sun and Moon, having been entrusted with care by Jupiter, entered into a contest to fill the earth with animals. Thus, the Lion was shaped by the Sun, but the Moon, spurred on by rivalry, produced the cat—an animal very similar to the lion. The Greeks, borrowing this from the Egyptians, describe it in this manner:

<margin>The Fable.</margin>
They say that man was produced by Apollo <note>The god of the Sun.</note>, and in turn, to mock Apollo, a Monkey leaped forth from the hands of Hecate <note>A goddess often associated with the Moon.</note>. But a little later, the terrifying Lion was produced by Apollo, which disrupted Hecate's laughter. Then, indignant, she created the cat as a rival to the Lion. At this, Apollo dissolved into even greater laughter, and to mock Hecate further, he produced the mouse; she, even more enraged and turning to cunning, incited the Monkey against the Lion and the cat sharply against the mouse. From this, the worship of both the Monkey and the cat remained among later generations.

<margin>The cat as the dwelling of Isis.</margin>
However, I believe more truly that this feline worship proceeded from the very belief by which the ancients persuaded themselves that the living Cat was a dwelling place for Isis. For they believed that through this animal, she appeared to men, taught them various things, and turned away evils from them.

<margin>Ovid.</margin>
Ovid appears to allude clearly to this in the fifth book of his *Metamorphoses*, where he relates that during the transformation of the gods—when each assumed different animal forms for themselves—Diana, or the Moon, assumed the form of a cat.

> And the leader of the flock, he said, became Jupiter, whence
> Lybian Ammon is even now depicted with curved horns.
> Apollo <note>Delius</note> hid in a crow, the son of Semele <note>Bacchus</note> in a goat,
> The sister of Phoebus <note>Diana/the Moon</note> in a cat, the daughter of Saturn <note>Juno</note> in a snow-white cow,
> Venus lay hidden in a fish, and Mercury <note>Cyllenius</note> in the wings of an Ibis.

<margin>Giraldus.</margin>
Giraldus asserts that for this reason, they established a four-sided statue with a cat-shaped <note>original Greek: αἰλουρόμορφον</note> head; the four sides represented the four elements, while the feline form signified the Moon.

<margin>The ridiculous worship of cats among the Egyptians.</margin>
Because of this, the Egyptians not only held living cats in great esteem, but also, according to Herodotus, mourned their deaths with great lamentation. Finally, they would carry their carcasses to sacred buildings and bury them with mourning in the City of Bubastis, where Diana was worshipped. Indeed, to have killed a cat, whether by intent or accident, was a crime to be atoned for by death; see the truly ridiculous history in Diodorus concerning a Roman killed in Egypt because of a cat.

<margin>The hieroglyphic meaning of cats.</margin>
It is not surprising, therefore, that the cat, as a sacred animal, was transferred into the register of hieroglyphics and signified various things under various symbols. First, they expressed the Sun by the male cat, as Horus <note>Horapollo, a writer on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> says in Book 1, Hieroglyph 10, when he states:

"For they say that the male cat changes his pupils according to the courses of the sun. For they expand toward the hour of the god's rising into a circular shape, they contract in the middle of the day, and they appear dimmer as the sun is about to set; hence the statue of the god in Heliopolis <note>The 'City of the Sun.'</note> is cat-shaped." <note>original Greek: Φασὶ γὰρ τὸν ἄρρενα αἴλουρον συμμεταβάλλειν τὰς κόρας ταῖς τοῦ ἡλίου δρόμοις. ἐπεκτείνονται μὲν γὰρ περὶ ὥραν τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀνατολὴν εἰς κυκλοειδὲς τέκνονται κᾱ μέσον τῆς ἡμέρας, ἀμαυρότεραι δὲ φαίνονται, δύσιν μέλλοντος τοῦ ἡλίου; ὅθεν καὶ τὸ ἐν ἡλίου πόλει ξόανον τοῦ Θεοῦ αἰλουρόμορφον ὑπάρχειν.</note>

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

The male cat changes its pupils according to the varying state and course of the Sun; at sunrise in the morning they are somewhat extended, but towards midday they become round, as it were; as the Sun presses toward its setting, they appear more blunt and darker. For this reason, the statue of the Sun-God at Heliopolis <note>A major city of ancient Egypt, whose name means "City of the Sun."</note> has the appearance of a cat.

Hieroglyphically, therefore, through the cat, they signified the following: through a seated cat with an *Ankh* <note>original: "Crux ansata," the "cross with a handle," a symbol of life.</note>, they signified, first, the power to ward off evils; second, the Lunar power diffused throughout the elements. The first will be shown in the explanation of the *Ankh* or Tautic character <note>Kircher refers to the *Ankh* as the "Tautic" character, identifying it with the god Thoth (Taautus).</note>; the second has already been demonstrated in the preceding sections by mystical reasoning based on the agreement it has with the Moon. Furthermore, the cat sits to indicate the stability which this Lunar Genius <note>A guiding spirit or divine force associated with the Moon.</note> confers upon the elemental world; just as will be more fully declared in the following pages concerning the placement of hieroglyphic statues.

Thirdly, hinting also at solar power, the Egyptians fashioned a seated statue (with hands placed on its knees, the left of which held an *Ankh*) covered with a linen cloth from the navel to the feet, otherwise naked, with swelling breasts and a cat-shaped head <term>cat-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: *ailouromorphō*.</note>, which a circle surrounded, from whose neck a flame flashed out. And this is that statue of which Horus, cited a little earlier, makes mention; a representation of which is offered to be seen in the Hieroglyphic Theater at figure 36. The circle with the flame denotes the power of the Sun which it provides through its circular motion, and because of the greatest fertility which it confers upon the world. But consider this figure explained elsewhere. And these are the things which I thought should be said in brief concerning the hieroglyphic of the cat.

# HIEROGRAMMATISM VIII.

## Concerning Amphibians, or

### On the Hieroglyphic Significance of the Hippopotamus.

In this place, we have thought it opportune to subjoin the hieroglyphic significance of the amphibious animals, the Hippopotamus and the Crocodile; let us therefore make a beginning with the Hippopotamus.

<margin>The Hippopotamus denotes Typhon.</margin>
The Hippopotamus, an amphibious animal, gave the Egyptians various occasions for hieroglyphics, both in moral and physical doctrine. First, wishing to express Typhon, the adversary <term>adversary</term> <note>original Greek: *antitheon*, a divine opponent or "anti-god."</note> of the deity Osiris, they fashioned the hippopotamus. For since they recognized this animal as harmful and born to inflict damage, moreover being monstrous in its cunning and impiety, it perfectly expressed the nature of Typhon. Thus, they noted not incongruously that Typhon was tamed by Osiris. <margin>Pausanias.</margin> For by Osiris they denote the Nile, and by the Hippopotamus they denote Typhon, that malignant, putrid, and poisonous force by which the crops...

### HIEROGLYPHICS.

...they secretly hinted that fruits and crops would be corrupted. This is confirmed by a statue at Hermopolis which, according to Pausanias, depicts a hawk hovering over a snake and fighting it; this beautifully exhibits the battle between Osiris and Typhon that we have described. Hecataeus also, in his book *On Sacred Philosophy*, confirms our stated opinion when he clearly records that Typhon, having been transformed into a hippopotamus, contends perpetually with Osiris. I have thought it necessary to include his words here:

<note>original Greek: Φασὶ δὲ Τύφωνα ἀντίθεον καὶ ἀντίτεχνον ἱπποποταμόμορφον, μετὰ τοῦ Ὀσείριδος συνεχῶς πολεμίζειν, φύσιν μὲν κάκεργον διὰ Τύφωνος, καὶ ἔνδικον δι' Ὀσείριδος σημαίνοντες.</note>
"They say that Typhon, the adversary and rival, in the form of a hippopotamus, continually fights with Osiris, signifying a wicked nature through Typhon and a just one through Osiris."
*They say Typhon the antagonist, under the form of a Hippopotamus, perpetually decertates with Osiris, signifying a malignant nature through Typhon; a good one through Osiris.*

<margin>The Hippopotamus is a symbol of ingratitude and impiety.</margin>
Secondly, since no animal (according to Suidas) expresses the vice of an ungrateful mind, impiety, and injustice more than the Hippopotamus (according to Horus <note>Kircher refers here to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>), those who depicted it—either in whole or in part—denoted sometimes ingratitude, sometimes impiety, and at other times impudence. For as the Poet rightly says:

->The foul beast enters his mother after having killed his father<-
->Where the fertile Nile waters the fat fields.<-

<margin>The scepters of Kings had the hooves of the hippopotamus placed beneath them.</margin>
For it enters into a fight with its father, and once he is overcome, it rages with incestuous lust toward its mother, as Horus testifies. Hence, according to the same Horus, they placed the <term>Cucupha</term> <note>A scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, traditionally a symbol of filial devotion or piety in Egyptian lore.</note> upon the scepters of Kings with a hippopotamus placed beneath it, or they placed two of its hooves under the scepter, because piety ought to suppress impiety, and clemency should suppress cruelty. Indeed, nothing is more becoming of Kings or Princes than gentleness, beneficence, and moderation of soul; so that as much as they excel others in command and power, they should just as much master themselves through humanity and a gentle disposition of mind. On their scepters, they also placed the image of a Stork at the top and a hippopotamus at the bottom, to hint that violence (symbolized by the hippopotamus) is subject to justice (symbolized by the Stork).

For this reason, before the vestibule of the temple dedicated to Pallas <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian goddess Neith.</note> in the Sais district, these figures were seen engraved, according to Clement in the 6th book of the *Stromata*: the face of a child and of an old man, a hawk, a fish, and a hippopotamus. Since we have interpreted this hieroglyphic sequence in the third part on page 198, we refer the reader there. Junius ingeniously alludes to this in the following four-line verse:

->The swift Hawk, the fish inhabiting the Nile, the dire<-
->Horse, which follows in order,<-
->Speak this symbol. Three symbols for the Egyptian people:<-
->God hates impudence.<-

<margin>What the Hippopotamus denotes.</margin>
Thirdly, Horapollo records that through the Hippopotamus, the Egyptians indicated sometimes spring and sometimes the hours. The reason for the former is that as soon as the meadows begin to turn green in the springtime, the Hippopotamus is accustomed to come out from the Nile to graze on the grass. As for the hours: because it remains hidden under the water during the day, but at night emerges from the river into the fields—not in a hurry, but like a mower hired for a specific task—it grazes upon the harvest evenly. By completing its activities throughout the night and day as if by measuring time, they quite appropriately used it to indicate the hours. See the cited passage...

# HIEROGRAMMATIC REPRESENTATION IX.

## The Crocodile, or

### On the Hieroglyphic Significance of the Crocodile.

<margin>The Crocodile denotes the nature of the divine essence.</margin>
The Crocodile, an amphibious animal, is of such great renown among the Egyptians that it has given rise to a diverse lineage of hieroglyphic meanings. First, the more secret initiates <term>mystæ; those initiated into the religious mysteries</term> indicated a certain aspect of the divine essence through the nature of this animal. Just as this animal, while lurking under the waters, looks at others through a transparent membrane covering its pupil, with only its eyes protruding above the water while the rest of it remains hidden and <gloss>unseen; original Greek: ἀφάνῳ</gloss>; so too does God behold all things, and nothing is so impassable that the eyes of the divine mind are not directed toward it, even though He Himself is most remote from the senses of all mortals—invisible and <gloss>unseen; original Greek: ἀοράτῳ</gloss>—even as He is intimately present to all things. Furthermore, since the crocodile is unique among animals in being without a tongue <note>A common ancient biological misconception; crocodiles do have tongues, but they are attached to the floor of the mouth and do not move freely.</note>, they used to paint the crocodile to designate the ineffable nature of God. Thus says Abenephi:

<margin>Abenephi <note>This refers to the Arab author Ibn Wahshiyya, whom Kircher frequently cites.</note></note>
<note>original Arabic: ولان الطبيعة الله لاتتغير ولا تدرك وهي غير منظرة من عين الناس لذلك ومعها كان يريدون يدلون الطبيعة الله التي هي غير منظرة وكانوا رسموا صورة التمساح ان هذا الحيوان تحت الما يرا ولا يرة وان التمساح بلالسان لذلك كان يعنوا بصورة الطبيعة الله غير مدركة وغير موصوفة ۞</note>

---

<margin>The ineffable nature of God</margin>
> ۞ *And because the nature of God is incomprehensible and immutable, invisible to the eyes of the sons of man, therefore when they wished to signify the invisible nature of God, they carved the figure of a crocodile; for this animal sees and is not seen, and since the crocodile is tongueless, they thereby noted the nature of God as incomprehensible and ineffable.*

Valerianus confirms these points according to the mind of Horus, who signified the head and the unknown substance of God by a painting of a crocodile lurking in a cave with only its tail visible. By the appearing tail, he signified that God can only be recognized <term>a posteriori; through His works and effects rather than His internal essence</term>, that is, from His works.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>It marks the motion of the Sun.</margin>
Secondly, furthermore, when the Priests wished to signify the motion of the Sun, they would paint an image of the Sun in a ship carried by a crocodile. By this, they secretly noted the motion of the Sun through moisture for the generation of things; the crocodile represents the fresh water which the Sun purifies by its heat. Thus says Eusebius in Book 3, Chapter 3 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*: <margin>Eusebius</margin> "They signify the sun sometimes by a man embarked on a ship lying upon a crocodile. The ship shows the motion in moisture; the crocodile represents the drinkable water in which the sun is carried. It signifies, therefore, that the sun performs its circuit through moist and sweet air." <note>original Greek: ἥλιον δὲ σημαίνουσι ποτὲ μὲν δι᾿ ἀνθρώπου ἐπιβεβηκότος τῷ πλοίῳ ἐπὶ κροκοδείλου κειμένου. δηλοῖ τι τὸ μὲν πλοῖον τὴν ἐν ὑγρῷ κίνησιν: ὁ δὲ κροκόδειλος, πότιμον ὕδωρ ἐν ᾧ φέρεται ὁ ἥλιος. ἐσήμαινε τοίνυν ὁ ἥλιος δι᾿ ἀέρος ὑγροῦ καὶ γλυκέος τὴν περιπόλησιν ποιεῖσθαι.</note>

<margin>The eyes of the crocodile are a symbol of the sunrise.</margin>
Thirdly, when they were about to indicate the sunrise, they depicted the eyes of a crocodile, either because this animal is endowed with prominent eyes, or because it emerges into the light from the egg without any incubation by the parents. Thus says Horus <note>Kircher refers to the author Horapollo</note>: "To describe the East, they paint two eyes of a crocodile; for from the whole body of a living creature, the eyes appear out of the depths." <note>original Greek: Ἀνατολὴν δὲ λέγοντες δύο ὀφθαλμοὺς κροκοδείλου ζωγραφοῦσιν; ἐπειδήπερ παντὸς σώματος ζώου οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἐκ τοῦ βυθοῦ ἀναφαίνονται.</note> To signify the Sunset, according to Horus, "they paint a stooped crocodile." <note>original Greek: κροκόδειλον κεκυφότα ζωγραφοῦσιν.</note> They paint the crocodile bent over and bowing prostrate to the ground because, just as the sun remains above the horizon all day and below the horizon at sunset, so the crocodile is said to dwell above the earth by day with vigorous eyes, but at night under the waters with dimmed vision. What the Egyptians signified through the crocodile in moral discipline shall be discussed elsewhere.

<margin>The crocodile is a symbol of Egypt.</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting an Egyptian deity with an ibis head, wearing a complex headdress featuring a sun disk and horns. The figure is seated on a throne decorated with a grid pattern. One hand holds a scepter, while the other rests on the lap holding an ankh symbol. Beneath the seated figure's feet and the throne, a crocodile lies flat on the ground.</image-desc>
Fourthly, the crocodile indicates the land of Egypt or the Nile, because this animal is native to Egypt; hence, after the Emperor Augustus reduced Egypt under the power of the Roman people, he struck a coin with a palm and a crocodile.

Fifthly, when they wished to signify Sunrise and Sunset, and the power over the substance of the moist element—as well as the Lunar Genius presiding over the moisture necessary for the generation of things—they depicted *Isis ibimorpha* <term>Ibis-formed Isis; Isis shown with the head of an ibis bird</term>, or Isis conspicuous with the head of an ibis on a square seat, beneath which two crocodiles looking in opposite directions are laid prostrate. This arrangement is seen in the third space of the middle of the Bembine Table <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with pseudo-Egyptian hieroglyphs popular in the Renaissance</note>; since we cannot explain it in this place due to the great variety of things contained under it and the multitude of mysteries, and because of the brevity of time, we have deliberately reserved its interpretation for our *Oedipus*. <note>Refers to Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempted to "solve" the riddle of hieroglyphs.</note>

BOOK IV. IDEAS

# SACRED WRITING X.
## The Hawk; or,
### *Concerning the hieroglyphic significance of the Hawk.*

<margin>The Hawk was worshipped with the highest honor among the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>Various transformations of the Hawk.</margin>
<margin>Meanings of the Hawk</margin>
**A**lthough in various places in this work we have touched upon the mysteries of the present hieroglyphic, because this was done on the occasion of other discussions, it seemed appropriate in this place to truly and explicitly unlock the hidden meanings of this hawk-symbol. This is done so that the context of the symbols and the clever Architecture of the ancients in establishing symbols might become more deeply known, and also so that many faulty passages regarding the meaning of this hieroglyphic might be corrected and the truth revealed. Plutarch reports that by depicting a hawk, the Egyptians always intended to represent Osiris, that god and sacred King of theirs, who was adorned with every kind of glory and honor. Since this is the case, I believe I will do nothing more pleasing to the curious reader than if I show that something of divinity was thought to reside in the hawk by superstitious antiquity, and for what cause they bestowed honors upon it with such great zeal. For just as most nations, entangled in the worst errors and mocked by the cunning of the demon—some, on account of certain benefits, adored Jupiter, Apollo, and Minerva; others Juno, others Venus, others another God or Goddess, or even fever and hunger—so the Egyptians, more superstitious than the rest, held the hawk in the greatest honor above all, next to the Crocodile and the Ibis. They did not only designate Osiris through this, but they honored the bird itself as their primary God, as Plutarch has left witnessed in several places. Indeed, that the hawk was of the highest consideration among the Egyptians is evidenced by its images represented in various forms on almost all obelisks, and the sacred patterns <term>Hierogrammatismi refers to the symbolic "sacred writing" or characters used by Egyptian priests</term> of hawk-form <term>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφον (hierakomorphon), meaning shaped like a hawk</term>. You may see it now wearing a high cap [tutulus], now human-formed <term>original Greek: ἀνθρωπόμορφον (anthropomorphon), meaning having a human shape</term>—that is, composed of a man and a hawk—now transformed into one made of a serpent and a hawk <term>original Greek: ὀφιόμορφον (ophiomorphon), meaning serpent-shaped</term>. Now you may see it marked by a crest, now by a cap like a tiara or a priestly miter; now with its wings extended as if to seek the heights, now again with the same wings folded, brought down from the high to the low. Now suddenly with a wild face and feathered head passing into the charms of a human face; with feet ending in fingers instead of claws, and with hands stretched out in upright duties, it takes on a human form <term>anthropomorphon</term>; now with feet passing into serpentine coils and volumes, it appears terrifying, reflecting the asp and the Dragon. Concerning all of these, something must be said so that finally a limit may be set to such confusion of things. Concerning the "human-shaped" hawk, we have already spoken in the preceding pages. Now let us see what they signified by the hawk wearing a high cap or crest. And first, indeed, Abenephius <note>Kircher frequently cites "Abenephius," an Arabic author he identified as an authority on Egyptian lore, likely Ibn Wahshiyya</note> asserts that it signified the Soul of the Sun: — "By the image of the hawk they used to signify the Soul of the Sun." <note>original Arabic: بصورة البازي كان يدلّون النفس الشمس</note>

<summary>Kircher explains that the hawk was one of the most significant Egyptian symbols, representing the god Osiris and the sun. He describes its various artistic forms—mixing human, avian, and serpentine features—and cites ancient authors like Plutarch and Abenephius to justify its divine status.</summary>

### HIEROGLYPHICS

And by the figure of a hawk, they denoted the soul of the Sun.

<margin>Horus:</margin>
To this, Horus <note>original: *Horus*, referring to Horapollo, the author of a famous 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics</note> agrees: *“Furthermore, since it seems to be an image of the sun beyond all other birds due to its rays, it is sharp-sighted; for which reason physicians also use the ‘hawk-weed’ herb for the healing of eyes, whence it is also called the ‘healer’ as if it were the master of sound sight, etc.”* <note>original Greek: *Ἔτι γε μὴν ἐπεὶ καὶ δοκεῖ εἴδωλον ἡλίου ὑπάρχειν παρὰ πάντα τὰ πτηνὰ πρὸς τὰς αὐτοῦ ἀκτῖνας, ὀξυωπεῖ ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ οἱ ἰατροὶ πρὸς ἴασιν ὀφθαλμῶν τῇ ἱερακίᾳ βοτάνῃ χρῶνται, ὅθεν καὶ τὸ ἦχον ὡς κύριον ὄντα ὁ ἐάσας, &c.*</note>

<margin>Hieracion: The herb of the Hawk.</margin>
Then also, because it seems to be a likeness of the Sun above all other birds, it is endowed with a certain peculiar and hidden power of nature, as it sustains the Sun's rays with eyes un-turned, contrary to the habit of other birds. From this it follows that physicians, to heal the defects and discomforts of the eyes, use the herb *hieracio* <note>The plant *Hieracium*, commonly known as hawkweed; ancient naturalists believed hawks ate it to sharpen their vision</note>. From this also it follows that they sometimes painted the Sun in the form of a Hawk, as if it were the guardian and Lord of sight. Hence, as *Aelian* <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> testifies: The Egyptians also consecrate the hawk to Apollo and worship it; <margin>Aelian.</margin> calling this God *Horus* in their own language; however, they call a bird of this kind *Thaustum*; <margin>The Hawk: Sacred to Apollo</margin> they say it has a similarity with Apollo <note>Apollo was frequently identified with the Egyptian Horus and the Sun</note> because, among birds, only hawks gaze toward the rays of the Sun always without difficulty, and they are not burdened by taking their path upward with intent eyes, nor are they offended by that divine flame. Likewise, they are most hostile to venomous beasts, such as horned vipers and scorpions. The *Scholiast* <note>An ancient commentator</note> on the *Birds* of Aristophanes also says: *“The hawk is most sacred to Apollo.”* <note>original Greek: *ἱέραξ ἱερώτατος τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι*</note> The Hawk is sacred to the Sun, both on account of the speed of its movement (for as the Sun is most swift, so is the hawk most rapid in its flight) and because of the relationship in the origin of its name; for it is called *hierax* <note>the Greek word for hawk</note> from the phrase “to go easily” <note>original Greek: *ῥᾳδίως ἰέναι*</note>, that is, from easy motion, which indeed most greatly suits the Sun. Indeed, *Varinus* and *Eusebius* in their notes on Homer say it is so named from the celestial impulse of the spheres, namely: *“on account of flying sacredly/powerfully,”* <note>original Greek: *παρὰ τὸ ἱερῶς πέτεσθαι*</note> because it is carried so easily, as if it were flying by divine power. <margin>Porphyry.</margin> *Porphyry* also in book 4 of *On Abstinence* says: the ancients called the Gods by the names of certain animals, such as the Cat, the Lizard, the Lion, the Dragon, and the Hawk. *Giraldus* also attributes to Apollo a genus of hawk which he calls *hierakopteron* <note>literally "hawk-winged"</note>; *Plutarch* also in *On Isis and Osiris* says: The Egyptians often paint Osiris in the form of a hawk; for this bird excels in the sharpness of its seeing and the force of its flying; *“for it surpasses in the sharpness of its sight and the swiftness of its flight.”* <note>original Greek: *ὀξυτάτη γὰρ ὄψεως ὑπερβάλλει καὶ πτήσεως ὀξύτητι*</note> Furthermore, according to *Eusebius*, the hawk was a symbol of light and spirit among the Egyptians; for the Hawk is of the keenest sight and the greatest speed.

<margin>Wonderful properties of the Hawk.</margin>
The Egyptians, therefore, considering the admirable properties of the Hawk, could hardly have devised a more fitting symbol to indicate the nature of the Sun and of fire. For just as the Sun is removed from every mass of earthly corruption, yet nevertheless illumines all things with its rays, touches all things, fertilizes all things, and separates the impure from the pure; so the Hawk, when it has raised itself to the highest point even to the clouds, with wings outstretched, looking down upon all that space where it rains and snows, betakes itself to that place where there is room for neither lightning nor thunderbolt; it seems to enjoy, so to speak, the very summit of the more divine air. From which place, as if from some high watchtower, with remarkable agility of body, it glides like an arrow in any direction; it directs the sailing oars of its wings with any slight steering of its tail; now with a lingering flight, hanging almost in the same place, it looks around and seeks where best to hurl itself from above upon its prey, and soon like a thunderbolt from heaven, it falls unlooked for upon the flocks of the fields and at once upon the [beasts] <note>The text cuts off at "fe-", likely *feras* (wild beasts)</note> of the mountains...

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

...[viewing the lands] under the same impulse, from where it might pierce with its beak or tear with its claws—be it a careless lamb, a fearful hare, or whatever living thing chance offers for its meal or destruction—all of which can be perfectly adapted to the nature of the Sun.

<margin>It emulates the virtues of the Sun in all things.</margin>
Added to this is the multifaceted flight of the hawk, which mirrors the movement of natural things with the utmost precision. Just as it is carried in a straight flight upward, so if it glides down to the earth from above, it does not do so through a winding or crooked path, but follows a straight course toward us. Certainly, just as those various coils, which it traces gradually in the air with a spiral flight, represent nothing other than the spiral motion of the Sun and the rest of the stars; so that straight and, as it were, perpendicular motion—which it constantly maintains whether descending to strike a flock of chicks or ascending toward a dove high in the clouds—seems to signify nothing other than the linear motion of the elements. Truly, this motion belongs to no other bird except the hawk and the eagle; for all other birds, if they take flight toward the heights, are forced to move in an oblique path and through curved spaces. What else is denoted by those sparkling orbits of the eyes, but the shining bodies of the luminaries and the power of hidden fire diffused everywhere? Furthermore, just as the Sun perpetually seethes with the motion of life-giving heat, so the hawk, swelling with the most vigorous blood and spirit, emulates the perpetuity of the Sun in its own long-lived vitality. And since the Sun, by the projection of its rays, surveys all things in the lower world as if with certain eyes, hence Plutarch, in his book *On Isis and Osiris*, quite appropriately asserts that it was customary for the Egyptians to denote the Sun by the image of a hawk, because of its extraordinary power of sight. On account of this same gift, <margin>Epies the Egyptian, interpreter of the Gods.</margin> <term>the all-seeing hawk</term> <note>original Greek: ἱέραξ παντόφθαλμος (hierax pantophthalmos)</note>, that is, the "many-eyed," was so named, just as Osiris was. To this also belongs what Epies, the greatest interpreter of the Gods among the Egyptians, says—as recorded in Eusebius, Book 1, Chapter 7—that the most divine serpent having the head of a hawk is a very pleasing thing; if it raised its eyelids, it filled its entire region with primordial light, but when it kept them closed, darkness was poured out. Thus there is no doubt that they considered its nature to be supremely fiery, and wished to demonstrate those effects of the Sun through the gestures of the hawk.

To this exceptional power of sight is added its speed of flight, by which it deservedly takes the prize from all other birds; a fact which the ancients indicated in many ways through symbols and parables. The Ethiopians indeed, as Clement records in the fifth book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: *Stromata*</note>, used the hawk to signify speed, just as the Egyptians used it to denote a "thing quickly done." Hence, as will be said in its proper place, when painting the wind, they painted a flying hawk. Because of this velocity of motion, says Varinus, they anciently dedicated the hawk to Apollo, or the Sun; whence <margin>Homer.</margin> Homer, comparing Apollo to a hawk, speaks thus:

> <term>He descended from the Idaean mountains like a hawk,</term> <note>original Greek: Βῆ δὲ κατ᾿ ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἴρηκι ἐοικὼς</note>
> <term>the swift slayer of pigeons, which is the swiftest of birds.</term> <note>original Greek: Ωκέϊ φασσοφόνῳ ὃς ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hawk as a solar symbol, transitioning from its physical flight patterns to its symbolic role in Egyptian religion, royal iconography, and its mythical association with the gods Apollo and Mercury.</meta>

# HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
<margin>Statue of Isis among the Ethiopians clothed in hawk wings.</margin>
Porphyry, in Book 4 of *On Abstinence*, states: "The Egyptians," he says, "regard the hawk as an image of the Sun. They claim its entire substance consists of blood and spirit, and that it is moved by compassion for humanity; it even mourns the dead and casts earth upon their eyes." For this reason, it was the custom of the Egyptians to adorn the statue of Isis with hawk wings as a sign of her excellence. Aelian relates that it was common among the Kings of Persia to wear a purple garment made remarkable by a hawk’s feather.

<margin>What did the hawk denote in moral matters?</margin>
<margin>What is the Baieth?</margin>
From these and similar gifts of character and nature, they used the hawk to signify not only the Sun, but also other concepts such as the soul, victory, and glory, as Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a famous treatise on hieroglyphs</note> rightly notes. Hence, in the Egyptian language, they called it the *Baieth* <note>original: βαιηθ</note>, which signifies the heart, or the proper seat of the soul; the hawk was also a symbol of the soul according to Horus. Furthermore, *Baieth* is a compound word derived from *bai*, which signifies life or soul—or as I believe, from the ancient Greek *bios* <note>life</note> and *eth*, which signifies the heart. These people were fond of using such compound words when they wished to signify the very origin and nature of a thing, or something similar. This practice is also very frequent among the Hebrews, as shown by the word *Shamayim* <note>original: שמים, meaning "Heavens"</note>, by which they suggested that the heavens consist of water and fire. But now let us see what connection the soul has with the heart itself. It was the opinion of the Egyptians that the heart is the receptacle of the soul. Through the combination of those two syllables, *bai* and *eth*, into one word, the term *Baieth* is formed, which means "Hawk." Therefore, just as they believed the seat of the soul was in the heart, so they believed the soul of the world resided in the Sun. Furthermore, since the blood <margin>The hawk denotes blood.</margin> which exists in the heart is the vehicle of the soul, the Egyptians also painted the hawk as a symbol for blood; for they believed the bird lived and was nourished by a diet of blood.

<margin>Apollo transformed into a hawk.</margin>
There are many reasons why they dedicated the hawk especially to Mercury—whom we have demonstrated in our previous apparatus to be the same as Apollo. First, they imagined that Apollo frequently transformed himself into this bird, just as they elsewhere feign that he took on the form of a lizard, a lion, or a dragon. For this reason, they often honored this god as Phoebus <note>a title for Apollo meaning "bright" or "radiant"</note>—a name by which they understood and worshipped the Sun—and frequently designated him by the name of a hawk. Because of the great similarity between the nature of the hawk and the Sun, the poets tell fables that this bird was held to be Apollo's chief messenger and the interpreter of his will. Hence Ovid, writing of the maiden Arachne contending with Minerva in the art of weaving, sings thus in Book 6 of the *Metamorphoses*:

> *There Phœbus is in the image of a countryman,*
> *Now using the feathers of a hawk, now the back of a lion.*

<margin>The hawk is the messenger of Apollo.</margin>
Homer says: "The hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo" <note>original Greek: Κίρκος Απόλλωνος ταχύς άγγελος</note>. The poets also babble that Daedalion was turned into this bird. But regarding this fable, read Ovid in Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*. For the hawk is a solar animal, and by a certain hidden likeness of nature, it is drawn toward solar things. Hence, it clears its eyes with a solar herb. From this comes its great sympathy for that subterranean sun—I mean gold. <margin>The bones of a hawk attract gold.</margin> That the bones of a hawk attract gold in the manner of a magnet was known not only to the Egyptians, but to Pliny himself, who writes: *Among the Arabs also, I have found it written that fire is drawn forth from the bones of a hawk, and gold is attracted.* <margin>Aelian.</margin> Aelian, in Book 10, Chapter 14 of *On Animals*, says:
