### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...says: *The shinbone of a hawk, if it is brought near gold, attracts the gold to itself by a certain wonderful allure, not unlike a magnet attracting iron, drawing it through a kind of enchantment and capture.* But these matters are discussed at length in our *Hieroglyphic Alchemy*.

<margin>The Hawk is sacred to Mercury on account of divination.</margin>
Second, hawks—especially goshawks—were considered sacred to Mercury, according to Pliny (Book 12, Chapter 4), because of a remarkable power of foreknowledge regarding future events which they possess. Additionally, they were of great use in the taking of auguries <note>Augury was the Roman practice of interpreting the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds</note>; for this reason, certain ministers were assigned to the care of hawks, which they raised for specific purposes, as Diodorus states (Book 2, Chapter 4). This care was so great that they would throw cut meat to the birds while they were in flight, inviting them with a loud voice until they took the meat. They also worshipped dead hawks because they believed their souls were endowed with the power of prophecy. Hence Aelian says in Book 1 of *On Antiquity*: while the hawk lives, it is considered exceptionally dear to God by the Egyptians; then, after its departure from life, they believe it reveals the future and that the interpretation of dreams originates from it. There is also a report among these same people that there was once a "tripod of the hawk," from which oracles were poured out to those consulting them, inspired by divine instinct. Eusebius also states (Book 2, Chapter 1) that the animal was held to be divine by the Egyptians, and this is evident from the fact that they depicted that "Good Spirit" <note>This refers to the *Agathodaemon*, a protective spirit in Egyptian and Greek mythology</note>—by whose benefit and will they believed all things subsist, flourish, and are sustained—with the body of a serpent and the head of a hawk. For this reason, they also honored the dead with public funeral rites; see Herodotus in his book *Euterpe*, and Diodorus, Book 2.

<margin>The power of foreknowledge in the hawk.</margin>
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
Third, they dedicated the hawk to Mercury, <term>because it examines all things and makes them invisible</term> <note>original Greek: Πάντα γὰρ ἐξελέγχει καὶ ἀόρατα ποιεῖ</note>. For just as Mercury is the winged messenger of the Gods, or as the Sun reveals all secret and unknown things by the benefit of light, so also the hawk was held as the messenger and interpreter of the divine will. This opinion was so prevalent among all people that some believe the bird's name [accipiter] was derived from auguries, as if it were called the bird "received three times" [*ter accepta*] and a most joyful messenger in the taking of omens. Indeed, they believed this power of foretelling in the hawk was so strong that they thought it did not die with the dying bird, but could be transferred into others; they believed that by devouring its entrails, the power could be acquired. Even that impious man Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher often criticized by Christian writers like Kircher for his "pagan" views</note> did not hesitate to assert this in these words: *Those who wish to receive into themselves the souls of animals powerful in prophecy, by devouring the principal parts of their bodies—such as the hearts of crows, moles, or hawks—receive the soul of each one, present and entering into them, and foreseeing future things like a God.*

<margin>Strabo.</margin>
<margin>Why the hawk was called Thaustus.</margin>
Strabo supports this in Book 17, where he says: *The inhabitants of Philae (which was a common settlement of Egyptians and Ethiopians) had Egyptian temples where a bird called a hawk was worshipped. Hence the ancient Egyptians called it Thaustus in their tongue, which is the same as Tuutum in the Phoenician tongue; Thaut in the Egyptian language is the same as Thoth or Mercury.*

Hawks were therefore called "Mercurial" on account of the remarkable discovery of things, which they attributed to Mercury. We shall now explain how this was demonstrated through this bird. First, the method for healing eyes using the herb <term>named after the hawk</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶ ἱέρακος, referring to the plant Hierakium or Hawkweed, which was anciently believed to be used by hawks to sharpen their sight</note>...

<margin>The hawk-herb called Hawkweed is an excellent eye-salve.</margin>
From the Hawk, the "hawkweed"—also known as the "hawk-herb"—derives its name <note>original: *hieracium* or *accipitrina*</note> and reveals itself as a most perfect eye-salve. It is a certain herb of the chicory family which, borrowing its name from the hawk <note>original: *hierax* in Greek</note>, is generally called *hieracium* by the Greeks and Latins, and even used in the feminine form by some. It is said that the Hawk, by anointing and smearing its eyes with the juice of this plant when it has been plucked or scratched, restores its lost keenness of sight to wholeness and recovers its former clarity. This herb is commonly called "Lion's Tooth" <note>original: *dens Leonis*; we know this today as the dandelion, though the author is discussing various plants in the hawkweed family</note>. Country folk in Germany, because of a similar outcome, call it *Weyenschwanz* or "Hawk's Tail." Indeed, the flowers of this plant—much like lettuce, Cretan hawkweed, and certain other varieties—flow with a milky <margin>Description of Hawkweed.</margin> juice when broken. Since this juice is bitter and endowed with a remarkable cleansing power, it is no wonder if it dispels dimness from the eyes of hawks when rubbed upon them. Botanists dispute whether the true "Hawkweed" is the endive, the spurge-like *Tithymalus*, the wild chicory, the dragon-herb with a stem marked like a hawk, the "hawk-foot" <note>original: *hieraciopodion*</note>, or the rose campion. I personally believe it is that *hieracium* which we previously called *Tithymalus*-like; for this plant possesses an extraordinary scouring power and, for that reason, benefits defects of the eyes, just like Greater Celandine and other such plants. Prosper Alpinus <note>A famous 16th-century physician and botanist known for his study of Egyptian plants</note> testifies that a great abundance of this grows in Egypt. And from this comes the origin of the eye-salves which physicians call "hawk-salves" <note>original: *hieracia*</note>; such is the "Phoenix" variety of eye-salve by Apollonius, which was nicknamed "The Hawk" in the writings of Galen, as some more recent doctors prefer. It was composed by a certain Hierax but taken into use by Apollonius.

<margin>The Tau character resembles a hawk's head.</margin>
Furthermore, they attributed that Mercurial character, or the sign of Isis known as the "Tau," to this bird. For when the Egyptians noted that the hawk's head, beak, and eyes shaped something resembling the character "Tau," they marveled at it as a mark of Mercury’s presence. They venerated this character as most mysterious, being derived (as they saw it) from the countenance of both the Bull <note>The word "Tau" sounds like the Latin *Taurus* (Bull), leading to this symbolic wordplay</note> and the Hawk. They included it among the four letters usually carried about by the Egyptians in the "Gomasian" solemnities <note>Ancient Egyptian festivals involving the processing of sacred symbols</note>, as we have intimated above. For the Egyptians were, above all others, studious to the point of superstition in the careful observation of animal forms and figures.

<margin>What is the Tau?</margin>
We have stated above that Mercury [Thoth] converted the Hebrew sign *Tau*, which was adapted to other mysteries, for use in Egyptian sacred rites; indeed, with a few changes, he called it *Thath* after his own name. Or, according to the Phoenician language, *Tauutus*, which means "fortunate spirit" or <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>original: *ἀγαθοδαίμονα*, a "Good Spirit" or protective deity</note>. He signified this by a hawk's head placed upon a serpent and enclosed in a circle. Through the hawk's head, which depicts the aforementioned character, they aptly express nothing other than life, which the power of the divine Osiris and that fertile, creative virtue indicated by the serpent communicates to the whole world. But lest we seem to have devised anything moved only by our own perception, let us hear Eusebius (Book 1, Chapter 7) discussing this not so much learnedly as, above all, appropriately:

> From Misor was born Tauutus, who first wrote down the elements of letters; the Egyptians call him Thaauth, the Alexandrians Thoth, and the Greeks Mercury. And in the same chapter...

### BOOK IV: IDEAS

...in the chapter, near the middle: *"But when Mercury sought the Southern Regions, having bestowed all of Egypt upon the God Taautus <note>Taautus is the Phoenician name for the Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes and the Romans with Mercury</note>, he appointed him King there."* And those things which follow: and afterwards: *"Taautus himself considered the nature of dragons and serpents to be divine, and after him, the Phoenicians and Egyptians did as well; for it is the most breath-filled <note>original: spirituosissimum; referring to the 'pneuma' or vital spirit</note> of all animals and the most fiery; the Phoenicians call it a 'Good Spirit' <note>original: Agathodaimon</note>; but the Egyptians called it Cneph <note>Kneph, an Egyptian creator deity</note>, to whom they attach the head of a hawk, on account of its singular activity, and for that reason Epies <term>because of his active nature <note>original: dia to praktikon</note></term> (whom the Egyptians considered the highest interpreter of the Gods), a scribe of the sacred letters whose books Arius translated into the Greek language, handing this down allegorically, says word for word: 'The serpent is a most divine animal and, having the head of a hawk, is exceedingly pleasant; if it raises its eyelids, it used to fill its entire region with first-born light; but when it kept its eyes closed, darkness was poured forth.'"* And toward the end: *"Indeed, the Egyptians, depicting the whole world, being led by this opinion, stretch out a <term>hawk-shaped <note>original: hierakomorphon</note></term> serpent—representing the air passing through and the fire poured around the surface—in the shape of the Greek letter Theta <note>The letter Θ</note>. Indicating the magnitude and form of the world by the circle: but by the <term>hawk-shaped serpent</term> which is placed in the middle of the circle, they show the good spirit, the preserver of all things, by whose power the world is contained."* And from this it is clear why the Hawk is also counted among the four letters <note>Likely referring to the four elemental or cardinal symbols</note>, and from whence it arose that the Greeks afterwards fashioned the caduceus of Mercury out of serpents.

And from this also, they used the figure of the hawk in place of an amulet against the malignant assaults of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>, as can be seen in the hieroglyphic description which appears today on the bases of the sphinx, or Lion, at the Fountain of the "Aqua Felice" <note>The Fontana dell'Acqua Felice, a famous Roman fountain commissioned by Pope Sixtus V</note> near the Baths of Diocletian. There, our "Thautic" character <note>The 'Ankh' or Tau cross</note>, placed together with two hawks on either side, signifies nothing other than a certain amulet placed against Typhon—that is, against the fiery dryness or the blasts of the Etesian winds <note>Annual Mediterranean winds</note> by which the water of the Nile dries up, and thus, by preventing the fertile flooding of the Nile, brings about sterility. For the Egyptians believe that by this character of Isis, the incursions of all evils are warded off, Osiris is enticed by these means, and the Spirit of the World is drawn in. HIEROGLYPHICS.

Furthermore, the figures are repeated from the sunrise to the sunset to ward off ill-omened powers; for it was believed that these powers, while presiding over the east and west, could be turned away by this doubled series of symbols, as if by opposing and hostile signs.

And for this reason, these hieroglyphics were specifically placed on the bases of Sphinxes and located along the banks of the Nile. They served as a kind of <term>phylactery <note>a protective charm or amulet</note></term> against drought and the fiery force that dries up the Nile—which, according to Plutarch, they called Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos, storms, and the parching heat of the desert</note>. It should be added that elsewhere, Abenephi <note>likely referring to the medieval author Ibn Wahshiyya, whose work on hieroglyphs was a key source for Renaissance scholars</note> calls these instruments, marked with the numbers 6 and 7, "the engines of Typhon." He does not provide a reason, but I suspect they are nothing other than the instruments or ropes with which Typhon once trapped Osiris in a chest, according to the history narrated by Plutarch. This opinion is confirmed by the fact that in the same collection of hieroglyphics, a Hawk appearing with these instruments—along with a fly and a sea-reed—signifies nothing other than Osiris as the repeller of Typhon's mechanical devices. Regarding these matters, see Plutarch’s more extensive treatment, as well as his full explanation reserved for other passages.

# HIEROGRAMMATISM XI.
### The Owl, or
## Concerning the Hieroglyphic Meaning of the Owl.

<margin>The owl signifies three things in particular.</margin>
I find that the Owl signified three things among the Egyptians. First, wisdom compared to silence. Second, GOD. Third, an averting demon, an <term>opponent of the god <note>original Greek: ἀντίθεον (antitheon)</note></term> to Osiris, or anything ill-omened and portentous. Since this type of symbol is extremely frequent among the other hieroglyphics seen on Obelisks and is displayed in various ways, I have decided to discuss it more extensively in this place, under the best possible conditions, so that the meaning of this hieroglyphic may be revealed more clearly.

<margin>The nature of the owl.</margin>
It should be understood that as they carefully considered the nature of this animal—seeing it as a hidden bird that stays awake at night and flies while all others are sleeping, and whose vision grows sharp in the darkness (where other birds rest with clouded eyes)—it moves about in its work and foresees things to come. Conversely, during the day, which is subject to the troublesome noise and clamor of various disturbances where other birds are active, the owl rests sweetly within the solitary ruins of old buildings as if in a certain delightful contemplation. Thus, they quite aptly compared wisdom, which is characterized by silence, through this bird.
<margin>The Owl as a symbol of Wisdom compared to silence.</margin>
> For watchful skill leads sleepless cares. <note>original Latin verse: "Nam vigil insomnes ducit solertia curas"</note>

<margin>In what wisdom consists.</margin>
Wisdom also acquires its own splendor by seeing through the greatest darkness of errors, and it discerns evil from good; for nothing is so hidden or so obscure that wisdom cannot perceive it. And where the [sight] of other men...

BOOK IV. IDEAS

While the common crowd of men is utterly occupied, wisdom takes its rest; and where the common people see nothing—being blinded by the usage of this worldly light—wisdom then becomes opportunely clear-sighted in carrying out affairs. For it is the mark of a wise man to take rest in those matters with which the crowd is occupied, and conversely, to exercise himself most where the crowd sees nothing to be done. In doing this, he can be said to beautifully imitate the owl. Abenephi <note>likely referring to the medieval author Ibn Wahshiyya</note> confirms all this with his own calculation in these words:

<margin>Abenephius</margin>
The owl is a sign of wisdom obtained through silence, because just as the owl works in the night and rests during the day, so the scholars abandon worldly tasks and remain much in their contemplation, just as the owl is guided by silence.
<note>original: "والهامه هى علامة الحكمة..." Kircher provides the Latin translation immediately following this Arabic passage.</note>
---
that is, *The owl is a sign of Wisdom acquired in silence, because just as the owl works at night and rests by day; so the wise, who flee the tumult of the world’s business, lead a tranquil life in their contemplations, just as the owl does in the night and in silence.*

All of this is beautifully taught by a figure inserted into the Herwartian theater of hieroglyphics <note>referring to the *Thesaurus Hieroglyphicorum* of Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, a 17th-century collection of Egyptian artifacts</note>, where Harpocrates <margin>A beautiful hieroglyphic of Harpocrates.</margin> is shown in the form of a seated boy, with snake-shaped <note>original: ὀφιομόρφοις (*ophiomorphois*)</note> hair, or rather hair degenerating into serpents. He urges silence with a finger pressed to his lips. In his other hand, he holds forward a torch with three poppy heads, from whose top emerges an ear into which a leaf of the <term>Persea <note>a tree sacred to ancient Egyptians, often identified with the *Mimusops laurifolia*; its leaves and fruit were thought to resemble the tongue and heart</note></term> is inserted, along with the character of a crescent Moon. A quiver is also seen behind his back with a bow cast down carelessly, to whose side are joined, first, an Owl, from whose head an ear emerges with a Persea leaf likewise inserted; then a rooster, as it appears here in the

### HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>The Persea leaf.</margin>
<margin>What the poppy signifies.</margin>
<margin>What the discarded quiver signifies.</margin>
<margin>Why the Athenians used the owl as a symbol.</margin>
...the rooster is a messenger, and is accustomed to rouse men with its voice to those duties; therefore, just as Harpocrates <note>The Hellenized form of the Egyptian god Har-pa-khered (Horus the Child), often depicted with a finger to his lips as a symbol of silence.</note> presses his lips with his finger, so he also restrains the throat of the rooster—that troublesome interrupter of rest—as if a certain silent and internal urge were being felt in its throat, just as it was preparing its voice. The ear, into which a <term>Persea leaf</term> <note>A tree sacred to the Egyptians, often identified as the *Mimusops schimperi*, whose leaves and fruit were compared to the tongue and heart.</note> is inserted, has a leaf placed upon the head; according to the testimony of Horus <note>Horapollo, the purported author of an ancient Greek treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, just as the leaf represents the tongue, so its fruit expresses the shape of the heart. This is because a wise man ought to hear much, and what he has learned through the tongue of a wise Master, he must commit deeply to the inner recesses of the heart through frequent contemplation. He carries poppies with a lit torch, because a wise man must especially occupy himself in the meditation on death (which is signified by the poppies) and on heavenly and most high matters (which are indicated by the lit torch). The quiver behind the back and the carelessly discarded bow indicate that whoever wishes to enter the inner sanctuaries of Wisdom must, above all, renounce the love of earthly things. He must utterly forget those things subject to corruption, which, according to Horus, are indicated by the moon and the serpent, the symbols of fleeting time. I would prove all these things at length from various authorities, had I not reserved them for the proper places for such symbols; therefore, we refer the reader to those sections. The owl, therefore, was a symbol of Wisdom compared to silence. For this reason, not only did the Athenians adopt the owl as the emblem of their City, but they also wished it to be sacred to Athena—that is, <term>Minerva</term> <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom, identified with the Greek Athena.</note>, the protectress of the City—as shown by almost innumerable coins found in the works of Paruta, Augustinus, Choul, and others, all marked with the image of the owl.

<margin>What *glaux* is and why Minerva is called *Glaucopis*.</margin>
<margin>The multitude of owls in Athens gave rise to a proverb.</margin>
<margin>What is to be understood by the owl as a symbol of victory.</margin>
<margin>Why it is dedicated to Aesculapius.</margin>
Indeed, *glaux* <note>original: γλαυξ (*glaux*)</note> is the same as the owl, named from the bluish-gray color of its eyes; hence <term>Athena Glaucopis</term> <note>original: Ἀθηνᾶ γλαυκῶπις (*Athena glaukōpis*)</note>, or Minerva the "gray-eyed," was so called either because she had bluish-gray eyes or because of the azure color of the air (for they interpreted Minerva as the air). From this, all who had bluish-gray eyes were considered men of the highest genius, as if they were the children of Minerva. Moreover, the City of the Athenians was so filled with these birds that a proverb arose from it: *to carry owls to Athens* <note>original: γλαῦκας εἰς Ἀθήνας φέρειν (*glaukas eis Athēnas pherein*)</note>, which is said against those who foolishly bring merchandise to a place where it already flows in abundance. As for the fact that some assert the owl to be a symbol of victory, I believe this was done because the owl was an image of the Wisdom and prudence which Pallas <note>Another name for Athena/Minerva.</note>, born from her father's brain, would grant; matters administered by these qualities undoubtedly achieve their desired end. For Wisdom is prepared by nightly contemplation and long vigils, as was clear from the symbols brought forward just a moment ago; in both of these, the owl seems to excel beyond all other birds. Indeed, it is the part of a wise man to discern through premeditation those things which are in darkness, and, having rejected talkativeness, to look to the proper place and time for acting. For the same reason, the owl is also dedicated to <term>Aesculapius</term> <note>The god of medicine and healing.</note>; because, in imitation of this bird, a physician must watchfully study day and night for the health of the sick.

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

...that owl's eggs are said to possess such power that if they are given to drunkards in wine for three days, they bring about a loathing of wine and make them sober. But let these remarks suffice concerning the first symbol of wisdom.

<margin>
The owl denotes a malignant demon.
Hecataeus according to Malchus.
Superstition of the Egyptians.
</margin>
We have discussed what the owl indicated among the Greeks; now let us reveal what it noted among the Egyptians. Among the Egyptians, therefore, it primarily signified a <term>Rival God</term> <note>original: *ἀντίτεχνον* (antitechnon). This refers to a deity acting as a spiritual competitor or adversary.</note> to Osiris, or a malignant demon—the Adversary of Osiris—who portends dire and terrible things, even if it might occasionally signify a messenger of prosperity, as will be said later. The reason for this significance took its origin from here: The Egyptians say, on the testimony of Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera, a Greek historian and philosopher who wrote about Egypt.</note>, that the followers of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and the rival of Osiris.</note> were each accustomed to take on the forms of those animals whose character and natural gifts were at odds with the sacred animals. Under these forms, they portended dire things to mortals and harassed them in various ways. Thus, just as Typhon occasionally took the form of a crocodile, or an ass, and sometimes a hippopotamus, so too did he sometimes take the form of a dragon or an owl (as has been proven elsewhere) in order to mock men and agitate them with various persuasions. The words of Hecataeus: <note>original: Τύφων ὁ μετασχηματιζόμενος εἰς γλαῦκα τερατολογέμενος ἔτυχε.</note> *Typhon, having been transformed into an owl, happened to portend terrible things.* Taking this occasion, whenever the Egyptians wished to signify a "Dragon" <note>In this context, a "dragon" often refers to a generic monstrous or malevolent force.</note>, they painted an owl. And just as they strived to appease the opposing powers of the sacred gods with certain sacrifices, so also they sought to venerate this <term>Rival God</term> visible under the form of an owl. They did this for the sake of averting evil, using various materials appropriate to the owl, treating it as a malignant demon, a hater of light, and an inhabitant of darkness, so that it might not harm them and that they might turn away all dire omens. For the Egyptians were the most superstitious of all mortals, as they drew omens from everything they might see, hear, or dream. It is no wonder, then, that Menander <note>A famous Greek dramatist; the text uses "Meandrum."</note>, speaking in the persona of the Egyptians, complained about all such dire omens:

> We are distressed if someone sneezes; we are angry
> if one speaks ill; we are very much afraid if someone
> has seen a dream; we tremble if any owl cries.

<margin>
The owl is an ill-omened bird.
</margin>
From here, this belief about the owl's deathly song and ominous moaning passed to almost all peoples and nations. Hence, we read so many unhappy epithets attributed to the owl everywhere among the poets, by which it was believed to be a most ill-omened bird to the human race while it screeches its "horrendous" sound, bringing sad fates. According to Ovid:

> And it becomes a foul bird, a messenger of coming grief,
> The sluggish owl, a dire omen for mortals.

And Virgil:

> And the owl was seen alone on the rooftops to lament
> with a deathly song, and to draw out long nights into weeping.

<margin>
The owl as a symbol of the day.
</margin>

...the name and Power <note>original: *Numen*</note> of the universal [deity], sends the owl as his messenger to men; through it, he signifies future events, warns of sinister outcomes, and teaches by its example what must be prudently done when a certain calamity is imminent. For they signified through the actions of the owl that true Wisdom is the only thing capable of meeting and resisting all sinister events and oncoming disasters. As appears even from this, this hieroglyphic accords best of all with Wisdom; so says Abenephius: <note>Abenephius, or Ibn Wahshiyya, was an author Kircher frequently cited for "Chaldean" and Egyptian wisdom.</note>

For they believed that the Owl is the messenger of the Deity Hemphta, who is the first divinity among them, and the announcer of all things that would happen to men. Certainly, what Abenephius says of Hemphta, Diodorus (Book 1, Chapter 2) confirms in open words regarding Isis—whom Plutarch interprets as the prudent progress of nature—when he says:

> Isis appears everywhere in dreams to those who worship her, offering aid for the diseases of those who are not well, giving advice for health, and urging men during the night through sleep and various visions both to avoid evils and to pursue good things.

Touching even more closely on this, Porphyry (Book 4, *On Abstinence*) openly says <margin>Porphyry, Book 4</margin> that among the *oscines* <note>Birds whose calls or songs were used by Roman augurs to predict the future.</note>, the owl is the one that announces the will concerning future events of Minerva (whom we asserted in the third book was the same as Isis). Plutarch, pursuing this at greater length in his *Life of Themistocles*, attached this story: When Neptune, defeated by Minerva, could not take possession of the Attic region, he was angered and sent them <term>δυσβουλίας</term> <note>original Greek: *dysboulias*</note>, that is, light and foolish counsels; however, since the bird of Pallas [the owl] was believed to open her mind to men, from this the proverb was born, *The owl has flown*, which was customarily said when things were done successfully and according to one's heart's desire, or turned out well. Whence Plutarch himself says it came about that the owl was adopted as a symbol of victory, which we were discussing above. Porphyry explains all these things quite appropriately in Book 3 of *On Abstinence* with these words:

> But the Gods indeed indicate matters by keeping silent, and birds perceive their signs more quickly than men, and having perceived them, they report them to us in the way they can. And different birds are the messengers of different Gods to men: the eagle of Jupiter, the hawk of Apollo, the owl of Minerva, the crane of Ceres, and others for the rest.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

*And at first they used to worship an idol whose name was Al-Laylah; they called it the Moon and named it Al-Laylah because she is the Mistress and Queen of the Night.* <note>Translated from the Arabic: "ولا وأول كان يعبدون الصنم اسمه الليله يقولونه القمر ويسمونه الليله لانها السيده وملكة الليل"</note>

The Ancients, he says, also worshiped a Goddess whom they called *Alilath*, and they said she was a *Lunar Spirit* <note>original: *Dæmonium*</note>; they called her *Alilath* because she was the *Mistress and Queen of the night*. Herodotus agrees with this, for in his book *Euterpe*, he asserts that the Arabs worshiped a Goddess by the name of *Alitta*. I believe that in place of the corrupted word *Alitta*, it should be read as *Alilath*. *They call Aphrodite Mylitta, but the Arabs call her Alitta.* <note>original Greek: Καλέουσι δὲ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην Μύλιτταν, Ἀράβιοι δὲ Ἀλίττα.</note> Although Mor Isaac the Syrian <note>A 7th-century ascetic and theologian.</note> wishes for *Mylitta* to be so named from the act of giving birth; for where he treats the goddess Astarte of the Assyrians, he says:

<image-desc>A line of Syriac script enclosed within two horizontal decorative lines</image-desc>

*Astaruth*, he says, is one of the seven wandering stars or planets, which is also called the Mother and the Midwife, because she is like the mother of all things, the producer of all things, and the preserver of all that exists in the world. Whatever the case may be—whether *Mylitta* is derived from *Valed* (that is, "to give birth"), or from *lail*, *Alilath*, and *Lilith* (that is, from "night")—it will certainly be admitted by anyone who rightly compares the actions of each and the mythological authors (as well as what we have written elsewhere on these matters) that all the names reviewed so far—Ilithya, Mylitta, Alilath, and Lilith—refer to the same Goddess. She is conflated with Lucina <note>Roman goddess of childbirth</note>, Hecate, Proserpina, Isis (or the subterranean Venus), Nephthe, Empusa, Lamia, and the Lemures or nocturnal demons. This is beautifully demonstrated through the owls indicated symbolically on the coins and medals of Paruta <note>Filippo Paruta, a famous 17th-century numismatist.</note>, which are inscribed sometimes to Juno, sometimes to Pallas, and now to Proserpina, as will be seen in the proper place. We have chosen to pursue all these matters more extensively here so that the consensus of authors <margin>Consensus of the cited symbols</margin> among all peoples regarding that nocturnal spirit—portending either prosperity or adversity and represented by the Egyptians through the owl—might be more clearly revealed. It also shows how the owl, through its natural behaviors, beautifully demonstrates how Wisdom might resist all adversities. (This Wisdom is taught by the Egyptian deity *Hempthay*—whom Eusebius calls *Emet* and Iamblichus corruptly calls *Cneph*—through the owl as the messenger of his will). We teach all these things more fully in our *Hieroglyphic Theology of the Egyptians*, where, explaining the mentioned symbols according to their higher spiritual meanings <note>original: *anagogicos sensus*</note>, we demonstrate the wonderful power of divine providence; and we clearly show that the Priests of the Sacred Rites <note>original: *Hieromantas*</note> did not differ much from the doctrine of orthodox theologians. But back to the subject.

<margin>The discord of nature through the owl and the crow.</margin>
<margin>The blood of the owl mixed with the blood of the crow does not combine.</margin>
Thirdly, I find that some have signified the discord of nature, which they call *Antipathy*, through the owl and the crow. This is because these two birds differ with such irreconcilable hatred that the blood of a crow, when mixed with the blood of an owl, is said never to cohere. If what is said is true, this certainly shows an entirely different temperament and a maximum discord of their natures. However, since I have found nothing regarding this kind of symbol among the Egyptians, I have chosen to present nothing further on it. Yet Horus <note>Kircher refers here to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics.</note> says that whenever the Egyptians wished to signify a man fleeing to someone's altars for the sake of protection or safety with a failed outcome, they used a sparrow and an owl...

<margin>Horapollo, Book 1, Chapter 51.</margin>
...he hopes to escape danger through protection, but instead, he is received by that very person with far more hostility. <note>original Greek: Ἄνθρωπον προσφύγοντα τῷ ἰδίῳ πάτρωνι καὶ μὴ βοηθεῖσθαι θέλοντες δηλῶσαι, στρουθὸν καὶ γλαῦκα, ζωγραφῶσι. Ὅτε γὰρ θηρευόμενος, πρὸς τὴν γλαῦκα φεύγει, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὴν πιέζεται.</note> "When they wish to show a man who flees to his own patron and is not assisted by his help, they paint a sparrow and an owl. For when the sparrow is sought in the hunt by bird-catchers, it flees to the owl, by whom it is soon crushed."

<margin>What various symbols attached to the Owl denote.</margin>
However, since symbols of this kind recounted by Horapollo have not yet been found among actual hieroglyphic schemes, we have deemed it more correct to relegate them to the category of Egyptian emblems and <term>apophthegms</term><note>Brief, pithy sayings or principles.</note>. Furthermore, the symbol of the owl signifies different things depending on the various objects joined to it. Thus, an Owl with a <term>Tautic character</term><note>A sign associated with Thoth, often resembling a cross or the ankh.</note> denotes a protective or "averting" spirit. The same with a curved staff denotes wisdom; with a figure denoting water, it signifies protection from the waters; with a Serpent, protection from the earth; with a <term>Nilometer</term><note>An instrument used to measure the height of the Nile's flood.</note>, protection from the Nile; and it has other meanings with other things. For the Athenians, an owl with a branch of laurel or palm, which it carried in its mouth with wings spread, signified victory; however, when flying over a reclining Lion, it suggested that strength had yielded to prudence. For the Owl is, as shown above, a symbol of the vigilance most necessary for scholars, which ought to be cultivated and preserved by sobriety; for this reason, we read that the <term>Attics</term><note>People of Athens/Attica.</note> depicted the Owl in such a way that it seemed to press down with its feet upon an inverted jar or vat, empty of wine. Let these remarks suffice concerning the hieroglyphic of the Owl.

## HIEROGRAM XII.

->The Quail, or<-

->*On the hieroglyphic significance of the Quail.*<-

<margin>The nature of the quail.</margin>
<margin>A symbol of ingratitude.</margin>
<margin>What its voice signifies.</margin>
Since the figure of the Quail occurs twice on our <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term><note>The Agonalis Obelisk now in the Piazza Navona, Rome.</note>, it must now be explained what the sages signified by it. Thus, since I find that the Quail has some sort of discord with the Moon—for when the Moon rises, the bird immediately raises ill-omened cries against her, not as if wishing the Goddess well or pursuing her with praise (as roosters are accustomed to do), but giving the most manifest signs of indignation against her—above all else, it digs into the earth and repeatedly <term>marks its own pupils</term><note>This refers to an ancient belief that quails scratched at their eyes or blinked excessively in the presence of celestial light they disliked.</note>, as if it cannot bear the appearance of the Moon, whom it does not even allow itself to look upon. It does this same thing at the rising of the Sun, that divine star. Since among the Egyptians, who were the greatest worshipers of the Sun and Moon, this was considered a sign of the highest impiety and ingratitude, they would secretly signify something impious, malignant, and hateful by painting the Quail, a bird of degenerate and <term>Typhonian nature</term><note>Associated with Typhon (Set), the god of chaos and enemy of Osiris.</note>. For they observed in it a certain Typhonian power hostile to Osiris and Isis, which the bird itself confessed with its natural voice. For with its cry it continually calls out *Ke Pa Ke*, which in the Egyptian language signifies the same as...

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

far from here, where he showed the greatest hatred toward the aforementioned Divinities, as Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera was an ancient Greek historian and philosopher who wrote about Egypt.</note> witnesses, it was believed he cried out; he proves this is true with these words, Horus <note>Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> in Book 1, Hieroglyph 49. <margin>Horapollo Book 1, Ch. 49.</margin> "When they wish to depict **Impurity**, they paint a quail <note>original Greek: ὄρτυγα. The author notes a manuscript correction here: "for thus the manuscript in my possession has it; not ὄρυχα [an oryx or antelope]"</note>, since when the moon rises in the east, looking intently at the goddess, it makes a loud cry. Not blessing her, nor with any favorable acclaim? Indeed, the sign is most clear then: for digging up the earth with its legs, it fixes its own pupils on the ground; as if indignant and unwilling to see the rising of the goddess. It does the same at the rising of the star of the lord god <note>The Sun</note>."

Furthermore, when marking an impure and wicked soul, they paint a Quail, because as the Moon approaches its rising, the bird looks toward the Goddess with intent eyes and cries out, neither blessing her nor following her with any favorable shout or congratulation. The clearest proof of this behavior is that it digs at the earth with its legs and fixes its own pupils into the ground, as if painting them there, appearing indignant and unwilling to behold the rising of the Goddess.

It does the same at the rising of the God—I mean the Sun. Finally, how perverse and <margin>The malice of the Quail.</margin> hostile the nature of the Quail is, and how it envies all other living creatures of any good thing, Horus pursues at length in the cited passage. For whenever it finds any place in the desert bubbling with water, after it has drunk, it disturbs the water with its beak, mixes mud into it, and throws dust into it with its feet, so that the water is unfit for any other living creature to drink. And although the Moon produces, increases, and nourishes everything useful in the whole world, the bird nevertheless seems to despise her: "for it does not even perform its duty, though the Goddess herself brings forth and increases all things that are now useful to the world" <note>original Greek: οὐ δὲ γὰρ οὐ δὲ τοῦτο καθῆκον ἐργάζεται, τῆς θεοῦ αὐτῆς πάντα γενώσης καὶ αὐξανέσης ὅσα νῦν τὸν κόσμον ἐστὶ χρήσιμα.</note>. And this it testifies openly with its voice, as Hecataeus also notes in these words: "more boastfully with the 'kepaka' <note>A phonetic representation of the quail's cry.</note> cry of the mother-quail <note>original Greek: ὀρτυγομήτρας</note>, as if it were despising the greatness of the gods with its voice." What is more unworthy than the "kepaka" cry of the Quail, by which it seems to some extent to scorn and mock the greatness of the Gods? But let these things suffice concerning the Quail; let he who desires more consult our *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he explains Egyptian mysteries in greater detail.</note> where we have pursued all things more extensively.

### Hierogram of the Rooster.

It is well known that to the Greeks, the Rooster signified many things, but to the Egyptians, it was hardly used, and then only in symbolic emblems. Therefore, since I have found no <margin>The Rooster is not found in these hieroglyphics.</margin> trace of it in the hieroglyphic literature marked on the Obelisks, nor in other inscriptions of the same kind, I have also judged it superfluous to deal with its meaning at length; therefore, let us proceed to other things.

## HIEROGRAMMATISM XIII. <note>A "Hierogrammatism" refers to a sacred symbolic lesson or entry regarding a specific sign.</note>

-> The Dove, or <-

### Concerning the hieroglyphic significance of the Dove.

**C**oncerning the hieroglyphics of the Dove, various authors devise various things. It is certain that it was held in the highest reverence not so much by the Egyptians as by the Assyrians especially...

# HIEROGLYPHICS

...to have been held in veneration. The reason for the cult was that some relate Semiramis, or more truly others relate Derceto <note>The text says "Decretam," likely a variation of Derceto, the Syrian fish-goddess and mother of the legendary Queen Semiramis.</note> the daughter of Semiramis, was turned into a Dove. Concerning this, since we have treated it very extensively in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's own work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>, in the *Pantheon of the Hebrews*, and in the treatises on the Decree, Dagon, and Oannes, we refer the reader there.

<margin>Moral actions through the symbols of the dove.</margin>
I have found, however, that the Egyptians signified moral actions through the dove. For instance, they signify pure air, free from all contagion of pestilential breath, through the Dove, because the eating of the Dove is an excellent prophylactic <note>A preventative treatment against disease.</note>, and thus it should serve as food for kings and chaste ministers of the sacred rites in times of contagion; concerning which see Horus <note>Horapollo, the traditional author of a treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> Book 1, Hieroglyph 57. Secondly, wishing to indicate a man who has restored himself to his former health through an oracle, they paint a ring-dove <note>Latin: *palumbum*.</note>, because by bringing a laurel leaf into its nest, it heals diseases. See Horus, Book 2, Hieroglyph 46. Thirdly, wishing to signify a widowed woman who has remained in that state of life until death, they paint a black Dove, for as long as she is a widow, she does not mix with another man. See Horus, Book 2, Hieroglyph 32.

<margin>Doves are not counted among the hieroglyphics.</margin>
From these things it is clear that the Egyptians did not transfer all animals into the register of sacred letters <note>Meaning the formal system of hieroglyphic writing used on monuments.</note>, but only those which were held sacred to the Egyptian Gods, due to a certain similarity and analogy to the operations of the Gods. Of this kind are almost all those we have explained so far. But some indeed—such as the horse, elephant, hare, donkey, deer, scorpion, weasel, ichneumon <note>A species of mongoose famous in antiquity for attacking snakes and crocodiles.</note>, leopard, pig, hyena, eagle, rooster, dove, sparrow, and similar ones mentioned by Horus—were not "sacred letters," but were only assumed to indicate moral actions through their properties, of the kind that are today called <term>phrenoschemata</term> <note>From Greek, meaning "mental patterns" or symbolic schemas used for teaching or meditation.</note>, emblems, proverbs, and the like. The reason for this, which we also suggested above, is that none of the cited animals are found on any obelisk, nor on Sphinxes, nor on the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet (the Mensa Isiaca) depicting Egyptian deities and pseudo-hieroglyphs.</note>, nor in any other hieroglyphic inscription which they were accustomed to paint on Isiac statues, mummies, and Canopic jars; undoubtedly they would have included them had not a mystical reason stood in the way.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>
The Ibis is very frequent in hieroglyphics.
</margin>
...[no other animal] has supplied so great a wealth of hieroglyphic material as the ibis. For as was said above, it was under the guidance of this bird that Hermes <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of wisdom and writing.</note> first discovered letters. With its help, the Egyptians perceived the elements of arithmetic, geometry, and those principles pertaining to the ratios of measurement. From its marvelous properties, the arts necessary to the human race—especially those pertaining to medicine and the science of divination—boast that they were discovered. 

<margin>
The usefulness of the Ibis.
</margin>
Through its benefits, the people were liberated from the countless evils by which the land of Egypt was continually infested, both from the multitude of venomous animals and from the savagery of crocodiles. By translating its actions not only into moral principles, but also into physical and archetypal ones, they denoted the vast mysteries of both the sensible and the insensible and supramundane spheres. 

<margin>
The ibis: a living dwelling-place of Mercury.
</margin>
Hence they called it the living dwelling-place of divinity; for they thought that Mercury—whom they called now Phthah, now Thoth, and sometimes Taut—clothed in the form of this animal, traveled around Egypt teaching men the discovery of various things and the worship of the Gods. Whence in the Egyptian language, as we have shown in our Dictionary <note>Referring to Kircher's *Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta*.</note>, they called him sometimes *Hermanuphta*, that is, the God of interpretation, and sometimes *Hermanubis Zeuda*, that is, the Ibis-Mercury teaching under the form of an ibis. See what we have treated extensively concerning their etymology in the supplement to the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher's *Prodromus Coptus*, an early work on the Coptic language.</note>. For they believed that the great Phthah, namely Mercury, who had provided them with the inventions of such great things, having been admitted into the fellowship of the Gods, did not cease to instruct men in whatever ways possible: while under the form of the Ibis he pours forth various oracles by his presence; while he instructs them through the hidden actions of this bird to form their character; while he averts all dire things by a happy omen, and many other things which we shall discuss in what follows.

<margin>
The Ibis as a symbol of the letter A.
</margin>
Therefore, the Ibis was the Hieroglyphic for the first letter **A**, and was called <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>original: "Ἀγαθοδαίμων"; a 'Good Spirit' or protective deity.</note>. Just as the Ibis indicated this, so with its beak inserted between its two legs, it beautifully expressed the same <term>destiny-writing</term> <note>original: "μοιρογραφικῶς" (*moirographikos*); a Greek term meaning to write or record one's fate or portion.</note>. But he who desires to know many curious things concerning the first construction of Egyptian characters, taken from the form and position of animals, let him read Book 2, chapter 7, on the construction of Egyptian letters; there we have shown at length, from various and most approved authors, six forms of different characters taken from the Ibis, so that it would be superfluous to repeat the same authorities here.

<margin>
2. It denotes Egypt.
</margin>
Secondly, when those ancient Egyptians intended to signify their own region, they primarily depicted the Ibis; first, because this bird so loves Egypt that it cannot live outside of it, and if exported, it dies as quickly as possible. 

<margin>
Aelian on the Ibis.
</margin>
> *Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author and zoologist.</note> says: the ibis never goes forth outside of Egypt, because that state of the Sky is moist, and the Moon is the most humid of all the planets. For if anyone should export it from Egypt by force and violence, it takes vengeance upon its captors, even to its own great ruin; for by bringing death upon itself through hunger, it shows the captors that their effort in exporting it outside of Egypt is in vain;* 

Hence it is no wonder if, as Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer.</note> witnesses, every crossroads in Alexandria is full of them. Since, therefore, this bird is unique to Egypt alone, it is no wonder [that they used] it in the [representation] of the same region...

### HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>The Ibis, deliverer of letters.</margin>
...taken as the hieroglyph of the region. Secondly, since the Ibis, while at rest, forms a triangle <note>the Greek letter Delta, Δ</note> with its spread legs and the line of the ground—as was proven in the cited seventh chapter—the Egyptians called this same region (formed by two branches of the Nile and the stretch of the sea) "Delta" from its resemblance to the shape, or in Coptic **the good field** <note>original: "ⲁⲗⲗⲏϯ"</note>. They referred to it by this monogram A, **the good spirit** <note>original: "ⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲇⲁⲓⲙⲟⲛⲁ"</note>, as we proved in the cited passage. And since the Ibis, by the spreading of <margin>From which comes the Egyptian Δ.</margin> its legs, had taught the branching of the Nile, by painting the Ibis in this posture, they denoted this part of Egypt as being fertile above all others. Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, dedicates this bird to Mercury. "I have heard," he says, "that near **Naucratis** in Egypt, there was one of the ancient gods to whom the bird called the **ibis** was sacred; the name of the god himself was **Thoth**." <note>Thoth is the Egyptian equivalent of the Greek Hermes or Roman Mercury.</note> I find six reasons why it was sacred to Mercury. The first is that <margin>Why it is sacred to Mercury.</margin> Mercury, to avoid the furies of Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian chaos-god Set</note>, transformed himself into an Ibis while other gods assumed other animal forms. Thus Ovid says in Book 5, cited above. The second reason is that Mercury, traveling about in the form of this bird, revealed the use of various things to men; so says Abenephius. <note>Kircher frequently cites "Abenephius," likely the Arab writer Ibn Wahshiyya.</note>

->*The Ibis is the bird of Hermes, and the people of Egypt mean that Hermes appeared to them under its form because of his knowledge.* <note>original: "برلوجه هي الطير هرميس ويقصردوا الاهل مصر لان هرميس تحت صورتة براي لهم لعلمه"</note><-

*The Ibis, or the stork, is called the bird of Mercury; for they thought that Hermes appeared to men in its shape to teach them.*

<margin>Mercury, presiding officer of the heart and reason.</margin>
The third reason is because Mercury is the presiding officer and moderator of the heart and reason; hence, when the Egyptians wished to signify the heart, they would paint an Ibis, because the bird itself is largely similar to the heart. Thus says **Horus**: <margin>Horus.</margin> *"Wishing to indicate the **Heart**, they paint an **ibis**, for this animal is attributed and dedicated to Mercury, the presiding officer and moderator of the heart and of all reason. For the ibis itself is largely similar to the heart, a matter about which there is much discussion among the Egyptians."* <note>original: "Καρδίαν βυλόμενοι γράφειν, ἴβιν ζωγραφᾶσι..."</note> Whence Pherecydes says in a hymn to Mercury: <margin>Pherecydes.</margin>

> O Ibis-shaped Hermes,
> Leader of the heart,
> Pourer forth of letters,
> And of all measurement.

*O Ibis-shaped Hermes, Leader of the heart, you are the Author of Letters and of all measurement.*

<margin>The weight of the ibis just hatched from the egg weighs as much as the heart of a newborn infant.</margin>
Hence the Egyptians, those keen observers of nature, found that an ibis newly hatched from its egg weighed exactly as much as the heart of a newborn babe—specifically, two drachmas. From this similarity between the heart and the ibis, they came to the conclusion that the heart was a member dedicated to Mercury, as was the ibis. They believed the heart reflected Mercury through a hidden property of shape, weight, and measure; indeed, that the bird designated these same things by the fixed intervals between its feet and its beak, as it formed an equilateral triangle, like a certain image and form of the heart. Thus says Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris*.

<margin>Aelian on the mystical shape of the Ibis.</margin>
Aelian relates the fourth cause in these words: *"They say the Ibis is beloved by Mercury, the father of speech, because it bears a likeness and specimen of speech; for its..."*

# BOOK IV. IDEAS.

Its black feathers can be compared to silent and as-yet-unspoken speech; however, the white feathers can be compared to the spoken word, which acts as the herald of our innermost feelings. Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a famous humanist scholar known as Volaterranus from his birthplace, Volterra.</note> explains this in the following way: *The ibis,* he says, *is selected by Mercury because it suits his nature; for since both black and white are found in this species, the one signifies the silent thoughts conceived in the mind, while the other represents the messenger of speech, heard and brought forth externally.*

<margin>Aelian on the Ibis. Plutarch.</margin>
The fifth reason is that while they asserted Mercury was Hermaphroditic, or "Moon-Solar," just as they designated his Solar power through the fervor of the heart and the source of heat, they designated his Lunar power by depicting the Ibis. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 2nd century who wrote on the nature of animals.</note> writes that they depicted the Ibis with expanded wings because the bird hatches its eggs in the same number of days as the moon waxes and wanes; furthermore, its very intestines are said to be compressed as the moon grows.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
Plutarch provides another cause: namely, that its black feathers are so arranged among the white ones that they resemble the **gibbous moon** <note>original: "αμφίκυρτον" (amphikyrtos), meaning curved on both sides or bulging.</note>, which is why it is also said to have been sacred to Isis. Clement of Alexandria confirms this in the 5th book of his *Stromata* regarding the "Solemnities of the Commasiae" <note>Public processions of Egyptian idols.</note>. There, among the other images carried about, was an image of the Ibis, by which they denoted the Moon. We have discussed this solemnity in several places throughout this work.

<margin>Cicero on the nature of the Ibis and its utility.</margin>
Cicero assigns a sixth cause for such "insane" worship of the Ibis in these words: *Ibises destroy a great force of snakes; they are tall birds with stiff legs and long, horny beaks.* Therefore, the cause for its consecration was its utility. For when winged snakes arrive from Arabia into Egypt, the Ibises move to meet them and destroy them, as well as their eggs (as Herodotus, Solinus, and Juvenal also report). By this service, the land is purged and liberated from many nuisances.

<margin>Herodotus book 2. Diodorus. Cicero.</margin>
And these are the reasons why the Ibis was held in such high honor, so much so that anyone who killed an Ibis—even by accident—would pay with their life, according to Herodotus, who notes this law also extended to those who killed Hawks. Diodorus Siculus testifies to the same regarding the Ibis, adding as an eyewitness that the same penalty awaited even involuntary killers, as was said above. Cicero adds to these in his 5th *Tusculan Disputation*: *the Asp, the Dog, the Crocodile.* Pomponius Mela <note>An early Roman geographer.</note> was therefore correct when he wrote: *The Egyptians worship the images of many animals, and the animals themselves even more; but different people worship different ones, so much so that it is a capital crime to have killed certain ones even by mistake.* This superstition was prudently used by Cambyses <note>A Persian King who conquered Egypt.</note> while he was besieging Pelusium. When the Egyptians harassed his army with missiles, he placed **dogs, sheep, cats, and ibises** <note>original: "κύνας, πρόβατα, αἰλούρους, ἴβιδας"</note> before the front line as a clever strategy. The Egyptians ceased their bombardment, fearing that by killing the sacred animals, they would bring a great crime upon themselves.

<margin>The Ibis: Symbol of the Lunar Genius and therefore Sacred to Mercury.</margin>
But let us return to our purpose. Thus, in the fourth place, the Ibis was—beyond the symbols we have mentioned—a hieroglyphic of the **Lunar Genius** <note>A "Genius" here refers to a presiding spirit or deity.</note>, or the protector of the element of moisture. For this reason, we indicated a little earlier that it was also sacred to the Moon, or Isis. And under this significance, that hieroglyphic is used in the **Bembine Tablet** <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, an elaborate bronze tablet depicting Egyptian-style mysteries, famous in the Renaissance.</note>, where an **ibis-shaped** <note>original: "ἰβίμορφον" (ibimorphon)</note> image sits upon a cube, holding in its left hand a staff with the head of Horus...

<summary>This page explains the symbolic links between the Ibis, Mercury (Thoth), and the Moon, citing the bird's feathers as symbols of speech and its utility in killing snakes as the basis for its sacred legal status in Egypt.</summary>

**Fifthly**, the wing of an ibis joined with a Crocodile indicated a certain power for averting evils; for just as the Ibis, by its mere touch, paralyzes <note>original: "siderat," literally "strikes with the power of the stars," meaning to stun or fix in place.</note> the Crocodile—that is, renders it motionless—so the Tutelary Spirit, by its superior dominant power, dissipates and puts to flight all **Typhonian** force <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms, often associated with the crocodile.</note> (indicated by the Crocodile, as said above) by its presence, or what is the same, stops the onset of imminent evils and renders them powerless. Thus says Horapollo: <margin>Horapollo, Book 2, chapter 18.</margin> *When they wish to signify someone rapacious or inactive, they paint a Crocodile having the wing of an ibis on its head; for if you touch it with the feather of an ibis, you will find it motionless.* <note>original Greek: Ἅρπαγα δὲ ἢ ἀνενέργητον βελόμενοι σημῆναι, Κροκόδειλον ἔχοντα ἴβεως πτερόν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς ζωγραϕᾶσι, τῶτε γὰρ τοῦ ἴβεως πτεροῦ θίγῃς ἀκίνητον αὐτὸν εὑρήσῃς.</note> And although Horapollo transfers these things to moral actions, the Egyptians nevertheless understand the rapacious Crocodile to mean Typhon, whom they believed had been turned into a crocodile (according to Plutarch), as has been said elsewhere.

**Sixthly**, this same bird—since it is thought to have discovered the **clyster** <note>An early form of the enema. Ancient naturalists claimed the ibis used its long beak to wash out its own digestive tract with seawater.</note>, or that type of remedy which was in very frequent use among the Egyptians for preserving and inducing health—depicted as holding its beak inserted into its rear, was a symbol of health to these same Egyptians. But let these remarks on the meaning of the Ibis suffice.

# HIEROGRAMMATISM XV.

->Of the Hoopoe, or<-

->*On the hieroglyphic significance of the Hoopoe.*<-

Although a complete figure of a Hoopoe does not appear among the hieroglyphics of our obelisk, because its head is nonetheless frequently seen placed upon a scepter among other things, it seemed appropriate to explain here what they indicated by the hoopoe and the scepter marked with its head.

Among the other portable items with which the statues of the **Comasiae** <note>Processional statues of Egyptian deities described by Clement of Alexandria.</note> appeared decorated, there was also a scepter <term>koukouphomorphon</term> <note>original Greek: κουκουϕόμορϕον, meaning "shaped like a hoopoe" or "cucupha."</note>, or distinguished by the head of a hoopoe; ignorance of this has provided many with a great source of errors. Pierius <note>Pierio Valeriano (1477–1558), author of a massive Renaissance compendium on hieroglyphics.</note> indeed thought it was the head not of a hoopoe or *cucupha*, but of a *cicuma*—that is, a stork's head...

It then introduces the symbolism of the hoopoe, particularly its appearance on the "cucupha" scepter used in religious processions.</summary>

<header>BOOK IV. IDEAS</header>

...thinks it to be. That this is false is evident from Festus and Isidore, who interpreted it as an owl <note>original: "noctuam"</note>. Goropius Becanus, in his usual imaginative way, tried to thrust upon us a crested lark <note>original: "galeritam," referring to the crested lark</note> by way of the *cucupha* <note>The Coptic word for hoopoe</note>, perhaps deceived by the crest. Others assert it is the head of a Stork, but who has ever seen a crested Stork? Unless perhaps by "stork" he means a turkey-cock <note>original: "gallum calecuticum," literally "cock of Calicut," a common early name for the turkey</note>. However, the source of this error seems to have been the great parental love <note>term: "philostorgia," the natural affection of parents for offspring and vice versa</note> found in both birds. To finally resolve the difficulty that authors find in untying this knot, we say that this is nothing other than the head of a **Hoopoe** <note>original: "upupæ"</note>, which will be easily clear from the Arabic. For Abenephius in this passage calls the scepter <margin>What the *Hodhod* is properly called by the Arabs.</margin> one "marked with the head of a hoopoe": *a scepter whose end is the head of the Hodhod* <note>original Arabic: قصبة بصورة الراس الهدهد</note>, which Camus <note>Referring to the *Al-Qamus*, a famous Arabic dictionary</note> aptly describes under the word *Hodhod*.

Furthermore, in the ancient Egyptian or Coptic language, the Hoopoe—the *Hodhod* of the Arabs—is the same as the **Koukoupha**, as can be seen in our *Egyptian and Coptic Thesaurus*, in the chapter on animals, which we recently published translated from Arabic into Latin.

<margin>A scepter marked with the head of a Hoopoe.</margin> And from this it appears that the Hoopoe is rightly understood by the word *Cucupha*. For the Hoopoe is a lover of "books" <note>likely referring to the Hoopoe's symbolic association with secret knowledge or the "letters" of the crest</note>, and the Hoopoe is the mark and ornament of divine scepters, as Horus witnesses in Book 1, chapter 55: <margin>Horus.</margin> *When writing "gratitude," they paint a hoopoe. For this alone of the irrational animals, once it has been reared by its parents, returns the same favor to them when they have grown old; for which reason the hoopoe is preferred for the divine scepter.* The *Cucupha* also does not seem to differ much from the **Duchiphath**, which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX)</note> in Leviticus 11 translate as "Hoopoe." There, Rabbi Solomon <note>The commentator Rashi</note> explains it as a "wood-cock with a double crest," from which <margin>The Hoopoe is conspicuous for its double crest.</margin> its name is derived, as if it were *Du Kephath*, meaning *having crests*. His words are: *The Duchiphath is a cock of the forest... which is adorned with a double crest.* Kimchi and Abenezra follow him, and Pagninus, following their version, says the Hoopoe is a bird with crests emerging from its head, like a helmet. This Rabbinic version is not displeasing: for the Hoopoe is even called by certain Greeks the "wild rooster," and by some the "bird of paradise." And because the Hoopoe matches the lark in its crest, the owl <note>original: "cicuma"</note> in its solitary life, the stork in its parental love <note>philostorgia</note>, and finally the cuckoo in its song, hence <margin>The Hoopoe, Owl, and Stork are reconciled.</margin> arose the differing opinions of various authors in determining the species of the Hoopoe; thus Goropius confused it with the Lark, Pierius with the Stork, and Aeschylus with the Cuckoo.

Since, therefore, the Hoopoe was a mark and ornament of hieroglyphic scepters, we must now see what they understood by such a <margin>What is meant by the hoopoe-shaped scepter.</margin> **hoopoe-shaped** <note>original: "κουκουφόμορφον" (koukouphomorphon)</note> scepter. It is known from Horus that the Hoopoe, placed by itself, is a symbol of gratitude; but when placed on a scepter, it is clear from what was cited above that it suggests the **unchangeable variety of things**. For the Egyptians saw that the bird was multi-colored, beautiful, equipped with a folding crest, and adorned with other rare virtues, and they did not want it to be absent from their catalog of hieroglyphics. For the Hoopoe is a bird, according to Aldrovandus and Pausanias, <margin>Pausanias. Aldrovandus on the Hoopoe.</margin> exceeding the quail in size, with a sharp head, like the one Philicles the Comic writer...

He explains its symbolism as representing both gratitude (due to its legendary care for elderly parents) and the "unchangeable variety of things" (due to its colorful plumage).</summary>

<meta>catchword: in</meta>

<margin>Description of the hoopoe.</margin>...as Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world.</note> writes it to have been, with a beak somewhat sickle-shaped, blackish like that of a treecreeper <note>original: "Certhiæ," a small insect-eating bird</note>, somewhat round, yet slightly flattened at the sides, and with an admirable crest. This crest consists of twenty-six feathers—though the Egyptians attribute twenty-eight to it, as will be said later—of which some are longer than others; their tips are blackish, followed by a white band. The rest of the bird is a chestnut color bordering on yellow; the eyelid, as in the poultry kind, covers the eye. Furthermore, it is said to raise or lower its crest at will, doubtless with the help of certain muscles. The neck, where it joins the head, is somewhat reddish, eventually fading into an ashy gray toward the back. From the back down to the tail, it is clothed in ashy feathers with white intervals and distinct spots. It has a tail six fingers wide; in the middle, a broad white transverse line is seen, inserted by nature to represent the image of the crescent Moon’s first quarter <note>This "lunar" marking on the tail is a key piece of evidence for Kircher's symbolic argument.</note>. The entire tail consists of ten feathers; the legs are short and lead-colored. It has black wings, distinguished by broad, high transverse lines; some of these wing feathers are black at the ends, while others are white. The tail extends beyond the wings; beneath the belly toward the rump it is white, but the breast is reddish. It has a triangular tongue, broad at the base and sharp at the tip, like a perfect equilateral triangle. From this minute and most exact description, it is likely that this most beautiful bird is imbued with a certain mystical color and variety of plumage; thus, it excels greatly in the hidden gifts of nature. This is evident from Abenephius <note>Kircher's name for an Arabic author he frequently cites, likely Ibn Wahshiyya</note>, who believes the Egyptians indicated the variety of worldly things through this bird, because they could not better represent it than through the symbol of the Hoopoe, which we <margin>The hoopoe is "all-colored"</margin> may not undeservedly call <term>παντοχρώματον</term> <note>original Greek: pantochromaton; "all-colored" or "possessing every hue"</note>. Hence Kiranides <note>A legendary author of a book on the magico-medical properties of plants, animals, and stones</note> assigns to it a diversity of colors and the four seasons of the year; these are his words:

> *The hoopoe is seven-colored, having a crown on its head two fingers high, which opens and closes; it possesses four colors corresponding to the four seasons of the year.*

<margin>The 7-colored hoopoe</margin> The hoopoe therefore has seven colors, by which it is likely the Egyptians signified the rays of the seven planets. By the mixing of these rays—just as by a certain tempering of colors—all lower things are what they are. Furthermore, through the four colors which Kiranides indicates the hoopoe's crest consists of, it is probable they understood not only the four seasons, but everything analogous to them: such as the four elements, the four phases of the Moon, the four quarters of the world, the four triplicities of the Zodiac <note>In astrology, the twelve signs are divided into four groups (triplicities) corresponding to fire, earth, air, and water</note>, and similar things. According to <margin>It marks the 4 Elements.</margin> the description above, the hoopoe's crest has black, whitish-yellow, red, and ashy colors, which beautifully correspond to the four elements: so that black corresponds to earth, blue to water, white to air, and yellowish-brown to fire. These, as primary colors mixed with others, produce infinite diversities of colors. Just so, the elements, stirred by celestial rays and joined in mixtures, produce infinite species of things. Thus the Moon, completing its periodic course in exactly as many days as the Egyptians say <margin>The hoopoe's crest as a symbol of the Moon.</margin> the hoopoe has feathers in its crest—namely twenty-eight, though others say twenty-six—governs the entire Lunar year.

330 BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>What does Horus with the scepter signify?</margin>
...divided into four parts, which astrologers call quadrants, each of which possesses the quality of a specific element; so that the first is hot and dry, the second cold, etc., as is clear below. This can also be said <term>analogously <note>original: "ἀναλόγως"</note></term> regarding the quadrants of the sun in spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Indeed, in this four-part season of the year, the whole world is, as it were, reborn. And the Egyptians seem to have had this in mind when, wishing to signify Horus—that is, the world—they painted him as a boy in a reticulated <note>Checkered or net-like.</note> garment, with a hoopoe-shaped <note>original: "cucuphomorpho," referring to the *cucupha*, another name for the hoopoe bird.</note> scepter in his hands, as appears on our obelisk and the Bembine Tablet <note>Also known as the *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze plaque featuring Egyptian-style deities and symbols that fascinated Renaissance scholars.</note>; for without this scepter, Horus is seen painted nowhere, as appears here.

<image-desc>A circular emblem containing a profile illustration of Horus depicted as a child. He stands facing left, wearing a garment with a reticulated or checkered pattern. He holds a tall scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe bird (cucupha). The word "SYMBOLS" is printed to the left of the figure and "OF HORUS" to the right, both following the interior curve of the circle.</image-desc>

For the world is not unlike an infant, being born each year in the spring; it becomes youthful in the summer, reaches maturity in autumn, and finally dies as it grows old in winter. Having died, it soon rises again and reveals itself as conspicuous through the variety of things. All these things are beautifully and exactly represented by the colors visible in the crest of the hoopoe, whose scepter is the proper attribute of Horus. For this reason, this scepter is seen placed seven times on the Bembine Tablet, corresponding to the multitude of colors observed in the hoopoe’s crest—specifically, as many times as the colors are reckoned to be in the hoopoe by the *Kiranides* <note>A series of ancient and medieval books on the magical and medicinal properties of plants, animals, and stones.</note>. This was to show that this variety of things is found in seven primary sensible subjects of this world: in earth, water, air, fire, animals, plants, and minerals <note>original: "fossilibus," which in Kircher's time referred to anything dug from the earth, including ores and stones.</note>.

<margin>The Hoopoe, a sign of the variety of things.</margin>
But all these things will be explained more fully when we interpret the aforementioned Tablet. In the meantime, look at the following chart.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

And this is the variety of things which the Egyptians indicated through the head of the hoopoe shining upon the scepter of Horus. The nature of the bird itself indicates this variety of things to us in two ways: first, by its crest, which it can raise up and hide when pressed down, according to Pliny. Second, by the shedding of its feathers, by which it remains hidden and bare in winter and autumn, according to Theophrastus. From this it is clear that this variety of things is sometimes hidden and sometimes apparent, depending on whether that Horus—the true eye of the world—has retreated further or approached closer.

<margin>The magical properties of the hoopoe.</margin>
And it should also be noted here that wherever the Isiac character, or the <term>handled Tau <note>original: "Tau ansatum," referring to the Ankh symbol, which resembles the letter T with a loop on top.</note></term>, is placed on the Bembine Tablet, the <term>hoopoe-shaped <note>original: "cucuphomorphum"</note></term> scepter is also placed. This is also observed on our obelisk, which we will discuss later. By this, they surely wished to insinuate nothing other than the wonderful power of the <term>Spirit of the World <note>original: "spiritus mundi," a Neo-Platonic concept of a life force permeating the universe.</note></term>, which, through its miraculous diffusion throughout the universe, introduces the greatest variety of things into the world. Accordingly, the Egyptians ingeniously joined those two symbols together, as we shall indicate more extensively elsewhere; they even used both as an amulet, just as we said above regarding the Tautic character. This is supported by the testimony concerning the hoopoe from Albertus Magnus and Evax, who call it a bird entirely full of illusions and omens; and the Magi have always held it in great value.

<margin>Sylvaticus.</margin>
Hence the superstitious Sylvaticus says that a stone found in the nest of a hoopoe, if placed upon the chest of a sleeper, betrays secrets and stirs up visions.

<margin>Kyranides</margin>
The *Kyranides* <note>A collection of ancient texts on the magical and medicinal properties of plants, animals, and stones.</note>, no less superstitious than Sylvaticus, passes down this operation: *“If you swallow the heart of a hoopoe, removed while it is still living and pulsating, having turned toward the Sun at the start of the first or eighth hour on the day of Saturn, with the Moon rising, and drink the milk of a black cow with a little honey over it while reciting the composition; see that you swallow the heart healthy and whole, and you will have foreknowledge of those things which happen in heaven and on earth.”* O what a remarkable Prophet! *“And you will know what men are thinking,”* (provided that, as I believe, he first learned it from the devil).

<margin>Villanovanus, Book 1 on elements.</margin>
Then he recites a honey composition, which he says is better if one throws in the heart and liver of a *hoopoe*. Similar ridiculous things are said about the heart and blood of the hoopoe, which <term>Villanovanus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note></term> subscribes to in his second book on the mole: *“that the pulsating heart of a hoopoe, swallowed during a new moon, makes one know all things that exist, the minds of men, and many celestial matters.”*

<margin>Rhazes.</margin>
<term>Rhazes <note>A celebrated Persian physician and scholar of the Islamic Golden Age.</note></term> tells similar tales. But because these things are unworthy of wasting more time on them, let us prepare ourselves for other matters, since all those things arose from the discipline of the Magi.

<margin>Maidenhair fern is placed in the hoopoe's nest.</margin>
In the Greek *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore.</note>, book 15, chapter 1, under the authorship of *Zoroaster*, we read that the hoopoe places the herb <term>maidenhair <note>original: "adiantum"</note></term> in its nest as a protection against enchantments.

<margin>Aelianus.</margin>
However, Horus shows another use for <term>maidenhair</term> in the hoopoe, which <term>Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric.</note></term> also teaches, attributing to it a certain power of unlocking.

<margin>A fable about the hoopoe unlocking.</margin>
*“For,”* he says, *“when a man once found a hoopoe in a crack of a ruined and deserted wall, and the caretaker had noticed it, he filled and blocked the crack with mud. But the hoopoe, returning and seeing its hiding place closed and filled, brought a herb which, when applied to the mud, caused it to dissolve and flow away. The bird entered the hollow to its chicks. But later, when it went out again to seek food, that man again blocked the cavern; the bird, however, opened the crack with that very same herb,”* which...
