### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...which itself happened three times. The curator of the wall, understanding this, took that herb from the mud—not indeed for the uses the hoopoe employed it, but to unlock treasures (fantastic ones, I think) which were of no concern to him. Certainly, it appears from this that the delusions of such superstitions were passed down from the Egyptians to posterity. 

<margin>The hoopoe changes its appearance at certain times of the year.</margin>

Pausanias relates that the blood of the hoopoe was used in <term>Typhonian <note>Associated with Typhon (or Set), the Egyptian god of chaos, storms, and desert.</note></term> rites. For when the Egyptians saw that the bird changed its appearance at certain times of the year, they called this change the transition of Typhon into <term>Horus <note>The sun god and symbol of order; Kircher interprets the changing feathers as the movement between chaos and light.</note></term>. For they thought that Typhon repeatedly took on the forms of animals dedicated to Horus. By this, they judged—privately—that for the variety of things in this world, a mixture of Horus with Typhon was necessary; that is, the disagreement of contrary principles, from which the harmony of the whole is born, as if composed of consonants and dissonances. Plutarch has explained this quite elegantly elsewhere, and that fable in Aeschylus seems to allude to this, which he described in the following verses:

<note>Original Greek from Aeschylus’ lost play *Tereus*: "Τῦτον δ’ ἐπόπτην ἔποπα τὸν αὑτοῦ κακῶν...". Kircher provides a Latin translation below, which I have rendered into English.</note>

> This hoopoe, the overseer of his own evils,
> He has made variegated and displayed,
> A bold bird of the rocks in full armor;
> Who, when spring appears, beats the wing
> Of a white-tailed hawk. For he will appear in two forms
> From the single womb of his child;
> And when the grain of the new harvest grows,
> A wing with curved shoulders gives birth to him again.
> In hatred of the plain of Pallene,
> He haunts the deserted forests or the frost-covered heights.

->Which we interpret thus:<-

> *This hoopoe, witness of its own calamity,*
> *He made varied; and he holds him, struck by fear—*
> *Once fierce and armed, now a bird of the rocks.*
> *When spring appears, it shakes new feathers*
> *Like a white-bellied hawk. For its figure is twofold:*
> *One color is on the youth's breast*
> *In autumn, and when that golden harvest has brought forth,*
> *It puts on other feathers again, changed, etc.*

<margin>Tereus turned into a hoopoe.</margin>

From these things it clearly appears that he alludes here to <term>Tereus <note>A mythical Thracian king who, after a cycle of violence and revenge involving his wife Procne and her sister Philomela, was transformed by the gods into a hoopoe.</note></term> being changed into a hoopoe, and beholding his own calamity in this face. Here he plays on the words *epops* <note>Greek for hoopoe</note> and *epoptes* <note>Greek for overseer or spectator</note>, as if to say: Jupiter (or whoever changed Tereus into a bird) made him a spectator of his own evils. Distinguished by varied feathers, that man who was previously fierce in his full armor was rendered into this same bird—for the long beak serves as a sword, and the crest as a helmet—now made fearful. I believe that here <note>Referring to the Greek text</note> *apodelosas* should be read with an *alpha* rather than an *epsilon*, so the verb *apodelan* signifies "to make clear," just as "to make variegated." And for *phainei* (appears), *phuei* (grows/produces) should be read, so the poem maintains the same sense. For *kampsinomese* (curve-shouldered), perhaps *kompsinomese*, that is, "it clothes and puts on," so the meaning is that it loses its feathers in springtime...

# HIEROGRAMMATISM XVI
->The Scarab, or<-
## Concerning the Hieroglyphic Significance of the Scarab

That the Scarab—which the Greeks call *Heliocantharos* <note>original: Ἡλιοκάνθαρον, meaning "Sun-beetle"</note> and *ailouromorphon* <note>original: αἰλουρόμορφον, meaning "cat-formed"</note> due to its shape—was a hieroglyphic for the Egyptians to indicate the Sun, is demonstrated more than sufficiently. This is shown not only by the double image of it inscribed on the present obelisk, but also by irrefutable testimonies brought from all antiquity and the ancient monuments of history. And to omit countless others, Suidas and Aelian testify in most brilliant words that the Egyptian priests, who worshipped scarabs with a certain singular honor, were accustomed to carve them onto sacred obelisks. Abenephi, writing on the antiquities of the Egyptians, agrees with them when he says: <margin>The excellence of the Sun represented through the scarab.</margin> *The Egyptian philosophers, to denote the excellence of the Sun, carved scarabs everywhere on their stones.* His words are:

<margin>Abenephi the Arab. The Beetle.</margin>
->The Egyptian wise men, when they wished to indicate the virtue of the Sun, engraved the image of the beetle into stones.<-
<note>Kircher provides the text in Arabic script: "الحكما مصر فلما يريدون ان يدلوا الفصله الشمس ونقشوا في الاحجار الصورة الخنفس"</note>

Manetho, in his epitome of natural history, and Hecataeus, in his work on the philosophy of the Egyptians (cited by Diogenes Laertius in *The Lives of the Philosophers*), also seem to agree: *The Egyptians,* he says, *spoke of a philosophy of this kind concerning the gods and justice: that primary matter was the beginning of things, that the elements were distinct, and that many living beings were perfect; that the Sun and Moon are Gods, one called Osiris and the other Isis; and that they expressed these through the scarab and the dragon carved into stones.*

Eusebius Pamphilus says: <margin>Eusebius Pamphilus, Book 3, Chapter 2.</margin> *Among other animals consecrated to the Sun, the Egyptians worshipped the scarab above all, thinking it to be a living image of the Sun.* This is supported by a letter written in the Ethiopic language, sent to <term>Peter de Comis<note>Likely a reference to an Abyssinian scholar or contact within the Ethiopian community in Rome during Kircher's time.</note></term>, an Abyssinian, from Ethiopia to Rome. A copy of this is kept in the Vatican Library, attached to a book of Ethiopic rites; in it, after discussing the antiquities of the Ethiopians, the author also writes about the scarab as follows, which I translate from the Ethiopic language: <margin>Ethiopic Letters.</margin> *There appear,* he says, *in these parts of ours, many monuments of the ancients, such as columns and stones, in which, besides other animals, many*

Note, therefore, that all those kinds of insects which are called <term>Coleoptera</term> <note>original: κολεόπτερα, meaning "sheath-winged"</note> by the Greeks—that is, those whose wings are hidden within a crust as if in a sheath—are grouped, according to Pliny, into the category of Scarabs (which the Greeks call 
<margin>

*cantharous*). They are distinguished from the *anelytra*, or insects lacking such a crust, because the latter are equipped with stingers and a proboscis and constantly traverse the air with the rowing of their wings. The former, lacking these instruments—having been equipped with teeth by Nature, the provident mistress of things, for the purpose of eating—are found everywhere in the dust and dung, right before men's eyes or under their feet, in all places and paths, provided excrement is present.

The Egyptians engraved this Scarab (which certainly holds a significant place among the other animals treated with divine honors) to indicate the powers of the Sun. In order to have a richer variety of

2. Bull-shaped.

The first species of Scarab is the cat-shaped <note>original: αἰολόμορφος</note>, which, because of its gleaming brilliance, we might not wrongly call—following Pliny and Aristotle—the <term>chrysocantharon</term> <note>Golden beetle</note>, or with Aristophanes, the *chrysomylo-keron*. The second kind was the *dikeros* <note>two-horned</note>, or bull-shaped, a true offspring of the bull, affecting something of the bovine. Finally, the third kind of Scarab was the *monokeros* <note>one-horned</note>, quite unlike the others; according to Horapollo, this was consecrated to Mercury <note>Thoth</note>, just as the preceding bull-shaped one was consecrated to the Moon, because of the Moon's "exaltation" in the sign of Taurus <note>In astrology, the Moon is believed to have its strongest influence in the zodiac sign of the Bull.</note>. One might rightly wonder which of these three types of Scarabs was most specifically consecrated to Osiris, the celestial Sun. But so that no spark of doubt remains in the readers' minds, I say that each was consecrated to Osiris, though representing different effects which that celestial Osiris causes in this world. For according to Plutarch, it was a familiar habit of the Egyptians to assign different names and symbols to the various effects of a single thing, as Girolamo Aleandro learnedly demonstrates in his *Heliadic Tables*, and as I show at length in my introduction or apparatus to the hieroglyphics. Horapollo testifies in these words that the scarab was dedicated by the Egyptians to Osiris—insofar as he was believed to be the Sun of the sensible world—on account of a certain likeness to the Sun's actions expressed in its own behaviors. <margin>Ch. 10. Horus, Book 1. Which scarab is dedicated to the Sun?</margin> "There are three forms of beetles," he says, "one is cat-shaped, and they dedicated it to the day and the sun because of its symbolism." <note>original Greek: εἰσί τε καὶ κάνθαροι ἰδέαι τρεῖς, μία μὲν αἰλουρόμορφος, κᾀκείνην ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡλίῳ ἀνέθεσαν διὰ τὸ σύμβολον.</note> He says there are three species of scarabs; the first indeed reflects the face of a cat and is distinguished by certain rays. They dedicated this to the Sun because of a certain resemblance: both because its brightness imitates the rays of the Sun, and, as is immediately apparent, because it seems to reflect the rising and setting of the sun through a cat-like <note>The author uses "aelurus" and "feles," both referring to cats.</note> expansion and contraction of its pupils. These pupils are strained at sunrise, become blunt at midday, and seem to set, growing dim, when the star <note>The Sun is often referred to as a "star" or "sidere" in classical contexts.</note> is about to set. And for this reason, the ancients used to engrave it on gemstones with a radiant head, as is shown here.

The bull-shaped scarab, however, they dedicated to the Moon, according to the testimony of <margin>Horapollo, cited place. Around the same time that the Sun runs through the "emergence" of the bull, the Moon rendered the earth fit and suitable for planting, sowing, and other labors of agriculture, of which the bull was the symbol. But let us hear Plutarch, who confirms the truth of these sayings with a most fitting testimony. For he says thus in his book *On Isis and Osiris*:

Furthermore, they say that the living Apis is the image of Osiris. Therefore, it also has a shape like the Moon with many bright parts covered by shadowy ones, and in the new moon of the month of <term>Phamenoth<note>The seventh month of the Egyptian calendar, falling in Spring.</note></term> they celebrate a festival which they call the "Entry of Osiris into the Moon," which is the beginning of spring. By placing the power of Osiris in the Moon in this way, they describe Isis as his wife, from whom he may generate offspring; therefore they also call the Moon the "mother of the world," and they fashion a nature for her mixed from both sexes, because being filled and made pregnant by the Sun, she in turn emits into the air and scatters the generative principles from herself. To the confirmation of these sayings is also added the fact that the scarab was held as a certain omen of the said springtime. This is because around the beginning of spring, revived by the returning heat of Phoebus <note>The Sun.</note> after its winter retreat, it begins gradually to gather dung, to form muddy balls for producing offspring, and to fill every path with its black brood.

BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>The solid-bodied Sun-beetle.</margin>
It seems that Phornutus and Albricus <note>Phornutus (Cornutus) and Albric of London were influential mythographers who interpreted ancient gods as symbols of natural forces.</note> intended to signify this. From this it is clearly evident that the Egyptians appropriately expressed one and the same Osiris through symbols of various scarabs—as if he were manifold in power and operation—but especially through that one which Horapollo calls at the beginning the *heliokantharon* [sun-beetle] or *chrysokantharon* [gold-beetle]. <note>original Greek: ἡλιοκάνθαρον or χρυσοκάνθαρον</note> This beetle, shining with the spread brightness of its wings like flickering rays, reflects the daytime light of the Sun; moreover, with the luster of its hindquarters, with which it flashes at night like sparks, it seems to represent the light of the Sun reflected from the Moon by no obscure argument. Furthermore, let us now see in what manner they expressed the world itself, its rotations, and the movements of the stars through that same celestial Scarab illuminated by rays.

<margin>The world compared to an egg. Eusebius.</margin>
It is established, according to Plutarch, that the Egyptians—under the teaching of Zoroaster—called the world an "egg," either by similarity, or by some hidden analogy of spiral motion or the oval boundary of the atmosphere, or for some other reason. Eusebius Pamphilus, in Book 3, signifies that world-egg produced by Ormazd <note>referred to as Orimazes, the Zoroastrian creator deity</note> in these words: > *This God, he says, produces an egg from his mouth, from which is born the God whom the Egyptians call Ptah and the Greeks call Vulcan [Hephaestus]; the world is signified by an egg of this kind;*
<margin>The composition of the egg and its comparison to the world.</margin>
Moreover, that the world has the greatest similarity to an egg will be easily clear from a comparison made between them. For just as an egg is composed of three parts—the shell, the white, and the yolk—so too is the world. In this way, the solid space of the heavens corresponds to the shell; the ether to the white; and finally the terrestrial region to the yolk. Just like the yolk in an egg (in which the whole power of the seed lies hidden), the earth is the recipient of all celestial influences and virtues.

These things being established, the individual parts of the Scarab also testify that it has a great affinity with the egg and the heavens, both in its own form and its mode of operation. The crusty structure of its entire body, mimicking an oval and shell-like shape, suggests this; its thin, transparent, and foldable wings correspond to the aerial and fiery space, just as the rest of its body, the receptacle of seminal power, corresponds to the terrestrial sphere—the place of all corruption. What else are those five lines appearing on its back but a representation of the five zones of the world? <note>In ancient geography, the world was divided into five climate zones: two frigid, two temperate, and one torrid zone.</note>
<margin>The Scarab has 30 digits.</margin>
It is added that every Scarab is equipped with thirty "digits" <note>small segments on the beetle's legs</note> on its six forked feet; by which surely nothing else seems to be signified but the monthly spaces of thirty days in which the Sun runs through each sign in the Zodiac.
<margin>Ruellius, On the Nature of Plants.</margin>
All of this Jean Ruel <note>a French physician and botanist known for his 1536 work "De Natura Stirpium"</note> aptly confirms in Book 2 of *On the Nature of Plants* in these words: > *Because the Scarab, an animal known to all, rests upon as many digits, or rather feet, as there are days in a month—during which the rising Sun pursues its courses—it clearly demonstrates to us the conjunction of the Sun and Moon. For, rolling a ball of ox-dung from east to west, it shapes it into the image of a sphere; it then buries it in a small pit in the ground for 28 days, until the Moon, circling the zodiac and returning to the inter-lunar period, falls silent. Then, opening the sphere, it brings forth new offspring; nor does it know any other origin of birth.*
<margin>Pliny.</margin>
Pliny also, speaking of the same: "On account of this," he says...

# HIEROGLYPHICS

[Pliny] says in Book 30, chapter 11: *“A great part of Egypt worships Scarabs among the Divinities, according to the curious interpretation of Apion, through which he concludes that a likeness to the works of the Sun exists in this animal, as we have said above.”* <note>original Latin: "Ægypti magna pars Scarabæos inter Numina colit..."</note> Horus Apollo confirms the aforementioned in the clearest words in Book 1, chapter 10; for he says thus: <margin>Horus.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἔχει δὲ πᾶς κάνθαρος καὶ δακτύλους τριάκοντα διὰ τὴν τριακονταήμερον τοῦ μηνὸς, ἐν αἷς ὁ ἥλιος ἀνατέλλων τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ποιεῖται δρόμον.</note> *Every beetle, he says, has thirty fingers, representing the thirty days of the month, during which the rising Sun completes its own course through each of the signs of the Zodiac.* Furthermore, it is clear that the Scarab emulates the Sun in all things, not only by its likeness or by a certain <term>anagogical</term> <note>Anagogical interpretation looks for a higher, spiritual, or mystical meaning within physical objects or behaviors.</note> representation of its parts, but also by its movement and its method of operating; for they fashion those little balls, from which the Scarabs take their origin, into the very form and image of the world. For when they have found the excrement of an ox or another beast of burden, <margin>The actions of the scarab are analogous to solar movements.</margin> they fashion little balls which they roll from the rising toward the setting sun [East to West], and pushing with their hind feet, they propel them with an unceasing rotation; meanwhile, they themselves look toward the sunrise—according to the testimony of Horus in the cited passage—as if they were intentionally taking pains to express the image of the heaven by gazing upon its model. Indeed, what of the fact that, while pushing from the <term>Subsolanus</term> <note>The East wind, representing the East.</note> toward the <term>Africus</term> <note>The South-West wind.</note>, it seems to strive to meet the rising of the stars—which is the proper movement from the West toward the East—do they not seem in this also to affect the proper motion of the Sun? What shall I say of the time destined for hatching the offspring, which is certainly ordered most exactly to the motion of the Sun and Moon, as is clear from the authors cited above? For those spheres of dung, fabricated by the Scarab after the model of the world and buried in the earth, are kept for as long a space of days as the periodic motion of the Moon lasts; <margin>It observes the motion of the Moon.</margin> they will be seen to gradually come to life, first indeed into little worms, and soon into scarabs, yet still enclosed in their own small casing. On the twenty-ninth day, the father comes forth from the nest, gathers the balls, and rolls each one into the water by pushing it, as we said; for he is not ignorant that this same day reconciles the rising of the Sun and Moon, and therefore, as the New Moon begins, he strives to represent a certain generation of the world itself. Once these balls have first been softened in the waters and opened not long after, the now-formed scarabs are excluded—a "black troop" moving through the fields. 

Thus the wise Egyptians, weighing more deeply the admirable workmanship of this little creature, gradually arrived at a profound investigation of the workmanship of this world. <margin>The Egyptians learn the motions of the Heavens from the motions of the Scarab.</margin> Indeed, with the scarab as a master, they reached the spiral motion of the stars, the Sun, and the Moon, and finally of the universe; the spiral progress of the human mind; and lastly, the reflected (if one may speak thus) agitations and motions of the revolutions of the archetypal world. Finally, with the workmanship of the scarab proposed as a kind of archetype, the <term>Lyncean</term> <note>Referring to "lynx-eyed" observers—philosophers who possessed deep, piercing insight into the secrets of nature.</note> philosophers of the first ages, working upon the stupendous mysteries of nature and the most hidden <term>Sacraments of both Medicines</term> <note>Likely referring to the Alchemical 'medicines' of the soul and the body, or the dual paths of physical and spiritual healing.</note>, penetrated them by the guidance of the scarab alone. <margin>Dee in the Monas Hieroglyphica.</margin> John Dee <note>original: "Deenus"</note> certainly seems to philosophize beautifully in his *Hieroglyphic Monad* concerning these mysteries already related—driven not so much by prepared speech as by a kind of sacred instinct; his words...

<margin>Alchemical discourse</margin>
*astronomers; and as it is said, a word to the wise is sufficient. From this, let Alchemists learn what is the true water of egg whites, what is the oil from yolks, and what is the <term>calx</term> <note>Calx refers to the powdery residue left after a substance has been consumed or transformed by fire; in alchemy, it often refers to a purified state.</note> of eggs. Here we have almost everything proportioned by nature. This is that aquiline [eagle's] egg which the Scarab once broke because of the injury and cruelty that the violence of that bird inflicted upon timid and brutish men; for although some fled to the Scarab’s burrow to implore help, they were not liberated from there. However, the Scarab alone, judging that this injury must be avenged by every means—being of a spirited mind and constant will—lacked neither the strength nor the ingenuity to perform it. Thus, pursuing the eagle through various attempts, the Scarab used its most subtle art and finally caused the eagle's egg—even when deposited in the lap of Jupiter—to be cast down to the ground and shattered. In the same way and for other reasons, the Scarab would have eventually deleted the entire eagle species from the earth, had not Jupiter intervened to prevent such an evil. Indeed, during the time when the Eagles solicitously care for their eggs, no Scarabs fly about. Nevertheless, I would advise those who are vexed by the cruelty of that bird to learn a most*

Thus a great metamorphosis of the egg occurs; the white now disappearing and being, as it were, enveloped by the liquid of the yolk. Furthermore, the eagle’s egg, through the artifice of the Scarab, will easily become known to the "Sons of Hermes" <note>An alchemical term for practitioners of the hermetic arts.</note> from the described hieroglyphic account. # HIEROGLYPHS

But lest, while I act the part of Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; here, the author uses him as a metaphor for a translator or decipherer of mysteries.</note> unraveling hieroglyphs, I might seem to play the Sphinx <note>The Sphinx was known for posing obscure riddles; the author is saying he wants to be clear rather than confusing.</note> in representing things obscurely, I have chosen to represent here a symbol of the origin and process of the triple world <note>The "triple world" usually refers to the three realms of existence: the elemental (earthly), celestial (heavenly), and intellectual (divine).</note> as shown in the workmanship of the Scarab. This will undoubtedly please the diligent stewards of nature.

The upper spiral is smaller and contains the words "helical progress" <note>original: "helicus progressus"</note> and "Spirit of the world" <note>original: "Spiritus mundi"</note>. Labels near the beetle include "Hieroglyphs of the Scarab" and "Idea of the ball" <note>Refers to the ball of dung the beetle rolls, which ancients saw as a model of the sun or the earth.</note>.</image-desc>

These, therefore, are those ideal spirals of divinity which involve the triple world within the workmanship of the Scarab. They are represented here as if in a rough model, through which the entire philosophy of the Egyptians—and indeed of all other ancient Sages—is completed. This includes their teachings concerning GOD, the <term>Architect Mind</term> <note>The "Opifex mens," often associated with the Demiurge or the divine intelligence that shaped the universe.</note>, the World Soul, Angels and Daemons, the World itself, and man, who is the son of the world.

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

The Poet <note>Referring to Virgil.</note> suggests with very clear words that the Egyptians alluded to these volumes of ideal spirals when he sings in the *Aeneid*, book 6:

<margin>Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.</margin>
> The Spirit nourishes within, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body.
<note>original: "Spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus / Mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet."</note>

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
<margin>The spirals of the divine Gods.</margin>
Orpheus also—in the writings of Symphorien Champier <note>original: "Symphorianum Camperius," a French Renaissance physician and humanist.</note>—confirmed the same thing with very few words, yet they clearly indicate the logic of this entire workmanship of the world. He says that God turns a swift impetus upon a perpetual hinge; for, as Champier rightly says in the cited passage, God is the universal hinge of all things, perpetually turning essence, life, mind, nature, and matter as if they were certain hinges. And, to speak with Plato: through the property of each rank, He turns the hinge itself; through the one essence, He turns all essences; through life, all lives; through mind, all minds; through soul, all souls; through nature, all natures; and through matter, all matters—perpetually, I say, turning a swift impetus upon the hinge. All of these things are confirmed in even clearer words by the famous Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius ille Trismegistus"</note> in his eighth dialogue to Tat <note>A figure in the Hermetic texts, often depicted as the son or disciple of Hermes.</note> with these words: *“But God, full of ideas, bringing qualities from the Father into the sphere, has circumscribed every quality as if in a circle.”* Furthermore, since the Egyptians noticed a triple order of all those things which are and can be—namely, the intellectual, the corporeal, and those mixed from these—

<margin>The triple order of things in the triple world.</margin>
they also established a triple world, according to the testimony of Pico della Mirandola in his preface to the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's 1489 work providing a seven-fold explanation of the creation story in Genesis.</note>: the highest is the "ultramundane," which theologians call the Angelic world and philosophers call the Intellectual and Archetypal world, which is well-celebrated. Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, places the celestial, the ethereal, the sublunary, and the human next to this.

<margin>All things in each individual world.</margin>
In the fourfold order of these worlds, one must observe that these four worlds are one, not only because they are all referred back to one principle and one end, or because they are gathered together by appropriate numbers and a certain harmonic kinship of nature (to speak with Pico) and a best-ordered series of steps; but because whatever exists in all worlds simultaneously exists in each one individually. There is not any single one among them in which all things that exist in the others are not present. Pico testifies in his preface to the *Heptaplus* that Anaxagoras was of this opinion, along with the Platonists and Pythagoreans.

<margin>How all things are in all things.</margin>
Truly, the things that are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but of a better quality; likewise, those that are in the higher worlds are seen in the lowest, but in a degenerate condition and a "corrupted" nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elemental quality; in the celestial bodies, it is a heating power; in the human body, it is a certain heat which Physicians call the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>Humidum radicale: a medieval medical concept referring to the innate life-sustaining fluid or "fuel" within a living being.</note>; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me say something more expressive: Among us, there is fire, which is an element; the Sun is the fire in the heavens; in the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>, the heart is a fire boiling with desires; in the ultramundane region, fire is the Seraphic intellect <note>Referring to the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning."</note>. But see how they differ: the elemental burns, the celestial gives life, the microcosmic illustrates and animates, and the super-celestial loves. There is water among us; there is water in the heavens, which is its nurse and mistress—namely, the Moon, the vestibule of the heavens.

The divine essence, or that triform intelligible world, is square. <note>original: "$\tau\epsilon\tau\rho\alpha\gamma\omega\nu o\varsigma$" (tetragonos).</note> Hence we read in the *Leviticus Rabbah* <note>original: "Vaicra Rabba," a homiletic commentary on the book of Leviticus.</note> regarding Chapter 4 of Leviticus, and in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A commentary on the Psalms.</note> the following words: <note>original Hebrew: רבכן אמרו מה הנפש המלאה את הגוף כן הקב"ה סובל את העולם</note> "Our Rabbis said: as the soul fills the body, so the Holy One, blessed be He, sustains the world." From these things it also appears why the Arab Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Albumajar," a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> says that the most high GOD, by ideally knowing His own essence, generates in His identity a Mind and Wisdom similar to Himself in all things; and again, that GOD produced all things by a fixed state and a revolution. Martianus Capella <note>Author of an influential 5th-century encyclopedia; he describes Philology purging herself to ascend to heaven.</note> also describes Philosophy, as she penetrated the abyss of divinity, vomiting up circles and spheres. It appears as well why Hermes Trismegistus said GOD is a circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere; and why Plato said GOD is always occupied with forming circles when he said: "God always geometrizes," <note>original: "$\delta \theta\epsilon\grave{\delta}\varsigma \dot\alpha\epsilon\grave{\iota} \gamma\epsilon\omega\mu\epsilon\tau\rho\epsilon\tilde{\iota}$"</note> which agrees with what Pico says in Book 1 of his *Heptaplus*, Chapter 1, concerning the human world. Man consists of soul and body; the rational soul is called heaven, for Aristotle also calls heaven a living being moved by itself, and our soul, as the Platonists prove, is a substance that moves itself. Heaven is a circle, and the soul is that same circle; indeed, as Plotinus writes, heaven is a circle precisely because its soul is a circle. Heaven is moved in an orbit; the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects and again returning from effects to causes, is revolved in the orbit of reasoning. For what else is that reasoning—which philosophers call a syllogism—but a certain spiral motion of the soul, which is completed in three parts: simple apprehension, composition (or the discovery of the "middle term"), and the conclusion (which is the same as the enjoyment of the truth already investigated). Furthermore, just as the divine essence is square, <note>original: "$\tau\epsilon\tau\rho\alpha\gamma\omega\nu o\varsigma$" (tetragonos).</note> so too is our soul. Hence, in the Tree of the Sephiroth among the Kabbalists, three *middot* <note>term: *middot* (Hebrew for "measures" or "attributes").</note> or three properties are attributed to GOD, namely **Keter**, **Hokhmah**, and **Binah** (Crown, Wisdom, and Intelligence), by which they record that GOD made all things; these three seem to correspond exactly to what has been said, etc. But a more ample opportunity for speaking on all these matters will be given elsewhere; for this reason, we wished here to indicate only in passing the philosophy and theology of the Egyptians, and how they may be investigated through hieroglyphics.

drawn from the inner depths, that there is nothing in heaven which is not, according to analogy, also in the ether and the elements, and nothing in all of those which is not in man. For there is in us a certain celestial portion, another that is sublunary <note>The region below the moon, traditionally the realm of change and decay.</note>, and a third placed at the boundary of both; as if some ether joins the powers from both sides. This is especially true if you consider the harmony—either of the internal organs with the external spheres through the intermediate channels of humors and spirits, or among the organs themselves. It has its own vital, animal, and natural spirit; its own desiring, emotional, and rational soul. Thus, among philosophers, no saying is more true or more famous than that "all things are in all things," and that even the smallest things perpetually possess the qualities of the greatest. 

Hence Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on "theurgy" or divine magic.</note>, in his book *On Magic and Sacrifice*, said that the priests of old and the truest lovers of wisdom progressed from that beauty which appears to the senses toward the divine beauty, by means of the senses. This was because they observed in the things of nature a certain kinship and the laws of an eternal fellowship, by which they seem both to nourish one another and to contribute their powers. Thus, at last, with the affections of love mixing all things together, this entire matter was judged by Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE.</note> to be <term>inhalation and exhalation</term> <note>original: ἀπνόα καὶ ἐκπνόα (apnoa kai ekpnoa), referring to the "universal breathing" or consensus of all parts of a living organism.</note>—that is, a certain animal that is altogether "breathing together" and "breathing out." From this, they composed their science under the logic of true magic, fixed in that mutual conspiracy of causes and effects among all universal parts. But because all these things will be treated more fully below, we stop here.

### A Recapitulation of What Has Been Said.

<margin>Comparison of the scarab beetle to the Sun, Moon, and Stars.</margin>
Since, according to the testimony of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*.</note>, it was familiar to the Egyptians in ancient times to heap divine honors upon such animals that had some similarity or analogy with the Gods to whom they were dedicated—that is, the Sun or the Moon and others—drawn from their heat, shape, movement, number of limbs, and arrangement; or animals in which the sympathetic character of said Gods shone forth, impressed by that "all-forming" <note>original: "panthomorpha"</note> likeness of nature. 

Certainly, from all that has been so extensively proven thus far, it is most clearly evident that we have not incongruously interpreted the scarab beetle to be the Sun, the moderator of the world, because of the remarkable signs and symbols it portrays, as will appear clearly in what follows. The Sun is radiant, and there is in it a certain night-shining power reflected to us from the Moon as if from a mirror; and the scarab has a certain diurnal light from the mirrors of its wings, which it vibrates as it is surrounded on all sides; and it also has a certain night-shining glow, which it has in common with all the worms called glow-worms <note>original: "cincindelas"</note>, with which, like the Moon, it dispels the darkness of the night. The Sun is round, and so is the scarab. There are twelve signs of the Zodiac in heaven, through which each...

# BOOK IV. IDEAS.

If a single cycle is completed in thirty days, finishing the year with a double motion, who would dare deny these things to our Sun-Beetle <term>Heliocantharus</term><note>A Greek-Latin hybrid term for the scarab beetle, literally "Sun-Beetle," which was believed to embody solar cycles.</note>? Provided one carefully considers its six little legs—each of which splits again into two like a fork—and its thirty digits, which antiquity attributed to it; what are these but the thirty-day revolutions by which the Sun joins with the Moon every month to fertilize the lower world and refill it with new offspring? The scarab follows this example: for having gathered a ball from dung, it hides it for twenty-eight days after infusing it with seed; once this time has passed, it removes the hidden ball, animated by its usual craft, and finally presents its dark offspring to the world. The Heaven is distributed into five Zones <note>Traditional climate divisions of the Earth or the celestial sphere (two frigid, two temperate, and one torrid zone).</note>, acting as boundaries for the solar rays; so too is the scarab, as is clear from its image placed above. All things that occur in the world seek a circular or spiral motion; who will deny this to the scarab, once he has more closely examined those spherical volumes of mud, cemented together as if from a manifold sequence of spirals—a true work of spiral progression?

<margin>Horapollo <note>original: "Horus"</note>, Book 1, Ch. 10.</margin>
Just as the sun is "only-begotten" <note>Unique or of a single kind; self-created.</note>, ignorant of the female sex, and imbued with a certain masculine power and strength, so too is the scarab. As Horapollo shows in these words: <note>original: "μονογενὲς μὲν ὅτι αὐτογενές ἐστι τὸ ζῷον, ὑπὸ θηλείας μὴ κυοφορούμενον· μόνη γὰρ γένεσις αὐτῷ τοιαύτη ἐστίν. ἄνδρα τε ἐπειδὴ θηλυκὸν γένος ἐν αὐτοῖς οὐ γίνεται."</note> "It is unique because the creature is self-generated, not carried by a female; for its birth is of such a kind. And it is male, since the female sex does not exist among them." With this Aristotle (History of Animals, book 5, chapter 19) and Pliny (Natural History, book 11, chapter 28) also agree. By this, clever antiquity truly seems to have represented nothing other than a certain masculine power of the sun, shown through the works of Osiris.

<margin>Diodorus</margin>
Whom Diodorus (Library of History, book 1, chapter 2) relates to have subdued the entire world after assembling a vast army. Certainly, poetic wit ingeniously shows the Sun subduing the whole world by the diffusive power of its rays, when it depicted the image of the Sun, or Apollo, equipped with a quiver, a bow, and arrows. But since these matters were treated at length in the preceding apparatus, I remain silent; he who desires more should consult the most learned commentary of Aleandro on the Solar Tablet <note>original: "Heliacam Tabulam". Likely referring to the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style reliefs.</note>, and Macrobius in his commentary on *Scipio’s Dream*, as well as Fulgentius, Phornutus, and Ausonius.

<margin>The scarab represents leaders of war.</margin>
But perhaps some unskilled person might say here: What does a scarab have to do with the war-leader Osiris? What has it to do with the arrow-bearing Sun? The objector will easily be silenced if he observes how the scarab shines all over with armor, striking those who look at it with a kind of martial lightning; how it is equipped with sharper protrusions like arrows; and how it has no part of its body not diligently fortified by shells and a shield. Indeed, it seems that even Homer’s Mars <note>original: "Mauors"</note> does not appear better armed when he dons his greatest panoply <term>panoplia</term><note>A complete suit of armor.</note>. Listen to its military drone, with a terrifying and panic-inducing buzz; contemplate its industry and persistence in boring through mud, as if digging tunnels <note>original: "cuniculis" – military mines or tunnels used to collapse enemy walls during a siege.</note>. Behold its continuous labors in the gathering and rounding of muddy material, as if in the construction of ramparts; all of which truly seem most suited to a General or a leader of war. And for the same reason, the Egyptians—on the testimony of the cited Horapollo—by depicting a scarab, signified a warlike man endowed with a certain masculine virtue, ignorant of female company, or finally, the very offspring of Osiris. From this, also, their images on rings...

HIEROGLYPHICS.

...bore [scarabs] engraved on rings, as Plutarch <note>A Greek-born Roman philosopher and historian (c. 46–120 AD).</note> testifies, the reason for which Caelius Calcagninus <note>Celio Calcagnini (1479–1541), an Italian humanist scholar who wrote extensively on Egyptian lore.</note> indicates with the following words: <margin>Scarab engraved on rings.</margin> *A scarab engraved on rings signifies that a man ought to be of a manly spirit, and not effeminate, just as the scarab is masculine only, knowing no female.* <note>Ancient naturalists mistakenly believed that all scarabs were male and reproduced by rolling balls of dung without females, thus making them symbols of self-sufficiency and virility.</note> And that saying of Horace seems to allude to this:

> Tyrtaeus sharpened manly spirits for Martian <note>Referring to Mars, the god of war.</note> wars with his verses.

Hence the Egyptians depicted Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian creator-god Ptah, the divine craftsman.</note>, the maker of arms, through a scarab, as Horus <note>Horapollo, the supposed author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a primary source for Renaissance understandings of Egyptian symbols.</note> testifies in Book 1, Chapter 13. The words of Horus are: <note>original Greek: "Ηφαιστoν τe γϱαφoνtes κάνθαϱoν ϰαὶ γύπα ζωoγϱαφῶσι, ἀθηνᾶν τe ϰαὶ πᾶν, ϰάνθαϱoν"</note> that is: *Indicating Vulcan, they paint a scarab and a vulture; but for Minerva, a vulture and a scarab.* This text brings with it a certain inconsistency and incongruity, as Caelius Calcagninus well noted in this place; for how could two opposite symbols correspond to one [deity]? Therefore, let us emend the aforementioned text, as it is flawed and corrupt, so that the meaning is: *Indicating Vulcan, they paint a scarab; but for Minerva together with Vulcan, they paint a vulture and a scarab.*

Furthermore, when a scarab occurs in hieroglyphics, so that you may understand its genuine meaning, the better authors hand down this rule: <margin>Symbols of the Serpent.</margin> A flying scarab with expanded wings—or even with a radiant head, or with a human head, or with a circle or triangle—always designates something divine, such as Osiris, the Sun, or the world and its governance. But with folded wings, engraved on rings, it designated fortitude of soul and a manly spirit. From all these things it is clear that the Egyptians expressed the concepts of things by symbols adapted not at all randomly, but with the greatest ingenuity.

# SACRED SYMBOLISM XVII.

-> Of the Serpent, the Asp, and the Dragon. <-

Since nothing occurs more frequently among hieroglyphic symbols than the Serpent, what the Egyptians indicated through symbols of this kind must be explained in this place. It should be known, therefore, that the Egyptians were as curious investigators of the nature of almost all animals proper to Egypt as they were of the Serpent. For when they saw that the serpent proceeded with no help from hands or feet, but by the mere drawing along of its oblong body; that it consisted of no limb besides the mouth; that it was an animal full of fiery spirit and long-lived, restoring its youth every year by shedding its old skin—they believed it impossible but that something great, excellent, and entirely divine lay hidden under these things. <margin>The serpent expresses all figures by its motion.</margin> It also happened that by that wavy motion of its pliable body, they could express nearly all figures; for instance, while now moving the tail to the head they form a circle; now, by coiling into spirals, they exhibit the volumes of the celestial spheres; now extended at length, a straight line; now a curve; now flat; sometimes, by the erection of the body, a perpendicular line; now glittering with a manifold order of scales like so many stars, and formidable with its hiss and three-forked tongue—when they contemplated these things, I say...

BOOK IV. IDEAS

...found in the serpent, they employed it as a most profound symbol of the most excellent things. But let us see what, and what sort of things, they signified through it.

<margin>Eusebius, Book 1, Chapter 7.</margin> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian who preserved many fragments of older, lost pagan texts.</note>
First, therefore, Epies the Phoenician says in the works of Eusebius that the GOD Emepht <note>A creator deity in Egyptian mythology, often associated with the breath of life.</note> was signified by the Serpent, or Asp, in these words: <note>The following is translated from the original Greek and the author's Latin paraphrase.</note> *Tautus <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the inventor of writing and culture.</note> himself (as did the Phoenicians and Egyptians) considered the nature of the Dragon and of Serpents to be divine; for it was handed down by him that this animal is the most spiritual of all reptiles, and fiery. For by its spirit, without the aid of hands or feet, or indeed any of the external organs by which we see other animals move, it attains an extraordinary speed; and in its progress, it produces various figures and forms, performing its movement with a coiled and winding gait at whatever speed it wishes. It is also long-lived; not only does it become young again by shedding its old age with its skin, but it is also naturally capable of greater growth. When it has fulfilled its allotted measure, it is consumed into itself, just as Tautus himself similarly established in the sacred writings. For this reason, this animal was included in sacred rites and mysteries. We have spoken more extensively about it in the commentaries entitled "Thothica," in which it is established that the creature is immortal and is resolved into itself, as was said before. For this animal does not die a natural death, unless it perishes by a violent blow. Hence the Phoenicians call it a "Good Spirit" <note>original Greek: agathodaemon</note>, just as the Egyptians name it Kneph.*

<margin>The Serpent as a symbol of health.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius, Book 3, Chapter 3.</margin>
Thus, they aptly noted the divine nature through the nature and operations of the serpent, all of which are clear from what has been said. Hence the Greeks, on the testimony of the same Eusebius, represented Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>, the Deity of health, by a serpent, as a symbol of saving power. *A coiled serpent carries the symbol of the health of the body and soul. For natural philosophers, contemplating the world, say that while other reptiles are of a coarser and more earthy substance, the Serpent is a most spiritual animal, which sheds the weakness of the body and seems most fit for medicine. For it is said to have discovered a remedy for sharpening the sight, and to know a certain herb for the labor of rebirth <note>original Latin: reuiuescendum - literally "to live again," referring to the shedding of skin.</note>.* Furthermore, the Egyptians, signifying the world,

### HIEROGLYPHICS.

...they used to paint it distinguished by various spots, about which Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a Latin poet known for his descriptions of nature and mythology.</note> wrote:

> Living forever in its scales, and devouring its tail
> with its mouth drawn back, retracing its beginnings with a silent gliding motion.
> <note>original Latin: "Perpetuumque vivens squamis, caudamque reducto / Ore vorans tacito relegens exordia lapsu."</note>

<margin>To signify that the affairs of the world are perpetually revolving into themselves?</margin>
Which undoubtedly signifies that everything generated in the world by divine providence is dissolved by that same providence more quickly, or is gradually diminished and fails, only to be received back into itself and become that thing once more. This follows the principle that "we are resolved back into that from which we come," which Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a historian who often quoted older Phoenician sources.</note> beautifully indicates a little earlier in these words from the Phoenician tradition, when speaking of the nature of the serpent: "and it is dissolved into itself as was said before" <note>original Greek: "καὶ εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀναλύεται ὡς προείρηται"</note>; so that from this it appears that the world is nourished by itself and revolves back into itself. For since the elements are eternal and are changed by no corruption or variation in themselves, they nevertheless seem subject to corruption and variation in that aspect where they are mixed to give form to specific things. Yet their power remains unharmed, not otherwise than typographic letters, which when joined signify something; but as soon as they have served the uses of the typesetters, they are dissolved and restored to their original integrity and their kind, and are reserved for the use of another form—a concept you may see learnedly described in the works of Pacuvius and Lucretius <note>Roman poets who discussed the "atoms" or basic building blocks of the universe.</note>. Therefore, with the serpent devouring its own tail, the author ingeniously indicates the immortality of the "kinds" of things with which **GOD** has distinguished nature. They teach that the beginning is directed toward the end, and the end reflects back to the beginning; for they believed nothing in the world truly perishes. Instead, as Virgil testifies, only the appearances of those things we see in the meantime are changed—for he said there is no place for death. Similarly, Democritus <note>The ancient Greek "laughing philosopher" who proposed that the world is made of indivisible atoms.</note>, by that perennial flow of atoms, seems to have intended to indicate nothing else (contrary to certain modern pseudo-philosophers) than those individual bodies which, when they have been disjoined, are neither destroyed nor receive total extinction, nor are divided by further cutting, but retain an infinite solidity within themselves through all time. This is what that "child-eating" of Saturn <note>original Greek: παιδοφαγία (paidophagia); refers to the myth of Cronos/Saturn swallowing his children.</note> alludes to: namely, that he swallowed a stone placed in the way of Jupiter. By this kind of fiction, they aptly indicate that terrestrial things are mostly subject to corruption and variation, but the soul is immortal; this is according to the verse of Hesiod, singing profoundly and according to the mind of the Egyptians:

<margin>Democritus's philosophy regarding atoms.</margin>

<margin>Hesiod.</margin>
> And these great Saturn swallowed down, as each one 
> came from the holy womb to the mother’s knees.
> <note>original Greek: "Καὶ τοὺς μὲν κατέπινε κρόνος μέγας, ὅστις ἕκαστος / Νηδύος ἐξ ἱερῆς μητρὸς προσγίνοιτο."</note>

Which I interpret thus: the species of things are born from the earth, and soon recede back into the earth; for Rhea <note>A Titaness and mother of the gods; here used as a metaphor for the flow of matter.</note> represents the flux and corruption of the world. Therefore, whatever time has brought forth, time consumes the same. All of these things Horus <note>Refers to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> explains in almost the same words in Book 1, Chapters 1 and 2, which I have thought should be omitted here since we shall cite them in the following pages.

Again, when they saw that the Serpent—being of a terrestrial substance and for the most part born from decay—represented the beginnings of fluctuation with the twisting pull of its body; the air with its hiss and fearsome sound; and moreover, with its whole substance decorated with the ornament of shining scales, expressed something fiery; they thought it not incongruous that the four elements...

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...they were accustomed to indicate through it: by the body, which is earthy and very heavy, **Earth**; by the winding path of the body, as it expresses the fluctuations of waves, quite aptly **Water**; by the hiss, truly **Air**, the subject of sound; and finally **Fire**, by the vigor of its whole substance and its three-pronged tongue, an appropriate symbol of fire. All of these meanings are suggested by Horapollo <note>Horapollo, the purported author of the *Hieroglyphica*, an ancient treatise on Egyptian symbols that was highly influential during the Renaissance.</note> in Book 1, chapter 2. Furthermore, although they expressed the four elements mentioned through the serpent, they did not set them out in the same way, but through different positions and configurations of the serpent. Thus, the vital spirit of the earth, or the earth itself—which they call *Oiph* or *Phnouti* <note>Coptic: ⲱⲓⲫ or ⲫⲛⲟⲩϯ. These terms refer to a divine or animating principle.</note>, as taught on page 127 (for so they call the *Genius* <term>Genius: a guardian spirit or animating force inherent in a place or substance</term> that governs all things, indicated by the serpent)—they depict as animating through its fiery power by a prostrate and two-horned serpent, of which nothing is more frequent on our obelisk.

Furthermore, intending to signify Fire, they painted an erect asp, placed either upon an altar or upon the heads of the Gods, with a globe resting on its head; by which they used to indicate a certain fiery force permeating the universe, as will be shown in its proper place in Book V; and the things we cited a little earlier from Eusebius and Horapollo relate to this.

They also noted this power through a circle in which a serpent was inserted, expressing the Greek or Coptic letter *Theta* (Θ), which they called *Tauta*; by which, according to Eusebius, they aptly signaled the fiery spirit infused into the whole universe. We pursue these things amply elsewhere in what follows, as well as on page 129.

Moreover, Horapollo openly testifies in Book 1, chapter 2, that the Egyptians signified an *age* or *eternity* by the Basilisk, where some manuscripts take *obaion* <note>original Greek: ὀβάιον or ὀβαῖον</note> for the Basilisk. We, restoring the genuine name of the Basilisk from the remains of the Egyptian language, have found it to be *mophion*. For I judge it should be read thus: "which the Egyptians call *mophion*, which in Greek is *basiliskos*." <note>original: "ὃν καλᾶσιν Αἰγύπτιοι, μοφίον, ὃ ἔστι ἑλληνιστὶ βασιλίσκος"</note> The reason why they established eternity through the Basilisk was roughly this: that among the types of serpents, this one alone could not be killed by force; since, as Horapollo testifies, it has such great power that it puts all other animals to flight by its hiss alone; hearing which, they say all songs of birds...

# HIEROGLYPHS

<margin>The wondrous power of the Basilisk.</margin>
...not only by its bite, but by its scent and its mere glance. Hence Archelaus, as cited in Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals."</note>, relates that when a beast of burden perished in the African desert, many serpents immediately flocked together to feed upon it; however, upon hearing the hiss of the Basilisk, they all fled or hid themselves in the sand. The Basilisk then moved forward at its leisure, without any disturbance from others, and ate as much as it wished. When it was full and about to leave, it let out its usual hiss again, as if granting the remaining serpents the power to feed on what was left.

I am well aware that at this time, the history of the Basilisk is considered more of a fable than a true history. Nevertheless, anyone who knows the character of the Egyptians will be forced to assert that they frequently invented many things regarding animals that suited their mystical reasoning—things which, like what they say of the Phoenix, conflict with modern experiments. Therefore, they did not strictly attend to the actual properties of animals, but rather explained the gifts and duties of the Gods, for the most part, through these sorts of invented properties. In this way, when they wished to signify the supreme deity or **Agathodaemon** <term>Agathodaemon: from the Greek for "good spirit," a protective deity often depicted in the form of a serpent or a winged snake</term>, they painted a Basilisk or an asp. Its hiss represented the commanding nod of a King which all living creatures obey, secretly suggesting the power and potency of the Supreme Deity over all things subject to it, and their subsequent obedience.

Hence, they most often placed it upon the heads of the Gods, as Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of an ancient guide to Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> testifies. Traces of this occur frequently both on the **Bembine Table** <note>The *Tabula Bembina* or *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze tablet of the 1st century AD covered in Egyptian-style motifs that Renaissance scholars studied to decode hieroglyphs.</note> and on other monuments. One such example was found while I was writing this, in the foundations of the Church under the name of **Minerva**, also known as the Church of the Order of Preachers <note>The Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, built over the site of an ancient temple to Isis.</note>, as shown by the copperplate engraving placed just before. In it, you see a headdress set between two asps, marked with ears of grain and flowers; from its base, a bifurcated flame erupts, which aptly illustrates what has been said thus far. Furthermore, they sometimes fashioned this asp with the head of a hawk, making it a fearsome sight, with eyes so skillfully crafted that they could be closed and opened. As soon as they brought it forth with open eyes, all of Egypt was bathed in joy and cheerfulness, just as if the eyes of the Gods were looking upon them and promising immediate help; therefore, everyone felt they were in the light and devoted themselves to laughter, jokes, and banquets. But if they brought it out with closed eyes, then everyone would retreat into darkness and shadowy inner rooms, and each person would strive with miserable lamentation to drive away the indignation of the Gods by whatever means they could. But for those who desire more on the mysteries of serpents, let them consult Horus and **Pherecydes** <note>An early Greek thinker; the author refers to a fragment preserved by the historian Eusebius.</note> as quoted in Eusebius, where one will find many truly wonderful things regarding this subject. Since we shall describe all these matters extensively in the following sections with various citations of authorities, we refer the reader to those.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific symbolism of serpents and basilisks to a broader classification of how the Egyptians depicted their deities through hybrid human-animal forms. # BOOK IV: IDEAS

### HIEROGRAMMATISM XVIII
#### On the various transformations of the human figure made from the aforementioned animals.

<margin>A simple idol.</margin>
**F**irst, the Egyptians considered several elements in a hieroglyphic statue: its form, position, gesture, clothing, ornaments, and instruments—all of which denoted different things. Initially, a statue was either simple and natural, or composite and multiform. A statue might represent a human head with the rest of the body transformed into one of the sacred animals; these were called **Sphinxes** and **Androsphinxes** <note>original: *androsphynges*; from the Greek for "man-sphinx," usually a lion's body with a human head</note>, and they were signs of a hidden divinity. A statue is called "simple" when it exhibits the human figure exactly and simply, without any transformation. It is called **multiform** <note>original: *πολύμορφος* (polymorphos)</note> when, in place of the human head, the body of any other sacred animal is attached—such as a Hawk, a Dog, an Ibis, an Ox, a Cat, a Goat, an Ape, or a Lion. Conversely, a human head might be placed upon the body or trunk of one of the listed animals; in this way, they are called sacred statues.

<margin>Multiform.</margin>

| :--- | :---: | :--- | :---: | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| Hawk-formed | | Hawk-like shape | | Hawk-headed | | With a Hawk head |
| Cat-formed | | Cat-like shape | | Cat-headed | | With a Cat head |
| Ram-formed | | Ram-like shape | | Ram-headed | | With a Ram head |
| Dog-formed | | Dog-like shape | | Dog-headed | | With a Dog head |

| Ape-formed | | Ape-like shape | | Ape-headed | | With an Ape head |
| Scarab-formed | | Beetle-like shape | | Scarab-headed | | With a Scarab head |

<margin>The logic of hands and feet.</margin>
Furthermore, one must observe the transformation regarding the other limbs, such as the hands or feet. You may occasionally see statues wrapped up without hands or feet, as in **canopic jars** <term>Canopic jars: ritual vessels used by the Egyptians to hold internal organs, often topped with heads of deities</term>; sometimes you may find some equipped with hands but without feet, and vice versa.

<margin>Position.</margin>
Additionally, the position must be diligently explored. A statue either sits, stands, lies down, or is bent in the manner of a crawling creature. Finally, the positions of all the limbs can be wonderfully transformed into various letters or **monograms** <note>symbols consisting of several letters interwoven together</note>, examples of which will be provided in the following pages. The hands of the statues are seen sometimes extended, sometimes contracted or hanging, now applied to the knees, occasionally as if pressing something, and very often closed, or open and occupied with other sacred instruments.

<margin>The condition of the Hands and Feet.</margin>
The feet are also seen to be either separate, or folded, or straight, or spread wide, or adapted into a running position, or even bent in the manner of suppliants. As for their clothing, they are either naked, or dressed in a simple tunic, or variously adorned with hawk feathers, or with **headdresses and diadems** <note>original: *tutulis & diadematis*; ritual caps and crowns</note>, or conspicuous without these. To declare the differences and secret meanings of all these things is a task of almost infinite labor—

# HIEROGLYPHICS

Since this is a work of great labor, we have more prudently reserved those matters for our *Oedipus* <note>original: *Oedipo*; refers to Kircher’s "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," his massive study of Egyptian lore</note>, in which we will, in due time, establish a perfect arrangement of each individual combination. Just as they attributed different virtues and operations to different limbs, they signified that different meanings were displayed when these limbs were joined to the things already listed, as will be seen in various ways in the following pages. Porphyry explains this beautifully in the fourth book of *On Abstinence* with these words:

> *Setting out from this practice and conjunction with God, they knew that divinity passed not through man alone, nor that the soul inhabited a tabernacle on earth in man alone, but that it passed through almost all animals. Wherefore, in the construction of the statues of the Gods, they took up every animal alongside man; in which they mixed the bodies of brutes, humans, and birds. For among them, individual statues of the Gods show a human likeness as far as the neck, but have the head of a bird, or a lion, or some other animal placed upon it; or conversely, they show the body of another animal placed beneath a human head.*

By these means, they clearly signify that these beings have associations with one another according to the will of the Gods, and that creatures—both tame and wild—are related not without a certain divine purpose. <note>original Greek: φανερὸν γὰρ ὅτι τοῖς αἰγυπτίοις...; This Greek passage mirrors the Latin text above, stating that Egyptian priests signified unspoken mysteries by combining various forms into one, such as an ibis or hawk head on a human body.</note> And Abenephi the Egyptian <note>An Arabic author Kircher frequently cited as an ancient Egyptian authority</note> confirms this with these words:

<note>original Arabic: "The philosophers of Egypt used to record their secrets either in the form of animals or birds, by calculations, by signs, and by geometric shapes, or by their limbs—meaning by their heads, their hands, and their feet—joining them with parts of the signs and with the form of wands and geometric signs and other similar things."</note>

---

->☼<-

The Egyptian philosophers displayed their great secrets most often through the figures of four-legged animals or birds, or herbs, or instruments, or geometric figures, or their extremities—namely, through their heads, hands, and feet—joining them to other instruments, figures of herbs, geometric shapes, and things similar to these. But, as I have said: since we shall treat the meanings of each of these listed combinations of symbols specifically in our *Oedipus*, I have thought it unnecessary to dwell on them any longer.

# HIEROGRAMMATISM XIX.

## On the Hieroglyphics of Plants.

->§. I.<-

## On the Cane, the Nile Reed, and Thyrsuses, or the staffs usually made from them.

<margin>Kamus, an Arabic Dictionary</margin>
Among the hieroglyphics, there is a certain scepter curved like a crook <note>original: *litui*; a curved wand used by Roman augurs</note>, which we interpret as being made of cane or papyrus from the Arabic قصبه, *Kasbe* <note>Qasaba</note>. For this name is the same as a sprout, a thyrsus <note>a staff topped with a pine cone</note>, a cane, an instrument, a shaft, a pole, a rod, or a whip, as seen in the *Kamus* <note>The "Al-Qamus al-Muhit," a famous 14th-century Arabic dictionary</note> or Arabic and Granadan Dictionary.

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>What the thyrsus was made of.</margin>
As appears in the Lexicon, we call the thyrsus "fennel-like" because a thyrsus was not necessarily made from the clusters of a vine, but was the name given to any long, rounded stalk or branch used as a spear, such as the giant fennel. They carried this object around because the thyrsus and the fennel-stalk were attributed to the Egyptian Bacchus or Dionysus; hence he is frequently called <term>narthekophoros</term> <note>original: $\nu\alpha\rho\theta\eta\kappa o\phi\acute{o}\rho o\varsigma$; literally "fennel-bearer"</note>, as we have taught elsewhere. This is supported by the words of Statius:

> *Who [carries] the soft thyrsi and the horns of Bacchus.*

And in another place: *Yet I did not bear the smooth thyrsi, nor the soft [garments] of Pentheus.* He mentions it elsewhere too: *Arming their soft arms with Nyphean thyrsi.* Ovid also writes in the sixth book of his *Metamorphoses*: *And they cast thyrsi green with foliage.* You will find many similar examples in his third book. Sidonius likewise says: *Bromius [Bacchus] whirls the Indian rites with the Echionian thyrsus.*

They carried these fennel-thyrsi in place of symbols because Dionysus bore them; for this reason, in the second book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, Eusebius calls him <term>narthekophoros</term> or <term>thyrsophoros</term> <note>original: $\theta\upsilon\rho\sigma o\phi\acute{o}\rho o\varsigma$; "thyrsus-bearer"</note>. He is addressed as the Lord of the Thyrsus: *[O thou who] in the night, mingled with goodly shouts, art the fennel-bearing lord of the thyrsus* <note>original Greek: $\nu\upsilon\kappa\tau\grave{\iota}\ \delta\grave{\iota}\ \epsilon\upsilon\beta\alpha\lambda\epsilon\upsilon\mu\acute{\iota}\xi\eta\text{-}\phi\acute{o}\rho\epsilon\ \theta\upsilon\rho\sigma\alpha\nu\acute{\alpha}\kappa\tau\alpha$; Kircher translates this as "he who reigns with the thyrsus"</note>. Hence Orpheus, in his *Hymns*, worshipfully adores him with the incense of Storax, saying:

> *I invoke the law-bearing, fennel-bearing Dionysus, the praised seed of Eubulus; who has many names, the sacred and chaste Mises, the venerable lord; who is both male and female, the double-natured Lyaeus, Iacchus; whether the sacred temple of Eleusis delights you, or you perform mysteries with the Phrygian Mother of the Gods; or whether Cytherean Cyprus holds you with your adorned hair; or you rejoice in the fruitful fields with the honorable Mother Goddess [Ceres], together with the chaste, serpent-bearing Isis near the river of Egypt.*

<margin>Why they carry fennel stalks in the processions of Bacchus.</margin>
Various authors give various reasons why the fennel-stalk thyrsus is assigned to Father Liber (or the Egyptian Dionysus, whom we proved in the third book to be the same as Osiris or the Sun). Eusebius calls him <term>narthekophoron</term>, that is, "fennel-bearer," and explains the reason: because men who are drunk are driven into a frenzy and strike one another; so that they do not stab each other with fatal wounds, they use fennel stalks, whose blow is slow and not lethal. Plutarch, in his *Symposium*, assigns another reason: that the fennel stalk and forgetfulness are given to Bacchus because it is hardly fitting for someone to remember offenses committed over drinks; or, if a fault is committed, a light and childish reprimand should suffice, just as children are punished with a fennel switch. Others say that the fennel is most suitable for Bacchus so that those weakened by drunkenness might guide their staggering feet with this light support. Among the Latins, it is called <margin>Ferula named from "bearing."</margin> *ferula* from "bearing" (*ferendo*), because its stalks served the elderly in place of supporting canes.

<margin>Description of the fennel.</margin>
Theophrastus describes it thus: the fennel rises quite large, with a single stalk, and is jointed; from these joints grow large, multi-cleft leaves, thinned like hair; the largest leaves, which are closest to the ground, clasp the stalk like reeds; it has seeds like Dill, etc. It grows in great abundance in Egypt; the Egyptian ones are hollow, while others usually have a spongy pith inside. But leaving these matters aside, let us see why the Egyptians used these fennel-thyrsi as symbols. First, it is attributed to Osiris (the Egyptian Dionysus) because he first taught how to plant the vine—

### HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>Why the fennel-thyrsus is sacred to Osiris.</margin>
...to plant it, and to attach it to a fennel-thyrsus, as if to a support most suitable for sustaining the vine. For since giant fennel stalks <note>Latin: *ferulae*</note>, according to Theophrastus, frequently grow to five or six cubits in Egypt in great abundance, Tibullus teaches that Osiris first used them in place of stakes for the planting of wine:

> *He taught how to join the tender Vine to stakes,*
> *And to prune the green foliage with a hard sickle.*

<margin>Why the vine is sacred to Isis.</margin>
Therefore, that fennel-thyrsus was a symbol among the Egyptians of the use of wine and the vine; for this reason, it is attributed indiscriminately to both Osiris and Isis on the Bembine Tablet <note>The *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze tablet of Egyptian style popular in Renaissance studies</note>. Because of this use, Pliny writes that the reed was also primarily cultivated in Italy, or perhaps because the "pan-pipes" <note>Latin: *fistula*</note> were constructed from its joined segments, as Ovid says, *from seven reed-canes*. For the ancients called a joined reed <term>zygen</term> <note>original Greek: $\zeta\acute{\upsilon}\gamma\eta\nu$; meaning "yoked" or "joined"</note>, using pairs and <term>mesogonia</term> <note>original Greek: $\mu\epsilon\sigma o\gamma\acute{o}\nu\iota\alpha$; the "middle-joints" of a plant</note> suitable for manufacturing musical instruments. Into the hollows of <margin>Why the Thyrsi were curved.</margin> these, according to Macrobius, they would place the tender clusters of the vine and ivy; from this they were bent at the upper part, which was not without its mystery. Furthermore, Herodotus testifies that trumpets <note>Latin: *lituos*; specifically J-shaped ritual trumpets</note> were fashioned from fennel-thyrsi just as they were from reeds. Moreover, since they attributed to Osiris not only the invention of wine through the <margin>Trumpets were made from them.</margin> fennel-thyrsi, as has been said, but also the invention of Music, according to Diodorus; certainly they could express it through no other symbol better than through the fennel and reeds. Pliny (Book 16, ch. 36) and Theophrastus (Book 4, ch. 12) testify that Music drew its first origin in Egypt from these, since both plants accept a bend and both grow hollow in Egypt. For since Egypt abounds in marshy places, and is therefore by no means lacking in plants in said places where fennel and reeds usually grow, they discovered among other things many kinds of fennel and reeds that could be bent and were hollow inside. Seeing that they were fit for producing sound, eventually both provided the opportunity for inventing pipes and trumpets through frequent experience, as in that passage from Ovid, Book 11:

> *And he plays a light song on the waxed reed.*

From this comes the Greek word <term>kalamos</term> <note>original Greek: $\kappa\acute{\alpha}\lambda\alpha\mu o\varsigma$; a reed or pen</note>, a term also widely adopted by Latin poets, as Manilius says when discussing the power of Music:

> *And the slender reeds, and words set to strings*
> *Before blowing the sonorous ones.*
> *Pan, learned in the reeds.*

<margin>What is the "zygites"?</margin>
The reed in Theophrastus (Book 24, ch. 11) is called <term>zygites</term> <note>original Greek: $\zeta\upsilon\gamma\acute{\iota}\tau\eta\varsigma$; the "yoking" reed</note>, which Gaza, in his translation, thinks should be called the "yoking-straw," as it is that by which vines are bound to a yoke. Columella teaches this method of binding the vine <margin>Two kinds of reeds.</margin> in Book 4, ch. 17. Furthermore, Theophrastus, in the cited passage, identifies two kinds of reeds: the first <term>auletikon</term> <note>original Greek: $\alpha\upsilon\lambda\eta\tau\iota\kappa\grave{o}\nu$; "flute-like"</note>, which Pliny interprets as "tibial" <note>relating to the *tibia* or flute</note>, and the other <term>plokimon</term> <note>original Greek: $\pi\lambda\acute{o}\kappa\iota\mu o\nu$; "plaiting" or "weaving"</note>, that is, "textile" or "woven," according to Gaza's interpretation; perhaps because mats, coils, and other things of that kind were made from its leaves. In this instance, Pliny, due to the similarity of the words in Theophrastus, read <term>ploion</term> <note>original Greek: $\pi\lambda\acute{o}\ddot{\iota}o\nu$; "floating"</note> instead of *plokimon*, as if it were a "floating reed." There are also reeds for the Egyptians, as Pliny testifies, as well as for the Cretans, which they call <term>toxikous</term> <note>original Greek: $\tau o\xi\iota\kappa o\acute{\upsilon}\varsigma$; "for arrows" or "archery"</note>...
