# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>When they were typically cut.</margin>
...because arrows were best made from them. These reeds, according to the testimony of Theophrastus in the passage cited, were typically cut at the appropriate time before the era of Antigenes—back when they played the flute <term>tibia</term> <note>a type of ancient reed instrument, often double-piped</note> in a simpler fashion—under the constellation of Arcturus in the month of September. For reeds cut then would remain useful for many years, though they required much practice to produce sound; however, the "mouths of the tongues" <note>original: *ora linguarum*; referring to the reeds or mouthpieces of the instruments</note> would close up, which was more useful for signaling things to the people. But after musical variety and artifice were added, the timing of the cutting was changed.

<margin>Apuleius.</margin>
Apuleius mentions these reeds used in Egyptian ceremonies in these words:

> *There went also the pipers dedicated to the great Serapis, who, by means of a slanted reed stretched out toward the right ear, repeated the familiar melody of the temple and the God.* <note>original Latin: "Ibant & dicati magno Serapidi tibicines, qui per obliquū calamum ad aurem porrectum dextram, familiare templi, Deique modulum frequentabāt."</note>

Indeed, to summarize many things in few words: we say that the Egyptians, through this symbol of fennel-thyrsi <note>stalks of the giant fennel plant, *Ferula communis*</note>—which were seen partly held in the hands of the Gods and partly carried in the more solemn festivals—denoted nothing other than the planting of the Vine and the invention of Music. This represents the "liquid of life" and the harmony inherent in individual things, with which the supreme mind enriched the world and all that exists in it. For Osiris, as Diodorus testifies, was delighted by music above all else and was never without the company of Satyrs and Muses; thus, what he had wisely and harmonically arranged through the Muses, he might preserve through the Satyrs—that is, through a fertile life. Therefore, this flute-like scepter or thyrsus is attributed to Osiris to denote his power over the harmony of the world. 

Three things must therefore be considered in this hieroglyphic: first, the method of planting the vine by applying it to a fennel-stalk or stake, an invention we have proved above to be his own. Second, the construction of flutes and trumpets <note>original: *fistularum & lituorum*</note>, which has also been shown in various ways to have been first fashioned by Pan or Mercury from reeds of this kind; from these, the proportions of music later flowed. <margin>Mystical meanings of the curved thyrsus.</margin> Third and finally, this is seen in the place of a scepter in the hands of Osiris and Isis; in this manner, such a flute-thyrsus and curved scepter, stretched out in the manner of an oblique reed, is represented six times on the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet, also known as the *Mensa Isiaca*, depicting Egyptian-style deities and symbols</note>. By this, they intended to signify, quite clearly, the power and the harmonic excellence of the things they invented and arranged in this economy of the world. Why this thyrsus is found exactly six times on the Bembine Tablet is a supreme mystery in the nature of things, which will be discussed most extensively in its own proper place. Therefore, this sign is nothing other than a fennel or reed thyrsus, a hieroglyphic symbol of the aforementioned things, as we have demonstrated; but now let us proceed to the third symbol.

### §. II.
### *Concerning the Papyrus and Rush Thyrsus.*

The third place in order is held by the Nile Rush <note>Latin: *Iuncus Niloticus*</note>, or if you prefer, the smooth and knotless Bulrush, which is confounded with papyrus or paper-reed by Pliny, Hermolaus, and Donatus. By this, the Egyptians wished to signify nothing other than the rarity of letters...

<header>HIEROGLYPHICS.</header>

<margin>
The discovery of letters through the papyrus staff.
A definition of papyrus.
</margin>

<margin>
What is a bulrush?
The use of reeds.
</margin>

The rare and noble discovery of writing was first found by the Egyptian Mercury <note>also known as the god Thoth, often identified with Hermes/Mercury</note>, or as you might prefer, Osiris and Isis, as Diodorus testifies in Book 3, Chapter 2. The plant itself is light and vigorous <note>original Greek: εὔζωος</note>; in place of leaves, it produces stalks or stems—straight, round, thin, smooth, and without knots. They grow to a height of one or one-and-a-half cubits, are green with an herbaceous color, have sharp tips, and are filled with a white pith, resembling and serving the purpose of a lamp wick. Theophrastus says: The bulrush <term>scirpus</term> <note>a water plant used for weaving</note> is a certain species of reed, light and knotless, from which they make sieves in Egypt. Others attribute the use of reeds to sea-nets; others, according to Pliny, use the pith of the reed for the light of lamps, as a wick.

<margin>
Meanings of papyrus or the Egyptian reed.
</margin>

This reed has as many meanings as the objects it is placed with; for it has one meaning when positioned alone, another with a sieve, another with a fly, and another with other things. Hence, when joined to the symbols of the inventions made by Osiris, it signifies nothing other than the noble discovery of letters; the reason for this must be briefly examined. It is well known that the reed, the bulrush, or if you prefer, the papyrus (for these are confounded by most authors, as Hermolaus and Donatus show from Pliny) is a plant of the kind we described above from Dioscorides, Theophrastus, and Pliny. And that this grows nowhere more frequently than in Egypt is testified by all the authors who have written and handed down accounts of it. That this reed, because of its excellent and manifold uses, was also adopted everywhere for various symbols, will be clearly seen in what follows. Now, that the symbol placed here represents the letters discovered by Osiris is testified by Horus himself <note>Horus Apollo, the supposed author of an ancient treatise on hieroglyphs</note> in Book 1, Chapter 38, in these words: *Thus the Egyptians,* he says, *when they wish to signify letters, or a sacred scribe, or an end, would place down ink, a sieve, and a reed; all of these have different meanings, but the Egyptian letters are signified because all writing among them is completed by these: for they write properly with a reed and no other.* Therefore, they gladly adopted as a symbol for letters that instrument which first gave them the occasion for writing; for the reed provides not only the pens <term>calami</term> but also the paper <term>charta</term>, for both are made from the same plant, as Theophrastus and Pliny testify; and after them Prosper Alpinus and his most learned commentator Johannes Westling, the chief physician of Padua. Whence 

<margin>
Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*.
</margin>

Apuleius, in these words: *To graze the wit of the Nilotic reed <note>original: Nilotici calami</note> implies Egyptian papyrus;* and another: *Those who commit words to thin papyrus;* and Martial in Book 13: *O Muses, lose my losses on Nilotic papyrus.* Thus the Egyptians signified an abundance of all necessary things by placing a papyrus reed with a thistle-shaped <note>original Greek: ἀκανθομόρφῳ</note> butterfly; but let these things suffice concerning the reed or papyrus.

Since we have treated at length the Reed, Papyrus, Cane, fennel-stalk, and similar things, it remains for us to say something briefly about the other hieroglyphic plants,

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>
The Lotus: The herb of Osiris and Isis.
</margin>

...and first, we encounter among the not infrequent hieroglyphics <note>symbolic Egyptian picture-writing</note> the Lotus, an Egyptian plant. Some authors confuse this entirely with the Water Lily <note>original: "Nenuphare" or "Nymphaea"</note>, while others mistake it for the Egyptian bean. While we reject the latter opinion, we gladly accept the former. Indeed, the Lotus is nothing other than the Egyptian Water Lily, a marsh herb that dances in a luxurious garment among the pools of stagnant waters. Some believe this most beautiful plant was born from the embrace of Osiris and Isis. Although it is the same species as our common water lily, it differs from the larger yellow variety—which stretches its roots out long—and from the well-known white variety. It differs in the delicate composition of its fibers, its size, and because its edges are hollowed out with light but wide notches, woven through with even more numerous small veins. Furthermore, its seeds are enclosed in a poppy-like pod <term>capsa papaveracea</term>, and it possesses a greater size and visibility than the common water lily.

<margin>
Meanings of the Lotus.
</margin>

But to return to our purpose: the Egyptians first indicated the Sun, or the movement of the Sun from east to west, through the Lotus. This was due to a certain natural sympathy the plant has with the Sun. Most, however, also recognized it as a symbol for the region where the Sun rises. I believe this hieroglyphic meaning was adopted because, before the Sun emerges, the plant has its leaves folded together; these then gradually unfold and open as the radiance of the Sun rises higher and higher. They are most fully spread when the Sun has completed half its journey <note>at noon</note>. As the Sun departs, the leaves in turn begin to contract and fold back together, withdrawing as if they wish to obey no one except the Deity whom they venerate; thus, in whatever way they can, they confine themselves within their own enclosures as the Sun departs. As Proclus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says, this behavior was observed by the Magi, leading them to believe the plant was entirely sacred to Apollo <note>the god of the Sun</note>. But let us hear Theophrastus <note>an ancient Greek botanist</note> on this marvel, who describes the plant in Book 4 in these words:

> The plant called the Lotus <note>original Greek: Τὸ καλῶτο (lotus)</note> grows mostly in the plains when the land is covered with water. Its leaf is similar to that of the bean <note>original Greek: κυάμου</note>, and its petals are likewise struck but do not stand upright; its flower is white, resembling that of the white lily. When the sun rises, and until the middle of the day, it follows the movement of the sun, and the flower head <note>original Greek: κοδίαν</note> stays together. At the same time as the sunrise, it opens its flower upon the water, even before the sun is high, until the head is fully formed and the flowers fall. <note>original: "ταῦτα δὲ ὅταν μὲν ὁ ἥλιος ἀνατέλλῃ..."</note>

And a little later: 

> From the lotus, both in the water and above the water, it opens until midnight and stands deep and upright; as it goes deeper and above the water, the flower opens. Once opened, it remains active by day until the sun comes again, and the flower opens. Then at the proper hour, it closes and enters the water. It frequently opens at the same time as the water rises.

This means: The plant called the Lotus grows for the most part in flat areas when the countryside is flooded. By nature, its stalk is similar to a bean, and its fruit 

<margin>
The Lotus follows the movement of the Sun.
</margin>

is formed in the same way, but smaller and more slender. The fruit is born at the head; the flower is white, very close to the narrowness of lily leaves, and many fruits emerge densely and indiscriminately. At sunset, they compress themselves and hide the head with wonderful industry; at sunrise, they open and rise up above the water. It continues this until the head is fully formed and the flowers fall away. And a little later: In the Euphrates river, they report that the head and flowers are submerged and descend even until the middle of the night; they go so deep into the depths that they cannot be reached even by reaching out a hand. Then, at dawn, they return, and more so as the day progresses. As the sun rises, they emerge from the waves and open the flower; once opened, they rise even further, as if they were clearly departing from the waters.

### HIEROGLYPHICS

Therefore, it should by no means seem surprising if they pursued this flower with such great honor. Furthermore, through this flower they indicated the sympathy <note>The "doctrine of signatures" or natural resonance between earthly objects and heavenly forces.</note> of lower things with the higher, as will be shown at length in its proper place in the interpretation of the Obelisk itself.

<margin>What is the meaning of Harpocrates upon the Lotus?</margin>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Egyptian deity Harpocrates (Horus the child) seated upon a blooming lotus flower. The figure is nude, holding a finger to his lips in a gesture of silence, and carries a flail or scourge over his right shoulder. The lotus rests upon a stylized representation of water.</image-desc>

Again, a GOD sitting upon a Lotus indicates the supereminence of divine leadership over all things; so Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> narrates, whose words are as follows:

> This is also confirmed by the symbol that follows, where GOD is brought forth sitting above the Lotus, which is an aquatic tree; this signifies that GOD, by His leadership, transcends the mundane mud and does not touch it even while governing it; instead, He exercises a leadership that is entirely intellectual and empyrean <note>belonging to the highest heaven of pure fire or light</note>. For everything in the Lotus is round, both the fruit and the leaves; by this is signified the circular action of the mind, namely through the same things and remaining in the same state. God Himself, therefore, stands above this action within Himself, surpassing such leadership, holy and venerable, and resting entirely within Himself, which is indeed signified by the act of sitting.

From this, I believe, was born that hieroglyphic of Harpocrates sitting upon the Lotus and pressing his finger to his lips as if urging silence; examples of this sort frequently occur on various medals, as you see in the illustration. He is the same as Horus, or the sensible world <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> according to Plutarch, whose archetype is the intellect; according to an anagogical <note>spiritual or mystical</note> interpretation, he is that supreme supramundane Divinity: the Ideal or Reflected Sun <note>original Greek: "ινδαλμικός" (indalmikos), meaning an image or reflection</note>, governing and preserving all things by his power, and toward whom, like the Lotus, all things higher and lower are turned by the radiant motion of their actions.

The Gnostics <note>Early Christian-era mystical sects</note> also display this in their seals, showing him sitting on a Lotus with a whip or scourge, in which region these words are placed: *IAO* and *SEBEO*; these, being corrupted from the Hebrew, denote the same as *Jehovah* or *Adonai Sabaoth*: "The Lord of Hosts" <note>original Hebrew: יהוה צבאות (YHVH Tzevaot)</note>. By His power, every force and ferocity of opposing powers is weakened and banished; these are aptly indicated by the scourge, a symbol for the driving away of evils. He urges silence with his finger to indicate that His nature is ineffable <note>beyond words</note>, and therefore to be venerated by silence alone. Consequently, they not inappropriately attached to him the name of God, *IAW*, though corrupted; this is the same name of God, the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, which the Hebrews assert is <margin>What do foreign names denote?</margin> "unspeakable and unutterable" <note>original Greek: "ἀῤῥητον καὶ ἀνεκφώνητον" (arrheton kai anekphoneton)</note>. See what we have handed down elsewhere copiously regarding this name. For the Egyptians very willingly accepted names of this kind. For as Iamblichus says, all names of this sort signify something among the Gods, even if the meanings are unknown to us in some cases; yet some are known, he says, the interpretation of which we have received divinely, though the mode of meaning in them is entirely ineffable. Nor is it according to human imaginations, but according to the intellect within us which is divine. However, the question is asked: why, among the names of the divine...

# BOOK IV.

...preferred "barbarous" <note>In the classical sense, "barbarous" refers to any non-Greek language, specifically those of the ancient Near East.</note> names over others. *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> responds: Because the Gods approved the entire language of the sacred nations, such as the *Egyptians and Assyrians*, as being most consistent with reality; therefore, we believe that common expressions and modes of speaking should be applied to the language and speech akin to the Gods, especially because that mode of speaking was the most ancient and original. The meaning of *Harpocrates* sitting upon the Lotus is therefore clear. From this, the Gnostics called him *Iao* and the Greeks *Ioua*, a name corrupted from the same Hebrew origin <note>original: "Ιαω" and "Ioua," likely derived from the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH.</note>, whom many—as was clear in Book 3—confuse with *Horus*; for *Jupiter* is nothing other than the world, or a part of the world, just like *Horus*. Hence, antiquity called the Sun the "eye of *Jupiter*," and *Jupiter* (or the Sky) the "mind of the World"; and the *Egyptians* called the Sun and Moon the "eyes of *Horus*." But more will be said about this *Harpocrates* or *Horus* in its proper place.

->§. IV.<-
->On the Hieroglyphic **Persea**, and its **Thyrsis** <note>A ceremonial staff or wand, often topped with a pinecone or vine leaves, here associated with Egyptian botany.</note>.<-

<margin>
The nature of the Persea.
</margin>
<margin>
The meanings of the Persea.
</margin>
The Persea is a plant of Egypt, which *Theophrastus* describes in these words:
> *There is in Egypt another tree called the Persea, great and beautiful in appearance; in its leaf, flower, branch, and overall shape, it is most similar to a pear tree; except that it is evergreen, whereas the other is deciduous.* And a little later: *From this tree they once made sacred images, tables, and similar items belonging to the sacred furniture. Those who thought the fruit of this tree was poisonous when grown in Persia were perhaps deceived by the similarity of the name. For more diligent writers report that the Persian tree is altogether different, similar to reddish plums (these are plums grafted onto service-trees), which is lethal in Ethiopia but healthy in Egypt.* <note>The "Persea" discussed here is the Mimusops laurifolia, a tree sacred to ancient Egyptians, often confused in antiquity with the peach (Prunus persica) which was rumored to be poisonous if moved from Persia.</note>
The Egyptian sages made great use of the leaves, fruits, and branches of this tree in their sacred carvings. First, they signify silence, and they accordingly dedicated it to *Harpocrates Sigalion* <note>Harpocrates the Silencer; from the Greek "sigao" meaning to be silent.</note>. Since it has fruit shaped like a heart and a leaf shaped like a tongue, they obscurely indicate that speech—which is the fruit of intelligence—ought to have its seat in the heart and not just on the tongue. Hence, it was also a symbol of the heart, as found in *Plutarch*; for when they discovered that Nature had impressed the shape of a heart upon it, and that the fruit was wonderfully beneficial to the heart (revealing by its very appearance and "signature" for which part of the body it was created), they not inappropriately adopted it as a symbol of the heart and consecrated it to *Isis*. Since *the Truth* <note>original: "τό ἀληθές" (to alethes)</note> belongs to *Isis*, this indicates that wisdom is first conceived in the intellect, but it is of little use unless it is also expressed for the benefit of mortals. Sometimes they display the fruit together with the leaf, and then it figured as a symbol of truth. Indeed, that image shows the tongue joined to the heart, and thus speech opens the innermost chambers of the heart itself; one should not think one thing and say another. All sages confess that speech should be noble and without deceit. Thus, "Truth" was held in such high regard among the Egyptians that they used amulets <note>original: "phylacterijs"</note> made from the *persea* to acquire it. So says *Plutarch*: *Hence, on the 20th day of the first month, celebrating a festival day for Mercury [Thoth],*

# HIEROGLYPHICA:
361

...[those celebrating] eat honey and figs, saying together, "Truth is sweet" <note>original Greek: γλυκὺ ἡ ἀλήθεια; Latin: Dulcis est veritas.</note>. The amulet of Isis, which they fabulate she hung upon herself, when interpreted signifies "True Voice" <note>original Greek: φωνὴ ἀληθὴς; Latin: vox vera.</note>. Harpocrates <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Horus the Child.</note> should not be considered an imperfect God or an infant; nor should he be thought of as a legume. Rather, he is the overseer and corrector of the recent, imperfect, and uncomposed opinions humans hold regarding the Gods. For this reason, he holds a finger pressed to his mouth, a sign of silence and quietness; and in the month of Mesore <note>The twelfth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, those offering him legumes say:

<margin>The tongue is fortune; the tongue is a spirit.</margin>
"The tongue is fortune, the tongue is a spirit" <note>original Greek: Γλῶσσα τύχη, γλῶσσα δαίμων</note>. Of the plants in Egypt, they say the **Persea** is most specially consecrated to the God, because its fruit resembles the heart, and its leaf the tongue.

<margin>The Persea is a symbol of the heart and the tongue.</margin>
*Of Egyptian plants, they say the **Persea** is most highly consecrated to GOD; because its fruit bears the appearance of the heart, and its leaf the appearance of the tongue. Indeed, of all things that can happen to a human being, nothing is more divine than speech—especially regarding the Gods—nor does any other thing bring greater momentum toward happiness. Therefore, one about to enter an oracle is commanded to think holily and speak modestly. Hence, you may very frequently see the Persea joined to the images of Gods and Goddesses on the **Bembine Tablet** <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet of Egyptian-style imagery influential in the Renaissance.</note>. This was carried around in processions instituted in honor of the Gods, as will be seen later; from its wood, sacred statues were both manufactured and adorned with its leaves and fruits, as will be explained more fully shortly.*

->§. V.<-
->**Hieroglyphic Branches.**<-

Clement of Alexandria, in the sixth book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "stromatum" or *Stromata*, a work by the 2nd-century Christian theologian.</note>, testifies that branches were carried in the sacred solemnities and processions of the Egyptians, in these words:
"Through symbols, just as the wheel is turned and drawn by the Egyptians in the precincts of the Gods, branches are also given to those who come to worship" <note>translated from the original Greek and Latin provided in the text.</note>. These symbols are explained in the verses of Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek poet and musician.</note> cited by the same Clement in this manner:

<margin>The meanings of Branches.</margin>
> But to those for whom human and earthly branches are a care,
> Fates do not stand in one place; in the mind, all things
> Revolve around, nor is it permitted to remain in one part,
> Just as a course begins; indeed, an equal part is for anyone.

Branches, moreover, are a symbol of primary nourishment, so that the common people may know that while fruits indeed germinate and grow entirely, and remain for a very long time, they themselves have received but a brief span of life; and for that reason, they desire branches to be given. Certainly, among the Athenians, there was a festive day distinguished by the name of branches, on which they carried forward <term>oschoi</term> <note>original Greek: ὀσχοὶ</note> in honor of Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy.</note>, which are like *moschoi*, that is, tender branches, specifically of the vine. From this, the solemnity obtained the name <term>Oschophoria</term> <note>An ancient Greek festival of "branch-bearing."</note> and the branch-bearers the name <term>oschophoroi</term>.

<margin>What is the Oschophoria?</margin>
The ministers of the sacred rites, having received the small vine branches from the temple of Bacchus, carried them to the shrine of Minerva Schirras <note>A title for the goddess Athena, associated with a particular sanctuary at Phalerum.</note>. As the commentator on Nicander <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek poet.</note> testifies: "The Oschophoroi are children at Athens who, competing according to their tribes, take vine shoots from the temple of Dionysus and run to the temple of Athena Schirras." # BOOK IV. IDEAS
362

<margin>The use of branches in sacred rites.</margin> Indeed, those venerating the Gods would move both their hand and a branch toward God according to the ancient rite of adoration; hence, Saint Jerome correctly translates, *and they applied a branch to their noses* <note>original Latin: "& applicabant ad nares suas ramum"</note>, specifically as a sign of the adoration they were offering to the Sun. Josephus, in the third book of his *Antiquities*, clearly testifies that the Hebrews also used these same ceremonies in the worship of God during that festival which they call <term>סוכות</term> <note>original Hebrew: Sukkot</note>, that is, the Feast of Tabernacles, as do the Holy Scriptures. His words are: <term>at that time offering burnt offerings and sacrificing thanksgivings to God, carrying in their hands a bouquet of myrtle and willow, along with a branch of palm to which the fruit of the persea was attached</term> <note>original Greek: ὁλοκαυτεῖν τε καὶ θύειν τῷ Θεῷ τότε χαριστήρια φέροντας ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν εἰρεσιώνην μυρσίνης, καὶ ἰτέας συγκράδῃ φοίνικος πεποιημένη τῷ μήλῳ τῷ τῆς περσεας προσόντος .</note>. *Sacrificing victims to GOD, and at the same time sacrificing through an act of thanksgiving, they meanwhile carry in their hands branches of myrtle and palm, from which the fruits of the persea hung;* In these things they imitated the Egyptians, as is clear from Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, where they venerate Horus with branches of Persea and Lotus, to signify that the heart and the tongue must be dedicated to God. That the Ethiopians also imitated these customs is clear from the third book of Heliodorus. <margin>Heliodorus of Ethiopia.</margin> Those receiving Kings or Great Men: *They came to meet them, crowned with Lotus and shaking palm branches in his honor.* His words are: <term>having crowned their heads with the Nile lotus and shaking palm branches in their hands</term> <note>original Greek: τὰς κεφαλὰς τῷ Νειλαίῳ λώτῳ καταστέψαντες καὶ φοινίκων πθόρτας ταῖς χερσὶ κατασείοντες;</note>. Therefore, if they wished to signify that someone was honored with the signal favor of the people and received with the most famous applause and joy of all, they called this person <term>one pelted with leaves</term> <note>original Greek: φυλλοβολούμενον (phylloboloumenon)</note>; <margin>What is a "phyllobolomenos"?</margin> for they not only presented those branches, but furthermore they scattered leaves and flowers upon those who had served well, which kind of honor and benevolence they named <term>leaf-throwing and flower-throwing</term> <note>original Greek: φυλλοβολίαν καὶ ἀνθοβολίαν (phyllobolia and anthobolia)</note>. Whence Philo, in his book on the embassy to Gaius, says that Agrippa was <term>pelted with leaves and flowers on account of his piety</term> <note>original Greek: φυλλοβολούμενον καὶ ἀνθοβολούμενον ἐπ’ εὐσεβείᾳ .</note>. Not content with this sign of favor alone, they were also accustomed to fasten branches, especially of palms, to the doors of distinguished men, a kind of honor which Lucian says is noteworthy: <term>the green palms arranged in wreaths upon the door</term> <note>original Greek: οἱ φοίνικες δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ θύρᾳ χλωροὶ ἐστεφανωμένοι</note>. Hence Christ also, as King and God—Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and Bishop</note> calls him <term>Christ, the World-Architect Wisdom</term> <note>original Greek: Χριστὸς σοφία κοσμοτεχνιτής</note>—was received by the Hebrew People with branches of palms, which the Poet correctly noted:

> And along the path they prepared garments as for a king
> And strewed tree-foliage and fragrant wreaths on the soil
> Beneath his feet, all confessing Him God with one voice.

<margin>What are the Baïa and Baïophoria of the Greeks?</margin> Furthermore, it is worthy of observation that this ceremony, which the Church venerates with an annual religious rite, was very celebrated among the Greeks; the Sunday which we call "Palm Sunday" is called by them <term>Baïophoria</term> <note>original Greek: βαϊοφόρια (carrying of palm branches)</note>, from <term>baïs</term> <note>original Greek: βάϊς</note>, because *baïs* in the Egyptian language—as Horus teaches in Book 1, Chapter 4—is a branch of a palm. From this also <term>baïa</term> <note>original Greek: βάϊα</note> is the name given to the distributions and gifts which were distributed by the Emperor and the Patriarch in that week which precedes Palm Sunday, according to the testimony of Balsamon <note>Theodore Balsamon, a high-ranking Byzantine jurist and canonist</note>, who treats the censures of the Patriarch copiously in these words: <term>the most high oversight of the divine Emperors and the magnificence of the Patriarchs was made no less than the others, being also the annual gifts of the palm-branches</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν ὑψηλοτάτην τῶν θείων αὐτοκρατόρων περιωπὴν, καὶ τῶν πατριαρχῶν τὴν μεγαλοπρέπεια μὴ τῶν ἄλλων ἐσόμενην καὶ ἐτήσιοι εἶναι πότε καὶ βαΐων φιλοτιμήματα</note>. *The eminent circumspection of the divine Emperors and the magnificence of the Patriarchs,* he says, *they made august along with the rest, both by annual payments and the munificent distribution of gifts which are called* <term>baïa</term> <note>palm branches or gifts associated with the feast</note>. Liutprand <note>Liutprand of Cremona, a 10th-century historian and diplomat</note> brings forward more of this kind in the third book, chapter 5 of his *History of Europe*. It is clear, therefore, that no ceremony was held among the Egyptians without the carrying around of branches...

# HIEROGLYPHICS
363

...the solemnity had been completed; for indeed they were accustomed to carry these branches in the Isiac, Mithraic, Ithyphallic, or Dionysian rites <note>These refer to the mystery cults of Isis, Mithras, and Dionysus (Bacchus); "Ithyphallic" refers to rites celebrating fertility.</note>, and they performed no divination, no casting of lots, nor any consultations without them, as will be shown elsewhere. Why the Egyptians used these specific signs and symbols in particular, Porphyry teaches in his book *On Abstinence*: <note>original Greek: "οἱ πάλαιοι ἄνθρωποι οὔτε λιβάνωτον, οὔτε ἄλλο θῦμα προσέφερον, ἀλλὰ χλόης οἵον τινα τῆς γονίμου φύσεως χρὲν ταῖς χερσὶν ἀράμενος κατέκαιον."</note> *The ancient people, he says, offered neither frankincense nor any other sacrifice, but greenery, as if it were the first downy growth of budding nature, plucked with their hands; by the power of which, herbs, crops, and fruits—all things, in short, born from the earth—would be produced and grow to maturity.*

<margin>Which branches are sacred to which Gods?</margin>
Just as they designated the diverse powers of the Gods through the branches of various trees, so too in the solemnities of those same Gods, they carried forward the branches that best agreed with their virtues. Thus, in the festivals of Mercury <note>The Roman equivalent of the Egyptian Thoth.</note>, they carried branches of the Persea, which are symbols of the heart and the tongue; in those of Isis, the Palm, southernwood, and *seriphium* (or sea wormwood); in the processions of Hippocrates or Horus <note>Specifically Harpocrates, the child Horus.</note>, the Lotus and the Egyptian Bean;

<margin>What is the Thryo?</margin>
in the Dionysian rites, they carried fig branches, because their leaf expressed the male organ <note>original Latin: "veretrum"</note>, and they called them *Thryo*, according to the testimony of Plutarch; for the fertility of this Deity, they also used vine branches to indicate the power of wine, over which he presided. In the festivals of other gods, they carried various other branches; nor did they stop there, but they also twisted those same branches into various figures so that nothing in the mysteries would be left without meaning.

In this way, when they were about to represent the Agathodaemon <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity often depicted as a serpent.</note>, they transformed a branch into the shape of an **A**, as the figure in the margin shows; likewise, they expressed the branches of the Persea—sacred to Mercury, Isis, and Harpocrates—in this form which you see in the figure below, shown in an inverted position.

->**A**<-

[A botanical diagram representing a plant structure with three distinct branches emerging from a central base. Each branch corresponds to a four-month period of the year, labeled at the bottom: "1st four-month period," "2nd four-month period," and "3rd four-month period." The branches are further divided into four leaves each, with each leaf inscribed with the name of a Coptic/Egyptian month. Branch I (left) contains Thoth, Paophi, Athyr, and Choiak. Branch II (center) contains Tybi, Mechir, Phamenoth, and Pharmuthi. Branch III (right) contains Pachon, Payni, Epiphi, and Mesori. Each leaf consists of four smaller leaflets. A circular element tops the central branch. Below the main diagram are two smaller glyph-like symbols: one resembles a stylized "M" with a central vertical stroke, and the other is a tripod or stylized "A".]

<margin>The meanings of the triple branch</margin>
By these symbols, it was secretly signaled that the generation of things usually occurs throughout the entire course of the year; through the triple branch, the three parts of the year were indicated; through the twelve leaves, each of which contains four other parts, they hinted at the twelve months. Having seen the branch, let us now explore the mysteries hidden beneath it. Just as the seed of the Persea, once committed to the earth in the first part of the year—that is, in the four-month winter space—is animated through the heat of genital conception after being decomposed; and in the second part of the year—that is, in the second four-month spring space—it bursts forth into shoots, leaves, buds, and flowers; and finally in the third part of the year—that is, in the four-month summer space—it swells into fruits, which are brought to maturity by the blowing of the Etesian winds <note>Annual Mediterranean winds that provided relief from summer heat and aided agriculture.</note>, producing a new abundance of seed for the following year; so, I say, does all generation of vegetables happen.

For the seed, first entrusted to the earth and decomposed, is gradually prepared for life; which being done, it soon breaks out into shoots, leaves, and flowers; finally, by the Sun...

BOOK IV. IDEAS
364

...its power is refined into new fruits—which is the ultimate goal of vegetable nature—within the span of a year. The ancients seem to have expressed this circular motion of vegetation quite appropriately through an inverted branch; for unless a plant or tree is in some way inverted, and the higher things become lower—following that pronouncement of more secret philosophy, *that which is above becomes like that which is below* <note>original: "quod superius est, fit sicut id quod inferius"; this is a famous maxim from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, central to alchemical thought</note>—it cannot happen. That is to say, unless the fruits, which first occupy the higher place on the tree, become lower by falling to the earth and rotting so that they may pour forth a new 
<margin>☩ All things are generated with corruption preceding them.</margin>
offspring of generation. This follows that saying of eternal wisdom: *unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth a hundredfold fruit.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24.</note> Thus, the ancients seem to have beautifully suggested the mystery of generation through this triple inverted branch. 

But because every sowing or planting is in vain unless Osiris—that celestial Sun—approaching in his motion through the twelve mansions of heaven, brings it to life; and unless Isis—the Moon—by her influence, nourishes and increases that same life through moisture, as if by perpetual irrigation; 
<margin>To whom is the triple branch sacred?</margin>
and finally, unless Mercury—that is, the logic of agriculture—approaching, leads those things to perfection through human industry; hence, they appropriately carried forward that triple mystical branch in their solemnities. The first part of the branch was dedicated to Osiris (the Sun), the second to Isis (the Moon), and the third to Mercury <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian Thoth with the Roman Mercury, the god of wisdom and calculation.</note>. For they believed that under the guidance of these three, all things obtained their perfection throughout the entire course of the year. By these three Divinities and the triple branch, they seemed to supplicate with a kind of mystical veneration and implore their aid. They valued this symbol so much that they added this character to the register of hieroglyphics and inscribed it on every obelisk; you may find it most clearly expressed among all the leaves and flowers on the Ramesside or Lateran Obelisk <note>The Lateran Obelisk is the largest standing ancient Egyptian obelisk in the world, located in Rome.</note>. 

Let these remarks suffice concerning the hieroglyphics of vegetables. Much more could be said about the *colocasia* <note>an edible tuber</note>, the Egyptian bean, the *schenofyris*, and the *seriphium*, but since these do not appear on our Obelisk, we have decided it more advisable to defer them to the *Botanical Hierography* of our *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his massive work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>. Concerning the sprout of the "tetradics," the curious reader may see the treatise in its proper place in Book V.

...you will find the hieroglyphic soul, where the mystery of the embossed Cross <note>original: "mysteriolum Crucis ektypon"; *ektypon* is a Greek term for something stamped or in relief</note> does not immediately occur.

<margin>Does the hieroglyphic Cross denote the life to come?</margin>
From this, various men, driven by different and diverse sentiments and opinions, have produced various explanations or, rather, conjectures. Ruffinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and historian known for translating Greek patristic works into Latin.</note> in Book 11, <margin>Ruffinus</margin> Chapter 29, thinks it signified the life to come. These are his words: *This Lordly sign of the Cross is said to be among those letters the Egyptians call* priestly <note>original: "hieratikas"</note>, *that is, Sacerdotical letters, as one of the elements of their writing. Of this letter or word, they offer this interpretation: "The life to come."*

<margin>Sozomenus</margin>
Sozomenus <note>Salamanes Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the Christian Church.</note> in Book 7 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Chapter 15, writes: <note>original Greek: Φασὶ δὲ τοῦ ναοῦ... ζωὴν ἐπερχομένην</note> *They say that when the temple of Serapis was being destroyed and torn down, certain characters called hieroglyphics appeared inscribed on the stones, similar to the sign of the cross. By those who were learned in such things, it was explained that this writing signified the life to come.*

<margin>The Handled Cross as a symbol of the life to come</margin>
In the history of Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD), another major historian of the early Church.</note> this is also briefly mentioned: <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ Θεοδοσίου... ζωὴν ἐπερχομένην</note> *During the reign of Theodosius the Great, when the temples of the gentiles were being demolished, hieroglyphic letters having the form of a Cross were found in the temple of Serapis. Seeing these, those of the gentiles who had already been converted to Christ said that, among those who understood hieroglyphic letters, the Cross signified the life to come.*

<margin>Lipsius</margin>
Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous Flemish humanist whose work "De Cruce" (On the Cross) studied the history of crucifixion and the symbol of the cross.</note> in his little treatise *On the Cross*, when he had considered this mystical embossed Cross with great wonder, finally admits frankly that he does not know what it signifies, or why it is found carved so many times in all hieroglyphic arrangements. <margin>Gretser on the Cross.</margin> Gretser <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625), a Jesuit scholar who wrote extensively on the history of the cross.</note> wishes that the ring placed upon it signifies an eye; and through the eye, the Egyptians signified the Sun, whence they also call it the eye of Jupiter.

But from these and similar ideas, it appears that neither Lipsius nor Gretser had seen the Obelisks that are now found in the City <note>Rome</note>, or if they did see them, they did not carry out an exact comparison of this figure with others occurring everywhere here and there. This seems to have provided the occasion for the error in which they think this symbol is represented solely by the sign of the T <note>The Tau cross</note>; whereas it does not occur only in that shape which our Gretser describes, but in entirely different forms. Jacobus Bosio <note>Giacomo Bosio (1544–1627), a historian of the Order of St. John, who wrote a massive work on the history of the Cross.</note> is also mistaken, although he is sharper than the others in this matter, for he claims it is placed everywhere only in that shape which you see drawn here: ☥. His Italian words sound like this: <margin>Bosio on the Cross.</margin> *Because the ring or circle stands above the Tau, or rather above the Cross, it is not shaped in just any way, but everywhere it is carved and sculpted as seen in the following figure, not only on the obelisks, but on all the other stones and fragments of Egyptian hieroglyphic antiquities found in Rome.* With all due respect to the good man, I would say that this is false, as will be most clearly evident to those who make a slightly more diligent comparison of this symbol with others. I, certainly, who have left nothing unattempted in this hieroglyphic business, when I recall my calculations and weigh everything with singular scrutiny, find in the actual specimens this character twelve and more times...

<margin>Origin of the Handled Cross</margin>
From these figures, it is clearly recognized that in all of them, something circular is mixed with the figure of the Cross, which must be considered by no means lacking in mystery, as we shall see later. However, so that something certain may be established about this figure after so many and such diverse attempts by various minds, we shall set out to show what ought to be concluded. First, let us hear concerning the origin of this figure and by what means it was passed down to the Egyptians. Thus says Abenephi <note>Kircher frequently cites "Abenephi" (Ibn Wahshiyya), an Arabic author associated with Hermetic and occult knowledge, though these specific genealogies are often legendary.</note>: "Mizraim <note>The biblical ancestor of the Egyptians.</note> received the circular cross from Noah through his father Ham, and he from Adam; it is indeed nothing other than a mysterious character by whose help the Angel Raziel <note>In Jewish mysticism, Raziel is the "Angel of Secrets" who gave Adam a book of hidden wisdom.</note> taught Adam all the greatest mysteries. This character, through a continuous succession in later times, reached Ham through Noah, and from him through Mizraim to the Egyptians. Ham also converted it to magical use and performed many miracles and wonders with it. Hence the Egyptians, being struck with wonder, adapted it in various ways, turned it to their own use, and employed it as an amulet; they symbolically represented the process of nature in things under this sign, and called it the vehicle of the Spirit of the World <note>original: "Spiritus Mundi"; a vitalizing force connecting the soul and the physical body of the universe.</note>." Thus far Abenephi, whose cited Arabic words you may see in Book V.

And this is the opinion of Abenephi concerning this sign, by which he surely intends to suggest nothing other than that mysterious character, known to all, the T or Tau: alluding to that common branch of the Tree of Life, which they say the Angel gave to Adam after his transgression. That this may be better understood, let us hear other Rabbis speaking more clearly on these matters. That great Rabbi among them, whom they call *Our Holy Teacher* <note>original Hebrew: רבנו הקדוש (Rabbenu HaKadosh); referring to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> on account of the singular sanctity of his life and excellence of his learning, in the book which he calls *The Revealer of Secrets* <note>original: "Raze Galeia"</note>. Here, at the petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the City of Rome <note>Likely referring to the legendary dialogues between Rabbi Judah and a Roman Emperor, often identified as Marcus Aurelius or Antoninus Pius.</note>, who had asked him from what tree the rod was cut with which Moses performed miracles, and from where he had obtained it, he replied thus: "Regarding what you ask me, to give you knowledge of the rod of Moses, I will tell you what I found written concerning this very thing by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>A famous 2nd-century sage to whom the *Zohar* is traditionally attributed.</note> in the book called *The Investigator of Secrets* <note>original Hebrew: מחוקר הסודות (Mechoker HaSodot)</note>, who says thus:

<margin>Iechnides</margin>
> *That rod, with which Moses and Aaron performed miracles in the land of Egypt and which later blossomed in the desert and produced buds, was cut from that tree which Moses pointed out in the desert so that the bitter waters might become sweet. And this tree was cut from the Tree of Life, which was placed in Paradise by the hands of angels; they indeed sent it to Adam when he had sent his son Seth to Paradise to implore the mercy of God.*

Seth received this tree, or rather a branch of it, and planted it in the desert. Moses later found it and cut his staff from it, and for this reason, it was called the "Staff of GOD." Furthermore, when Israel stayed at Marah and could not drink those waters <note>According to Exodus 15, the waters of Marah were too bitter to drink until Moses threw a piece of wood into them.</note>, GOD showed Moses this tree, so that he might make those waters sweet. This is also that tree upon which Moses placed the serpent, through which GOD intended to save the entire world and send His mercy upon Adam when the Messiah comes. For then this tree will bear fruits, by which the bitter waters shall for a second time be made sweet; it will purge the first sin and all the transgressions which men have committed or will commit. 

And a little later: *I have taught you this secret: when you contemplate the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and furthermore the tree of life, which was situated in paradise, and also the serpent who came to tempt Eve, you may understand why the Staff of Moses, cast upon the ground, was made into a serpent, and then, seized by the tail and lifted from the earth, returned to a staff as it was, and swallowed all the Staffs of the Egyptian Magicians who did the same, just as it is said in Zechariah, chapter 13:* <note>original: "והיה ביום ההוא נאם יהוה צבאות אכרות כל עצבים מן האדמה ולא יזכרו עוד"</note> *And it shall be on that day, says the GOD of hosts, I will cut off all the trees* <note>original Latin: "arbores". Furthermore, what Abenephi <note>A pseudonym used by Kircher for an Arabic source he claimed to possess.</note> says—that this sign was a mysterious symbol of the Cross—is attested by a Kabbalistic fragment found in Galatinus <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino, an influential 16th-century Christian Kabbalist.</note>, regarding that verse of Psalm 139: *Behind and before you formed me, and you have placed your life upon me, namely your hand.*

<margin>The mystical reasoning of the Tree of the Sephiroth.</margin>
From this, the Kabbalists in their more hidden Theology form the tree of the <term>Sephiroth<gloss>The ten divine emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite interacts with the universe</gloss></term> in such a way that the three properties, or <term>Middot<gloss>measures or divine attributes</gloss></term> as they call them, together with the Sephirah <term>Tiphareth<gloss>the central Sephirah, representing Beauty and Balance</gloss></term>—which they say is the tree of life planted in the middle of paradise—constitute the perfect figure of a Cross. They attribute four Angels to each divine Sephirah, whom we have represented here. And they say this mystery was first represented to Adam after his transgression in the branch which the Angel sent to him from paradise, as was said before. Read Raphael Aquilinus in his treatise on the Holy Trinity.

<margin>Each of the first Patriarchs had their own assigned Angels.</margin>

From the sacred scriptures, one might add Raphael as the teacher of Tobias, Gabriel for Daniel in the vision of the Anti-Christ, and likewise for the Blessed Virgin Mary. And this is that salvific sign <term>Tau<gloss>the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet</gloss></term>, with which Ezekiel says the faithful were marked to perceive the fruits of life; which Saint Jerome testifies has the figure of a Cross in his commentary on this passage.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

The Greeks received many of our holy sacraments <note>original: "sacramenta"; here meaning sacred rites or symbols of faith.</note> from the Egyptians, and the Egyptians in turn from the Israelites. For Epiphanius <note>Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a Church Father known for his writings on religious traditions.</note> is the authority who states that the Egyptians—remembering that day when the Israelites were freed from the slaughter of the Angel because they had smeared the doorposts of their houses with the blood of a lamb—were accustomed at the onset of the spring equinox to take red ochre <note>original: "rubricam"; a red earthy pigment or clay.</note> and smear all their trees and their entire houses. They did this while crying out that at this time, fire once destroyed all things; against such a plague, they believed the blood-colored red ochre was a remedy. <margin>Thephillin, or Totaphoth <note>These are the Hebrew terms for phylacteries (tefillin), the ritual boxes containing scripture worn during prayer.</note></margin> Formerly, by the command of God, they also used to fasten these to their arms and foreheads as *Thephilim* or *Totaphoth*, inscribed upon the purest parchment of a lamb in the shape of a Cross, containing four sentences drawn from Holy Scripture. You will find much concerning these in the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought, or Kabbalah.</note> and everywhere among the Cabalists.

Since, therefore, the sign **T** was a mystical character and held in the highest veneration specifically by the Hebrews, and since the Egyptians received most things from the ancient Hebrews (as we have already often shown from the writings of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Hebrew scripture.</note>), it is probable—both from what has been said and from the reasoning of Abenephius <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, an Arabic author whose works Kircher frequently used to interpret Egyptian lore.</note>—that the Egyptians also borrowed this character from the Hebrews, being themselves curious observers of figures. To both peoples it was indeed mystical, but its meaning was spread across different mysteries. <margin>What the handled Tau <note>The "Tau ansatum" is the Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life.</note> properly signifies.</margin> We say, therefore, that among the Egyptians, this character does not precisely signify "the life to come," as Ruffinus, Suidas, and other authors cited above wish; rather, it is likely that this whole rumor arose from the Jews who were wandering as exiles through Egypt at that time. For seeing this sign **T** repeated so many times in the Egyptian images, they interpreted it everywhere as their own salvation or the "life to come" according to the tradition of their fathers, as was said. But we shall speak more consistently with Abenephius: that among the Egyptians, this character signified nothing other than the movement and diffusion of the Divine Mind in the production of all things. Let us, therefore, more deeply discuss how deep and sublime the things were that the Egyptians denoted through this character.

<margin>The first formation of astronomical characters from the handled Tau.</margin> We say, then, that this mystical character was received from the first patriarchs, but that other astronomical characters were first invented with its help—partly by Zoroaster (whom we previously identified with Ham and Mizraim <note>Kircher often conflated biblical figures with legendary founders of pagan wisdom.</note>), and partly by Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt.</note>, about whom we have already dealt at length in the first book. This was done so that he might ingeniously represent the process of things being born into this world. <margin>Marsilio Ficino <note>The 15th-century Italian scholar who translated the Hermetic corpus into Latin.</note></margin> Marsilio Ficino confirms this opinion of ours in his *Platonic Philosophy*, chapter 29: *"For Zoroaster and his priests had a certain peculiar way of writing different from the common way; Zoroaster himself instituted it and formed letters with the celestial characters of the signs and stars, from whom Mercury Trismegistus was later instructed and handed it down to the Egyptians."* <margin>Hermes Trismegistus transferred the Tau into the number of his letters.</margin> Whether Zoroaster or Mercury first discovered it, or received it by tradition and increased it with their own inventions, it is all the same. ...they seem to have placed before our eyes, as if in a mirror, the idea of all-formed nature <note>original: "naturae pantamorphae"; a concept suggesting nature can take all shapes and forms</note>. But since that character is found in so many forms in the sacred carvings, we shall deal here only with the character specific to this place, as we see it most often attached to sacred images. Regarding the other character that takes the form of the St. Andrew’s Cross, we have dealt with it more extensively in the *Prodromus* <note>A reference to Kircher's earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus* (1636)</note> and will do so again in the explanation of the Bembine Table <note>The "Mensa Isiaca," a famous bronze tablet of Egyptian-style imagery</note>, although these characters are fundamentally the same, as will be shown later.

<margin>Composition of the Tautic character.</margin>
This Character consists of two different parts—circular and straight lines—and it appears to be nothing other than the character used by ancient astronomers, following the Egyptians, to denote Mercury, like so: ☿; hence, they called it the Tautic character <note>named after Thoth, or Tat, the Egyptian equivalent of Mercury/Hermes</note>. Through the circle, they denoted the diffusion of the divine mind into the starry world; and through the Cross, its diffusion into the elements. We see this "fall" into the material world expressed most elegantly in hieroglyphic form in the third hierogram <note>a sacred symbolic drawing</note> on the first side of the Lateran Obelisk, in this replica:

Indeed, the circle represents nothing other than the movement of the divine mind, as we have demonstrated at length above. The hawk-formed serpent is nothing other than the spirit of that mind, which is diffused through the entire mass of the World—as was discussed extensively in the seventeenth hierogram regarding the serpent.

Jonathan Ben Uziel <note>A famous translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic; Kircher is citing his "Targum"</note> and other Hebrew commentators agree on this point. Consequently, if you carefully consider the levels and the order of the words brought forth by Mercury <note>Kircher refers here to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage thought to be a contemporary of Moses</note>, you will clearly see in his writings that Mercury is very much like Moses. For Moses saw darkness upon the face of the deep and the Spirit of the Lord brooding over the waters; Mercury, however, saw a "horrendous shadow" migrating into a moist nature, which the Word of the Lord created. The former announces all created things by the powerful Word of the Lord; the latter asserted that: *That shining Word, the seed of the mind, is the Son of GOD; and that the Mind, the Father, and the Word of the mind—the Son—do not differ in nature, for he was indeed consubstantial with Him.* Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with the Torah</note> also explains this passage of Genesis with similar words in his book *On the Creation of the World*.

<margin>Pacuvius.</margin>
Most appropriately, therefore, the Egyptians exhibited the first creation of all things, and the processing of those same things from the First Cause and the "Architect Mind," through this hieroglyphic sign. Pacuvius <note>An early Roman tragic poet</note> alludes to this fittingly in these verses:

> ->Whatever this is, it animates, forms, and nourishes all things.<-
> ->It increases, creates, buries, and receives all things back into itself.<-
> ->And while it is the Father, it is likewise the same Mother;<-
> ->The things that were, fall back into that same source to begin anew.<-

<margin>A double mode of signifying used by the Egyptians.</margin>
It must be noted, however, that the Egyptians exhibited their secrets through a twofold hieroglyphic system. Some represented the nature of things through the virtues and properties of living creatures; others through certain characters devised with the greatest ingenuity, or geometric marks. To avoid amassing too many symbols and to prevent those wishing to learn from being entangled in long-winded complexities—since they claimed to clearly know all the obscurity of nature and possessed a discipline passed down as if by hand—they realized that neither a circle could be drawn without a line, nor a straight path made without a point. Content with this single hieroglyphic consisting of straight lines and a circle, they intended the entire condition of the world and a certain universal appearance of things to be expressed. For, taught by long experience and imbued with the knowledge of various things, they saw the first and simplest production and representation of all things—both those not yet existing and those hidden in the veils of nature—only through the straight line and the circle. Thus, the famous John Dee <note>original: "Deenus"; refers to the English polymath John Dee (1527–1608)</note> excellently shows in his *Monadic Hieroglyph* <note>Dee’s "Monas Hieroglyphica" (1564), a treatise on a universal symbol combining the signs of the planets and the cross</note>, in the first and second Theorems, that the essence and beginning of things lie in the principle of the point and the monad <note>the number one or the concept of unity</note>, and that things affected by a periphery (no matter how large they may be) can in no way lack the service of the point.
<margin>Through the circle and straight lines, the Egyptians explain all things in the world.</margin>

<margin>What is noted by the Cross.</margin>
Therefore, by the **Circle**, they noted the Celestial Orbs, with which the Spirit of the World first mixes itself by communicating its power to them; by the **Cross**, they noted the power of the four elements in the sublunary world <note>the world below the moon, i.e., the Earthly realm</note>, through the mediation of the celestial bodies, from which the generation of all things arises. All of this they beautifully expressed through the numbers hidden beneath this crossed figure. Indeed, the Circle resting upon the Cross appropriately signifies both the "ternary" <note>the number 3</note> and the "quaternary" <note>the number 4</note>.

The **Ternary** <note>The number three</note>, when it consists of two straight lines and a point that joins them both. The **Quaternary** <note>The number four</note> indeed consists of four straight lines intersecting each other at four right angles; from which, out of four straight lines encompassing four angles, the mystical **Octonary** <note>The number eight</note> also results, concerning which we have dealt extensively above when we were treating the mysteries of the pyramids. By the aid of these numbers **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, disciples of the Egyptians, showed the machine of the entire world and the visible orb, as we showed in the cited place.

Pythagoras

Two simple motions in nature: straight and circular.

For the Egyptians noticed two simple motions especially shining forth in the nature of things, the straight and the circular; they showed the latter by a circle, the former by straight lines. For they proved by experiment that when the **Elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> are moved out of their natural seats, they make their return to them in no other way than by straight lines. Therefore, not incongruously, by four straight lines running out into opposite parts from a single and individual point, they hint at the mystery of the four elements (into which each elementary thing can finally be resolved). This is confirmed by those things which I remember having noted in the *Saracenic Cabala* <note>original Arabic: اهل الفلسفة وطبا مصر وفرس والهند والروم فلما يريدون ان يدلون العامه راوج كتبهم والمرجع بدورة الصليـــــــب — "The people of philosophy and the physicians of Egypt, Persia, India, and Rome, when they wanted to guide the common people, circulated their books, and the reference was to the cycle [or form] of the Cross." Origin of astronomical letters.

And first indeed I assume from **Clement of Alexandria** and **Eusebius** that the Egyptians had a twofold way of representing their symbolic mysteries: one through the virtues of animals, herbs, and plants; the other through geometric characters, aptly representing the intended mysteries. ...especially the **Sun** and **Moon** (☉ and ☽). Indeed, the Circle and those things which are circular pertain to the age <note>Latin: *seculo*, referring to vast cycles of time or the "aeon"</note>, to celestial motion, and to the Zones and circles which are understood to exist in Heaven. We explain these according to the mind of the ancients in this way: the Egyptians depicted a circle by which they represented the Sun, the prince of all stars and the Divinity of the heavens, from whose light all might participate. However, since they recognized all its power only in the Elemental World, they added a crossed sign or character (♀) to the circle, by which they noted the spirit of the World permeating all things, and fertility; whence the Greeks also adopted that same symbol to express **Venus**, as if she were the Goddess of generation. 

When they observed this virtue of Venus scattered and sown by God through all parts of the world—namely, the spirit of the *Anima Mundi* <note>The Soul of the World</note>, or of the Sun, giving form, life, essence, and duration to each thing—and when, I say, they saw it found in all things (in man, in beasts, in earth, water, air, fire, in rivers, in mountains, plains, valleys, forests, meadows, deserts, plants, animals, and even in the heavens and stars), they added the semi-circle of the **Moon** (☽) to it, and that most celebrated and sacred character of **Mercury** (☿) was born. In our third book, we interpreted this as the Spirit of the World, or the Sun of the Egyptians, attracting all things to itself.

<margin>The origin of the character of Mercury (☿).</margin>

**John Dee** <note>original: "Deenus"</note>, in his *Monad Hieroglyphica*, agrees with our thinking in a wonderful way; hence his words, worthy of preservation <note>original: "cedro digna," literally "worthy of cedar oil" used to preserve precious manuscripts</note>, are these:

And for the same cause it also held the name of **Jupiter**, and maintained that more secret figure (♃). And the Moon, "elementated" <note>refined through the elements</note> for a third time, they noted more obscurely as (☿), which they are accustomed to call **Mercury**; do you see how Lunar he is?

### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...referring to Book 1, folio 22. The ancient Egyptian priests signified this same thing to us through that wonderful and mysterious hieroglyph. According to Plato and Aristotle, the material world is composed of eight Heavens, four elements, and the various things found within them. This hieroglyph encompasses all of this within itself, being composed of the characters or signs
<margin>The composition of astronomical characters</margin>
of each of these things, which can be clearly perceived there. Indeed, if one performs an "anatomy" of the symbol and divides it into its parts, it will be clearly seen that it first consists of a perfect circle, the hieroglyph of the **Sun** (☉). Next, it consists of a semicircle, the sign of the **Moon** (☽); a cross, the symbol of the **four elements** (+); and the sign of **Aries** (♈). The other four hieroglyphs—namely those of **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, and **Venus**—are then formed from the character of the Sun or the Moon, with the addition of the cross (or part of it) or the sign of Aries. The hieroglyph of **Saturn** (♄) is composed of that of the Moon joined with that of the Elements; that of **Jupiter** (♃) consists of the same, and is identical except that it is positioned differently. The character of **Mars** (♂) is composed of that of the Sun and that of Aries, joined together by the straight line of the cross. The sign of **Venus** (♀) is formed from that of the Sun and the Elements; and finally, the hieroglyph of **Aries** (♈) is formed from two semicircles connected at a common point.

Do you see, therefore, how wonderful such a hieroglyph appears, and how aptly the great Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus</note> represented that greatest Mercurial spirit and soul of the universe, the unique "cause of causes"? The Platonists affirm that this celestial spirit of Mercury is found in all things, and that similarly all things are contained within that same spirit.
<margin>Proclus</margin>
Hence Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, in his book *On Magic and Sacrifice*, says: The ancient priests knew best that "all things are in all things" <note>original Latin: "omnia in omnibus esse"</note>; that in Heaven, earthly things exist in a celestial way, and on Earth, celestial things exist in a certain terrestrial way, just as we interpreted above regarding
<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
the mystical pyramid. Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> also seems to subscribe to this by saying: all things are in all things. Hermes also, in his mysterious
<margin>The Emerald Tablet of Hermes</margin>
*Emerald Tablet* <note>A foundational text of alchemy and Hermeticism</note>, expresses this concept skillfully when he says: "That which is above is like that which is below" <note>original: "Quod est supra, est sicut, quod est infra"</note>; but these things have been discussed elsewhere. The most ancient Artephius <note>A famous alchemist, often claimed to have lived for a thousand years</note> also seems to allude to this at the beginning of his work *On Abstruse Secrets*: "The World," he says, "is known by the first of all things." Furthermore, since that spirit of the world—that celestial Mercury—fills all things with numbers, proportions, and harmony, they cannot be understood without numbers. For according to Pythagoras, the nature of numbers
<margin>Artephius</margin>
passes through all things, and the knowledge of it is that true divine and incorruptible wisdom, concerning which the most ancient Artephius writes in his *Book of Secrets*: "By the knowledge of number, you shall know how the notice of all things is held through it," and elsewhere: "from the calculations of the first man, the science of all arts and all knowledge is found." For all things that exist in the world (as Boethius <note>A Roman philosopher and mathematician who transmitted Greek logic and music theory to the Middle Ages</note> testifies) consist of numbers. In this Mercurial character, all numbers also seem to be represented; for if you unfold it into its parts as has been said—that is, into the Sun (☉), Moon (☽), Cross (†), and Aries (♈)—you will soon have that wonderful Pythagorean Tetractys <note>original Greek: "τετρακτὺν" – a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows: one, two, three, and four</note>, which he called the "fountain of perpetual nature" <note>original: "fontem perpetuæ naturæ"</note>, the idea of all created things and of knowledge itself.

# HIEROGLYPHICS

...in the divine mind working rationally: this <term>tetrad<gloss>the number four, representing stability and the physical world</gloss></term> was also called mystical according to Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Pythagorean number symbolism and Egyptian mysteries.</note>, by which the four parts of the world were represented by the Egyptians; as we shall say in the progression of this work. ### BOOK IV. IDEAS

...of the mind: substance, quantity, quality, and motion. Under bodily substance: the essential, the vegetable, the sensitive, and the intellectual. Quantities are divided into the point, length, width, and depth; quality into four: the dry, the cold, the moist, and the hot; Motion into ascending, descending, straight, and circular. The Earth is divided into four spaces.

Furthermore, it is not incorrectly said that the <term>Tetractys<gloss>a mystical Pythagorean figure of ten points arranged in four rows, symbolizing the harmony of the universe</gloss></term> contains all things, since the number four—as we have shown elsewhere—is potentially the number ten (the most perfect and absolute of all numbers), and thus becomes the Idea of all things, beyond which no other number is found, as shown above in Book 2, Chapter 10. <margin>The Cabalists reduce all things to ten.</margin> The Jewish <term>Cabalists<gloss>practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism</gloss></term> also reduced this to the ten <term>Zephiroth<gloss>Sefirot: the ten emanations or attributes through which the Infinite reveals itself</gloss></term>, which are divine attributes and measures by which they are accustomed to describe God, divine providence, and the immensity of things. But so that what has been said so far may be condensed into a summary, I have thought it best to propose the preceding figure, in which we place before the eyes of the curious reader the idea of the whole speculation considered in the <term>Tautic character<gloss>a symbol based on the letter Tau or a cross, here specifically the Hieroglyphic Monad or the sign of Mercury</gloss></term>. The figure consists of a circle, a segment of the Moon, and a cross. Through the circle, the starry world is divided into its planetary orbits; the Moon, intersecting it, forms the character of Mercury, composed of the Sun and Moon. The cross, indeed, denotes the elemental world, into which the starry world exerts its power through the <term>soul of the world<gloss>Anima Mundi: an intrinsic spirit believed to animate all nature</gloss></term> pervading everything; the four extremities of the cross contain four presiding statues of the four elements, indicated by the four quarters of the world. The topmost statue is hawk-formed <note>original: "accipitriformis," likely referring to the god Horus</note> and denotes fire, situated in the shape of a 'Y' <note>original: "ypsilonomorpho"</note>, the mystery of which we shall reveal in what follows.

The second statue is dog-formed <note>original: "caniformis," likely referring to Anubis</note> for Air; the third is ibis-formed <note>original: "ibiformis," referring to Thoth</note> for Water; and finally, the fourth is human-formed <note>original: "ἀνθρωπόμορφος" (anthropomorphos)</note> for Earth, from which a serpent breaks forth as a sign of fertility, by which the earth is impregnated through the diffusion of the mundane spirit. All are positioned in the form of a 'Y' (the letter upsilon), whose mystery will be opened later; all are equipped with <term>handled crosses<gloss>cruces ansatas: the Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life</gloss></term> to indicate the power they draw from the spirit of the world. The whole cross is filled with handled crosses to indicate the Ideas of the divine mind, of which that whole character is a symbol. Added are the horn of Aries with a small moon, and the heads of an ox and a scarab, from which elements the Tautic character is constituted; thus the whole figure expresses the character of Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note>, as it was discovered by him and composed of all worldly materials. Since the other secrets of the character have been explained at length in this whole <term>hierogrammatism<gloss>sacred symbolic writing or diagram</gloss></term>, I thought it superfluous to deal with them more verbosely here. Let it suffice, therefore, that this exhibition of the most mysterious expanded character placed here is grasped as if in a certain summary.

<margin>Why the handled Tau is seen so often among hieroglyphics.</margin> Furthermore, why that mystical character of the cross so often appears in the <term>Bembine Table<gloss>also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet from antiquity featuring Egyptian motifs</gloss></term> and other idols recently brought from Egypt, held in their hands—this might perhaps seem wonderful to someone. But it now remains for us to explain it.

It must be noted, therefore, that the Egyptians always held mysterious characters of this kind in great veneration, not only because of the supreme [mysteries] they contained within themselves...
