### HIEROGLYPHICS

...contained mysteries; but most especially because they believed that celestial spirits <note>original: "Genios cœlestes"; here referring to guardian spirits or divine intelligences</note> were attracted by a character of this kind through a certain natural sympathy. For since they believed the world to be a kind of living animal, in which the parts, however distant in location, are drawn toward one another because of a single shared nature, and that the mediator of the world itself and the common cause of all mixtures draws the parts to one another by its very nature (as Iamblichus says); hence they judged that such attractions and appetites could be increased beyond the ordinary order by a certain art. Hence, as Iamblichus rightly says:

<margin>The Tautic character as an effective amulet for the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, Part 1, folio 140. Basel Edition.</margin>
> *The Egyptians, imitating the very nature of the universe and the workmanship of the Gods, themselves also displayed certain images of mystical and hidden notions in the fashioning of symbols, just as nature expresses hidden reasons in apparent forms as if through symbols, and the Gods explain the truth of ideas through manifest images; especially since they perceived that all higher things are delighted by the likeness of lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from the superiors, insofar as they may imitate them according to their strength; rightly, they themselves also offer a mode of action agreeable to the celestial powers according to their strength, when they insert hidden mysteries into manifest symbols, in the interpretation of which, put away the words and receive the meanings.*

The Egyptians, therefore, fashioned this kind of symbol under specific times and celestial positions, most especially under Aries and Mercury, from which signs (as we have demonstrated above) the character was constituted. For they judged that when the Sun was exalted in Aries, and the Moon with Mercury, they acquired the greatest power from heaven for drawing forth spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note> to perfect divinations and the investigation of things, and for repelling the opposing <term>Typhonian spirits<gloss>entities associated with Typhon or Set, representing chaos, darkness, and obstruction</gloss></term>. But Marsilio <note>referring to Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> describes all these things aptly and clearly in Book 3 of *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*.

*But someone may ask which celestial figures the Egyptians were most accustomed to imprint upon their images. For there are forms there very conspicuous to the eyes, and depicted by many for what they are, such as Aries (♈), Taurus (♉), and similar figures of the Zodiac, and those which are manifest outside the Zodiac. There are, furthermore, many forms there not so much visible as imaginable, proceeding from or at least devised by the Indians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans through the "faces" <note>referring to the Decans, or ten-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign</note> of the signs. Just as in the first face of Virgo, there is a beautiful Virgin sitting, having twin ears of corn in her hand, and nursing a boy. Finally, there are certain characters of the signs and planets designated by the Egyptians. They wish, therefore, for all these to be engraved on images; so that if one expects a particular benefit from Mercury (☿), he ought to place him in Virgo (♍), or at least there with an aspect of Mercury, and then fashion the image from tin or silver, in which is the whole sign of the Virgin, its character, and the character of Mercury. Some established their entire form in a round shape according to the likeness of the heavens,* <margin>The Cross used by the ancient astronomers.</margin> *but the more ancient ones preferred the figure of the cross above all others. This is because bodies act through power upon a surface already spread out; and the first surface is described by a cross. For in the first instance, it possesses length and width; and this figure is the first and most straight of all; and it contains four right angles. Indeed, the effects of the heavenly bodies result most especially through the straightness of rays and angles. For then the stars are most powerful when they hold the four angles of heaven—namely, the <term>Cardinal Points<gloss>the four "hinges" of the sky: the Rising (East), Setting (West), and the upper and lower mid-heavens</gloss></term>—and being thus disposed, they hurl their rays into one another in such a way that they constitute a cross therefrom...*

### BOOK IV. THE IDEA

...should constitute it; therefore, the ancients used to say that the Cross was a figure created by the strength of the stars, and was a receptacle for that same celestial strength. For this reason, it was believed to possess the highest power in images and to receive the spirits of the planets. This opinion was either introduced or strongly confirmed by the Egyptians, among whom the cross was one of the most distinguished characters, signifying their "future life" <note>original: "vitam eorum futuram"; Kircher interprets the Egyptian Ankh as a pagan prophecy of the Christian promise of eternal life</note>. They used to engrave its shape on the breast of Serapis <note>A major Greco-Egyptian deity representing the sun and the afterlife</note>, and this character was also imprinted upon many other things. I, however, believe that the excellence of the cross among the Egyptians before Christ was not so much a testimony to the gift of the stars, but rather a presage of the power that it was destined to receive through Christ. On the other hand, the astrologers who lived immediately after Christ, seeing the wonderful things performed by Christians through the cross, but being either ignorant of or unwilling to credit so much to JESUS, referred these powers back to the heavens. Thus says Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous Renaissance philosopher who attempted to reconcile Platonic philosophy with Christianity</note>, in whom—as if in a brief compendium—all those things which have been discussed at length so far are confirmed.

<margin>An anonymous Arab,</margin>
Furthermore, these points are confirmed by a certain anonymous Arab writer, who in a manuscript book speaks as follows:

-> We have received from the ancients that there is great power in the form of the cross. <-
---

> We have received from the ancients that there is great force and efficacy in the decussated <note>intersecting in the shape of an X or cross</note> figure, that is, the symbol of the cross.

From all of this, it is clear that this magical character was the primary Egyptian phylactery <note>a protective charm or amulet</note> and amulet. By its power, they would undoubtedly bind demons into idols and compel them to give answers <margin>Carved on the forehead of Serapis.</margin>, and they would shatter the "Typhonian" <note>referring to Typhon or Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note> assaults; for this reason, it was engraved on the forehead of Serapis, who was the symbol of the worldly mass and the greatest oracle of the Egyptians. And from this, the Caduceus of Mercury seems to have drawn its origin.

<margin>The Caduceus of Mercury had its origin from the Tautic character.</margin>

The serpent denotes the Spirit. The circular and hemispherical figure, created as the serpent transforms itself into them by winding, signifies the Sun, the Moon, and the stars, as we have said based on Horus <note>Horapollo, an author of a famous treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> and other writers on hieroglyphics. The Cross, which is formed by the reed-like rod with wings attached on either side, represents the elements which the Spirit of the World pervades. All these things are seen beautifully represented in the hieroglyphic scheme which we provided above in the "Hierogrammatism of the Dog" on page <margin>Description of Mercury</margin> 294; there, Mercury (or Anubis) is depicted by later Egyptians with a dog's head and a caduceus, standing upon a crocodile, with the heads of Ammon <term>ram-faced <gloss>original: κριοπρόσωπος</gloss></term> and Apis <term>ox-faced <gloss>original: βουπρόσωπος</gloss></term> <margin>Explanation of the figures shown in Scheme IV.</margin> added to the side with inscriptions, as you see. # HIEROGLYPHICS.

...the Mercurial spirit; by the sphere, however, they signify the governor of the World and the Leader <note>original: "Choragum," literally the leader of a choir or dance</note> of harmonic order. By the Crocodile, they represent the fertile moisture of the spirit of the World, which is required for the generation of all things. For the crocodile is a fertile animal that rejoices in the fertile moisture of the Nile; and indeed, all generation consists of the moist and the warm. By the joined heads of Ammon and Apis, they wished to indicate that Anubis-Mercury, Ammon, and Apis are the same thing, differing only in their effects, as the inscription teaches; however, you will find these matters explained more expansively in the preceding sections.

### §. II.

### Concerning the Sphere, and the Circle.

<margin>The ancients noted the highest mysteries through geometric forms.</margin>
By the consensus of all learned Doctors, it is established that sensible things—those we can perceive with our senses—are like images of those things which are invisible. Consequently, God can be seen by the human intellect through knowledge in no other way than as if in a mirror or a riddle <note>This is a common Renaissance reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, suggesting that we see divine truth indirectly through the physical world</note>. Since all things have a certain proportion to one another (though it remains hidden and incomprehensible to us), a single universe arises out of everything; and all things within that one greatest whole are themselves one. Furthermore, because these concepts cannot be grasped without an image or likeness, many wise men primarily employed those images and similarities in their contemplations of higher beings which, by being simpler and more abstract, could more aptly express the logic of the heavens. Such are the contemplations of mathematical things. Because these are mostly occupied with numbers and geometric figures, they produced such an abundance of speculation that none of the great men of antiquity approached the arduous mysteries of divine things by any path other than this. 

Hence, Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who bridged classical Greek thought and the Middle Ages</note> appropriately says that no one who is <term>unversed in geometry</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀγεωμέτρητον" (ageōmetrēton)</note> can reach the science of divine things. For this reason, Pythagoras, Plato, and their followers placed the entirety of the search for truth within numbers and geometric figures. Indeed, Saint Augustine proves from Plato that the "number" of things to be created was the primary model in the mind of the Creator. 

<margin>Numbers and figures denote the ideas of things.</margin>
Aristotle himself could not hand down the distinction between different mathematical types to us in any other way than through the comparison of numbers. When he wished to teach the science of how natural forms exist one within another, he deemed it necessary to take refuge in mathematical forms, saying: <term>Just as the triangle is in the quadrangle, so is the lower in the superior</term> <note>original Greek: "Καθάπερ τρίγωνον ἐν τῷ τετραγώνω, ἕτως ὕπατον ἐν τῷ ὑπερτάτῳ"</note>. Thus, as Boethius witnesses, the entire doctrine of truth is comprised of "multitude" (number) and "magnitude" (size/geometry). There should be no doubt that the ancient Greeks drew all these ideas from the Egyptians. For the Egyptians were not only the first inventors of Letters and mathematics, but relying on that knowledge, they used these forms to denote the greatest mysteries and secrets of higher beings. To demonstrate this, we shall begin our discussion with the circle.

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

<margin>Wonders of the circle.</margin>
Aristotle, when he was searching deeply for the cause of the wonderful and prodigious effects which occur everywhere in mechanics concerning the lever and the balance—to the great admiration of all—found at last no other cause for these effects except the circle, which is the most astonishing of all marvelous things. And not without reason: for it is most consistent with reason that wonderful effects proceed from a wonderful cause. <margin>Definition of the circle.</margin> A circle is a plane figure contained by only one line, which is called the circumference, toward which all straight lines proceeding from one point (which they call the center) are equal to one another. Therefore, in this figure, a most wonderful existence of opposites occurs; for every circle is made from that which moves and that which remains still—with one foot of the compass standing fixed and the other driven around into a periphery. <margin>A wonderful property of the circle.</margin> Furthermore, it is most marvelous that the line which encompasses the orb of the circle—called a *helix* <note>original: "ἕλιϰα"</note> by the Greeks—although it is entirely devoid of width, also admits a certain agreement of opposites: namely, the concave and the convex <note>The original uses "curuum" (curved), here implying the outer curve or convex side to contrast with the inner concave side</note>. These are opposites in the same way that "large" and "small" are; for the middle point of the latter is "equal," while the middle of the former is "straight." For indeed, everything that is large, in order to become small, or small to become large, must necessarily reach the "equal" before it reaches the other extreme. In the same way, a curved line, before it becomes concave, must become as if straight; and a concave line, to pass over to the convex and circular, must similarly first be in some way straight.

<margin>The ancients thought something divine was in the circle.</margin>
The Egyptians seem to have been by no other means ignorant of these admirable qualities and virtues of the circle. For when they looked upon certain cyclical *states* <note>original: "στάσεις", referring to fixed points or stages in a cycle</note> shining forth among all things contained in the circuit of this world, they contemplated with the highest admiration the spiral ideas affected by that supreme Architect. He affects something spherical both in Himself and in His works—which, as we said above on the testimony of Plutarch, were made according to no other pattern than the circle. Thus, they judged that something divine resided in the circle, so much so that whenever they wished to indicate something great, wonderful, or excellent in which some traces of divinity appeared, they demonstrated it by applying a circle or a sphere. From this, that truly Thrice-Great Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the beginning of hermetic philosophy</note>, in defining the divine nature, took the circle as his means; for when asked, "What is GOD?" he replied:

> ->*God is a circle, or an intelligible sphere, whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.*<-

Since GOD is not a body, nor can He be one (because He is supremely simple, and because everything most perfect must be most simple and devoid of all composition, since every composite thing is posterior to its components), he therefore says He is an *intelligible sphere* to distinguish Him from a physical sphere. <margin>God is a circle and how this is to be understood.</margin> Wherefore, by the "center"—which is something tiny and most simple compared to the circumference—understand the divine simplicity; but by the "circumference"—which is the greatest—take the divine immensity. Therefore, the sense of the aforementioned description is: GOD is a sphere, that is, lacking beginning and end, much more so than a material circle or sphere, so that His eternity may be noted; He is *intelligible*, so that His immateriality may be noted; His center, that is, the indivisible essence...

### HIEROGLYPHICS

His essence is entirely everywhere; but His circumference—that is, His immensity—is nowhere, because it cannot be contained by any place. We also compare GOD to the center of a circle, around which all things exist, and from which all things proceed in a certain order into a Sphere, until the complete universe of things is finished. For just as a center is neither a magnitude, nor a circle, nor a sphere, but is the principle <note>In this context, "principle" means the source or foundational origin.</note> of all circles and spheres; by the same measure, GOD is none of those things which are in the world, nor is He the whole world itself, but He is nevertheless the principle of the whole world. To this center, therefore, the highest point of all creatures is bounded, just as in a circle all parts are finished by the form of a pyramid from the circumference to the center. 

And from this doctrine of Trismegistus <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and hermetic philosophy.</note>, our Pythagoras received <margin>How Pythagoras understood that God was to be worshiped by the rotation of the body.</margin> that ceremony which he later handed down: namely, that GOD must be worshiped by the rotation of the body, "to move around while fluttering about" <note>original: "περίκινειν περιπετόμενον"</note>. Pierio Valeriano <note>An Italian Renaissance humanist, author of a famous work on hieroglyphics.</note> in Book 39 is the authority that this was also an institution of Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites.</note>; for he commanded that before anyone worshiped GOD, they should turn themselves in a circle, and having completed the circle, they should offer worship to GOD. They did this because they venerated Him who was to be signified through the circle, the perfect figure. Pliny, cited in Pierio, says that in the act of adoration, we bring the right hand to the mouth and turn the whole body around. 

Truly, I wanted to note these things here, although <margin>What happiness is.</margin> they may perhaps seem like "secondary matters" <note>original: "παρέργα"</note>; namely, that circular motion—through which a body is revolved back to the same point from which it ascended—is the most expressive image of true and eternal happiness. Through this happiness, the creature returns to that same principle from which it had proceeded. For they define happiness as the return of each thing to its own principle, because happiness is the highest good; moreover, the highest good is that which all things seek, and that which all things seek is the very thing which is the principle of all. But the principle of all is God, the one, the almighty; therefore, the end of all is the same as the principle of all. 

Hence those two names for God among the Pythagoreans: "The One" and "The Good." They name Him "The One" because He is the principle of all, just as we have said that unity is the principle of all number. But they name Him "The Good" because He is the end of all, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. Indeed, nothing moves in a circle except things that are immortal and incorruptible; nothing returns to God except an immortal and eternal substance. Although celestial things are suited to circular motion, they are not themselves sufficient to complete this motion; rather, there is need for a Divine Mover to turn and revolve them. It happens no differently for us <margin>How the return to God is made.</margin> as it does for the Angels: for we are such by nature that we cannot turn and reflect ourselves, but we can be turned by the power of the Moving Grace and be reflected back toward God. Hence that saying:

> Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. <note>original: "qui aguntur ſpiritu Dei, filij Dei ſunt," quoting Romans 8:14.</note>

The Motor Spirit <note>The "Spiritus Motor" or Divine Mover that initiates spiritual action.</note> constantly knocks at our soul; if we admit Him, we are immediately filled with God and are carried back to the Lord through the circle of religion, to possess life in Him forever—the same life we were even before we were made. This is true Religion, the true happiness of man, toward which Religion promotes, directs, and impels us.

# BOOK IV. IDEAS

...both for the reasons mentioned and because they saw this massive bulk of the Universe distinguished by a circular shape. For it is hidden from no one that this shape is the most suitable for the Heavens; just as it was necessary for the Universe to be the most capable, simplest, and most perfect, so the most wise Architect <note>A common Renaissance term for God as the creator-designer of the world.</note> chose the most capable, simplest, and most perfect figure for its construction. For it is most perfect when it possesses all its own parts, nor is it possible for it to suffer even the slightest loss. It is the simplest because, as the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who emphasized the mathematical and ideal nature of the cosmos.</note> believe, there is nothing from which it could be made or into which it could be dissolved; otherwise, it would be subject to birth and decay. It is the most capable because it leaves nothing outside of itself but embraces all things within. That the sphere is of this kind is shown by the fact that it holds the same relationship to other solids as the circle does to its own planes.

<margin>The Property of the Circle.</margin>
First, indeed, the figure of the circle is the most capable of all <term>isoperimetric</term> <note>isoperimetrarum: referring to shapes that have the same perimeter length but different areas; the circle encloses the greatest area for its circumference.</note> shapes; furthermore, it is the most perfect because it undergoes no increase or decrease, and it is the simplest because it is contained by only one line. Thus, the sphere is a solid figure contained by a single surface, to which all straight lines drawn from a single central point are equal. Therefore, the sphere is also the most capable because it has the circle as its boundary; it is the most perfect since, unlike an angular body, it does not grow or shrink in any place; and indeed it is the simplest, for it is enclosed by a single surface. To this cause is added another reason for such great veneration: through the straight line and the circle, there was the first and simplest production and representation of things into the light—both those things not yet existing and those hidden in the veils of nature. But a circle can be made neither rightly nor skillfully without a point; therefore, by the logic of the point and the <term>monad</term> <note>monadis: the number one, representing unity or the source of all numbers.</note>, things both began to exist first, and those things which are shaped by a circumference, no matter how great they may be, can in no way lack the service of the central point.

<margin>Why the Egyptians placed circular crowns or orbs on the heads of the Gods.</margin>
These things having been demonstrated in this way, it remains for us to say why the Egyptians placed a circle and a sphere on the heads of their statues, as can be seen from many of the images on our Obelisks.

Antiquity was accustomed to studiously venerate things considered religious and majestic in human opinion. Among these, the most noble is a certain orb sometimes drawn around the head, an index of veneration and of a majesty that exceeds the human. This is noted everywhere as being placed around Emperors (whom the Ancients looked up to as raised above the height of mortality), the Provinces of the Roman World, primary Cities, and even the animals of the Gods. Regarding the Augusti <note>A title for Roman Emperors.</note>, there exist bronze coins of Antoninus Pius and Constantius, which Laurentius Pignorius <note>Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631), an Italian antiquarian famous for his study of the "Bembine Tablet" or Mensa Isiaca.</note>, a man most skilled in antiquity, mentions in his exposition of the *Mensa Isiaca* <note>The Bembine Tablet, an elaborate bronze tablet featuring Egyptian-style iconography.</note>.

<margin>Laurentius Pignorius.</margin>
*The Egyptians,* he says, *placed this Orb on the very top of the head of their images. This may be noted both here and elsewhere; one may suspect that the Romans took this from them and varied it in style for the sake of decorum, so that a crown might be fitted in that position to a head in which they thought something divine resided. However, this ornament, through the moderation of subsequent princes and the silent consent of all, passed entirely to God and His Saints—as many things did—and it has retained the ancient name of "diadem" to this day. Thus far Pignorius, who is supported by those things which Pierius says in Book 29, page 4.*

<margin>What the Pierian circle denotes.</margin>
*A single circle,* he says, *described either simply or upon some other...*

## HIEROGLYPHICS

...enclosed by a picture and a sign, the Egyptians signified sometimes "always," sometimes "perpetual and eternal," and sometimes "all things" (the All <note>original Greek: τὸ πᾶν, *to pan*</note>), namely because in that figure neither beginning nor end can be found, which is the specific quality of eternity. And a little later: *Taking into account the reason of its never-appearing beginning and end, the Egyptians understood God from the hieroglyph of the circle.* Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note>, cited in Eusebius <note>A Greek historian of Christianity (c. 260–339 AD).</note>, Book 3 of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, testifies that a sphere <note>original Latin: *pila*, literally a ball or globe.</note> was attributed to the Gods by the Egyptians with these words: *The sphere and all round things are attributed to the world, and especially to the Sun and Moon; they fashioned their altars and temples in the shape of a circle.*

<margin>Jupiter as the circle of the heavens.</margin>
<margin>God as a circle</margin>
The Persians also, according to the testimony of Brissonius <note>Barnabé Brisson (1531–1591), a jurist who wrote on Persian customs.</note>: *When they spoke of Jupiter as the Lord of Heaven, they believed they were performing sacrifices to him when they ascended the highest lookout point and called Jupiter the "circle of Heaven."* The same custom passed to the Turks; hence those morning proclamations from a certain high tower: *la alla elle alla* <note>Kircher's phonetic rendering of the Shahada: *La ilaha illa Allah* ("There is no god but God").</note>, etc. The meaning of these words is that God exists always and will be always, and is nothing else—except that they also greet their own Muhammad. The Saracens <note>A term used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for Arabs or Muslims.</note> and many other nations also called God a circle, and from this they concluded that eternity was expressed. The Mughals <note>original Latin: *Mogores*. Kircher refers to the Mughal Emperors of India.</note> also depict their King, whom they venerate with almost divine honors, shining with a radiant head.

<margin>What the radiant orb around the heads of saints signifies.</margin>
<margin>What a Nimbus is</margin>
<margin>Lucian.</margin>
From this Egyptian custom, the origin of the Greeks and Romans seems to have flowed, in that they adorned their Gods with a radiant circle; all of which are shown by infinite medals and coins, which you may see in the works of Fulvius Ursinus, Paruta, and other antiquarians. For it was sometimes customary for a crown of rays, or a certain shining light, to be painted on all the Gods, as I have discussed at length in my *Hieroglyphic Apparatus*; and they called this by the specific name <term>nimbus</term> <note>Now commonly known as a halo.</note>, as Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentaries on Virgil.</note> testifies in many places. Nor should anyone think that a solid, continuous light was usually painted for the other divinities while the Sun's light was divided into rays; for rays in the manner of a circle were also given to those men to whom divinity was attributed. Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist (c. 125–180 AD).</note>, in *The Syrian Goddess*, says: *he wears rays upon his head* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ ἀκτῖνας φορέει</note>; and in *The Misanthrope* he describes Jove: *holding a thunderbolt in his right hand, and with rays upon his head* <note>original Greek: κεραυνὸν ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ ἔχοντα, καὶ ἀκτῖνας ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ</note>. Heliodorus <note>Author of the ancient Greek novel *Aethiopica*.</note> testifies that the Ethiopians also had this custom, who in Book 9 of the *Ethiopian History* elegantly describes these arrangements of rays:

> *They placed a woven thing,* he says, *which was circular, around the head, and having pierced it with arrows around the circle, they turned the feathered ends of the arrows toward the head, while the sharp points projected outward like rays.* <note>Kircher provides both the Greek original and a Latin translation of this passage from Heliodorus.</note>

By these things, they wished to indicate nothing other than the signs of hidden divinity, according to the Egyptian mind, as will be declared more fully in Book V.

How the Egyptians demonstrated God as infinite through the circle, and how they learned from the circle that the line, the circle, the triangle, and the square are the same in GOD, remains to be explained. Since they recognized that God, by the necessity of His nature, is necessarily infinite, they first, from the limits and properties of the circle, proceeded by a truly subtle reasoning to the properties of the infinite...

<margin>
How will they show the infinity of God from a circle?
</margin>
...were rolled out; for the larger a circle is, the more obtuse <note>In this geometric context, "obtuse" refers to the flattening of the curve. As a circle grows larger, its arc becomes less curved and more like a straight line.</note> they saw its circumference to be. Thus, if circles were made ever larger and larger toward infinity, it followed necessarily that the one which reached the limit of infinity, so to speak, would be infinite, and therefore would coincide with an infinite straight line. Thus, if circles D, E, and F, made ever larger toward infinity, are all imagined touching one another at point C, it is certain that the largest of all—and thus the infinite one, stripped of all curvature—coincides with the equally infinite line AB. Let us now imagine the triangle CDB moving from the center, becoming more and more obtuse toward DEF by the leg DB; it is certain that this triangle, extended into the infinite circle at F, would be infinite, and the same would be true of the diameter CF. Since we suppose this diameter to be infinite, the triangle would also be infinite; and thus the straight line, the circle, and the triangle coincide into one in infinite magnitude.

A triangle (CDB) is inscribed within the circles, used to demonstrate geometric principles approaching infinity.
</image-desc>

<margin>
How the circle, triangle, and straight line are the same in GOD.

See the most abstruse things we have taught concerning these and similar matters in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry* <note>Kircher refers here to his own theories on "sacred geometry" where mathematical shapes act as symbols for divine truths.</note>; from these few points it should be more than clear how subtly the ancients investigated the immense nature of God, and how aptly they penetrated little by little from sensible things to the invisible things that are inaccessible to the human intellect. It is also clear from these points how the definition of God is to be understood from the description of the intellectual, infinite circle proposed a little earlier by Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed. This refers to the famous maxim: "God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere."</note>. Having seen the reasoning by which they hinted at the supreme Divinity through geometric figures, let us now examine how they indicated His operations in the sensible world through the same figures.

## §. III.

## Concerning the Circle and Angular Figures

<margin>
Proclus in Book 5 [of his commentary on] Euclid.
</margin>
Since the Egyptians had noted a circular property in GOD as if in the Archetype <term>Archetype: the original model or "blueprint" of all things in the divine mind.</term> of all things, they rightly chose the same as a symbol of the sensible world; so that the thing formed <note>original Latin: *ideatum*, the physical manifestation of an Idea.</note> would perfectly correspond to its Idea in every way. For, observing the circular traces and actions of all things, they called the world and the things in the world "sensible circles"; but incorporeal intelligences they called "invisible circles." Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note> explains this cleverly in his usual manner in Book 5 [of his commentary] on Euclid: *All mathematical things,* he says, *are first in the soul itself: numbers before numbers that move by themselves, vital figures before visible figures, harmonic ratios before things that are composed, and invisible circles were produced before bodies that move in a circular motion.* For since they knew that the rays of the stars, resting upon the earth as if on a center, described circles by their rotation, they deemed this a property of the divine...

### HIEROGLYPHICS

...considering it a work of divine faculty. When they wished to indicate either divinity, the world, or the heavens with their symbols, they expressed it by a circle, or a sphere, or by some other symbol chosen from lower things that was not dissimilar. From this, I believe, arose the practice where shrines, altars, and the instruments with which sacred rites were administered were all fashioned in a circular arrangement. Their ceremonies, gestures, and movements were also performed in a circle. Since we have discussed these matters in various parts of this work, we only wish to indicate them briefly here. Let us therefore proceed from the circle to other angular figures. When the ancients noted that a line is born from the center—or from the imaginary flow of a point—where one end remains unmoved and the other is led around to describe a curved line (which they called a circle), they progressed a little further in their contemplation and imagined something angular within the circle itself. For an angle is established within it, which is a symbol of pyramidal influence. Furthermore, any other line cutting the diameter at the center constitutes a <term>decussis</term> <note>The Latin term *decussis* refers to the Roman numeral X or any cross-shaped intersection.</note>. If this was done at right angles, it constituted a perfect cross, a symbol of influence into the four quarters of the world. If done at acute angles, it properly formed a <margin>What is a *chasma*? And its meanings.</margin> <term>chasma</term> <note>original Greek: χάσμα (*chasma*). While it often means a "yawning gap" or "abyss," in this geometric and Platonic context it refers to the crossing point of two lines forming an X.</note>, or a *decussis*, which is a symbol of the pyramidal influence of the Gods.

<image-desc>A small circular diagram containing a decussis or X-shaped cross, positioned in the right margin to illustrate the geometric intersection discussed in the text.</image-desc>

The former point is proved by Justin Martyr, who, speaking of the world being founded by God, says, <note>original Greek: "ἐχίαζεν αὐτὸν, ἐν τῷ παντὶ"</note> "He formed it into the shape of a Chi (X) in the universe," alluding to the mystery of the cross, just as he shows in his second *Apology* about three pages from the end: <note>original: "ὅπως ἔδωκεν ἀναγνὼς τῷ Πλάτωνι..."</note> "Thus, having read [the scriptures], **Plato** gave and acknowledged this, though not knowing it accurately, nor understanding it to be the type of a cross, but perceiving only the logic of a decussis—namely, that the power following the first God was made in the shape of a decussis throughout the universe." He had explained the mystery of the bronze serpent as referring to Christ, which he draws from this Platonic idea. Sylburgius adds the very words of **Plato** <margin>Plato.</margin> in his notes to Justin: <note>original Greek from the *Timaeus*: "Ταύτην τὴν ξὺν οὖσαν πᾶσαν..."</note> "Splitting this whole composition in two along its length, and joining them together at their centers like the letter X, he bent them into a circle." Which, in the work *On the Universe*, he translates thus: "*Splitting this whole double conjunction lengthwise, and fitting the middle to the middle, he joined them as if in a decussis.*" This mystery of the *chasma* or *decussis* was undoubtedly drawn by him from the Egyptians.

They [the Egyptians] adopted the *decussis* into their number of letters quite willingly, both for the reasons demonstrated on page 126 and because of the extraordinary mysteries hidden beneath it. From this character, indeed, countless others found their origin—among them the **ankh** <note>original: "crux ansata," the "cross with a handle," the Egyptian symbol of life.</note>, the mysteries of which we declared in the preceding pages. Other equally varied types of *decusses* also emerged, which occur throughout this Obelisk of ours and which we shall explain in their proper place. For first, the letter **Λ** [Lambda], discovered from the gait of the **Ibis**, denoted the influence of the Deity into the lower material worlds; whereas the **V**, from the open beak of the Ibis, denoted the return of the Deity from the lower things to the higher. When these were joined at their vertices, the **X** emerged—that famous and mysterious *decussis* which aptly hinted at the process of the world-spirit <note>original Greek: "ἄνω καὶ κάτω" (*anō kai katō*)</note> "upward and downward." By this, too, the number ten is the symbol of the totality of things, as **Horus** <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> most clearly teaches in Book 2, Chapter 30, with these words: <note>original Greek: "γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία..."</note> "A single straight line together with a bent line divided horizontally signifies..."

Straight... <note>Catchword: "Recta" (Straight), leading to the next page.</note>

*A straight line together with another curved at the top signifies ten flat lines.*
*But since this passage is entirely faulty in all copies,*
*let us see how it should be restored; we have consulted printed books*
*and manuscripts, and almost all the corrupt ones read as follows:* <note>original Greek: γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία ἅμα γραμμῆ ἐπικεκλυμένη δέκα γραμμὰς ἐπιπέδους σημαίνει</note> *“One straight line together with a curved line signifies ten flat lines.” The sense is entirely unsuitable; in other manuscripts, it is read less corruptly as:* <note>original Greek: γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία ἅμα γραμμῆ ἐπικεκλημένη, . . . . ἢ δέκα γραμμὰς ἐπιπέδους σημαίνει</note> *“One straight line together with an inclined line, either . . . . . . or 10 flat lines signify,” where you may see that the space marked with dots signifies something is missing. Therefore, I believe it should be read thus:* <note>original Greek: γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία ἅμα γραμμῆ ἐπιτεταμμένη, ἢ χίασμα, ἢ δέκα γραμμαὶ ἐπιπέδους σημαίνει</note> *that is: “A straight line where another line is stretched across it, in this manner X, or a cross-shape <term>chiasma</term> <note>The Greek term *chiasma* refers to the shape of the letter Chi (X).</note>, or ten lines on a plane in this manner ||||||||||, signify [ten].” Thus, by designating the <term>decussis</term> <note>A Latin term for the number ten or the shape of an X.</note> in the form of a cross in this manner X, they expressed the number ten, a custom which has been accepted by posterity even to this day.*

<margin>
How the ancients formed numbers
</margin>

*But how ten flat lines expressed this same ten remains to be explained;*
*it should be known that the ancients, before they had invented fixed figures for numbers,*
*expressed their numbers with as many small lines as the number signified;*
*hence, indicating one, two, three, four, etc., they placed one, two, three, four, up to ten lines: I. II. III. IIII; in this manner ||||||||||;*
*by which they simply placed the number indicated by the cross-shape before the eyes through ten lines; and this is what the words of Horus seem to indicate:* <note>original Greek: γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία, ἅμα γραμμῆ ἐπιτεταμμένη δέκα, ἢ χίασμα, ἢ δέκα γραμμαὶ ἐπιπέδους σημαίνει</note> *“One straight line, with a line stretched across it, or a cross-shape, or ten lines on a plane signify [ten],” and with this number, as with 10, they secretly denoted the completion of all things;*
*for beyond 10, all numbers are nothing other than a repetition of the first ones. Some traces of this still seem to exist among the Ancient Romans,*
*when they indicated the <term>Duumviri</term>, <term>Triumviri</term>, <term>Septemviri</term>, and <term>Decemviri</term> <note>These were Roman boards or commissions of two, three, seven, or ten men, respectively.</note> by these linear numbers: II vir, III vir, IIII vir, etc. We have chosen to explain this more at length so that the text of Horus might be restored and it might become clear how they indicated ten through those marks. For through this crossing <note>decussationem</note> of two lines, there arose a sort of double pyramid connected at a common apex, of which the first would tend upward and the second downward—a genuine symbol of the progression of the <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>The "World Soul," a concept from Platonic philosophy representing the animating spirit of the universe.</note> "upward and downward" <note>original Greek: ἄνω καὶ κάτω (*anō kai katō*)</note>. See what we have handed down concerning these on pages 126, 169, and 171.*

The first pyramid ABC denotes the gliding of the supreme <term>monad</term> <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate One or the divine source of all numbers and existence.</note> into multiplicity; the pyramid BCD, however, denotes the return of that same monad from the lower or material world into the world of light—or what is the same thing, the active influx of the Deity through the pyramid ABC, which becomes the expansion of point B into multiplicity or the width of AC; the passive influx...*

# HIEROGLYPHICS

...they indicated the reception of an active influence in the lower world through the inverted pyramid BCD; see what we have discussed more extensively on page 171 regarding these matters. However, since the <insert>

</insert> Genius <note>Here, "Genius" refers to the guiding spirit or characteristic intellectual method of the Egyptian people.</note> of the Egyptians was inclined toward this—namely, that they might represent the progression of all other sensible things shining forth in generation and corruption according to a certain analogy fitting the archetype—they quite aptly exhibit, through this figure, the progression of the **spermatic virtue** <note>The "spermatic virtue" refers to the inherent life-force or "seed-power" within nature that drives growth and reproduction.</note>. By this, all things contained in the material worlds <note>original: "hylæis mundis"</note> are shown, which are indicated by the <term>quaternary</term> (the number four), the <term>septenary</term> (the number seven), and the <term>decussis</term> (the X-shape) of the <term>denary</term> (the number ten). But I shall explain the mystery in a few words, using the example of vegetables. Since a tree proceeds from a seed, and from the tree a seed is made again; the latter is indeed subsequent, the former prior. The end also, in number, does not coincide with the first, but the end of the outflow coincides with the beginning of the reflux; thus the number seven rightly arises, and from there, the number ten.

->**[Image: A geometric diagram featuring two intersecting triangles (pyramis recta/upright pyramid and pyramis inversâ/inverted pyramid). The top is labeled "Above" (Greek: ἄνω) and the bottom "Below" (Greek: κάτω). The points are labeled with letters A through K, showing a flow from the bottom vertex A, through a central point G, to the top vertex D, and back.]**<-

For if **A** is like the seed, **D** is like the tree, **G** is like another seed, and **K** is like another tree; then **A** proceeds through **BC** into **D**. **D** then proceeds into **G** through **EF**, and the **septenary** (seven) is closed. Then **G** ascends into **K** through **HI**, and thus the **denary** (ten) is completed. <margin>Hieroglyph for the generation and corruption of things.</margin> Therefore, the individual contraction of the species (as the Schools <note>Refers to "Scholasticism," the medieval and Renaissance system of logic and philosophy taught in universities.</note> say) in the seed **A** is corruptible in itself, but incorruptible in the species. Striving to preserve itself through the power of the contracted species existing within it, and resolving itself into the species, it sheds the individuality of the seed so that it might draw out something like itself through the mediation of the species. Therefore, it ascends into the tree by a quaternary (four-step) progression, since without that medium, it cannot multiply itself in specific likeness. Thus, **A** intends to produce **G**; and since it cannot accomplish this without ascending into **D**, it ascends into **D** to reach its goal. **D**, the existing tree, seeing that it can only preserve itself in a similar tree, intends **K**; but it cannot reach **K** without **G**, therefore it descends into **G** so that by its mediation it might reach **K**. Thus, a double appetite is joined in **A**: the natural appetite which ends in **G**, and the accidental appetite which ends in **K**. Likewise in **D**, a double appetite is joined: the natural which finds its end in **K**, and the accidental which ends in **G**. Therefore, the quaternary (four) moves the appetite, with one appetite stimulating the other, so that there is a certain continuation of generation and a succession of corruption.

However, the Egyptians explain this discourse—which we have proposed in the Scholastic manner—allegorically as follows: **Osiris** is the moisture, **Isis** is the earth with which Osiris is mixed, from which **Horus**, the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"</note> nourishing and fertilizing all things, is born from the seed. **Isis** resuscitates **Horus** from the lower regions when the seed committed to the earth sprouts into a plant, tree, leaves, flowers, and fruits. But with the scorching power and dryness of **Typhon** <note>Typhon represents the destructive, drying heat of the sun or desert that withers vegetation.</note> lying in wait for **Horus**, which happens in the Autumn season, **Horus** is slain by **Typhon**—that is, the falling fruit provides a new sowing. This, hidden in the earth, is once again restored by **Isis** through the industry of **Anubis**, that is, the Mercurial skill of the Farmer <note>Anubis is here linked to Mercury (Hermes), representing the cleverness and labor of agriculture.</note>. By this likeness, they speak not only of the vicissitude of the generation and corruption of things exerting itself in the vegetable seed, but also in the sensible, and even in the rational and...

<header>BOOK IV. IDEAS</header>

<margin>What is the rational tree?</margin>
...they reasoned symbolically in an intellectual manner. For from the seed of wonder, the **rational tree** arises, which bears fruit similar to wonder; indeed, through the wonder it elicits, it raises a similar tree of reason. Thus, from the seminal principle of demonstration, the intellectual tree proceeds, putting forth seminal principles from itself, through which an intellectual tree rises again. From all these things—narrated perhaps more extensively than was proper—it is clear by what subtle reasoning they indicated the change of generable things <note>The "change of generable things" refers to the constant cycle of birth, growth, and decay in the physical world.</note>, even under this most humble **three-lined letter** <note>original: "trigráma litera"; likely referring to a symbol like the 'Y' or a three-pronged figure representing the branching of paths or the stages of growth.</note>; and how that **world spirit** <note>The "spiritus mundanus" or World Spirit was envisioned as a vital, animating force that links the divine realm to the material world.</note> lurking in the seeds of all things gradually ascends and descends, so that it may ascend again, instilling the generative principles into each and every thing; thus the world is preserved in its being, which would not happen at all without this cycle.

### §. IV.
## On the Triangle, Square, etc.

<margin>
What the equilateral, isosceles, and scalene triangles signify
</margin>
Having now explained the mystical progression of angular lines, it remains for us to reason in the same way about the symbols of polygons. The Egyptians, therefore, secretly indicated the generation of things through lines, angles, and figures: thus, they considered the progression of the **world spirit** according to the generation of shapes and bodies resulting from points, lines, and surfaces. This spirit, unfolded from the point of its unity—or center—first forms something angular in the lower world; then, returning from here as it permeates all the bodies of the world, it seems to describe innumerable figures by a kind of reflected <note>original: "anacamptico"; a term derived from Greek meaning a "bending back" or reflection, often used in optics.</note> and varied motion of radiation. The first of these is the triangle, which is three-fold: either equilateral, isosceles, or scalene. And first indeed, it was shown extensively in Book V, Interpretation I of the *Schematismus*, that the **equilateral triangle** was a symbol of the Supreme Divinity diffused into the sensible, elemental world; let us now see what they thought of the Isosceles and the Scalene. Proclus, in his *Commentary on Euclid*, writes according to the mind of Pythagoras and Plato that the first triangular figure is a sign and image of the **constriction** <note>original: "coarctationis"; here implying the way divine power "binds" or "squeezes" disparate elements together into a single form.</note> inherent in divine things, and the principle of order which collects divided things into one, partible things into an impartible nature, and joins many things into a community. Therefore, the angular junctions of figures are called **nodes** <note>original: "nodos"; literally "knots."</note> by the oracles, because they are images of the binding unions and divine conjunctions through which things that are naturally distinct cling to one another. Next, he adds that those angles seen on surfaces express the unions of things themselves in a way that is more immaterial, simpler, and more perfect. But those found in solids now progress toward lower things, providing a community for more disjointed things and a union of the same nature to things that are entirely divisible. Again, of those angles on surfaces, some depict the primary forms of these things and mixed forms, while others...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of symbolic geometry from page 388, specifically exploring how different types of angles and triangles represent divine providence and the physical elements in the thought of Pythagoras, Plato, and Proclus.</meta>

<page-num>389</page-num>
<header>HIEROGLYPHICS.</header>

...which embrace the infinity of progressions existing within them. Some unite "intelligent forms," such as those pertaining to circles; others are adapted to sensible <note>In this context, "sensible" refers to things that can be perceived by the senses (the physical world) rather than "reasonable."</note> things and provide the conjunction of the reasons <note>original: "rationum"; here referring to the underlying mathematical ratios or principles.</note> existing within them, such as the rectilinear; others are mixed, joining those which occupy a middle place between the former and the latter. These points lead us to understand why Alcinous <note>Alcinous was a Middle Platonist philosopher who summarized Plato's teachings.</note>, following Plato, takes for the principles of the elements—which are the primary sensible bodies—only those angles which are seen in planes and consist of straight lines.

<margin>To whom the right angle is sacred.</margin>
Since there are three species of rectilinear angles—the right, the obtuse, and the acute—Pythagoras consecrates the **right angles** to the pure and immaculate Gods. He views them as the Authors of divine providence, by which lower things are ruled, because right angles are all similar and identical to one another.

<margin>What acute and obtuse angles denote.</margin>
But because **acute and obtuse angles** are distinguished by the inequality of being "greater" or "lesser," and because they possess an infinite motion according to these very qualities, the Pythagoreans refer them to the Gods of progression and motion. These deities are said to bestow various faculties upon the things constituted by nature. This also explains why Plato, in the triangles first constituting the elements, especially favored the right angle, yet could not explain its origin without the obtuse and acute.

<margin>Proclus.</margin>
For as the same Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on geometry and theology.</note> says, the **obtuse angle** bestows universal substance upon the elements, and its ratio increases material forms into magnitude and into every kind of change; the **acute angle**, however, makes their nature divisible. He adds further that, for this reason, the **equilateral triangle** among triangles—as it is of an immutable essence—is the best of all, and is most closely related to the circle and to divine souls by its equality and simplicity. Since, he says, "equality is the measure of the unequal," just as divinity is the measure of all lower things, it is clear why Plato did not use the equilateral triangle in the first principles of the elements, and why we said above that it is the symbol of God diffused into the sensible world. Hence the cited Proclus, following the opinion of the Pythagoreans, was content with the triangle in explaining the causes of the primary bodies, so that he might teach that it is the principle of the origin and conformation of all things.

The Pythagorean Philolaus <note>Philolaus was a contemporary of Socrates and a key figure in Pythagorean thought.</note>, observing these things diligently, is said to have consecrated the angle of the triangle to four Gods: **Saturn, Pluto, Mars, and Bacchus**. Through these, he encompassed the adornment of the four elements, which proceeds from heaven itself or from the four segments of the Zodiac; for Saturn constitutes the moist and cold essence; Mars the burning; Pluto the earthy; and Bacchus the moist and warm.

<margin>The angle of the triangle dedicated to 4 Gods.</margin>
However, since we have pursued all these matters most extensively in Book V, in the interpretation of Figure 1, the Reader may refer there so that we are not forced to repeat the same things so often. There, one will find the genesis of the five **regular bodies** <note>Also known as the "Platonic Solids."</note>, which are the symbol of the formation of the elementary bodies, perfectly demonstrated.

### BOOK IV. ON IDEAS

...they held, they received into the register of hieroglyphics. These are of various kinds: some served as symbolic head ornaments for sacred statues, such as *tutuli* <note>original: "tutuli"; a conical hairstyle or hat often worn by Roman priests</note>, *struppi* <note>original: "struppi"; garlands or headbands used in religious ceremonies</note>, *cidares* <note>original: "cidares"; a type of ancient Persian or Armenian head-dress</note>, and tiaras, made of various materials. Some were carried in the hands of the Gods, such as staffs, scepters, the tautic character <note>original: "tauticus character"; a reference to the Ankh symbol, which Kircher identifies with the letter "Tau"</note>, *sistra* <note>original: "sistra"; ancient Egyptian rattles used in the worship of Isis</note>, and innumerable others; which, according to the diversity of the Divinities, were also made of different materials. Regarding these, see the sacred symbolism <note>original: "hierogrammatismum"</note> of plants, in the section concerning scepters and the *thyrsus* <note>original: "thyrso"; a wand or staff topped with a pine cone, carried by Dionysus and his followers</note>. There were, moreover, various forms of seats <note>refers to thrones or ceremonial chairs</note> upon which the sitting Divinities, as if endowed with supreme power, seemed to rule over things. The mystical reasons for all of these will be explained in Book V in their proper places, so that I have therefore thought it superfluous to attach specific descriptions of these symbols in this place.

<margin>What the kyriological symbols are.</margin>
Finally, those are called **Kyriological** <note>original: "Kyriologica"; from the Greek "kyrios" (proper/standard), referring to signs that represent the physical object literally rather than metaphorically</note> hieroglyphics which are appropriated to the things themselves. Thus, when they were about to express the Sun and Moon, they painted a circle or a segment of a circle; if a gate, the figure of a gate; if a chain, a chain; if a sacred mixing bowl <note>original: "craterem"</note>, a mixing bowl; if the enclosure of Apis <note>The sacred bull of ancient Egyptian religion</note>, an enclosure; if a sacred bier, a bier; if a sacred bar <note>original: "barram"; likely a bolt or ceremonial rod</note>, a bar. The same judgment must be made concerning innumerable other figures which occur everywhere both on this our obelisk and on others.

However, let no one persuade himself that they employed such similar things without mysteries. For since they flourished with the greatest genius, they exhibited even individual things—the smallest and most common—with such mysterious subtlety that one ignorant of the matters might perceive indeed the literal meaning of the thing, the bare husk <note>original: "nudumque corticem"</note>, but would by no means look through to the kernel, or the mystical reasons. For even if they exhibited the Sun through a circle, they nevertheless displayed, under the various properties of the circle, various excellences and prerogatives of the Solar Divinity <note>original: "Solaris Numinis"</note>, known only to the initiates <note>original: "mystis"</note>. In this way, not content with the bare figure of those gates through which access to the sacred sanctuaries <note>original: "adyta"</note> was opened, they formed them with an architecture full of mysteries. The same must be thought of the chain, the bier, the bar, the mixing bowl, and the receptacle of sacred water <note>original: "sacræ lymphæ"</note>. Concerning all of which, as I have said, a more copious matter for discussion will be given in the following proper places. And these are the things which I thought should be briefly touched upon concerning hieroglyphic ideas.

### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'P' showing a woman in classical robes leaning against a stone pedestal, set against a background of swirling vines and leaves.</image-desc>

*AFTER the laborious comparison of the materials presented in the preceding books, we at last begin the actual interpretation of the Hieroglyphics arranged in order on the Obelisk, under the happy auspices of the divine Will. In this task, we shall so occupy ourselves through the grace of the same divine Father of Lights <note>original: "Patris luminum"; a biblical reference to God as the source of all knowledge</note> that we shall leave nothing, however small or meager, without explanation; and once explained, we shall confirm it with appropriate authorities drawn from every branch of learning. The reader will indeed discover by the facts themselves that I have not indulged in mere conjectures, as some might imagine, but that I have, if I am not mistaken, so successfully combined this doctrine of the Egyptians—drawn from the monuments of the most approved ancient authors—and so connected what had been scattered by the passage of time, that I seem to have restored that chain of hieroglyphic context so long desired. Furthermore, since the context of hieroglyphic literature is "ideal" <note>Kircher means "ideal" in the sense of communicating pure ideas or concepts directly, rather than phonetically</note> and involves the entire meaning of either natural or divine matters, let no one here expect that type of reading which arises from the joining of letters into words and sentences. Instead, let him contemplate the corresponding reading <note>original: "ανάγνωσιν" (anagnōsin); Greek for "reading" or "interpretation"</note> which indicates the hidden meanings of the Egyptians lying hidden under symbolic coverings. All these things will become clearly manifest to the curious reader from what follows.*

*We have established the interpretation in this manner: First, we express each sacred mark <note>original: "hierogrammata"; sacred carvings or symbols</note> as they occur in order by their names; we indicate the actions of the figures or the transformations of the images; then we add the mystical significations of each, which we confirm from approved authors in such a way that, if there is any place for human faith, the reader will have no doubt regarding the knowledge of the truth.*

<page-num>392</page-num>

<header>BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK</header>

*As for those matters which, because of their multiple meanings, required a greater explanation, we have explained them at length in our own Hierogrammatisms <note>original: "Hierogrammatismus"; Kircher's term for sacred symbolic diagrams or priestly writings</note>, to which we refer the reader, lest he become confused by the sheer quantity of material and lose the thread of the context.*

*To these, finally, we apply the method of "ideal reading" <note>An "ideal" reading refers to Kircher's belief that hieroglyphs represent complex Neoplatonic concepts rather than phonetic sounds</note> to each of the arrangements. And so the reader may know how the reading of the context corresponds to the figures, we have marked individual hieroglyphs with their own numbers or letters; we have placed these same numbers and letters next to the corresponding words, names, and sentences in the reading of the text. Furthermore, we have placed these at the beginning of the explanation of each item, so that we might not seem to have omitted anything necessary for communicating the knowledge of these most obscure matters clearly, sincerely, and faithfully.*

*One must know, however, that the vastness and scope of this hieroglyphic doctrine is so great that if we had wished to discuss the reasons for every detail and the inner secrets of these most hidden sciences, not even three volumes would have sufficed to properly complete the interpretation of this single Obelisk. Therefore, having set aside the rituals, ceremonies, and various methods of divining and healing through such symbols, and a more extensive explanation, we have decided to present here only the intent of the Egyptians regarding the meanings of this Obelisk's literary context through appropriate authorities, reserving a more extensive interpretation of each for our Oedipus <note>original: "Oedipo"; referring to his monumental work "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he attempted a universal decoding of Egyptian lore</note>.*

*But if at times we bring forward the reasoning behind the dogmas of the Ancient Egyptians, I would not want the reader to persuade himself that I subscribe to their views or approve of them by my own judgment. Rather, as befits an interpreter, I set aside such things and aim only for the meaning of the latent truth. These are the things of which we first wanted the reader to be warned. Nothing remains, therefore, except to set our hands to the work we have undertaken.*

# CHAPTER I.

## The Articulation or Anatomy of the Pamphilian Obelisk.

->that is,<-

## On the various division and composition of the hieroglyphs contained on the Pamphilian Obelisk.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central vessel or lamp flanked by scrolling floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>THE EGYPTIANS, excelling in intellect and taught and led by long experience of things, used symbols composed of several parts—rather than just simple ones—to represent the vast number of their mysteries in various ways. It seemed right to explain the variety of these in this chapter, so that the goal of our intended interpretation might be more clearly recognized. There are, therefore, various symbols on this Obelisk, shown according to the various meanings of hidden things, which we divide into four classes. The first class consists of things pertaining to the condition of animal nature; for they are either human likenesses, notable for the structure of the human form, some of which

<meta>This page follows page 392, where Kircher described his methodology for reading the Pamphilian Obelisk. Here, he begins the formal classification of the hieroglyphic symbols into four distinct categories based on their form: natural animals, composite/multiform creatures, individual body parts, and plants/tools.</meta>

# INTERPRETATION

Some symbols vary by position, some by gesture; others by dress and ornaments, namely the *tutuli* <term>tutuli: high-piled hairstyles or ceremonial hats worn by priests</term>, *struppi* <term>struppi: ritual headbands or wreaths</term>, crowns, and *epomides* <term>epomides: shoulder-bands or vestments</term>; they are distinguished by every kind of garment and various tools. Furthermore, there are four-legged animals; such as the Ox, Lion, Dog, Cat, Long-tailed Monkey, He-goat, and Ram, all adorned with various gestures, positions, and ornaments. Among the birds are the Falcon, Ibis, Guinea-fowl (or Pharaoh’s Hen), Dove, Hoopoe, Heron, Owl, Vulture, Goose, Crow, Swallow, and Quail. Among the water-dwellers are the *Phagrus* <term>phagrus: a species of sea-bream or similar fish associated with the Nile</term> and the *Oxyrhynchus* <term>oxyrhynchus: a sacred sharp-snouted fish famous in Egyptian myth</term>; among the amphibians, the Crocodile and Hippopotamus. Then follow the insects: the Asp, the *Cerastes* <term>cerastes: a horned viper</term>, the serpent conspicuous for its horns, various serpent figures, and the "dragon-shaped" <note>original: "δρακοντόμορφος"</note> Beetle or the Fly of the Nile. We will provide the interpretation of these shortly.

<margin>II. Class of Hieroglyphs</margin>
The second class is the "multiformity" <note>original: "πολυμόρφωσις"</note> of the aforementioned things, or the arrangement of things transformed in various ways; here we behold with wonder a human joined with any of the said animals, pressed together as if into one. Thus the whole emerges as entirely multiform <note>original: "πολυμορφος"</note>—at one moment threatening in human form with a falcon's face, now deformed with the face of an ibis, then ridiculous in the form of a goat, and immediately showing himself formidable with a lion's maw. At times he appears "human-faced" <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπρόσωπος"</note>, or with only the head and face being human, while the rest of the body is substituted by that of an Ibis, falcon, lion, cat, scorpion, or beetle. Therefore, I am not surprised that Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman historian who recorded the appearance of obelisks in Rome but admitted he did not fully understand their symbolic language</note>, ignorant of the mysteries hidden beneath them, thought the Obelisks were filled with animals of this kind because of their excessive transformation, as if they were taken from another world. Nor does transformation take place only in the head and body of different animals joined into one; but sometimes human arms are given to birds, or the claws of insects, as can be seen in the hieroglyph of the fourth side near the end, where a Falcon is seen ridiculously transformed with one wing, one human arm, and the claw of a beetle.

<margin>III. Class</margin>
The third class is the "Articulated" <term>arthrotica: from the Greek 'arthron', meaning joints or limbs; referring here to isolated body parts</term>, that is, the various members of the human body or even of other animals shown separately from the rest of the body, exhibiting differences in position, gesture, and dress. You may often see a human head variously adorned; an arm, sometimes closed, sometimes open, now equipped with other objects; feet, sometimes single, sometimes separate, sometimes joined with some other thing. Eyes are also not lacking on this Obelisk, now shining upon a scepter, now on a leaf of the *persea* <term>persea: a sacred Egyptian fruit tree, often associated with the heart or the sun</term>, and sometimes inserted into a phallus. The "eye-shaped" <note>original: "ὀφθαλμόμορφος"</note> phallus or human male organ is frequent. From the remaining bodies of animals, you may similarly see heads by themselves—such as those of the lion, ram, cat, and ox—or thighs and feet being placed; from the birds, sometimes heads, sometimes feathers or wings, now one, now a pair, sometimes feet, likewise either one or two, sometimes separate, sometimes joined, which they used to secretly denote their sacred mysteries—a practice they also observed with Insects.

<margin>IV. Class</margin>
The fourth class consists of vegetable and instrumental things, fashioned with ingenious artifice. Among the vegetables, you may see here the Lotus, the "sun-delighting" <note>original: "ἡλιότερπον"</note> *persea*, the Nile reed, the *colocasia* <term>colocasia: the taro plant or Egyptian bean</term>; the water-lily, the *seriphium* <term>seriphium: likely a type of wormwood or sea-grape</term>, and other...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher categorizes the hieroglyphs of the Pamphilian Obelisk into four classes: natural animals, composite multiform figures (hybrids), isolated body parts (articulated limbs), and plants or tools. He critiques earlier historians like Ammianus Marcellinus for failing to see the hidden philosophical mysteries within these seemingly monstrous transformations.</summary>

<margin>Stones.</margin>
...and these, which will be declared in their proper place, along with flowers, fruits, and seeds; stones are also not lacking, such as Mnizuris <note>possibly a variant of a precious stone name like "minerals"</note>, Pyrope <term>pyrope: a deep red gemstone, often a type of garnet</term>, amethyst, crystal, emerald, topaz, lapis lazuli, turquoise, and onyx, with all of which they signaled diverse mysteries.

<margin>Metals.</margin>
From metallic bodies, gold, silver, lead, and iron; the meanings of all these we have learned, not from color (which is absent in the stone carvings) or from hidden individual properties, but from context and authoritative sources.

<margin>Instruments & ornaments.</margin>
From the supply of instruments, you may see here various seats, bases, sceptres, hooks, vessels, tripods, tables, staffs, cornices, and spears. From ornaments, *tutuli* <term>tutuli: ceremonial conical hats or high-piled hairstyles worn by priests</term>, mitres, *cydaris* <term>cydaris: an ancient royal headdress or tiara</term>, crowns, and veils.

<margin>Geometric figures.</margin>
From geometric figures: triangles, squares, pyramids, trapeziums, stars, *decusses* <term>decusses: figures in the shape of an X, representing the number ten or a crossing</term>, circles, spheres, and their segments, and other oval patterns. From artificial signs of "personification" <note>original: "ἰδιοποιΐας"</note> or "literal representation" <note>original: "κυριολογίας"</note>, there are figures of various letters, gates, harbors, walls, the Sun, the Moon, and similar things which, God willing, will be treated in the course of the work.

Therefore, having seen the articulation and "anatomy" of the things contained in the said Obelisk, nothing now remains but that we turn our pen to the interpretation of each one.

## CHAPTER II.
### The Subject Matter of the Pamphilian Obelisk.

Mercurius Trismegistus, a philosopher from the lineage of Canaan—shrewd, sharp-witted, and endowed with a certain divine vigor of mind—was a contemporary <note>original: "συγχρονος"</note> of Abraham. He was spurred by an immense desire for knowledge, both of natural things and especially those pertaining to the inquiry of divine notions; he left nothing undone to obtain a full and perfect knowledge of them and to entrust it to posterity.

<margin>From where the first seeds of hieroglyphic literature arose.</margin>
Since the first Patriarchs, instructed by Adam, the "first-formed" <term>protoplast: Adam, as the first created human</term> of the human race, had received by a certain continuous and successive tradition many things by word of mouth concerning the nature of GOD, the benefits bestowed and to be bestowed upon the human race, the Angels, their nature and ministry, and various offices in the "worldly economy" <term>economy: in this context, the divine administration or management of the universe</term>, the founding, structure, and fabrication of the world, and the orders, virtues, and uses of natural things.

<margin>Noah and his sons propagate the knowledge of things before the flood to posterity.</margin>
Then especially Noah <note>original: "Noëmus"</note>, the witness of both worlds <note>meaning the world before and the world after the Great Flood</note> and the future preserver of the human race, together with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, undoubtedly drank in a perfect knowledge of those things so necessary for the human race.

<margin>Mercury, participating in these same things, explains them.</margin>
Therefore, Mercury [Trismegistus], by frequent association with the sons of Noah—who were still surviving at that time—learned by word of mouth from those to whom he was closest in blood the perfect history of things done and believed immediately both before and after the flood, as has been proven at length in the first book. Then, among other things, he drank in some knowledge concerning the profound mystery of the Triune GOD, the Word of the same to be incarnated, as well as grace, nature, and other mysteries revealed by GOD to the first propagators of the world and the human race.

He argues that Egyptian wisdom originated from a direct oral tradition passed from Adam and Noah to Hermes, preserving divine truths from before the Great Flood.</summary>
