Equipped with these very tools and himself contemplating many matters, he <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-king of Egypt</note> applied his mind to recording them for posterity. Lest the memory of such remarkable things be erased by the passage of time, he followed the custom of his predecessors and carved them into the hardest stones as if to last forever. However, so that such sublime secrets would not be accessible to any common person, he wrapped them in an allegorical display of various symbols. He exposed these to the world in such a way that their deeper understanding remained only with the Priests (whom he established for this purpose) and the Leaders of the Kingdom. Furthermore, to ensure everything remained mysterious, he chose a most mysterious shape for the stones: that through this mystical form itself, the loftiness of the sacraments might be displayed. 

Following this institution, their descendants placed these stone masses everywhere in temples and sacred places. Because they imitate the form of rays, they called them the "Fingers of the Sun"—that is, of the Archetypal Divinity—and *Ambras*, which means "sacred books." <term>Ambras: Kircher's term for the obelisks as "lithic books" containing the totality of Egyptian secret knowledge.</term> The Greeks, from their shape, called them Obelisks. The symbols or letters with which they carved the sacred doctrine received from Hermes onto the stones were called "sacred letters," and later the Greeks named them "Hieroglyphics." 

In subsequent ages, they devoted themselves to this practice with such zeal that hardly any place in Egypt was free from such Obelisks. This resulted in such a great reputation for their name and wisdom that no one was considered a Philosopher among foreign nations who had not had the Egyptians as Masters—even if, as time went on, the Priests (following the decrees of the degenerate lineage of Ham, as usually happens) shrouded many things in various superstitions. <note>Kircher refers to the biblical tradition that the Egyptians descended from Ham, whose line was often associated with the origin of magic and idolatry after the Flood.</note> 

Among such Obelisks is our **Pamphilian Obelisk**, which shines above the rest in its contemplation of sublime things. Indeed, I do not know by what providence it happened that the interpretation of this Obelisk—filled with mysteries not unlike the Christian faith—should come forth, hidden for so many centuries, at the very time when a **Pamphilius** <note>A reference to Pope Innocent X, born Giovanni Battista Pamphilj, who commissioned the re-erection of this obelisk in the Piazza Navona.</note> rules the world as the Head of the Christian Religion. But before we proceed to the actual interpretation, we shall first set before the eyes of the curious Reader the general Theme of the whole work, to invite and encourage him to weigh what follows with greater attention.

<margin>
The central essence of the triform divinity, and how it generates.
</margin>

This Pamphilian Obelisk contains, first, the internal and external operations of the Triune Divinity, or the Universal Triform Soul of the World, which the Egyptians call **Hemphta**. <term>Hemphta: Kircher’s name for the supreme Egyptian deity, whom he equated with the Holy Trinity or the Platonic "World Soul."</term> It shows how that supreme Triform Divinity, before the constitution of any created thing, generated in the solitary unity of its essence the "Creator Mind," and then the "Third Mind," the life-giving spirit of all things.

<margin>
The Divinity falling into multiplicity.
</margin>

Next, it shows how this Triune Divinity, falling from its solitary unity into multiplicity, first produced the Intellectual or Angelic World, which the Egyptians call "Genial." 

<margin>
Explanation of the class of the Angelic and Genial World.
</margin>

It explains how the Divinity flows into that world continuously—as if through the most perfect and immediate patterns of the divine mind—bestowing life, motion, and power upon all lower things. Those who participate in this influx directly from the supreme deity **Hemphta** exert their influence upon the four quarters of the world (indicated by the four sides of the Obelisk). Thus, they are divided into various classes, some of whom are Rulers and Leaders, while others are ministering spirits who carry out commands...

The attraction of good spirits; the repelling of evil.

The Obelisk beautifully teaches by what analogous things—drawn from every class of natural objects—the Spirits of the individual parts of the world are to be attracted; by what rituals and sacrifices they are to be won over; and by what oaths, hymns, songs, and incenses they are to be lured, according to a certain analogy corresponding to the nature and property of each. It teaches how they are to be appeased for the good of the world if they should ever be angry, and how they are to be urged to provide for our well-being. Finally, it shows how the harmful power of adverse Spirits is to be restrained and driven back. It also contains the medicines with which the evils of encroaching sicknesses and diseases—sent by adverse Spirits—are to be cured, and by what preventative measures they may be turned away. Since it is often necessary to know the outcomes of future events, whether to avoid evils or to acquire good things, this Obelisk teaches how the science of prophecy is obtained through dreams, through omens <note>augury: the ancient practice of interpreting the will of the gods from the flight or songs of birds</note>, and through various and manifold types of divination. It teaches what diet, clothing, and posture should be used in religious business and the performance of sacred rites to obtain similar results from the supreme Divinity and the Spirits.

Superstitions.

It shows how each of these Spirits is to be worshipped and invoked in the inner sanctuaries <note>adytis isiacis: the most secret, holy chambers of the temples dedicated to the goddess Isis</note>; with what ceremonies and exorcisms (hidden under a complex allegory of fables) they should be called upon; and from what material they should construct consecrated statues <note>original Greek: *τετελεσμένας* (tetelesmenas), meaning "consecrated" or "perfected" objects</note>—which the Greeks now call *talismata* <note>talismans</note> and sometimes *stoicheia* <note>original Greek: *στοιχεῖα*, meaning "elements" or "elementary spirits"</note>, and the Arabs call *Talleshmath*. And this is the summary of the matters contained in the present Obelisk. All these things are presented within an ingenious architecture of symbols, some of which reveal excellent mysteries in both Theology and natural philosophy; while others are entangled in magical and superstitious arts, such as...

# CHAPTER III.
## Division of the Interpretation of the Pamphilian Obelisk.

We finally approach, with the help of the good God, that which we intended from the beginning: namely, the actual interpretation of the entire Obelisk. This task is as arduous and difficult, and truly a work of profound speculation and most sublime construction, as it seemed to demand deep foundations by its own right. Indeed, everything we have laboriously produced throughout this entire work by means of the "fourfold apparatus" <note>This refers to the four preliminary books or sections of Kircher's work that laid the theoretical groundwork</note> seems to aim toward this single goal of an exact interpretation. To proceed methodically in such an intricate business, we shall dissect the entire Obelisk into twenty-four Schematisms <term>Schematism: A complex symbolic arrangement or diagram representing a specific concept</term> or, what is the same thing, divide each side into six parts; each of these is again divided into six other hierogrammatisms <term>Hierogrammatism: A specific grouping or 'sentence' of hieroglyphs</term>. Thus, each Schematism, explained in order, might more perfectly and clearly place the subject of the entire Obelisk before the eyes of the curious Reader. <margin>Division of the Obelisk into 24 Schematisms, each of which contains 6 other hierogrammatisms.</margin> By "schematism," we mean a certain collection of either hierograms or hierogrammatisms; by "hierogram," a simple hieroglyphic letter; and by "hierogrammatism," a hieroglyphic composition forged from various symbols. We wished to establish these first so that you might not be confused by the multitude of terms. And first, for each schematism, we will propose the simple meaning of the entire ideal concept; then, we will add scholia <note>original: *scholia* — explanatory notes or commentaries</note> to confirm the reading with the proper authorities. And lest the thread of the interpretation be interrupted by the multitude and abundance of things to be said and authorities cited, having omitted the longer [citations] here...

### CHAPTER III. BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

We refer the eager reader to the authorities cited copiously in the preceding pages. For we trust that by doing so, the truth of the matters demonstrated will be more clearly revealed; but in order that the logic of the **ideal concept** <term>Ideal concept: Kircher’s term for the mental image or spiritual reality that a symbol represents, rather than just a literal word</term>, and the multitude and variety of things signified may be more deeply scrutinized by the wise, we shall temper physical interpretations with **anagogical** ones <term>Anagogical: A method of interpretation that finds hidden spiritual or mystical meanings leading the mind toward divine things</term>, and these with moral, magical, and mystical interpretations **according to analogy** <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν (*kata tēn analogian*)</note> and allegorical mysteries. In this way, the intention and scope of the ancient priests may be more precisely discerned even from this chapter, along with the vast collection of knowledge and sciences they indicated under a few symbols. Furthermore, the Obelisk consists of four sides so arranged that each corresponds to a specific side of the world, following secret reasons to be disclosed shortly. Thus, side **A** corresponds to the **Eastern** region; **B** to the **Southern**; **C** to the **Western**; and **D** to the **Northern**. Each side exactly corresponds to the **Genii** <note>Genii: Guardian spirits or presiding deities believed by the ancients to govern specific geographic directions</note> presiding over those regions, both to appease them and to attract common or private benefits through similar things, as was stated in the argument. But leaving aside verbal ambiguities, let us approach the matter itself directly. While we do this, let no one imagine that this hieroglyphic writing is performed in the same way as our usual writing composed of alphabetic letters, syllables, words, and syntax; rather, since this is a **symbolic writing of ideal concepts**, it must be presented to the reader’s mind through an **ideal reading**. In reading these, to speak with **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus: A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>: *discard the words, receive the meanings.* See what we have treated extensively regarding the nature of this in Book 2 on the symbolic writing of the Egyptians.

<margin>What does the circle or globe signify?</margin>

By the globe or sphere—according to the testimony of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus: A legendary figure often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of sacred texts on philosophy, medicine, and magic</note>—they signified that immense, incomprehensible, supra-mundane, and **archetypal** circle. That is, they represented that eternal and immense essence of **GOD**, defined by no limits, pure and simple, which Trismegistus calls at times the Father, at times the First Mind, and at other times the Supreme Intellect.

<margin>Asclepius <note>original: *Asclep.*; referring to the *Asclepius*, a famous Hermetic dialogue</note></margin>
<margin>What is meant by the wings.</margin>
By the serpent emerging from the globe, they signified the fruitful nature of God, or a certain form existing within and coexisting with God that gives life and soul to all things. Trismegistus calls this the **Word** <note>original: *Verbum*</note>; Plato calls it the **Mind** <note>original: *Mentem*</note>, the **Maker** <term>Maker: Referring to the *Demiurge* or Divine Craftsman in Platonic philosophy who shapes the material world</term>. By the wings, however, they signified the motive power within God, or a certain penetrative form of all things, which Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus: A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy</note> calls the **Spirit of the World** <note>original: *Spiritum mundi*</note> and Trismegistus calls **Love**; Plotinus called it the **Third Mind**, while others called it by other names. We have, therefore, in the threefold deity **Hemphta** <note>Hemphta: A name Kircher uses for a primary Egyptian creator deity, often associated with Kneph or Phtha, representing the divine breath or spirit</note>, a meaning explained by a secret logic through this threefold symbol. It remains for us to establish such a wondrous philosophy with appropriate authorities; so that this may be done as well as possible, let us begin this matter, so worthy of consideration, from a slightly deeper point.

<margin>Mercurius Trismegistus, author of the hieroglyphic discipline.</margin>
<margin>What is contained on the Obelisks.</margin>
Mercurius Trismegistus was the first author and founder of the hieroglyphic discipline, as we have shown extensively in the first and second books. Since he had received the highest mysteries of the Divinity from the primeval Patriarchs of the world before the flood (among which, without a doubt, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity and the mystery of the Incarnate Word held the chief place), he was wonderfully—as he was most gifted—swept away by a certain weight into divine contemplations of this kind. Journeying to Egypt (where these divine mysteries, already made public by Ham <note>Ham: The son of Noah; in Kircher’s chronology, Ham’s descendants brought corrupted versions of antediluvian wisdom to Egypt</note> and contaminated and corrupted in many various ways, were degenerating into an obvious nursery of superstitions), he spread his teachings far and wide. However, so that traditions of such great importance might survive for posterity and be propagated without contamination according to the pure tradition of the Fathers, and so that the mysteries might remain accessible only to the Wise and the Priests—safe from the dim intellect of the common people—he designed this hieroglyphic literature. This system proposed to posterity (as we have taught elsewhere) reasonings about the wondrous properties of the Divine nature, about the production of the world through it, and the nature of things by the art of God, about Angels and Spirits, and similar difficult and sublime Sacraments, all covered in ingenious symbols and carved into stones against every injury of time. # CHAPTER III. 400 BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK

This established the system of order and the dogmas discovered by Mercury <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Thoth, often called Hermes Trismegistus</note> as if by a Divine genius. These doctrines, propagated through all time, provided the occasion and custom for Obelisks, which were distinguished by this manifold exhibition of learning. Thus, there was no Obelisk that was not marked by his teaching, of which our Pamphylian Obelisk here was one. In it, the secrets of the more hidden Theology and Philosophy of the Ancients are so graphically displayed that they seem to be sketched not by Pagans, but by orthodox Teachers. Indeed, posterity could never have devised such sublime things unless they were equal in genius to Hermes; as **Abenvašchia** <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century scholar known for his work on ancient scripts and Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> well notes in his book on the *Worship of the Egyptians* in these words:

<margin>Abenvašchia on the worship of the Egyptians.</margin>
*Truly, many of the people of this Region are ignorant of what such enigmas signify; and this is because the natives did not consecrate them, but a certain man once withdrew to us from the land of Canaan. He was eminent in Wisdom, and in Grammar, Geometry, Music, Arithmetic, Philosophy, and the rest of the designated sciences, which those who note the disciplines call "teachings"; and he offered these figures as a gift, that they might be sacred to God.* But with these warnings, let us now proceed to the proof of individual points.

<margin>The Essence of GOD is denoted by a circle.</margin>
<margin>Hermes.</margin>
<margin>Egyptian Theology according to Aristotle.</margin>
**Trismegistus** showed in plain words that the Essence of **GOD** is denoted by a circle. Defining **GOD**, he said He is an intellectual circle, *whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere*; since He can by no means be open to the senses, he placed the circle, or sensible sphere, as an indicator of the given definition. It is as if he were saying that the intrinsic essence and nature of **GOD**, though indivisible, nevertheless exceeds all spaces that can be conceived by the mind by the extension of His infinite magnitude. He said the circumference is nowhere—that is, circumscribed by no limits—yet he called it a circle because of the actions of the divine mind, which are analogous to the properties of a circle. All these things are beautifully explained by the *Theology of the Egyptians*, which Plato published in speech and Aristotle in writings <note>Kircher refers to the "Theology of Aristotle," a Neo-Platonic text long misattributed to Aristotle</note>, and which some thereafter wish to have been produced by Numenius. For thus he says in book 4, chapter 4: *The Intellect (namely the first) is the center of a circle, which contains whatever of angles, sides, lines, surfaces, and other imaginable things exists in the circle itself and other figures; but it is itself indivisible and <term>amerès</term> <note>original: ἀμερὲς; meaning "without parts" or "indivisible"</note>, and all the lines of the circle flow from it and flow back to it; therefore it is called the center.* And in the *Pimander* <note>The first book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note>, Hermes asserts that God is moved in circles. And on page 29 of the Basel edition: *Mind and reason, embracing itself, free from all bodily mass, impassive, intangible, assisting itself, purifying and preserving all things, whose rays are the good, the principal light, and the primary form of souls.* Plato seems to have alluded to this when he said: *God always measures by circles.* <note>original Greek: Θεὸν ἀεὶ κυκλομετρεῖν</note>

INTERPRETATION. 401 CHAP. III.

...if any other material thing could, the eternal essence of GOD—restricted by no limits and the first form of the Divinity (to speak in the Egyptian manner)—is most appropriately and properly expressed here. <margin>The serpent denotes the second form of the divinity.</margin>
<margin>The serpent is a most lively animal.</margin>
<margin>Epies, according to Eusebius.</margin>
<margin>Pherecydes, according to Eusebius.</margin>
There follows the Serpent, which emerges from the sphere. By this truly remarkable symbol, the second form of the Divinity is expressed, and it denotes the fecundity of GOD. For just as the serpent—according to the Egyptian beliefs—is born partly without seed from rot (that is, from itself) and partly from the mixing of both sexes, it is fertile with manifold offspring. It is, moreover, a most lively creature, and does not know how to die except by a violent killing; and when it reaches old age, as Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> testifies, it recovers its youth by the shedding of its skin. In the same way, GOD, with no other being existing before Him, necessarily exists of Himself, free from all old age, eternal, immense, and immortal. Yet He is not unfruitful; since He is the Father of all, He begets a fertile mind—not only externally in creation, but internally. Because this mind is the "harmonizing" <note>original Greek: ἁρμόζουσα (harmozousa), meaning fitting together or arranging</note> power that disposes and adapts all things, it is most appropriately expressed through the nature of the serpent. 

But let us hear from Epies, as cited in Eusebius, book one, chapter seven: <note>original Greek: Τὸ πρῶτον θειότατον ὄφις ἐστὶ... translated as: "The most divine animal is the serpent, having the form of a hawk, very pleasant; if it raised its eyelids, it filled its entire first-born region with light; but when it kept its eyes closed, darkness was poured out."</note> *He says the serpent is a most divine animal, having the form of a hawk and being very pleasant; if it raised its eyelids, it filled its entire first-born region with light; but when it kept its eyes closed, darkness was poured out.* Hence Epies said that its fiery nature was handed down by the Phoenicians. What else is meant by the Hawk-form but the "First Mind," and by the serpent but the "Second Mind" begotten from the First Mind? See the wonderful things Pherecydes tells of this Ophionean <note>Serpent-like</note> GOD in the cited passage of Eusebius. 

Furthermore, Horus indicates in Book 1, Chapter 2, near the end, that the providence of GOD (which the Platonists call the "Second Craftsman Mind" <note>The Demiurge, or creator-mind</note>) is indicated by the serpent in these words: <note>original Greek: Τὸ δὲ ὡς τροφῇ χρῆσθαι... translated as: "The fact that the serpent uses its own body as food signifies that whatever things are generated in the world by divine providence return again into it and undergo a reduction into the same source."</note> *The fact that the serpent uses its own body as food signifies that whatever things are generated in the world by divine providence return again into it and are resolved back into the same.* Indeed, see more regarding the serpent in its own specific hierogrammatism on page 348.

<margin>What is the meaning of the serpent raised up by Moses?</margin>
Certainly, when Moses raised the bronze serpent in the desert as a remedy for salvation, it is believed by the common consensus of all that he was looking toward the Word Incarnate <note>Jesus Christ</note>. This he was able to know in some way, not only through revelation, but also from the tradition of the writings of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> accepted and propagated from the first Patriarchs. Since Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, especially their Theology, it is likely that such a great mystery was by no means hidden from him. Additionally, Truth Himself <note>Christ</note> called Himself a serpent in the Holy Gospel of John: *As Moses lifted up the serpent, etc.* and perhaps the double nature <note>Divine and Human</note> in the Incarnate Word is indicated by the double head of the serpent—but this is my own conjecture, which Clement [of Alexandria] supports in Book 6 of the *Stromata*, which we cite elsewhere. Thus, the serpent appropriately represents the Craftsman Mind of GOD, the se-

### CHAPTER III. 402 BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

<margin>Horus.</margin>
...the second form of the divinity was signified according to the Egyptians, in which all the ideas of seminal reasons are coiled up. These, as Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a late antique work on hieroglyphs</note> testifies in Book 1, Chapter 2, they indicated quite appropriately through a **serpent** marked with various scales, like the stars that serve as signs for astral ideas.

<margin>What is the winged globe?</margin>
Thirdly, through the **wings of a Hawk** attached to a globe, they beautifully indicate the third form of the Divinity. The Platonists call this sometimes the "spirit of the universe" and sometimes the "soul of the world." This is nothing other than the penetrating power of the whole, and the movement of the Divinity into the sensible and material <term>hylæos; matter-based</term> worlds. Thus says Abenephius:

<margin>Abenephius the Arab.</margin>
<note>original Arabic: وبصورة الدايرة دي جناحان البزي كانوا يدلون علي الروح الدنية</note>
And by the figure of the circle provided with two hawk wings, they denoted the divine spirit.

<margin>What do the two wings on the head of Saturn mean?</margin>
Since, according to the testimony of Sanchuniathon <note>A Phoenician author whose works survive only in fragments quoted by others</note>, Saturn is nothing other to the Phoenicians than the spirit permeating the whole world, they fashioned two wings upon his head. This alluded to the present Egyptian hieroglyph, which Eusebius reports to be as follows:

<margin>Eusebius, Book 1, Ch. 7, near the end.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κείνῳ τὸ πάλιν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς πτέρα δύο, ἓν ἐπὶ τῷ ἡγεμονικωτάτῳ νῷ, ἓν ἐπὶ τῇ αἰσθήσει.</note>
To Saturn, moreover, there were two wings around the head, one of which denoted the sovereignty of the mind, and the other, sensation. Furthermore, they did not take the wings of just any bird for this purpose, but those of a hawk, which is not without mystery;

<margin>The Hawk is **bainthi** in the Egyptian language.</margin>
for we have said in the preceding pages that the name of the Hawk, **bainthi**, in the Egyptian language is composed of two words, **bai** and **ethi**. The first of these signified "soul," and the other "heart." By this, they secretly hinted that just as the soul resides chiefly in the heart—the center of the vital faculty—so too does the Soul of the World reside chiefly in the Sun, as if in the heart of the mundane fabric. From there, it exercises its powers everywhere through movement, as if by flight, reaching all things that exist in the world.

<margin>What are the winged sphinxes in the temples?</margin>
For this reason, the Egyptians placed sphinx figures everywhere in their temples, being winged creatures <note>original Greek: πτερόμορφα (pteromorpha)</note>, to indicate the actions of sublime things; for as Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note> rightly says in Book 5 of the *Stromata*:

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, Book 5, *Stromata*.</margin>
> *The face indeed is a symbol of the intellectual soul. The wings, however, are the ministries and sublime operations of the powers on the right and the left; together they hint at the supreme intellect lying hidden beneath a cloud, difficult to find, and ineffable in its power.*

So also Porphyry in Book 4 of *On Abstinence*: <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν πτερῶν φύσις ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ κεῖται διὰ τὸ δυσέρετον & κεκρυμμένον</note> *The nature of the wings consists upon the head because God is difficult to find and hidden.* For this same reason, Moses also placed the **Cherubim** as winged beings; he did so only to indicate the secret and most sublime reasons of the incomprehensible GOD, and to demonstrate the swiftest speed of the actions which He executes through the readiness of His ministers—conforming in all things to the will of the supreme Deity. This is the opinion of St. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> and the interpreters commenting on Exodus 25. Therefore, the wing was always a symbol of Divine motion, which Plato also beautifully handed down in the *Phaedrus*, and which is explained by Plutarch in these words:

<margin>Plutarch, in *Platonic Questions*.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πῶς πότε ἐν τῷ Φαίδρῳ λέγεται τὸ τὴν τῶν πτερῶν φύσιν, ὑφ' ἧς ἄνω τὸ ἐμβριθὲς ἀνάγεται κεκοινωνηκέναι μάλιστα τῶν περὶ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. Πότερον, ὅτι περὶ ἔρωτος ὁ λόγος ἐστὶ, κάλλοις τέ τε περὶ τὸ σῶμα ὁ ἔρως. Τὸ δὲ κάλλος ὁμοιότητι τῇ πρὸς τὰ θεῖα κινεῖ ἀναμιμνῆσκον τὴν ψυχὴν; ἢ μᾶλλον, οὐδὲν περίεργασίον, ἀλλ' ἁπλῶς ἀκουστέον, ὅτι τῶν περὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ψυχῆς δυνάμεων πλειόνων οὐσῶν, ἡ διαλογιστικὴ...</note>
How is it ever said in the *Phaedrus* that the nature of wings—by which that which is heavy is led upward—has shared most in the things concerning the body of God? Is it because the discourse is about love, and love is about the beauty of the body? And does beauty, by its likeness to things divine, move the soul by reminding it? Or rather, is nothing too elaborate, but it is simply to be heard, that while the powers of the soul concerning the body are many, the reasoning power...

INTERPRETATION. 403 CHAPTER III.

...the intellectual faculty has most truly participated in God. Therefore, wings grew from divine and heavenly things; for which reason they also attached wings to it, as the soul is raised up from humble and mortal things. <note>original Greek: ἡ διανοητικὴ μάλιστα τοῦ Θεοῦ κεκοινώνηκεν... This is a reference to the soul's ascent.</note> When, he says, it is stated in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul, beauty, and love</note> that the nature of the wing—by which that which is heavy is carried upward—participates most in those things which are around the body of GOD. Is it because the discourse is about love? For love is attached to the beauty of the body; and beauty, by its resemblance to divine things, moves the soul and brings things back to its memory. Or rather, without any overly complex interpretation, are the words to be taken simply? Namely, that while many faculties of the soul are occupied with the body, the power of reasoning and understanding participates most in the divine nature. Having called this power capable of divine and celestial things, he [Plato] not without reason called it a "wing," as it lifts the soul away from humble and fleeting things.

Thus the divine spirit, stirred by wings through the corporeal world, gives life to all things and excites them into its own love; by which the winged soul, having left behind the weights of earthly things, is joined to the creator, as the oracles of Zoroaster <note>The "Chaldean Oracles," ancient mystical texts attributed to the Persian sage</note> beautifully hand down, as explained at length in Book 2, Chapter 10.

We have, therefore, a triple form of divinity exhibited in a single <term>ophio-cyclo-pteromorphous; having the form of a serpent, a circle, and wings</term> symbol; that is, one Deity displayed with a triple power. Abenephius, in his book *On the Religion of the Egyptians*, shows this shadowed in the aforementioned symbols in very clear words:

<note>original Arabic: اولئك فلما كانوا يريدون ان يخبروا علي القوه وصفة الله مثلثه...</note>
*When they wished to indicate the three divine powers or properties, they would draw a winged circle from which a serpent emerged. By the figure of the circle, they signified the nature of GOD—incomprehensible, inseparable, eternal, and devoid of any beginning or end. By the figure of the serpent, the creative power of GOD over all things; and by the figure of the two wings, the power of GOD which, through motion, gives life to all things in the world.*

I do not see what could be said more clearly than these words. A fragment of Sanchuniathon <note>A legendary Phoenician author</note> regarding the ancient religion of the Phoenicians, written in the Chaldean or Phoenician language, agrees with these in almost as many words:

<margin>Fragment of Sanchuniathon.</margin>
<note>original Syriac/Chaldean: ܗܘ ܗܘ ܐܣܦܝܪܐ ܙܒܝܐܝܬܐ ܡܢܗ ܐܪܚ ܚܘܝܐ...</note>
*Jupiter is a winged sphere; from it is produced the serpent. The circle shows the divine nature without beginning or end; the serpent shows His word which animates and makes the world fruitful; and the wings show the spirit of GOD, who gives life to the world through motion.*

From these things it clearly appears that Hermes Trismegistus <note>The "Thrice-Great Hermes," the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom</note>, the instructor of hieroglyphic literature, quite appropriately shadowed the Holy Triad, whether through revelation or tradition. He expressed this in the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, a foundational Hermetic text</note> with words far exceeding all limits of human genius: <margin>Hermes in the *Pimander*.</margin> "But Mind, being God, being both male and female, and existing as Life and Light, brought forth by a Word another Mind, the Creator." <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ νοῦς ὁ Θεὸς ἀρσενοθῆλυς ὤν ζωὴ καὶ φῶς ὑπάρχων...</note>

# CHAPTER III. BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

<margin>*Pymander*, page 13, Basel edition.</margin>
"For God is Mind, most full of the fecundity of both sexes, life and light; and with His Word, He brought forth another Creator Mind, who is indeed the God of fire and the Spirit of Divinity." All these things so aptly fit what has been handed down so far that he seems to have explained the mentioned symbol in these very words. Do you see how aptly the circle represents the Divine Mind? How beautifully he marked the offspring of the fecund God—that is, the second Mind, which he calls the Word—proceeding from the Divine mouth as life and light through the serpent? The serpent is a fecund and long-lived animal, which, according to Horapollo, consists of no other member besides its mouth: <note>original Greek: ὁ ὄφις οὐδενὶ ἑτέρῳ τῶν μελῶν ἰσχύει, εἰ μὴ τῷ σώματι μόνον. Kircher interprets this "body" as the "mouth" or "breath" in his Latin commentary.</note> "The serpent prevails in no other limb except the mouth alone." For this reason, those signifying the "mouth" <note>The breath or spirit of God</note> would paint a serpent, according to the verse: *By the Spirit of God the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their power.* Furthermore, Horapollo in Book 1, Chapter 64, shows in express words that the Spirit of God permeating all things was indicated by the serpent: <note>original Greek: Παντοκράτορα δὲ ὑπὸ τοῦ ζώου τούτου σημαίνουσι πάλιν τὴν ὁλόκληρον ὄφιν ζωγραφούντες, ἢ τὸ παρ' αὐτοῖς τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου τὸ διῆκον ἐστὶ πνεῦμα.</note> "They signify the Ruler of all things through the perfection of this same animal, again painting a complete snake; so it is among them the spirit that permeates through the universal world." Finally, how congruently they expressed the life-giving spirit of the world through the wings of a hawk; Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> seems to touch upon this with these words: <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ δημιουργὸς νοῦς σὺν τῷ λόγῳ ὁ περιέχων τοὺς κύκλους, καὶ δινῶν; ῥοίζῳ ἔστρεψε τὰ ἑαυτοῦ δημιουργήματα καὶ εἴασε στρέφεσθαι, ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἀορίστου εἰς ἀπέραντον τέλος; ἄρχεται γὰρ πῆ λήγει.</note> That is: *The Creator Mind, indeed, together with the Word, containing the circles and turning them with a celerity, revolved its own machine back toward itself, and commanded it to be turned from a beginning without beginning to an end without end; for it always begins there, where it finishes;* or as it says elsewhere: *The Monad <note>The "Unit" or "The One"</note> begat the monad, and reflected its love back into itself.* Who does not see clearly that the first Mind is signified by the circle; the Creator Word implanted in the circle by the serpent; and finally, that the life-giving spirit of the world is signified by the swift and agile wings of the hawk, which moves through the archetypal circles in its flight?

<margin>Mercury was called "Trismegistus" because he asserted a triple God.</margin>
Certainly, Mercury—a man of such admirable doctrine—was called <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>From the Greek "Tris-megistos," meaning "Thrice-Greatest."</note> (or "thrice maximum") for no other reason than that he asserted a triple God, and that he had found three greatest powers within the unity of the Divine essence. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* teaches this in these words: <note>original Greek: Ἐν τούτοις μὲν ταῦτα χρόνοις ἐβασίλευσεν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων πρῶτος ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς τοῦ Χὰμ Σεσοστρεις, ὃς ἦν Ἑρμῆς ὁ Τρισμέγιστος, ἀνὴρ φοβερὸς ἐν σοφίᾳ, ὅστις ἔφρασεν τρεῖς μεγίστας δυνάμεις εἶναι, τὸ τοῦ ἀρρήτου καὶ δημιουργοῦ Θεοῦ ὄνομα μίαν Θεότητα εἶπεν εἶναι. Διὸ καὶ ἐκλήθη ὑπὸ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων Τρισμέγιστος Ἑρμῆς.</note> 

<margin>The *Alexandrian Chronicle*.</margin>
That is: *At those times, there reigned first among the Egyptians, from the family of Ham, Sesostris* (in the version by Rader, "Sesostris" is written incorrectly, as we have shown elsewhere; it ought to be, according to the dialect, <term>Sesoostris</term>, which means "the seed of Osiris"), *a man venerable in wisdom, awesome—that is, of admirable doctrine—who asserted that there were three greatest powers, virtues, or forms in God, and stated that the name of the ineffable and creator God was one Deity; for which cause he was called by the Egyptians Mercury Thrice-Great.* Suidas also hands down these things in these words: <note>Suidas was a 10th-century Greek lexicographer. Original Greek: Ἐκέκλητο δὲ Τρισμέγιστος, διὰ τὸ περὶ Τριάδος ἐφθέγξατο εἰπὼν ἐν Τριάδι μίαν εἶναι Θεότητα· ἔπας, ἦν φῶς νοερόν, πρὸ φωτὸς νοεροῦ; καὶ ἦν ἀεὶ νοῦς νοὸς φωτεινὸς καὶ οὐδὲν ἕτερον ἦν ἢ τούτου ἑνότης, ἢ πνεῦμα πάντα περιέχον ἐκτὸς τούτου οὐ Θεός, οὐκ ἄγγελος, οὐκ οὐσία tis ἄλλη. Πάντων γὰρ κύριος, καὶ πατὴρ καὶ Θεὸς, καὶ πάντα ὑπ' αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐστὶν, ὁ γὰρ λόγος αὐτοῦ...</note>

# INTERPRETATION. CHAPTER III. PAGE 405

Being all things, and fecund, and the creator in a fecund nature. <note>original Greek: παντήιος ὤν, ϗ̓ γόνιμος, ϗ̓ δημιουργὸς ἐν γονίμῳ φύσει</note> He was called "Thrice Great" because he spoke of the <margin>God Three and One.</margin> Trinity, saying that in the Trinity **there is one Deity, thus: There was an intelligible light before the intelligible light, and there was always a Mind shining from Mind, and the unity of this was nothing other than the Spirit encompassing all things: outside of this there is no Angel, nor any other substance. For He is the Lord of all, and Father, and GOD, and all things are under Him and in Him. For His Word is most absolute, and fecund, and the Creator in a fecund nature.** What else can be gathered from this, if not the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity expressed in clear words? In this mystery, three persons (to speak in the orthodox manner) subsisting in the unity of the Divine essence and nature, denote a God who is both three and one. According to Mercury’s testimony in the *Pimander*, <note>Mercury is the Latin name for Hermes Trismegistus; the *Pimander* is his most famous philosophical work.</note> this mystery has remained hidden from the human race until this day. This is also clearly shown by that inscription cited in the third book: **I am whatever was, is, and shall be, and no mortal has yet uncovered my veil.** <note>This refers to the famous inscription at the Temple of Neith in Sais, which Kircher associates with Hermetic wisdom.</note>
<margin>*Pimander*, page 46, Basel edition.</margin> These words aptly correspond to the words of Trismegistus in the *Pimander*: **That which truly is not, You are yourself; You are all that has been born, and all that was never born; indeed, the understanding Mind, and the fabricating Father, God the effector of good, making all things good.** And on page 13: <margin>page 13.</margin> **I am that light, Mind your God; but the seed of the mind, the shining Word, is the Son of God, whose union is life.**
<margin>Whether Hermes knew the mystery by revelation, or from elsewhere?</margin> It is a matter of doubt, however, whether he possessed such great mysteries from elsewhere or from revelation. It is possible he drew some obscure principles from the first Patriarchs regarding the ineffable Name of GOD, which is mentioned here. As has been shown elsewhere, this Name was held in the highest veneration by the first Patriarchs, as is evident from the Kabbalah of the Hebrews, and it implicitly contained the mystery of the Trinity. He also shows in the *Pimander* that he partly drew this knowledge through the revelation of the "Pimander"—that is, the Word of GOD—with these words: **These things happened to me from the Mind that draws forth, that is, the Pimander, the Word of divine power; whence I myself, inspired by the divine Spirit, was made a master of the truth. Wherefore with all my strength I give thanks to God the Father.**

->***Father of all, Holy God, whose will is fulfilled by His own powers.***<-
->***Holy God, who is known to His own kin; Holy are You, who established all things by the Word; Holy are You, of whom all nature is an image; Holy are You, whom no nature ever formed; Holy are You, more powerful than all omnipotence; Holy are You, greater than all excellence; Holy are You, better than all praise, etc.***<-

He repeats ***Holy*** nine times, yet in such a way that he sings this admirable "thrice-holy" <term>Trisagion</term> <note>A standard hymn in Christian liturgy, "Holy, Holy, Holy," which Kircher finds prefigured here.</note> three times for each of the three subsistences or persons. This is more sublime than the heavenly powers, and is constituted from three triads, as will be said later, according to the oracles of Zoroaster.

Therefore, from what has been said, it is clear that Hermes Trismegistus was the first to assert the Holy Trinity, whether through tradition received from the Hebrews or through the revelation of the Pimander. He exhibited this wondrous mystery both through other symbols and especially through this "snake-circle-wing-shaped" <note>original Greek: ὀφιο-κυκλο-πτερόμορπον (ophio-kyklo-pteromorphon)</note> hieroglyph. Thus, whatever he discussed with sublime reasoning in the *Pimander* can be called a living interpretation of this symbol, as we shall declare more fully later. <margin>The Hebrews drew some knowledge of the Holy Trinity through successive tradition.</margin> I read in the Kabbalah of the Hebrews that the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity was exhibited in a not dissimilar manner, which no doubt reached our times through a continuous succession from the first Patriarchs. It is held thus in the *Jezirah*, or book...

### INTERPRETATION. CHAPTER III.

<margin>
The secret theology of the Hebrews concerning the three properties of GOD.
</margin>
...to emerge from the inaccessible abyss of the fountain of infinite light, yet in such a way that nothing is understood to emanate or proceed from it by which this most brilliant splendor of the Deity is dilated or spread, or its incomprehensible depth diminished. These three enumerations, emanations, or modes of existence are in a most unique and perfect unity, suffering no division within themselves; though by reason of their procession, one is distinguished from the other in its own order as prior or posterior, even if any of these can by no means be measured or circumscribed in itself. 

The first of these, therefore, as has been said, is called the **Supreme Crown**, and for that reason its sanctuary is called admirable or hidden; for in the contemplation of it, the minds of all go dark, tongues grow mute, every voice is silent, and the soul fails on account of its impenetrable height. This one, however, has this peculiar and proper quality: that all enumerations proceed from it, while it proceeds from no other. 

Behold the Father in Divine things, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—GOD, three in unity and one in trinity—described so graphically that nothing more clear could be said by the orthodox. Writers of mystical matters also exhibit this enclosed in a triangle within a circle, in the middle of which are three <term>Yod</term>s <note>The letter י, the first letter of the Tetragrammaton</note> with a <term>Kametz</term> <note>A Hebrew vowel mark ( ָ ) written below a letter</note> written below them, acting as indicators of the Name of GOD, as if you were to say י. י. י. *Iah, Iah, Iah* <note>A shortened form of the divine name Yahweh</note>, ONE GOD in Trinity, and three in unity. 

Although modern Hebrews, out of obstinacy, do not concede these things at all, but assert they should be taken as three attributes fitting for GOD, they are nevertheless convicted both by various places in Holy Scripture and from their own <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note>. They must confess that the Holy Trinity is precisely indicated to them here, a topic we shall discuss in the proper place in my work *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his massive study of Egyptian lore, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. Furthermore, all the Egyptian priests and philosophers who followed, and the Greeks after them, asserted this admirable philosophy of the triform Deity, held both by the Hebrews and by <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many ancient mystical texts were attributed</note>, as is evident from their writings, in which mention of a triform Deity occurs everywhere.

<margin>
The oracles of Zoroaster.
</margin>
<margin>
The Monad generates the dyad and the triad.
</margin>
**Zoroaster**, a contemporary of Mercury <note>Kircher identifies Hermes Trismegistus with the Roman god Mercury</note>, first calls God the *paternal monad* <note>original: "πατρικὴν μονάδα"</note>, containing all things in himself. If he is Father, therefore he generates; and what does he generate? Surely that which is first by nature after him, and these are called two, as his words have it: *The monad is extended, which generates two* <note>original: "παντὶ γὰρ μονὰς, ἥ δύο γεννᾷ"</note>. If the extended monad generates two, the <term>dyad</term> <note>a group or set of two</note> with the monad necessarily make a **Triad**, shining everywhere; for he says: *For in every world the Triad shines, of which the monad is the principle* <note>original: "παντὶ γὰρ ἐν κόσμῳ λάμπει Τριὰς, ἧς μονὰς ἀρχή"</note>. And elsewhere: *The Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the second mind* <note>original: "πάντα ἐξετέλεσε πατὴρ καὶ τῷ παρέδωκε τῷ δευτέρῳ"</note>. And then: *For that is the Mind of Mind, which is the architect of the fiery world* <note>original: "νοῦ γὰρ νᾶς ἐστιν, ὁ κόσμῳ τεχνίτης πυρός"</note>. 

We have, therefore, from Zoroaster: that GOD is a monad; that it is generative; that it is called the paternal mind; that being extended it generates a dyad; that with the dyad it generates a triad; that the triad is the principle and the end of the paternal depth; that it shines everywhere; and finally, that with the dyad and triad he produced the world or universe. All of these points are consistent with the doctrine of Trismegistus. **Orpheus**, himself also instructed by the Egyptians in the doctrine of Hermes, placed this triad in GOD...

### CHAPTER III. 408 BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISC

<margin>The names brought forth by Orpheus refer to the Holy Triad.</margin>...she who is the creator of all things, he [Orpheus] sang quite fittingly in his sacred theme, where he calls the first power in GOD *Pinuti* in the Egyptian language <note>Kircher uses his own reconstruction of Coptic; "Pinuti" is his interpretation of "the God"</note>, which means *the Father*. This word has been understood by no one until now, and has been corruptly called *Phanetas* <note>Referring to Phanes, the Orphic primeval deity</note> by all other authors. The second he calls *Phranum*, that is, *Uranus* [the Sky], which is the mind born from the first—namely, from the Father—and is called heaven. The third he calls *Chronum* [Time], namely, the Crafting Mind, which is also called Saturn; the Phoenicians used to express this through the two wings of a hawk, as was shown a little earlier. If, therefore, GOD is *Pinuti*, that is, the Father, he must have a son; but who? *Uranus*, who is the second subsistence, the mind

<margin>Philo. Plethon on the Oracles of Zoroaster.</margin>of the Father; for "nature," according to Philo, "by its intellectual Word <note>original: τῇ νοερᾷ αὐτῷ λόῳ (tē noera autō logō)</note>, is a generative and creative nature" <note>original: φύσις ἐστὶ γεννητικὴ κὴ δημιουργική (physis esti gennētikē kē dēmiourgikē)</note>. For the intellectual nature of the Word itself is the generator and founder of things; it is followed by another Crafting Mind, which he calls Cronus or Saturn, depending upon both.

<margin>Pythagoras. Plato.</margin>Pythagoras also says that all things that ever exist in the world consist of this triad. Plato—who, according to Iamblichus, learned most of his things from the columns of Mercury <note>The "Columns of Hermes/Mercury" were legendary pillars inscribed with ancient Egyptian wisdom</note>—everywhere subscribes to Mercury regarding the triform Divinity. He sometimes calls the first mind "the Father," sometimes "the First," "the True," "the Good," "the One," or the "First Substance" in divine matters. The second he calls the "Divine Intellect," the "unparticipated first mind," the "first Archetypal world," the "son of the first Good," the "eternal reason of GOD," the "eternal Word," and the "divine Wisdom of GOD." The third power he calls the "Soul of the World," the "King of the universe," the "Leader of all," and the "Cause of the whole." Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Numenius, Proclus, Syrianus, and his other followers explain nearly the same things in almost the same words. Iamblichus, how-

> *The first GOD, before Being and alone, is the Father of the first GOD, whom he generates while remaining in his solitary unity; and that is the super-intelligible. It is the exemplar of himself, which is called his own father, his own son, the Sole-Father, and the truly good GOD. For he is greater, and first, and the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, the ideas. And these are the most ancient principles of all. There is an intellect understanding itself, and turning its understandings back into itself, which in the Egyptian language is called Emeph (better, Hemphta). Before this, he places the indivisible One, which he calls the first exemplar, the expression or image, which he calls Icthon, in which is the first understanding and the first thing understood, which is worshipped only with silence. But insofar as it proceeds into generation, it brings the hidden power of latent reasons into the light, and in the Egyptian language is called Amun.*

See these matters treated more extensively in the third book. But having brought these points forward, let us now return to the Obelisk.

<margin>Why this winged globe is placed at the apex of the Obelisk.</margin>This serpent-circle-wing-shaped <note>original: ὀφι-κυκλο-πτερόμορφοv (ophi-kyklo-pteromorphon)</note> symbol is placed at the head of the Obelisk like a title and inscription for the whole Obelisk concerning the Triform Deity. It is placed on each of the sides of the Obelisk, which faces the fourfold face of the world, to show that there is no part or place in the world so hidden and secluded that it is not animated and brought to life by the power of this triform GOD.

...which is placed in a triangle, or rather within the triangular side of the pyramid, so that they might indicate that all things harmonize in signifying the Trinity; for the triangle has been shown elsewhere to be the symbol of the Sacred Triad. Therefore, having explained the Inscription of the Obelisk, nothing further remains except to explain the process of the triform Divinity spreading itself into the intellectual, angelic, or "genial" <note>Referring to the world of *genii* or spirits</note> world, as the Egyptians call it. This process, which the Egyptians call divine radiance <note>original: επιαυγωσιν (*epiaugōsin*), meaning an out-shining or divine illumination</note>, is shown to us by the second hieroglyphic arrangement of the first schematic.

## OF SCHEMATISM I.
### HIEROGRAMMATISM II.

->*Which shows the outflow of the triform Divinity into the Genial world.*<-

The second hieroglyphic arrangement is expressed by this array of symbols. In the middle space, a female human figure, naked in her upper part and covered in the rest, sits upon a variegated seat with her feet joined together. In her right hand, she holds a scepter marked with the head of a hoopoe <term>upupa: a bird often used in Egyptian symbolism to represent filial piety or spiritual vigilance</term>; with her left hand effectively pulled back, she supports a *tutulus* <term>a high, conical headdress</term> upon her head <margin>Explanation of the figures of Hierogrammatism II, Schematism I.</margin> that is flame-shaped <note>original: πυρο-πέρ-μορφος (*pyro-per-morphos*), literally "fire-form"</note>—that is, emerging from a bifurcated flame at the top of the head. It is composed of two asps with swollen necks, a circle, and wings. To her right and left stand two other images in human form, notable for their flowing hair and separated feet. The first of these, marked with the letter B, carries a scepter marked with a lotus flower in her right hand and a basket in the other, supporting on her head an ornament composed of a lotus flower. The other, marked with the letter C, holds a feather in her left hand and a scepter notable for a lotus flower in her right, with a basket placed upon her head.

### CHAPTER III.
## BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK
#### 410

...with a basket containing a Lotus flower. We have already presented the description of the hieroglyphic arrangement <term>hierogrammatismi: A term Kircher uses to describe a specific grouping of hieroglyphic symbols that form a complete theological "sentence" or concept</term>; now let us see the meaning of the individual symbols we encounter. It was stated in the preceding pages that the circle-sphere-serpent symbol denotes a triform Divinity <note>original: *Numen triforme*</note> set apart from all contagion of matter, retracting and concealing itself in the ineffable retreat of the Divinity and the inaccessible abyss of the fontal light. From this, a most brilliant, naked, and immanent splendor—clothed in no garments of attributes or properties, as the Egyptians say—pours forth and expands, content only in the ineffable contemplation of its own essence. This shadows forth the monad-triad <note>original: μοναδο τριάδα (*monado triada*)</note>, that is, the uni-trine form of GOD, if one may speak this way. Now, the priests <note>original: *Hieromantæ*</note> instructed by Mercury <note>Kircher refers here to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom</note>, proceed to show in the second hieroglyphic arrangement, under the secret likenesses of symbols, how this triform Divinity comes forth to the outside, and how it gradually becomes known to the sensible world through the effects of natural things. This present arrangement places this beautifully before our eyes, in which the headdress is shaped like a flame-circle-wing-serpent <note>original: φλογο κυκλο-πτερόμορφος (*phlogo kyklo-pteromorphos*)</note>. This denotes the same thing as the triform Divinity above, such that the first mind is indicated by the circle; the second mind—that is, the fecundity of the Creator’s mind hidden in the center of the Divinity—is indicated by the serpent; and a certain fiery power is indicated by the flame, just as the motion, flight, and divine impulse of the Spirit is aptly suggested by the wings.

<margin>What is the all-formed Genius?</margin>
Therefore, the Genius marked "A" represents the process of the triform Divinity, set in motion through the circles, into the intellectual world or the world of Genii <note>In Kircher's system, "Genii" are equivalent to angels or celestial intelligences</note>. This Genius is called "all-formed" <note>original: παντόμορφος (*pantomorphos*)</note>, according to the testimony of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>, because it changes itself into every form, being closest to the Divinity. It wears the character of the triform Divinity on its head to express within itself the wondrous providence of the supreme Divinity in the administration of things. Thus, the triform Divinity is understood to be set in motion into the intellectual world under the form of this very Genius. Consequently, the Egyptians frequently confuse this Genius with the supreme Divinity itself. This name fits beautifully with what the sacred scriptures say concerning the Angel in Exodus 23; for there, God the Best and Greatest says in express words that he must be treated with the highest honor and reverence, because His name was written in the midst of him. But let us hear the words of the sacred text:

> *Behold, I send my Angel before your face, to guard you on the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared for you. Observe him, and hear his voice, and do not resist him, for he will not let your sins go unpunished, because my name is in the midst of him.* <note>Kircher provides the Hebrew text for Exodus 23:20-21 above this Latin translation</note>

Or as the Chaldean paraphrase of Onkelos <note>The Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Torah</note> has it: *because in my name is his Word* <note>original Aramaic: ארום בשמי מימריה (*arum bishmi memreia*)</note>. This means you shall receive him as an envoy executing affairs in my name—as if He were saying that the Angel, marked with my name, is the immediate likeness and pattern of myself. He has the power to direct, administer, and perfect all my works, being the sole executor of my will in the earthly Economy. In no different way did the Egyptians regard their "secondary gods" or Genii as the primary ministers of the supreme Divinity...

### INTERPRETATION. CHAPTER III
#### 411

...his ministers with the same name, or what is the same, with the corresponding symbol, namely the **serpent-circle-winged-form** <note>original Greek: ὀφι-κυκλο-πτερόμορ-φω (*ophi-kyklo-pteromorpho*)</note>; so that they might show that in his name and word, they fulfill all things in the world. And from this it is clear why Timaeus the Pythagorean calls God the **exemplary world** <note>original Greek: κόσμον ἐνδαλματικὸν (*kosmon endalmatikon*)</note>; for just as the world encircles all things in its embrace, so God does most of all—as the Pythagoreans say—as a universal nature present everywhere, seeing all, hearing all, containing all things, yet contained by the boundary of nothing. He is the greatest world of Wisdom, holiness, intelligence, life, reasons, and forms, which Plato indeed beautifully amplifies in his own way with these words: *For holding all intelligible living beings within himself, he possesses them, just as the world contains us and whatever other visible creatures have been formed.*

<margin>Explanation of the Second Diagram.</margin>
But to the point: The human figure is seen to be youthful and feminine, so that its beauty and fecundity <note>fruitfulness or ability to produce life</note> in the Angelic intellectual world might be indicated. The upper part is seen naked, because although God is present in all created things, his simplicity and purity are infected by no contagion from them; the lower part is covered, because the reasons of the **seminal ideas** <term>seminal ideas: In Kircher's Neoplatonic view, these are the "blueprints" or hidden spiritual seeds from which all physical things grow</term> are hidden. It has indistinct <note>joined or unseparated</note> feet, because God, even if he is always in motion, is nevertheless always immobile by his own nature. But the figure sits upon a square, both to indicate the stability and immutable nature of the divine Power, and the stable, firm, and unshakable order of nature. The base of the seat is marked with five **handled crosses** <note>original: *ansatis crucibus*. This refers to the Ankh, which Kircher interpreted as a symbol of the four elements governed by a central divine power</note>, to show that the Divinity acts primarily upon five classes and orders of natural beings: obtaining its dominion over intellectual, rational, sensitive, and vegetable things, and all bodies devoid of life. This is beautifully shown by the scepter marked with the head of a **hoopoe bird** <note>original: *upupa*</note>, for by this bird, the variety of created things is graphically expressed, as has been explained in the specific **hierogrammatism** <term>hierogrammatism: A sacred symbolic arrangement of images that functions like a sentence</term> of the hoopoe.

...it is shown that they are clothed in no covering of earthly mixture <note>This means they are pure spirits, untainted by physical matter.</note>; their feet are separated and as if urged to run, so that their readiness in executing the commands of the Supreme Divinity, and their speed of motion in the administration of created things, may be expressed. The first of these, distinguished by a **scepter topped with a lotus flower**, denotes power over all things subject to the East; the **Basket** <note>original: *Calathus*, a wicker basket often used in religious processions</note> denotes the abundance that results from their administration of the world. The other figure, similarly possessing a lotus-shaped scepter, also holds a **feather** in her left hand, an indicator of speed in actions. <margin>What the matching basket represents.</margin> On her head, each figure holds a basket conspicuous with a lotus flower, by which they secretly signify the movement, reverence, and obedience with which they perpetually bow toward the **Supreme Divinity** and the **all-formed Hemphta** <note>Hemphta is Kircher’s name for the Egyptian creative spirit or Demiurge</note>. This follows the nature and property of the Egyptian lotus flower, which, by a certain hidden love and harmony, is so drawn to the presence of the Sun that it rises out of the water with the rising Sun and is submerged as it sets, as if it were indignant at being deprived of the sight of it. For this reason, the lotus flower was appropriately adopted by the Egyptians as a symbol of the Eastern region; but all these things are discussed more extensively in the examination of the hierogram of the Lotus on page 358. And this is the brief and succinct interpretation of the second Hierogrammatism; it remains for us to prove that the matter stands as described with solid and varied learning.

We have shown in the preceding pages how the Egyptians, through the symbol of the **all-formed** <note>original Greek: παντόμορφον (*pantomorphon*)</note>, beautifully demonstrate three distinct modes or forms of existence in GOD; and how they exhibited GOD according to the reasons of His ineffable essence. Now, proceeding further, through another diagram linked to the previous one, they show how this triform Divinity, through the production of the sensible world, gradually becomes sensible from the insensible; and how, first flowing into the intellectual world, He distributes the economy of the world to the **Genii**, the ministers of divine commands, the "fecund Gods," the presidents and stewards of the world. For, as the Egyptian Abenragel <note>likely the Arab astrologer Abu l-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal</note> rightly reports from the mind of the Egyptians:

> الله كل اقوات بدو وانتهارهم بطابع ويعطي للملايکة الذين بقوة شکلية رسم كل ما في سما وفي النجو—

> *GOD is the beginning and end of all powers; He gave the seal of ideas to the Angels, who, by ideal power, mark all things in the heavens and the stars.* 

That is: GOD, the beginning and end of all powers, provides the seal of ideas to his ministering intelligences; who, like faithful executors of things, mark each thing entrusted to them with an ideal power. Meanwhile, the heavens and stars, acting as instruments, dispose the matter to receive those forms which reside in the Divine Majesty—as Plato says in the *Timaeus*—to be brought down through the stars. These forms the **Giver of Forms** <term>δοτήρ εἰδῶν: Doter eidon; a Platonic term for the source of all shapes and structures in the world</term> distributes through the ministry of the intelligences, whom He has appointed as rulers and guardians over His works. To them is entrusted the faculty over the things committed to them, so that all the virtue of stones, herbs, metals, and all other things comes from those very intelligences, presiding and ruling; and afterward they are disposed by the aspects of the heavens...

...remaining things, and furthermore from the arranged combinations of the elements, which correspond to the influences of the heavens by which the elements themselves are disposed. Therefore, these operations possess expressed forms in the lower things themselves, but in the heavens they act through disposing virtues, in the <term>Intelligences</term><note>Celestial spirits or angels that govern the spheres</note> through mediating virtues, and in the **Archetype** <note>The original divine mind or blueprint of the universe</note> through ideas and exemplary forms. If anyone weighs these matters a little more precisely, they will see that they correspond with a truly beautiful connection to the context of our hieroglyphic scheme. After <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note> showed the generation of the Word from the Father in the first chapter, he says the following in the third chapter of the *Pimander*:
> *The holy light was sent forth, and the elements were solidified under the sand from the moist essence; and all the Gods distribute the nature of sowing;* 
and a little later: 
> *And the sky appeared in seven circles, and the Gods appeared in the figures of the stars, together with all their forms; and they were distinguished along with those Gods who are within them, and the circular revolution is bounded by the circling air, and moved by the divine spirit; and each GOD produced, by a particular virtue, that which had been commanded to him.* 
So says Mercury. Hence the Greeks thought that **Hercules**, a Solar Deity situated in the Sun, was carried around with it, but that **Mercury** was in the Moon, according to the testimony of <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer</note>; his words are:
<note>original Greek: "Οἱ μὲν ἡλίῳ τὸν Ἡρακλέα μυθολογοῦσιν ἐνιδρυμένον συμπεριπολεῖν, τῇ τε σελήνῃ τὸν Ἑρμῆν."</note>
> *And they mythologize that Hercules, situated in the Sun, is carried around with it, and Mercury in the Moon; for the things which the Moon effects are similar to the works of speech and wisdom, but the City of the Sun is effected by force and strength; for some will have it that the Sun is nourished by the sea, but the Moon sends up a sweet and soft exhalation from springs and terrestrial waters.* 

<margin>What is denoted by figure A?</margin>
**Figure A**, the **Hemphta of the Holy Deity**, veiled under the solar deity of the "all-formed" <term>Genius</term> <note>A guiding spirit or minor divinity</note>, refers first to the process into the intellectual world (or the world of Genii), which the human figure aptly expresses, as we shall explain later; then, through these, it refers to the further process into the sensible <note>perceivable by the senses</note> world, which is beautifully indicated by the staff or scepter he holds in his hand, distinguished by the **head of a hoopoe** <note>original: *upupa*; a bird with a distinctive crown of feathers</note>; 

<margin>What does the head of the hoopoe denote?</margin>
for since, as was said in the discussion of the <term>hierogram</term> <note>A sacred symbolic character or image</note> of the hoopoe, this bird is found to be painted by nature with seven different colors, and changes four times in a year according to the four seasons, it indicates quite appropriately by the seven colors the qualities of the seven planets, by which they act upon the fourfold elemental nature with continuous mutations. And thus <term>Abenephius</term> <note>Kircher's name for an Arabic source, likely Ibn Wahshiyya</note> explains it: 
<note>original Arabic: ۞ ——— القصيبة التي فيها راس الهدهد تدل علي التحويل الذي ———</note>
that is:
> *(The scepter, in which the head of the hoopoe is found, indicates the perpetual variety of things in the world; possession, stability, or the firm and stable empire of GOD over the earth.)* 

All these things are explained at length in the hierogram of the **seats**; and this meaning is so true that all posterity, having been taught by the Egyptians, deservedly adopted the **seat** to denote stability and dominion. 

<margin>The seat is a sign of stability.</margin>
Hence <term>Apollodorus</term> <note>An ancient Greek scholar</note> says: <note>original Greek: "οἱ παλαιοὶ ἔγραφον τὸν Δία καθί- ζοντα, θεὸς σημαίνων ἀκινήτου τοῦ Θεοῦ δύναμιν."</note> *The ancients depicted Zeus sitting, a god signifying the immovable power of God.* 

<margin>Numa Pompilius.</margin>
Hence **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome</note>, when he instituted the Priesthood, imitating the Egyptian Priests, ordained among other ornaments a **chair** <note>original: *sella*</note> as a symbol of immutable and unshakable stability and the likeness which the Religion of the Priesthood confers. ...also in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato</note>, while the twelve orders have departed from the house and follow the winged chariot of Jove, Vesta alone remains; since she represents the stable, firm, and solid earth, she deservedly sits alone while the other gods move. Our triform Deity, **Hemphtha**, truly reflects this same figure—seated and distinguished by a feathered <term>tutulus</term><note>A high, conical headdress or hair decoration</note> and a scepter. Eusebius describes this in these words: "They depict the image of **Cneph** (or better, as we showed above, **Hemphtha**) as a human figure of a blue color, surrounded by a belt, holding a scepter in his hand and wearing a feather on his head. The seat is variegated and square, denoting the stable or solid earth, filled with a variety of things." Why he is shown with unseparated feet, however, is explained by Heliodorus in Book 3, page 148.

<margin>
Heliodorus, Book 3, page 148.
What the unseparated feet mean.
</margin>
<note>Original Greek: ἀλλ' αὖϑι Θεοὶ τοῖς τὲ ὀφϑαλμοῖς ἀνεωγόσι...</note> *But the Gods, with eyes always open and looking steadily, never closing their eyelids... and in their gait, they move not by a joining of the feet or by taking steps, but by a certain airy rush and an unimpeded impulse, cleaving the divine air rather than walking through it. For this reason, the Egyptians also set up the statues of the Gods with their feet joined together as if united. Homer, knowing these things as an Egyptian would, having been taught the sacred education, left these matters to be recognized symbolically in his verses by those who are able to understand.* <note>Kircher suggests Homer was essentially "Egyptian" in his philosophical training</note>. The arrival of the greatest of the Gods is marked by their gait; it does not consist of the movement or transposition of the feet, but of a certain airy impulse and the swift power of those who cleave the breezes rather than passing through them. For this reason, the Egyptians place the statues of their Gods with the feet joined and, as it were, united. Homer, knowing this as one instructed in sacred doctrine, rendered this secretly and involvedly in his verses, leaving it to be understood by those who can. This agrees with what Eusebius relates concerning a statue of this kind, which he asserts was a <term>hieroglyphic</term> of the World: that the "man" had his feet folded together, wore a robe reaching to the ankles, and supported a golden ball on his head. By this form, they noted the immovable constitution, the roundness, and the variety of the stars, signifying that all things are ruled and sustained by GOD, and that the minds of men are led into the knowledge of GOD.

<margin>
What the covered private parts mean.
Herodotus and Plutarch.
</margin>
Nudity signifies the simplicity of essence, while the concealment of the private parts signifies the hidden nature of the <term>seminal reasons</term><note>In Stoic and Neoplatonic philosophy, these are the "blueprints" or generative principles inherent in nature</note>, as Herodotus in his description of Pan in *Euterpe*, and Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*, demonstrate. See what we have treated more extensively regarding this kind of significance in the chapter on the <term>hierogrammatism</term> <note>The sacred symbolic drawing or writing system</note> of the human figure.

Furthermore, regarding the base, which is marked with a five-fold character of the **ansated cross** <note>The Ankh symbol</note>, they signified the production of the five-fold mixtures through the four elements by the Genii of the triform Deity. You will find this most amply proven in the chapter on the *Hierogrammatism of the Ansated Cross*, where you will also find many wonderful things worthy of the highest consideration concerning this character, confirmed by the various doctrines and authorities of writers.

Moreover, Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher</note> asserts that the standing figures—naked and distinguished by lotus-shaped baskets and scepters—indicate the **Genii** <note>Guardian spirits or presiding deities</note> who preside over the Eastern region, in these words:

### INTERPRETATION. 415 CHAPTER III.

...Indeed, from the blossom of the Water Lily or Lotus <note>original: "Nenupharis seu Nymphæa"</note>, which we have already shown above to be the same as the Lotus, they designated the region of the rising Sun. Furthermore, through the baskets <note>ornamental vessels or crowns</note> clearly visible on the heads of both Lotuses, they ingeniously signified the inclination, readiness, and obedience of the Genii <note>Spirits or guiding intelligences</note>, and the immutable law of consensus by which they are joined to that divine, otherworldly Sun. In the Lotus, everything is round—the root, the stalk, the leaves, the flowers—by which they secretly hint at how all things, according to a certain analogy, must be conformed to the supreme Divinity with the greatest readiness and haste. We showed above from Heliodorus that they also suggested this through feet that were not separated, as if urged on to run. For according to Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, God affects circles; the intellectual nature of the Genii affects circles; the world affects circles; and all things in the world affect circles, aptly expressed through the roundness of every part of the Lotus. Hermes says in book 14 of the Basel edition: *The creative Mind, indeed being one with the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift speed, has reflected its machine back upon itself, and commanded it to revolve from a beginning without beginning to an end without end.* <note>original Latin: "Mens quidē opifex vna cum verbo circulos continens..."</note> For it always begins there where it finishes. *Truly the circuit of all these things, just as the Mind itself willed, etc.* The curious reader will also be able to see from the interpretation of the sacred inscriptions <term>hierogrammatismi</term><note>The study or interpretation of sacred Egyptian writing</note> that the Lotus was a symbol of the consensus of lower things with higher things, turning itself toward the sun with a certain natural and insatiable love. All these things are beautifully indicated through the boy Harpocrates sitting on a Lotus and pressing his finger to his lips.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the Egyptian deity Harpocrates as a young child. He is seated on a large, stylized lotus flower. He holds one hand to his mouth with a finger pressed against his lips in a gesture of silence, and in his other hand, he holds a tall, thin staff or scepter. <margin>What does Harpocrates sitting on the Lotus mean?</margin>
Harpocrates denotes the world full of divinity—for "all things are full of Jove," as the poet testifies. By pressing his lips, he commands silence, to show that the sacred mysteries of this <term>empsychosis</term> <note>original: "empsychofeos," referring to the infusion of soul or life into the world</note> must be suppressed in deep silence from the ears of the profane. He sits on the Lotus in the form of a boy to signify the generation of things—by which the World is continually rejuvenated, as if by the power of the solar Genius—emerging from moisture. The flower of the Lotus, emerging from the waters at the presence of the sun, is a certain likeness and exemplar of this. Furthermore, why are the statues nude? Why are they conspicuous with scepters? Why should the lower parts be covered? Why in human form? Why do they sit? These are beautifully declared by Eusebius in Book 3, Chapter 3, with these words: *They fashioned the image of Jove into a human likeness because he was the Mind, into whose exemplar he might look in the procreation of things, and by whose seminal reasons, as it were, he might perfect all things. Indeed, he sits so that he might signify the constant stability of his power:* <note>original Greek: κάθηται δὲ τὸ ἑδραῖον τῆς δυνάμεως αἰνιττόμενος.</note> *He has his upper parts naked because he is manifest in the intellectual and celestial parts of the world.* <note>original Greek: γυμνὰ δὲ ἔχει τὰ ἄνω, ὅτι φανερὸς ἐν τοῖς νοεροῖς & τοῖς οὐρανίοις τοῦ κόσμου μέρεσίν ἐστι.</note> *His lower parts, conversely, are covered because he himself lurks hidden in the lowest and most deeply recessed things.* <note>original Greek: σκέπεται δὲ αὐτῷ τὰ ἀφόδια, ὅτι ἀφανὴς τοῖς κάτω κεκρυμμένος.</note> *And indeed he holds the scepter in his left hand, because in that part of the body, the heart—the most commanding and intellectual reason—resides.* <note>original Greek: ἔχει δὲ τῇ μὲν λαιᾷ τὸ σκῆπτρον, καθ' ὅ μάλιστα τῆς τοῦ σώματος μοίρας, τὸ ἡγεμονικώτατον καὶ νοερώτατον ὑποικουρεῖ λόγος ἡ καρδία.</note> *And he holds*
