rests, because out of all parts of the human body, it is especially in that side that the heart—easily the prince of the rest, and the organ containing the greatest power of understanding—reposes as if in its own proper dwelling. Moreover, that the world is an intellectual one, distinguished into various orders of Spirits <note>Kircher uses the term "Genii" to refer to intermediate spiritual intelligences or guiding spirits</note>, Iamblichus clearly shows on page 306 of the cited edition, where he says:
> The multitude of deities is like a world, having many orders conspiring into one; similarly, sacrifices must have an order of deities, likewise conspiring into one order, so that individual rites correspond rightly to individual deities. Similarly, the things around us and in us are manifold; they should not correspond to the divine causes of our affairs from only one part, but from all parts congruously, and thus ascend to the leaders above.

<margin>Symbols also denote the manner of proceeding in sacrifices.</margin>
Hence the ingenious Egyptian priests, not only through these sacred writings <note>original: "hierogrammatismos," referring to hieroglyphic inscriptions</note>, noted the operations of the triform Divinity and its outward progression, as has been said; but with these symbolic schemes they also demonstrated, through a certain hidden analogy, the way in which they could not only attract this triform Deity through ceremonies, sacrifices, rites, and prayers analogous to it, and make it favorable to themselves, but even become thoroughly <term>theomorphoi | god-shaped</term> <note>original: θεόμορφοι</note> or "deiform." This <term>theomorphōsin | deiformity</term> <note>original: θεόμορφωσιν</note> or supreme happiness they regarded as the ultimate goal—just as it truly is in our own orthodox Theology, in the opinion of all Theologians—namely, *that we may be called and truly be the sons of God.* They indicated that from this state all good, all health, peace, rest, tranquility, and the ultimate blessedness of man depends, as is clear from the words of Iamblichus cited just before.

<margin>Mercury in the Pimander.</margin>
Mercury Trismegistus <note>The legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> beautifully shows all these things in the *Pimander*, where he seems to aim at this one point almost exclusively: how one can emerge <term>theomorphos | god-shaped</term> through actions pleasing to GOD. You may see this treated more extensively in Porphyry, Plutarch, and others whom we cite throughout. Moreover, the image itself teaches most excellently with what ceremonies the sacrifices should be instituted. For first:

<margin>The method for performing sacrifices.</margin>
To draw God to themselves, the Priests kept a Statue of the Deity placed in the innermost sanctuaries <note>original: "adytis," the most sacred, restricted parts of a temple</note> in places most remote from the company of men, marked with that array of symbols which you see here. Hence, so that they might become similar in dress, ceremony, and sacrifice, they were naked, clothed in no garment of the earthly body; having washed, they were seen carrying thyrsi <note>ritual staffs or wands</note> in one hand, and in the other a basket and a feather—just like the Spirits <note>Genii</note>—and on their heads they carried lotus-bearing baskets in the same manner. These were symbols of actions expressing the likeness of the Eastern Spirits and the Triform Deity they represent. For by this likeness and analogy of symbols, they believed both the Deity and the powerful Spirits were attracted. Thus, this sacred writing is first a kind of uplifting display of the virtues proper to GOD; then it is a living picture and representation of priestly operations. By these operations, instituted correctly according to the present image, they thought they were snatched up into GOD and reached the goal of intended happiness. They are shown with slender and thin bodies, so that from this, priests might be warned that divine rites are to be approached not with bodies stuffed and fattened with food and drink, but with abstinence and purity, as if by preparation—

Thus Plutarch says: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ εὐταλῆ καὶ κῦφα ταῖς ψυχαῖς περικεῖσθαι τὰ σώματα, καὶ μὴ πιέζειν, μηδὲ θλίβειν ἰσχύοντα τὸ θνητὸν, καὶ βαρύνειν τὸ θεῖον."</note> *rather, they wish that bodies be draped around souls in a light and graceful way, so that the mortal part does not overpower or burden the divine part.* Regarding these matters, since we shall deal with them here and there in what follows, we only wished in this place to hint at the intention of the wise men in the display of these sculptures; we shall reserve more copious authorities for their proper places. For as the clever Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> teaches according to the mind of the Egyptians on page 220: *The proper observance of the precepts and divine works—which surpass all human understanding—along with the wondrous power of symbols and sacraments, grants us a deifying union with the gods.* And a little 
<margin>Iamblichus, Basel edition, page 220.</margin> later: *Just as in agriculture, medicine, the art of making images, or human procreation, man seizes the opportunity of the matter, but a higher and universal cause provides the form; so in sacrifices, when symbols and tokens <note>original: "synthemata"</note> are made, the priests use certain material things, namely, in imitation of natural powers in the order which beauty established, but GOD impresses the effective power into the Sacraments.* Hence on page 238 of the Basel edition: *And so, He is suddenly present, and He uses the Prophet as an instrument, who meanwhile is neither in control of himself, nor notices what he speaks; he even ignores where he is. Indeed, before drinking the water, he abstains from food day and night, and withdraws himself to certain sacred things inaccessible to the common people. Therefore, because of this separation from human affairs, he renders himself pure and fit to look upon GOD; hence the Priest, before he performs the sacrifices for the divine oracles in the many rituals, observes holiness, is washed, abstains from food for three days, dwells in the inner sanctums <note>original: "adytis," the most private part of a temple</note>, and thus gradually begins to be illuminated and to rejoice wonderfully.* Having thus explained the process of the Supreme Deity into the intellectual world, let us next explain how it proceeds into the sensible world, or the world of the stars.

# SACRED SCHEME III.
<note>original: "Hierogrammatismus"</note>
->Showing the influence of the Triform Deity into the World of the Stars.<-

After the priests, through the two preceding Sacred Schemes, represented the actions of the triform Deity—both internally and externally—into the intellectual world, and through that into this sensible world, they now proceed to more particular things. Under this third sacred scheme, they beautifully show both what that triform Deity performs in the principal part of this sensible World—that is, in the Sun—and how it gradually becomes known through the sensible images of the worldly machine.

Three symbols are therefore seen in this place: a variegated Hawk, upon whose head is a basket laden with the fruit of the persea tree <note>The persea was a sacred Egyptian tree often associated with the heart and the goddess Seshat</note>, which reveals something secret and worthy of veneration; behind it, an asp with an erect and swollen neck rests upon a globe.
<margin>The influence of the Triform Deity into the Starry World.</margin>

# INTERPRETATION.

<margin>What the hawk signifies.</margin>
"GOD," he says, *has the head of a hawk; He is incorruptible and first, eternal, unbegotten, without parts, most similar to Himself, the driver of all good things who expects no rewards, the best of the good, the wisest of the wise, the father of justice, self-taught, perfect by nature, Wise, and the Inventor of Sacred Nature.* And that He is such a being is indicated mystically through the tiara or headdress <note>original: "cidarim"</note> which He carries on His head in the form of a protruding basket, with the fruit of a persea <note>The Persea (Mimusops laurifolia) was a sacred tree in ancient Egypt; its fruit was often compared to the shape of a human heart.</note> inserted into it. By the basket indeed—as Rhodiginus and Macrobius <note>Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus and Macrobius were classical and Renaissance scholars who wrote on ancient myths and symbolism.</note> testify—is denoted the regal power of the Supreme Divinity who draws all things toward the sublime; hence it is placed upon the head, as if upon the citadel of all reason and power, the origin and the source. The fruit of the persea, similar in figure to a heart, indicates the wisdom shining forth in the administration of the World’s machinery and in the invention of things necessary for the World. <margin>What the Basket with the fruit of the Persea placed on the head signifies.</margin> For this is the divine Osiris, as was rightly shown a little earlier, who is <note>original: "ἱερᾷ φυσικῶς μόνος εὑρετής"</note> the only inventor of sacred nature; hence the basket ended in a sort of cone with the pointed fruit, to signify the sharpness of the mind, which is necessary for the investigation of things. These are the words of Clement of Alexandria: <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
> *The hawk is the symbol of the sun, because it is of a fiery nature and has the strength to kill.*

To which Porphyry subscribes in book 5, chapter 3, with these words: <margin>Porphyry.</margin>
> *The hawk, he says, is dedicated to the Sun because it is a symbol of light and spirit: the one because of the speed of its motion, the other because it flies into higher regions, which are more luminous than those below.*

The Greeks likewise, even if they did not worship the hawk as the Egyptians were accustomed to do, nevertheless held it in great esteem, considering it a bird of the best omen and believing it to be the swiftest messenger of Apollo—that is, of the Sun. Origen seems to silently suggest this with these words: <margin>The hawk is the messenger of Apollo.</margin> <margin>Origen.</margin>
> *Indeed, even "Apollo" signifies certain omens of the hawk, and it is called the swift messenger of this GOD:* 

And therefore, whenever they wished to represent the light of the Sun, they painted the head of a hawk with a circle or sphere placed above it, to show that something divine, as mentioned above, was present in such a head; this is aptly displayed on the Flaminian Obelisk, concerning which more will be said in its proper place.

They therefore formed the image of Osiris under the form of a Hawk to indicate the fiery and luminous power of the sun, penetrating the whole lower and upper world with its rays. Porphyry again: <margin>Porphyry.</margin>
> *The hawk is dedicated to the sun: because it is a symbol of light and spirit; the one due to the speed of motion, and the other because it flies into higher places, which are more luminous than those below.*

Let us also hear Plutarch from his book *On Isis and Osiris*, subscribing to Porphyry. <margin>Plutarch, Book 4 on Abstinence.</margin> <note>While the margin cites Porphyry's "On Abstinence," the main text correctly identifies Plutarch's famous essay "On Isis and Osiris."</note>
> *They say that those painted as hawks often represent Osiris, for that bird excels in the sharpness of its sight and the speed of its flight.* 

But whoever desires these things to be established from all-encompassing learning should read what we have handed down in the specific <term>hierogrammatism</term> <note>A term for a sacred symbolic writing or "sacred inscription" used by the author to describe Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> of the Hawk. Now, let us establish what the winged globe portends by appropriate authority.

The globe surrounded by an asp <note>The "asp" or cobra (uraeus) often encircles the solar disk in Egyptian iconography.</note>, as we have said above, designates nothing else but that fiery power penetrating all places of the world, making all things fertile, which Abenephius <note>A name used by Kircher to refer to an Arabic source, often identified as Ibn Wahshiyya.</note> records concerning the sacred letters of the Egyptians in these words:

<sig>Ggg</sig> ->The Sun<- <note>original Arabic: "دعمورة" (likely a transliteration or variation of a term for the sun or a solar deity).</note>

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

->"Through the form of the circle they indicated the fiery power that is in the Sun, and through the form of the serpent which is in the containing circle, [they indicated] matter, and the result is the world."<- <note>original Arabic: بصورة الدايرة كانوا يدلّون القوة النارية التي في الشمس وبصورة الحيّة التي هي في الدايرة الحاوية والهيولي والنتيجه العالم</note>
->--- ۞ ---<-

*By the figure,* he says, *they designated the fiery power shining in the Sun, and by the figure of the asp surrounding the sphere, the life, motion, and fecundity of the World.* Almost these very words are endorsed by Sanchuniathon <note>Sanchuniathon was a purported Phoenician author whose works survive only in fragments quoted by later writers.</note> in the works of Eusebius.

<margin>
Sanchuniathon
in Eusebius,
Book 1, Chapter 7,
Cologne edition.
</margin>

"Tautus <note>The Phoenician name for the Egyptian god Thoth, the inventor of writing and wisdom.</note> himself declared the nature of the dragon and serpents to be divine, and after him, the Phoenicians and Egyptians did likewise. For this animal was handed down by him as the most spiritual of all reptiles and full of fire. Because of this, it also displays unsurpassed speed through its spirit, without feet or hands, or any other external organs by which other animals move. It produces many different shapes and forms, and in its progress, it moves with spiral-like impulses at whatever speed it wishes. It is also very long-lived; not only does it renew its youth by shedding its old age, but it is naturally capable of even greater growth. And when it has fulfilled its allotted measure, it is consumed into itself, just as Tautus himself arranged in the sacred writings. Therefore, this animal has also been included in sacred rites and mysteries." <note>original: Τὴν μὲν οὖν τοῦ δράκοντος φύσιν... συμπαρείληπται.</note>

*Tautus himself considered the nature of dragons and serpents to be divine, and after him also the Phoenicians and Egyptians; for it is the most spiritual animal of all, and fiery. For by its Spirit, without the aid of hands or feet, or indeed any external organ—as we see other animals are carried—it achieves extraordinary speed, and completing various figures and forms, moving in coils and loops adorned in the shape of a spiral, it performs with the greatest ease whatever speed of gait it wishes; it is also long-lived and of many years, and not only does it become young again by laying aside its old age with its skin, but it even grows when returned to youth; and when it has filled its determined limits, turned back into itself, it flourishes again, though always less so; just as Tautus himself established them in the sacred letters, therefore in sacred things this animal, and in mysteries, has always been adopted.* These words explain everything so beautifully that it seems nothing can be taken away or added. Thus, not without reason, through the Asp surrounded by a globe, they indicated the divine power and hidden operation of Osiris—as well as the Spirit and life which they signaled to the individual parts of the world, the heavens, and the elements—through the various forms of the serpent depicted in its movement. This is why the Phoenicians call it the *Agathodaemon* <note>Greek for "Good Spirit."</note>; while the Egyptians name it *Kneph*. They also add the head of a hawk to it, on account of the hawk's singular activity. *They called it the Good Spirit, but the Egyptians called it Kneph, to which they add the head of a Hawk, because of the unique activity of the hawk.*

<margin>
Epies, the inter-
preter of the Gods
and sacred scribe,
in Eusebius.
</margin>

From this, Epies, the highest interpreter of the Gods and scribe of the Sacred Letters—whose books, according to Eusebius, Arius translated into the Greek language—says: "The first divine thing of the universe is a serpent having the form of a hawk." <note>original Greek: τὸ πρῶτον θεῖον τοῦ παντὸς ὄφις ἐστὶν ἱέρακος ἔχων μορφήν.</note> *The first and most divine of all is a serpent having the form of a hawk.* And although in other places, as we said a little before, it may be seen under the figure of a hawk-headed asp <note>original: "aspidis ἱερακοκεφάλου"</note> transformed with a hawk’s face; yet here, both the hawk is seen alone, and the asp with the globe is seen alone, which is not without its mystery. For by the meaning of each of these symbols placed separately, the dispersion of divine perfections in the Solar light, or Osiris, was indicated. It is therefore clear from what has been said that the solar Divinity is aptly expressed through the Hawk, and its penetrating and fertilizing power through the globe animated by the serpent. Let us now proceed to the secrets of the fourth hierogram <term>hierogrammatismus: a sacred symbolic writing or inscription</term>.

INTERPRETATION.
<meta>Schematic of the Latin Orientation in top right corner; catchword: rearum</meta>
Ggg 2

# HIEROGRAMMATISM IV.

->Showing the influx of the Triform Deity into the Elemental World.<-

In the preceding sections, it was shown how the Triform Deity <note>original: "Triforme Numen," referring to a three-fold manifestation of the divine</note> proceeds outward into the intellectual and starry worlds. Now, in this fourth hierogrammatism <note>A "hierogrammatism" is a sacred inscription or symbolic diagram</note>, it is shown how it glides from the starry world into the elemental world, and from here into the sphere of generation. From this sphere, having taken up wings again, it makes its return to the solitary monad <note>The "monad" refers to the original, indivisible unity of God from which all things began</note>; but let us explain the Symbols.

<image-desc>A vertical rectangular woodcut illustration. At the top is a hawk (accipiter) facing left, wearing a crown and sun disk, labeled with numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. To the right of the hawk is a coiled serpent marked with 6 and 7. Below the hawk is a sequence of symbols: a horizontal staff marked 'a' and 'b', three circles marked 'c', a grid with squares 'e', right-angled triangles 'f', and a vertical staff with a circular base 'h'. The symbols rest on a rectangular platform 'g' above a row of vertical recessed panels resembling an Egyptian temple or palace facade.</image-desc>

<margin>Explanation of the symbols contained in the fourth hierogrammatism.</margin>
First, after the hawk, there occurs a figure of the Ibis-like letter <term>a</term> <note>original: "literæ Ibiacæ"; Kircher believed some Egyptian letters were modeled after the positions of the Ibis bird</note> transformed into the shape of the letter Alpha. After this follows a staff <term>b</term> or line connected to the preceding letter. After this are three circles <term>c</term>. After these is another staff <term>d</term> with three squares <term>e</term>, followed by five right-angled triangles <term>f</term>, one of which is positioned across from the squares; the remaining four triangles are placed below along with a cycle-shaped staff <term>h</term>. All of these are placed above a pedestal <term>g</term>. By this array of symbols, the greatest and most significant mysteries are hinted at, as will be clear from the interpretation. And first, indeed, the character laid out in the form of an Alpha is the same as the <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>original Greek: "Agathos Daimon," meaning the Good Spirit or protective deity</note>, or the Good Genius. It is an alphabetic character holding the first place in the Egyptian alphabet; it is called "Ibis-like" because it was first discovered by the Egyptians from the posture of the Ibis. Concerning this, see page 149 and page 236.

<margin>What the three circles are.</margin>
There follow three circles or orbs. Beneath the orbs is a figure in the linear form of a scepter with an extended leg. This indicates that just as the archetypal Good Spirit <note>Agathodæmon</note> is triform, so too by its triform power it flows into the threefold heaven: namely, the heaven of the fixed stars, the solar-planetary heaven, and the lunar heaven.

<margin>What the three squares are.</margin>
Through the staff with three squares, however, a further progression is indicated: from the circular Triad <note>The group of three</note> into the <term>tetrad</term> or quaternary <note>The group of four</note>, which number represents corporeal things... <note>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "rearum" indicating the next word is "corporearum," meaning "of bodily things."</note>

<summary>This page explains the fourth "hierogrammatism," a symbolic diagram showing how divine power flows from the heavens into the physical world of elements and "generation." It details specific symbols like the Ibis-shaped Alpha and triple circles, representing the Agathodæmon's influence across different celestial spheres.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Fourth Hierogrammatism," specifically detailing the symbolic meaning of geometric shapes (triangles and squares) and their relation to the creation of the elemental world. BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK

[Unive]rsality in the world is noted; and from here a progression into a **triad** or **angular ternary**, which they represent through the figure of a right-angled triangle placed in that same series, and it is a mark of generation, as will be shown later. After these, four other right-angled triangles are placed, by which the progression of the genetic triad into a **quadrangle** <note>original: "τετράγωνον" (tetragonon)</note> is shown—that is, the **Elemental Quaternary**. From the conjunction of this quaternary with the ternary (3+4), the **mystic number seven** <note>The number seven was considered "mystic" because it combined the spiritual triad (3) with the material quaternary (4)</note> is born, which contains the harmony of the whole. This is the "great genetic triangle," composed of five other triangles which signify the five subjects of generatable things in the Elemental World.

These five subjects are:
1. First, the **atmospheric phenomena** <note>original: "μετέωρα" (meteors/meteora), referring to anything occurring in the sky or air</note>.
2. Second, **inanimate bodies** <note>original: "ἄψυχα" (apsycha)</note> or minerals.
3. Third, things of a **vegetative nature** <note>original: "ἔμψυχα" (empsycha), literally "having a soul" in the Aristotelian sense of life</note>.
4. Fourth, things of a **sensitive nature** <note>original: "αἰσθητικά" (aisthetika), referring to animals with senses</note>.
5. Fifth, those composed of both sensitive and vegetative nature, which the Greeks call **zoophytes** <note>original: "ζῳόφυτα" (zoophyta), organisms like sponges or corals that seem to be both plant and animal</note>.

If a rational and intellectual nature is added to these, we will have that mystic **septenary** <note>The number seven</note>, the limit of all things, from which whatever lies hidden in the entire universe of things is constituted. Furthermore, through the **cycle-shaped staff** ☿ <note>The symbol for Mercury</note>, the cyclic process of the Supreme Deity is shown, moving from the circle into lines (that is, from the celestial into the elemental) and then from there back into circles, signifying a return to the **solitary monad** <note>The singular, divine unity</note>. Finally, at the base, a **bier** <note>original: "pheretrum," a litter or frame for carrying a corpse or sacred object</note> is placed as a sign of divine worship or veneration, by which the manner and reason for the veneration and attraction of this **Three-Doored Deity** <note>original: "Numinis Triforis," a reference to the triform nature of the divine power</note> lurking in all things is shown.

<margin>
What is meant by ☿
<image-desc>A small diagram of three triangles arranged in a pyramid formation, with a fourth triangle placed to the right.</image-desc>
</margin>

And this is the interpretation of the fourth hierogrammatism. The proper order now requires us to show that this is so by using proper authorities, so that we do not appear to have fabricated anything by our own conjecture. It must be known that the Egyptians, as has been proven elsewhere, did not only display their secret mysteries under the ingenious architecture of sacred animals, but also under various geometric figures. They were, in fact, the inventors of **Geometry**, and were more skilled in it than other mortals, being thoroughly aware of its secrets; hence they were called **Arpedonaptae** <note>original: "Ἀρπεδοναπται," usually translated as "rope-stretchers," the ancient Egyptian surveyors who laid out fields and temple foundations</note>. While such sciences were held in the highest honor and value among other nations, which had few experts in them, according to the testimony of Clement and Philo, they were almost commonplace in Egypt. Clement mentions this in Book 1 of his *Stromata*, when he speaks of a certain Democritus who boasted too immoderately of his own erudition in these words:

<margin>Who were the Arpedonaptae?</margin>

> "I have listened to many learned men, and in the composition of lines with proof, no one has yet surpassed me, not even those among the Egyptians called **Arpedonaptae**." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ λογίων ἀνθρώπων πλείστων ἐπήκουσα καὶ γραμμέων συνθέσιος μετ' ἀποδείξεως οὐδείς κώ με παρήλαξεν, οὐд' οἱ Αἰγυπτίων καλεόμενοι Ἀρπεδονάπται."</note>

This word is truly Egyptian and signifies "ingenious engineers," as is clear from our Lexicon. The **sacred scribes** <note>original: "ἱερογραμματέας" (hierogrammateas)</note> were of the class of Priests, called **interpreters of sacred oracles** <note>original: "τῶν ἱερῶν λογίων ἑρμηνευταὶ"</note>. They are also called **sacred carriers** <note>original: "ἱεροφόροι" (hierophori)</note> and **sacred robe-keepers** <note>original: "ἱερόστολοι" (hierostoli)</note>: *because they carry the sacred doctrine, pure from all superstition and meddling, in their soul as if in a chest...* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι τὴν περὶ θεῶν πάσης καθαρεύοντα δεισιδαιμονίας, καὶ περιεργίας ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ φέροντες, ὥσπερ ἐν κίστη τῇ περιστέλλοντες."</note>

<meta>The catchword "cista" (chest) at the bottom of the page suggests the sentence continues to describe the hidden nature of Egyptian priestly knowledge.</meta>

Kircher cites classical authors to argue that Egyptian priests used geometry as a secret language for divine truths.</summary>

# INTERPRETATION

...they carry and contain in a chest. So says Plutarch in *On Osiris and Isis*. Suidas also implies they were prophets: "These among the Egyptians were the bark <note>original: "ὁ φλοὶ" (ho phloi). This is a difficult reading in the original Greek of Suidas; it may refer to a outer covering or a specific class of seer</note>, and they spoke the truth about things to come." Such were those most ancient figures Bitis and Jachim, "experts in all things divine and super-worldly," <note>original Greek: "τῶν θείων πάντων καὶ ὑπερκοσμίων ἐπιϚήμονες" (tōn theiōn pantōn kai hyperkosmiōn epistēmones)</note> who are said to have predicted to Pharaoh the power of Moses over the Egyptians. For the other ranks of the priestly order, see them cited throughout this work and described at length by Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who provided detailed accounts of Egyptian rituals</note> in Book 6, where the functions of each are graphically explained. Regarding the **Entaphiastae** <term>embalmers</term>, **Odi** <term>singers of hymns</term>, **Horoscopi** <term>astrologers or time-keepers</term>, **Stolistae** <term>masters of the sacred wardrobe</term>, **Prophets**, and **Pastophori** <term>shrine-bearers</term>, since Clement treats them most extensively in the cited place, the reader may consult him there; it is therefore clear how the **Arpedonaptae** <note>original: "Ardenadaptæ"; these were the "rope-stretchers" or sacred surveyors who measured the land after the Nile flooded</note> are distinguished from the sacred rites and the priests.

Furthermore, the priests, being rightly imbued with geometric rites, just as they prepared their minds for the higher mysteries of philosophy, so they were accustomed to employ geometric figures and numerical science for perfect philosophizing. This has been ingeniously achieved in this hierogrammatism <term>a sacred symbolic composition</term> partly through numbers and partly through geometric figures. Indeed, by weighing the nature of secret things more deeply, they found that **GOD** affects numbers, geometric figures (such as triangles, squares, and circles), and harmonic proportions in His operations. Surely, they could not exhibit these things in a better or more comprehensible way than through the said forms. Following them, Pythagoras and Plato—the wise disciples of wise masters—expressed all the greatest mysteries under these same forms. But to the matter at hand.

The first figure of this hierogrammatism is **A**, by which they signified the **Agathodaemon** <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent or a protective deity in Hellenistic-Egyptian belief</note>. It is an "ibiac" character, discovered by Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes/Thoth</note> from the gait and posture of the ibis bird. Concerning this, see many curious and most worthy considerations in the *Mystical Fabric of the Egyptian Alphabet* and in the specific hierogrammatism of this figure. For through this character, they first signify movement from the supernal to the infernal regions, as its pyramidal shape shows. Indeed, just as it held primacy among the letters, so it designated the primacy of this Spirit, whom the Egyptians called the Agathodaemon, or Good Spirit; and it is expressed as the **Agathodaemon of Egypt**, with the initial letters compressed into one.

<margin>
[Aga]thos
**A**
[Da]imon
<image-desc>A large capital letter 'A' with the right leg extended into a flail or whip with three lashes.</image-desc>
Figure of the Agathodaemon
</margin>

For here, besides the capital letters of the said words as I have mentioned, it also expresses the figure of that portion of Egypt which they everywhere call **Delta** <note>The Greek letter Δ</note>, or *alanti* in Coptic—that is, the "good field." They used to carry this character, usually composed of three stalks of either the *persea* tree or papyrus thyrsi adapted into the shape of the first alphabetic letter, before the statues of the Gods during the solemnities of the *Comasiae* <term>festive processions</term>. Please see what we have discussed more extensively regarding this monogram in the *Coptic Prodromus*, page 231, and in the hierogrammatisms concerning the *persea*, the sacred bier, and the character A; for neither the shortness of time nor the bulk of this work permits every detail to be repeated here. Let it suffice that we have indicated here that this character is the symbol of the Agathodaemon, having demonstrated it more fully elsewhere. Therefore, the character of the Agathodaemon is placed in the first position to show his rule over the lower and sensible world, which is beautifully expressed by the staff <note>The flail or whip shown in the margin</note> attached to one of the legs of the character.

...[character]; also, the character is not upright but prostrate. By this, they indicated that the **Agathodaemon’s** <term>Agathodaemon: literally the "Good Spirit," often depicted in Egyptian-themed Renaissance texts as a serpent or a protective deity</term> rule was not absolute (for they indicated absolute rule through symbols placed in an upright position), but vicarious or dependent upon the direction of a higher Divinity. This dependency they denoted through prostrate symbols, as will be shown more extensively in the following sections; but for now, let us turn our pen to interpreting the remaining symbols.

<margin>What is denoted by the 3 circles.</margin>
<image-desc>Three circles arranged horizontally: OOO</image-desc> By the three circles is understood the influence and dominion of the triform Divinity, appearing under the form of the Agathodaemon, over the specific presiding powers of the three Worlds: the Empyrean <note>the highest, most spiritual heaven of fire and light</note>, the Sidereal <note>the realm of the stars and planets</note>, and the Elemental <note>the terrestrial realm of the four elements</note>. These are denoted by three circles because of the perfect analogy—which will be discussed later—that each world holds with the supreme and supra-mundane circle of the Deity. By the transverse rod and the three squares, we understand the dominion and influence of that same triform Divinity which, through the mediation of the three "genial" <note>pertaining to "genii" or guiding spirits</note> worlds, acts upon the three corporeal and material worlds.

<margin>What is denoted by the 3 □ □ □</margin>
<image-desc>Three squares arranged horizontally: □ □ □</image-desc> These material worlds are those which the philosophers call "hylaeic" <term>hylaeic: from the Greek word "hyle," meaning matter or substance</term>. The first is the world of airy bodies, the second of aquatic bodies, and the third of terrestrial bodies. They are marked by three squares, both because of the similarity of squares to corporeal things (as will be explained later), and because of the composition of the four elements from which they exist. Furthermore, by the three circles, the figure of the triple World is indicated—the Empyrean, Sidereal, and Elemental—into which the supreme Divinity exerts its power, goodness, and beauty. Thus say the Egyptians in "Aristotle," Book 11, chapters 3 and 4: 

<margin>The Egyptian Philosophy of Aristotle.</margin>
<note>Kircher is quoting the "Theology of Aristotle," a Neoplatonic text actually based on Plotinus that was widely attributed to Aristotle during the Renaissance.</note> 
*The human mind itself, when it has perceived the intellectual sphere, reports to us that it is the first created work, distinguished by the highest beauty, effortless and unafflicted; indeed, it is joyful in its own light, and contains within itself substances exultantly flowing forth from other essences. Of these, the planet Jupiter is the primary exemplar of all its beings; nor indeed is it placed nowhere, but in another secondary sphere, which is nonetheless good, illustrious, and perpetual, and filled with the image of that first sphere. Wherefore it is also fitting for it to be good and absolute, since it is a metatype <note>a derivative or secondary type</note> and similar to the archetype. Again: this lowest world is similar to the celestial one; just as the celestial is perpetual through life, essence, and causative goodness, so this world is in some way perpetual through continuous successive generation. Since all our life is a likeness of the higher, it is continued from that continuous sphere by the supreme principle. And in the following chapter: Since, therefore, the infinite light of the Prince of essences is never corrupted, it will also never cease to illuminate the super-celestial sphere, and that sphere the celestial; therefore also this secondary Lord of the lowest world always exists, as if the first image of that primary Prince. And although the Prince of the higher world differs little from the lower, he nonetheless strives to preserve it; the preserver of the intellectual world is the primeval light; but of the celestial world it is the super-celestial or Genial world; and of this lowest sensible world, it is that middle celestial world. All, however, are preserved and consist by the power of the first Author, who supports and sustains them by the strength of his administration, as one who adorns him upon whom the others depend.*

# -> INTERPRETATION. <-

In the motion of the Elements, a twofold position of lines must be considered, corresponding to the twofold placement of the Elements. **Earth** and **Water**, being opposites, occupy the base and the side opposite to it in the hieroglyphic square; they always obtain a position that is flat, or—as mathematicians say—parallel to the earth or the Horizon, one placed above the other. **Air** and **Fire**, however, because they tend upward, constitute the sides in the hieroglyphic square, standing <note>original: "ἐγγὺς τὰς ἀρχὰς", meaning "near the origins"</note> upon the previous lines. These perfectly declare the nature of air and fire tending upward; and thus the qualities of the four Elements are aptly expressed through the four sides of the square. All of these matters will be explained at length in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry*. 

<image-desc>
A square diagram representing the four elements. 
The top side is labeled "Water".
The bottom side is labeled "Earth".
The left side is labeled "Fire".
The right side is labeled "Air".
</image-desc>

Since the sun, traversing the Zodiac, most strongly incites the mixture of elemental or compound bodies and disposes them toward the generation of things, they [the Egyptians] signaled the year through three squares quite appropriately. According to the witness of Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>, the year was divided by the Egyptians into three parts: namely, Spring, Summer, and Winter. These parts were denoted by the three squares, just as the four months or four signs of the Zodiac that made up each third of the year were denoted by the four sides. For through these "twelfth-parts" <note>the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> the divine sun—that **Osiris**, the **Agathodaemon** <term>Agathodaemon: the "Good Spirit," a protective deity often associated with the sun and life-giving force</term> of Egypt—passing through, excites the elements to the production of all things. 

<image-desc>

The second square contains 6 at the top, 8 at the bottom, 5 on the left, and 7 on the right.

</image-desc>

And Horus <note>Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on hieroglyphics</note> does not differ from this interpretation of ours with these words: <note>original: "ἔτος τὸ ἐνιαυτὸν γράφοντες, τέταρτον ἀρούρας γράφουσιν· ἔστι δὲ μεῖζον τῆς ἡ ἀρούρα πηχῶν ἑκατον βαλόμενοι τὸ ἔτος αὐτῶν, τετάρτον λέγουσι. &c."</note>

<margin>
How did the Egyptians denote the year?
</margin>

> *When signifying the current year, they write a fourth part of an **aroura** <term>aroura: a classical Egyptian unit of land area</term>. Now, an **aroura** or "Field" is a measure of land encompassing one hundred cubits. And they do this because from one rising of **Sothis** <note>the star Sirius, whose rising marked the Egyptian New Year</note> to the next, a fourth part of a day is interspersed.*

For since the Solar year is completed in 365 days, the Egyptians intercalated a redundant day every fourth year, which they call *epagomenon* <term>epagomenon: a "brought-in" or intercalary day added to the calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year</term>; for four quadrants of a day complete a full day. See the most curious details we provide regarding this hieroglyphic in the *Prodromus*, and later at length in our *Hieroglyphic Astronomy*. 

You see, therefore, how that supra-mundane, triform **Agathodaemon**—proceeding from that triad of intellectual worlds which is incorruptible, eternal, and indicated by circles—moves into the tetradic triad (the three sets of four) of the three elemental worlds. That is, it is carried from the simple and immutable into the angular form, subject to corruptions, representing the varied face of material mixing, which the square figure aptly represents. In order that these things may be clarified a little more deeply:

<image-desc>Three geometric diagrams of triangles are positioned in the left margin. The top diagram is an equilateral triangle labeled with 'A'. The middle diagram is an isosceles triangle labeled with 'B'. The bottom diagram is a scalene triangle labeled with 'C'.</image-desc>

They observed the triangle most highly; and within it, three specific conditions. For a triangle consists either of three equal sides and is called **equilateral** <note>original: "isopleuron"</note>, or of only two equal sides and is called **Isosceles**, or of three unequal sides and is called **Scalene**. Through the **Equilateral** triangle, they denoted the procession of the three-fold divinity into the corporeal world—which is why, according to the witness of Plato, it was dedicated to the Gods who preside over the physical World. Through the **Isosceles**, they denoted the procession of that same divinity into the World of the stars. Through the **Scalene**, which has three unequal angles (the first being a right angle, the second being two-thirds of a right angle, and the third being one-third), they denoted the World of alteration, which is the elementary world <note>The "elementary world" refers to the Earthly realm where the four elements—earth, water, air, fire—constantly change and decay</note>. However, through the **Circle**, they aptly denoted the solitary, triune nature of GOD, as will be discussed later. How they showed this order and the series of the generation of all things is deduced beautifully and at length by *Alcinous the Platonist*.

<margin>
Alcinous.
ch. 11.
</margin>
Now, since there are two things from which the world is constituted—body and soul—the former is visible and tangible, while the latter is neither visible nor tangible, and the power and constitution of each are different. For the body itself is joined together from fire, earth, water, and air. Indeed, these four elements, which certainly had no order before, were formed by the creator of the world into the **Pyramid** <note>Also known as the tetrahedron</note>, the **Cube**, the **Octahedron**, the **Icosahedron**, and beyond all these, the **Dodecahedron**. For as much as Matter took on the figure of the **Pyramid**, it became **fire**; because this shape is most suited for cutting and dividing, consists of fewer triangles, and is therefore the rarest <note>meaning the least dense</note>. Insofar as it became an **Octahedron**, it simultaneously took on the quality of **air**, just as water took on the form of the **Icosahedron**. However, he attributed the figure of the **Cube** to the **earth**, as it is the most solid and firm of all. But the **Dodecahedron** he adapted to the **Universe** itself. Furthermore, the nature of planes reaches toward the primary principles more than all these things, since planes are prior to solids. Truly, the two "progenitors" of the nature of planes are two most beautiful right-angled triangles: one **Scalene**, the other **Isosceles**. And when the **Scalene** has one right angle, another containing two-thirds of a right angle <note>60 degrees</note>, and the remaining part a third of the same <note>30 degrees</note>, I call this the primary triangle. This **Scalene** triangle is the element of the **pyramid**, the **octahedron**, and the **icosahedron**. For the **Pyramid** is constituted from four triangles having all sides equal; any one of which can be distributed into six **Scalene** triangles of the kind just mentioned. The **Octahedron** is made from eight, each of which is similarly divided into six **Scalenes**. The same applies to the **Icosahedron**, which is made from twenty. The other triangle (I mean the **Isosceles**) is fit for constituting the cube. For four triangles of this type, joined together, complete a square, just as six squares complete a cube. God used the **Dodecahedron**, however, for the **Universe**. Because the twelve signs are seen in the heavens in the **Zodiac**, each of which is cut into thirty parts; just as in the dodecahedron composed of twelve pentagons, each of these is divided into five triangles, and each of those contains six triangles; thus in the whole dodecahedron, three hundred and sixty triangles are found, which is exactly the number of sections in the **Zodiac**. Therefore, matter, expressed by God through these figures, was moved: first indeed in rough traces without order, then brought into order by Him, according to that ratio which all things obtain among themselves in that joining. Yet these do not remain separate in one place, but are in perpetual agitation, and bring the same to matter. Since by the circuit of the world...

# INTERPRETATION. 427

...driven by the constriction of their surroundings, they are moved by alternating pulses: those parts that are thinner move toward the region of the denser ones. For this reason, nothing at all is left empty or void of body; and the permanent inequality in them causes a shaking, since matter is agitated by these things, and these things by matter.

Truly, how Plato—following the mind of the Egyptians—composed the four regular figures <note>These are the Platonic solids, the geometric building blocks of the universe: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, and icosahedron</note> from scalene triangles where one angle is a right angle, another is two-thirds of a right angle, and the third is one-third of a right angle (that is, a triangle whose angles are 90, 60, and 30 degrees), is a matter that has remained hidden from his commentators until now. We have considered it our task to demonstrate this here through geometric reasoning. First, they described an equilateral triangle **ABC**, from whose angles **A**, **B**, and **C** they drew three perpendicular lines, **AD**, **FC**, and **EB**. Thus, the equilateral triangle was divided into 6 scalene triangles, all equal and similar, as the numbers show. Each of these has one right angle, while the others are 60 and 30 degrees. Specifically, those meeting at the center point **S** are 60 degrees; those ending at points **A**, **B**, and **C** of the triangle are 30 degrees; and finally, those consisting of the middle sides at points **F**, **D**, and **E** are 90 degrees. Their sides are allotted in the same proportion as the numbers 3, 4, and 5; the mystery of which will be explained later <note>This refers to the Pythagorean triple (3, 4, 5), which was considered sacred in ancient Egyptian and Greek mathematics</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an equilateral triangle ABC subdivided into six smaller triangles by perpendicular lines AD, FC, and EB, which meet at a center point S. The smaller triangles are numbered 1 through 6. Below it is a right-angled triangle labeled P with vertices B (at the right angle), C, and A.</image-desc>

<margin>What is the genetic triangle?</margin>
Therefore, they called a triangle of this kind sometimes the **genetic** triangle, sometimes the *generative* <note>original Greek: γονιμὸν (gonimon)</note>, or the **nuptial figure**, because it was the principle of the generation of all sublunary things <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earthly world beneath the moon, which is subject to change, growth, and decay</note>. They did so in this manner: by the base **BA** they denoted the passive principle of things, namely moisture, or **Isis**; by the perpendicular **CB** standing upon **AB**, they suggested the active principle of things, namely heat or **Osiris**, the masculine power; and by the hypotenuse **AC**, they denoted **Horus**, who is composed of both—as was shown at length in Book 3. Now let us see how from triangles of this kind—the Isosceles and the Scalene—acting as first principles, the four regular figures are produced, and consequently the four elements of which they are symbols. In considering these, two steps must be observed, in this manner:

<margin>What is the symbol of Earth?</margin>
They constructed the **cube**, the symbol of Earth, in this way: first, they quadrupled the Isosceles triangle **a b c**, and the square **a b e d** resulted; this, multiplied by 6, constituted the cube **a b e d i f g**. Thus, according to the testimony of Proclus <note>Proclus was a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the mystical properties of geometry</note>, the Isosceles triangle was the first principle of earth, while the square was the proximate principle.

<image-desc>A perspective drawing of a cube with vertices labeled with lowercase letters: a, b, d, e, f, g. Internal lines show the cube's structure and diagonals.</image-desc>

<margin>What is the symbol of Fire?</margin>
Furthermore, they constructed the **pyramid**, or **tetrahedron**, the symbol of fire, as follows. Since the tetrahedron consists of 4 equilateral triangles, each of which (as shown shortly before) is in turn composed of six scalene triangles, 4 multiplied by 6 produced 24 **genetic scalenes** (for so we shall call this kind of triangle hereafter). Thus, the four-sided pyramid denoted not only fire but also the whole universe, into which the fiery force secretly diffused itself. This is how they brought it into bodily form.

<meta>This page continues the geometric and mystical analysis of the five Platonic solids, which the author attributes to ancient Egyptian wisdom filtered through Plato and Pythagoras. # BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

<margin>
How the tetrahedron is made.
</margin>
By dividing the equilateral triangle <note>original: "Isopleùrum"</note> **ACD** in half, they formed two scalene triangles **ABC** and **BAD**. By these, they signified the procession of the Divinity from the Archetypal World into the World of changes and mutations—which was represented by the scalene triangle described. Dividing these scalene triangles in half again, they produced the isosceles triangles **BFA** and **BEA**, which serve as indicators of the divine influence through the influx of the stars. They divided these isosceles triangles once more through the line **FE**, producing four equilateral triangles **AFE**, **FEB**, **EBD**, and **FCB**. When these were folded together, they formed the first of all solid bodies, the *tetrahedron* <note>A four-faced pyramid</note>. Thus, the triad <note>the number three</note> passes into the tetrad <note>the number four</note>; that is, from the figure of a triangle arises a solid of four planes, or a three-sided pyramid, and from three corners, twelve angles are born. Thus, in this single figure, they possessed the entire sequence of the whole world, both sidereal <note>relating to the stars</note> and elemental.

<margin>
Mystical Philosophy in the Tetrahedron.
</margin>
For the triangle, through its triad, expressed the generation of things (as will be shown later); the four sides represented the elements. Three and four joined together gave the number seven <note>the septenary</note> of the sidereal world, visible in the circles of the seven planets. The twelve angles denoted the dimensions of the <term>Aplanes<gloss>The sphere of the fixed stars, specifically the twelve signs of the Zodiac</gloss></term>. The figure was sharp and pyramidal, by which they suggested fire or heat—the active principle of the generation of things, which permeates the elements, the planets, the Zodiac, and in a word, everything.

[A geometric diagram of a large equilateral triangle labeled with vertices A, B, and C. A perpendicular line descends from vertex A to point D on the base. The triangle is further subdivided by horizontal and oblique lines passing through points labeled F and E, creating smaller internal triangles.]

<margin>
What the Octahedron denotes.
</margin>
Furthermore, since the *octahedron* <note>An eight-faced solid</note> is composed of eight equilateral triangles, each of which is again made up of six "genetic" scalene triangles, multiplying 8 by 6 gave 48 scalenes, which constitute the octahedron as a symbol of Air. Finally, since the *icosahedron* <note>A twenty-faced solid</note> consists of 20 equilateral triangles, and each of those consists of 6 scalenes, multiplying these by 20 gives 120 scalenes. From these principles, the icosahedron is formed, and it was therefore adopted as the symbol of Water. We have, then, 24 genetic scalenes in the tetrahedron pyramid, 48 in the octahedron, and finally 120 in the icosahedron. By comparing these, *Plato*—taught by the *Egyptians* and *Pythagoreans*—came to understand the proportion of the elements that each maintains toward the other. 

<margin>
What the Icosahedron denotes.
</margin>
For because fire, air, and water have the scalene triangle as their first principle, while the earth has the isosceles triangle, he concluded that the earth could by no means be dissolved and transformed into the other three—the Earth, I say, compared to the remaining three. But the three—air, water, and fire—could be dissolved and transformed into one another in practice because they share a common genetic principle.

<margin>
What the Cube denotes.
</margin>
He also indicated that the same proportion existing between the numbers of triangles (from which the three elements consist as their first principles)—namely 24, 48, and 120—is the same proportion found in the density and rarity of the substances of fire, air, and water. Specifically, fire is twice as rare as air, just as water is four times thinner than the same; and they relate to each other as the 24 scalenes of the tetrahedron do to the 48 of the octahedron and the 120 scalenes of the icosahedron. The *cube*, however, is the symbol of Earth; since it is composed of a heterogeneous source—namely, the isosceles triangle—so...

# INTERPRETATION

...he also judged that the cube <note>the symbol for Earth</note> could not be transformed into the remaining three elements. Yet, he recognized that beneath the cube, which serves as the symbol of Earth, there lies a certain harmony that governs the entire harmony of the world. He discerned this from its constituent parts—namely, from the six planes, twelve lines, eight solid angles, and twenty-four triangles <note>original: "planis"; here referring to the constituent triangles that make up the faces</note> of which the cube consists. These represent the harmonic proportions: 6 to 12 is a double ratio, the *diapason* <term>diapason: an octave</term>; 
<margin>
The Cube contains the harmony of the whole.
</margin>
6 to 8 is a sesquialter ratio, the *diapente* <term>diapente: a perfect fifth</term>; 12 to 8 is a sesquitertian ratio, the *diatessaron* <term>diatessaron: a perfect fourth</term>; 8 to 24 is a triple ratio, the *diapason-diapente* <term>an octave plus a fifth</term>; and finally, 6 to 24 is a quadruple ratio, the *disdiapason* <term>a double octave</term>. 

But since, besides these four solid regular figures, they saw that a fifth could also be constructed from pentagons—where three joined together would form a solid angle and thus complete a figure of twelve bases, or a *dodecahedron*—they sought to ensure that the bodies existing in nature corresponded entirely to the mathematical forms. These forms, which the Pythagoreans (following the Egyptians) called the primary principles of natural things, were assigned to the universe. They ascribed this dodecahedron to the whole, not as some believe to a "fifth essence" <note>the aether or quintessence</note> above the moon, but to the fifth great body of the universe composed of the four primary simple bodies. In this way: they saw that 
<margin>
The Dodecahedron denotes the universe.
</margin>
twelve equilateral pentagons <note>original: "pentagonos isopleuros"</note>, each of which was divided into five isosceles triangles, could be joined together so that no vacuum remained between the junctions of the sides. Furthermore, these joined at the center of a circle to form twelve pentagonal pyramids. Sensing here the mystery of the universe, they first related the twelve sides of the dodecahedron to the twelve seats of the Zodiac, which they called the boundary of the entire universe. For these seats, as if by the radiant influx of the stars joined at the center of the earth, constituted as many five-sided pyramids—a symbol of the twelve inner chambers <note>original: "penetralium"</note> through which the Divine Powers <note>original: "Numina"</note> flow into the lower world. Concerning the mystical reasoning of these, as we have already dealt with on page 177, the reader may consult that section. 

Therefore, just as these twelve five-sided pyramids, connected by their vertices at the center of the earth, are so aptly joined that they leave no intermediate vacuum, so the life of the world is diffused through the Divine Powers that preside over the dodecahedra of the Zodiac through all things, such that there is nothing that does not participate in it. Again, just as the cube (the symbol of Earth) is composed of isosceles triangles, so too are the pentagons of the dodecahedron. By this mystery, they noted a certain hidden consensus between the male Zodiac and the female Earth, from whose union all things were said to be born.

For just as from the bisection of the isosceles triangles in the cube and the pentagons of the dodecahedron, scalene triangles are born, so from the earth as a passive principle, and from the motion of the Planets under the twelve signs of the Firmament (which are like an active principle), an influx is made upon the earth. From this, "genetic scalenes" <note>triangles of generation</note> are born—that is, all the diverse kinds of beings in the sensible world.

You see, therefore, how they proceeded from the first and simplest lines and figures to the birth of bodies and the secret of all corporeal nature. And just as they denoted the triune divinity by the circle (tri-one by center, radius, and circumference), 
<margin>
The equilateral triangle denotes God as Creator.
</margin>
so by the equilateral triangle they noted the triune divinity exhibiting itself in the works of creation, as has been said; and indeed the circle...

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISKS

<margin>
What the
Scalene Triangle
signifies.

...it produces from itself, as it were the completion and the greatest of all polygons consisting of infinite sides <note>The author is likely referring to the circle as the limit of polygons</note>; thus it secretly signifies the solitary unit in trinity. The triangle, however, is the beginning of all generation, the father of all remaining things, whether they be polygonal figures or solid bodies, as was shown just before. Closely following this is the **isosceles** triangle <note>a triangle with two equal sides</note>, a symbol of the earth and the firmament. Next follows the **right-angled scalene** triangle, used to indicate the highest mysteries of generative nature. As stated above, the scalene triangle consists of three unequal sides and as many angles: one right angle and two acute. By the right angle, they represented the constant and immutable law of nature in its operation; by the remaining two, they indicated the ratios of change: one representing the greater "sub-double" motion of growth <note>original: *subduplum*; a 1:2 ratio</note>, and the third representing the "sub-sesquialter" ratio of diminution and division <note>original: *subsesquialterum*; a 2:3 ratio</note>. Furthermore, by the lower line which constitutes the base of the triangle, they signified—on the testimony of **Plutarch**—the passive principle of things, specifically the Earth or **Isis**. By the perpendicular line standing straight upon it, they signified the active principle of things: form, **Osiris**, or the Sun. Finally, by the hypotenuse <note>original: *hypotenusam* or *subtensam*</note> joining both lines, they cleverly indicated the "composite" reality, **Horus**, the son born from both. (See folio 201).

<image-desc>A right-angled triangle diagram. The vertical leg is labeled "Form: Osiris", the horizontal base is labeled "Matter: Isis", and the hypotenuse is labeled "The Composite: Horus".</image-desc>

But let us now see the secret of the whole world hidden within the figure of the aforementioned scalene triangle; its sides relate to one another as 3, 4, and 5, as is clear in the figure. There you see the **equilateral** triangle <note>original: *isopleurum*</note> under the number three, and the **isosceles** under the number four, which two constitute the square and then the cube. Furthermore, 3, 4, and 5 joined together make 12, the "dodecahedron of nature." Just as numbers are contained within numbers, lines within lines, and figures within figures, they secretly prefigured by these means that "all things are in all things." Moreover, side AB (3) multiplied by itself makes 9; side BC (4) multiplied by itself makes 16; joined together, these make exactly as much as side AC (5) multiplied by itself, namely 25. This is a massive secret in mathematics and fertile with infinite discoveries; it was first found by the **Egyptians**, but was published by **Pythagoras** under his own name. By this "genetic triangle," they indicated the origin <note>original: *genesin*</note> of worldly bodies and indeed of the entire universe through subtle reasoning; but we shall treat this at length in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry*.

...are composed of matter and form, they aptly indicated these through just as many generative triangles <note>original: *triangulos geneticos*</note>; they arranged these triangles into one larger triangle to show the fivefold generation in the world. Since we have shown all these things most extensively from various monuments of hidden writings—both in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, in the treatise on *Hieroglyphic Geometry*, and in our own hieroglyphic descriptions of the triangle, square, and circle—we did not wish to be more verbose here.

Among the five scalene triangles, another figure occurs <image-desc>A symbol consisting of a circle with a vertical line extending downwards from the bottom edge, intersected by a horizontal crossbar</image-desc>, by which they wished to indicate nothing other than the progression of the Divine Mind through innumerable circles and figures. This is the descent through the sphere of Spirits <note>original: *Geniorum orbem*</note> into the sidereal and elemental world, and finally from this lowest level—indicated by rectilinear figures—a return back into the sphere of divinity, that is, into itself. <margin>What the circle-like figure signifies.</margin> This present figure aptly indicates this process by a straight line attached to a circle. But lest I seem to have fabricated anything, let us hear Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher</note> on Plato, chapter 14, who so beautifully describes these things according to the mind of the Egyptians that he seems to have had this very figure in view. Here, where he treats at length the progression of the divine mind into the corporeal world through various circles, he finally concludes his discourse with these words:

> Finally, from all the revolutions and turnings, the absolute number and time will be completed when the stars, reaching the same point, receive such an order that if any straight line were considered from the highest circle down to the earth according to a perpendicular, the centers of all things would be seen within it.

Finally, there occurs the figure of the bier <image-desc>A symbol resembling a squared horizontal bracket or a low table frame with legs</image-desc>, by which they indicated the honor and reverence they owed to this supreme Deity. This figure is called the sacred bier, in Egyptian <term>†cλH</term> <note>transliterated as *Tisle*</note>. To make the reason for its meaning more clear, we begin from its very origins. It is known from Clement of Alexandria, Book 6 of the *Stromata*, and from Apuleius's *Metamorphoses*, that in the Isiac processions, four images—which they called the "four letters"—were carried about. The instrument by which these were carried was fashioned in the shape of a rectangular parallelogram, so that it might correspond in every way to the mystery of the four letters. It had slightly extended opposite legs so that the bier could be more easily received upon the shoulders of the bearers; an instrument almost identical to those used today for carrying out the dead. The form commonly found on obelisks shows well enough that it was made in two ways: <margin>What the bier denotes.</margin> first, as a bare rectangle upon which they placed both the sacred images and the hidden chest of the sacred objects; second, as a chest inserted into a rectangle, according to which form it is likewise presented to be viewed. We read that this instrument was so common among the Egyptians that, for the mystical reasons of the "quaternary" <note>the number four</note>, they included it in the register of hieroglyphs, just like all the other instruments that served in any way for sacrifices and ceremonies. For by the four sides, they indicated the four-part region of the world, or the four elements, into which they believed the four Spirits—whom they carried placed above—poured out their power. ### BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK

...of the same chest were stored; namely, the phallus of Osiris made of fig-wood, the ribbons of Isis, the <note>original: ἀείαπλα & καὶ πέταλα</note> ornaments and metal leaves of Horus, and similar absurdities held in great price and esteem among them. From this it was called the "sacred chest," a container for sacred objects, as Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek lexicographer</note> testifies: <note>original: κίσται ἱεραὶ</note> "sacred chests," and those carrying it were called <note>original: κιστηφόροι</note> "chest-bearers."

<margin>What is the Sacred Chest?</margin>
It was called "sacred" because it was covered and not exposed to the eyes of the uninitiated. Apuleius, in his *Metamorphoses* <note>Also known as "The Golden Ass," a 2nd-century Roman novel</note>, teaches us that this chest was carried around with the greatest solemnity, placed upon a bier, using these words: *Furthermore, the chest, capable of holding secrets, deeply concealing the hidden things of a magnificent religion.* It is also called a "mystery" by Suidas: <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ μύειν τὸ στόμα</note> "from the closing of the mouth," because it is fitting for those who hear and see the divine ceremonies and the secrets of religion to seal their mouths and not reveal them to any mortal. Indeed, to increase the grandeur, not just anyone but the most prominent men were chosen to carry it; so much so that Lampridius and Aelius Spartianus <note>Authors of the *Augustan History*</note> say that the Emperor Commodus, having once been initiated into these rites, did not disdain to submit his shoulders to this ridiculous burden; while he practiced the rites of Isis, he shaved his head and carried the statue of Anubis. Hence, as Plutarch also testifies, it was customary for a phallus to be carried behind the <term>Kanephoroi<gloss>Basket-bearers; young women of noble birth who carried ceremonial baskets</gloss></term>, and for a phallic song to be sung. These Kanephoroi were virgins carrying a basket on their heads, in which all the first fruits were placed; but let us hear Aristophanes in the *Acharnians* describing them aptly:

<margin>Aristophanes.</margin>
->Step forward a little, basket-bearer<-
->Let Xanthias set the phallus upright<-
->And I, following, will sing the phallic song.<-

->Where the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on the text</note> says: In Athens, noble virgins carried baskets during the Dionysia, in which there were baskets made of gold upon which they placed the first fruits of all things.<-

Furthermore, what kind of images they carried in this type of bier is described by Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who wrote extensively on pagan rites</note>; since we cite his words throughout this work on pages 121 and 128, the curious reader may consult them there.

<margin>What is a Bier?</margin>
Therefore, since the bier was intended for these specific sacred uses—both because of its mystical shape and for other purposes—it found a place among the hieroglyphic symbols; thus, when they wished to signify that Gods and Divinities were to be celebrated with due honor, they would paint this bier. The origin and meaning of the bier are thus clear.

However, so that everything we have said so far about the "Genial World" <note>the world of generation and procreation</note>, the actions of the priests appropriate to it, the public processions, and the use of biers within them may gain full authority, I shall here add the words of Apuleius from Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*, in which he describes these things so exactly that he might seem to have been present at them:

And in this, they alluded to the bifurcated flame emerging from the head of the all-formed one <note>referring to a deity with many forms, likely Serapis or a composite deity</note>. The second was similar in dress, but carried in both hands altars—that is, the "helps"—by which...*

...gave the proper name of the Supreme Goddess to the auxiliary <term>providence</term> <note>Kircher refers to "Providentia," seeing the Egyptian gods as manifestations of divine foresight</note>. And a statue of this kind occurs on the <note>original: "senniferteo"</note> obelisk, which is the Flaminian obelisk, around its base. This indeed alludes to the images which are placed in the Hieroglyphic Schemes I, II, and III, notable for their palms and <term>handled crosses</term> <note>original: "crux ansata"; the Ankh symbol</note>; for the Egyptians, this handled cross is the same as the caduceus of Mercury. A fourth person showed the sign of equity: a fashioned left hand with the palm stretched out, which, by its natural "laziness"—being endowed with no cleverness or skill—seemed more suited to equity than the right hand. This same person carried a small golden vessel rounded in the fashion of a breast, from which he offered libations of milk. You may see traces of this everywhere in the <term>Bembine Table</term> <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet of the 1st century AD covered in Egyptian-style imagery</note>. A fifth carried a golden winnowing fan heaped with golden twigs; and another carried an amphora. Without delay, the Gods, deigning to walk with human feet, move forward: here one raises the terrifying, high neck of a dog <note>Anubis</note>; another is the messenger of the worlds above and below, now with a dark face, now a golden one, held high, carrying a caduceus in his left hand and shaking a green palm branch in his right. Immediately following his footsteps was a bull <note>The Apis bull</note> raised into a standing position. There was also a second image of the omnipotent Goddess; one of the blessed ministry carried this, resting it upon his shoulders with a theatrical gait. Another carried the chest capable of secrets, deeply concealing the hidden things of a magnificent religion. Yet another carried in his happy bosom the venerable effigy of the Supreme Divinity, which was not like any beast, bird, or wild animal—nor even like man himself—but was a thing to be revered for its very novelty, a clever invention: an ineffable proof of a deeper religion that must be covered in great silence (perhaps a winged globe). Furthermore, in this same manner, there was a small urn fashioned of shining gold, most skillfully hollowed out with a rounded bottom, and decorated on the outside with the wondrous images of the Egyptians. Its mouth was not raised very high but extended into a spout, protruding in a long stream; on the other side, receding far back with a wide curve, was a handle upon which sat an Asp in a twisted knot, its scaly neck swollen and raised high. Thus far Apuleius <note>Kircher is quoting from Book 11 of *The Golden Ass*</note>. This is the very procession we see today most elegantly engraved on a fragment of a column found in the <term>Medici Gardens</term> <note>The Villa Medici in Rome</note>, in the region of that side of the Obelisk which faces the hanging gardens and the Pincian Way; I would have gladly inserted it here, had the narrowness of time not delayed my intent.

Certainly, it can be clear only to one who has some knowledge of Egyptian affairs that Apuleius, being an initiate of the Egyptian rites, has here truly and properly described the sacred ceremonies and processions of the Priests usually celebrated during the solemnities of the Gods.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological interpretation of Egyptian symbols, moving from the description of the sacred procession and specific deities to a metaphysical discussion of geometric forms as representations of the Divine. It connects the abstract mathematical concepts of the infinite to the symbolic "schemes" found on the obelisks.</meta>

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

...center, nature, *and the all of all things*. For since the <term>divine essence</term> <note>original: "essentia diuina"; the fundamental, unchanging nature of God</note> is infinite, a Circle will rightly be infinite; and since it is a square, it will rightly be an infinite square; and since it is a triangle, it will rightly be an infinite triangle; and since it is a line and a center, these will rightly be infinite in God. Therefore, the circle, the sphere, the square, the triangle, the line, and the center are exactly the same in God. Thus, a point will be a line, a triangle, a square, a circle, and a sphere; all of which you will find demonstrated by geometric reasoning on *folio 383*. 

For since the diameter of a circle is a straight line, and the circumference is a curved line larger than the diameter, it follows that the circumference of the "greatest circle"—one so large that nothing larger can exist—will be the least curved, and therefore the most straight. Thus, the greatest will coincide with the smallest, and the circumference and the diameter of the circle will be the same <note>Kircher is employing the "coincidence of opposites," a philosophical concept where in the infinite, contradictory properties like "straight" and "curved" become one</note>. Furthermore, since a diameter rotated around a stationary center describes a triangle at any point, and when fully rotated describes a circle, if the diameter is infinite, then the triangle and the circle it describes will also be infinite. 

It is well-established that a triangle with one infinite side cannot have other sides that are smaller; and since any part of the infinite is itself infinite, the sides of an infinite triangle must necessarily be infinite. And because there cannot be multiple "infinites" of the same kind, reason dictates that the infinite cannot be composed of multiple lines. Although it is the greatest, truest, uncomposed, and simplest triangle—and because it is a "truest" triangle it cannot exist without three lines—one infinite line will necessarily be three lines, and three lines will be one most simple line, in which one angle is three. You should not think of this kind of "greatest triangle" as a physical quantity, nor as being composed of sides and angles; rather, in it, the infinite line and the angle are one and the same, so that the line is the angle, because the triangle is the line. All these things are contrary to the shapes we perceive with our senses or measure as quantities. 

The same must be understood regarding the circle, the square, and polygons. From this you may understand the subtle genius of the *Egyptians*, and what a wonderful Theology they wished to hint at through a certain hidden allegory in this first <term>hieroglyphic scheme</term> <note>original: "hieroglyphico Schematismo"; Kircher’s term for the complex symbolic diagrams he used to interpret Egyptian thought</note>, by means of those circles, squares, triangles, and lines.

Therefore, having explained the first Scheme, nothing remains except that we place before the eyes of the *Curious Reader* a summary of all that has perhaps been shown more diffusely until now, presented through a certain ideal discourse denoted by hieroglyphics.

# INTERPRETATION.

# Inscription of the Obelisk: SCHEME I.
## The Eastern Part.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a fragment of an Egyptian obelisk, labeled "Pars Orientalis." The image is divided into three main horizontal registers within a triangular top. 

At the very top, within the apex of the triangle, is a winged sun disk containing a hawk-headed figure (labeled 1) holding a scepter and an ankh. Below this, in the main triangular field, are three figures: on the left, a kneeling priest-like figure (B) with a bird head; in the center, a seated deity on a throne (A) with a complex headdress; and on the right, a standing figure (C) offering something to the deity. Letters D, G, K, F, E, H, and I are scattered around these figures.

The middle register shows a large, detailed hawk or ibis standing on a pedestal. It is numbered with 1 (above its head), 2 (on its wing), 3 (along its back), and 4 (above its head/beak). To the right of its head is a coiled serpent figure (numbered 6 and 7).

The bottom register consists of a rectangular panel filled with smaller symbolic boxes and hieroglyphic-like icons, including a horizontal eye (a), various geometric shapes, a scepter (h), several triangles (f), and lines of stylized text or patterns. Letters a through k are used to label specific elements within this grid.</image-desc>
