# This is the reading of the Ideal Concept.

<margin>Hierogram I.</margin>
<margin>I. The Archetypal World.</margin>
¹ To the triform Deity <term>Hemphta</term> <note>A name used by Kircher for the supreme creator god, likely derived from Kneph or Ptah</note>, the First Mind and mover of all things; ³ to the Second Mind, the craftsman; ² to the all-shaping spirit; triune, eternal, ⁴ lacking beginning and end; the Origin of the secondary Gods. This Deity, from its solitary <term>Monad</term> <note>The absolute unity or "The One"</note>—acting as a center and an apex—diffused into the breadth of the worldly pyramid. Out of its own goodness, it first bestowed upon the intelligible World of the secondary Gods the guardianship of the East; and, marked with the character of the triform divinity, it established the guardians of the triple World.

<margin>Hierogram II.</margin>
<margin>II. The Angelic World.</margin>
⁵ The supreme <term>Genius</term> <note>A protective or guiding spirit, comparable to an angel in this philosophical system</note> in his order and choir, shares in the power received from Hemphta; through his followers, the <sup>EF</sup> Genii who are most obedient to his commands,³ he bestows a continuous influx upon the lower World <sup>HI</sup>. From this comes the <sup>K</sup> variety of all things; here is the origin in the lower World <sup>HI</sup> of things now being <sup>DE</sup> born, now <sup>GN</sup> perishing so that they may be born again. Thus, finally, human happiness is completed—an exemplar set before the priests to be imitated in their sacred rites.

<margin>Hierogram III.</margin>
<margin>III. The Sidereal World.</margin>
¹ Hemphta, from the center of his Monad ¹¹ into the <term>Dyad</term> <note>The number two, representing the first step away from unity toward multiplicity</note>, and from there through the Dyad—that is, the Angelic Minds—into the <term>Triad</term> <note>The number three</note>, diffused into the third world; that is, into the sensible <term>sidereal world</term> <note>The realm of the stars and planets</note>. He communicated himself to the supreme Osiris, who is the guardian of the solar world. This deity, having shared in the power of the Soul of the sidereal World, was established as the ¹ leader and moderator, the ² mover of the heavens. With the help of the sensible Gods (the planets), ⁶ he gives life to the entire World, which is marked with the character of the triform Deity; ⁷ he fertilizes it, and ⁷ enriches it.

<margin>Hierogram IV.</margin>
<margin>IV. The Elemental World.</margin>
⁴ The Monad, diffused through the <sup>b</sup> Dyad into the <sup>c</sup> Triad, and from this into the <sup>d</sup> <term>Tetrad</term> <note>The number four, representing the material elements of earth, air, fire, and water</note> <sup>IV</sup>—which is the fourth world, the <sup>e</sup> elemental world—propagates <sup>h</sup> its power and its <sup>i</sup> triple diffusion within it through the powerful <sup>g</sup> <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent in Egyptian-themed art, representing divine providence in nature</note>. This power extends <sup>f</sup> into the triple face of the Elemental World, or the worlds of <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Hyleos Mundos"; matter or the material substance of the universe</note>. From here, descending into the Sphere of generation <sup>f</sup>—which is distinguished by a fivefold order of beings—he stimulates all things toward <sup>f</sup> generation, ⁷ fertility, and ⁷ abundance. Finally, once the circular <sup>h</sup> appetite of his goodness is fulfilled, he returns from the <sup>k</sup> lowest mixture of the material worlds back into his solitary <sup>h</sup> Monad; a Deity to be worshipped and adored by all with divine cult and honor.

# INTERPRETATION
## OF SCHEME II.
### II. The Southern Side.

->*Which shows the diffusion of the Triform Deity into the Southern region of the World.*<-

The first diagram of the Southern side contains four hierograms <note>A "hierogram" is Kircher’s term for a sacred symbol or "priestly writing"</note> just as the previous one did; the first and third are the same as before, while the second and fourth are different. Just as they differ in appearance, they also signify something different from the others.

The first Hierogram is therefore the globe with three-circled wings <note>original Greek: *tri-kyklo-pteromorphos*</note>, a symbol of the **Triform Deity**. Since we have explained this at length in the preceding diagram, we refer the reader to that section.

<margin>Explanation of the Figure.</margin>
The second Hierogram is as follows: A primary female figure **A**, distinguished by a headdress or tiara in the shape of a basket filled with the fruit of the *persea* tree <term>persea</term> <note>A sacred Egyptian tree often confused by early modern scholars with the peach or laurel; it symbolized the heart or eternal life</note>, is depicted nude with swelling breasts. Her private parts, however, are covered by leggings, and her feet are joined together; she sits upon a variegated square seat **IK**. In her right hand **B** she holds a scourge <note>A ritual flail, often held by deities and Pharaohs as a symbol of power</note>, and in her left hand she holds a scepter **C** shaped like a **Cucupha** <term>Cucupha</term> <note>A staff topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, representing purity or divine power</note>. Assisting this figure are two statues **D** and **E**. The first, **E**, is in male form and nude, except for the private parts covered by a linen loincloth; his feet **H** are separated and positioned as if running. A headband covers his head, supporting a feathered cap **F**, in the middle of which a circle is placed. In his right hand, the statue holds a **Y-shaped** object **N**, and in his left he holds a **Tautic character** or "handled cross" **O** <term>Ankh</term> <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian Ankh as a form of the letter 'Tau,' symbolizing life or the world to come</note>. The other statue, **D**, is entirely nude with flowing hair and swelling breasts, representing a female; her head is marked by two forked feathers **F** with a circle between them. In her right hand **M**, she offers a basket-shaped headdress or tiara to the seated figure, while she holds her other hand pulled back. We shall now proceed to interpret what the ancient Egyptians intended by this hieroglyphic arrangement.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration contained within a triangular frame, depicting Egyptian-style figures and symbols labeled with letters and numbers. # INTERPRETATION.

<margin>What is the Hoopoe-headed Scepter?</margin>
<margin>Psellus on the Zoroastrian Oracles.</margin>
...those whom all and each of the southern region ordains, disposes, and moderates. And first indeed, through the first figure sitting on a square seat, they denoted one of the **Usiarchs** <term>Usiarchs</term> <note>From the Greek 'ousia' (essence) and 'archein' (to rule); these are principal spirits who govern the essential nature of things</note>, that is, the principal Genii. He is naked because he is removed from all contagion of earthly mixture; his private parts are visible <note>original: 'verendis operis visitur'</note> because he imparts the hidden mixtures of "seminal reasons" <note>A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of the 'seeds' or blueprints of all physical things</note> to all things through a ministry concealed from men. He wears a basket shaped like a *persea* fruit <term>persea-form</term> <note>The fruit of the persea tree, sacred in Egypt, which Kircher identifies as a symbol of divine abundance and the heart</note> in place of a tiara, to suggest the abundance which he confers. He holds a scourge in his right hand to drive away and dispel the **Typhonic force** <note>The destructive, chaotic power named after Typhon (the Greek equivalent of the Egyptian god Set)</note>—that is, all adversity—from the things committed to his care. The scepter which he holds in his left hand is **hoopoe-headed** <term>cucuphomorphon</term> <note>Topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, known in Egyptian lore as the 'Cucupha'; it symbolizes the variety of nature</note>, which is an index of the variety of things to be produced in the World. He sits upon a square and variegated seat to indicate the dominion and power which he holds over all things of that region subject to him. The remaining two figures signify attendant Genii of a lower order, whom the Egyptians call **Zone-spirits** <term>Zonęos</term> <note>Spirits that preside over specific zones or spheres of the cosmos</note>, according to the testimony of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century scholar who preserved ancient Orphic and Zoroastrian fragments</note>. They appear in male and female dress to show the active and passive principles of generation, for they are the presiding spirits over generation and incite things toward generating and producing. They also wear feathered caps <term>tutuli</term> on their heads to denote the promptness and speed of their will in obeying the commands of the prince-Usiarch, which they also demonstrate by their feet being set apart as if stirred to run. The first of these holds a statue in his right hand to indicate what honor he ought to be worshipped with; in his left hand he carries the **Tautic character** <term>Tautic character</term> <note>The Ankh or 'handled cross,' which Kircher calls 'Tautic' after Taautus (Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus)</note>, a most powerful amulet and a sign of the influence of the **Triform Deity** <note>The supreme Egyptian Trinity in Kircher’s system</note> flowing into the elemental World through the Genii. The other, a female figure, offers a basket with her right hand and holds the other hand contracted; the protection of abundance is indicated by the basket, while efficacy in action is shown by the contraction of the hand. Having presented the interpretation, it only remains now for us to establish it with suitable testimonies.

## Explanation of the Second Hierogram.

And first indeed regarding the winged globe, since it was extensively explained in the preceding pages on folio 400, it is not necessary to speak of it here. Therefore, let us proceed to the second hierogram, in which exactly the same figures occur as in the second scheme of the preceding side; this difference alone intervenes: that they are equipped with different instruments and headdresses. And first indeed, what the scepter marked with the head of a **Cucupha** [hoopoe] means, what the *persea*-shaped basket (the ornament of the head) means, what the posture of the one sitting and of the standing attendants, what the nudity, and what the square seat mean, has been sufficiently shown and established from various authors in the preceding scheme.

In this place, it falls to us with the greatest care only to prove by various authorities what the scourge in the hand of the sitter, what the statue, what the Tautic character (or **handled cross** <term>crux ansata</term>) in the left hand of the image, what the contraction of the left hand in the other, what the basket-shaped tiara in the right hand, and finally what the feathered caps properly mean.

<margin>The mystical significance is explained.</margin>
We have said in the preceding sections that the second scheme represents the Intellectual or **Genial World** <note>The realm of spirits or 'Genii' that bridges the gap between the divine mind and the physical world</note>, into which the Triform Deity first flows; and consequently these Genii, through various and different instruments...

<meta>This page continues Kircher's systematic interpretation of the Egyptian "world-economy" and its spiritual hierarchy. # BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK.

...[the symbols] with which they are equipped signify nothing other than the diverse duties which they perform in this world-economy, destined as if to distinct offices by the **Triform Deity** <note>Kircher's term for the Egyptian concept of a Triple Divinity, which he often equates with the Christian Trinity in a Hermetic context</note>. Some of these preside over the Eastern region (of which we spoke in the preceding diagram), others over the Southern, others the Western, and finally the Northern. For the world is full of Gods or Genii; whoever knows these, as the Egyptians believed, was thought to be filled with the happiness of all things. From this arose the sacred art of invoking the Deities and the attraction of desired Genii through things suitable and agreeable to them, all of which Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy (divine magic)</note> shows in almost as many words:

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*</margin>
> "When," he says, "the distribution of Deities occurs through the different regions of the world, understand that different regions receive the gifts of the Gods in different ways according to their own property. Considering this, the art of sacred works uses proper invocations which seem agreeable to such distribution and the property of the Deities. For any part of the world receives something from any God; for every God is present in his entirety to any part of the world, but different parts receive him differently: the ether receives in an ethereal manner, the air in an aerial way. For by certain materials and invocations, the gifts of the Gods are naturally attracted."

These words are so clear that they seem to have almost explained the diagram itself.

Let us further explain what is signified by the whip <term>scutica</term> <note>original: "scutica"; in modern Egyptology, this is the flail, part of the "crook and flail" regalia representing the Pharaoh’s or Osiris's power to provide and punish</note> which the supreme president of the Southern region holds. The Egyptians believed that there were not only benign and tutelary <note>protective</note> spirits, but also certain implacable powers—concerning which consult **Psellus** on the **Oracles of Zoroaster** <note>Michael Psellus (11th century) commented on these mystical texts, which Kircher used to link Egyptian and Chaldean wisdom</note>—which they called the **Typhonic offspring**. These, endowed with a certain harmful and destructive force, full of snares, deceits, frauds, and envy, were perpetually at odds in implacable war with the tutelary Genii. Against these Typhonic powers, however, the tutelary Gods were accustomed to fortify themselves; being stronger, as they are closer to God, they easily resist the malignant Deities of the Typhonic crowd and protect and defend all things committed to their care. The symbol of this protection was the whip, which they placed in the hands of the tutelary images. It was most often made from the tail of a sacred bull; for they believed this had the greatest power for routing adverse powers, for the reason cited above in the hieroglyph of the bull; and it was of various shapes.

<margin>Of what material the averting whip was made.</margin>
Hence one can see all the statues and images of the tutelary Deities equipped with whips of this kind. I have a great abundance of these sent to me from various parts of the world; such is a small statue sent to me not long ago by the most excellent Paduan physician, Giovanni Rhodio <note>John Rhode (1587–1659), a Danish scholar and physician active in Padua and a frequent correspondent of Kircher</note>, a man truly of rare wide-learning <term>polyistōr</term> <note>original: πολυΐστωρ; a person of great and varied learning</note>.

<margin>Hieroglyphic figures equipped with a whip.</margin>
Such are those which Giovanni Nardi <note>Giovanni Nardi (c. 1585–1654), a Florentine physician</note>, a most famous physician and philosopher, placed among the hieroglyphic images in his truly brilliant commentary on Lucretius, on page 648. There, in a certain inner sanctum <term>adyton</term> <note>The innermost, restricted chamber of a temple</note>, you see a tutelary deity with joined feet, holding a whip in his left hand and something like a dog's tail in the other—signs for **averting** <term>averruncative</term> <note>From the Latin 'averruncare,' meaning to ward off or avert evil; in Roman religion, Averruncus was a deity who turned away calamity</note> contrary powers. At his sides are four other tutelary figures: Anubis in the form of a dog; a hawk in the form of Osiris; Mercury in the form of a dog-headed baboon <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>original: "Cynocephali"; from the Greek for "dog-head"</note>; and Isis in human form, each indeed [holding] a whip—

<margin>Explanation of Diagram II.</margin>
Therefore, the whip in the hand of the image indicates a protective power <note>original: *tutelare Numen*</note>; the basket-shaped tiara <note>a *modius* or *calathos* crown, often symbolizing fertility or divinity</note> indicates sovereignty; the extended hand, as well as the seated posture, indicates authority and dominion. Conversely, the posture of the standing figures nearby indicates a certain subjection and readiness to obey the higher presiding Genius, just as was shown and proven in the preceding second diagram. For as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries</note> rightly shows in these words:

> The Gods show the Gods or Angels standing around them.

In their hands they hold, first in the left, the **handled cross** <note>original: *crucem ansatam*, now commonly known as the Ankh</note>, or the "Tautic character"; the right hand carries a statue in the form of a V <note>likely a specific hieroglyphic vessel or symbol of offering</note>. Another figure, presenting a tiara to the ruling Genius, holds the other hand contracted. All of these have the greatest significance in the contemplation of the nature of things.

<margin>What the handled cross signifies in the hand of the Genii.</margin>
The Tautic character, or **handled cross**, is familiar to every Egyptian statue. As it is constructed from all the elements of the world, it was rightly judged by the Egyptians to be the most effective amulet against adverse powers. Furthermore, it indicates the progression of the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima mundi*, the spiritual essence thought to animate the physical universe</note> through all the parts of the world. Since we have discussed this character extensively and by profession in an entire treatise—which we call the *Hierogrammatism of the Tautic Character*—we refer the reader there, where they will find altogether wonderful and paradoxical things hidden under this symbol.

Moreover, Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, likely referring to Ibn Wahshiyya or a similar occult source</note> teaches how it passed from the Hebrews to the Egyptians, and what meanings it held among them, in these words:

<note>The following Arabic text describes the "Handled Cross" (Ankh). Kircher provides a Latin translation immediately below, which is rendered here into English.</note>

The shape of the cross which has at its top a circle in the form of a handle is a character that Egypt received from Ham, and Ham from Noah his father, and Noah from Enoch who is Idris, peace be upon him, and Enoch from Seth, and Seth from Adam, peace be upon him, and Adam from Raziel his angel. And Ham performed great wonders through it; and from him Hermes <note>Associated with the Egyptian god Thoth</note> received it, peace be upon him, and placed it among the "bird-letters" <note>Kircher's term for hieroglyphs</note>. It signifies the spirit of the world, and it was a sensible stamp and a great secret in their talismans, and a powerful protection against demons.

---

The figure of the cross in whose head is a circle in the manner of a handle <note>The Ankh</note>: Mesra <note>Mizraim, the biblical progenitor of the Egyptians</note> received it from Ham, and Ham from Noah, and Noah from Hanuch, who is Idris <note>The Islamic name for the prophet Enoch</note>, peace be upon him, and Hanuch from Seth, and Seth from Adam his father, peace be upon him, and Adam from his Angel Raziel. Ham truly performed great wonders by its power, and from him Hermes received it, peace be upon him, and placed it among the "bird-letters" <note>original: *literas auium*, meaning hieroglyphs</note>; this character is the sign of the process and motion of the <term>spirit of the world</term> <note>original: *spiritus mundi*, the vital force connecting all things</note>, and it was a magical seal, and a secret in their <term>talismans</term> <note>original: *telesmatis*</note>, and a ring against demons and malignant powers.

<margin>
What the carrying of the small statue in the hand of the Genii means.
</margin>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a standing figure (a Genius) holding a staff or tall object topped with an ankh (ansated cross). The figure is dressed in robes and stands on a small base.</image-desc>

The statue, however, which he carries in his other hand, indicates with what honor and ritual that principal Genius <note>A guardian spirit or tutelary deity</note> ought to be worshipped and bound. We call this statue <term>ypsilon-shaped</term> <note>original: *υψιλομορφον* (upsilomorphon)</note>, that is, in the form of the letter Y, because this letter signifies a luminous pyramid, which is the path of light by which lower things are illuminated by higher things and participate in divine influences. For this reason, they also twisted statues into the form of this letter for a certain mystical reason, so that nothing should be lacking from the sacred rites that was not full of mysteries; see what we have said extensively regarding this character in the structure of the *Mystic Alphabet* on page 129, and in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher’s *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note> regarding the hieroglyphic statues twisted into the forms of all the letters.

<margin>
Iamblichus:
</margin>

Whence Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> rightly says: *To the various Orders of the Gods there correspond in the World various species, certain ones to certain orders; and from these truly flow various melodies, which they compose similarly through their own movements according to certain Orders of the Gods, the principles of motions, and the rest*, which follow aptly to our subject. For as was rightly proven in the *Hierogrammatism* <note>The study of sacred symbols/writing</note> of statues, the Egyptians worshipped with great reason in the position and gestures of the statues; the more hidden these were, the greater the power they were thought to contain—according to the testimony of Iamblichus—for attracting or repelling [forces]. See what we have produced in the preceding pages from Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the ancient world</note> concerning an argument of this kind.

<margin>
The Priests performed everything in sacrifices according to the pattern of the Symbols with which the Genii were equipped.
</margin>

Furthermore, although a likeness of this kind referred to the World of Genii, it also simultaneously displayed to the Priests the manner of rightly worshipping the Gods, and of instituting sacrifices according to mystical and legitimate Ceremonies; so that such as the Genii showed themselves to be, such should the Priests present themselves in the Sacrifices, so that they might become more conformed in their sacred operations to the tutelary Genii to whom sacrifice was being made, and finally obtain what they sought.

<margin>
Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*.
</margin>

### INTERPRETATION

[He] says, <note>Kircher is quoting Iamblichus’s *De Mysteriis*, a foundational text on Egyptian ritual</note> *“in material things, beyond corporeal qualities, there also lie hidden incorporeal and divine ratios, and species, and measures, through which the things that are applied are made suitable for the gods. For a certain small congruence of our things to the Gods is sufficient for us to draw [grace] from them; for they are always most ready for this, because of their natural goodness and marvelous power; indeed, a powerful cause acts upon matter even if it is only slightly prepared.”* And in another place, *“neither the gods nor their followers transform their nature into any images, nor do they produce these from themselves into something else, but they illustrate and demonstrate the true forms of themselves in the true characters of the soul.”*

<margin>The various meanings of symbols</margin>
Therefore, the Genii <term>Genius: a guardian spirit or tutelary deity believed to preside over specific places or functions</term> displayed with this collection of symbols showed what they wished to be done by the Priests. Hence the Priests used to sacrifice to appease them with the exact same rite, ceremonies, form, clothing, and position which the Genii—as presiding over some worldly region—represented; as was clear a little while ago from Iamblichus. This was so much the case that this figure, as we also hinted in the preceding diagram, besides being a figure by which it refers to the World of Spirits, is also a figure of the sacrifices to be established by the same rite, which it suffices to have indicated in this place. The Genius holding a Tiara in his left hand indicates the power of influence over the lower things committed to his faith; with the left hand contracted, it signifies efficacy in working, as we have proved elsewhere. And let these things suffice concerning the second hierogrammatism <term>hierogrammatismus: Kircher’s term for a complex grouping of sacred symbols or "holy writing"</term>.

To its left is a circular emblem depicting a coiled serpent, labeled '2'. Numbers '3' and '4' are placed near the bird's back. The lower compartment features a bull labeled 'a' walking to the right. The third hierogrammatism is a **Crested Hawk**, together with a **serpent-bearing globe**. Since we described this hieroglyphic extensively in the preceding diagram as being the same as this one, we refer the reader there. For it denotes a triform Deity <term>triforme Numen: a divinity with three aspects or forms, common in Kircher's Neoplatonic view of Egyptian religion</term> having descended into the sidereal World, and manifesting itself most powerfully in the Sun, of which the hawk is the hieroglyphic, as Hermes beautifully teaches—whom we have cited elsewhere in the *Asclepius* <note>The *Asclepius* is a famous Hermetic dialogue discussing how spirits are "drawn down" into statues</note>.

The fourth Hierogrammatismus is as follows: first, there presents itself in it the figure of an **ox**, beneath which is a **decussis** <term>decussis: a symbol in the shape of the letter X, representing the number ten or a cosmic crossing</term>; this is followed by an **extended arm holding a grapevine shoot** in its hand, after which a figure...

### BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

...of the Agathodaemon <note>original: "Agathodæmonis" — a 'good spirit' or protector deity, often represented as a serpent in Egyptian-Greco thought</note>, which is finally followed by a statue situated in the form of the letter **V**. But let us explain the individual parts.

<margin>What the Bull indicates.</margin>
By the Bull, they denoted the God of Agriculture, Osiris or Apis, whose mystical reasons and hidden secrets in the Hierogram <term>Hierogrammatismus: the sacred symbolic composition or "priestly writing"</term> of the Bull we have proven extensively from all the doctrine of the Orientals. The Crossing <note>original: "Decussis" — referring to an X-shaped alignment or intersection</note> shows the ascent and descent of the Soul of the World, or of the Triform Deity operating in the Sun; for just as it flows into Osiris, so here it flows into the invention and supply of all things necessary for the human race, which the extended hand equipped with a vine tendril <note>original: "Capreolo vitis"</note> also aptly teaches. All of this Abenephius <note>Kircher's name for Ibn Wahshiyya, a 10th-century author he believed recorded ancient Egyptian wisdom</note> teaches in these words: <note>original Arabic: بصورة الثور كانوا يعنوا العبده الارض ويد مبسوطة المحسنة الارواح</note> *That is, by the sign of the Bull they indicated the servitude of the earth, but by the extended hand, the beneficence of the Spirits.* What indeed is meant by the vine tendril? (A tendril is nothing other than that extreme and most tender final part of a vine, or a gourd, or Dodder <term>Cuscuta: a genus of parasitic climbing plants</term>, which is twisted into spiral-like lines; they are like the "hands" of the vine ordained by nature to support themselves, for whatever it catches, it wraps itself around so tenaciously that it can hardly be disentangled.) With this tendril they beautifully indicated the appetite of vegetable nature, by which plants are carried toward higher things from which they obtain life. 

<margin>What is meant by the vine tendril.</margin>
Furthermore, by this tendril they also referred to the invention of the vine, which they attributed to Osiris, as witnessed by Herodotus, Diodorus, Eusebius, and Clement. Hence in sacrifices they carried branches of this kind of vine, as well as of the persea <term>Persea: a sacred Egyptian fruit tree (Mimusops schimperi), not to be confused with the modern avocado</term>, myrtle, and palm in their hands, about which we have written extensively on page 362, and which you see cited in their own Hierogram. The figure A follows, which we showed and proved signifies the Agathodaemon on page 125.

But the idol indicates Isis, or the Earth, with whom Osiris-Agathodaemon conjoining, as witnessed by Eusebius and Plutarch, produces the variety of things in Egypt; hence she has a position suited for receiving, and on her head she has a jar <note>original: "vrnam"</note> to demonstrate the abundance that arises from this mixture. These symbols indeed have a double meaning: either the Bull represents the Sun and Isis the Moon; or the Bull represents the Earth and Isis represents Water, or the Nile. Plutarch asserts that both of these interpretations were accepted by the Egyptians; for when water and earth conjoin, that marvelous fertility of the land results, which authors so greatly praise. They expressed this beneficence through the extended arm with the hand holding the tendril, as witnessed by Diodorus in the works of Caussinus: <note>original Greek: ἡ μὲν δεξία τοὺς δακτύλους ἐκτεταμένους ἔχουσα, σημαίνει βίου πορισμὸν</note> *The right hand having extended fingers signifies the supply of necessary things*, <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ εὐώνυμος τήρησιν καὶ φυλακὴν χρημάτων</note> *but the left hand contracted signifies the preservation and guarding of resources.* Indeed, Abenragel <note>An 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> beautifully teaches in his description of the Nile that the very land of Egypt is designated by an arm.

<note>original Arabic: والارض مصر التي هي مبسوطة من جنوب الى الشمال تحت صورة الذراع الانسان الذي وجهه تلاوه ملكي مثل النيل واودايه مثل اعمياء</note>
*That is, Egypt is extended in a straight line from the South to the North, like the likeness of a human arm...*

### INTERPRETATION.

*...human [body], and the Nile passing through the middle of it like a cardiac vein; and when it has approached the Sea, it then divides the land as if into certain fingers of a hand; wherefore it was also called the "arm of Osiris" by the ancient Egyptians. See the more numerous and curious details we bring forth on this argument in our* Chorography of Egypt *in the* Oedipus <note>Kircher refers to his own massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652–54), where he attempted to decode hieroglyphs and Egyptian geography.</note>; *and indeed, from this the "Good Spirits"* <note>original: "Agathodæmones" — protector deities often associated with the fertility of the Nile</note> *of Egypt received their name, as has been proven elsewhere in this work. But since the Nile stretches straight from the South into the North, and the entire land of Egypt maintains the same position under the same longitude, for this reason (according to Plutarch) they called the Southern region the "efflux of Osiris," because the Nile originates in it. This beneficial efflux the "Typhonian Tyranny"—that is, the scorching and parching power of the Sun—strives to impede. Hence, they placed these tutelary Spirits of Egypt in opposition to the adverse powers, appointing them as presidents of this southern region to break the Typhonian force, as if setting them in defense; just as the oracle of Zoroaster* <note>Referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, ancient mystical texts Kircher attributed to Zoroaster.</note> *holds: "The intellectual world possesses unbending sustainers"* <note>original Greek: ἔχει κόσμος νοερός ἀνοχῆας ἀκαμπῆϲ</note>. *Psellus* <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar who wrote commentaries on these oracles.</note> *explains the said oracle more fully in these words: "The Chaldeans and Egyptians placed powers in the world which they named world-leaders or rectors, because they rule the world with the care of providence through their motions. These powers or faculties, therefore, the oracle calls 'sustainers' because they support the entire universe; and indeed, their firm and stable strength is declared by their 'immobility,' while their 'sustenance' signifies their care for protection and conservation." This is exactly what we hinted at above through the Genii sitting and leaning on staffs. Psellus continues further: "Moreover, they designate these faculties through the causes of the worlds alone, and through immobility. There are, however, some other powers which they call 'implacable,' which are strong and fixed in power, and never bend toward lower things; they are the reason why minds are in no way enticed by the allurements of physical effects; there are also certain harmful powers, having a perpetual inclination toward hurting and subverting; 'adversaries of the Good Spirits'"* <note>original Greek: ἀγαθοδαιμόνων ἀντίτεχνοι</note>. *But regarding these, see our discussions elsewhere. You see, therefore, the context of the sacred symbols* <term>hierogrammatismorum: the arrangement of sacred symbols or "priestly writings"</term>, *which we place before the eyes of the curious Reader in this conceptual discourse, with this epigraph of words, as follows.*

BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK

## The Inscription of the Obelisk: A Reading of the Ideal Concept
# SCHEMATISM I. This is it.
## On the Second (Southern) Side.

---

<margin>I. The Archetypal World.</margin>
To the triform Deity <term>Hemphta</term> <note>Kircher's name for a supreme Egyptian creator-god, often identified with Ptah or Ammon-Ra</note>, the first Mind and mover of all things, the second Mind and Craftsman, the all-shaping Spirit—to this Triune Deity, eternal and without beginning or end; the Origin of the Secondary Gods; who, from a <term>Monad</term> <note>The number one, signifying absolute unity and the source of all being</note> as if from a single point, spreads out into the vastness of the mundane 
<margin>Hierogram I.</margin>
pyramid, first communicates its goodness to the intellectual World of <term>Genii</term> <note>Spirits or guardian beings that act as intermediaries between the divine and the physical</note>. These spirits, under the Tutelary Leader of the Southern Choir, and through their swift, effective, and ready attendant Genii **hh**—who are simple substances free from matter—communicate their shared virtue and power to the lower World. This is a model proposed to the Priests, so that they might perform their duties in sacrifices with an analogous ritual to win the favor of these beings. From these, the virtue communicated by the supreme Deity

<margin>II. The Angelic World.</margin>
<margin>Hierogram II.</margin>
is derived into the starry World, where Osiris—the powerful Deity of the perceptible sun—fertilizes all things by his virtue, and grants essence, life, and motion. Being the true soul of the perceptible World, the Leader, moderator, and mover of the heavens, he enlivens, fertilizes, and enriches the perceptible World (which is marked with the character of the triform Deity) by the aid of the attendant spirits of the perceptible world.

<margin>III. The Starry World.</margin>
<margin>Hierogram III.</margin>
Here is <term>Apis</term> or <term>Serapis</term>, the fertile Guardian Spirit of Egypt, who, being beneficent, distributes the virtue received from the powers above through a fourfold influx into all things subject to the South. He does this through the Guardian Spirit of the Nile, <term>Nephthen</term> <note>Referring to Nephthys, whom Kircher associates here with the Nile's fertility</note>, the <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>original: "Agathodæmonem" — a "good spirit" or protective deity often depicted as a serpent</note> of Egypt; from which flows the 
<margin>Hierogram IV.</margin>
plenty and abundance of all things necessary for the human race, through which at last human happiness is fulfilled.

<margin>IV. The Elemental World.</margin>
Let the Reader see the explanations and reasoning for all these matters both in the preceding sections and in the specific hieroglyphic interpretations provided.

# DIAGRAM I.
## Of the Third Western Side.

*Showing the influence of the Triform Deity into the intellectual, starry, and elemental World, and into the Western region.*

The first <term>Sacred Symbol</term> <note>original Latin: Hierogrammatiſmus</note> on this side is the winged globe, the meaning of which has already been stated: namely, the nature of the triform Deity.

<margin>Explanation of all the symbols.</margin>
The second Sacred Symbol denotes the <term>World of Genii</term> <note>original: Genialem Mundum; refers to the realm of intermediary spirits or "genii" that bridge the gap between the divine and the material</note>, into which the triform Deity first exerts its influence. Here, the leader of this choir—as was clear in the preceding Diagram—sits upon a square seat and is likewise equipped with a whip. With his right hand, as if giving a command, he expresses the supreme authority and dominion he holds over his ministers. With the whip, however, he suggests protection against sinister powers. As for the rest, since they were explained in the preceding sections, there is no need to repeat them here. The attendant Spirits <note>original: Aſſeclæ Genij</note>, by their nakedness, position, gesture, and their being equipped with <term>ansated crosses</term> <note>the Ankh, which Kircher interpreted as a symbol of the flow of life or spirit</note>, indicate what they intend (as has often been said). By their feathered headdresses <note>original: tutulis pennigeris</note>, they indicate power and participation in the supreme Deity. They stretch the ansated crosses downward to indicate a desire to influence the lower things committed to their faith. They hold feathers in their hands as if presenting them to the Prince of the Genii, to show the speed and readiness with which they stand at his command, which they also indicate by their feet, urged on to hasten. One of these on the left is <term>ibis-headed</term> <note>original Greek: ἰβικέφαλος (ibikephalos)</note>, the other <term>lion-headed</term> <note>original Greek: λεοντοκέφαλος (leontocephalos)</note>; the former, being ibis-headed, shows himself to be of the Lunar class, while the other, being lion-headed, is of the Solar class. That this is so, we clearly teach on page 325 in what was proposed regarding the Sacred Symbols of the Ibis and the Lion; and <term>Eusebius</term> <note>a 4th-century Christian historian and bishop</note> clearly teaches the reason for this transformation in Book 1: *They say, therefore, that these gods traverse the entire Earth, appearing to men sometimes in the form of sacred animals, sometimes with the face of men, and sometimes covered in some other likeness; they are seen at times because they are the ones by whom all things are truly procreated. Thus the poet, when he had arrived in Egypt and the priests had shared such discourses with him, celebrated it in a certain passage of his poetry as if it were a common occurrence:*

> Indeed, sometimes the Deities with foreign faces
> Are wont to traverse our towns in a thousand new forms;
> They discern right and wrong together with a closer light.

The third Sacred Symbol, namely the crested hawk with the serpent-bearing globe, and what it signifies, has also been discussed in the preceding pages.

Let us therefore proceed to the fourth Sacred Symbol, in which first occurs a <term>dog-like chain</term> <note>original Greek: κυνολογικὴ (kynologikē)</note> figure, which secretly indicates the concatenation of the three Worlds (marked by circles) described thus far. So says <term>Abenephius</term> <note>An Arabic author, likely Ibn Wahshiyya, whom Kircher frequently cited as a source for "ancient" Egyptian wisdom</note>: <note>original Arabic: السلسلة هي علامة النظام العالم عالي مع العالم تحتي</note> "The chain is the sign of the system of the upper world with the lower world." There follows <term>Anubis</term> hidden under the figure of a dog, who, according to the testimony of Plutarch and Diodorus, suggests the guardianship of Osiris, and indicates one of the four principal Protectors of Egypt, who in the

### BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK

In the heavens, Sirius or the Little Dog-star corresponds to this, called *Sothis* in the Egyptian language according to Horus <note>Kircher refers here to Horapollo, an author of a late-antique treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, or the *Astrocyon* (the Dog-star), which influences the moist nature of things. <margin>Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris</margin> Plutarch describes all of this quite beautifully in these words: *Of the stars, they assign Sirius to Isis, because it leads or brings the water.* <margin>What is the Nilotic Vessel?</margin> The truth of this is shown by the "Urn" or Nilotic Vessel which is placed beneath the dog.

A Nilotic vessel, or Water-Jar, is joined to this figure to indicate the protection and the rising of the Nile. This same <term>Sacred Symbol</term> <note>original: Hierogrammatismus</note> shows that this Nilotic vessel signifies nothing else in another hieroglyphic monument—or rather a fragment—which can be seen in the house of the most noble Knight Hippolytus Vitelleschi, a very famous antiquarian. There, next to a statue of Isis, a dog is placed with a Nilotic vessel; the body of the vessel bulges out excessively, with a very wide lip and a very narrow neck, as is clear in Figure B. I am well aware that these vessels had various shapes, which you will see in due time in the section on the <term>Sacred Symbolism of the Water-Jar</term>, where we have displayed the differences between them all according to various mystical reasons.

<margin>What is Anubis or the Dog?</margin> Therefore, in this place, Anubis, the tutelary Spirit <note>original: Genius; a protective or guiding spirit</note> of Egypt, beautifully indicates the protection of the Nile's increase by means of the Nilotic vessel. That the Dog and Anubis are the same thing has already been proven in the section on the <term>Sacred Symbolism of the Dog</term>. It is also sufficiently clear from the words of Plutarch that the dog is related to Isis. Furthermore, the image of Isis—with swollen breasts, holding a vine-tendril in one hand and a Nilotic vessel in the other—expresses this quite clearly in the Sacred Symbols. Through these, two things are beautifully indicated: first, the protective guardianship over the moist element of nature, namely the Nile, by which the earth (which Isis represented) is irrigated throughout the course of the year and brought to life for the procreation of plants. This was indicated symbolically (as said previously) by the vine-tendril, representing the first-fruits of all vegetation, while her swollen breasts indicate this same fertility. Indeed, Horus <margin>Horapollo</margin> teaches that all these things are so in express words in Book 1, Chapter 3: *When they wish to represent the Year, they paint Isis, that is, a woman; by this same sign, they signify the Goddess. Among them, Isis is a star called Sothis in Egyptian, and Astrocyon [Dog-star] in Greek.* This corresponds quite beautifully to the context of the symbols. Therefore, it was not incongruous for them to place a dog above Isis, for as Plutarch testifies, water is chiefly "led" by this, which, when drawn forth by Isis, is the cause of the generation of all earthly things.

The statue, however, is shaped in such a way that by the very configuration of its limbs it expresses the logic of the "influence" flowing from higher powers—both how it is received and how it is communicated to lower things. This is aptly expressed through the <term>X-shaped</term> <note>original: decussiforme; shaped like the Roman numeral X, often referring to crossed arms in Kircher's analysis</note> image, which will be discussed more fully in the following pages. The feet are joined together (undifferentiated) to designate the immobility of the earthly Deity and the condition of the passive principle in properly forming conceptions. From this source, an abundance of blessings flows forth, bestowed upon the land of Egypt by the beneficence and liberality of this Deity, which is aptly indicated by the outstretched arm holding the vine-tendril. For as Diodorus rightly says (cited by Causinus): just as the contracted left hand signifies the conservation and guarding of resources, so the extended fingers incongruously designate the supply of things necessary for life.

He interprets the physical posture of Egyptian statues as symbols of divine influence and the distribution of life-sustaining resources.</summary>

# SCHEMATIC III.
## Inscription of the Obelisk
### Side III. West.

In front stands a hawk-headed figure (F) holding a staff and ankh, labeled H, K, and B. Symbols C and D are at the base.
3. The main central register features a large standing falcon (representing Horus or Osiris as mentioned in the text), wearing a double crown (Pschent) topped with a disk and uraeus. It is surrounded by numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4.
4. The bottom register shows a rectangular panel containing a lion (a) at the top, a jar or vessel (b) to the right, and a figure (c) seated in a boat at the bottom. A coiled snake (d) is to the left. Other labels (e, f, g) point to features of the boat and the ground.
5. The very bottom of the obelisk face shows a series of four vertical recessed panels or doors.</image-desc>

->is as follows:<-

|---|---|---|
| <margin>Sacred Symbol I.</margin> | <margin>I. The Archetypal World.</margin> To the Triform Deity Hempha <note>original: "Hemphæ"; Kircher’s name for a supreme Egyptian creator-god, often linked to the "world-soul"</note>; 1 to the first Mind, the Mover of all; 2 to the second Mind, the Craftsman; 3 to the all-forming Spirit; to the Triune Deity, 1 eternal, 2 incorruptible, 3 possessing neither beginning nor end. The origin of the secondary powers; | |
| <margin>Sacred Symbol II.</margin> | <margin>II. The Angelic World.</margin> which, diffused from its Monad <note>The "One" or the singular source of all being</note>—as if from a center—into the breadth of the Mundane Pyramid, communicates its goodness to the intellectual World of Spirits. These spirits are the presiding lords of the Western World and ministers of the supreme Deity under the supreme Leader A, the Guardian B whose command [k] they obey; this Leader A, marked with the character of Archetypal power, participates in the virtue of A, and communicates it to the Moon-Sun Spirits E and F; these spirits, quickly channeling the influence [I] they have received, derive it into the economy of the lower World [C and D] subject to the West. Through their various bearings, symbols, and gestures, they teach what ought to be done in the performance of sacrifices to dispel adverse powers and to win the favor of good spirits. | |
| <margin>Sacred Symbol III.</margin> | <margin>III. The Starry World.</margin> From these, virtue is derived into the Starry World, where 1 Osiris—the Solar Deity of the Sensible World <note>The physical world that can be perceived by the senses</note>—along with his 4 attendant planets, 2 fertilizes all things by his virtue; he bestows essence, life, and motion upon all things. He is the true Soul of the Sensible World, the Leader, Moderator, 4 and mover of the heavens; he 3 vivifies, 3 fertilizes, and enriches the Sensible World (which is marked with the character of the triform Deity); and here... | |
| <margin>Sacred Symbol IV.</margin> | <margin>IV. The Elemental World.</margin> ...he derives the shared virtue into the Elemental World, and within it, propagates those things that fall under the domain of the West. In this part of the Elemental World, a Anubis and b Isis, receiving the c concatenated <note>chained or linked together</note> influence from the heavens, imprint it upon the remaining things committed to their care and guardianship; from this flows the d e fertility of the Nile and the f beneficence and g liberality of the Deities, and consequently the abundance of all things necessary for Egypt—the very completion of human happiness. | |

The reader may see the mystical reasons for these things explained both in the preceding explanation and in the individual <term>Sacred Symbols</term> <note>original: hierogrammatismus</note> themselves.

<header>BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK</header>

# SCHEMATIC I
## Side IV. North.

->*Showing the influence of the Triple Godhead into the triple world and the northern region.*<-

This Schematic is likewise divided into four other Hierograms <note>Kircher uses "Hierogrammatismus" to mean a sacred symbolic arrangement or "holy writing" of hieroglyphs</note>. First, what is indicated by the globe in the form of a winged-circle-and-serpent <note>original Greek: ὀφι-κυκλοπτερόμορϕον</note> was explained and proven in the Schematic of the first side of this Obelisk.

<margin>
The mysterious headdress of the central figure.
<br/>
The sculptor, by error, omitted the snakes in the headdress.
</margin>
<image-desc>An engraving of the top of an obelisk fragment (pyramidion). At the very peak is a winged solar disk or globe with pendant serpents. Below this, in a central register, is a seated deity on a throne, wearing an elaborate headdress (tutulus) consisting of a split flame above a circle containing a scarab, flanked by leaves and serpents. Two standing human figures face the central deity; the one on the left holds a staff and the one on the right has arms raised. Various hieroglyphic symbols like an eye, a bird, and vertical strokes are dispersed around the figures.</image-desc>

There follows the second Hierogram of the Genial World <note>The "Genial World" refers to the realm of spirits or "Genii" that bridge the gap between the divine and the physical</note>, into which the Triple Godhead (indicated by the aforementioned winged globe) flows immediately. Therefore, the first figure of this second Hierogram has everything in common with the other three previously reviewed Hierograms of the second order, except for the headdress <term>tutulus<gloss>a high, ceremonial headdress or crown worn by priests or deities</gloss></term>. Since this headdress is exceedingly mysterious, I have decided to explain it at somewhat greater length. It is composed of a forked flame emerging from the head, with a circle in the middle from which two asps <note>Egyptian cobras or uraei</note> emerge with swollen necks, along with the leaves of a *persea* tree; finally, the figure of a Scarab marks the center of the circle. I say, therefore, that the principal Genius of this region is denoted by this, imbued with many privileges and qualities by the Triple Godhead, which the diversity of symbols shining forth in the headdress aptly indicates.

<margin>
Explanation of the figure.
<br/>
What the flame, the snakes, and the scarab signify.
</margin>
By the flames, a fiery force emerging within him is noted—or rather, as we have said elsewhere, the highest peak of intellectual power and a subtlety that penetrates all things. For this reason, it is placed on the head. Through the snakes, both fertility and vitality in the production of forms are signified. The leaf of the *persea* <note>An Egyptian evergreen tree, often associated with the "Tree of Life" and the heart</note> represents Wisdom, shining forth in the constant and perpetual arrangement of the matters committed to its trust. Finally, the Scarab in the center of the circle denotes its diffusion into the universal World, which they indicated through the symbol of the Scarab. Regarding this symbol, I ask the reader to see what we have carefully handed down in the 16th Hierogram.

<margin>
The scarab as a sign of the world.
<br/>
Horapollo.
</margin>
Horapollo <note>A 5th-century author who wrote a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, often used by Kircher despite its inaccuracies</note> teaches in Book 1, Hieroglyph 10, that the Egyptians signified the World by the scarab: "To signify the only-begotten, or birth, or father, or the world, or a man, they draw a scarab." <note>original Greek: μονογενές δὲ δηλῶντες, ἢ γένεσιν ἢ πατέρα, ἢ κόσμον, ἢ ἄνδρα, κάνθαρον ζωγραφῶσι.</note> And a little later: "They signify the world by the scarab because it performs the production of its offspring in a world-shaped form." <note>original Greek: κόσμον δὲ ἐπειδὴ κοσμοειδῆ τὴν γένεσιν ποιεῖται.</note> For at a certain time of the year, having obtained ox dung, it takes that material upon itself to be worked. As Aristophanes says at the very beginning of his verse in *The Peace*: "Bring the cake as quickly as possible for the beetle," <note>original Greek: αἶρε μάζαν ὡς τάχισα κανθάρῳ</note> in which passage the poet uses "cake" <note>maza</note> to mean excrement. In any case, it first makes pills from it, so that at the very beginning it imitates the form of the World itself.

<header>I N T E R P R E T A T I O N</header>

<margin>Clement.</margin>
...or as Clement says in Book 5 of the *Stromata* <note>original Greek: ἐπειδὴ κυκλοτερὲς ἐκ τῆς βοείας κόπρȣ σχῆμα πλάσσάμενος ἀντιπρόσωπος κυλινδᾷ;—"since, having fashioned a spherical shape out of cow dung, he rolls it forward while facing it?"</note>; and later: Soon, having placed his feet toward it, he pushes the ball from the rising to the setting sun <note>from East to West</note> and thrusts it forward with uninterrupted rotation; meanwhile, he himself, turned away, gazes at the Sphere, 
<margin>Mystical operations of the Scarab.</margin>
as if he were intentionally taking care to express an image of the heavens by gazing upon their exemplar. But what of this: that while pushing, he is carried from the east wind toward the southwest wind <note>original: "à subsolano in Africum"</note>, as if he were striving to meet the course of the stars, which indeed moves by its own motion from the southwest to the east? Truly, since we have most amply handed down all the secrets of this hieroglyph in its proper Sacred Symbolic Arrangement <note>term: Hierogrammatismo; Kircher refers to his own systematic study of sacred images</note> according to all the doctrine of the Orientals, the curious reader may consult that work, where he will find certain wonders noted by the Egyptians concerning the nature of this animal. Therefore, it was not without cause that the Egyptians represented a Spirit <note>term: Geniū; an intermediary power or "Genius" in the Neoplatonic sense</note> of great power over all the bodies of the World, distinguished by this scarab-shaped headdress. The attendants of this Spirit have nothing different from the symbols of the preceding diagram, except for the ibis-shaped Spirit standing on 
<margin>What is the ibis-shaped image?</margin>
the right, offering with his hand a globe encircled by a serpent. By this they wished to secretly suggest a Spirit of a lunar nature, or the presiding power of the moist element, which is aptly indicated by the head of the ibis while he offers the serpent-bearing globe to the principal Spirit. This is because, even if moisture is required for all 
<margin>What is the serpent-bearing globe?</margin>
generation, it is indicated that we can attain no effect in natural things unless a fiery spirit or fertilizing heat is added—which, as we showed in the first Diagram, the serpent-bearing globe represents. For all generation consists of the hot and the moist. Thus, he seems to pray to the principal Spirit that he might communicate, through his influence, his own power of heat, fertility, and the vigor of life to the moist element. The other Spirit, however, proffers a statue, so that by the infusion of the spirit it may acquire the power of accomplishing that which is intended. Hence, in sacrifices, the Priests used similar rites, gestures, and symbols to obtain such things from the Spirits, as has been shown in innumerable places in this work; and so this Sacred Symbolic Arrangement of the Spirits is a kind of exemplar and "Idea" of the sacrifices to be established by the Priests so that they might have efficacy.

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK

...as is appropriately indicated; since we have extensively explained its symbolic apparatus in the first Schematic Arrangement <note>Kircher refers to his own systematic diagrams of Egyptian symbols earlier in the volume</note>, we refer the reader to that section.

<margin>What the Chain is.</margin> The fourth Sacred Diagram <note>term: Hierogrammatismus; a sacred or symbolic writing system</note> is presented as follows: first, it offers the representative figure of a chain, a symbol of the three Worlds linked together, indicated by three circles; for this reason, it is called *seira* <note>original Greek: σειρά</note> in Egyptian—that is, a *connection*. For there is a certain chained-together influence of the Triform Deity <note>The "Triform Deity" refers to Kircher’s concept of the Trinity reflected in Egyptian theology</note> into the Intellectual World of the Spirits <note>term: Geniorum; intermediary beings between the divine and the material</note>, and from there into the Sidereal <note>pertaining to the stars</note> world, and finally from this into the Elemental world. This present fourth Sacred Diagram represents this; the figure of the chain is a symbol of this influence, which is confirmed by the testimony of the Arab Algaziel <note>Al-Ghazali, a famous Persian theologian and philosopher</note>, who says the following in his book *On Influences*: "Whoever knows the chain by which the upper world is joined with the lower, knows the secrets of nature and will act as a performer of miracles in everything he desires." <note>Kircher provides the original Arabic: كل من يعرف السلسله التي تلفق بها العالم العالي مع التحتي هو يعرف الاسرار الطبيعة ويفعل معجزات بكل ما يريد</note>

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure believed by Kircher to be a contemporary of Moses and the author of Egyptian wisdom</note> also explicitly describes this chain as being connected by three rings—fate, necessity, and order—in the *Asclepius* with these words: *Fate therefore, O Asclepius, or Destiny <note>original Greek: ειμαρμένην</note>, is that necessity of all things that are carried out, always joined by chained links;* and a little later: *This Destiny or fate produces the beginnings of all things, while another [necessity] compels the effect which depends on those primordials. Order follows these—that is, the weaving together and the marking of time for the things that must be completed.* In all these things, this World is perfect; therefore, all things are joined by an inseparable glue.

<margin>Folio 140, Basel edition.</margin> Corresponding to the chain on the opposite side is the figure of the sacred bowl <note>term: crater; a large vessel used for mixing wine and water, here used as a mystical symbol</note>, which they were accustomed to use in the libations of sacrifices. This is taught by the hieroglyphic Arrangement found on a certain Egyptian Amphora (a drawing of which was sent to me from the workshop of Peiresc <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, a famous French scholar and patron of Kircher</note>). In this drawing, the priests about to sacrifice to the God Mophta, or the Spirit of the Nile, held this figure in their hands like a bowl containing the liquid appropriate for the Gods. From this, the meaning of this figure first became known to me. By the bowl, we should first note the Divine Mind, within which souls are immersed; having obtained the contemplation of divine things and the understanding of God, the soul is made **conformed to the same image** <note>original Greek: ὁμοιόμορφος</note>. Thus Trismegistus teaches in the *Pimander*, folio 36: *When He had filled a wide bowl with Mind, He sent a herald, commanding him to announce such things to the souls of men: "Immerse yourself in this bowl, whoever is able—you who believe that the bowl will lead the soul back to Him who sent it, and who know the purpose for which you were born." Whoever therefore heard the herald’s proclamation and immersed themselves in the Mind, they became partakers of knowledge...*

Behind him is a rectangular pillar or altar adorned with hieroglyphs, including a prominent Ankh symbol at the top.</image-desc>

# INTERPRETATION

...they were made participants, and looking up towards perfect men, they emerged; they did not remain submerged in ignorance. And this is the knowledge of the mind according to Tat <note>Tat is a character in the Hermetic texts, often represented as the son or disciple of Hermes Trismegistus (Thoth)</note>; namely, the contemplation of divine things and the understanding of God within the divine "bowl" that exists. From this, the Greeks also attributed a bowl to Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, in which all things were mixed; but more of this elsewhere. So much for the anagogical <note>term: anagogical; a spiritual or mystical interpretation that leads the mind toward divine things</note> sense.

Secondly, by the letter **a**, they denoted this bowl according to the physical sense: the influence of the supernal mind first upon the Genial <note>pertaining to the world of "Genii" or intermediary spirits</note> world, and then, by means of this, into the moisture of the sidereal and elemental world. These things were certainly aptly indicated by the underlying Urn **c**, which is the Nilotic Jar resting on the head of the Ibis **a**. According to the testimony of Herodotus and Plutarch, they used this in sacred rites and placed it before the doors during certain festivals in memory of the benefits they received through Sothis (or Mercury) and Osiris (or the Nile). Indeed, Hecataeus, in his book *On Sacrifices*, testifies that the Urn was dedicated to Sothis or Osiris; for he says it was the custom "to wrap the vessel in a garment during the holy rites" <note>original Greek: ἐσϑῆτι δὲ περιϰεῖσϑαι τὴν χόαν ἐν ταῖς ὀσίαις</note> by which they worshiped the God. Moreover, they were accustomed to bring forth the urn in sacred ceremonies, as has been said elsewhere, and Hecataeus (cited in Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani, author of a famous Renaissance work on hieroglyphics</note>) continues with these words:

> *And so they followed a certain huge water-jar with the highest cult and almost astonished veneration; which, once obtained and received with pure religion, they carried into the temple in a solemn procession. When they had arrived there, prostrating themselves on the ground with hands raised to Heaven, they gave thanks to those who had first shared the gifts of divine kindness for mortal use, as they were persuaded that all things arise from moisture.*

From this, they also transformed similar urns into various figures proper to the Nilotic Genii—from which you, Reader, may recognize the origin of the Canopic jars. But see what we have discussed concerning the Canopic jars and their various differences both in the *Prodromus* and in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his previous works, *Prodromus Coptus* and *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>. Furthermore, Plutarch teaches that they represent Bacchus (or Osiris)—whom they make the lord and prince not only of wine but of all moist nature—by this urn or Nilotic vessel carried around in the sacred rites, using these words:

<margin>Plutarch, in the book *On Osiris and Isis*</margin>
> *Bacchus, the giver of joy, fertilizes the trees with grateful fruits. This is the reason why it is a sin for the worshipers of Osiris to destroy a garden tree or to block a spring of water. They call not only the Nile, but all moisture simply the "efflux of Osiris"* <note>original Greek: ὀσίριδος ἀποῤῥοὴν</note>*, and before the sacred rites in the procession, a water vessel always precedes in honor of the GOD. With a fig leaf, they depict the King and the southern climate of the world; they interpret the fig leaf as the irrigation and fecundation of all things, and it seems similar in nature to the genital member.* <note>For more on this, Kircher directs the reader to his sections on the phallus and the Dionysian rites.</note>

<margin>What the Hook is.</margin>
Shortly after this urn, the head of the ibis **d** corresponds, together with the hook **e**, or the sacred grappling-hook emerging from the region, by which they indicated the protection of the Nilotic Genius or Mercury <note>The Egyptian god Thoth</note>. For, as was shown in the Sacred Description <note>term: Hierogrammatismus; a symbolic or priestly writing</note> of the Ibis, the Ibis and its members were a proper symbol of Mercurial matters.
<margin>What the head of the ibis means</margin>
It was one of the four Genii of Egypt exercising its protection over moisture. But let us see how the hook or grappling-hook indicates protection. This hieroglyphic is very frequent everywhere on all the Obelisks, and...

He interprets these figures both spiritually as divine knowledge and physically as the natural influence of the Nile.</summary>

# BOOK IV. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK

<margin>A hook made in the form of an Ibis.</margin>
...it signifies the extraction of Horus, who was submerged in water, by the Ibis; for this reason, and to commemorate the event, they fashioned this sacred hook <note>original: *harpago*; a grappling iron or hook</note> into the shape of a neck with a protruding beak reaching into a void. As we have shown in the structure of the *Mystic Alphabet*, they called this in the Egyptian tongue by the name <unclear>Camat</unclear> <note>original: *χαεατ*</note>, meaning a rule, or an "extraction." For
<margin>The sacred hook, in Egyptian *Camat*, that is, extraction.</margin>
Hecataeus, according to Sophianus, clearly teaches that it was first detected by the ibis, and that the Body of Horus—which had been cast into the Nile by Typhon and the Titans, as Diodorus witnesses—was extracted and preserved. But see what we have discussed more copiously elsewhere regarding this hieroglyphic hook. And from this, the Egyptians displayed the sacred hook under the form of an ibis's neck with its beak, which had great
<margin>How is Horus, submerged in the waters, rescued by Mercury?</margin>
use and significance both in sacrifices and in hieroglyphics. For they beautifully hinted at this tropologically <note>term: tropologically; a method of interpretation that finds moral or figurative meaning in a text or symbol</note>: that Horus, who was the archetype of the sensible world <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note>, being submerged under water, represented the oblivion and ignorance of the things contained within the worldly machine. From this ignorance, Mercury <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian Thoth with the Roman Mercury</note> liberated them, dredging up the hidden things of the world and bringing into the sight of men those things necessary for the human race to know; he taught these under the
<margin>What are the quadrangles?</margin>
form of the ibis. This is also shown by the following hieroglyphic of three larger quadrangles and three smaller quadrangles. Through the quadrangles, he noted the fourfold triplicity in the Zodiac <note>referring to the grouping of zodiac signs into "triplicities" or elements</note>, by which the three seasons of the year are established. Or, to speak a little more clearly, he noted the fourfold triplicity of the Zodiac, each part of which contains four "mansions" <note>astrological divisions</note> indicated by the four sides of the quadrangles. For the Sun, passing through these, creates the difference between the three seasons of the year—namely, spring, summer, and winter. (For the year was distributed into so many parts by the ancient Egyptians, and these were called "hours.") Again, by the said quadrangle triad, the twelve months were indicated, which the Sun produced by passing through the twelve signs. They further added three smaller quadrangles, which noted the number of parts into which they divided the individual days and nights of the whole year—one might call them "little months." This was done according to a certain analogy to the twelve months, so that the time of individual days—the morning—corresponded to spring; the midday to summer; and the evening and night to winter. By this distribution, ingeniously made by Mercury, they denoted the generation and production of all things in the Elemental World. Diodorus confirms this in these words in Book 1, Chapter 2:
<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
> For they [the Egyptians], he says, then completed a year in four months according to three seasons: namely summer, spring, and winter; which was the reason why certain Greeks called years *Horoi* <note>original: "Horos"; likely a Greek wordplay on the name of the god Horus and the word for seasons/hours</note>, as if you were to say the seasons of the year, and annual records *horographies*.

For since Horus is the son of Osiris and Isis—that is, the sensible world—it is perfected through the Sun and the Moon. Hence Diodorus says in the same chapter:

> *Thinking these to be Gods, they claim they travel around the entire world, and nourish and increase all things by the three seasons of the year, completing the circuit [of the Zodiac] by a continuous motion: in Spring, summer, and winter. These, though contrary to each other, complete the year in firm concord. The nature of these Gods contributes much to the generation of all living things: since one is fiery (indicated by the hawk placed nearby), the other is moist and cold (indicated by the head of the Ibis with an urn placed above it), while the air is common to both.*

Indeed, this wondrous harmony of the seasons, Mercury...

<meta>catchword: Mercu-</meta>

He further interprets the geometric quadrangles as symbols of the Egyptian three-season calendar and the zodiacal cycles as organized by Thoth-Mercury.</summary>

### INTERPRETATION

Diodorus teaches that Mercury was indicated in the form of an ibis in these words: *Mercury was, above all, an observer of the stars; he discovered the harmonies of voices and was furthermore the inventor of the lyre made of three strings, patterned after the three seasons of the year. For he established three tones: the high, the low, and the middle. He took the high pitch from summer, the low from winter, and the middle from spring; these show a wonderful harmony with the aforementioned symbols.* <note>original Latin: "Imprimis astrorum obseruator fuit Mercurius..." This quote attributes the invention of music and the division of the year to Thoth/Mercury.</note> Furthermore, that a quadrangle indicates a year is expressly taught by Horus in Book 1, Chapter 5: *When they wish to write "the current year," they paint the fourth part of an arura.* <note>original Greek: ἔτος τὸ ἐνιστάμενον γράφοντες, τέταρτον ἀρούρας γράφουσιν. Kircher is citing Horapollo, a late antique author who wrote on hieroglyphs.</note> For an <term>Arura</term> <note>A traditional Egyptian unit of land area.</note> is a space comprising 100 cubits, of which a whole field would be 400 cubits, and consequently, the side of its square is 20. Why they assumed the space of a quarter of a field as the indicator of a year is described by Horus in the cited passage, and we have treated it extensively elsewhere.

And this is that Horus who was extracted from the waters of ignorance by Mercury and led into the light, by which life is given to the world, as the placed figure of Horus—positioned beneath the quadrangles along with the serpent—designates. Plutarch teaches with many words that by Horus (whom among the hieroglyphics a child’s head, as if wrapped in bandages, signifies), the "sensible world" <note>the physical world perceived through the senses</note> is denoted. Indeed, he recites an Egyptian fable from Eudoxus: namely, that Jupiter <note>Kircher often uses Roman names for Egyptian gods; here likely referring to Osiris or Amun.</note>, who was struggling with his feet grown together, was freed for walking by Isis. The <term>epimythium</term> <note>the moral or underlying meaning of a fable</note> of this story was this: that the mind of God is by its nature inconspicuous and hidden, but it proceeded through motion toward the procreation of things. Hence they express him either through a child’s head, or through the feet, or as through the lattice-patterned garment in which we showed him wrapped on page 212. And from this also flowed the description of Horus, whom the Moon (or Isis, the mother of the world), having found him in the water, restored to life and made immortal, as they tell in fables. For the generative power of water and the Moon, the Queen of sublunary things, both fertilize the world and make it, as it were, immortal through the various changes of things. Hence among these same Egyptians the opinion prevailed that the Moon and the Sun were the eyes of Horus; and even that he was first nourished by Latona in the marshes near Buto. All of these things allude to our interpretation.

The <term>Cerastes</term> <note>a horned viper, common in Egyptian iconography</note> placed upon the head of Horus clearly teaches this as well. For we have shown in our study of sacred writing <note>original: "hierogrammatismo"</note> that the serpent, whether a Cerastes or one conspicuous for its two horns, being a "moist-warm" animal, signifies life. This is on account of two things, namely, moisture and heat, by which life is preserved in all living creatures. Therefore, a certain wonderful context of hieroglyphs is evident from what has been said. Now that the diagrams of the four sides of the Obelisk have been explained, nothing remains except that we now show in summary the harmony of each part playing together. This will be done appropriately once we have first placed before the eyes of the curious reader a condensed reading of the entire ideal concept shining forth in the individual diagrams.

<header>INTERPRETATION.</header>

# A SUMMARY BY WAY OF QUESTIONING,
## IN WHICH

Several difficulties, which could render the mind of the Reader doubtful—as they reflect in various ways upon what was said above regarding the confirmation of the matters presented—are solved and disentangled through short questions.

Lest any scruple remain in the mind of the Curious Reader who seeks inward truths, I have thought it timely to attach this Question-and-Answer Recapitulation <note>original: "Anacephaleosis Erotematica," a Greek-derived term for a summary conducted through a series of questions and answers.</note> at this point; in which we trust we shall fully satisfy the Reader's wishes.

---

->Reflections concerning the symbols of Hierogram I.<-

<margin>Why is the winged globe placed at the apex of the pyramid?</margin>
It is asked, therefore, first: Why is the character **shaped like a serpent, circle, and wings** <note>original: "όφι-κυκλο-πτερόμορφος" (ophi-kyklo-pteromorphos). This refers to the common Egyptian "Winged Sun" motif which Kircher interprets as a representation of the Trinity.</note> of the **Triform Deity** placed immediately under the apex of the Obelisk? **I answer**, because since the Egyptians signified the fourfold breadth of the Universe through the pyramid or Obelisk, they quite aptly indicated the supreme Deity through the apex, at which all lines converge, and are united in it as if in the center of all things. This Deity, having fallen from its unity <term>Monad<gloss>The ultimate, indivisible One from which all existence originates in Neoplatonic philosophy.</gloss></term> into a multitude, is the cause, life, and soul of all things, just as all things return to the same, as if to the Author and Producer of all, upon whom they essentially depend; regarding these matters, see the final chapter of the second book on the mysteries of the pyramid.

<margin>What do the three rows of feathers in the wings of the globe mean?</margin>
It is asked, secondly: What is signified by the three rows of feathers in the winged globes? **I answer** that the Egyptians signified by these the eternal ideas of the supreme **Archetypal Triform Deity**, and the patterns of things shining forth in the classes of the three Worlds. For, as Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who wrote extensively on Egyptian symbols.</note> rightly notes, the Egyptians were accustomed to use small, humble things to indicate great matters.

<margin>Why does the serpent emerge below the globe?</margin>
It is asked, thirdly: Why does the Serpent emerge not above the globe, but below it? **I answer**, they indicated by this the natural appetite and, as it were, a certain striving of the Creator-Mind to communicate itself to the lower worlds.

<margin>What is the fastener?</margin>
It is asked, fourthly: Why is the globe of the serpent-circle-wing shape separated in a triangle from the rest by the figure of a fastener <note>original: "retinaculum." In Kircher's diagrams, this is often a bar or bracket that separates segments of the hieroglyphic column.</note> (which was a sign of division for them)? **I answer** that they signified by this very thing the triune essence of the Deity (which both the triangle and the winged globe with serpents indicated) absorbed in the abyss of eternity, enjoying the contemplation of its own blessedness in such a way that it nevertheless always possessed an appetite for creation—which the triangle, projected further outward, beautifully indicates.

It is asked, fifthly: Why in each part of the Obelisk is that triform...
