they placed the symbol; I answer, so that they might indicate by it the omnipresent influence of the supreme **Deity** <note>original: "Numinis"</note>, which is signified through the fourfold region of the World.

->Reflections concerning the symbols of Hierogram II.<-

<margin>Why fire is included in a triangle with the winged globe.</margin>
First, it is asked: Why are these symbols of the Second Hierogram included in a triangle together with the triform symbol? **I answer**, that by this they wished to indicate that the **Genial World** <note>original: "Mundum Genialem." In Kircher's system, this refers to the world of "Genii" or angelic spirits that mediate between God and the physical world.</note>, or the Angelic substance, is the immediate work of the Creator, and is most similar to Him: simple, incorporeal, and completing all things by intellect alone. Because it is the most expressive and immediate image of God—into which the Deity flows directly, as if into a subject most similar to Himself—they have, on account of this similarity with God, quite beautifully included it within the same triangle. This triangle is marked as the character of the supreme Deity on each side of the Obelisk to show that the World is committed to their governance, and that by their ministry even the smallest parts of the sensible World are arranged and cared for.

<margin>Regarding the variety of symbols in the configurations of the genial world.</margin>
Second, it is asked: Why are these **Genii** distinguished by so many and such varied symbols, positions, gestures, and bodily habits? **I answer**, that they wished to signify the diverse and distinct duties which they hold in the World and in its specific parts. Hence the middle Genius, notable for his sitting posture and a **head-dress** <term>tutulo<gloss>A conical headdress or hairstyle, used here to denote high status or priestly authority.</gloss></term> more conspicuous than the others, and furthermore equipped with a scepter, indicates the leadership of his own order and choir; he further represents dominion and supreme power over the others subject to him. The rest, however, appear standing with their feet poised as if ready to run, exhibiting a certain promptness to carry out the commands of their Leader.

<margin>What the "struppi" are.</margin>
Third, it is asked: Why are those <term>struppi<gloss>Originally ritual headbands or garlands, used by Kircher here to describe the complex Egyptian crowns or headdresses.</gloss></term>, or head-dresses marked with multiform symbols, worn primarily on the head? **I answer**, that they wished to signify that all power, dominion, leadership, life, and influence flows first from the supreme Deity into the genial or intelligible World—that is, into the intellect and reason. The brain is the organ of this faculty (following a certain analogy to the human form), being the part of the rational faculty and the unique archetype for all actions to be performed. However, through the symbols which they carry in their hands, the operative and executive power—which carries out what the intellect prescribes—is shown.

<margin>Why the statues are of so many forms.</margin>
Fourth, it is asked: Why are these Genii transformed, appearing now with the face of a man, now with the form of a hawk, an ibis, a cat, a cow, or a dog? **I answer**, that by this they wished to signify the diverse offices by which they administer everything in the world. These Genii are partly "insensible" <note>meaning spiritual or beyond the reach of the physical senses</note> and partly "sensible." Through those painted with a human face, they represent the insensible Genii, who moderate all things by intellect alone and by a certain invisible assistance. Through the others appearing in the forms of animals, they indicate the "sensible Gods" who, according to the testimony of **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note>, travel through the whole world in the forms of animals to instruct the human race. Thus, they represent **Mercury** <note>The Roman equivalent of the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> under the form—

He interprets their headdresses as symbols of intellectual power and their hand-held objects as symbols of executive action.</summary>

<note>The sentence begins mid-word from the previous page's catchword "ma".</note> ...the Dog-star <note>original: "Canis"</note> under the form of a Dog, Osiris under the form of an Ox, Isis under the form of a Cat, and so with the others, as has been shown throughout this book. For this reason, we see those transformed beings, for the most part, covered with clothing; whereas the others, who are imperceptible <note>original: "insensibiles," meaning spiritual or non-physical</note>, are shown with a naked and subtle body, as they are simple and separated from all contamination of matter.

<margin>What do the masculine and feminine forms signify?</margin>
It is asked fifthly: Why are they expressed under feminine and masculine forms? **I answer**, to show that they are the presidents of all generation, and moreover, that there is in the **Intellectual World** <note>original: "Mundo intellectuali"</note> a certain distinction of sex, according to a certain analogy made to man and animals; from which, clearly, an intellectual birth results, from which an infinite variety of things is born.

<margin>Why are there only 3 Genii on one face?</margin>
It is asked sixthly: Why are only three Genii placed on each side, and twelve placed on all sides joined together? **I answer**, so that they might express the process of divine reason from the **Monad** <note>the number one, representing unity or God</note> into the **Dyad** <note>the number two, representing multiplicity</note>. Since this number [two] suggests a certain imperfection, they aptly used it to indicate the Second World from the **Archetype** <note>the original blueprint in the mind of God</note>, namely the **Genial World** <note>the realm of spirits</note>; for it denotes a certain imperfection with respect to the essence of the supreme Deity, which is indicated by the number two, or multiplicity, as I have said, and as was explained in the section on the Dyad of the Obelisk. Yet it also moves from the Monad into the **Triad** <note>the number three</note>, which is indicated by the triangle in which they are included and the number of the Genii. This is because the immediate work proceeding from the supreme Deity, as I said, is the **Angelic World**, which can be called the first created Triad, because of the supreme perfection it holds among created things; just as the **Triform Deity** <note>the Trinity</note> is called the uncreated Triad. If indeed the three Genii of one side are multiplied by the four sides, twelve are produced; by which number they aptly noted the universality of things, as has been explained elsewhere. Therefore, through the three Genii, both the excellence of the angelic nature and the three classes or orders into which they are distinguished for the protection of lower things are understood; and through the twelve, the administration of the entire World performed by them is understood. Be careful, however, not to confuse the triad of order with the triad of perfection.

## Reflections concerning Hierogrammatic Symbols III and IV.

It is asked first: Why, after the Genial World, did they place the figure of a **Hawk** <note>original: "Accipitris"</note> in a quadrangle? **I answer**, to indicate the **Sensible World** <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note>, or the corporeal world, which is aptly indicated by a quadrangle, as we have proved above from Plato. For the further the series of Worlds recedes from the first circular Archetypal World, the more imperfect they are due to the variety of angles and shapes, and the further they recede from the Monad and the Triad. Hence, between the Monad and the **Tetrad** <note>the number four, or the square</note>, they aptly placed the angelic Triad, to indicate that the influx into the corporeal world (the Tetrad) occurs by the mediation of the Genii.

<margin>What do the streaks in the wings of the hawk mean?</margin>
It is asked secondly: What is the meaning of those linear and circular streaks in the wings of the hawk? **I answer**, that they wished to indicate that the revolutions of the heavens are made...

**Thirdly**, it is asked: Why is the fourth sacred diagram <term>hierogrammatismus</term> <note>a symbolic or sacred diagram used by Egyptian priests</note>, likewise enclosed in a square, further enclosed in a larger square? **I answer**: Since the said diagram represents the Elemental World <note>the world of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note>, they appropriately represented it through a distinct smaller square enclosed in a larger one, as it is contained and governed by the Sidereal World <note>the world of the stars and planets</note>, like a thing contained by its container. Hence, Osiris, the ruler of the sacred world <gloss>hierokosmos</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἱεροκόσμος</note>, stands upon it to indicate the most absolute dominion he holds over it.

<margin>What is meant by the linear paths.</margin>
**Fourthly**, it is asked: What is intended by the exhibition of the four mutually linked Worlds through those transverse lines *a*, *b*, *c*, and through the seven lines perpendicular to the upper ones—of which those marked with numbers *d, f, g, h* are disjointed, while *i, k, l* are joined to the upper ones—all contained within the space *RSXZ*? Furthermore, what did they wish to indicate by the sum of ten, which is constituted by adding 3 to 7? I know many will think these are mere trifles <note>original: "parerga," meaning secondary works or ornaments</note> and serve only as decoration. However, whoever scrutinizes the sharp wit of the Egyptians more deeply will see that among the sacred scribes <term>hierogrammatistae</term>, just as nothing is devoid of mystery, so too these linear paths were not without hidden mysteries.

<columns>2</columns>
<margin>Explanation of the linear diagrams and schemes seen contained within the space RSXZ at the base of the present figure.</margin>
**I answer**: They have shown through these lines—just like numerical figures—the entire context of the aforementioned things, as if in a certain numerical idea. For just as the highest Archetypal World <note>the divine realm of pure ideas</note> flows through the **Dyad** <note>the number two, representing the first step into multiplicity</note> into the **Triad** <note>the number three</note> and the Angelic **Tetrad** <note>the number four</note>, so Osiris, the Leader and Moderator of the corporeal world, unfolds from his **Monad** <note>the number one, representing unity</note>—that is, from the center of the Sun, in which he resides as the soul. He unfolds first into the dyad of the two worlds, the Sidereal and the Elemental (*c* and *e*). From there, he descends into the corporeal triad of things—that is, the sphere of generation, which is aptly suggested by the three transverse lines *a, b, c*. He then passes through the tetrad—that is, the fourfold gate of the corporeal world, indicated by the four perpendicular lines *d, f, g, h*. Finally, he flows as if through channels into the individual things of the entire universe, which [follow] in order through the hieroglyphics on each side...

<header>INTERPRETATION.</header>

...are indicated, it is aptly shown; however, the three transverse parallelograms *a, b, c*, along with four *d, f, g, h* placed normally <note>meaning perpendicular or at right angles</note> and disjointed, make up 7, the mystic number of the **harmony of the world** <note>original: "harmoniæ mundi"</note>. This number is also indicated by the seven lines marked with letters *d, i, f, k, g, l, h*, which, joined to the three upper transverse lines, constitute ten—the symbol of the **mystic decade** <note>original: "decadis mysticæ"</note>, representing the return of all things to their source <note>original: "principium"</note>. Moreover, that the seven normal lines are joined with the three transverse *a, b, c* indicates that from the corporeal triad <note>the physical world of three dimensions</note>, the influence of the higher realms continues through the **four gates of the world** into the entire lower scope of individual things. Thus, whatever we showed as mysterious in the chapter on the mysterious figure of the obelisk, let us see it here contained in a kind of epitome <note>a summary or condensed version</note>. See what we have discussed at length from folio 126 to folio 130 concerning these matters.

<margin>What do the garments and instruments of the Spirits signify?</margin>
Fifthly, it is asked: What does that varied clothing of the **Spirits** <term>Genii</term> <note>guardian deities or supernatural beings often depicted on Egyptian monuments</note> indicate, since besides their various transformations, they carry now statues, now a serpent-bearing globe, now feathers, now something similar in their hands? I answer: they wished to indicate by this the method of establishing sacrifices, which had to be instituted by priests for the purpose of propitiating the Spirits by a thoroughly analogous rite. Hence the priests, as we have shown elsewhere, when about to sacrifice in the inner sanctuaries <term>adyta</term> <note>the most sacred, private parts of a temple</note>, proceeded in that clothing, position, gesture, and with that apparatus of symbols in which they saw the Spirits—whom they intended to propitiate—represented by **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage associated with Thoth</note> on the Obelisks. For they believed that nothing was more powerful for either pleasing or attracting the Divinities than to perform sacred rites with an apparatus of things and ceremonies analogous to them; all of which have been proven elsewhere from **Plutarch**, **Iamblichus**, and others. 

But let us hear **Porphyry** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, who in his book *On Abstinence* so beautifully confirms everything explained in this **Summary** <term>Anacephaleosis</term> that he seems to have alluded to what has been said: "We shall therefore imitate the holy and ancient ones, dedicating as if first-fruits to the Divinities from that very contemplation which the higher beings have granted us, and whose use is necessary for our true salvation. Hence the **Pythagoreans**, being occupied with numbers and lines, attributed much to the Gods from these as well, naming one number **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>, another **Diana** <note>Artemis</note>, and another **Apollo**; again, another Justice, another Temperance, and similarly with figures; and so with similar sacrifices, they pleased the Gods so much that they would call upon each of the Gods with their own offerings, and by their benefit they frequently used divination and prophecy. To the Gods, however, who are within Heaven, whether wandering in a certain way in their course or not wandering <note>referring to the 'wandering stars' or planets versus the 'fixed stars'</note>, among whom the **Sun** must be thought to hold the primacy, and then the **Moon**, it was fitting to approach and offer fire as if related to them."

And a little later, speaking of the **Platonists**, he says: "They hand down in this manner: the first **GOD**, since he is incorporeal, immobile, and impassible in nothing, nor even restrained within himself, needs nothing external; nor even does the **Soul of the World** need external things. For it possesses and contains that itself which is perfected in triple dimension <note>representing the physical world of length, width, and height</note>, and a faculty naturally moving itself, which has decided by its own nature to move well and orderly, and to move the **Body of the World** according to the best reasons; moreover, it has received and embraced the body within itself, although in..."

BOOK V. THE PAMPHYLIAN OBELISK
<meta>catchword: Theo-</meta>

...therefore, let it be corporeal and thus free from every passion. To the other Gods, the World, and the Stars—all of which consist of soul and body—one must sacrifice inanimate things with eyes wide open <note>meaning with clear awareness or manifest intent</note>. See Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his book *On Sacrifices and Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: "de sacrificijs, & abstinentia animalium"</note>.

<margin>The Hieroglyphics displayed here are in harmony with the Orthodox religion.</margin>
You see, therefore, from these few questions, that nothing was so trivial to the Egyptians that they did not adopt it to display their hidden mysteries. You have here also how the Father generates the Son, and how the Spirit proceeds from these; you have how this World was produced by the Triune Deity <note>original: "Triuno Numine"</note>; you have the orders of Angels distributed into various choirs; you have the World committed to their protection and preservation. But let us hear the golden words of Hugh of St. Victor <note>A famous 12th-century mystic and theologian</note>, who explains the mind of the ancients in a certain sermon so aptly that he seems to have looked toward this very subject:

<margin>Hugh of St. Victor.</margin>
> *GOD the Creator of the World is perceived through the contemplation of the World; and He who cannot be seen made that which could be seen, and was seen through that which He made. For His invisible things are understood and perceived from the Creation of the World through those things that have been made. Weighing this passage, the Scholiast asserts that philosophers were able, by natural light <note>reason unaided by divine revelation</note>, to arrive at the attributes of the three divine persons; for as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> rightly teaches in his third homily on the Song of Canticles, this visible World depends upon the invisible, and this earthly arrangement contains certain patterns of Heavenly things, so that from these things that are below we might be able to ascend to those that are above, and from those things we see on earth, to sense and understand those things held in the Heavens; for since it is impossible for a man living in the flesh to recognize anything of hidden and invisible things unless he receives some image and likeness from visible things; for this reason I judge that He who made all things in Wisdom created each visible form on earth in such a way that He placed in them the teaching and recognition of invisible and heavenly things, so that through these the human mind might ascend to spiritual understanding.*

Therefore, after it was not enough for God to enjoy the contemplation of Himself alone, but it seemed worth the effort to diffuse and derive Himself more widely so that more might feel the benefit, He first conceived in thought the Angelic and celestial powers. This thought then passed into work, which was completed by the Word and perfected by the Spirit; for the Father is the "conceiving cause" of created things, the Son is the "effecting cause," and the Spirit is the "perfecting cause." Thus, by the will of the Father, the ministering spirits exist; by the action of the Son, they are produced in the nature of things; and by the presence of the Spirit, they obtain perfection and their final completion. These are established as certain fruitful splendors, the ministers of that first light. But after this first workmanship pleased the Architect Himself and the Designing Mind, He expressed another world in thought—or in the Word—which would consist of matter and through this would be open to corporeal eyes; namely, this entire universe composed and arranged from heaven and earth and all things contained in them.

The Angelic orders are contained under the square of the ternary <note>the number three</note>; for the Triad is "triply first" <note>original: "Trias triniter prima," referring to the Trinity as the fundamental principle of all things</note>, the principle of that highest good even by all Orthodox...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher argues that Egyptian hieroglyphs contain seeds of Christian truth, specifically regarding the Trinity and the hierarchy of angels. He cites classical and medieval scholars to show that the visible world is a mirror through which we can understand the invisible divine realm.</summary>

<header>INTERPRETATION.</header>

It is celebrated by theologians as existing in the unity of the same substance under a Trinity of persons without any division of itself. Therefore, it is reasonable that the sacred number of the first principle—namely the triad multiplied by itself—brought forth the great multitude of Celestial Genii <note>The "Genii" refers to the various ranks of spirits or angels in the celestial hierarchy</note> and immaterial substances. Hence Zoroaster, by a tripled Triad, established nine choirs, which Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and historian</note> explains in these words:

<note>original Greek: "Μίαν ἀρχὴν τῶν πάντων δοξάζουσι καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ὑπομνέουσιν· εἶτα πατρικόν τίνα βυθὸν σέβονται ἐκ τριῶν τριάδων συγκείμενον· ἑκάστη δὲ τριὰς ἔχει πατέρα, δύναμιν, καὶ νοῦν."</note>
"They glorify one principle of all things and in it they acknowledge the Good; then they worship a certain paternal depth composed of three trinities; but each trinity has a Father, a Power, and a Mind."

They consider there to be a single principle of all things, and they profess this to be the true and the good; then they worship a certain paternal foundation composed of three trinities, each of which has a Father, a Power, and a Mind. You see how these three trinities square beautifully with the things explained; these shine forth first in the intellectual world and the Genii; then in the Sidereal <note>relating to the stars</note> world, in the three classes of stars—namely in the fixed stars, the Sun, and the planets—which fill all things with light, rays, and heat; and in their effects, by which they provide essence, life, and sense.

Therefore, of the one World, there is fecundity <note>the capacity to produce life</note>, offspring, and love; nor is fecundity one world, and offspring another, and love another; but they are one and the same world. For the fecundity of the world, its offspring, and its love are participated in by angels angelically; in humans humanly; in beasts like animals; in beings as beings; in elements elementally; and in each of the others in its own way. Indeed, the world possesses nothing except from Him who, being Triune, communicates His perfection to it in the best and most capable way possible. The oracle of Serapis <note>Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity; his "oracles" were often cited by later scholars to show pagan "anticipation" of Christian truths</note> harmonizes beautifully with all of this:

> ->First is God, then the Word, and the Spirit with them<-
> ->These three are innate, and all things tend toward the one.<-
> ->*God is the Principle, then the Word, and with these the Spirit is one.*<-
> ->*These three are born together, and all these things tend toward the one.*<-

Sixthly, it is asked: Why are hieroglyphic compositions of this kind occasionally seen outside of obelisks, carved on statues—specifically Sphinxes—and on tablets? I respond that the obelisks were like certain mysterious Archetypes or prototypes, in which the Egyptians prefigured an entire science concerning God and the Gods. This science they carved into massive, extremely hard, and very spacious stones so that it would not be lost to the ravages of time; they did this both so that the perennial brilliance of the doctrine might strike the eyes of everyone, and so that they might serve as a kind of Archive. From these archives, particular arrangements <term>Schematisms<gloss>specific symbolic patterns or layouts</gloss></term> suitable for individual gods could be drawn—whether for the consecration of statues and images, or for the private use of Amulets. Hence, you will find everywhere that the symbols explained extensively on the obelisks are inserted here and there in hieroglyphic inscriptions, especially those seen enclosed in an oval figure <note>A reference to "cartouches," which Kircher correctly identifies as containing significant specific names or concepts</note>. But more on these matters in what follows. Of this argument, besides countless others occurring here and there, there is that one which follows.

<header>INTERPRETATION.</header>

## Interpretation
# THE HIEROGLYPHIC TABLE
->*Drawn from the Barberini Treasury, in which everything discussed thus far is contained as if in a certain summary.*<-

Whatever, therefore, was discussed at length in these first four Diagrams, the Egyptians presented in a condensed form in their mystical statues. Only a fragment of these has reached me through the kindness of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, who, just as he first emerged as the promoter of my labors, has not ceased to support them out of his affection for the Republic of Letters <note>The "Republic of Letters" refers to the long-distance intellectual community of scholars in the late 17th century</note>. This small tablet is made of black Parian stone, which is extremely hard; its thickness is nearly a thumb <note>approximately one inch</note>, its width equals half a palm, but its length could not be determined because of a break made through the middle, as is apparent in the present diagram. However, because I remembered seeing something similar in an Egyptian statue—a copy of which Marcus Milesius, <term>I.C.</term> <note>Latin: *Iuris Consultus*, a legal expert or consultant</note>, once shared with me, and which is now in the possession of the aforementioned Francesco Angelomo—I shall easily restore every missing part from it. 

The Barberini statue shows only the lower part, while the Milesian statue is complete, although it does not possess such a grand display of hieroglyphs as the Barberini one. For this one <note>the Barberini fragment</note> is seen to be illustrious, featuring fourteen columns of hieroglyphs on the back, and on the sides, the bottom, and indeed on every part, hieroglyphs incised by a subtle hand with the most exact and distinct detail. The other <note>the Milesian statue</note> shows only the main figure intact. I thought both should be placed here so that the Reader, by comparing one with the other, might easily supply the missing pieces. 

The central statue takes the form of a seated figure, holding in his hand a staff, and at the same time a scorpion and two serpents, while grasping the tail of a lion that is struggling downward. His feet rest upon the heads of two crocodiles looking in opposite directions. The Milesian statue has a head armed with a ram's horn, with a lion's head inserted into a crescent moon; in the left hand it holds two serpents and a lion grasped by the tail, struggling below and seemingly looking back; in the right hand it holds a scorpion and a dog. The tablet is shaped into an arch at the top, near which a winged globe with expanded wings is stretched out as if brooding over the things below. 

Furthermore, below the crocodiles, the Barberini tablet displays sixteen statues of Gods variously transformed into sacred animals. In the middle of this, a Serpent, with a wavy contraction of its body, bites its own tail <note>original: "Serpens... caudam suam mordet"; this is the Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity or the cyclical nature of the universe</note>. Upon its coils sit five <term>mystagogic</term> <note>from *mystagogue*, one who initiates others into sacred mysteries</note> statues. Images standing outside the coils of the wavy serpent take the form of a hawk, a lion, a cat, a dog, and an ibis, and they are equipped in their hands with various <term>averruncative</term> <note>from the Latin *averruncare*, meaning to ward off or avert evil omens</note> symbols. Those looming over the coils of the serpent, however, are in a seated position, and are likewise accompanied by various hieroglyphs—

BOOK V. THE PAMPHILJ OBELISK

<margin>Explanation of the Barberini Tablet.</margin>

...notable for their arrangement. Let us see what each one indicates. The **wing-shaped circle** <note>original: *κυκλο-πτερόμορφος* (kyklo-pteromorphos)</note> globe shows the unity of the triform Deity, dwelling in solitary contemplation of itself. The principal figure, however, indicates the descent of the same triform, **all-shaped** <note>original: *pantamorphi*</note> Deity into the vastness of all Nature. Upon its head, it wears a lion's head inserted into a textile moon, by which power and dominion over the Sun and Moon are shown; this power is also declared by its seated posture. It carries a ram's horn to demonstrate its fertility and its **Ammonian virtue** <note>Referring to the Egyptian god Amun, often depicted with ram's horns as a symbol of creative power</note>. With its right hand, it holds a scorpion by the tail and a dog; by which **Anubis** and **Typhon** are aptly indicated, according to the testimony of Plutarch; this represents the drying power of the Sun, which is most active when the Sun enters Scorpio, as the trees are stripped of leaves and the earth of its grasses. The folded left hand holds a Scorpion, two serpents, and a lion-shape entwined with a staff; by these, power and authority over life and death, generation and corruption, good and evil, and the Kingdom of **Mophta** <note>A term Kircher uses to describe a specific Egyptian creative or elemental force, often associated with water or craftsmanship</note> are indicated. Thus, according to the testimony of Horus <note>Horapollo, an ancient author on hieroglyphs</note>, death and the destruction of things (or the preparation of evils) are indicated by the Scorpion, a deadly animal; the double life of the celestial and elemental world is shown by the two serpents; and Momphta, the overseer of moist nature, is aptly indicated by the Lion. 

Furthermore, through the images placed around the many-shaped Deity—equipped with serpents and other hoopoe-headed staffs <note>term: <term>Cucuphomorphis</term>; staffs topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, symbolizing purity or surveillance</note>, a whip, and **ankh crosses** <note>original: *ansatis crucibus* ("handled crosses")</note>—under the figures of a boy, a lion, a hawk, and an ibis, they show the vital fertility which they flow into the World, the Sun, the Moon, and the Elements for the variety of things; all of which will be explained at length in their proper places. It tramples the heads of two Crocodiles looking in different directions, by which it is beautifully indicated that all destructive Typhonian and Arimanian <note>Refers to Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of evil and darkness</note> force is held perfectly subject to itself, wherever the east and west extend. 

Under the crocodiles, an arched surface is seen with the Genii <note>Spirits or divine attendants</note> who are followers of the all-shaped Deity and the tutelary administrators of things; by these, the entire kingdom of Mophta is governed through the fit arrangement of the seasons. Some of these are standing, others are sitting; the first three on the right and the three on the left are standing; the five in the middle are in a sitting posture. Starting from the right, the first is a **lion-headed** <note>original: *λεοντοκέφαλος* (leontokephalos)</note> Genius, holding a grappling hook in its hand, clothed in a sacred veil, and holding a globe on its head; by this is noted the Genius conferring a corroborative force and a solidifying power to things against the dissipating force of things. Following is a **hawk-shaped** <note>original: *ἱερακόμορφος* (hierakomorphos)</note> Genius, that is, with a hawk-like face, distinguished by a hoopoe-headed staff, by which the solar force in heat and moisture (which is the cause of the variety of things) is indicated. There follows a third **cat-shaped** <note>original: *αἰλουρόμορφος* (ailouromorphos)</note> Genius, or in the likeness of a Cat—or what is the same thing, a baboon-headed lunar Genius. Three other Genii correspond to these from the opposite side: the first of which, sitting with a hawk-like face and a feather in its hand, shows the swift power of the Solar motion; the second, in the form of an Ibis with a feather in its hand, shows the swift power of the Lunar motion; the third, under the form of a dog, indicates Anubis, the guardian of the Horizon, according to the testimony of Plutarch.

In the middle is the figure of a serpent, biting its tail in a wavy coil; this is the figure by which the year or the Zodiac is aptly indicated, according to the testimony of Horus. It is wavy...

# INTERPRETATION.

...whether arranged in the figure of flowing water, so as to express the spirals which the Sun [traces] as if in the waves of the celestial sea through the twelve signs and as many months. While it completes its motion, it is the cause of the production of all things that exist in the world; the twelve signs or months are aptly indicated by these spirals, each of which we have marked with its own number, as appears in the figure. Because, however, five days are missing from the solar year to reach 360, they wished to signify these through five principal spirals, over which as many Genii <note>Spirits or guardian deities</note> preside. The mythology, according to the mind of **Plutarch**, is as follows. They say that **Rhea** <note>The Greek name used here for the Egyptian goddess Nut</note>, having secretly slept with **Saturn** <note>The god Geb</note>, was cursed by the **Sun** <note>The god Ra</note>, who had discovered the crime, so that she could give birth neither in a month nor in a year. But **Mercury** <note>The god Thoth</note>, captivated by love for the Goddess, lay with her; afterward, playing a game with the **Moon**, he emerged victorious and took away the seventieth part of every day, adding these to the 360 days of the year. These five days are now called *Misi* by the **Egyptians**, and by the **Greeks** *epagomenoi* <note>original: ἐπαγομένοι; meaning "added" or "intercalary" days</note>, that is, "added days." On these days, the **festivals of the birthdays of the Gods** are celebrated. On the first of these days, **Osiris**, the lord of all things, was born. On the second day, **Arueris** was born, whom some call **Apollo**, and others the elder **Horus**. On the third, **Typhon** leapt out, not at his proper time or place, but having broken through a wound in his mother's side. On the fourth, **Isis** [was born] in the festivals. On the fifth, **Nephthys**, whom they also name "the End," and "**Venus**," and "Victory." We, however, have restored these five minor deities from hieroglyphic doctrine in such a way that we understand the first day to be dedicated to **Hermanubis**; the second to **Anubis**; the third to **Isis**; the fourth to **Horus**; and the fifth to **Osiris**, as the true tutelary <note>protective</note> deities of **Egypt**, whom the figure expressed here denotes. For **Hermanubis**, or the *Ibis-like Hermes*, is expressed by an ibis-shaped statue; **Anubis** by a *kynomorphon* <note>original: κυνόμορφον; dog-faced</note> or canine face; **Isis** by a female face with her veil; **Horus** by a child's face; and finally **Osiris** by a lion-like and maned countenance. They hold wings in their hands to hint at the hidden motion of their driving force. The circles on the heads of the first, second, and fifth indicate divine power and authority over the world. The **eyed phallus** <note>A symbolic representation of generative power combined with divine providence</note> placed above the head of **Isis** in the middle indicates the multitude of seminal abundance, over which **Isis** stands as the passive principle of things. Finally, the fifth figure, **Osiris**, carries a serpent-bearing globe on his head, to show that he is the active principle of worldly life.

And these are the moderators of the year, and the tutors and preservers of all things born in the lower world during the course of the entire year. However, because the happiness indicated by the said five tutelary Genii for lower things has opposing powers, by whose malice the things of nature could be variously disturbed, they have aptly placed at the sides tutelary *averruncant* <note>original: auerruncos; deities who ward off or "turn away" evil</note> Genii. These are indicated by symbols of warding-off power, such as hooks, whips, and similar items, by which the malignant force of the [evil] Genii is driven away, and the intended variety and abundance of things is preserved. Below these, indeed, are two images: the first pierces a **hippopotamus** with a lance, the other a crocodile. By these, the **Bebonian** force—for so **Manetho** in **Plutarch** names the **Typhonic** force—is denoted as an obstacle or impediment. Because the **hippopotamus** and the **Typhonic crocodile** [stand] against things proceeding rightly and tending toward their end...

466 BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

...might stand; whom, however, the spirit of Horus and Osiris finally destroys and scatters. This harmonizes beautifully with what **Plutarch** records in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, where he says that at **Hermopolis** <note>An ancient Egyptian city, known as the "City of Hermes" (Thoth)</note> a statue is shown of **Typhon** as a **hippopotamus** <note>original: ἵππον ποταμον (hippon potamon)</note> upon which stands a **hawk** fighting a **snake**. By the horse they signify **Typhon**, and by the hawk they signify power and sovereignty, which he, having acquired by force, is disturbed by and causes disturbance through his malice.
<gloss>*A river horse upon which a hawk stands fighting a snake; the horse indicates Typhon, the hawk indicates the power and principle through which, having obtained it by force, he is often restless, disturbed by and causing disturbance through malice.*</gloss>
You see in this figure a **Deity in the form of a hawk** <note>original: ἱερακόμορφον (hierakomorphon)</note> holding a snake in his left hand and with his right hurling a spear at the hippopotamus. For **Osiris**, the life of all things, by the power of his rays—like spears being struck—easily overcomes that **Beastly force** <note>Referring to the chaotic power of Typhon/Set</note> and kills that which is hostile to the end of natural things. Against this force, **Mophta** <note>In Kircher’s system, Mophta is a "Genius" or spirit associated with the creative power of the Nile</note> presents himself as a diligent antagonist, indicated by the **lion-shaped statue** equipped with a **hoopoe-headed staff** <note>original: baculo cucuphomorpho; Kircher identifies the Egyptian 'Was' scepter as being topped with the head of a hoopoe bird</note> following from behind and breaking his power. This same thing is shown on the opposite side by the figure of a hawk piercing a **crocodile** with a weapon. See **Plutarch** in the cited place: they used to say all evil and harmful events, which have a certain repugnance to nature, were the effects and works of **Typhon**; these the **Sun**, while he kills them, at the same time restores the world to a **pure** <note>original: ἄκρατον (akraton); meaning unmixed or temperate</note> climate. 

Moreover, by the **dogs** at the sides, lying near the wavy snake, the guarding of the **Sun's approach and withdrawal** <note>The solstices</note> is indicated; or, as Plutarch wishes, it refers to the **rising of the Nile**, which the celestial dogs <note>The star Sirius, known as the Dog Star, whose rising coincided with the Nile flood</note> move and promote by their rising. **Clement of Alexandria** demonstrates that these things are so in very clear words in the 5th book of his *Stromata*: *There are those who would have the Tropics signified by the dogs, who guard and, like doorkeepers, observe the Sun’s approach to the South and the North.*

And from these things it is clear that whatever has been said regarding the influence of the **Triform Deity** <note>The supreme divine power acting through three aspects</note> upon the **Angelic World** through its many-formed nature, and from there into the **Celestial** and **Elemental Worlds**, is contained in this hieroglyphic fragment as if in a certain epitome and recapitulation.

With these things established, nothing remains but for us to proceed with equal daring to unravel the context of the sacred symbols in each of the following sides of the obelisk.

And indeed, just as the earlier Schematisms were placed in the position of an inscription <note>Literally "as a title or epigraph"</note>, they also provide a universal knowledge of the doctrine contained in this obelisk. In the remaining sides of the obelisk, the doctrine taught universally descends, as it were, to particulars: what its use may be in human affairs, what in nature, and what in the human soul; how...

## REPRESENTATION I.
### Of the First Side: The Eastern Side.

<margin>Of the 1st Eastern Side of the Obelisk.</margin>
This Representation <note>original: Schematismus</note> exhibits the influx of the Triple-Formed Deity first into the Archetype <note>The original "blueprint" or ideal pattern in the mind of God</note>, then into the spiritual, the starry, and the elemental realms. Since these were treated at length on page 400, we refer the reader there. But before we proceed further to other Representations, it seemed appropriate to offer a brief prelude, so that the truth in the following explanations might become more clearly known. 

The question is asked, therefore: how can God, being immaterial, involve Himself in material things? Second, why did the Egyptians appoint gods over each of the world's quarters, locations, and inner chambers? Why did they fashion statues of gods from every kind of sensible matter? And why did they call animals the "dwellings of the gods"? Finally, why did they reject certain materials as being contrary to the gods? 

As for the first point, since GOD is the cause of all causes and is distant from nothing—as all things would vanish into nothingness without His perpetual influx—it is necessary that He be intimately present in all things. Although the Egyptians held this orthodox doctrine, handed down from Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Egyptians attributed their wisdom</note>, they lacked the light of supernal faith. Thus, they scattered this hidden unity within all things into a multitude of material objects. Consequently, they assigned to individual things their own Spirits <note>original: Genios</note>, as if they were specific particles of the divine Power, and worshipped them in place of the true Gods. Hence they believed all matter was fit for receiving the gods, which **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians"</note> shows with his usual subtlety in these words on page 307 of the Basel edition:

*Truly, the abundance of power in the highest causes of the universe is such that, just as it surpasses lower things in other ways, so it greatly surpasses them in this: namely, in the very amplitude of its presence. As the greatest causes of all, they are most present to all things, so that the power of each cause is always present everywhere in its entirety, without hindrance. By this reasoning, the very first things assist even the last; immaterial principles are present in material things in an immaterial way. Let no one wonder if we say there is a certain matter that is pure and divine. For since matter itself was made by the Creator and Father of all, it has deservedly acquired a certain perfection of its own, making it fit to receive the gods. Furthermore, nothing prevents higher beings from diffusing their light to lower ones; therefore, they do not permit matter to be devoid of higher things. Quapropter <note>Therefore</note> whatever matter is perfect, pure, and god-like <note>original: Deiforme</note> is not unfit for the reception of the gods. For since it was necessary that even earthly things should in no way be devoid of divine communication, the earth itself received a certain divine portion and lot within it, sufficient to receive the gods. From this it followed that they would select whatever materials were congruent to the gods for use in sacrifices, while rejecting incongruous symbols as belonging to rival powers* <note>original: ἀντιτέχνων (antitechnōn), meaning "rival craftsmen" or opposing forces</note> *or adverse ones; hence with such great study and care, sin-*

# BOOK V. OF THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK

...for the individual Gods, they prepared individual Statues, fashioned from those materials which they knew to possess a certain rational correspondence <margin>rational justification <note>original Greek: αποδολογία (apologia)</note></margin> to the properties of the said Gods, and which they superstitiously believed were under their protection. Hence, they fashioned Serapis—the "mind of the world," as we have proved elsewhere—from all the sensible materials of the world: herbs, roots, seeds, and every kind of stone and earth. 

Thus, when about to make a statue, they would especially select those materials that grew in the lands of Egypt, over which they believed the Guardian Spirit <note>original: Genius</note> of the one whose statue they were preparing presided. Furthermore, they strictly observed the quarters of the world, so that they might select those things which, by a certain analogy, corresponded to the quality of that specific Spirit presiding over a particular quarter; they took the greatest care not to confuse things belonging to one quarter with things of another, as if they did not belong to the proper Spirit. 

From this came the cult of sacred animals, some of which they worshipped with divine honors because the Divinities <note>original: Numina</note> taught the mortal race from within them as if from dwellings, and provided omens of future events. By observing and worshipping these, they thought they could win for themselves the intimacy of the Gods. Some they slaughtered and burned, honoring the immaterial Divinities through this worship by means of the resolution into the four elements <note>The process of burning reduced the physical animal back into its constituent elements: fire, air, earth, and water</note>, giving to each what is proper to a God.

But whatever has been said thus far is taught so clearly by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note> that to have heard him is to have understood their entire doctrine. He speaks thus on page 308 of the Basel edition:

> *Therefore, this sacred wisdom, having contemplated these things and thus diligently finding suitable receptacles <note>original: susceptacula; physical objects capable of holding divine essence</note> for each of the Gods according to their harmony, often combines into one: stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar sacred, perfect, and God-like things. From all these, it then fabricates a pure and complete receptacle. For it is not lawful to despise all matter, but only that which is alien to the Gods. One should choose what is proper to them, as that which is able to harmonize with and contribute to the dwellings of the Gods, the foundations of the statues, and the works of sacrifice. For in no other way can any possession or portion of divine things reach earthly places and the men living here, unless such a foundation has first been laid.* 
>
> *One must believe the secret discourses, which testify that through blessed visions a certain matter was handed down from the Gods; this matter is therefore kindred to those who handed it down. Such matter in sacrifice rouses the Gods to show themselves, and immediately calls them to be understood, takes hold of them as present, and demonstrates them perfectly. One can learn the same things even from the distribution of divinity made according to location, and from the very prefecture divided among individual things, whatever lots of this kind may have been obtained throughout the various orders, whether greater or lesser.* 
>
> *For it is certain that for the Gods who are rulers of certain places, a sacrifice made from those same things that grow there will be most fitting; the things governed will please the governors, and those things belonging to them will be pleasing. Their own works are always most grateful to the creators, and those who first produce something hold such things as most acceptable in turn. Whether, therefore, they be certain animals or plants, or other things dispensed by the vision of those above, they have at the same time obtained a prefecture under them, and they procure for us an indivisible communion with the higher powers. Some of these, therefore, insofar as they are preserved and held—*

<header>INTERPRETATION.</header>

<margin>Eastern Side of the Obelisk.</margin>
...[they are increased], they increase the intimacy of those who possess them toward the Gods. Such, among the Egyptians, are the sacred animals, and everywhere the "sacred man"; indeed, there are some things which, when slaughtered and burned, effect a clearer intimacy, namely because they ensure a more certain resolution into the principle of the first elements <note>The four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note> for the sake of the higher powers, and are rendered more sacred according to the rite. Hence the Egyptians alone held the secret methods for fashioning Idols of this kind; concerning which <margin>Diodorus, Book 1.</margin> Diodorus writes in Book 2, chapter 3, in these words: 

> A type of art unknown to the Greeks, but known by use among the Egyptians. For the Egyptians alone did not measure the composition of the whole statue by sight, but by dimension, so that the statue was perfected from various and many stones reduced into one body according to a certain measure. It is truly an admirable thing that different craftsmen in various places could agree so perfectly on a single measurement, so that sometimes a single statue was constructed from 20 or even 40 separate parts.

Seeing, therefore, that all things were marked with the seal of divinity, the Egyptians adorned their more secret philosophy according to the markings and characteristics impressed upon individual things. This philosophy is, in fact, nothing other than a certain hidden analogy of sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses.</note> to the virtues of the insensible Gods. When they employed these things in their sacred rites through a certain secret mixture, there necessarily arose—as they believed—a certain Divine Transformation <note>original Greek: Θεομόρφωσις (Theomorphosis)</note> from these things most acceptable to the Gods. From this came the attraction and union with the Divinity, which is the ultimate end and fulfillment of all happiness. And this is what the remaining diagrams of this Obelisk teach, which you may see as follows:

And a little later, Horus <note>The author of the *Hieroglyphica*, known as Horapollo, whose work was a primary source for Renaissance attempts to decode Egyptian symbols.</note> says: *“others say [the water comes] from above the Ocean, for from then the water of Egypt rises up, in the time of the manifestation [the flood].”* <note>original Greek: ἕτεροι δὲ... ὑπὲρ τὰ Ὠκεανῶ, καὶ γὰρ ἀπὸ τότε ὕδωρ ἀναγίνεται τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ἐν τῇ ἀναφάσεως καιρῷ.</note> This is another cause by which, at the time of the inundation, the water overflows into Egypt. The strength of this overflow marks the coming year through a square <gloss>10</gloss>, which, according to Horus in Book 1, Chapter 5, signifies that the year acquires great fertility. Egypt is blessed by the generosity, beneficence, and benevolent offering of the Deity, which are aptly indicated by the two <gloss>11 12</gloss> following arms, along with a two-knotted scepter to indicate the dominion of both the celestial and terrestrial Momphta <note>Kircher's name for a supreme creative spirit or "World Mind" in his Egyptian system</note> mentioned above.

Furthermore, after the two-knotted scepter, there follows a <gloss>14</gloss> prostrate human figure, and below that figure a <gloss>15</gloss> parallelogram ending on both sides in the letter V, with three lines in the middle. After this is a <gloss>16</gloss> Cerastes, a horned serpent, and below this a <gloss>17</gloss> scalene triangle with three <gloss>a b c</gloss> squares. Beneath these is a "hydroschema," or <gloss>18</gloss> figure of water, which is followed by a <gloss>19</gloss> bifurcated scepter; this scepter is <gloss>21</gloss> eye-shaped, or having the form of an eye. This is followed by a <gloss>23</gloss> receptacle for sacred water, which is <gloss>24</gloss> square; then an <gloss>25</gloss> extended hand, beneath which are a <gloss>26</gloss> Cerastes, a <gloss>27</gloss> rudder-shaped club with an arm and a <gloss>28</gloss> quail, followed by a <gloss>29</gloss> circular segment with an ember, or a receptacle for <gloss>29</gloss> sacred water.

->But let us explain each one.<-

<margin>The Priests shaped the rites according to the mystical proportions of the statues.</margin>

The <gloss>14</gloss> human figure represents Mophta, or Momphta (for it is called both), whose name it expresses through the position of its limbs. For, as we correctly stated in our work on the construction of the mystical alphabet, it was a particular custom of the Egyptians to represent statues in such positions that they would express the Name of the God they were invoking. This present figure teaches us this very thing: it represents the name of the Genius <term>ⲙⲱⲙⲫⲧ</term> <note>Mompht</note> transformed into letters by the position of the limbs. In this way, the two arms with the space between them <gloss>ⲙⲙ</gloss> express the Coptic letter M; the head represents the letter <term>ⲱ</term> <note>Omega/O</note>; the arms with the belly represent <term>ⲫ</term> <note>Phi/Ph</note>; and finally, the feet represent the bifurcated cross <term>ⲧ</term> <note>Tau/T</note>, a type of hieroglyphic mark we have shown to be very frequent. Indeed, see the figure to the side, along with its resolution into Coptic characters. 

They believed that nothing could be more powerful for performing wonders or attracting divine influence than constructing a statue with this ingenious structure. Moreover, through this prostrate figure, they showed the rite to be performed by the Priests during its consecration, which had to conform to the statue itself. Thus, the Priest, prostrate on the floor in the inner sanctuary, silently expressed the Name through a similar position of his limbs, while also invoking it with a spoken formula of words. We see this same rite used by the Hebrews themselves, who expressed the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter sacred name of God, YHWH</note> Name of God in their sacred ceremonies by disposing their fingers in a certain way; regarding this, see the *Prodromus* and *Oedipus*, which treat the subject extensively. The Kabbalists also—as that most recondite book they call the *Pardes* <note>The *Pardes Rimonim* (Orchard of Pomegranates) by Moses Cordovero, a key text of Jewish Kabbalah</note> clearly shows—express all the limbs of a man through the divine names. He uses these words: *“And this explicit Name you shall put upon you, and you shall place the drawing of the letters within it with the limbs of your body.”* <note>original Hebrew: וזה שם המפרש תשים עליך וצירת האותיות בו תשום עם אברי גופך</note>

*“And you shall place this explained name of God upon you, and you shall mark the figures of its letters upon the members of your body.”* Indeed, the Chaldean Targum <note>A Targum is an ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> on chapter 3 of the Song of Songs, verse 17, teaches in these words that the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note> name of God was not only expressed with the fingers, but also engraved upon sacred ornaments:

*“And they shall be prepared, and there shall be engraved upon them the Great Name, explained through seventy names.”* <note>original Hebrew: ויתתקון וינהון דחקיק בה שמא רבא מפרש בשבעין שמהן</note>

<margin>Why do the Hebrews and Greeks express the name of God and Christ with their fingers?</margin>
*“And they took off the ornaments of their weapons, in which was engraved the Great Name explained in seventy names.”* Thus, these secret rites flowed not only from the Egyptians to the Hebrews (or, if you prefer, from the latter to the former), but also to the Greeks and Arabs, who proceed in their sacred rites with a similar cult of ceremonies to this very day. For it is better known than it needs to be said that the Greek Patriarchs and Bishops, in their solemn blessing, express the name of Christ ☧ with their fingers formed in a certain way. We would show all these things more extensively if the bulk of this book did not stand in the way, and if we had not treated this material elsewhere as a professional study. Therefore, let it suffice to have merely indicated these things.

Now that the rite has been explained, let us see the effect emerging from it. The figure extends the right hand as if to designate something; that designation was the following 15th figure, which, according to the author of the *Great Coptic Scale*, <note>A reference to a Coptic-Arabic dictionary or "Scala" used by Kircher for his linguistic studies.</note>

<margin>The sacred baris.</margin>
they called the sacred “barra” or, in Egyptian, *baris* <note>original Coptic/Greek: ϐⲁⲣⲓⲥ. A "baris" was a type of flat-bottomed boat used on the Nile, often used in religious processions to carry statues of deities.</note>. The sacred baris was an instrument similar to a bier or litter, in which the Priests, having placed the sacred statues, consecrated them with legitimate rites and mysterious operations. It had three divisions in the middle designated for the three parts of the year; its horns, ☽ and ☾, indicated the Rising and Setting [of the sun], according to which regions it was hiddenly arranged. In its receptacles were placed the "witnesses" of Osiris, the bandages of Isis, the amulets of Horus, and similar things. Sometimes it was constructed in a lunar or crescent shape, of which Plutarch speaks in his book *On Isis and Osiris*: *“Cutting the wood in the burial of Osiris, as they call it, he prepares a chest in a lunar shape; for the Moon, approaching the Sun, becomes crescent-shaped and is hidden.”* By means of these things, they sought a benefit through a triple influx during the three parts of the year, from the rising and the conjunction at the setting. From this followed 16 life in heat (which they indicated by the cerastes, <gloss>16</gloss> the fiery serpent) and the 17 generation of things, through the 17 genetic scalene triangle, in the triple elementary ᵃ ᵇ ᶜ World (through the three squares), as was said above; and 18 moisture (which they indicated by the 18 *hydroschema* or figure of water) flowed forth. There follows the 19 forked staff, a symbol of support <term>κυριολογικῶς</term> <note>original Greek: "kyriologikōs," meaning in a literal or primary sense.</note>, as if they were saying that through the action

<margin>The forked staff, what it means.</margin>
indicated above, life and the generation of all things contained in the triple elementary World, consisting in heat and moisture, procures the true 20 support of the coming year, indicated by the 20 □ square. But, so that the Reader may more clearly know the origin of this forked staff, it must be understood that the Egyptian Priests transferred all instruments used in sacred rites into the register of hieroglyphics because they consisted of a certain mystical principle. This mentioned scepter was also one of these, with which they supported the sacred bier carried about in the processions of the Gods, as well as the sacred baris, whenever they had to rest. It was made from a certain wood appropriate to the Gods they were carrying, and the staff terminated in the shape of a V, because with the symbol of celestial influx...

<margin>Pausanias in *Description of Greece: Corinth*.</margin>
*Corinthiacs*, with these words: *The priest-ministers went before, equipped with sacred prongs*; <note>original: "sacris instructi fuscinis"</note> and a trace of this is still seen in a coin of Pietro Stephanoni once shared with me. <margin>What is the eye-shaped scepter?</margin>
There follows ²¹ an arm with an ²² eye-shaped scepter and the figure of a ²³ <term>favissa</term> <note>In Roman antiquity, a *favissa* was an underground cellar or cistern near a temple; Kircher uses it here to mean a sacred water-receptacle.</note> or sacred receptacle. By these, they indicated the beneficence of Osiris, or the Celestial Eye; the former through the arm, the latter through the scepter adapted into the shape of an eye. For, as was said above, the Egyptians, when intending to represent Osiris, placed a scepter with the figure of an eye, according to the testimony of Macrobius and Plutarch: <note>original Greek: "Τὸν δὲ Ὅσιριν αὖ πάλιν ὀφθαλμῷ καὶ σκήπτρῳ γράφουσιν ὧν τὸ μὲν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐμφαίνει τὸ δὲ τὴν δύναμιν, ὡς Ὅμηρος τὸν ἄρχοντα καὶ βασιλεύοντα πάντων Ζὴν ὕπατον καὶ μήστωρα καλῶν."</note> *They depict Osiris again with an eye and a scepter, indicating providence by the eye and power by the scepter; in this way Homer calls Jove, the King and Prince of all, the most high and the counselor.* Since frequent mention of this is made everywhere, we shall not linger on it, and we have shown elsewhere that the Egyptians were accustomed to carry this kind of mystical scepter in the solemnities of their processions.

<margin>The nature of the *favissa*, or sacred cistern or pool.</margin>
Figure ²³ denotes a *Favissa*, or sacred cistern—that is, a receptacle for Celestial water. According to Festus, it is called a *Favissa*, meaning "Sacred Water," preserved in sacred inner-sanctums for holy use. Abenephius <note>A reference to the 10th-century writer Ibn Wahshiyya, whom Kircher believed was an ancient authority on hieroglyphs.</note> calls it a sacred pool:

<note>original Arabic: "وكان بكل هيكل بركه تحت الصوره التي هي موافقه لاسراره"</note>
*For there was in every temple a pool beneath the image, which was suitable for their mysteries.* For the Priests had, in the more secluded places, a receptacle for the water of the Nile, introduced into it through hidden channels, which they used in performing sacrifices. This is expressly shown in the following figure, where a priest-minister, carrying a sacred bowl, stands on a pavement where you see the figure of a sacred cistern exactly like the one shown in the present hieroglyphic. Into this cistern, water flows from a lion's head, through which the beneficence of <term>Mophta</term> <note>In Kircher's system, Mophta is the "genius" or spirit of the Nile's generative moisture, often symbolized by a lion.</note> toward the element of moisture is indicated. This figure was once sent to me by Peiresc <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a famous French humanist and patron of learning.</note>, having been taken from a certain ancient amphora. By this, the coming year ²⁴ is ²⁵ blessed with ²⁶ life and abundance of things, and ²⁷ equality...

...and the proper balance of things is shown through the yoke of the scale (30), a symbol of <term>pyrelogikon</term> <note>original Greek: "πυρελόγικων," likely referring to solar or celestial calculations or the "logic of fire."</note>. The hostile demon (28), however, is driven away from the receptacle (T) of the sacred water (29). As has been said, the year is indicated by the square; life, which consists of heat and moisture, is represented by the <term>horned viper</term> <note>original: "cerasten bicornem"</note>. Generosity is shown by the arm (25). Through the lotus-shaped club (27), upon which a quarter-measure of a field, or <term>arura</term> <note>An ancient Egyptian unit of area.</note>, is placed, they indicated the stability of things subject to the East (which is represented by the Lotus), as well as the abundance (27) of the fields. Through the arm (T) with the Quail (28), beneath which a <term>favissa</term> <note>A sacred underground cistern or cellar.</note> is placed, the repelling of the hostile Spirit (28) from the sacred pool is indicated (concerning which, see more in the Hieroglyph of the Quail). Porphyry, in the second book of *On Abstinence*, explains why the Egyptians studied to appease both good and evil spirits with such exactness and care through sacrifices and ceremonies in these words:

> *Regarding all these matters, men are convinced that demons, if they become angry because they are neglected and deprived of the established worship, will inflict harm; on the other hand, they will do good for those who have made them favorable to themselves through vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other things of this kind. Thus, while these spirits harm the mortal race of men in many areas—and sometimes in the greatest matters—the good demons never cease their specific duties. They show us the dangers hanging over us from evildoers to the best of their power, making signs to us through dreams, through a divinely inspired soul, and many other means. If anyone were able to distinguish those things which are signified, he would know and guard against all frauds; for they signify to everyone, but not all perceive the things being signified.*

> *These are the ones who are delighted by libations and the smell of burnt offerings; for they live on vapors and incense, and are strengthened in various ways by various things, particularly by the smells from blood and flesh. Therefore, a wise and temperate man will be careful to use such sacrifices by which he might attract such demons to himself, and will study to purify his soul in every way; for such spirits are not accustomed to invade a pure soul because of the dissimilarity they have with it.*

All of these things are confirmed by what is read in Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy.</note> to this effect: for we are accustomed to call upon the Gods through such animals who clearly preside over those animals, especially those which they govern by a close and almost kindred condition. Likewise, the demons are divided by provinces and regions and, as guardians of the parts of the world, they take such great care of the individual parts entrusted to them that they cannot tolerate even a word contrary to the order and dispensation of that part; they are, in fact, the obstinate guardians of the eternal and immutable perseverance of worldly things. But concerning these matters, we shall speak more diffusely in the following sections; now let us proceed to the Third Schema.

## Ideal Conception of the Reading.

A mystical **protective statue** ${}^{1}$ <note>original: "Statua prophylactica"</note> must be constructed when the ${}^{2}$ **Sun** is in the **rear part of Leo**, with the ${}^{3}$ **Moon rising**; it must be positioned toward the East (1. 6.). Furthermore, this statue ${}^{4}$ must be dedicated to both the ${}^{5}$ **Celestial** and ${}^{4}$ **Terrestrial Mophta** <note>Kircher identifies "Mophta" as a divine spirit or "genius" of the Nile, often depicted as a lion-headed figure representing fertility and the power of water.</note> through a sacred rite. From this ${}^{7}$ benevolence of the Deity, an abundance of ${}^{8}$ things that are born and ${}^{8}$ grow is granted; through the ${}^{9}$ **water** surging into Egypt in the subterranean regions, the ${}^{10}$ coming year is filled with the happiness and abundance of the ${}^{12}$ benevolent **Deity** ${}^{11}$ who is powerful in a ${}^{13}$ double dominion.

Furthermore, the ${}^{14}$ **Priest** in the sacred rites, by conforming himself into the form of Mophta, shall perform the ${}^{15}$ **sacred ceremonies** upon the ${}^{15}$ sacred boat.

For from these things, ${}^{16}$ **life** and the ${}^{17}$ **generation** of all things contained within the triple elemental World (a, b, c)—consisting of the ${}^{18}$ **hot** and the ${}^{18}$ **moist**—there flows the unique ${}^{19}$ support of the ${}^{20}$ coming year. From this also, the ${}^{21}$ generosity of **King Osiris**, the celestial eye (22), is poured back through the ${}^{23}$ **afflux of sacred water**, or <term>favissa</term> <note>A sacred underground cistern or reservoir used to hold ritual waters or discarded sacred objects.</note>, into the ${}^{25}$ benevolence of the Deity for the ${}^{24}$ coming year’s happiness.

And finally, the **life** ${}^{26}$ of things ${}^{27}$ subject to the **East** is granted with an ${}^{30}$ equal temperament; the ${}^{28}$ **hostile power** is kept away and restrained by the ${}^{30}$ protection of the benevolent Deity through the ${}^{29}$ influx of the *favissa* or sacred water.

BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK

### S C H E M A T I S M III.

#### *Interpretation of the First Eastern Side.*

<margin>Explanation of the names of the symbols.</margin>
In this third Schematism <note>A "schematism" refers to a structured diagram or a specific arrangement of figures used in Kircher’s analysis.</note> of the first Eastern side, there occurs in the first place: 1. the figure of a labyrinth; then 2. two crows, beneath which is 3. a two-horned viper <note>original: "Cerastes bicornis," a Saharan horned viper common in Egyptian iconography.</note>; followed by 4. an Ibis, whose head is surrounded by 5. twelve small circles; opposed to which is 6. a Beetle <note>original: "Scarabæus"</note> enclosed by 7. a square and 8. a triangle; then follows 9. the head of a boy, whose neck is divided into three zones, across from which is placed 10. the figure of a gate distinguished by three projections; beneath which is placed 11. a two-horned viper; and 12. a prostrate owl with the figure of an extended hand; after which follow statues or idols, of which 14. the first is in a wondrous posture, and 14. the other 13. is distinguished by a high headdress <note>original: "tutulo," a conical priest’s cap or hairstyle.</note>, exhibiting I know not what mysteries; beneath these is placed 16. a two-horned viper; then 18. two stars with 17. a mystical statue and the head of a boy with a three-zoned neck, with 19. an altar placed beneath; after these 20. a scepter cutting through three parallelograms, beneath which is placed 22. an eyed phallus, with 21. a hawk across from it; this is followed by a figure similar to the Greek letter Π, which includes 24. an Ο; then six 25. 26. quadrangles with three 27. grappling hooks <note>original: "harpagonibus"</note> adapted into the shape of a goat’s head; after which is 28. an extended hand, then 29. a Spheroid figure, after which are three idols with spreading legs joined by their hands, each of which 30. has a 31. 32. vessel placed upon its head, and each vessel is of a different shape; afterward 36. a serpent occurs, beneath which are five 37. quadrangles with 38. a Spheroid; then 39. the figure of a mechanical restraint, with 40. an egg-bearing <note>original: "ὠοφόρῳ" (oophorō)</note> arm. We have thus the nomenclature of the individual symbols; let us now subjoin the mystical reasons for each.

<margin>The Labyrinth indicates that nature is difficult to access.</margin>
The Labyrinth occurs in the first place; by this symbol, the Egyptians suggested the nature of things; for just as it is situated in the hidden abyss of the Divine Power, so they appropriately noted it as abstruse, impassable, and difficult to find by means of the labyrinth. Hence, according to the testimony of Hecataeus, they placed a labyrinth everywhere at the temple of the Spirit <note>original: "Genii"</note> of nature. *The people of Memphis, by an ancient tradition, were accustomed to place a labyrinth at the shrine of the Agathodaemon <note>The "Good Spirit" or protective deity of a place or of nature itself.</note> of nature, to signify that the path toward her is most difficult.* <note>original Greek: οἱ Μεμφῖται τῷ ἱερῷ τοῦ Ἀγαθοδαίμονος τῆς φύσεως, λαβύρινθον ἐκ παλαιᾶς τινος παραδόσεως ἔθος περιτιθέναι, προσημαίνειν χαλεπωτάτην πάροδον πρὸς αὐτήν.</note>

<margin>What do the two crows represent?</margin>
The two Crows following the labyrinth indicate the male and the female, or the active and passive principles of things, which nature uses as instruments in the production of things. For the Egyptians observed that this animal never lays more than two eggs, and from these a male and a female always emerge; hence, they very aptly denoted the male and female by two painted crows, representing Mars and Venus, of whom the former refers to the active principle and the latter to the passive principle in the nature of things; Horapollo <note>An author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics which Kircher relied upon heavily, though it was only partially accurate.</note> testifies to these things in Book 1, Chapter 8, with these words: *And others, when depicting Mars and Venus, paint two crows.* <note>original Greek: ἕτερος δὲ τὸν Ἄρεα καὶ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην γράφοντες, δύο κορώνας ζωγραφίζουσι</note>
<margin>Horapollo.</margin>

INTERPRETATION.
<page-num>477</page-num>
Ooo 2
<meta>catchword: called</meta>

...as man and woman. Since this animal brings forth two eggs, from which a male and a female must be born. <note>original Greek: ὡς ἄνδρα καὶ γυναῖκα. ἐπεὶ τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον δύο ὠὰ γεννᾷ, ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἄῤῥεν καὶ θῆλυ γεννᾶσθαι δεῖ.</note>
In another way, when writing of Mars and Venus, they paint two crows to represent the male and female, because this animal is accustomed to laying twin eggs, from which a male and a female are produced. But since Nature perfects the generation of things from an active and passive principle, and generation itself consists of heat and moisture—and from these, the life of things and the increase of all births occurs—they quite aptly placed beneath the two crows the Cerastes <gloss>3</gloss>, a two-horned Serpent, as a symbol of life consisting in heat and moisture, as was shown in the specific sacred description of the serpent.

<margin>The horned viper [Cerastes] as a sign of life consisting in heat and moisture</margin>
Furthermore, because the generation of things cannot be perfected without the motion of the Sun and Moon under the Zodiac—for these stars, by their various movements, move and alter the seminal reasons <note>A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept (*rationes seminales*) referring to the formative principles or "seeds" inherent in matter that guide development.</note> enclosed within the world, disposing them to take on forms, and finally perfecting the generation of things—hence the great gate <gloss>10</gloss> of the life of things is opened. All of this is beautifully seen through the Ibis <gloss>4</gloss>, whose head <gloss>5</gloss> you see crowned with twelve small circles distributed as if in the circumference of a ring. That they indicated the Moon through the Ibis has been explained at length in the sacred description of the Ibis;

<margin>What the head of the Ibis surrounded by 12 small circles means.</margin>
through the twelve small circles, the twelve parts of the great circle or the twelve signs of the Zodiac <note>original: "dodecamoria," the twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note> are noted, which the moon traverses in individual months. These are circumscribed around the head of the Ibis to demonstrate that this wondrous division proceeded from the mind of Mercury <note>The god Thoth, often identified with Hermes/Mercury, credited with inventing the calendar and writing.</note>. For as we have shown at length in the cited description of the Ibis, the Egyptians believed that the Mercurial deity, appearing in the form of an ibis, first handed down to men both the forms of letters and the division of the year, as well as the knowledge of the stars.

<margin>The Ibis as a mark of the Moon.</margin>
Because the Moon is of no use without the aspect of the Sun perpetually nourishing her, they placed in that region the Scarab <gloss>6</gloss> [Beetle] as a symbol of the Sun, on account of the wondrous analogy of its works to the works of the Sun. For the Sun, coming together with her twelve times through the space of the whole year, perfects the generation of all things; just as the Moon, completing the circuit of the twelve signs, constitutes a month (namely, the lunar year), so the Sun, by traversing the twelve signs, constitutes the Solar year. In this, a wondrous convergence is shown of the elemental power indicated by the square <gloss>7</gloss> toward the generation of all things, indicated by the genetic triangle <gloss>8</gloss>.

<margin>What does the Beetle [Scarab] denote?</margin>
Since we have treated all these matters most fully in the sacred description of the Scarab, we refer the reader there. Indeed, that the square signifies the elements and the triangle signifies generation was demonstrated copiously in the first diagram on page 388.

<margin>What the □ and ▽ mean</margin>
Since the influence of the Sun and Moon belongs to the whole world, as if they were the gates of the life of things, they placed next to the symbols of the Sun and Moon the head <gloss>9</gloss> of a boy, whose neck is encircled by three bands or zones. Opposite this, they established the figure of a gate <gloss>10</gloss>. By the head of the boy, they signify Horus, whom Plutarch, in his book *On Isis and Osiris*, calls the "mundane house"; others, as shown in the third book, call him the whole sensible world, distinguished into three zones: the Solar, the Lunar, and the Elemental. Or perhaps he represents the three hours—that is, the three parts of the year: Spring, Summer, and Winter—so called by Horus, according to Diodorus and Plutarch.

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
