...said to be indicated by those same nine zones of the neck. They depict it in the form of a child because, through the cycles of days and years and the generations of things, it seems to grow young again; for more on this, see Diodorus and Plutarch in the cited passage.
<margin>A gate is a figure proper to the thing signified.</margin>
The great gate <gloss>10</gloss> of life is opened; and the figure of the gate itself indicates a "gate" <term>kyriologically</term> <note>original Greek: κυριολογικῶς; Kircher uses this to mean a sign that represents an object literally or through its own form rather than metaphorically.</note>. For it was characteristic of the Egyptians to use "proper figures" (which represent the actual object) instead of sacred symbols in their sacred rites, as Clement of Alexandria testifies in Book 6 of the *Stromata*; regarding these, consult the section on the priestly writing of literal figures on page 364. Furthermore, it has already been frequently stated that life is suggested by the serpent <gloss>11</gloss>. You see, therefore, how beautifully the Egyptians wove their symbols together; let us follow the thread further so that you may see this tapestry more clearly.

<margin>Prophylactic statues are amulets against adverse powers.</margin>
However, because the generation of things can be hindered in various ways by contrary powers envious of human happiness, they invented certain astrological outcomes or amulets fashioned from sacred symbols and worldly materials, made analogous to the benefits of the *Genii* <note>Guardian or tutelary spirits that act as intermediaries between the divine and the material world.</note>. Such are the images marked <gloss>14</gloss> and <gloss>15</gloss>, the first of which, with its strange <note>original: *ridicula*, meaning odd or unusual in form</note> body shape, refers to the name of a Genius in the customary manner, as we have said elsewhere. For the early sages thought that this transformation contributed much to appeasing and attracting a Genius; for while these spirits take unique delight in things suited to them—such as the letters of the mystic Alphabet fashioned after the patterns of nature—they seemed to readily obey those performing the sacrifices and to grant their requests, as Iamblichus testifies. On the other hand, the adverse powers, which they indicate by an owl <gloss>12</gloss> with an arm, are restrained, and their opposition <term>antimachia</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντιμαχίαν; a state of resistance or combat.</note> is routed by the Good Spirits <note>original: *Agathodaemonum*</note> as if by symbols hostile to them. Moreover, we taught on page 315 that the owl is a symbol of an ill-omened Divinity. Furthermore, it has been stated elsewhere that the figure marked <gloss>15</gloss>, distinguished by a headdress <note>original: *tutulo*</note> with a segment of a circle placed beneath it, denotes power over lower things. A two-horned serpent <gloss>16</gloss> is placed beneath the statues to indicate the life which it preserves. Furthermore, since
<margin>The Egyptians thought that statues could be animated by the astrological art.</margin>
images of this kind draw all their force and power from the Astral Genii, they placed stars <gloss>18</gloss> beneath the serpent, along with the prophylactic image and the head of Horus. This indicates that through the astrological art and appropriate sacred rites—which the form of an altar <gloss>19</gloss> placed beneath Horus aptly indicates—such images must be consecrated so that a vital influence may be derived into them through the stars and their presiding Genii. For by a star, they indicated God, fate, the star itself, its Genius, and the divination which they believed they drew from the knowledge of future things by its help—a triple meaning shown under the single figure of a star, as we have shown elsewhere. Beneath Horus is placed a scepter <gloss>20</gloss> that cuts three quadrangles; by this symbol, they indicated the dominion of Horus over the three elemental worlds, as we prove elsewhere; and by the altar <gloss>19</gloss>, they noted the sacred rites due to Horus, all of which, as I said, are described elsewhere.

# INTERPRETATION.

<margin>The Vulture as a symbol of the Sun.</margin>
All these things are beautifully stated through the <gloss>21</gloss> vulture, and through the <gloss>22</gloss> eyed phallus and the equipment of the following lines. For just as the Sun, in a space of 120 days—which they called Spring—stirs the mixture of seminal things; and in another space of 120 days—which they call Summer—it incubates the offspring of the things conceived; and in another space of 120 days—which they call Winter—it rejoices in the fruits produced as if they were births, and remains quiet and free from generation; for by these three sets of three, the three parts of the year, together with the five corresponding days, the year is completed. As witness to this, Horapollo <note>Horapollo was the supposed author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a 5th-century treatise that provided symbolic (though often factually incorrect) explanations for Egyptian hieroglyphs, which Kircher used extensively.</note> says in Book 1, Chapter 11: <gloss>12</gloss> The vulture, a symbol of annual time, conceives from the wind over five days when its womb is opened to the breeze; then it carries the womb for 120 days, and for another 120 days it rears its chicks; for the final 120 days, being at leisure, it attends only to its own affairs, intent neither on pregnancy nor on rearing. Three times 120 makes 360, to which if you add the five days in which it conceives its offspring by the wind, the result is exactly the number of 365 days, by which the year is completed according to the Egyptian institution, with five "added days" <term>epagomenis</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπαγομένοις; these were the five extra days added to the twelve 30-day months of the Egyptian calendar to align it with the solar year.</note> joined to them.

Because the Sun would do nothing unless it surveyed all things by its motion made from east to west, the daily time is distributed into morning, noon, and evening. This corresponds exactly in every way to the three seasons of the year—if we assign the morning to the springtime, the noon to the summertime, and the evening to the wintertime. This "daily year" can not incongruously be said to be the cycle in which the concepts of things, their incubations, and finally their births are produced, proportioned to the daily motion of the Sun. Considering this motion to be of great importance in the worldly republic, they beautifully expressed it through the motion of the vulture, which, according to Horapollo, looks toward the west when the Sun rises, but when the Sun declines from noon toward its setting, the vulture looks toward the East with its womb turned toward the sun as if to receive the fertile power of the Sun. Moreover, they express this motion by two <gloss>23</gloss> isosceles triangles situated in opposite directions, as if always accompanying the Sun in the middle. Horapollo explains all these things beautifully in Book 1, Chapter 11; since he describes this hieroglyphic at greater length, we refer the reader there.

<margin>What is the eyed Phallus?</margin>
Since the end of motion is heat, and heat stimulates moisture, and from these the generation of things is perfected, they appropriately placed the <gloss>22</gloss> eyed phallus opposite the vulture. By this they suggest that Osiris—or the fertile Sun—perfects the generation of things through this celestial eye of his, via the annual time and the cycles of the days, in the management of the six lower worlds, which are designated by as many <gloss>25 26</gloss> rectangles.

Furthermore, because they found through continuous observation that the vulture lays only thirteen eggs, from which only females always emerge (no male existing among them), they beautifully indicated the Moon by this symbol, which is joined with the Sun thirteen times in an annual space. Thus, they noted the whole heaven by the vulture, because, like a female, it generates within itself all the works of the Sun and Moon. Through this <gloss>24</gloss> gate to the material worlds, indicated by the <gloss>25</gloss> rectangles <gloss>26</gloss> and the fertile dominion represented by the <gloss>27</gloss> three scepters distinguished by goat heads, the way is opened; by the benevolence of the <gloss>39</gloss> Divinity, the heavens are filled—the symbol of which is an extended hand of benevolence...

<margin>What *Iauta* means in Egyptian. And the statues made in the form of the Egyptian letter *Iauta*.</margin>
...ness and the liberality of the Deity; the circular figure is an indicator of the heavens, as has been proved elsewhere. Because the subject of celestial influx is moisture, they placed <gloss>29</gloss> <gloss>31</gloss> <gloss>34</gloss> <gloss>33</gloss> three statues here, whose spread feet are joined with their hands in the form of <term>Iauta</term> <note>Kircher identifies this as a specific symbolic Egyptian letter, likely derived from his study of "Hermetic" alphabets, representing a mystical "beginning."</note>, which letter in Egyptian signifies the same as "the beginning." Through these three similar statues, they indicated the identity of the triform Deity and the influx by which it moves into lower things, and from there back to higher things, without itself moving, being immersed in material things without being contaminated by them; this is what the statues of spread feet joined with hands mystically express.

There are, therefore, three statues, similar in form; they hold three vessels placed upon their heads of different shapes, and they denote different effects. Namely, that health-giving supramundane liquor through the <gloss>32</gloss> circular vessel; through the second <gloss>31</gloss> vessel, mixed from straight and curved lines, the sidereal water; the third <gloss>30</gloss> rectilinear vessel denotes the elementary water. <margin>The triple Nile indicated through the various forms of the Nilotic vessels.</margin> For there is a supramundane Nile, a celestial Nile, and an elementary Egyptian Nile, each of which contributes water that is healthy for the soul and the body. Furthermore, the statues are seen positioned with a spread-out bend to indicate that the supreme triform Deity, even if it is immersed in material worlds, is nonetheless infected by no contagion therefrom—unlike men devoted to worldly things, who are necessarily defiled by worldly mud. To purify these men, supramundane water is needed. <margin>The custom of the priests in washing themselves.</margin> Hence the Priests of Egypt are accustomed to wash themselves three times a day in the water of the Nile; so says <term>Chaeremon</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest of the 1st century AD.</note> in Porphyry, Book 4: *Three times a day*, he says, *they washed in cold water: when they rose from bed, when they were about to dine, and finally when they went to bed.* Their bed was woven from palm branches, which they call *Bais*. For while they wash themselves with the water of the Nile, they simultaneously participate in the water of the celestial Nile, and through this, as if with a prepared soul, they drink in the liquid of the supramundane Nile; being sprinkled by this, they believe they have attained a life incapable of any misery, blessed by the company of the Gods. Whence this pronouncement of the Ethiopians regarding the celestial Nile seems to have emerged: *Gihon falah samui zaiflas V-uatu bemai, Madur tambla bebaala, Vuatamblu saabanu* <note>original Ethiopic: "Ge'ez" script transliterated. Kircher is quoting an Ethiopic liturgical or poetic fragment.</note>; that is: *The Nile is a celestial river, irrigating us with healthy waters, filling the earth with riches, and satiating us with abundance.*

-> For it is this which confers life not only to the five gates of the <term>megacosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the Universe at large.</note>, but also, according to a certain analogy, to the five gates of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," or the human being.</note>, which are the five senses; and so these are beautifully expressed through the <gloss>36</gloss> serpents placed beneath the Nilotic statues, and through the five quadrangles and the celestial figure marked with the number <gloss>38</gloss>. Although through the five quadrangles they also indicated the five gates of the worlds into which that aforementioned triple liquid flows: these are the Archetypal, Genial, Sidereal, Elementary, and Microcosmic worlds. For once this triple liquid is given, the egg <note>Referring to the "Orphic" or "Cosmic" Egg, a symbol of universal creation.</note> is animated, corresponding to each of the said worlds, heavy with manifold offspring; it confers a happiness of fruits and an abundance overflowing into each World, which surely the <gloss>40</gloss> arm, upon whose hand the figure of an egg is placed, aptly expresses. <-

## Reading of the Conceptual Discourse.

1 The hidden nature of things, which is difficult to discover, employs two principles: 2 an active and 2 a passive one, both necessary for the generation of things, by which 3 the life of the universe is granted. This life consists in <gloss>o:</gloss> heat and <gloss>P:</gloss> moisture. The latter, <gloss>4</gloss> the Moon, promotes through <gloss>5</gloss> twelve months and in that same monthly space through <gloss>5</gloss> twelve mansions of the great circle; the former, the <gloss>6</gloss> Sun, promotes in an annual <gloss>7</gloss> span. From this comes again the <gloss>8</gloss> generation of things in <gloss>9</gloss> Horus, or the worldly house; and this is the <gloss>10</gloss> great gate of the <gloss>11</gloss> life of things.
   However, because the hostile force of <gloss>12</gloss> Typhon <note>original: "Typhonis." Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, whom Kircher views here as a symbol of chaos, drought, and destructive forces.</note> is contrary to these—either by immoderate cold or the parching power of immoderate heat—it usually brings about great devastation and sterility. 
   Hence, <gloss>14</gloss> statues or warding images <note>original: "simulachra auerrunca." These were statues meant to avert evil or disaster.</note> must be fashioned as Typhon’s <term>opposing reflections</term> <note>original: "ἀντίσχια" (antischia). A Greek term meaning "opposite shadows," used here to mean symbolic counter-forces or remedies.</note>, directed toward the east, expressing the names of the Genii <gloss>14</gloss> Mophta and <gloss>15</gloss> Nephta <note>Kircher identifies these as specific Egyptian spirits; Mophta is often linked to the creative spirit of the Nile.</note>, whom they represent. By their formation, the opposing power is restrained, and the life of <gloss>16</gloss> things remains safe and secure.
   Furthermore, under a certain <gloss>18</gloss> constellation, the <gloss>17</gloss> statue of Mophta must be made, which expresses the name itself, and that of <gloss>18</gloss> Horus with the three <gloss>20</gloss> <term>material</term> <note>original: "hylæis," from the Greek "hyle" meaning matter.</note> worlds under the power of the presiding ruler. For just as <gloss>21</gloss> Mophta, the <gloss>24</gloss> Lord, by the <gloss>23</gloss> rising and setting influx, governs the three <gloss>25</gloss> material worlds; so <gloss>18</gloss> Horus, <gloss>22</gloss> keeping watch with a <gloss>27</gloss> triple influx, <gloss>22</gloss> fertilizes and <gloss>28</gloss> blesses the three <gloss>26</gloss> material worlds.
   By these, <gloss>29</gloss> Heaven flows into the <gloss>30</gloss> <gloss>31</gloss> <gloss>32</gloss> Nile, whose increase arises from a triple cause and a triple virtue: <gloss>35</gloss> supramundane, <gloss>34</gloss> celestial, and <gloss>33</gloss> elementary. That is, the <gloss>33</gloss> water concurs as a triple force: <gloss>35</gloss> supramundane, <gloss>34</gloss> sidereal [star-driven], and <gloss>33</gloss> material, by which the soul of the one performing the sacrifice is prepared to obtain what he intends. And from here, <gloss>36</gloss> life overflows through the five <gloss>37</gloss> gates of <gloss>38</gloss> heaven into <gloss>40</gloss> Egypt, the beneficial and fertile mother of <gloss>40</gloss> all things.

Furthermore, regarding what follows on the Obelisk, three or four symbols have been erased, so that we cannot know what they were; the hunger of time, or the cruelty of Cambyses or the Goths <note>Kircher frequently blames the Persian King Cambyses II or the invading Goths for the physical damage to Egyptian monuments.</note>, has begrudged us this knowledge.

<margin>What is meant by the Rudders or oars.</margin>
<margin>Hecataeus.</margin>
Since the Egyptians saw that the spirit of the world dwells in moisture, and moisture is threefold according to the triple world, they aptly placed three oars or rudders here as indicators of this passage through the three worlds. Hence Hecataeus <note>A Greek historian and geographer.</note> relates that the *Barys* <note>original: "Barym." A Greek term for a specific type of Egyptian flat-bottomed boat used on the Nile.</note>, the small ship of Isis, had three oars: one at the back, in place of a rudder, which was immobile; the other two at the sides, by which the *Barys* was moved through the waters. By the ship, he says, they indicated the movement of the world-soul through moisture; by the immobile rudder or oar, the providence that directs all things; through the two intermediate auxiliary oars, they indicated the abundance of Genii <note>original: "Geniorum copia." Here meaning protective or intermediary spirits that assist in the governance of the universe.</note>. Since all these things move within this machine of the worldly boat, it is necessary that from this movement heat and moisture—and consequently the storehouses of seminal things—are both moved and advanced. Since three things especially promote this passage of the spirit—the Stars, the Sun, and the Moon, moved from sunrise to sunset—they aptly placed beneath them three segments of a circle, curved-cut <note>original: "κυρτοτομας" (kyrtotomas). A Greek term for something cut in a convex or bowed shape.</note>; these are indicators, according to Eusebius and Plutarch, of the upper hemisphere. The 45 two-pointed fastener indicates the sunrise and sunset...

Lest the hostile force of the **"rival spirits"** <note>original Greek: "ἀντιτέχνων" (antitechnōn), spirits that work against the divine order</note> should hinder this fecundity, they placed near the ²⁷ **owl** the **Erica** <note>often identified as heather or tamarisk</note> or "tetradice" <note>a four-pointed or four-petaled plant</note> as a kind of amulet against malignant power. For it is said that when the ark of *Osiris* was thrown into the *Nile*, it was enveloped by a portentous growth of this shrub's offspring and hidden from the violence of *Typhon* <note>the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>. *Plutarch* shows in these words that it was therefore carried by kings as a sacred protective charm <note>original: "prophylacticum"</note> and placed in the Temple of *Isis*:

Even now, the people of Byblos worship that wood, which is situated in the Temple of Isis."

# INTERPRETATION

<margin>What is the sacred Baris?</margin>
...sacred <note>original: "Barra", likely referring to the *Baris*, the sacred boat of Osiris</note>, as we have said elsewhere, in which they believed Osiris was hidden and concealed from the attacks of Typhon by the Erica <note>A type of heath or heather plant</note> plant, they performed sacred rites to propitiate the Divinity or *Agathodaemon* <note>Greek for "Good Spirit"</note>; concerning these ceremonies, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and scholar of ancient religions</note> treats extensively in Book 1 of *On Abstinence*.

For once these ceremonies were performed, they believed that the benignity of the **Triform Deity** <note>A triple-natured god representing the three parts of the world</note>—bestowed upon the **triple world** (the **three circles** 32 describe the triple world, and the **extended arm** 33 describes his benignity)—was bound and constrained through the **small cord** 34 or the **ribbons of Osiris**, about which we have dealt elsewhere at length from Plutarch; by whose power, consequently, they believed **life** 37 was granted to the moist nature, indicated by the **water-symbol** 35 <note>original: "hydroschema"</note>.

<margin>The ritual of the Priests in the inner sanctuaries.</margin>
But so that the life of the said triple world might be attracted with greater efficacy, the Priests (according to Plutarch, whom we have cited elsewhere) would conform themselves in their sacrifices and psalms in the inner sanctuaries at morning, noon, and evening, with their arms extended toward heaven in such a position that their arms expressed the **letter U** <term>υ</term> <note>the Greek letter upsilon</note>, which they called <term>ueet</term> <note>Egyptian for "an open heart"</note>, which is the same word as <term>Hemphta</term> <note>The supreme demiurgic spirit or Divine Mind</note> <image-desc>A symbolic character consisting of a circle topped with a cross and lateral flourishes</image-desc>, and it represented the life of the Supreme Deity poured into the universe, as the statue marked with number 41 shows; see our *Egyptian Vocabulary* <note>original: "Onomasticum Aegyptiacum"</note>. For in this posture, they hoped they would more easily and abundantly obtain from the Triform Deity (indicated by the **three circles** 38 placed above the **upright arms**) the sum of all happiness: **life** 39, consisting in moisture (which is indeed indicated by the **two square urns**). For they thought that nothing moved the Gods more to succor our needs than a similar mystical preparation both of the body and of the other external apparatus. 

This same thing was signified by the mystagogic statue of **ueet** <note>meaning "open heart"</note> placed below, and by the altar marked with a **young goat** <note>original: "Capreolo"</note>; all of which are symbols of sacrifices to be rightly ordered. This was done so that the three pairs of arms represent the three-part time of the day, in which the Priests were accustomed to offer their prayers in that posture of the arms, which was both mystical and appropriately displayed the reception of the flowing Divinity. For as Porphyry rightly says in Book 4, quoting Chaeremon: 

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
> *They distributed the day into the worship of the Gods, in which three or four times—at morning, evening, and noon—they attended the Sun with hymns;*

Furthermore, they used to depict the arms alone with two sets of five fingers to show that the solitary **decad** <note>The number ten, considered a perfect number representing the totality of the divine</note> of divinity is derived into the two worldly sets of five through hidden and analogous operations suited to them. For according to Synesius <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and bishop</note>, nothing is more pleasing to the Divinity than to solicit it with hidden allusions of this kind. Hence, at one and the same time, they transformed the body into various symbolic figures, as the condition of the Deity they were soliciting required. This is sufficiently indicated by the following statue expressing the name **Hemphta** by the position of its body, where the bent arm with the leg reflected backward expresses the **stigma** <image-desc>A symbol resembling the Greek letter stigma ϛ</image-desc>; while **ee** <term>εε</term> expresses both arms with the breast; and **u** <term>υ</term> <note>the letter upsilon</note>, or rather the contracted **symbol of Mercury** <image-desc>The astronomical symbol for Mercury ☿</image-desc>, represents the head with the shoulders. Moreover, by the pyramidal bending of the arms—the former showing an upright pyramid and the latter an inverted one—the shortly-before-mentioned worlds...

...the pairs <note>original: "binarios"</note>, from whose conjunction is born the *decussis* <note>The Roman numeral X, representing ten</note> or the number ten, a symbol of the entire universe, over which **Emphta** <note>In Kircher’s system, Emphta is the supreme creative intellect or "Spirit of the World"</note> presides, they express this in a secret manner; see what we have treated extensively elsewhere regarding these things. Furthermore, at sunrise, they would entreat the Divinity lying hidden beneath the perceptible Sun with raised hands; they repeated this rite at noon, and finally in the evening at sunset, according to **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>. Indeed, they practice piety toward the Divinity in a certain peculiar way: for before the **Sun** rises, they speak nothing profane, but pour out certain ancestral prayers to him with hands extended toward heaven, as if supplicating that he might rise; the same is performed at noon and sunset. And **Virgil** seems to have looked toward this in the second book of the *Aeneid*, while describing the custom of **Anchises** <note>The father of the hero Aeneas</note> in prayer:

> *But father Anchises, joyful, raised his eyes*
> *to the stars, and stretched his palms to heaven*
> *with his voice: "Almighty Jupiter," etc.*

In this same manner, in the second book of the *Iliad*, **Chryses** <note>A priest of Apollo</note> is described by **Homer** praying to Apollo, **lifting up his hands** <note>original Greek: <greek>ἀνασχὼν τὰς χεῖρας</greek></note>, which **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century scholar and commentator on Homer</note> interprets as **stretched out in prayer** <note>original Greek: <greek>ἀνατείνας εἰς εὐχήν</greek></note>. Various authors confirm this same thing, whom **Stucchius** <note>Johann Wilhelm Stucki, a 16th-century scholar of ancient rituals</note> cites, describing it in these words in his book on rites and sacrifices, folio 87: *They likewise observed the **position or disposition** <note>original Greek: <greek>θέσιν ἢ διάθεσιν</greek></note>, site, gesture, or rather the gesticulation of the whole body as well as its individual parts and members. Of the whole body indeed, for they would prostrate themselves upon the ground, which prostration the Hebrews call **Histachauah** <note>original Hebrew: השתחוה, meaning to bow down or worship</note>, whence also the proverb among the followers of **Pythagoras**: **"after they had worshipped"** <note>original Greek: <greek>καθ' ἃς προσκυνήσαντες</greek></note>, they would sit down to pray;* so that he seems to have alluded to the position of these statues. Furthermore, they would turn the entire body toward this or that part of the world. **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure equated with Thoth</note> ordered those worshipping at midday to turn toward the south, at sunset toward the west, and if the **Sun** were just rising, toward the east. Thus, no differently than the **Lotus** <note>The water lily, which ancient authors believed followed the sun's path</note>, they would follow the Solar Divinity incessantly with their eyes and soul.

When these rites and gestures were completed, they sacrificed upon the altar—not the flesh of animals, but tender plants pleasing to the Gods, such as the vine tendril <note>original: "capreolum vitis"</note> you see placed upon the figure of the altar. For they hoped that they would obtain **life** (indicated by the serpent) and an **abundance of temporal goods** (indicated by the two Nilotic vessels) from the Divinity of the triform world (indicated by the three circles).

But so that the consensus of authors might correspond in every detail, I will add here what I have drawn from the remains of the ancient **Copts**. Not long ago, the most Illustrious Lord **Hannibal Albani** <note>Annibale Albani (1682–1751), a powerful Cardinal and Vatican librarian</note>, Prefect of the Vatican Library, a man exceedingly distinguished for both his humanity and varied erudition, granted me a manuscript codex to interpret. It was a **Coptic Ritual**, recently brought from Egypt by the Reverend Father **Marco de Luca** of the Order of Saint Francis, in which, among other things, the ancient ceremonies of the Egyptians are described so aptly that they seem to look back to the ancient ceremonies I described just a moment ago. Let them take care of the place of sacrifice, and after that, let the priest pray over the place of sacrifice with his hands in a venerable prayer, and let him raise the Gospel upward. After this, the bishop shall offer the incense and go around the place of sacrifice, and he shall bow to the horns of the altar <note>The Coptic text mentions "ⲛⲓϣⲉ-ⲛ̀ϣⲱⲟⲩϣⲓ," likely referring to the wooden structures or "horns" of the altar</note> and designate it for his brother; and let us pray to our God in the manner of the Eucharist over the place of sacrifice. That is: The Priest went around the altar, in whose hand was the sacred vestment, lifting the book above; by this figure of the **Copts**, I explain the **cross** as the **Tautic character** <note>The "Tautic character" refers to the "Tau" cross (shaped like a T), which Kircher believed was a bridge between ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics and Christian symbolism</note>, which he marks in the manner of a monogram; then the Priest lifts the Censer, and three times brings the sounding brass <note>likely referring to bells on a censer or cymbals</note> to life with sound; then three times he rouses the singing of hymns over the altar, with hands raised to heaven, saying prayers three times; finally he takes the sacred ointment, and signs the character of the cross on the four corners of the altar, corresponding to the four parts of the world. From which it is clear that the ancient Christians assumed many things from the ceremonies of the ancients, and employed them in the worship of the true God.

So that from these things it may be evident how much study the Egyptians placed in the proper administration of ceremonies and sacraments. How much these same things were in use not only among the Gentiles, but also the Hebrews and Orthodox Christians; and not without reason, for since man consists of the material and immaterial—that is, body and soul—besides the internal affections of the soul and intellectual operations, by which he might tend toward **GOD** as if lifted up on two wings (intellect and will), external signs were also seen to be necessary. These belong to the body, and by such outward gestures, the interior operation of the mind is testified. These are the ceremonies and mystic operations used in both private and public sacred rites, both to procure majesty for the rites and to more fervently arouse the vigor of the mind through external actions. That these have been pleasing and acceptable to **GOD** at all times is testified by the exact observance of those very things prescribed by **GOD** to Moses in the book of Leviticus. **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 245–325 AD</note> also says: *The constant observance of divine precepts and works, which exceeds all intelligence, and the wonderful power of symbols and sacraments, offers to us a deifying union through the prayers of the Gods alone. When, therefore, we operate in sacred rites, we do not accomplish it through intelligence. For otherwise, the sacraments and their action would be intellectual and would be produced by us. On the contrary, even when we do not understand, they perform this proper work, and the power of the Gods to which these refer recognizes the ineffable and proper images in themselves, not excited by our own thoughts.* What does Iamblichus indicate here other than that sacraments reconcile grace not only from the *work of the worker* <note>Latin: "ex opere operante," referring to the personal piety or merit of the person performing the ritual</note>, as the Schools <note>The Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages</note> say, but also from the *work worked* <note>Latin: "ex opere operato," the theological doctrine that a sacrament is effective by the very fact of being performed, provided the recipient does not place an obstacle in its way</note>? But now let us append the ideal reading of this whole discourse.

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILI OBELISK

### The Context of the Ideal Reading.

The Triform Deity <note>original: "Triforme Numen," Kircher’s term for a supreme god manifesting in three powers</note>, through a triple vehicle of $^1$ Stars, $^1$ Sun, and $^1$ Moon, spread through the three $^2$ celestial spaces from $^4$ East to $^5$ West, brings about the three $^6$ seasons of the year; and thus, $^8$ driven and bound by a hidden and $^{10}$ invisible motion and progression through the $^9$ humid medium mixed with $^{11}$ fire, provides life to the three $^7$ material worlds <note>original: "hylæis Mundis," from the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter</note>. It collects the $^{12}$ influx of the sacred liquid by a dual $^{13}$ power, both celestial and terrestrial, and ordains $^{14}$ two $^{16}$ principles of generation from $^{14}$ sunrise and $^{16}$ sunset. From this results the $^{15}$ fecundity of the lower $^{15}$ worlds and the coming $^{15}$ years, which the priests shall venerate with a sacred ritual. 

Furthermore, the Triform Deity, driven through the celestial spaces in the $^{21}$ rising, $^{19}$ midday, and $^{22}$ setting positions, restores $^{18}$ Horus—who was slain by the fierce force of the $^{26}$ malignant Typhonic power <note>referring to Typhon or Set, the Egyptian god of chaos</note>—through $^{23}$ Isis, the protector of the heat and moisture of the lower worlds. This restoration is achieved through the $^{27}$ seed of the fourfold <note>original: "tetradicis germine"</note> as a support for the two worlds, by which the upper and lower things are $^{29, 30}$ joined, once Typhon has been driven away and routed by a ritual performed in the sacred boat <note>original: "sacra barra," likely referring to the Baris, a sacred Egyptian vessel</note>. The $^{33}$ beneficial force of the three worlds, $^{34}$ bound during the $^{35}$ midday hour, $^{36}$ grants life to the humid nature. Hence the Priests, transformed into a $^{39}$ mystical figure <note>original: "mysteriola figura"</note> with $^{39}$ arms extended toward Heaven, must receive the life proceeding from the supreme Triform Deity to the three $^{38}$ worlds, every day, in the $^{39}$ morning, $^{39}$ noon, and $^{39}$ evening, through appropriate $^{40}$ prayers and $^{40}$ sacrifices, as well as through $^{41}$ statues prepared with a similar sacred rite.

honors, which was accustomed to be carried around on a bier in the <term>Comasia</term> <note>A festive procession of sacred images in ancient Egypt</note>; because, indeed, all generation has its origin from motion, you see placed beneath it the $^4$ three-pronged restraint along with the $^6$ <term>Favissa</term> <note>Usually a temple cellar, but here used by Kircher to mean a receptacle for sacred "influx"</note> or figure of the sacred influx. By this, they wished to indicate that by the motion of the $^2$ Moon, propitiated by sacred rite, moving from its rising through the south to its setting, the $^4$ seeds of $^3$ generations and the influx of $^6$ sacred water are promoted, and from this the $^8$ life of the $^7$ World is advanced. But although $^9$ Isis, the $^{10}$ Genius of the Lunar World, opens the $^{10}$ gate of $^{11, 12}$ procreative things and the $^{13}$ influx of sacred water; nevertheless, unless the $^{14}$ celestial eye of Osiris looks upon it and $^{15}$ vivifies the waters with his heat, they held the conviction and testimony that she could accomplish nothing in the $^{16}$ lower world. Hence they aptly placed beneath it the same Ibis with a $^{10}$ globe, and a $^{11, 12}$ lotus-bearing gate; the Favissa, the $^{13, 14}$ eye-shaped scepter with a <term>hydroscheme</term> <note>Kircher's term for a symbolic representation of water</note>, and a $^{16}$ spheroidal segment, and a $^{17}$ hawk sitting upon the spheroidal segment, the Lord of celestial, superior, and inferior things, by which they indicated all the secrets we have mentioned. For the $^9$ Moon and $^7$ Sun joined together $^{11}$ open the gate of the world, $^{12}$ strengthen the vegetation, $^{13}$ fertilize the sacred pool with the $^{14}$ mixing of rays, and grant $^{15}$ life to the waters, and animate all things $^{16}$ contained in the lower world, with $^{17}$ Osiris, the lord and moderator of the $^{18}$ heavens, acting as the primary agent. Regarding the earlier symbols, they have been treated at length in the preceding pages; it remains for us to explain what they meant by this $^{16}$ spheroidal segment. When the Egyptian Sages indicated that half of the sky is always visible and the other half always hidden, they called the superior, always visible part of the Horizon "Isis," and the hidden part "Nephthys"; 

<margin>Plutarch on Isis and Osiris.</margin>

but the part joined by a common line they called "Anubis," all of which has been discussed more fully elsewhere, and Plutarch indicates this in express words: *For Nephthys is that which is under the earth and is not seen; Isis is that which is above the earth and stands manifest; but the circle touching these and called the horizon, being common to both, is called Anubis.* <note>original Greek: "Νέφθυς γὰρ ἐστι τὸ ὑπὸ γῆν καὶ ἀφανές : Ἴσις δὲ τὸ ὑπὲρ γῆν καὶ φανερὸν . ὁ δὲ τούτῳ ὑποψαύων καὶ καλόμενος ὁρίζων κύκλος ἐπίκοινος ὢν ἀμφοῖν, Ἄνουβις κέκληται."</note> Hence they formed the lower part of the earth in the shape of a skiff, as you see here; so Diodorus in Book 1, Chapter 8, brings forward the private opinions regarding the earth, asserting that it is similar to a skiff and that it is hollow. You see, therefore, why they indicated the lower and upper parts of the earth with inverted segments; this segment thus signified the world with its inferior convexity...

...the lower, that is, the lower hemisphere, or the lower part of the horizon.

<margin>In what ways are the Solar-Lunar Genii to be attracted?</margin>
By what further rites these Solar-Lunar Genii <note>In Kircher’s system, Genii are intermediary spirits or forces associated with celestial bodies like the Sun and Moon.</note> are to be attracted for the good of the World, and what benefits come to them from this kind of worship, they declare in the following arrangement of symbols; for first there appears an oval figure 19, the lower part of which has a 19 pedestal <note>Latin: *abacum*</note> suitable for standing; which, according to the testimony of Iamblichus, they called the **sacred table**;

> *The priest, he says, standing at the door of the inner sanctuary, carrying the sacred table in his hand, rouses the God in the ancestral language of the Egyptians.* <note>original: "Sacerdos, inquit, in porta adyti stans satram tabulam manu gerens, patriâ Aegyptiorum linguâ Deum suscitat."</note>

<margin>Iamblichus. What is the Sacred Table?</margin>
For in this table, the sacred symbols collected and inscribed were thought to have great power for attracting benign Genii and dispelling malignant ones. Hence, they would engrave these kinds of sacred hieroglyphic arrangements—as if they were certain amulets <note>Latin: *phylacteria*</note> imbued with mystical reasons and thus most pleasing to the Gods—not only on Obelisks, but also on Canopic jars, Sphinxes, Statues of Isis, Mummies, and Tombs. They also carried these symbols engraved on various plates and applied to different members of the body; by their help, they believed themselves blessed by the company and conversation of the Gods; by their aid, they believed the purified soul after death would migrate into the most excellent bodies; and by their use, they thought themselves to be filled with an abundance of all good things. Hence, on all Obelisks and statues, these kinds of arrangements, or engraved sacred tables, are seen consecrated to the Gods as if containing something singular, and they regard those same Gods as being pregnant with mystical reasons. Therefore, in this place, they indicate this sacred table through the present figure, which is indeed empty of symbols, but which would serve as an index for the hieroglyphic arrangement to follow shortly after. Corresponding to this on the opposite side is the mystagogic statue <note>A statue that leads or initiates one into the "mysteries" or hidden religious truths.</note> of the Genius **Momphta**, the overseer of the humid Element, whose Nilotic vessel, which he carries on his head, is a sign; and he expresses the name of the Genius by <unclear>hieroglyphic characters</unclear> through the position of his body, as was indicated above. By this, they wished to indicate that through the rites to be explained shortly, the sacred table attracts to itself, by the power of the Genius, the Life of the celestial World, which the following 21 Cyclic figure denotes. 

Truly, by what rite this ought to be done, the following symbols show; and they do so under the form of a precept, as if they were saying: the minor priest, shaped into the form of a <term>Tautic character</term> <note>Also known as the *Crux Ansata* or Ankh; Kircher associates it with the god Thoth/Taut.</note>, or a handled cross, shall perform the sacred hymns; then he shall bend himself over the altar, expressing the 24 mystical character <unclear>portal-like character</unclear>, which letter 24 signifies the worldly house; then the 23rd signifies dominion and power over 23 vegetable nature, indicated by the vine-tendril as will be explained shortly. Since the <term>☉</term> Sun and <term>☽</term> Moon preside over these, their benign influences, stirred by the mystical sacrifice, will be derived into the lower realms by the appropriate Genii. From this derivation, 26 **Ammon**, the fecund Deity of heat and moisture, and consequently the 25 overseer of generation, will imbue all worldly bodies with 27 life. But so that we may look upon these things more closely in their source, let us fully explain the mystical subtleties and the hidden doctrine of each one.

<margin>Priests used to contort their bodies into the characters of the names of the Gods and symbols during sacrifices.</margin>

See, if you please, the secrets we have handed down regarding this character in its proper place, which are well worth knowing. Whatever was previously reported through expanded symbols is here gathered and condensed under this diagram.

<margin>Transformation of the Priests into various figures during the time of sacrifices.</margin>

Since the Tautic character was so great and overflowed with such illustrious mysteries, it is no wonder that the Priests used it in the performance of all mysteries, expressing it through the very shaping of their own bodies to solicit the Gods with greater efficacy.

I come now to another hieroglyphic, which they expressed by a similar transformation of the body; and so that you may see the marvelous operations of the ancient sages more clearly in sacred matters, it seemed best to begin the matter from a slightly deeper point. We said in the structure of the mystical Alphabet that the Egyptians constructed even their common characters according to mystical reasons. And first indeed, as we demonstrated in the *Prodromus* and the *Supplement to the Treasury of the Coptic Language*:

they expressed the name of God in two ways: through ☥ ☨, and through πδϲ <note>Likely a Greek/Coptic transliteration of a divine name, which Kircher interprets as "Lord."</note>. The first of these is joined from two characters, namely ◯ and ✝. The first was the symbol of the universe and of all things connected by love, concerning which see the *Prodromus*. The other, ☨, was the symbol of the influence of the Divinity into the material worlds, as we have proved elsewhere. From these was born ☥ ☨, the name of God, animating the entire World by His power. The other name of God was said to be **PDS** <note>original: πδϲ</note>, which in the Egyptian language signifies the same as "Lord." To the first letter they referred...

# INTERPRETATION

<margin>Lateran Obelisk I.</margin>
...they represented through $\Pi$, which they called the gate of the mundane house, while the other two letters $\odot$ and $C$ indicated the Sun and the Moon **kyriologically** <note>original: *κυριολογικῶς*; a term from Clement of Alexandria meaning the use of primary or literal symbols rather than metaphors</note>, according to the testimony of Clement. Thus, just as the Priests expressed the name $\Phi \nmid$ in the previous diagram, so in the second, through the conformation of the body, they expressed $\Pi \odot C$, as if silently imploring the Divinity or the Lord of the universe. Therefore, to represent this name hieroglyphically, they included $\odot$ and $C$ within $\Pi$, as is evident in this present hieroglyphic diagram. This was sent to me for interpretation by **Nicolaus Peiresc** <note>original: *Nicolaus Persefcius*; Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a renowned French polymath and collector who frequently corresponded with Kircher about antiquities.</note>, a man of immortal memory. I previously presented this in the supplement to the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher refers to his 1636 work *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus*.</note> while he was still living, and I have chosen to present it again here to confirm what has been said, as follows. Here you see the middle figure under the letter $\Pi$ holding the characters $\odot$ and $C$—that is, the Sun and the Moon—enclosed in the likeness of a gate. Just as this monogram signified "Lord" in the Egyptian language, it also silently hinted at the absolute dominion of the Sun and Moon, as secondary Gods, over the universe.

For by the gate $\Pi$ they indicated this worldly house; by $\odot$ the Sun; by $C$ the Moon; and by the serpent, the life-giving Divinity <note>Latin: *Numen viuificum*</note> which encompasses all things by its immensity. Furthermore, according to the testimony of **Horus** <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs which was highly influential but often historically inaccurate.</note>, the serpent represented the annual cycle, a type of divinity. By all these signs, they showed that the Sun and Moon, positioned in the middle, are the Lords of this mundane house and of time, possessing a power shared from the Supreme Divinity that encompasses all things. They arranged it so that all parts of the World (marked by the four **Genii** <note>Spiritual guardians or presiding deities of the cardinal directions.</note> placed according to the fourfold division of the World) might receive the benefit of these flowing influences. Hence, the $\Pi$ is open at the bottom to signify that the influence and emanation happen from higher things to lower things, and not the reverse. The symbol $\Phi \nmid$, along with the hieroglyphic statues assigned to each quarter, indicates the Genii presiding over those regions; according to the analogy of the qualities of said regions, they are transformed into the **Ibis**, the **Hawk**, the **Lion**, and the **Cat**. As for the letters assigned to each, they are **Coptic** letters and names, about which you may consult the supplement of the *Prodromus*, page 529, where we have explained everything at length.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>
<image-desc>A circular woodcut diagram encircled by an Ouroboros (a serpent biting its tail). In the center, a structure resembling the Greek letter Pi acts as a frame for symbols of the Sun and Moon. Surrounding this are four seated figures representing the cardinal points, each with a different animal head (Ibis, Hawk, Lion, and Cat). Various Coptic characters and the strings "NEPMET" and "EMΦSI+" are arranged around the figures.</image-desc>

<margin>Wondrous transformations of the Priests in sacred rites.</margin>
Since, therefore, the word was so mystical, it was not without reason that the Priests in their sacrifices expressed the name $\Pi \odot C$ just as they did $\Phi \nmid$. This is clearly taught by the hieroglyphic diagram, in which the figure marked with the numbers 22 expresses $\Phi \nmid$ in the form of a cross, and the other marked 24 expresses $\Pi \odot C$ by the over-extension of the body performed above the altar. In this position, the hands and feet, together with the chest and belly, express a perfect $\Pi$, as if they were saying:

> *O eternal Divinity, supreme in power over all things, Lord of the universe, hear our prayers and sacrifices, send your influence upon us and upon all things, for which we implore...*

# Context of the Ideal Reading.

<note>original: "Hic Obelifcus vel Cambyfis vel Gothorum incendijs defædatus figuris caruit unde eas prætermifimus."</note> This obelisk, defaced by the fires of either Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note> or the Goths <note>Referring to the various sacks of Rome where many obelisks were relocated</note>, lacked figures, and for that reason we have omitted them.

Through the balance of heat from the 1 rising and setting, the 2 **Lunar Spirit** <note>original: *Genius*; refers to a guiding intelligence or divine power</note> moving through the 4 rising, 4 noon, and 4 setting, 3 stimulates the **generation of things**, and 6 brings the variety of things and the 6 influx of the **sacred moisture**, and 8 brings **life** to the 7 **World**; 8 for that reason, in its 5 **processions** <note>original: *Comasijs*; refers to the public carrying of divine statues</note> its statue is to be carried around.

Furthermore, the 9 **Lunar Spirit**, 10 lord of its own sphere, 9 reflects with variety and 11 opens the **worldly gate**, while it 11 solidifies all things and 12 brings forth an **abundance** of things capable of being born, through the 13 influx of the sacred moisture—that is, through the 14 **celestial eye** and the influx of **Osiris**; from there comes 15 **life** to 16 **subterranean things**. The 17 **Solar Spirit**, however, 18 ruling over the celestial realms, 20 through a **mystically constructed image**, and through a 19 **sacred prophylactic tablet**, and through the 20 statue of its faithful Steward **Mophta** <note>In Kircher's system, Mophta is a spirit or "genius" associated with the Nile and the movement of water</note> fertilizes all things by bringing down the upper waters; so that this may be done more effectively, the **sacred rites** are to be performed in this manner.

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

## SCHEMATISM VI.

->Of the first Eastern Side.<-

<margin>Explanation of the Scheme</margin>
In this Scheme, there first occurs a cycloid <note>A curved, circle-like path or shape</note>, with an extended $_2$ arm, and a $_3$ bar; then a $_4$ Sphere, across from which is another $_7$ Sphere, supported by three props made of linked triangles, like a $_7$ tripod (which from here on we shall call the **Ideal Tripod**). Beneath this is a $_5$ segment of a spheroid, and afterwards three $_8$ circles, placed between two $_9$ scepters, which are followed by two $_9$ triangles, holding two enclosed $^{10}$ quadrangles. Finally, after these comes that sacred table mentioned in previous sections: a hieroglyphic arrangement, both protective and acting as an amulet, heavy with mystical symbols. But let us explain each part individually. After the symbols 1, 2, and 3 explained previously, there follows:

<margin>
What the circles signify.
</margin>
4 The Globe, or Sphere, which in this place indicates God—that eternal and immobile Divinity <note>original: *Numen*; a Latin term for a divine power or presiding spirit</note>, lacking beginning or end. This is that "Hermetic circle" whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. Consequently, Xenophanes (cited in the works of Pierius Valerianus <note>A 16th-century author famous for his massive encyclopedia of symbols, *Hieroglyphica*</note>) not without reason called it the **Archetypal Sphere**. Indeed, a single circle, or one drawn around any other simple figure or sign, according to Valeriano, signified to the Egyptians not only "now," "always," or "perpetual and eternal," but even "The All" <note>original: *τὸ πᾶν* (to pan)</note>. This is because in that figure, one can find neither a beginning nor an end—a quality proper to the eternal Divinity, that is, God. Because the circle is capable of containing all other shapes, it seems to embrace the entire universe within itself. He is, in fact, "the whole in the whole"—or rather, He is the Whole itself, embracing all things within and without Himself. Thus the Egyptians represented God, or the Triform Divinity (as shown in Scheme I of the 1st side), as He rests eternally in His solitary unity, content in His own blessedness and contemplation. The oracle of Zoroaster <note>Ancient Persian prophet to whom many "Chaldean Oracles" were attributed in the Renaissance</note> seems to have alluded to this: <note>original Greek: *ἑαυτὸν ὁ πατὴρ ἥρπασε, οὐ δ' ἐν ἑῇ δυνάμει νοερᾷ κλείσας ἴδιον πῦρ*</note> "The Father snatched Himself away, nor did He enclose His own fire within His intellectual power."

The property of the circle.

<margin>
What the ideal tripod is.
</margin>
Since God contains the "ideas" <note>The perfect blueprints or patterns of all things</note> of all created things within Himself, the Egyptians very beautifully placed another globe across from the first one, supported by three rays. These rays are made of linked triangles. By this symbol, they showed that the divine nature of the Triform Divinity, pregnant with ideas, proceeded outward through them to create the **Tripartite World** <note>The world divided into the Intellectual, Celestial, and Elemental realms</note> and all that it contains, and that He preserves what was created through a perpetual influx. Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary "thrice-great" Egyptian sage thought to be the author of the Hermetic corpus</note> touches upon this **Ideal Tripod** in the *Pimander* <note>The first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> on page 55 with these words: <note>original Latin: *Plenus autem ideis, omnibus qualitates pater inferens in Sphæram veluti in gyrum omni qualitate seipsum circumfcripsit.*</note> "Full of ideas, the Father, bestowing qualities upon all things, circumscribed Himself within the Sphere as if in a circuit with every quality." From this, they displayed those three triangle-shaped rays in the manner of a pyramid, derived from the center of the Divine Sphere and expanding into the vastness of created things. Since we have stated above that the equilateral triangle is a symbol...

# INTERPRETATION

<margin>Obelisk Side I</margin> ...to be a symbol of the triform Divinity <note>original: *Numen*; refers to the divine power or presiding spirit</note> proceeding outward. For this reason, they quite fittingly wove those three rays—which indicate the triple World: the Angelic, the Celestial, and the Elemental—beneath a certain chain of equilateral triangles. They did this to show that every single thing is marked by that triangular character and made according to the first model of God the Creator. As the author used to say, every thing participates in a certain "particle of divine breath" <note>original: *divinæ auræ*; a reference to the soul's spark or heavenly origin</note>. This participation happens more fully for each person the more they become like God through the study of contemplating the divinity, and the more they are purified through sacrifices and sacred ceremonies. This is indicated by the Oracle of Zoroaster in these words: "The paternal mind sowed symbols in souls" <note>original: *σύμβολα πατρικὸς νόος ἔσπειρε ψυχαῖς*</note>. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar who commented on the Chaldean Oracles</note> interprets these words as: "The fatherly mind implanted symbols into souls." Just as the book of Moses says that man was formed in the image of God, so too does Psellus say: <margin>Psellus on the Oracle of Zoroaster.</margin> *The Creator and Parent of the World implanted signs and marks of his own property into souls.* For not only were souls produced from the paternal seed, but all the higher orders also had their origin from there. However, in incorporeal substances, the signs are different—namely, they are incorporeal and indivisible—while in the worlds, there are signs and symbols of the unspeakable properties of God that far excel even the virtues themselves. Note that by "signs" here, "ideas" <note>In the Platonic sense: the eternal, perfect forms or blueprints of things</note> are understood. Therefore, to participate in divine gifts, they performed those rites which I explained a little earlier with such great zeal. According to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note>, they believed that if even one detail in these rites was omitted, they were laboring in a useless effort to summon the Divinity. Certainly, this single hieroglyphic—showing the connection of the divine ideas with their effects in the triple World—shines with such sublimity of mysteries that I would not say a small page, but not even an entire book would suffice to explain them according to their merits. On this point, let the reader consult in due time our *Hieroglyphic Theology*, which we are reserving for the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's massive work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, in which he attempted to "solve" the riddle of the hieroglyphs</note>. <margin>Oracle of Zoroaster.</margin> For as the Oracle of Zoroaster rightly says: "For the Father completed all things and delivered them to the second Mind" <note>original: *πάντα γὰρ ἐξετίλησε πατὴρ καὶ νοῷ παρέδωκε δευτέρῳ*</note>. All things were produced from one fire, because the Father perfected all things and handed them over to the second Mind.

But now let us return to the subject at hand. We have said, therefore, that the globe placed simply and without anything else signifies the nature of God hidden in the abyss of eternity. However, the $_7$ globe constructed with 7 rays as if by a certain triangular chain signifies God, or the triform Divinity, pregnant with the ideas according to which He works in the production of things. The following symbols beautifully demonstrate that this is so: the three $_8$ circles enclosed between two scepters. By this, first, the "procession" <note>The theological concept of how the many come from the One</note> of the triform Divinity, pregnant with ideas, is indicated as it moves into the triple World through the double dominion over things higher and lower, corruptible and incorporeal, Celestial and Elemental. From this procession, the subsequent $_9$ generation of things is indicated by the $_9$ scalene "genetic" triangles <note>Triangles with unequal sides, often used in mystical geometry to represent the diversity and "becoming" of the physical world</note>. This was indeed beautifully suggested as occurring in the material worlds <note>original: *mundis hylæis*; from the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter</note> signified by the $^{10}$ squares. But to show how this Divinity can be drawn near, and if ever it has been angered, how it may be appeased, they prescribe the following protective amulet <term>prophylacticum amuletum: a charm used to ward off evil or spiritual harm</term> as if on a sacred tablet, the use of which...

### BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

...they believed they would become participants in all good things. This is the sacred table: a scalene triangle <gloss>11</gloss> <note>A triangle with three unequal sides.</note> with an extended arm <gloss>12</gloss>, followed by two scepters, the first of which <gloss>13</gloss> has three knots, and the second <gloss>15</gloss> has two knots. These enclose a segment <gloss>14</gloss> of a sphere, which is a symbol of the lower hemisphere. This is followed by another segment <gloss>16</gloss> of a sphere, an indicator of the upper hemisphere, with a sacred basin <gloss>17</gloss> <note>original: *sauissa* or *favissa*; a term for a sacred underground reservoir or temple cellar</note> placed beneath it. These are followed by two feathers with two rhomboids <gloss>19</gloss>, another segment, and an extended arm <gloss>20</gloss>, beneath which is placed a water-pattern <term>hydro-schema</term> <note>A symbolic representation of water or fluid substance</note> and, finally, a two-knotted scepter.

The scalene triangle is a sign of generation. Regarding this, Plutarch writes: *The Egyptians likely compared the nature of the universe to the most beautiful of triangles—a comparison which Plato also seems to have used in his Republic when he composed the "nuptial figure." That triangle consists of three sides: the base is 4, the vertical side forming the right angle is 3, and the side extending between them <note>the hypotenuse</note> is 5. The square of the hypotenuse is equal to the squares of the sides that form it. We should understand the vertical line as the father, the base as the mother, and the hypotenuse as the offspring. Thus, Osiris represents the beginning, Isis the recipient <note>matter</note>, and Horus the finished effect. For the number three is the first odd and perfect number; the number four is a square whose side is the even number two; and five, which fits both the father and the mother, is composed of two and three. Among the Greeks, five is called "all" <note>original: πᾶν (*pan*)</note> as if you were saying "all things" <note>original: πάντα (*panta*)</note>, by which the universe is understood. Furthermore, five produces a square from itself that equals the number of letters in the Egyptian alphabet, and the number of years the Apis bull lived.* 

Thus Plutarch writes in his book *On Isis and Osiris*. Therefore, this "genetic triangle" <note>The triangle of generation</note> is the work of Osiris, the beneficent and fertile one, which is fittingly indicated by the extended arm. For as Plutarch rightly says in the cited passage: "For Osiris is a doer of good, and the name signifies many things; not least, it designates an active and beneficent power" <note>original: ὁ γὰρ Ὄσιρις ἀγαθοποιὸς, καὶ τὸ ὄνομα πολλὰ φράζει· οὐχ ἥκιστα δὲ κράτος ἐνεργὸν καὶ ἀγαθοποιὸν ὃ λέγουσι</note>. From this he is called *Omphis*, or more accurately *Ompha*, which is to say "the Beneficent Deity," according to the witness of Hermaeus. 

Since Osiris is therefore the Author of generation in the whole world, let us now see how they impressed the worldly mysteries upon the following scepters. There is a double scepter enclosing a segment; the first has three knots, having two square knots and a round one in the middle. Since these allude to the "Omphiac" triangle of generation, they indicate that the more divine nature consists of three parts: that which is perceived by the mind (indicated by the circular node), matter, and the world composed of both (indicated by the square nodes). As Plutarch says: "The better and more divine nature consists of three: the intelligible, the matter, and that which is from these, which they call the world" <note>original: ἡ κρείττων καὶ θειοτέρα φύσις ἐκ τριῶν ἐστι, τὸ νοητὸν, καὶ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τὸ ἐκ τούτων ὃν κόσμον λέγουσι</note>. 

You see, therefore, how the two scepters contain within themselves the numbers 2, 3, 4, and 5 indicated by the five knots; the squares of these numbers (4, 9, 16, 25) each indicate certain orders of beings in the world. These are those "sacred knots" of which Iamblichus speaks on page 164. By these, the favor of the Deity <gloss>12</gloss> is drawn into the sacred basin <gloss>17</gloss>, then into the air <gloss>18</gloss> and the fertility of the fields <gloss>91</gloss>. That is to say, the power of the Beneficent Deity is drawn into the moist substance of the lower world, from which life is granted through its influence and through the use of sacred amulets. Since the mystical reasons for all these things have been explained at length in the preceding pages, we have decided not to repeat them here. The reading follows.

### DIAGRAM II.
->Of the 2nd Southern side.<-

<margin>Explanation of the figures.</margin>
In this Diagram, there first appears 1. a Butterfly, <note>original: δρακοντόμορφος (drakontomorphos)</note> **dragon-shaped**, or in the form of a small dragon; 2. with a **papyrus staff** <note>original: "thyrso papyraceo"; a thyrsus is a ritual wand associated with Bacchus/Dionysus, but here made of papyrus.</note>; beneath these is placed 3. a **segment of a sphere**. Then follow two scepters, which include 4. **three circles**; after these, 5. a **vessel** <note>original: "crater"</note>, with 6. an **eye-shaped scepter**; 7. a **globe** with a scepter, and 8. **three quadrangles**; which 10. an **Ibis**, perched upon 9. a **globe** and 11. a **segment of a sphere**, receives. Beneath this are placed three **Wash-basins** <note>original: "Luteres"</note>, which are the three receptacles of the sacred water. Finally, the **sacred table** is shown. To demonstrate the meaning of all these things, it seemed best to begin from a slightly deeper source.

One must know, therefore, that the Egyptians displayed on this side the duties, effects, and rituals of worship belonging to the Genii <note>In Kircher’s context, these are intermediary spirits or "daemons" that govern natural forces.</note> who preside over the southern region, as well as the method of attracting them for both private and public good. Thus, having first presented the first Diagram as a kind of inscription <note>original: "Epigraphâ"</note> regarding the influx of the Supreme Deity into the fourfold World, they now descend to particulars. They show how the divine Power—operating in all things and through all things by means of <term>Attendant</term> <note>original: "Assectas"; spirits who follow or serve a higher deity as part of their retinue.</note> Genii—proceeds forward, indicating this through an ingenious and hidden arrangement of symbols, as will be clear from what is about to be said.

First, then, they believe that a certain power rules over the whole world which, as was shown above from Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy.</note>, they called <term>all-forming</term> <note>original: "pantamorpham"</note>. Some call this the ruler of the <term>material</term> <note>original: "hylęi"; from the Greek 'hyle' for matter.</note> world, and the Arabs called it the <term>Lord of the House</term> <note>original: "Colcodean"; a Latinization of the Arabic astrological term 'Al-Kokhoda', referring to the planet that governs the length of life or the "disposer" of forms.</note>. This is because it destines forms that are suitable and harmonious for individual things; from the proper distribution of these forms, that supreme variety of things emerges for the use of the human race in all necessary matters. And they have quite aptly indicated this Deity through a dragon-shaped butterfly. This animal is peculiar to Egypt, and is found everywhere among the papyrus beds—

<margin>The meanings of the multiform little dragon.</margin>
The Egyptians noted that an animal of this kind grows from a lowly worm first into a biped, then into a quadruped, and soon shows itself with wings imbued with an innumerable variety of patterns and also with horns. from matter—which hungers for forms, once the previous arrangements were introduced (as if from a certain chaos of an elementary mixture)—it produced first the variety of bipeds through two feet, then quadrupeds through four; then the variety of birds through variegated wings, the cloven-hoofed kind through two horns, and reptiles aptly indicated by a tail. 
<margin>The meanings of the papyrus staff.</margin>

By this, they simultaneously wished to secretly suggest the multiform <note>original: "πολύμορφε" (polymorphe)</note> care and vigilance of the Divinity for promoting the good of the lower World to which it is destined, and how all things also come forth from water or moisture as the principle of things. Diodorus and Herodotus in his *Clio* further mention this animal, where they speak of the little dragons flying annually from the Red Sea into Egypt: "God moves in reptiles because of their multiform nature" <note>original Greek: θεὸς κινεῖται τοῖς ἑρπετοῖς διὰ τό τε τὴν φύσιν πολύμορφον</note>. They worshipped reptiles because of the diversity of their nature; concerning which see also Eusebius, cited above. Nevertheless, this variety of things is seen not only in the Elementary World, but also in the triple Angelic, Starry, and Elementary World—that is, the Sun and Moon, and the subterranean parts. And first, indeed, the Angelic World, although it is incapable of material forms, nevertheless has its own fitting variety of forms according to a certain analogy, conceivable only to the wise. From this, the greatest variety in the production of things emerges during the 8 **three seasons** of the year. Then it flows into the 9 **globe** of the 10 **Lunar Genius**, by whose power the 12 **Plutonic Wash-basins** <note>term: Luteres Plutonici; ritual vessels associated with the underworld or subterranean depths</note>—or the 12 subterranean receptacles of the lower World—are filled with fertility and arranged for the production of innumerable forms.

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK. 502

...or can in no way be grasped by Angelic powers. For here He has established the hiding places of His glory; which, if the mind tries to break through, it is overwhelmed rather than illuminated. Therefore, signifying the immense obscurity of the divine nature, the Egyptians used to say that the first principle of all things is darkness placed above all intellect. Hence, to honor this in fitting places, performing their rites and ceremonies in subterranean chambers which they called "sacred cisterns," they invoked a thrice-unknown gloom—that is, God in three forms <note>original: "τριμόρφον" (trimorphon)</note>—signified through three separate receptacles. This was excellently noted among others by Damascius the Platonist in his work *On Principles*: <note>original: "περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν" (peri tōn archōn)</note> *They consider darkness, above all thought, unknown darkness, to be attributed to this.* <note>original Greek: "νομίζουσι σκότος, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν νόησιν, σκότος ἄγνωστον εἰς τοῦτο ἐπιφημίζοντες."</note> **The first principle they consider to be darkness, placed above all intellect; they thrice invoked the incomprehensible darkness.** See what we have handed down about these things elsewhere. Furthermore, all these things are beautifully indicated by distinct symbols. By the three 4 circles, indeed, the triple World is signified, as was said above; by the two 4 scepters, dominion over the upper and lower realms; regarding the 5 crater <note>a "crater" in this context refers to a mixing bowl or vessel used in libations</note> of Osiris, see what we have discussed above on page 450. Furthermore, since we touched upon the eye-shaped scepter of Osiris rather sparingly above, let us explain it somewhat more extensively in this place. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> calls the Sun the "mind and moderator of the World" in *Scipio’s Dream*. **And those most ancient Priests, when they wished to signify this Moderator hieroglyphically, were accustomed to create an eye and a scepter; Macrobius testifies to the same in these words: "Hence the Egyptians claim that Osiris is as the Sun; whenever they wish to express him in their hieroglyphic letters, they carve a scepter, and in it they express the appearance of an eye, and by this sign they demonstrate Osiris, signifying that this God is the Sun, and sublime in royal power, he looks down upon all things; hence antiquity calls the Sun the eye of Jove."** Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris*, and Isidore agree: *For they write the King and Lord Osiris with an eye and a scepter.* <note>original Greek: "τὸν γὰρ βασιλέα καὶ κύριον ὄσειν ὀφθαλμῷ καὶ σκήπτρῳ γράφουσι."</note> Moreover, they were accustomed, as is evident from various hieroglyphs, to represent scepters of this kind in many ways; for sometimes they placed the head of a bird or a man at the top of the scepter, sometimes an eye-bearing phallus; sometimes from branches twisted in a certain way, expressing the leaf of a Laurel or Persea <note>The Persea was a sacred Egyptian tree, often identified with *Mimusops schimperi*</note>, into which they inserted an eye, as you see done here, and the above-cited Macrobius in Pierio Valeriano, page 234, hands down in these words: **"Sometimes," he says, "they were accustomed to entwine little branches in the scepter itself, so that coming together in an embrace, they might form the appearance of an eye to be looked at in the middle, and by that appearance they wished to say Osiris was as if multi-eyed, so they understood it;"** you see certain sketches, as it were, of this in our hieroglyphic here.

<margin>Osiris was mostly fashioned from Laurel and Lotus.</margin>
Hence, as we have shown elsewhere, scepters were fashioned from Laurel, or Lotus, Persea, and similar leafy plants, so that by this hidden analogy, just as they suggested a more recondite meaning, they might also indicate a more pleasing operation to the Gods by presenting analogous things. It remains for us to say something about the 1. 2. receptacles of the three fluids. Three receptacles of fluid are placed here, corresponding to the triple World, into which a multiform <note>original: "πολύμορφα" (polymorpha)</note> force is derived; it performs the effects intended by the Moderator of Nature. The first receptacle, considered in the Angelic World, is the clarity and transparency of the Angelic intellect; in which, as if in a certain mirror, there shine forth...

<margin>Meanings of these receptacles.</margin>

He also details how sacred scepters were fashioned from specific plants like the Laurel and Lotus to create a sympathetic link with divine forces.</summary>

# INTERPRETATION.
## Obel. Lat. II.

...[transmit] the dictates of the supreme divinity, and the trust and care of each thing committed to them.

In the **Starry World**, the "receptacle of humors" <note>liquid essences or influences</note> is the transparent space itself, filled with celestial waters. Its fertility is drawn down by the various radiations of the **Sun** and **Moon** into the lower receptacles—that is, the *Craters of Nephthys* and *Mophta*—from whose fertilization the life of all things flows forth.

Having thus explained the effects and operations of the multiform Deity in the triple World, the following hieroglyphic composition now shows how and by what means he may become favorable to people. This is a "sacred table," which they believed would unfailingly make the Deity favorable to them by the wearing of it, much like a protective amulet. This is the sacred table:

<margin>Explanation of the sacred table.</margin>
**13** Two feet are arranged in the shape of a pyramid; as we said above, this signifies the progression of the multiform Deity through all things by his hidden influence. Together with this is **14** a Crow sitting upon **15** a Spheroid, by which they signified the "passive principle" of things, as we explained in the third diagram of the first side. There follows a reclining Lion, **16** *Momphta*, the Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the Nile’s increase, which has similarly been discussed at length both in its own hieroglyphic section and in the preceding parts. The remaining symbols that follow have been explained extensively in other places. There follows **17** an arm, with **18** a Spheroid enclosed by two two-knotted scepters; by these, we have shown that the benevolence of *Osiris*—distinguished by a fourfold dominion—indicated his influence first into heaven and then into the lower World, represented by the segment of the Sphere. Because this beneficence consists chiefly in the sharing of moisture, they fittingly placed below it the figure of the "outflowing of sacred water," the meaning of which I have decided to interpret.

It has already been shown in various places from *Plutarch* that the Egyptians pursued their Nile with divine honors, even to the point of great superstition. In all their rites, they used Nile water, which they also called "sacred Lymph." Hence, so that the worship of this beneficial water might be performed with greater care, it is said that they diverted the waves of the Nile through hidden channels into subterranean shrines, into **21** the receptacle of the inner sanctum. *Festus* <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian</note> called this a *Favissa* <note>a "favissa" was a sacred underground pit or cellar for storing discarded ritual objects or sacred water</note>, and the Egyptians called it *Monia* <note>original Greek: "Μονία"</note>, meaning the influx of sacred water; this was done so that the resource, which was of such great importance in sacrifices, would never be lacking.

For this reason, they fashioned the receptacle in the shape of a pool, which they called the "entrance of the God" and the "fertile influx of Osiris," as *Plutarch* testifies. They added its specific shape to the list of hieroglyphs as a symbol pleasing to the Gods, just as they did with most other furniture and instruments belonging to sacrifices. That this is so is taught by the diagram of the Isiac inner sanctum, visible in the hieroglyphs, which (as was mentioned elsewhere) was once sent to me from the *Museum of Peiresc* <note>Nicholas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a celebrated French scholar and collector</note> for interpretation. On its floor, this figure of the *Favissa* filled with Nilotic water is clearly seen engraved. Thus, whereas I was long anxious and perplexed regarding a mark of this kind, this single, clearly expressed symbol has entirely removed all my doubt. And this is the reasoning behind this hieroglyph: therefore, both the higher and lower Spirits take peculiar care of this receptacle...

...two feathers, symbols of the Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note>, and a segment with two rhomboids, which are indicators of the fields, as has been said elsewhere. There is also a hand, the mark of beneficence, and a <term>hydroschema</term> <note>a symbolic arrangement or "water-figure" representing the flow of moisture</note>, with two double-knotted scepters holding a bowl <note>original: "craterem"</note>. By these symbols, they indicated nothing other than that, through sacrifices performed at the receptacle of the sacred water, the bowl of **Osiris** (who is fourfold in power) is filled with abundance for the fourfold world, which the horns of the bowl represent.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration positioned on the right side of the page.
