From this, finally, the principles of seminal things—indicated by the egg—are awakened and sprout into a most rich fertility. To ensure this happens even more abundantly, they elegantly show the solemnities of the feasts and the honors to be paid to the Deity through a statue and a litter <note>original: "feretrum," a ceremonial frame for carrying a statue</note>. The priests used to carve this "sacred table" in public places everywhere as a protective <note>original: "prophylactica"</note> and attractive charm to draw the favor of the Deity. Furthermore, nothing remains but for us to provide the context of the **Ideal Reading** <note>Kircher's term for the symbolic or mystical interpretation of hieroglyphs</note> here, through which the reader may easily arrive at the secret reasons for these statements. 

For since most of the symbols that follow have already been explained in the preceding sections and other appropriate places, it seemed by no means fitting to repeat one and the same thing so many times. In the meantime, let it suffice for the curious reader to have understood the secret meanings of each symbol through the aforementioned context. Nor should the reader be troubled that we occasionally present one and the same thing by different names; for it will be known only to him who has more deeply examined the varied character of the **Egyptians** that this was done deliberately. They frequently impose different meanings on one and the same symbol; however, no one will easily understand the difference between them except from the other symbols joined to them here and there.

# Ideal Reading Schema II. Connection of the second, Southern Side.

1 The many-formed Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of nature (1) directs the use of things subject to the South, which are necessary for the lower parts (2), and first (3) derives it from the three Worlds, by the power and influence of the Three-formed Divinity (4), into the bowl (5) of the all-seeing Divinity (5), the celestial eye (7) that watches over the World and rules (7) over the lower regions; then it flows into the material <term>hyleos</term> <note>derived from the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter; referring to the physical, elemental world</note> worlds (8) through the Lunar globe (9). The Lunar Spirit (10) indeed destines this for the increase of moisture (11) into the subterranean receptacles of the inner shrines, which represent the lower world; to propitiate these Spirits, this sacred table of signs is arranged.

*Note: we call it a "sacred table" here to refer to all those symbols contained within the oval figure.*

The hidden and invisible motion and process (13) of the celestial **Osiris** (14-15), through the benefit of **Mophta** <note>In Kircher's system, Mophta is a "hemicranine" or lion-headed genius associated with the transformative power of nature</note> (16), distinguished by a fourfold (18) dominion of heaven (18), activates the lower regions by an influx (22) of sacred moisture, from which the fertilized fields (23) are cultivated (22) by the speed and beneficence of the Divinity; the moisture (25), equally powerful with a fourfold dominion (26) and in the fourfold region of the lower World (27), disposes the principles (29) of seminal things through **Isis** (30), and therefore they ought to be celebrated and worshipped with sacred ritual (31).

*See the mystical reasons for each of these in the preceding pages.*

## SCHEMATIC III.

->Of the second Southern Side.<-

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side II.
South.
</margin>
In the preceding Schematic, we displayed the sacred table that attracts the many-formed Divinity; in this Schematic, however, the effects of this sacred amulet are shown.

<margin>
The baboon <note>original: "Cynocephalus"</note> as a symbol of the rising Moon.

Horus, Book 1, 15.

What is the Hook <note>original: "Harpago"</note>?
</margin>
First, we encounter the $^1$ baboon, which is a symbol either of the Moon simply or of the rising Moon, according to the testimony of Horus. It is shown with a $^2$ sacred hook, which the Egyptians adopted among their hieroglyphs because, as Plutarch testifies, the body of Osiris—having been thrown into the Nile by Typhon—was pulled out with its help. The "body of Osiris" represents the sun, which is said to be "thrown into the Nile" when the solar heat (necessary for the generation of all things) is suffocated by the superfluous and destructive moisture of Typhon <note>In Kircher's Egyptian mythology, Typhon represents chaos and destructive excess, often associated with the parching wind or the overwhelming flood</note>. It is extracted, however, by the Spirit of the Nile, $^3$ **Mophta**, when he suppresses and tempers the destructive and excessive moisture. This is achieved by the power of the supreme Divinity, indicated by the solitary $^4$ globe; through his $^5$ hidden and invisible operation working in harmony, a $^6$ moisture proportioned to the needs of plant life is provided.

<margin>
What is meant by the globe and the arms holding the gourd?
</margin>
This is beautifully indicated by the $^5$ Nilotic vessel turned upside down, from which two $^5$ arms emerge, their hands $^6$ clutching a long gourd. Just as they signified the movement of the Divinity throughout the universe by the feet, they suggested the practical execution or hidden operation of the Divinity through the $^5$ arms and hands, as we have proven elsewhere. They place an inverted bowl with $^5$ arms emerging from it to show that the moisture of nature is derived from the supreme $^4$ bowl, through the beneficial arms and hands of the Divinity, into the world of plants (represented by the gourd, a very watery fruit). Thus, they secretly suggest that by the power of the sacred table, Typhon’s destructive force is brought to a temperate balance by the Spirit of the Nile, Mophta. Even the supreme Divinity is, as it were, compelled or driven to grant a temperate increase of the Nile by the power of the sacred protective charm <term>phylactery</term> <note>A religious amulet or "sacred table" of symbols used to invoke divine favor</note>. For they had learned by experience that if this increase deviated from the middle path—becoming either excessive or deficient—sterility would necessarily follow, to the great detriment of Egypt.

<margin>
What figure 8 indicates.
</margin>
Therefore, the $^8$ priests, equipped with the sacred table to appease the angry Divinity (as the figure marked with number 8 shows), transformed their bodies during sacrifices into the monogram of the guardian Spirit. They used a $^9$ gourd tilted in the right hand as a symbol of averting evil, in place of a whip; but the $^{10}$ measuring rod, which they held in the left hand as a sign of balance and proportion, they formed either into the name of the Divinity or into something like the shape of a seat. Within this seat, the Spirit is received, and being powerful in command, he promotes the balance of the $^{11}$ moisture after all excess has been removed. Through the gourd, he grants the tempered waters indicated by the $^{12}$ water-pattern <term>hydroschema</term>. Indeed, while the Nile's $^{13}$ flooding continues (indicated by the $^{14}$ reclining sphinx, as has been proven), the said Divinity was bound to grant what they requested;

<summary>Kircher explains the symbolic figures on the Southern side of the obelisk, interpreting the baboon, the hook, and the gourd as symbols of the Nile's flooding and the divine moderation of moisture. He describes how Egyptian priests used these "sacred tables" to ensure a balanced flood that would fertilize the land rather than destroy it.</summary>

### The Reading of the Conceptual Discourse.

By the power of this sacred table, the rising Moon—after Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, representing chaos and drought</note> has been driven away—is pacified. $^3$ **Mophta** <term>Mophta: Also spelled Momphta; in Kircher's system, the "Genius" or guardian spirit of the Nile's creative force</term> directs the $^4$ moisture $^4$ of the superior World into the reservoirs of the inferior World through $^5$ hidden and invisible effects of divine operation, for the $^6$ preservation of the $^7$ nature of water.

From this, the $^8$ Priest—utilizing a $^{11}$ long gourd <note>original: "cucurbitâ longâ"</note> as a symbol of this flowing influence, as well as a $^{10}$ staff and a $^9$ gourd-shaped scourge transformed into letters that indicate the Divinity or the figure of its seat—performs the sacred rites according to the ritual by which he knows the Gods are delighted, for the $^{12}$ increase of moisture.

For from this, the $^{14}$ Isis-shaped $^{13}$ **Mophta**, the author of all $^{15}$ Nilotic growth, bound by this $^{16}$ honorary rite through the life-giving power of the $^{17}$ Supreme Divinity encompassing the world, will grant $^{18}$ life to the $^{19}$ moisture.

INTERPRETATION.

# SCHEME IV.

### Interpretation of the Second Southern Side.

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side II.
South.
</margin>

The context of the meanings of the preceding symbols is continued with this present one. The Supreme Divinity is described by a **1 Crocodile** resting upon the symbol of the cycloid of the heavens; this is because an animal of this kind, since it mostly remains hidden, indicates the hidden and unsearchable Nature of God. Furthermore, since among other animals it has no tongue, it is therefore suggested that the said Divinity ought to be adored by silence alone. 

<margin>
What the Crocodile signifies in this place.
</margin>

Moreover, since its sight is most piercing, they have placed this symbol as suitable for God, who watches over all things with His providence and perfects the generation of things. And although this symbol of the crocodile also denotes the malignant nature of Typhon <note>Set, the god of chaos</note>, as well as Egypt, yet because in this place it lacks the symbols that constitute Typhon or Egypt, and instead stands resting upon the figure of the cycloid symbol of the heavens, it is certain that the Divine Divinity is signified here. But see the many things not unworthy of knowing which we have handed down regarding this symbol in its own sacred writing. 

Thus, this Divinity first indicates the **2 Heavens** and time, which they thought was produced by two opposite movements through their contrary bearings and motions; these are most aptly indicated, as Horapollo witnesses in Book 1, Chapter 2, by the contrary position of two **3, 4 serpents**, as St. Cyril against Julian, Censorinus, and Herodotus in Book 1 teach. Hence, they call it <term>the year's time <note>original Greek: ἐνιαύσιον χρόνον</note></term>, as if it were <term>a year turning or revolving about itself, because of its returning into itself <note>original Greek: περιπλόμενον ἢ περιελόμενον ἐνιαυτόν, τῷ διὰ τὸ εἶναι εἰς ἑαυτόν</note></term>. For as Censorinus correctly says in this passage: *“The turning year is the nature by which the sun, traversing the twelve signs, returns to the same place from which it set out.”* 

The **1 Divinity**, therefore, first influencing the **2 heavens** agitated by two opposite **3, 4 motions**, ordains time and its consequences; then, it fills the reservoirs—first the celestial, then the terrestrial—with fertility. From this, the **7 Mundane house** of **8 Horus**, which the following figure aptly notes (within which you will find a standing boy equipped with a **cucucomorphous** <note>original: "cucucomorpho"; a scepter topped with the head of a stylized animal, likely the 'was-scepter'</note> scepter, together with a **6 curved staff** placed at his side). Below the 22 **Spheroid**, they place a 23 **tongue**, because, as Horapollo witnesses, the head always distills moisture into the tongue, and thus the tongue always dwells in a moist environment; so too the head of the Sensible World—the heavens—distills that 24 **vital moisture** through the serpent first into the 25 **twelve mansions of the great citadel**. These are aptly indicated by the following figure stretched out like a wall, conspicuous for its twelve quadrangles. By this they denoted the Zodiac, whose twelve parts they called the towers or mansions of the Gods; this was because each part was consecrated to a specific God according to the diversity of the effects which the Sun and Moon, when positioned within them, brought about. Algazael <note>Al-Ghazali, a famous Persian theologian and philosopher</note> explains this beautifully in the introduction to his *Astrology* with these words:

> <note>Arabic text omitted in English prose, translated below</note>

That is: *The ancients placed twelve towers in the great circle like mansions of their gods, and in each of them was a presiding power and authority which operates there according to the manner suited to it.* They are represented as squares to indicate the twelve months or Lunar Years, which the Moon establishes by traversing the circle in a fourfold arrangement of phases. Since the Moon reaches the Sun twelve times during the space of a year, all things in the lower World are established by this varied conjunction of light—now full, now half, now diminished. The 26 **attendants** of the 27 **Spirit** 28 **Momphta** <note>In the author's system, Momphta represents the divine creative artisan or "Hemispheric Genius"</note> participate in this influx of moisture, as the initiating statues indicate a little further on. Those placed between two 26, 29 **water-configurations** with a 30 **scepter** are meant to show that these Spirits obtain full dominion over the upper and lower waters. The first of these, in a sitting position with feet joined and the left arm pressed to the hip, forms the letter 'Y' with the right hand; with swelling breasts, this symbolic portrayal of the statue indicated that Momphta communicates the power received from the supreme Deity to the heavens. This is noted by the gesture of the hand and the bend of the elbow formed into a pyramid, while the cycloid <note>a circular or curved path</note> indicated by the left hand and the rest of the body shows that from here, by an imperceptible motion (indicated by the single foot), it is communicated to the lower waters. This is sufficiently shown by the 28 **initiating statue** formed in the manner of a suppliant, with its feet and hands. For by this very act they wished to secretly denote a certain subordination of the Spirits, by which the lower strives to supplicate the higher, as it were, in fulfilling the prayers concerning the matters committed to its faith.

But so that you may better perceive the mind of the Egyptians, I have decided to set down the following context of the ideal reading; however, since the reasons for each part have been indicated in various preceding places, we refer the reader there to avoid the tedious repetition of every single detail.

# INTERPRETATION

### Context of the Ideal Reading

The Supreme $^1$ Deity, who is to be worshipped through silence alone, broods over the moist $^2$ passages and the hidden things of Heaven with a certain $^3$ invisible power; through the $^3$ $^4$ contrary motions of the heavens and the stars, he fills the receptacles of the sacred liquid and its inflows. From these, in the $^7$ mundane house of $^8$ Horus, the $^8$ variety and $^6$ harmony of all things emanate, once the $^{10}$ dissonant, $^{10}$ ruinous, and $^{10}$ destructive power of things has been eliminated.

This is accomplished through the $^{12}$ image of the <term>Genius<note>original: "Genii"; here referring to a presiding spirit or tutelary deity that governs a specific element or region of the cosmos.</note></term> presiding over the $^{11}$ Elemental World, using sacred ritual, worship, and symbols that are analogous for attracting the superior Deities. For from these, $^{13}$ Life flows from $^{14}$ Heaven, and $^{15}$ beneficence and abundance flow into the $^{16}$ sacred Bowl <note>original: "Craterem"; likely referring to the celestial constellation Crater or a symbolic vessel of divine influence.</note>, over which the Genii $^{17}$ Arueris <note>A Greek name for the Egyptian god 'Horus the Elder' (Heru-ur).</note> and $^{18}$ Nephthys preside (who are to be worshipped by this construction of images).

For he rules over the $^{20}$ moist element; they are the presiders of the inflow $^{21}$ into the receptacle of the sacred liquid. Moistening the $^{22}$ heaven, he $^{24}$ gives life, and it flows through the twelve $^{25}$ mansions of the Great Citadel <note>A Kircherian term for the Zodiac and its twelve signs.</note> into the $^{26}$ moist element. The $^{30}$ presiders of this $^{29}$ moisture are the $^{27}$ Mophtae and $^{28}$ Alseclae <note>Specific names assigned by Kircher to Egyptian decans or spirits; they represent the governing forces of the physical elements.</note>, who are to be expressed and worshipped in this arrangement of images.

The figure that follows is a <gloss>17</gloss> human figure turning a circle or wheel, across from which is a <term>sacred pit<note>original: "fauissa"; a subterranean cellar or pit in a temple for storing sacred objects.</note></term> or <gloss>18</gloss> receptacle of the sacred flow with two <gloss>19</gloss> spheroids, supported by two <gloss>20</gloss> feet. The circle or wheel which the first figure turns is called the circle or wheel of Hecate, which they were accustomed to turn in the inner sanctuaries of sacrifices to solicit the Gods, according to the testimony of <term>Psellus<note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar who wrote on the "Chaldean Oracles."</note></term>.
<margin>Psellus on the Oracle of Zoroaster.</margin>
It is written thus in the Oracles of Zoroaster: <note>original Greek: "ἐνέργει περὶ τὸν ἱκαπνὸν στρόφαλον"</note> *Work upon the Hecatine spinning-wheel*; a ceremony which Psellus describes in these words in his commentaries on the said oracles of Zoroaster: <note>original Greek: "ἱκαπνὸς στρόφαλος σφαῖρα ἐστὶ χρυσῆ , μέσον σάπφειρον περικλείουσα... ἃ δὴ δονῶντες τοὺς ἀσήμους ἢ κτηνώδεις ἐξεφώνουν ἤχους γελῶτες, καὶ τὸν ἀέρα μαστίζοντες. διδάσκει οὖν τὴν τελετὴν ἐνεργεῖν;"</note> *The Hecatine spinning-wheel is a golden sphere enclosing a sapphire in the middle, turned by a bull-hide thong, having characters engraved all over it. By spinning this, they performed their invocations. And they were accustomed to call such things "Iynges," whether they were spherical, triangular, or any other shape. While they rattled these, they emitted meaningless or beast-like sounds with shouting, laughing and lashing the air. Zoroaster therefore teaches how to perform the rite, namely the movement of such a spinning tool, as it possesses a secret power; it is called "Hecatine" because it is dedicated to Hecate.*

<margin>What the Hecatine circle is.</margin>
The Hecatine circle is a golden Orb containing an enclosed sapphire in the center, turned by a bull's thong, having various figures and characters on every side, which those performing invocations would rotate. Of this sort are the things they usually call <term>Iynges<note>original: "Iyngas"; magical spinning wheels or charms used in theurgy to attract divine favor or spirits.</note></term>, whether they have a circular, triangular, or any other shape. And while they spin that Orb, they emit unformed or even brutish sounds with a shout, laughing and striking the air with whips. Thus Zoroaster teaches the operation of the rite, or such a movement,

<margin>What the bands of Osiris signify.</margin>
Moreover, they considered double bands: they referred one set to Isis, namely the Moon; the others they ascribed to Osiris, as Macrobius says in the works of Pierius Valerianus:

<margin>Macrobius.</margin>
*For since Isis also mystically signifies matter, while the Sun signifies the form or the acting power, and the Moon so observes her Sun and always seeks to receive his rays, by which she may be illuminated; I seem to see that saying of Plato concerning the bride, who like a prostitute awaits a most eager groom, from whom she may conceive the species and renewal of things, and return them to the marriage bed, just as the Moon restores the light she has received with as much zeal as she can. And this obscure hieroglyphic is matter, which has not yet taken on any form; however, the variation of the figure in the Lunar globe demonstrates matter clearly enough; which, like soft wax, is fit to receive now this, now that impression from whatever seal. Hence those various and multicolored bands dedicated to Isis indicate not only those seven faces of the Moon, which the Greeks call phases <note>original: "φάσεις"</note>, and Heliodorus names conjunction <note>original: "σύνοδον"</note>, birth <note>original: "γένναν"</note>, rising <note>original: "ἀνατολὰν"</note>, crescent-shaped <note>original: "μηνοειδῆ"</note>, half-moon <note>original: "διχότομον"</note>, gibbous <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτον"</note>, and full moon <note>original: "πανσέληνον"</note>. But they also indicate her power, which is occupied with matter—namely, that which brings forth all things and conceives all things: light indeed and darkness, day and night, life and death, the beginning and the end. The bands of Osiris, however, were not stained by any shadow, but from every side they displayed a bright splendor, like solar rays. Hence the Priests, once they had taken these into their hands, immediately hid them away, not to be seen or touched any further.*

Now follow the Hawk with its neck contracted as if sleeping, resting on the horizon, followed by the Asp <term>Agathodæmon</term><note>The "Good Spirit," a protective deity often depicted in Egypt as a serpent. Moreover, there is the Asp which the Egyptians call the <term>Uraeus</term><note>original Greek: ὀυβαῖον (oubaion). This is the royal serpent symbol of Egypt</note>; which, since according to the beliefs of the Egyptians it is immortal and kills other animals by its breath alone, they found it a suitable symbol for the divine nature, which holds the power of life and death over all things. Hence, they everywhere placed <term>hawk-serpent-shaped</term><note>original Greek: ὀφι-ἱερακόμορφα</note> figures upon the heads of the Gods—as can be seen in the <term>Bembine Table</term><note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet covered in Egyptian-style imagery that served as a primary source for Renaissance scholars like Kircher</note>—designating them as the arbiters of life and death, day and night, light and darkness. *That which the Egyptians call the Uphæus in their own tongue, the Greeks call the Basilisk. They place the same, made of gold, around the Gods. Furthermore, the Egyptians say this animal signifies an age [eternity], because while there are three kinds of serpents, this alone among all is immortal, the others being mortal; for it kills any other animal by its breath alone. Wherefore, since it seems to have the power of life and death, it is quite rightly placed upon the heads of the Gods.* <note>original Greek: "Ὃν καλῶσιν Αἰγύπτιοι ὀυβαῖον, ὅ ἐστιν ἑλληνιστὶ βασιλίσκον. ὅνπερ χρυσῶν ποιοῦντες θεοῖς ἐπιτιθέασιν. αἰῶνα δὲ λέγουσιν Αἰγύπτιοι διὰ τὸ δὲ τὸ ζῶὸν μὴ θνητόν. ἐπειδὴ ζῶὸν γενῶν ὀφέων καθιστῶν, τὰ μὲν λοιπὰ θνητὰ ὑπάρχει, τὸ το δὲ μόνον ἀθάνατον, ὃ καὶ προσφυσῆσαν ἑτέρῳ πάντη ζώω. δίχα κὰ τοῦ δακεῖν ἀναιρεῖ. ὅθεν ἐπειδὴ δοκεῖ ζωῆς καὶ θανάτου κυριεύειν; διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς τῶν Θεῶν ἐπιτιθέασι."</note> But see the context of the following Ideal Reading.

# INTERPRETATION

<column-break/>

## Conceptual Discourse
### Reading

Through the waxing $^1$ and waning $^4$ $^5$ of the sacred Moon $^2$ $^3$, the supreme triple-formed $^6$ Deity $^7$—by means of its divine $^8$ and life-giving spirit—bestows life upon all things. This is achieved through the monthly $^9$ influence of rising $^{10}$ and setting upon the lower parts of the earth, governed by the arrangement of feminine principles $^{12}$. Anubis $^{13}$ and Nephthys $^{14}$, the presiding guardians of the three material $^{16}$ worlds <note>original Latin: "hylaeorum Mundorum," from the Greek "hyle" meaning matter</note>, protect the vessel of the sacred liquor $^{18}$—which is filled through the heavens $^{19}$—with the assistance of the divine Deity who passes through all things $^{20}$. Through the revolution and whirling noise of the Hecatine $^{17}$ circle <note>A ritual tool or spinning disc used in ancient theurgy to invoke divine presence</note>, they guard against opposing powers. From this, the life of the heavens $^{21}$ is reconciled through the sacred benevolence $^{23}$ of the Deity $^{22}$, as is the life $^{25}$ of moisture $^{24}$. Celestial $^{28}$ Osiris $^{27}$, by the power $^a, ^b, ^c$ communicated from the supreme triple-formed Deity and derived as a force into the lower $^n$ world, binds the Moon $^{29}$ by tempering its excessive moisture; from this bond of temperament, harmony $^s, ^t$ is born. While Osiris $^{31}$, the <term>Agathodæmon</term><note>The "Good Spirit," a protective deity often depicted as a serpent or a hawk</note>, is sleeping, all things waste away; but when he is awake $^{32}$, all things rejoice, and life and prosperity are granted to all lower beings.

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

<margin>Second Side of the Obelisk, South</margin>

### SCHEMATIC III.

#### *Interpretation of the Second Southern Side.*

<margin>A marvelous hieroglyphic metamorphosis.</margin>
In this schematic, we first encounter a marvelous and altogether exotic <term>metamorphosis</term><note>A transformation of shape or form, often used in ancient mythology to describe gods changing their appearance</note>. It is a bird possessing a single wing; in place of the second wing, a human arm is substituted. It has one foot, but the bird's claw transitions into the form of a serpent. Furthermore, it has the head of a Hawk and the remaining body of an Ibis. Let us see what they intended to signify by this admirable transformation.

The Egyptians, contemplating the multi-formed <note>original Greek: *polymorphon*</note> nature of reality, believed that the supreme Deity was likewise multi-formed, permeating all classes of natural things and bestowing life and fertility upon each—all while remaining unmoved in its own motion. To express this multi-formity <note>original Greek: *polymorphosin*</note> precisely, they gathered parts taken from various classes of beings and combined them into a single mystical figure. In this way, they could display a marvelous and exotic image that suited their genius, such as the symbol we see here. This figure seems to represent in epitome <note>original Greek: *epitomikōs*</note> everything they recorded at length on this side of the obelisk regarding the Multi-formed Deity. St. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his second oration against Julian, calls images of this sort "monstrous and composite forms." Tertullian, in Chapter 16 of his *Apology*, describes them with these words:

> But they ought to have immediately worshiped a dual-formed Deity, for they accepted gods mixed from the heads of dogs and lions, horned from goats and rams, resembling goats from the loins down, snakes from the legs, and winged from the soles and back.

From this, Porphyry (in his fourth book *On Abstinence*) drew arguments to defend his own heresy—namely, that in the composition of idols, any animal was once joined with a human, such as a hawk's or lion's face joined to a human body. This custom was, however, mocked in his usual manner by Lucian in his work *Hermotimus*. 

But let us return to the subject. Through this present symbol, the ancients signified the influence of the triple-formed, multi-formed Deity upon all things. Through the **hawk’s head**, they represent the immense God; for, according to Zoroaster, *He has the head of a hawk; He is the first of the incorruptible beings, eternal, unbegotten, perfect in nature, wise, and the sole discoverer of sacred nature.* Through the **human arm**, they intended to indicate nothing other than the "Second Mind," the creator of things or the executor of the Father's will (symbolized by the hand). For the Father, as was said above from Zoroaster, entrusted all things to the Second Mind, the Craftsman. Through the **wing**, the multi-formed spirit is indicated, proceeding from the First and Second Mind. In the power of this spirit—and the Craftsman Mind—rests the life of all things, indicated by the **foot transitioning into a serpent**. Thus, we have a representation of the triple-formed Deity contained within a single symbol. Now let us see how it is immersed in the triple world.

And first, indeed, in the Angelic World, the hawk's head hints at the fiery...

# INTERPRETATION

<margin>Obelisk. Side II. South.</margin>

The power of the fiery powers—that is, of the sublime Genii <note>Spirits or guardian beings</note> close to God, whom orthodox doctrine calls the fiery power of the Seraphim—is indicated here. Through the hands, we see the Genii who are the executors of all things, whom we call Archangels and Angels. Through the wing, the presiding powers of the World are shown; their swiftness and readiness are aptly represented by a wing extended for flight. These Genii are then distinguished into other classes according to the marvelous variety of duties and effects they perform. Regarding their order and arrangement, since we have treated this elsewhere, we refer the reader to that work. Thus, we have the <term>multi-form manifestation</term> <note>original Greek: πολυμόρφοσιν (polymorphosin)</note> of the triform Divinity in the Angelic world.

Now, let us see how this Divinity is multi-formed in the sidereal <note>relating to the stars and planets</note> world. First, what else does the variety of streaks and spots scattered across the body in Figure 14 indicate but the variety of stars in the firmament? By the head of the hawk, whom they called Osiris, what else is meant but the Sun? Truly, by the human arm, the execution of things is indicated as if by a hand. Thus, they said through this symbol that everything in the sidereal world is accomplished by the stars, the Sun, and the Moon. 

Finally, in the elementary world <note>The physical realm composed of the four elements</note>, fire is aptly denoted by the head of the hawk; water by the Ibis; air by the wing; and earth by the serpent's claw. From the various combinations of these elements, the various classes of natural things finally emerge. Thus, the class of human souls, prevailing with a certain fiery power, is indicated by the hawk; birds by the wing; aquatic creatures by the Ibis; quadrupeds <note>four-legged animals</note> by the foot; and the levels of insects are indicated by the serpent. In all these things, the triform Divinity works all in all, and through its crafting mind (indicated by the human arm), it produces every variety of things, signified by the spots. Furthermore, they formed this symbol into the shape of a cross (†), by which they conveyed the universal influence into all the bodies of the World, as has been said.

You see, therefore, how many great secrets they indicated by even a single symbol, under a perpetual analogy of the Worlds. Do you see how they established the sacred triad of the Divinity in the Archetypal World <note>The world of divine ideas and the mind of God</note>; the choirs of Genii conforming to the properties of the triform Divinity in the Angelic World; the Stars, Sun, and Moon as the living workshops of the triform Divinity in the Sidereal World; and finally, how they graphically displayed the levels of men, quadrupeds, winged creatures, aquatic creatures, and reptiles in the Elementary World? And how one and the same spirit works all things in all.

There follows the multi-formed symbol of a statue—either a mystagogic <note>related to religious mysteries</note> or magical one—which expresses the letters <term>pieech</term> <note>original Greek: πιεεχ</note>, that is, the "mother and eye of Osiris." They believed they could draw down this spirit of the universe through the power of the <term>hieromantic</term> <note>Sacred divination or priestly magic</note> art, by means of the <term>chain</term> <note>original Greek: σειραν (seiran)</note> of Osiris. Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar</note> explains this term as a series of Genii connected in the manner of a chain, which they showed through a <term>cord</term> <note>original Greek: σχοινίον (schoinion)</note> in the form of a chain with a triple spiral, indicating the triple world. The first circular spiral easily hinted at the Archetypal World; the second cycloid or oval spiral at the celestial world; the third interrupted spiral at the Elementary World. The Chaldeans called these "Zones," as will be clear later. Now the symbols follow...

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK

<margin>

Of the Genii, the Solar power is represented by an upright asp <note>A cobra or serpent, often used in Egyptian royalty and divinity</note>, distinguished by a triple dominion; from its region comes the $^8$ Nilotic vessel <note>A water jar or "canopic" vase representing the Nile</note>, which they used to aptly denote the power of heat acting upon the mixture of moist nature. For from the commingling of these two—heat and moisture—all things that exist in the world are composed. To show this more clearly, they proceed as if to an enumeration of parts, which they signify by the following symbols: the $^{10}$ sensible world <note>The physical world that can be perceived by the senses</note> is represented by the head of a boy; $^{11}$ Isis, representing terrestrial moisture, is shown by a female head subject to Horus; the $^{12}$ Mystagogue <note>A teacher or initiator into mystery religions</note> statue of Momphta represents the power that disposes or arranges all things; and finally $^{14}$ Sothis, that is, <term>Sioth</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲥⲓⲱⲑ</term>, whom the Greeks call the <term>Star-dog</term> <note>original Greek: Αστροκυωνα (Astrokuyona); referring to the star Sirius</note>, appears in the form of a sitting dog. The Phoenicians called him Thaut, that is, Mercury, while the Coptics called him <term>Sioth</term>. This is the <term>seira</term> <note>original Greek: σειρα; meaning a "chain" or "series"</note> or chain of Gods, which we recently cited from Psellus. These beings, under the guidance of the supreme Divinity, are <term>multiform</term> <note>original Greek: πολυμορφοι (polymorphoi)</note> and administer and dispense all things that exist in the world.

And so that everything said thus far may be confirmed by a single authority, let us hear Psellus, who explains everything so skillfully that he seems to have had these very symbols in mind. In his *Recapitulation of Chaldean Dogmas*—which are nothing other than commentaries on the Egyptian edition of the Oracles of Zoroaster (Paris edition by the author Opsopæus, page 116)—he says: <term>There are among them also the Azonoi Hecates; such as the Chaldean Triform-Giver, the Comas, and the Releasing One. Gods called "Azonoi" among them are Serapis, and Dionysus, and the chain of Osiris, and that of Apollo. They are called "Azonoi" [un-zoned] Gods because they freely exercise their power within the Zones, and are established over the manifest Gods.</term> <note>Kircher provides the Greek first, then translates it into Latin. The term "Azonoi" refers to deities not restricted to a single celestial "zone" or planetary sphere.</note>

But let us explain each part, so that the agreement of our interpretation with these authors may be known in every respect. What else is meant by the <term>Triform-Giver</term> <note>original Greek: Τριεκδοτιν (Triedkotin)</note> but the three-fold Divinity who was adored by the Chaldeans in a triple form? What is the <term>Comas</term> <note>original Greek: κωμας</note> but the "Builder Mind" (the Demiurge), which inserts itself into all the "villages" <note>A play on the Greek 'komas' (villages/wards), implying the divisions of the universe</note> of the world, working all things in all? Finally, what does the <term>Releasing One</term> <note>original Greek: εκλυστικην (eklystiken)</note> indicate but the Spirit of the World enclosed in all things? These descriptions fit aptly with the symbol of the various transformed birds, the Archetypal Hecate, or the Triform Divinity.

There follows the chain of Genii, by whose help all things are perfected: Serapis, who according to Eusebius is the Spirit of the World indicated by the upright asp; Bacchus (or Momphta), the overseer of moisture, indicated by the $^8$ Nilotic vessel. These are followed by $^{10}$ Horus (that is, Apollo), $^{11}$ Isis, $^{12}$ Nephte, and $^{14}$ Anubis—the followers of Hecate—to whom the life of things is committed, to be propagated into all $^{13}$ members of the world. Thus, what we set out to prove from the beginning is clear.

However, since these things have been handed down this way, I have decided to explain one symbol more fully in this place: the symbol of the sitting dog with a serpent-bearing globe. This is of great importance for confirming many things on this Obelisk. It was believed that Mercury—the inventor of both letters and things necessary for the human race—was translated to heaven after death. In that region occupied by the constellation Leo, specifically in Sirius (the Great Dog), he established his kingdom to indicate his sagacity <note>Wisdom or keenness of mind</note>. From this...

### INTERPRETATION

It is not without reason that the Egyptians call him Sothis—or in Coptic <unclear>Soti</unclear>—and the Phoenicians and Chaldeans call him Thoth (by changing the *S* into *Th*). He is the principal $^{14}$ Guardian Spirit and protector of Egypt, or the most faithful $^{15}$ Tutelary of the fatherland. He is the one who draws the influence of the $^{30}$ multiform spirit into the lower realms; from this source flows the $^{30}$ life of the $^{13}$ world, an abundance of all things, and complete happiness. All these qualities were indicated by his $^{14}$ seated posture, the $^{15}$ handled cross <note>The *Ankh*, an Egyptian symbol representing life and divine power</note>, the $^{13}$ globe marked by a serpent, and finally by $^{16}$ another serpent with a segment of a circle and a scepter.

Since this Spirit was of such character and greatness—most renowned for his earthly kingdom, priesthood, and wisdom, and the sole inventor of sacred letters <note>Hieroglyphs</note>—it is certain that later Kings were primarily focused on his worship in memory of his blessings. Most notably, the Erector of this Obelisk, who had taken the name Sothis for himself from this most wise King, Priest, and Philosopher Sothis, decided to erect this Obelisk in his honor, as the one from whom every good thing proceeded. To make this known to posterity, he saw to it that a $^{14}$ seated dog was depicted at the base of the Obelisk. This dog would represent both Mercury and the name of the erector, Sothis, as a symbol common to both. By this symbol, he left a witness of his gratitude to the $^{15}$ Protector of both the kingdom and royal power, from whom he had received everything. He placed this symbol on the southern side because Sothis rules most especially over the southern region, from which the outflow of Osiris—that is, the beginning of the Nile—emerges, of which Sothis is the guardian; consequently, every good thing flows from there. These are the things that remained to be explained regarding the second side of the Obelisk.

*Reader, take note that I have used the word "Asp" <note>original Latin: "Aspis"</note> sometimes in the masculine and sometimes in the feminine gender; I find many other authors have done the same. I mention this so that you do not think an error has perhaps crept into the text.*

## DIAGRAM II.
### Of the Third Western Side.

On this side, there first appear two 1 Ibis-shaped figures <note>original: "Ibimorpha"</note>, mystagogues <note>A "mystagogue" is a priest or guide who initiates others into sacred mysteries</note> with the head of an Ibis and clothed in a sacred veil, which sit upon hemispheres. These are followed by a 2 vulture 3 sitting upon the Heavens; then the head of a "three-zoned" 4 child <note>Likely referring to a child figure with three belts or bands, often representing a stage of initiation or a specific aspect of Horus</note> placed between two 5 retainers, followed by a 7 Hawk, to which is added a 9 serpent 8 encircling a globe, sitting upon a 10 mixing bowl <note>original: "crateri"</note> with a 11 two-knotted scepter and an Isiac receptacle, or 12 sacred cistern, beneath which is placed an 13 arm with an extended hand; then a 14 knotty staff, from which a serpent emerges along with a 15 water-symbol <term>hydroschemate: a symbolic representation of water or fluid</term>; this is followed by a 16 Papyrus thyrsus <note>A staff tipped with a pinecone or ornament, here made of papyrus</note>, with a 17 quail and two 18 19 serpents; these are followed by the said thyrsus and a 20 <term>dragon-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: δρακοντόμορφος (drakontomorphos)</note> butterfly with upper hemispheres and one 22 larger lower one; finally, two staffs follow, between which three 23 circles are placed, and then two 24 scalene figures, between which are two 25 squares. But let us explain each part.

<margin>What are the Ibis-shaped images?</margin>
Therefore, after they showed the influx of the triform Deity into the fourfold World in the first Diagram, now descending to particulars, they describe on this side the operations, effects, and worship of the Ibis-deity, the presiding lord of moisture <note>original: "humidi"</note> both of a superior and inferior nature, as has been aptly signified by the two Ibis-headed mystagogue images. For since they found the Western region to be filled with adversarial demons who continually infest the beneficial, moist, annual Libyan breeze, they placed here protective <note>original: "prophylactaicos"</note> Spirits <term>Genios: guardian spirits or presiding deities</term> facing the Western quarter as presiding lords of the moist nature. By their power, they believed themselves safe and unharmed against the hostile Spirits; they endeavored to appease them with various sacred rites, as follows shortly after. <margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*</margin> They wear a sacred veil, with which, as Plutarch testifies, they were accustomed to adorn these statues for reasons indicated elsewhere; on their heads they carry a gourd, a symbol of the moist nature. For just as the gourd, a pot-bellied fruit, draws all the moisture of the earth into itself, so the Spirit presiding over the moist nature attracts all moisture to himself, having dominion over every watery Elemen-

BOOK V. THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side II.
South.

What are the two hemispheres?

What is the position of the statues in a V-shape?

What is the vulture sitting on the cycloid?
</margin>
The powerful element <note>The element of moisture or water, as discussed in the preceding section</note> is placed upon the head to indicate the reason existing in the head, from which all force and power emanate. They sit upon two hemispheres to indicate that this power extends to all things within the horizon of the two hemispheres. With their arms and feet, they express the "V" symbol of the influx of the Supreme Deity <note>original: "Superni Numinis"</note>, which they are subject to, and in which they participate and receive. Because the Spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> are linked together, and the Spirit of the moist nature cannot achieve its purpose unless it is aided by celestial power, they have placed beneath it a ² vulture, the ³ indicator of the heavens. For the vulture, as I have said elsewhere, is always female in its kind; indeed, they claim the vulture conceives from the wind. It behaves as a passive principle, and by such a property—according to Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>—they aptly indicated the heaven, which is like a passive principle containing in its womb the seeds of all things that can be generated. It ³ sits upon a celestial figure to show that the moist nature accomplishes nothing unless it is first activated by heaven, as if in a womb, and prepared for the generation of things.

<margin>
What is Horus between two retainers?
</margin>
For this reason, beneath the vulture and within ⁴ ⁶ two retainers, there is aptly placed the ⁵ retainer of the Horus of the World, in the form of a child's head marked by three Zones. This was to indicate that the entire tripartite World is filled with "seminal reasons" <note>The Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of *logoi spermatikoi*, or the creative principles that form matter</note>, from which an abundance of all good things flows. This symbol is explained more fully in Plutarch. Horus is depicted in the form of a child's head to suggest that the World is always, as it were, growing young again through the continuous production of new things.

<margin>
What is the hawk with the globe?

What is the mixing bowl?

What is the sacred chest?
</margin>
Because the World profits nothing unless the Solar Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> approaches, they place beneath Horus the ⁷ hawk, the symbol of the Solar Spirit, together with the ⁸ globe ⁹ entwined by a serpent. By the power and efficacy of this globe, the World is animated and made fertile. It ¹⁰ stands upon a mixing bowl <note>original: "crateri"</note> because the force and power of the Sun, through its heat, acts most strongly upon the moist nature, tempering it and preparing it for the generation of things in the material worlds <note>original: "hylæis Mundis"</note> over which it exerts its power. But let us explain the ¹¹ staff. The hieroglyphic staff is sometimes smooth (without knots), and sometimes consists of one knot, which is either round or quadrangular; occasionally it consists of two or three knots, either circular or angular. By the staff without knots, they denoted simple dominion over higher and celestial things; by the quadrangular one, dominion over the lower elementary things. Again, a two-knotted staff indicated double dominion, and a three-knotted staff triple dominion over the higher or lower Worlds, depending on the shape of the knots. But see what we have treated more extensively regarding staffs and scepters, both in the preceding diagram and in the specific study of sacred writing <note>original: "hierogrammatiſmo"</note> according to the minds of various authors. They aptly included these knots on their scepters—which Iamblichus calls "sacred knots"—to indicate the extension of power over all things, and the connection of all things with the power and dominion of the Deity. Therefore, the staff in this place, marked with two quadrangular knots, indicates power over the lower Worlds, and especially over the moist nature filled with subterranean conceptions. This is aptly expressed by the ¹² sacred chest, the concealer of sacred things, placed beneath it.

### INTERPRETATION

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side III.
West.
</margin>

...where, through another knobby staff teeming with a snake, along with a water-symbol <note>original: "hydroschemate"; a diagram or figure representing water</note>, the life and fertility of the waters is indicated. And because the opposing powers lie in wait to ambush the efforts of the good Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note>, and are accustomed to hindering the life-giving spirit of the higher and lower things (suggested through the <gloss>18</gloss> two snakes) in various ways with their malignant machinations, these are indicated by the <gloss>16</gloss> papyrus thyrsus <note>A staff associated with ritual and nature</note> and the <gloss>17</gloss> quail. Hence they have placed the many-formed Spirit <gloss>21</gloss>, indicated by the <gloss>21</gloss> dragon-shaped <note>original: "δρακοντόμορφος" (drakontomorphos)</note> butterfly, opposite the malignant quail—that is, opposite the adverse powers. For by the strength and power of this Spirit, the use of necessary things is preserved in the <gloss>22</gloss> lower realms through the mark of the <gloss>29</gloss> thyrsus, and is defended from every ill-fated power. Since this Spirit is powerful in the triple World, it directs all the force of fertile <gloss>14</gloss> generation into the <gloss>25</gloss> elemental <gloss>24</gloss> worlds in various ways, which are aptly indicated by two scalene triangles and two squares, as we have said elsewhere.

For the Many-formed Spirit <note>A concept in Kircher's Neoplatonic Egyptian theology where a single divine force takes many shapes</note> works all things within individual Spirits: indeed, it promotes the moist, nourishing force of things in Dionysus or Bacchus; in Hercules or Mompha <note>A name Kircher associates with a specific Egyptian aspect of Hercules</note>, it promotes the solidifying force of things; in Ammon, the fertilizing and receptive force; in the Earth, the industrious force; in Nephte or Proserpina, and finally in the Moon or Isis, the moistening force. If, however, an excess or defect ever occurs in the worldly House of Horus <note>The physical universe or the sphere of change</note> regarding the disposition of things, this Spirit reduces it to a middle state and makes it harmonious through Typhon—this scorching and burning force, or superfluous moisture (for Typhon signifies everything excessive or defective in the nature of things). This is not unlike how, in bodies filled with pernicious humors, burning treatments or, in those that are overly dry, moisture-inducing <note>original: "hydrotica"</note> medicines are used. All these things are explained so beautifully by Plutarch that he seems to have had this very matter in mind. I provide his words here:

> *Again, when Isis receives Osiris and raises Horus—who grows strong through exhalations, mists, and clouds—Typhon is indeed overcome, but not killed. For the Goddess, who is the Mistress of the Earth, did not allow the nature contrary to moisture to be completely abolished; rather, she dismisses and relaxes it, desiring that a balance remain. This is because the world could not be perfect if the fiery nature were abolished. And a little later: For they give the name of Bacchus to the generative and nourishing spirit; the name of Hercules to that which has the power of striking and dividing; Ammon to the faculty of receiving; Ceres and Proserpina to that which penetrates through the earth and its fruits; and they call that which moves through the sea Neptune. Those who mix mathematical and astrological matters with these natural ones thought Typhon was the scorching force of the Sun, and Osiris the moistening force of the Moon. For they say the Moon, which has a generative and moistening light, is prosperous for both the procreation of animals and the budding of plants; but the Sun, with its immoderate fire, heats and dries the growing and flourishing plants more than is right, and by its heat has made a large part of the earth unfit for habitation, and often even the Moon is overcome by it. Therefore, the Egyptians call Typhon "Seth," a name signifying that which prevails by force.*

For this reason, the sacred table is immediately placed below, which—like a certain sacred amulet—both puts the adversary to flight and attracts and placates the benign Spirit.

BOOK V. OF THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK

# Context of the Ideal Reading.

(1) The Ibis-shaped <note>Associated with the god Thoth, often depicted as an ibis</note> Spirits <note>original: "Genij"</note> who preside over the moist nature in the lower regions are to be worshiped with sacred ritual, because these first diffuse the generative principles into the (3) heaven, which acts as the (2) passive principle and the receptacle of feminine reasons. (4) These <note>the generative principles</note> (5, 6) Horus, the bond of the sensible world, actuates and binds together; (7) Osiris indeed, brooding over them, (9) with vital spirit, fertilizes both the (8) World and the (10) sacred mixing-bowl <note>original: "craterem"; a vessel used in Neoplatonic thought to represent the receptacle of souls or divine influence</note>. To whose (11) doubly-powerful dominion over the lower things, the (12) hidden or subterranean chest is referred; and by whose (13) beneficent and (14) life-giving dominion, the (15) waters receive their increase. And from here flows an abundance of (16) necessary things, once every (17) Typhonian force <note>referring to Typhon or Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and destruction</note> has been dispelled. (18, 19) Life is propagated both in the superior and inferior world. Finally, the (21) Many-formed Spirit of nature <note>original: "Polymorphus... Genius"</note>, mixing himself into individual things, (22) furnishes the lower world with a new (20) abundance and variety of necessary things; (23) he is the ruler of the three worlds, and (24) the sole author of the generation of things in the material <note>original: "hylæis"; from the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter</note> worlds.

---

*You see therefore from these things, how the Lunar Spirits prepare the matter for the generation of things; the Solar Spirits actuate and fertilize that which has been prepared; while the Many-formed Spirit provides the final completion to that which has been actuated, by producing a variety of things.*

# DIAGRAM III.

->Of the third Western side<-

There now appears a sacred tablet, or a protective amulet <term>Amuletum prophylactycum: a defensive charm or symbol intended to ward off evil or misfortune</term> almost identical to the one seen in Diagram VI of Side I. Within this, in the first position, a 1 Scalene triangle <term>Scalenus: Kircher refers here to a right-angled triangle which, following Pythagorean and Plutarchian thought, represented the principle of generation</term> appears, with an 2 extended arm and two 3, 5 knotted scepters, between which a 4 spheroid is placed. There follows a 6 serpent, with a 7 receptacle of sacred influence, and two 8 wings with an 9 extended arm, to which is joined a 10 hydro-symbol <note>A symbol representing water or its properties</note> with a staff or 11 scepter. These are sacred symbols established by a certain secret logic, as we have proven in the specific descriptions of each; since they are constructed from things analogous to the "Good Spirit" <note>original: "benignum Genium"</note>, they believed they contracted a certain affinity or sympathy with that Spirit. Thus, they more superstitiously believed that he was attracted by these things and, conversely, encouraged to repel unfavorable powers. For as was said regarding the preceding symbols, the Scalene triangle is a figure filled with mysteries and a unique type of the principle of the generation of things; therefore, it was not ungracefully called a "fertile nuptial sign" <note>original Greek: "σῆμα γονιμὸν" (sēma gonimon)</note> by Plutarch. Since the remaining hieroglyphs have been explained in various places in the preceding sections, I did not wish to linger on untying them, as they can easily be understood by the curious reader from the following reading of the conceptual discourse.

Let us therefore follow the effects of this sacred tablet, which are ingeniously indicated through the following symbols; first, indeed, there appear a papyrus reed, a Nile vessel with the figure of a tongue, and a shell with a leaf of the persea tree. There follow a square with a Nile vessel and the figure of an Altar. Through the 12 reed thyrsus <note>A staff associated with ritual power</note>, the power of Chenosiris <note>A name used by Kircher for a deity associated with the Nile's vegetation</note> is shown; through the 13 Nile vessel with the 15 figure of a tongue placed beneath it, the refreshing moisture is denoted. Just as the tongue constantly dwells in moisture (according to the witness of Horus <note>Refers to Horapollo, an ancient author on hieroglyphs</note>) and derives moisture into the other limbs, so does the celestial Nile moisture flow into the remaining members of the world. Through the 16 square with the other 17 Nile vessel, he notes the annual increase of the Nile, by which an abundance of necessary things is granted. Furthermore, through the 14 shell, or a cup in the shape of a heart with a persea leaf and an altar placed beneath, it is indicated that for the preceding amulet to confer its power, the Divinity to whom it is inscribed must be solicited with "tongue and heart"—that is, by the heartfelt performance of hymns through the true study of wisdom joined to religion.

There follows Momphta <note>Kircher's term for a supreme creative deity or "Hyle," the Governor of the World's substance</note>, noted by a scepter <image-desc>hieroglyphic scepter resembling a 'was' scepter</image-desc>; for according to the testimony of Plutarch, they mostly placed the letters of the Spirit upon scepters, whose power and dominion they were describing. Thus, in this place, they mark the scepter of Momphta with the letter M, which <image-desc>hieroglyphic water ripple symbol</image-desc> denoted water; the deity Momphta was the overseer of this water. It is as if they were saying: <image-desc>three hieroglyphs: two water ripples followed by an ankh-like scepter symbol</image-desc> "The God of the increase of the waters," marked and indicated by the letter M. Moreover, by the feather, they aptly indicate sometimes speed, sometimes the wind, sometimes the soul, or the impulse of the divine Power, as has been shown elsewhere; here, however, it signifies the wind...

<header>BOOK V. THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK</header>

<margin>Obelisk Side III. West.</margin> They noted the west wind as a purifier of the air, and through the 20 Phagrus fish <note>A species of sea bream or similar fish found in the Nile</note> they signified malice—that is, a ruinous impression and Typhonian force <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and drought</note> that plagues the air with a certain parching quality. Thus, they held this fish as a symbol of abomination because it devoured Osiris’s genitals when Typhon cast them into the river, according to Plutarch. Moreover, the Phagrus is considered to "devour" the genitals of Osiris—meaning the fertile overflow of the Nile waters—when dry and parching Typhonian winds rise from the sea. By these winds, the generative moisture of the Nile and the hoped-for fertility are hindered. For the Phagrus is a marine fish of ill omen; when it is seen ascending from the sea into the Nile, it shows a meager hope of abundance, resulting from the shallowness of the Nile and the weakness of its rise. Hence, it is a symbol of evils and other things which Plutarch pursues at length in these words:

<margin>The member of Osiris devoured by the Phagrus fish.</margin> <note>original: "Συηνῖται δὲ φάγρῳ ἀνέχονται; δοκεῖ γὰρ ἐπιόντι τῷ Νείλῳ συνεπιφαίνεσθαι, & τὴν αὔξησιν ἀσμένοις αὐτάγγελος δεχόμενος."</note> *The people of Syene also abstain from the phagrus and avoid it; for it seems to appear alongside the rising Nile, and its sighting is received as a self-announced messenger of the longed-for increase.* Although in this passage Plutarch suggests that the fish announced the fertile increase of the Nile, anyone who weighs the words correctly will find that they were spoken through a kind of <term>antiphrasis</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a word is used in a sense opposite to its literal meaning, often for irony</note>. It is as if he were saying: it *seems* to announce the longed-for increase, yet that increase does not follow. Therefore, it is no wonder that the same fish was held in execration among the Egyptians, as it was a sight that mocked them with vain hope. They abstained from this fish not only because it was of a Typhonian nature and an indicator of a parching power during the Nile's weakness, but also because it had tasted of Osiris's member. That Plutarch’s cited words must be understood as an irony is clearly apparent from what follows; for he says a little later:

> *They relate, furthermore, that of all the members of Osiris, only the penis was found [missing] by Isis; for this had been immediately cast into the Nile and tasted by the Lepidotus, Phagrus, and Oxyrhynchus fish; which the Egyptians therefore abominate above all other fish.*

But to return to our purpose, there follows in Diagram 21 the 21 Monia <note>Kircher's term for a specific type of spirit or symbolic figure</note> with a 22 receptacle of sacred liquor, and a quadrilateral figure, a hemisphere, a quadrangle, and an 23 extended arm. By these, it is indicated through the Monia that power is carried down from the celestial heights into the fourfold world and the subterranean channels, whereby the receptacle of sacred liquor is filled by the benevolence of the Divinity, as was explained above. The 25 waters of the lower world are 26 brought to life by a 24 fourfold influx; the divine 25 Osiris, powerful with double dominion, 29 blesses the 28 heavens and the 20 lower world with 30 his influx and fills them with all good things. This influx they aptly indicate through the 30 pyramid which he 31 holds in his hand. There follows hereafter the Ideal Reading of the things mentioned:

## DIAGRAM IV.
### Of the third, Western side.

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side III.
West.

In this diagram, there first occur two ¹ **eyed scepters**; which are followed by ² a **triple-crowned tripod** <note>original: τριστέφανος (tristephanos)</note>, that is, one constructed with three supports in the form of triangular rings, with two ⁴ **owls**, and a ⁵ **mystagogue figure** <note>A 'mystagogue' is a person who initiates others into sacred mysteries; here, Kircher uses it to describe a priestly or guiding deity figure</note>. These follow: three ⁶ **quadrangles**, and a ⁷ **beam** conspicuous with twelve squares, three ⁸ **Nilotic vessels**, a ⁹ **staff** pregnant with a serpent, an ¹⁰ **eyed scepter**, with an ¹¹ **water-symbol** <note>original: hydroschemate; likely a reference to a specific hieroglyph representing water or irrigation</note>, and a ¹² **serpent**, under which a ¹³ **sacred bier** is placed. These follow: two ¹⁴ **spheroids** with an ¹⁶ **extended arm**, the hand holding a ¹⁵ **pyramid**; which is succeeded again by a ¹⁷ **beam** distinguished by twelve squares, with an ¹⁸ **water-symbol**, and under it a ¹⁹ **sacred table**, with a ²¹ **water-symbol**, and in that region a ²⁰ **gourd**. These follow: ²², ²³ **six mystagogue statues**, all similar to each other in position, except that the three upper ones are clothed in different tiaras <note>High, conical headdresses</note> than the lower ones.

Beneath these are placed ²⁴ the **head of Horus**, ²⁵ the **figure of a priest**, ²⁶ **Horus** again leaning upon an altar, with a ²⁷ **hawk**, under which are placed the figure of a ²⁸ **chain**, a ³⁰ **eyed** ²⁹ **phallus**, and a ³¹ **scarab**; let us see what each indicates.

<margin>
What is the triple-crowned tripod?
</margin>

1 The **eyed scepter**, as we have demonstrated extensively elsewhere from Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer often cited by Kircher for his theories on solar theology</note>, indicates the divine intellect, which they call the Archetypal or supramundane Osiris, illuminating all things with his crafting mind; they place two scepters for this reason: that just as the Sun and Moon are like two eyes of the world illuminating all lower things, so the supreme divinity, together with his crafting mind, works all things in all things through the Sun and Moon, and surveys all things. Moreover, to indicate how he, with his crafting mind and all-shaping spirit, works all things in all things through the divine ideas common to the **triform Deity** <note>original: triformi Numini; Kircher often equated the Egyptian "triform" nature of the sun or Osiris with a precursor to the Christian Trinity</note>; hence they quite aptly placed beneath the eyes a ³ **mystical tripod** with a ² **globe or circle**, from which three rays woven from triangles (note here in the figure the triangles were not closed, which the engraver omitted through carelessness; for on the Obelisk they are closed, and represent perfect triangles <note>original: trigonos</note>, as you can see in the copper-engraved figure) pour forth toward the lower parts. By this hieroglyphic they denoted nothing other than the procession of the triform Deity, pregnant with ideas, into the universe, communicating his ideas under the triangles of the classes of created things to each, insofar as they are capable of them; for from these is the origin of all, the existence of all; from these all things have their being, their life, their feeling, and their likeness to their maker. But concerning this symbol, see the more extensive treatise in the preceding sections.

<margin>
Two owls.
</margin>

These are followed by two ⁴ **owls**, a symbol of evils, placed opposite the two eyes, by which it is shown that the goodness of the triform Deity is devoid of all evil; indeed, he is the driver-away of all evils, which have their origin only from created things (which are marked by the pair of owls); since the best and most beneficent Deity by no means intends evils, but rather...

<margin>
Obelisk.
Side III.
West.
</margin>
...a certain rust of clay, as *Plutarch* says, results spontaneously from the nature of the iron itself. 

<margin>Mystagogue statue.</margin>
But the 5 **mystagogue statue** <note>A 'mystagogue' is one who initiates others into sacred mysteries; here, a guiding deity figure</note>, when it is established through the sacred rite which it expresses by the position of its body, is rendered fit to receive the power of the Triform Deity. It then becomes powerful and effective through its own virtue in routing all things contrary to the Deity—that is, the machinations of malignant powers. To show the influx of the Triform Deity more particularly, and to indicate the suitable arrangement of the year and seasons, 6 **three quadrangles** follow. Through these, they signify first the three corporeal Worlds, and then the three seasons of the year, as was proven by various authorities in the first diagram of the first side.

Since the three material worlds <note>original: mundi hylæi</note> do not complete their vital operations without the movement of the Sun and Moon through the twelve mansions of the great citadel, following that monthly process, they aptly placed beneath them a beam or 7 **wall with twelve squares**, representing the many mansions of the great citadel or the space of the Zodiac. We not incongruously call this the <term>Dodecapylon</term> <note>original: δωδεκάπυλον, meaning 'Twelve-Gated'</note>. 

<margin>What is the <term>Dodecapylon</term>?</margin>
Through these gates, the Moon (passing monthly) and the Sun (passing annually) arrange the calculation of the three seasons and stir the seeds of the material worlds toward the production of things that can be generated. By their progress, the 8 **Nile**, through a vital inundation, provides an abundance of celestial and terrestrial water (as Horus testifies), indicated by the three water-jars. The 10 **celestial eye of Osiris** 11 provides life to the 12 **waters**; therefore, it is to be worshipped with the highest 13 **cult**. Through the 14 **heavens**, by a 16 **beneficial** 15 **influx** into the 17 **twelve mansions** of the Great Citadel, and from there into 18 **moist nature**, it propagates life; these things are aptly indicated by symbols marked with corresponding numbers. 

The reason for this hieroglyph depends on this: the Egyptians, as shown elsewhere, surrounded the Temple of the Sun in the City of the Sun <note>Heliopolis</note> with a certain mystic wall arranged with 12 pyramids or square chariots. They dedicated each of these to one of the twelve signs of the Zodiac and to the Genii <note>protective spirits or presiding deities</note> who govern them. By this mystic arrangement, they were firmly persuaded that the Gods were enticed to favor the sacred rites being performed. Thus, they quite rightly included these symbols among their sacred objects; see what we have declared explicitly about these on page 170. We have seen the effects of the Deity; now let us see by what modes and rites it may be made "attractable."

First, therefore, there occurs a sacred 19 **table**, with an 18 **water-symbol** <note>original: hydroschemate</note> and a 20 **gourd**. They wish to indicate by this that a sacred table ought to be prepared, inscribed with the Genius of moisture. Next, statues are to be constructed with mystic apparatus: three for the 21 **three Lunar Genii**, and another three for the 23 **western and solar Genii**, as the Diagram shows. The first three hold a tiara <note>original: cidarin</note> in the shape of a gourd placed upon the head; the latter three hold a basket full of fruits. 

The figure of the statues resembles the letter **N**, which, as we said in its place, indicates both the flow and reception of celestial and terrestrial influx, since it represents a double pyramid (one upright and one inverted). Furthermore, it indicates the movement of the generation of things upward and downward. 

<margin>See page 387. What are the 3 Lunar and 3 Solar Statues?</margin>
Indeed, the arms twisted in the shape of a **V** indicate the celestial movement; the feet with the thigh contracted into the shape of an **A** indicate the terrestrial movement. They are depicted sitting for rest...

He describes the specific physical postures of these statues as symbolic of the 'N' shape, representing the flow of energy between the heavens and the earth.</summary>

...to indicate the quality by which material powers are made fit, as if by necessity, for the reception of forms. The higher Lunar figures wear a *cidaris* <note>A Persian-style headdress or turban</note> in the shape of a gourd, which is a symbol of moisture. The lower figures hold a *Calathus* <note>A Greek-style basket typically used for wool or grain</note> overflowing with fruit, a sign of Solar benevolence. By the former, the moist power of the Moon is suggested; by the latter, the mixture of heat within moisture is shown, which promises an abundance of vegetation. Three figures are placed here, partly to represent the ideas of the Triform Deity, and partly to distinguish the three seasons of the year over which they preside. These seasons, according to Diodorus, are called "hours," and are produced by both the Moon and the Sun as they traverse the mansions of the Great Citadel through these ministering spirits. For as was said previously, the Sun, in its annual course, creates three seasons according to the Egyptians—Spring, Summer, and Winter—each of which is defined by 120 days, or the signs of four mansions. The Moon, in its monthly course through the twelve mansions, completes a Lunar year likewise divided into three periods, each defined by a space of ten days. The first of these, from the New Moon to the <term>gibbous</term> <note>original: ἀμφίκυρτον (amphikyrton); referring to the Moon when it is more than half full</note> moon, corresponds to Spring; the second, from one gibbous phase to the next, to Summer; and the third, from the gibbous phase back to the New Moon or <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: συζυγίαν (syzygian)</note>, corresponds to Winter. These are aptly indicated by the wall marked with twelve squares placed just before. See all these points confirmed in other locations.

With these things thus secretly established, they believed the gate of the 24 houses of the world—or of the 24 Horuses—was opened, as indicated by the head of the boy with the figure of the gate placed beneath him. Furthermore, through this 26th Horus, noted by the other head and the altar placed beneath, they believed that through sacred rites, worship, and the Spirits 25 **Mophta** and 27 **Osiris**—who, in the economy of the world, are the presiding governors of the superior and inferior moisture and heat—the world was filled with fertility. This is indicated by the 25th Priest, transformed into the letters of the name **Mophta**, and by the 27th garment and position, as well as the 18th hawk. Finally, they trusted that <term>through the chain of good spirits</term> <note>original: διὰ τῆς σείρας τῶν ἀγαθοδαιμόνων (dia tēs seiras tōn agathodaimonōn)</note>, the seeds of lower things would be fostered by a benign gaze, and the world filled with fecundity and plenty. Thus, through...

and Mophta signify.

...the chain, the concatenation of Spirits and the things subject to them is designated; through the 30 **eyed phallus**, the seeds of things fostered by solar rays are shown; and through the 31 **scarab**, the universe is aptly represented. For it has been extensively proven in the study of its specific hierogram <note>A sacred symbol or character</note> that the scarab is placed sometimes for the Sun, sometimes for the universe, and sometimes for a combination of symbols. As for the 29 **eyed phallus** or member, it was a symbol of the fecundity of the all-seeing Sun, and it is seen engraved on nearly every hieroglyphic fragment. Its origin is as follows: when Isis anxiously sought the remains of Osiris, who had been murdered by his brother Typhon, and could not find that specific part, Diodorus testifies that she honored an image of it with divine worship. From this source, as if from a perennial spring of superstition, there emerged among the Greeks the Dionysian Pamylia and the *Ithyphallia*—not sacred rites, but crimes. In honor of Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, says Arnobius, Greece raises up these phalluses and statues...

-> ### I N T E R P R E T A T I O N: 531 Obelisk. Side III. West. ### <-

...all territories flourish with the images of male charms <note>original: *virilium fascinorum*; referring to phallic amulets or symbols intended to ward off evil and promote fertility</note>. According to Plutarch, these were made of fig-wood, because the *Thrio* <note>original: θρῖον; a fig leaf</note>, that is, the fig leaf, expresses the male genitals; or they were made of leather, hanging from the neck, as Herodotus and Nonnus relate. Indeed, that golden one of 120 cubits mentioned by Athenaeus was an extraordinary case. According to Eusebius, they worshipped that member of man because from it comes the birth of all things. From this, as recorded by Arnobius, Nicetas, and Hyginus, come the *Phallophoria* <note>Greek festivals in which phallic symbols were carried in procession</note> festivals; from this came those secret initiations in Cyprus where participants, in exchange for a donated fee, were presented with phalluses. From this flowed the <term>apotheosis</term> <note>original: ἀποθέωσις; the elevation of a mortal to divine status</note> of Fauns, Satyrs, and Silvani; from this the shameful secrets of Priapus and Beelphegor <note>The author identifies the biblical Baal-Peor with the Greco-Roman fertility god Priapus</note> emerged. From this the charm of Mercury, worshipped by the Cyllenians, was held sacred in the religion of the Athenians. From this the *Neurospasta* <note>original: νευρόσπαστα; string-controlled puppets or figurines</note> in Lucian were used as remedies; and that "shameful little thing" worn on the necks of boys, namely the *fascinus* <note>a phallic amulet</note>, which Pliny calls the guardian of infants. But regarding these things, see what is recorded elsewhere throughout various parts of this Work.

<margin>The reason why such a shameful idol was worshipped?</margin>
Furthermore, I find in authors the reason why, after the Egyptians, the Greeks and Romans (who drew these things from the said Egyptians) always worshipped these sacred rites with such zeal. It was because, through this cult, those evils that might hinder generation were turned away, as if by a counter-spell <note>original: *fascinata*</note>; and also because of that part of the body from which the origin of all things arises. For the first reason, we read that it was placed everywhere in gardens, among trees, and in other fruitful places, according to that line of Ovid:

> Let the red guardian be placed in the fruitful gardens
> So that Priapus may terrify the birds with his sacred sickle.

Columella says: *And venerate the name of the ancient tree of the Ithyphallus.* <note>Ithyphallus: a representation of the phallus, typically shown erect in ancient art</note>

<margin>The Hebrews worshipped Beelphegor to avert sterility.</margin>
With this established, moved by a certain false superstition, they promised themselves an abundance of all things. Another reason moved them: to avert impotence brought on by sorcery and to turn away the sterility of women, they wore these as <term>phylacteries</term> <note>amulets or protective charms</note> around the neck, hands, belt, and ears. It will be clear from the hieroglyphics that these were also attached to animals and beasts for the same reason, as nothing occurs more frequently in them than this phallus. We assert, therefore, that for the same reasons, the Hebrew people also embraced these most shameful rites—and all the more willingly and greedily as they were more prone to every kind of superstition and the pollutions of every type of luxury. For since the Egyptians ascribed all the happiness of the earth, as well as the fertility of humans and beasts, to the cult of this Priapus or Ithyphallus, nothing was easier for a nation among whom nothing was more disgraceful than sterility. This people, having loosened the reins of temperance and rushing miserably into every kind of lust, even under the honest pretext of human propagation, adopted those rites by which they might safely and with impunity do so under the mask of religion. Following the example of the Egyptians, they averted that shameful sterility, which was cursed in the Law, through the cult of Priapus.
