# SCHEMATIC V.

->Of Side III, West.<-

In this diagram, the following symbols follow in order: 1. A receptacle for the sacred liquid with a 2. Crocodile; a bifurcated figure with two 3. feathers and a 4. <term>mystagogue</term> <note>A "mystagogue" is a teacher or guide into religious mysteries; Kircher uses this to describe a figure that directs the flow of divine power.</note> statue of Momphta; and three 5. quadrangles, beneath which is placed a 6. <term>hydroschema</term> <note>original: *hydroſchema*; a "water-diagram" or symbolic representation of water.</note> with two 8. segments, one lower and the other upper. Attached to these are two 8. arms reaching upward in a U-shape, with a 9. papyrus <term>thyrsus</term> <note>A "thyrsus" is usually a staff topped with a pine cone, but here Kircher identifies it with a papyrus stalk.</note> and a Nilotic vase, flanked by two 7. Rhomboids, and three 10. squares placed below. These are followed by 11. a bird with extended wings in the act of attempting flight, beneath which lies a 15. reclining Lion with two 12. Rhomboids; then follows 12. a Roe-deer with a 13. feather, and the figure of 14. Momphta with a <term>hook</term> <note>original: *harpagone*; a grappling hook or harpoon.</note>. Furthermore, there are three quadrangles, under which are placed 8. a papyrus thyrsus, a 19. drooping Lotus flower emerging from a bulb, with a 20. statue of Momphta and a 21. two-horned serpent in an erect position. To these are joined 22. the head of an Ibis with a 23. <term>tendriled basket</term> <note>original: *calatho capreolato*; likely referring to a basket-like headdress with curved, horn-like decorations.</note> and three 24. two-horned serpents with a segment above; however, below these are another two segments with three quadrangles; then 25. the figure of a thyrsus, with a 26. tongue, a 27. swallow, and an erect 28. serpent-bearing staff; a 29. Tiara in the form of a tendriled basket, with a 30. <term>Cucucomorphous</term> <note>original: *Cucucomorpho*; Kircher’s term for a scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe bird (the Egyptian *was*-scepter).</note> scepter, and a 31. receptacle for the sacred liquid, beneath which is 32. the figure of a swallow; under this is a 33. band or binding-cord with a 34. serpent. To these is joined a drooping Ibis distinguished by a triple-branched tendril, with a cycloid, a segment, and an extended arm. Let us see what all these things signify.

Beneath the 1. Receptacle of sacred liquid is placed a Crocodile, which in this context, through the combination of symbols, indicates not a GOD, but a <term>Typhonic nature</term> <note>Typhon was the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, representing chaos, storms, and the enemy of the life-giving Nile.</note> that is hostile to the receptacle of the sacred humor. Indeed, the hook-like figure suggests a certain prohibition of this malignant power, which is driven away by favorable winds according to the threefold division of the year; all of these things are indicated by the feathers (the markers of the air and winds), the mystagogue statue, and the three quadrangles, as was demonstrated in the preceding pages.

Thus, the sacred effects and operations of the Amulet shown in the previous schematic are continued in this one. Therefore, beyond the stated effects, the Amulet restrains everything contrary and unfavorable to the moisture within the receptacle of the sacred humor and within the three seasons of the year, across the three <term>material</term> <note>original: *hylæis*; from the Greek *hyle*, referring to the physical or material worlds.</note> worlds. This occurs through the power of the Mophta image, which is appropriate to itself, dissipating the force of the raging winds that are hostile to the waters and moisture.

<margin>The mystical rationale of the statue.</margin> Note here that this statue, as well as the two following it, expresses by its posture the letters of the name **Mophta**. For the arms with the chest and the hanging hand express **M**; the head expresses **O**; the feet with the thigh express **N** <note>Kircher is attempting to show that the deity's body forms a "hidden" name.</note>. These express **Mon**, which indicates the "increase of the Nile," as we taught on page 283. For they believed nothing to be more effective than to use silent invocations of the Divinity in this manner; which is also shown by the two arms following shortly after...

BOOK V. THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK

<margin>Side III of the Obelisk. West.</margin>
As was explained above on page 48, the [figures] with arms extended toward the heavens indicate that through such ceremonies, they believed the presiding power of humors was powerfully moved to grant an abundance of water and necessary things. This was achieved through the fertile ^7^ rise of the Nile and the ^7^ irrigation of the fields. Note here that the annual irrigation of the fields is aptly signified by the ^7^ Nilotic urn flanked by two Rhomboids. A **Rhomboid** is nothing other than an *aroura* <note>An "aroura" was a traditional Egyptian unit of land area, roughly equivalent to a square of 100 cubits per side.</note> or field, or a fourth part of a field encompassing one hundred cubits. By this, they signaled both the space of the current year and the inundation of the fields, which usually occurs at the rising of Sothis <note>Sothis is the ancient Egyptian name for the star Sirius, whose "heliacal rising" coincided with the start of the Nile flood.</note>. See Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> Book 1, chapter 5, whom we have frequently cited. These are oblique quadrangles, partly to distinguish them from the rectangular quadrangles that symbolize the elementary world and the year, and partly because fields appear as oblique Rhomboids when viewed from a distance. Next follows ^11^ a Bird with extended wings forming a cross, representing an **Aerial Spirit**, the presider over the fourfold aerial zone, accompanied by the Leonine ^15^ Mophta <note>Mophta (or Momphta) is a name Kircher uses for a divine artisan or "heming" force in Egyptian theology.</note> and a ^13^ feather. This indicates that the Spirit agitates the air by sending forth wind; the air, thickened by this agitation and then dissolved by the heat of the Lion <note>Referring to the sun being in the zodiac sign of Leo during the peak of summer heat.</note>, descends as moisture. From this, finally, the ^12^ fertility of fields and vegetation—indicated by the two Rhomboids and the tendril—emanates, with the statue of ^14^ Mophta actively cooperating, equipped with a hook for warding off adverse powers. So that the supply of ^18^ necessary things does not fail, and so that the appetite for ^19^ vegetable things may be satisfied, the ^20^ statues of Mophta, the presiders over the ^15^ three material <note>original: *hylęorum*; Kircher uses "hylaeic" to refer to the physical, material realm.</note> worlds, must be fashioned with sacred and mystic ritual. For from here, ^21^ life drawn from heaven and channeled into the material worlds will bring great benefit. All these things are beautifully indicated: specifically, necessary things by the ^18^ papyrus thyrsus; the greatest abundance of things by the ^19^ Lotus flower emerging from its bulb; the expression of the mystic ritual by the ^20^ statue of Momphta; and the fertile life propagated from heaven by the ^21^ erect two-horned serpent.

<margin>
Irrigation of the fields.
What is a Rhomboid?
</margin>

Because nothing is rightly completed without the **Lunar Spirit**, they expressed him here as a cooperator with Mophta under the form of an ^22^ Ibis head. Having obtained ^23^ power over vegetation (which the tendriled basket indicates), he bestows ^24^ triple life upon the three material worlds, indicated by three two-horned serpents and the three squares placed beneath them, for an abundance of necessities and the ^26^ continuation of moisture.

<margin>What the Swallow signifies.</margin>
Because ^26^ moisture accomplishes nothing unless it is distributed in due proportion to individual things in the material worlds, they aptly indicated this distribution of water through the ^27^ **Swallow**. It is the nature of this bird to nourish its young with marvelous equality, imparting an equal share of food to each one, with such diligence that no one who has received once should receive twice, and thus the portion for all is provided fairly. For as Horus rightly says: <note>original: "Ἐκείνη γὰρ κυκλόθεν ἑαυτὴν εἰς πηλὸν & κτίζει τοῖς νεοττοῖς φωλεὸν μάλιστα πιθανῶς."</note> "For she builds a nest for her young out of mud, circling about most persuasively." <note>This quote from Horapollo actually describes the swallow's skill in construction, which Kircher links to the "just" distribution of materials.</note> Near death, she rolls herself up and prepares hiding places for her young; see Pierius <note>Giovan Pietro Valeriano Bolzani, author of *Hieroglyphica* (1556).</note>, under the heading "Swallow." Hence they were held sacred to Osiris and Isis, because these Deities—according to Diodorus—most especially instructed the minds of mortals in laws and justice for the tempering of life. By this equality of distribution...

...of distribution, especially since ^28^ life consists in the ^31^ receptacle of the sacred moisture. Furthermore, the Divinity—through this ^32^ equality and the careful distribution of individual things shining forth in the ^30^ variety of worldly affairs—being ^29^ powerful over plant life, ^34^ animates the ^35^ substance of moist nature with a ^33^ life-giving connection. Since, finally, the ^36^ Lunar Spirit <note>Kircher uses "Genius" to mean a presiding spirit or intelligence.</note> by its own nature inclines toward promoting the plant life committed to its faith, and does not cease to derive the beneficial power of the heavens into lower things, they quite aptly placed ^36^ here [the symbol of the Ibis], distinguished by a branch with a triple tendril and leaning toward lower things as if by a certain effort. This is a beautiful symbol of its own leaning toward the things committed to its protection; the beneficial ^38^ influence of heaven is indicated by the spheroid and the ^39^ extended arm working together. Through the three tendrils, they indicate the three benefits of vegetation: the first is provided in the abundance of herbs and legumes; the second in fruits of every kind; the third in the richness of animals. For as was shown on page 361, the ancients were accustomed not only to dedicate certain plants or branches to specific Gods but also to insert those same branches, twisted in a certain mystical fashion, into the hands of the statues of the Gods they represented. Thus, in this place, they attributed to the Ibis—that is, the Lunar Spirit—a branch marked with a triple tendril. Just as this stands by a mystical reasoning, so too does it involve much in its meaning; it is as if they were saying: the Lunar Spirit spreads the power communicated to it by the triform Deity into the triple material world <note>original: "mundum hyleum," from the Greek word "hyle" meaning matter.</note>, whence the triple benefit of the nature of vegetation flows into lower things from the tripartite division of the year, by celestial favor and benevolence. One may admire this hieroglyphic idea in a similar tripled branch of the *persea* tree <note>The Persea was a sacred fruit tree in ancient Egypt, often associated with the heart or the recording of names on its leaves.</note>, which, because we have explained it extensively on page 363, we refer the reader there; for this reason, we will only place its figure here to fill the space. Since the reasons for all these things have been explained in various places in the preceding pages, I have judged it superfluous to take up time repeating them. Let it suffice here merely to have determined the numbers of the sections in which they are treated. How indeed all these things may be applied to mystical, anagogical <note>spiritual or uplifting interpretations</note>, and allegorical senses shall be said in its own time in my *Oedipus* <note>Referring to his massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>. Nothing therefore remains but to provide the reading of the entire Ideal discourse.

# SCHEMATIC VI.
## Of the third Western side.

<margin>Explanation of the figures.</margin>
There occurs first in this Schematic a triple $^1$ lotus flower with a $^2$ quail, and a $^4$ roe-deer <note>original: "capreolo"—a small deer or goat, often representing a sacrificial animal or a specific spiritual influence in Kircher’s system</note>, and three $^5$ small squares, which are followed by three $^6$ female heads with three $^7$ jars; these are succeeded by the $^8$ vulture sitting upon the $^9$ sacred barque <note>original: "barra/barys"—a ritual boat used by the Egyptian gods</note>, then a globe with prostrate thyrsi <note>staffs topped with pine cones, associated with Dionysian or generative rites</note>, upon which a roe-deer rests. After this, an $^12$ ibis with a long rectangle, a $^{14}$ staff, and three $^{13}$ small squares, which a double-knotted scepter, a $^{15}$ water-symbol <note>original: "hydroschema"</note>, and an $^{14}$ extended arm follow; these again are followed by a double-knotted $^{18}$ scepter, a $^{19}$ serpent, and finally the $^{23}$ sacred barque, upon which stand a simple $^{20}$ <term>ankh</term> <note>original: "crux ansata"—literally "cross with a handle," the Egyptian symbol of life</note>, a $^{21}$ triple rudder marked by 6 protruding squares, and a $^{22}$ <term>hoopoe-headed scepter</term> <note>original: "sceptrum cucuphomorphum"—a scepter topped with the head of a Cucupha or hoopoe bird, symbolizing purity or alertness</note>; beneath these are placed again an $^{21}$ ankh, a $^{26}$ square with a $^{25}$ sphere rising above it, and a $^{27}$ handled Nilotic vase, decorated with a $^{28}$ serpent and a segment. But let us briefly touch upon these cited symbols.

<margin>Harmony of the World from Consonants and Dissonants.</margin>
Since the Egyptians, considering the nature of things deeply, found in some things wonderful attractions, but in others the greatest disagreements and perpetual strife; they believed that the former proceeded from the <term>Orimazian Genii</term> <note>referring to Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian spirit of light/goodness, whom Kircher syncretizes here with Egyptian thought</note>, that is, the benign and luminous ones, and the latter from the <term>Arimanian Genii</term> <note>referring to Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of darkness/evil</note>, that is, the malignant and shadowy ones, about which we have written extensively in Book 2, Chapter 10. Nevertheless, a fitting distribution by the Supreme Divinity ensures that all those things, however distant from one another, are brought into accord to finally produce a perfect harmony, as if from a mixture of consonant and dissonant notes—a harmony not only for the adornment of the World, but also entirely necessary for its preservation. And they noted this "concordant discord" especially in the lower, tripartite kingdom of Hecate or Isis, whence they beautifully displayed this <term>sympathy</term> <note>in the Hermetic sense: a natural attraction or "likeness" between things</note> through the triple $^1$ lotus flower, just as they showed <term>antipathy</term> <note>natural repulsion or "unlikeness"</note> through the $^2$ quail. By the lotus, they indicated the sympathy of lower things toward higher things; but by the quail—a bird ungrateful and hateful to other animals, and indeed to the Sun—they indicated antipathy, as was proved in its <term>hierogrammatism</term> <note>the symbolic meaning of its sacred writing</note>. For as Plutarch rightly says:
> *For the origin and composition of this world is mixed from contrary powers, but their forces are not equal; for the better one prevails, while it is a sin for the worse one to be utterly destroyed, since it clings strongly to the body and to the soul of the universe, and always resists the better. In the soul, therefore, the Mind—that which is ordered, equitable, and healthy—is the outflow and image of Osiris, visible in the successions of seasons, temperaments, and revolutions; Typhon, however, is the part of the soul void of reason, agitated by various movements, tumultuous and brutal, causing diseases in the body and intemperance and instability in the air.* <note>original Latin: Kircher is translating a passage from Plutarch's "De Iside et Osiride" into Latin; here translated into English</note>

<margin>Nature of the Lotus.</margin>
But let us return to the Lotus, in which the first flower looks toward the East, the middle one stands upright as if inclining toward the mid-heaven; the third, however, tends with a certain effort toward the western region; by which it is indicated that just as the Lotus follows the divine course of the Sun from the East through the South into the West...

### BOOK V. THE PAMPHILJAN OBELISK

<margin>Obelisk. Side III. West.</margin>
<margin>The world consists of good and evil things.</margin>
...it follows with a certain insatiable appetite that in individual things there are established certain orders, which the lower things in that same order look up to; they regard the superiors as certain leaders from whom they draw power, life, and every good, which is the foundation and basis of the entire <term>sympathetic connection</term> <note>Kircher refers to "sympathy," the Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected by hidden "spiritual strings."</note>. However, because this friendly confluence of things would least likely occur if there were not certain opposites in nature—which are said to incite the flight from evil and the pursuit of good—the Egyptians adopted symbols of the world's variety as if woven from dissonant-consonants and bad-goods. They expressed this quite aptly through the <term>Lotus</term> (a solar herb) and the <term>Quail</term> (a bird contrary to the Sun). Hence, according to Plutarch, Mercury fashioned a lyre <note>original: "cytharam"</note> from the severed nerves of <term>Typhon</term> <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, representing chaos and destruction. Mercury (Hermes/Thoth) turning his "nerves" into a musical instrument symbolizes order being brought out of chaos.</note>, by which the harmony of the world is secretly noted as being made of consonant and dissonant parts. The Author of Nature wished to use their mixture both for the preservation of the world and for the variety of things. Proclus describes all of this so fittingly in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic* that he seems to have had these hieroglyphics we are proposing in mind. His words are:

> Just as lovers progress by reason from the beauty that appears to the senses toward a divine beauty, so also the ancient Priests—when they considered a certain kinship and compassion <note>original: "compassionemque," here meaning "suffering with" or reacting in harmony with</note> of some things for others in natural objects, and of manifest things for hidden powers, and found all things in all things—constructed their sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest: in the heavens, earthly things exist according to their cause and in a heavenly manner; and on earth, heavenly things exist in a terrestrial manner. For from where else do we think those plants move toward the motion of the Sun, which they call <term>heliotropes</term> <note>original: "heliotropias," literally "Sun-turners"</note> (that is, sun-seekers)? Or the <term>selinotropes</term> <note>original: "selinotropias," literally "Moon-turners"</note> (that is, moon-seekers) turn toward the Moon? Truly, all things pray and sing hymns to the leaders of their order—some in an intellectual way, some in a rational way, others in a natural way, and still others in a sensible way. Thus the sun-seeker moves toward the Sun however it can; and if anyone could hear the pulsation produced by it in the circuit of the air, he would surely perceive that through such a sound, a certain melody is composed toward its king, such as a plant is able to produce. For this reason, one may see the Sun and Moon on earth, but according to their terrestrial quality; while in heaven one may see all plants, stones, and animals according to their heavenly nature, possessing intellectual life. Having contemplated these things, the ancients applied certain heavenly things to some earthly things, and certain earthly things to others, from which they drew down divine virtues into a lower place because of a certain similarity. For similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. Indeed, if someone warms hemp <note>original: "canabim"</note> or papyrus, and then brings it close to a lamp, even if he does not touch it, he will suddenly see the hemp ignited—though it did not touch the fire—and the ignition descending from above to the lower parts. Let us therefore compare the warmed hemp or papyrus to the kinship of lower things to higher ones; its approach to the lamp to the opportune timing, place, and matter of things; the movement of the fire to the hemp to the presence of the divine light; and finally, the ignition of the hemp to the deification of mortals and the illumination of material things, which are then carried upward like the ignited hemp because of a certain participation in the divine seed. What truly shall I say of the Lotus? The Lotus indeed folds its leaves within itself before the Sun’s...

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the Western side of the Pamphiljan Obelisk. Having established the concept of "sympathy" and the interplay of opposites, Kircher now explains how specific plants, stones, and animals participate in the "Solar" and "Lunar" chains of being, leading into a discussion of ancient theurgic practices.</meta>

### INTERPRETATION

...rise: indeed, when the sun rises, it unfolds little by little. And as far as the sun ascends to the middle region of heaven, so far does it spread its leaves; but as it seeks the setting from the midpoint, it gradually contracts its leaves. It seems that this plant honors the sun no less by the expansion and contraction of its leaves than humans do by the gestures of their cheeks and the movement of their lips. Indeed, one may behold an imitation and a certain participation in the supernal lights not only in plants, which possess a trace of life, but even in stones. For instance, the <term>Helites</term> <note>original: "Helites"; likely a reference to sunstone or a similar solar-reflecting mineral</note> stone imitates solar rays with its golden beams. Moreover, the stone called the "eye of heaven," or "eye of the Sun," has a shape similar to the pupil of an eye, and a ray flashes out from the center of the pupil. The stone <term>Selenites</term> <note>original: "Selenites"; moonstone</note>, that is, the lunar stone, similar in shape to the horned moon, follows the lunar movement by a certain change in itself. Finally, the stone <term>helioselenus</term> <note>original: "helioselenus"; literally "sun-moon"</note>, that is, the solar-lunar stone, imitates in a certain way the meeting of the sun and the moon, and represents it in color.

Thus, all things are full of divine things: earthly things indeed of celestial things, and celestial things of super-celestial things; and every order of things proceeds even unto the last. For those things which are gathered together in the One above the order of things, these are subsequently expanded in descending, where other souls are ordered under other divinities. Furthermore, there are many solar animals, such as Lions and Cocks, which are participants in a certain solar divinity according to their nature. Hence it is a wonder how much the lower things in the same order yield to the superior, even though they do not yield in size or power. For this reason, they say that the Cock is feared by the Lion above all else, and is almost revered. We cannot assign the cause of this matter to material or sense, but only to the contemplation of the supernal order: because, clearly, the presence of **Solar Virtue** is more suited to the Cock than to the Lion. This is also apparent because the Cock applauds the rising Sun with certain hymns, as it were, and calls out to it when it turns toward us from the mid-heaven of the Antipodes.

And sometimes certain solar angels have appeared, endowed with such forms; and although they themselves were without form within themselves, they nevertheless appeared formed to us, who are formed. Sometimes even solar demons have been seen with a leonine forehead; when a Cock was presented to them, they suddenly disappeared. This indeed proceeds from the fact that things constituted lower in the same order always revere the superior—just as many people, when looking upon images of divine men, are usually afraid to commit something shameful by that very sight.

But to speak briefly, some things revolve along with the revolutions of the Sun, such as the plants we mentioned; others imitate the shape of solar rays in some way, like the palm and the date; others the fiery nature of the Sun, like the laurel; others something else. One may surely see the properties that are gathered in the sun distributed here and there in the following things established in the solar order: namely, in angels, demons, souls, animals, plants, and stones. Wherefore the **authors of the ancient priesthood** <note>Kircher refers to theurgists, such as those in the Neoplatonic tradition like Proclus or Iamblichus, who practiced "divine work" through ritual.</note> discovered the worship of supernal powers from apparent things, while they mixed some things and purified others. They mixed many things together because they saw that some simple things possessed a property of a divinity, yet not individually sufficient for the summoning of that divinity. Therefore, by that very mixing of many things, they attracted supernal influences; and that which they themselves made into one from many by composing it, they made similar to the "One" itself, which is over the many, and they constructed statues mixed from many materials. Also, by gathering together composed scents into one through the art of divine symbols, and rendering them as one—such as the divine exists according to its essence—they certainly comprehended those powers...

# BOOK V. THE PAMPHILIAN OBELISK
<meta>catchword: species-</meta>

<margin>Obelisk. Side III. West.</margin>
...many: *Indeed, the division of these things weakens each one, but their mixing restores them to the idea of the exemplar. Sometimes a single herb or a single stone suffices for a divine work. For <term>Cnebison</term> <note>original: "Cnebison"; likely referring to the blessed thistle, *Cnicus benedictus*</note>, that is, the thistle, suffices for the sudden appearance of some deity; while for protection, the Laurel, <term>Raccinum</term> <note>original: "Raccinum"; a type of thorny shrub, possibly buckthorn</note>, that is, a genus of thorny shrub, the onion, the squill, coral, diamond, and jasper are used; but for prophecy, the heart of a mole; and for purification, sulfur and sea water. Therefore, the priests, through the mutual kinship and <term>compassion</term> <note>original: "compassionem"; in this context, it refers to "sympathy," the hidden natural resonance between objects</note> of things, gathered them into one, and by their repugnance <note>antipathy</note>, they expelled them, purifying when necessary with sulfur and asphalt, that is, bitumen, and sprinkling with sea water: for sulfur purifies by the sharpness of its scent, while sea water purifies because of its fiery portion.*

And they employed *animals suitable to the Gods in the worship of the Gods, and other things likewise. Wherefore, receiving from these and similar things, they first recognized the powers of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonum"; used here in the Neoplatonic sense of intermediary spirits or guardian entities, not necessarily evil beings</note>, namely that they are most closely linked to natural things and actions; and through these natural things to which they are near, they summoned them into their presence. Then, they proceeded from the daemons to the very powers and actions of the Gods—partly learning by the instruction of the daemons, and partly by their own diligence interpreting the fitting symbols—ascending into the proper understanding of the Gods. And finally, having set aside natural things and actions, and for the most part even the daemons, they were received into the company of the Gods.*

This sympathy and antipathy of things shines out most clearly in the inferior tripartite kingdom of **Hecate** <note>The Greek goddess of magic and the underworld, whom Kircher equates with Egyptian figures</note>; which they fittingly expressed through the three heads of **Isis**, and the three quadrangular vessels. For it has already been said elsewhere, and demonstrated extensively in Book 3, that Hecate is everywhere confused with **Isis**, **Nephthys**, **Teleuta**, and similar figures. Three heads are positioned to indicate the triform nature of this subterranean spirit; which <term>Psellus</term> <note>Michael Psellus, a prolific 11th-century Byzantine scholar known for his work on the occult and philosophy</note> describes quite beautifully in these words regarding the *Zoroastrian Oracles*: <note>original Greek: "Τῶν δὲ ζωογόνων ἀρχῶν, ἡ μὲν ἀκρότης, ἑκάτη καλεῖται. ἡ δὲ μεσότης, ψυχὴ ἀρχική, ἡ δὲ περάτωσις, ἀρετὴ ἀρχική..."</note> **That is:** *Among the life-procreating principles, the summit is called Hecate; the middle is the initiatory soul; the extremity is the initiatory virtue; and among them are the "Un-zoned" Hecates, such as Triecdotis, Comas, and Ecclystice.* She is called **Triecdotis** <note>original: "Triecdotis"; meaning "the triple-giver"</note> because she presides over the terrestrial world by granting life to its triple nature—namely, the sensitive, vegetative, and mineral natures. She is called **Comas** because she supplies nourishment distributed to each thing as if through certain receptacles and veins of subterranean channels. She is called **Ecclystice** <note>original: "Ecclysticè"; likely meaning "the releaser" or "the dissolver"</note> because she contains all the aforementioned things within herself as if in a womb, whence she is also called the center of all influx; in which things, mixed with consonant and dissonant elements, they produce the harmony intended by nature. In a word, this **Isis** or **Hecate**, marked with the seal of the triform Divinity, if taken <term>synagogically</term> <note>meaning collectively or as a synthesis</note> as we have also shown above, is the same as the triform Divinity which the three heads indicate. While she works all things in all in the terrestrial world, she is most aptly called **Hecate** from the innumerable variety of things she produces there. To this, **Plutarch** <note>The famous Greek biographer and priest of Apollo at Delphi</note> subscribes with these words:

*Isis is therefore that part of nature which, being as it were feminine, receives all births into herself, acting as a kind of nurse and the common receptacle of all things. She is called by Plato and many others: **Myrionymos**, that is, endowed with innumerable names; because reason transforms her into all forms...*

<summary>Kircher explains the "sympathetic magic" of the ancient Egyptians, detailing how priests used specific plants and minerals to contact spirits and deities. He identifies Isis/Hecate as the universal feminine principle that governs the earthly realm and provides the "nourishment" for all physical existence.</summary>

# INTERPRETATION
<margin>Obelisk. Side III. West.</margin>

...and it turns its forms; for since it intends the good and flees the evil, and is the receptacle and subject of both, it nevertheless always inclines toward the better by its own will. It offers itself to be filled and enriched by the <term>outflows</term> <note>original: "defluxibus"; referring to the Neoplatonic idea of divine influence flowing down from the heavens</note> and similarities, in which, being fruitful and fit for the generation of things, it rejoices and exults. Furthermore, that this is the head of Isis is sufficiently testified by the statues of Isis encountered everywhere in the Roman <term>treasuries</term> <note>original: "Gazophylacijs"; here meaning museums or collections of antiquities</note>.

Furthermore, since this sympathetic and antipathetic power of things has its hidden seeds primarily in the 8 sky as if in a certain womb, it is therefore fittingly indicated by the 8 vulture. Its genital power, through the sacred rites performed in the 9 Isiac <term>baris</term> <note>original: "barra"; the Egyptian sacred boat or skiff</note>, 11 is carried down into the 10 lunar Heaven. The 12 Lunar <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Genius"; a guiding intelligence or deity</note>, however, being instructed with divine power over plant life, 14 holding double dominion over the three lower 13 <term>material worlds</term> <note>original: "hylæos mũdos"; from the Greek 'hyle' for matter</note>, derives its nature into 15 moisture through a 16 beneficial 17 influx. From this 18 dominion, 19 both life in individual things and the motion toward the pursuit of good and the flight from evil is born.

Moreover, the Lunar Spirit, acting through that same dominion upon the 23 moist nature, provides life, which is derived through the "world-boat" into individual things by the universal 20 influx of the 21 triform Divinity <note>Likely referring to the moon's three phases or its association with Hecate</note>. This is conducted throughout all the bodies of the lower world of <term>Hecate's</term> kingdom <note>In Kircher's cosmology, Hecate/the Moon rules the sublunary or earthly realm</note> over an annual space of time, by which that 22 variety of things in the World is made wonderful. For this reason, according to the testimony of Plutarch:

> *They called the Moon the mother of the world, on account of her nature being composed and mixed of both sexes; since she is full and pregnant from the Sun, she in turn emits the genital principles into the air.*

Hence, through the life-giving 24, 27, 28 <term>amulets</term> <note>original: "periapta"; charms worn for protection or to draw celestial influence</note> of this influx, 28 life, prosperity, and desired happiness are communicated to those who carry them.

I have decided not to set forth the mystical reasons for each individual part, since all these things have already been explained at length in the preceding pages.

At this point, it seemed appropriate only to explain what the <term>Baris</term> is. The <term>Baris</term> <note>original: "Baryis"</note> is an Egyptian word denoting a certain type of vessel, similar to our common skiffs; it is made of papyrus or the thorny Lotus. They say that Isis escaped in this boat while fleeing from <term>Typhon</term> <note>The god of chaos and desert storms, the rival of Osiris and Isis</note> during the crossing of the Nile. For this reason, enrolling it among the number of sacred letters <note>hieroglyphs</note>, they indicated by it the motion of the supreme Deity through the moisture. Beneath it they often place a Crocodile, as is found in the writings of Eusebius; Diodorus, Propertius, and Herodotus (in Book 2) also mention it, where you will find its form exactly described. Iamblichus indeed hands down its mysteries in his book *On the Mysteries*, folio 343 of the Basel edition.

Its form is seen graphically expressed in the <term>Bembine Table</term> <note>The *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs that Kircher studied extensively</note>, and it corresponds to ours here. But regarding these things, I have written at length in the explanation of the said table.

Note also that this is not distinguished from the sign of the "lower hemisphere," except by the <term>sistra</term> <note>original: "siſtris"; ancient Egyptian rattles used in the cult of Isis</note> and the rudders placed upon it; for they likewise called the figure of the horizon or the lower hemisphere a "Skiff" from its similarity, as was proven above from Diodorus and Eusebius.

Nothing remains, therefore, except that we set down the idea of the whole discourse in a suitable reading.

### Context of the Ideal Reading.

From this, the 1 Sympathy and 2 Antipathy of things shines forth in the 6 three <term>material worlds</term> <note>original: "Mundi-læis," likely a contraction of the Greek-derived "mundis hylaeis," referring to the physical realms composed of matter</note>, and in the triple 6 lower kingdom of Hecate, or Isis; and the 7 moisture, having been activated as if in the 8 womb of the heavens, is drawn and brought down through the sacred 9 <term>baris</term> <note>original: "barram"; the sacred boat or skiff used in Egyptian ritual to represent the movement of gods and celestial influences</note>, the vehicle of the plant world, and fits all things into a beautiful harmony forged from dissonant and consonant parts. The 12 Lunar <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Genius"; a presiding deity or intelligence</note>, the 13 attraction of the three Worlds, having 14 attained power over the 15 waters, and being 16 doubly-powerful through a 17 beneficial influx, 19 fills the 23 mundane <term>boat</term> <note>original: "baryn"; another reference to the sacred baris boat</note> with life. Through this, the triple-formed 20 21 22 power and efficacy of the Divine is channeled through all the bodies of the World, and 22 produces the variety of all things. From this, the amulets of the 24 <term>Tautic cross</term> <note>original: "crucis Tauticæ"; the Ankh, associated by Kircher with Thoth (Taaut)</note>, the 25 circle, and the 26 mystic square—and from this, the 27 <term>charms</term> <note>original: "periapta"; from the Greek for "amulets" or things tied around the body</note> of the sacred vessel—28 draw the life which they communicate to all who carry them, leading them to the desired happiness.

## DIAGRAM II.
### Of Side IV, North.

In this second Diagram, in the first place is set (1) a fourfold <term>sistrum</term> <note>A ritual rattle used in Egyptian worship, often associated with Isis, intended to drive away evil spirits</note>, attached to (3) <term>favissae</term> <note>original: "Fauissæ"; these were traditionally underground cellars or repositories in temples used for sacred objects or liquids</note> or a receptacle for holy liquid (4), with the figure of (2) a sacred door; there follows (4) a square with (5) an extended arm, grasping a young goat; which is succeeded by (6) a two-horned serpent, two (7) squares, a pair of (8) feathers with a (9) papyrus <term>thyrsus</term> <note>A ceremonial staff or wand</note>, and (10) a water-symbol, and (11) two (12) serpents, by means of (13) a square. Finally, there follows a sacred tablet, in which are included (14) a square placed upon a Nilotic urn, with the figure of an altar marked with young goats, an (17) extended arm with (18) a water-symbol, and (20) a two-knotted staff, and at the end finally the figure of (19) a Star, with two (20) rhomboids and a quadrangle; beneath which are placed (26) an owl with an intervening (21) arm; the Diagram is closed by the figure of (22) a Priest with a staff, a (23) Nilotic vessel with (24) a tongue, and another (25) vessel, within which a (25) pyramidal figure is drawn; let us declare what each of these indicates.

On this Northern side are placed four (1) sistrums resting upon (2) a receptacle for holy liquid, with (3) a door, and this for a very significant reason. For since this region is infested by <term>Ahrimanic</term> <note>original: "Arimanijs"; referring to Ahriman, the spirit of evil and darkness in Zoroastrianism, whom Kircher equates here with Egyptian chaos-demons</note>, or <term>Typhonian</term> <note>original: "Typhonijs"; relating to Typhon (Set), the god of disorder, storms, and the desert</note> dark spirits, and those of a moist nature, infested by a biting cold, they fix their seat in the kingdom of darkness. They rightly say that the North Wind (<term>Boreas</term>) is the kingdom of Typhon, to whom also the Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major</note> is dedicated, as Plutarch teaches; and he says this is the allegorical reason for it: that Osiris joins with Nephthe, the wife of Typhon—that is, the Nile (which is the outflow of Osiris), flowing down from the South, when it is mixed with the sea at the Northern boundary, loses all its fertility. For this reason, calling it a symbol of evils and the "tear of Saturn," they used to pursue sailors and those devoted to maritime commerce with the greatest hatred, as if they were the sons of Typhon. Thus, for the reasons mentioned, they called this region "Typhonian," being full of hostile spirits, which they believed were driven away by the sound of these sistrums, leaving Egypt immune from every harmful force.

<margin>
Side IV of the Obelisk. North. Plutarch.
</margin>
For as Plutarch rightly says: *That Arimanian <note>A Latinized form of Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of darkness and destruction, whom Kircher equates with the Egyptian Typhon.</note> power, or Typhonian force, is nothing other than a certain violent inhibition, contrariety, or inversion, which the Egyptian words* Sith, Bebon, Smy *aptly signify: It is a cold and scorching force rushing from the Northern sea of Egypt, by which the fertile moisture of Egypt—namely the Nile, the outflow of Osiris—withers away.* And they believed for certain that this **Arimanian** force residing in the North was stopped and restrained by the sound of *sistrums* <note>A ritual rattle used in Egyptian worship to drive away evil and invite divine presence.</note> constructed through a certain secret method; but that the **Orimazaean** <note>Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian spirit of light and goodness.</note> power was drawn in and made present; hence, appropriately, the sistrum rests upon the receptacle for the sacred liquid. Furthermore, they indicated by the sistrum that all natural things are shaken and agitated by a never-ending motion, and if they should ever become sluggish or wither, they must be awakened; of which motion the birth of things, and the rising and falling of the Nile, was a symbol, according to Plutarch.

<margin>
Mystic reasons for the Sistrum.
</margin>
And indeed the sistrum, being round at the top, shows that four primary bodies, indicated by the fourfold bars of the sistrum, are shaken together. For that part of the world which is subject to birth and death is contained within the sphere of the Moon, in which all things move and change by reason of the four elements—namely fire, earth, water, and air; Plutarch recites these things in almost as many words, whom we cite at length in our discussion of the sacred writing of the sistrum, where you may contemplate its mystic figure along with various diagrams of sistrums in due time. Hence they were accustomed to carry the sistrum of Isis, while the Priests—distinguished by their shaven heads, clothed in linen garments, and equipped with sistrums—performed the sacred rites, as Martial testifies: *The linen-wearing <note>original: "nigeri", likely a transcription error for "linigeri" (linen-wearing), which fits the context of the Priests' garments.</note> shaven-headed ones and the sistrum-carrying crowd flee.*

<margin>
The agitation of the 4 Elements is signified by the sistrum.
</margin>
Therefore, the agitation of the four elements and the restraint of Typhonian violence are aptly shown by the sistrum. For by the power of this sound, after Typhon has been put to flight, the beneficent Divinity (noted by the arm) is awakened to grant Life to the lower world—a life which the **Arimanian** power, pouring out from the Northern sea, was striving to take away. By this, moreover, the 7 elementary movements of the world are agitated, the harmful power of the winds is dissipated, and an abundance of necessary things is granted, which are aptly indicated by the two squares, the two feathers, and the papyrus <term>thyrsus</term> <note>A ceremonial staff or wand.</note>. When the hostile Arimanian power has been dissipated, a double life—celestial and elementary—is granted to the watery element, which is indicated by the 10 water-symbol <note>original: "hydroschema", a symbolic representation of water waves.</note> and the two serpents with the square in between. Furthermore, they believed that by the sound of the sistrum, the Priests were inspired in various ways to perform the works of divination. Iamblichus beautifully explains these things in his own way with these words on page 234 of the Basel edition: *In the world, various kinds of motions correspond to the various orders of the Gods; and certainly from these, various melodies breathe forth, which likewise agree through their own motions with certain orders of the Gods, who are the principles of devotions. Since these are everywhere, and they especially obtain their own things, they are present primarily in those sounds and melodies that most suit them, and insinuating themselves into our spirits affected by them, they occupy the person, and soon thoroughly transform them with their own essence and power.*

There follows now the sacred tablet or prophylactic <note>protective</note> Amulet, in which first is (24) the Nilotic urn with a square placed upon it, the symbol of elemental moisture; there follows (15) an altar with (16) young goats, and (17) an extended arm, (18) a water-symbol, (19) a two-knotted sceptre, (19) a star, two (19) Rhomboids and a quadrangle; by means of the altar equipped with goats, they indicate that by sacred rites the beneficent Divinity...

...beneficent <note>The word begins with "neficum," completing "beneficum" from the previous page.</note> and powerful with a double dominion over the waters, must be continually entreated and drawn down through the influence of the <sup>19</sup> appropriate star, for the <sup>22</sup> second irrigation of the fields and for the <sup>16</sup> production of favorable harvests—all of which overflow with various meanings, providing for both the needs of the body and those instilled in the mind. For they believed that by this sacred amulet, all unlucky and unhappy things were driven away. They indicate this through <sup>26</sup> the owl <note>Original: "noctuam." In Kircher’s system, the owl often represents the darkness of Typhon or the "Arimanian" power.</note>, which <sup>21</sup> an extended, transverse arm seems to strive to prohibit. 

And since no one can achieve their prayer simply by carrying the sacred tablet, unless there is also <sup>22</sup> purity of life <note>Original: "castimonia vitæ."</note> and the <sup>22</sup> study of wisdom <note>Original: "sapientiæ studiū."</note>—by which things, as if by things similar to itself, the Divinity <note>Original: "Numen."</note> is uniquely drawn to provide help—hence the <sup>22</sup> priests, in order to derive the influence of the supernal Divinity into the <sup>23</sup> sacred water <note>Original: "lympham."</note>, continually entreated it with <sup>24</sup> tongue and heart. For this reason, the <sup>22</sup> Priest is depicted naked, with a feather placed on his head, his arm lowered and hand contracted, while the other hand carries a staff. 

By the feather, they indicated the sublimity of contemplation; by the arm with the contracted hand, efficacy in action; by the nakedness of the body, a soul immune to every stain of earthly corruption; and finally, by the staff, they indicated the dominion that he obtained over the things he requested in this manner. By the <sup>24</sup> tongue, the persistence of prayers and the recitation of hymns was signaled; and finally, by the <sup>23</sup> urn, it was signaled that the supernal moisture was derived from heaven into the lower world. These are aptly expressed through the <sup>23</sup> upper urn and through the <sup>25</sup> pyramidal shape which was derived into the <sup>26</sup> lower urn. 

You see, therefore, that in this present schematic <note>Original: "Schematismo."</note>, three things are primarily required for the attraction of the Divinity and the Guardian Spirits <note>Original: "Geniorumque."</note>: 
1. First, the routing of adverse powers through the sound of <term>sistrums</term> <note>Original: "sistrorum." A ritual rattle used to repel chaotic forces.</note> (for mystic reasons based on how such an instrument is constructed). 
2. Second, the amulet of the sacred tablet, by which they might be fortified against those same powers. 
3. Third and finally, through sacred ceremonies and rites, as well as actions pleasing to the Gods, such as the study of wisdom, purity of life, and efficacy in action. 

For by these things alone, it was believed that the worldly spirit was attracted to do good and to avert evil. But let us now set down the Reading.

^1 By the sacred sound of the sistra <note>sistrum: an ancient Egyptian percussion instrument or rattle used in religious ceremonies to ward off evil</note>, the ^2 great gate is opened to the ^3 receptacle of the influx of the sacred liquid.

The ^5 beneficent Divinity is awakened to the ^4 abundance of the vegetable fields, as well as to ^6 grant life to all things.

The ^7 terrestrial and ^8 aerial worlds, pregnant with ^9 Typhonian <note>Typhonian: referring to Typhon/Set, the god of chaos and drought, whose influence Kircher believes must be purged</note> impressions, are purged by the sound of the sistrum and provide the use of necessary things.

By whose help and protection, ^26 unlucky and destructive powers are ^21 restrained and tamed. The ^22 leader of the mystical rites—wise in sacred matters, prompt, effective, chaste, and powerful in dominion—is made ready; with heart and tongue in harmony, and drenched from heaven by the ^3 sacred liquid, he participates in the influx of the ^25 World Spirit through these preceding operations. This is also achieved through the amulet of the following sacred tablet.

Obelisk. Side IV. North.

# I N T E R P R E T A T I O N

## D I A G R A M III.

### Of the fourth Northern side.

In this diagram, in the first place, occurs the Sacred Tablet, which includes <gloss>1</gloss> a serpent, <gloss>2</gloss> two wings, <gloss>3</gloss> an extended arm with <gloss>4</gloss> a two-knotted staff; to these is added <gloss>5</gloss> a star with a square. After the sacred tablet follows <gloss>6</gloss> a cornucopia with <gloss>7</gloss> seven small squares; then <gloss>8</gloss> a four-banded wing; the image of <gloss>9</gloss> Mophta <note>Mophta: In Kircher's system, a "genius" or spirit associated with the Nile's fertility and moisture</note>, with the <gloss>10</gloss> Iynx <note>Iynx: A magical "spinning wheel" or bird-like spirit used in Neo-Platonic ritual to draw divine power down to earth</note>, which sits upon <gloss>11</gloss> a spheroid; this is followed by <gloss>12</gloss> Horus with <gloss>13</gloss> a spheroid, and <gloss>14</gloss> the figure of a restraint; <gloss>15</gloss> an upright Asp, with the figure of <gloss>16</gloss> a sleeping Hawk, which sit upon the <gloss>21, 22</gloss> segments; there follow <gloss>17</gloss> a Nilotic urn, <gloss>18</gloss> a cross, with <gloss>19</gloss> a star-gazer [astroscope]; closing the line of symbols is <gloss>20</gloss> an extended arm with <gloss>23</gloss> a young goat in the hand; but let us see what this context of symbols intends for itself.

What the figure of the sacred tablet signifies, and what mystical reasoning it possesses, has been indicated and declared throughout the preceding pages; it will also be made clear from the reading to be set down a little later. There follows <gloss>6</gloss> the cornucopia with <gloss>7</gloss> seven small squares, by which are indicated the seven mansions of the seven Governors of the World; for the school of Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster: An ancient Persian prophet whom Kircher and his contemporaries viewed as a source of "primeval wisdom" shared with the Egyptians</note> established just as many corporeal worlds with just as many governors, as witnessed by Psellus <note>Michael Psellos: A Byzantine scholar known for his commentaries on the Chaldean Oracles</note>, who, commenting on the oracles of Zoroaster, says:
> *They say there are seven corporeal worlds: one first empyrean <term>empyrean: the highest, fiery heaven</term> world; and next after it, three ethereal ones, and then three hylic <term>hylic: material or physical (from the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter)</term>, or material ones.* <note>original: "ἑπτὰ φασὶ σωματικοὺς κόσμους· ἐμπύριον ἕνα καὶ πρῶτον, καὶ ἑξῆς μετ’ αὐτὸν αἰθερέας, ἔπειτα τρεῖς ὑλαίους."</note>

And these correspond to the circles of the 7 planets, which they likewise call worlds; of which the first, the empyrean, is aptly assigned to the Sun because of the fiery power in which it excels; the remaining worlds correspond to the other 6 planets. Of these, the 3 higher ones are ethereal, and the 3 lower ones—due to a certain similarity and proximity which they hold to the elemental world—are called hylic, that is, material worlds. Regarding these, Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus: The legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed</note> says in the *Poimandres* <note>Poimandres: The first and most famous text of the Hermetic Corpus</note>, folio 24: *He then fashioned seven governors, who encompass the sensible world in circles, and their arrangement is called Fate*; and on folio 42: *The Sun is the most excellent God of the celestial Gods; the rest of the heavenly beings obey the Sun as their prince and king.* etc. Therefore, through these governors cited elsewhere, as if from a certain cornucopia of plenty, the entire system of distributing things is derived into the lower hylic worlds, which are aptly indicated by the four-banded wing placed beneath the cornucopia. For, as was correctly shown above from Plato in Plutarch, the wing was the symbol of the empire of divine intelligence, which, stimulated by love, embeds itself in the material worlds, having descended into the generation of things. These four hylic worlds—fiery, airy, watery, and earthy—are indicated by the wing divided by 4 zones; it is fashioned into the shape of a pyramid to indicate that its movement proceeds from the apex (as if from the center of divinity) into the breadth of material things. The multicolored variety of the wing shows the diversity of beings which it produces by its movement; finally, the wing is positioned so that the speed and readiness with which all things [are moved...]

<margin>Obelisk. Side IV. North.</margin>
...pervades the bodies of the lower world, is marked. Hence, quite appropriately, they placed below the wing the **Iynx** <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, an Iynx is a spiritual mediator or "spinning wheel" that draws divine influence down into the material realm</note>, a symbol of the aforementioned all-pervading intelligence, which Psellus calls the **intelligible mind** <note>original Greek: νοητὴν</note>, proceeding from the paternal mind; but let us hear Psellus:

> *There are, moreover, certain powers after the paternal depth composed of three unities, which understand through the paternal mind, which presents to them the cause of those things represented to itself in the form of unity.*

Furthermore, this **Iynx** has another image placed opposite it, transformed into the name **Mophta**, which signifies the presiding spirit of the humid nature; he has a water-jar, or Nilotic vessel, or a **modius** <term>modius: a grain-measure, often depicted as a crown on the heads of fertility gods like Serapis or Pluto to symbolize abundance</term> on his head, to indicate that the principal subject upon which the governors of the said worlds act through the Sphinx or Iynx is moisture; of which **Mophta** is the governor and dispenser. And because he is almost always confused with **Serapis** and **Pluto**, Servius is the authority that the ancients fashioned him with a measure or an urn on his head. We have, therefore, the manner in which the seven governors of the world act through the Iynx upon the fourfold elemental world. It follows next how the divine intelligence indicated by the Iynx distributes the power drawn from the supreme Deity through all the bodies of the world, and what effects result therefrom. Since, therefore, the reason for everything that the Iynx disposes concerning the world is inherent within it, it is appropriately placed upon the **cycloid** <note>A circular or spheroid shape</note>, which we generally call the symbol of the heavens.

This is to indicate the primary reasons of the paternal mind implanted in the heavens, through which they are then derived into the sensible world—that is, the <gloss>12</gloss> **three-zoned collar of Horus**, which acts as a kind of <gloss>14</gloss> **restraint** or "stay" for the heavens, and from there into lower things. For as Plutarch rightly says, **Horus** is sometimes called the movement of the visible Sun, sometimes the terrestrial world, and sometimes the temperament of the air surrounding all things; therefore, these things are appropriately indicated by the neck of the triple-zone. Hence, he is placed in the middle between two cycloids, because he appropriately tempers and connects the upper things with the lower, which is hinted at by the <gloss>14</gloss> **restraint**. Since, however, the world profits nothing unless each thing is directed to its ends by a providing and vivifying reason for all, hence that vital <gloss>15</gloss> **spirit of the universe**, the supreme **Agathodaemon** <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent</note> or <gloss>16</gloss> **Osiris**, stimulates the hidden virtues, as if to bring them into the light. If he should sleep, all things in the lower world (marked by the <gloss>21, 22</gloss> **segments** upon which they sit) are consumed by a certain squalor and decay; but when he is awake, all things are seen to dance with joy and gladness in the greatest abundance, according to the testimony of Eusebius. They indicated this appropriately through the <gloss>15</gloss> **upright asp**, distinguished by its scales and coils, as well as through the <gloss>16</gloss> **hawk** expressed under the figure of a sleeping bird; as these have been discussed more extensively in the preceding pages, we refer the reader to them. There follows the <gloss>17</gloss> **Nilotic urn** with the <gloss>18</gloss> **cross-mark** <note>original: decussi</note> and <gloss>19</gloss> **astrological quadrant**, and the <gloss>20</gloss> **extended arm** with the hand <gloss>23</gloss> **clutching a young goat**. By these inventions they indicate that the sacred moisture, into which the said governors of the worlds flow, finally confers a beneficial abundance of all things. The influence is indicated by the <gloss>18</gloss> **cross-mark** composed of two pyramids, like an **X**, of which one (upright) indicates active influence, and the other (inverted) indicates passive influence. The number ten <note>symbolized by the X or decussis</note> is born from the seven governors and the Iynx (which is composed of three unities), by which the whole is completed. As for the cross-mark, or the two lines crossing each other...

### INTERPRETATION.

...intersecting, to indicate a ten-count <note>original: denarium</note>, Horus clearly teaches in Book 3, Chapter 28, with these words: *“One straight line, together with another line cut across it, or a cross-shape, signifies ten flat lines.”* <note>original Greek: γραμμὴ ὀρϑὴ μία, ἅμα γραμμῇ ἐπιταμμένη, ἢ χασμα, ἢ δέκα γραμμὰς ἐπιπέδας σημαίνουσι</note> A straight line together with another bent over the first, or a decussis <note>an X-shape</note>, indicated ten flat lines; we have explained this more fully on page 385. Furthermore, the Bembine Tablet <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs</note> shows that the **Astroscopium** <term>Astroscopium: a specialized instrument for observing the positions of the stars and celestial bodies</term> was in use at that time; you will find it depicted here and there with degrees marked upon it. These instruments indicated that astrological diligence must be applied to perform everything according to the rites and to appease the aforementioned spirits.

<margin>Summary or recapitulation of the entire Schema.</margin>
Thus, once the sacred tablet is displayed, they now show its effects through the attraction of the linked Divine Powers. First, they indicate that when this sacred tablet is used in holy ceremonies with confidence and singular preparation, the seven princes of the world—the presiding governors of the seven celestial mansions—are stimulated to pour the abundance of their influence into the four-zoned face of the elemental world. But because these influences would achieve nothing unless they were first committed to **Momphtha**, their guardian and dispenser, he performs his role here. With the cooperation of the **Iynx** <note>The spiritual mediator that draws down divine ideas</note>, who disposes of things lying hidden in divine providence, Momphtha distributes the influences derived from the heavens across the entire face of the sensible world. This world is indicated by the head of **Horus**, acting as a kind of bond connecting the upper world to the lower. By the common consensus of the Gods, he distributes these influences, activates them within the world, and arranges the variety of things in the highest harmony. 

However, because **Osiris**—overwhelmed by worldly moisture—sometimes becomes as if sluggish, the fiery **Agathodaemon** <term>Agathodaemon: the "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent, representing a protective and life-giving solar force</term> is appointed to rouse him. The Agathodaemon, through his heat, consumes the excessive abundance of moisture—which would otherwise suffocate the storehouses of seminal things—and by removing the superfluous solar moisture, he restores him to a proper balance and leads him from lethargy to vigilance. Once this is done, the moisture is proportionately distributed across the fourfold regions of the elemental world, which, when combined with astrological skill, brings about an abundance of all things. If anyone thinks this arrangement is arbitrary, they will be immediately convinced otherwise by **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note>, who expressly states that the arrangement of sacred letters follows "linked ideal reasons" established with the greatest genius by the priests.

The three (1) quadrangles indicate the three elementary worlds, into which an (2) abundance of moisture has been sent down together with a circular segment. There follows the (3) hammer of Isis, which is both a hammer and a key at the same time, by which—after the ceremonies of certain strikes, according to the testimony of Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera, a Greek historian who wrote extensively about Egyptian customs</note>, whom we have cited elsewhere—the (6) Enclosure of the bull Mnevis or Apis is opened. Let us see what this Enclosure of Apis truly was, and with what mystical reasons it was distinguished. Strabo and Ammianus Marcellinus <note>Ancient Roman and Greek authors used as sources for Egyptian history before hieroglyphs were fully understood</note> say that the Bull Mnevis was raised in a certain enclosure; they say this Mnevis Bull was dedicated to the Moon. In the Sacred Writing <note>original: Hierogrammatismo</note> of the Bull it was shown in various ways, where we also expressed the spots and signs up to 29, by which they indicated the periodic motion of the Moon. Since they adorned the cow with so many and such great symbols appropriate to the Moon, they marked its Enclosure—being its dwelling—with the same apparatus of symbols. They did not disdain to receive this into the register of hieroglyphs, just as they did all other sacred furniture, of the kind found painted both here and elsewhere, as will be shown in its proper time and place. The Enclosure was a quadrangle formed of ten beams fixed in the earth, jagged with fourteen teeth in a row on both sides. Therefore, through the Cow, as I said, they indicated the Moon; through the quadrangular enclosure, the Elementary World; and through the ten beams descending perpendicularly, they indicated the influence of the Moon upon the ten degrees of beings in the elementary world. The four degrees of beings are, first, the four simple elements, then the six degrees of beings composed from their mixture, such as birds, aquatic creatures, quadrupeds, insects, vegetables, and minerals. <margin>Obelisk.
Side IV.
North.</margin>
With deliberate reason they expressed the Enclosure <term>Septum: A sacred pen or space, often associated with the holy bulls</term> with ten perpendicular lines; furthermore, to show that the Moon brings all things subject to itself to perfection through its monthly influence, they have roughened the outer beams with 14 teeth on each side, which joined together make 28. These express the number of the periodic lunar motion, by which it proceeds from its conjunction with the Sun by a continuous increase of 14 days until it reaches perfect fullness; from there, by a continuous decrease of 14 days, it returns to its desired Sun. This they aptly indicated through the 14 teeth fixed into the outer beams, as if by certain steps. Moreover, it was opened by a hammer and a key at the same time, constructed in the form of the Tautic character, or handled cross <note>original: "crucis anfatæ," commonly known today as the Ankh</note>, as appears here. From this mystical apparatus and these ceremonies, once all unlucky and destructive powers have been eliminated and expelled, they indicate that a triple life is diffused into the triple world and the fourfold region of the world, and that the (10) Bowl of the (9) Sun is filled with an abundance of supernal virtue. All these things are indicated by the 3 serpents, the crossed circle, the hook, and the hawk sitting upon the bowl, which are marked with corresponding numbers.

The (12) hawk sitting upon a spheroid, which is preceded by the figure of a (11) quadrangular gate, indicates that the celestial Osiris opens the (11) gate of the elements. Through this gate, both (14, 15) Momphta <note>Momphta: In Kircher's system, this refers to a divine creative power or "Spirit of the World" that presides over nature</note>, appeased by sacred worship, may complete the influence made upon the ten kinds of beings with its fruitful and beneficial power. However, the effort of Momphta would be invalid unless the (19) celestial eye of Osiris and the (23) Isis of the auxiliary Genii of the Sun and Moon were added. For these, departing into the (20) Orb, and establishing the difference of the (21) three (22) seasons of the (23) year, while they are joined twelve times in the annual span, consequently bestow life upon everyone in the lower world. These things are clearly seen expressed through the (19) eyed scepter with a (20) globe, beneath which is immediately placed the (22) head of an Ibis, which indicates the twelvefold conjunction of the Sun and Moon. It is also shown through the three quadrilaterals (21, 22, 23) representing the three seasons of the year; through the twelve sides shining forth in the three quadrilaterals representing the twelve months. By these twelve meetings of the Sun and Moon, the three elemental worlds—airy, watery, and earthly—indicated by these same quadrilaterals, draw a (25) double life, both heavenly and material <note>original: "vraniam & hylæam"</note>. This double life is aptly indicated by the (25) amphisbaena <note>A mythical serpent with a head at both ends</note>, conspicuous for its two heads. Through this Lunar-Solar conjunction, the (29) mundane boat <note>original: "barys," a specific type of Egyptian vessel described by ancient writers</note> equipped with (26, 28) sistra to drive away harmful power, also brings into the sacred images of Isis—that is, the kingdom of Isis and the entire mundane house of Horus—the benefit of the health-giving Tautic character or handled (27) Cross, which the little streams flowing from it demonstrate as influencing all things. They represent Isis with a (30) statue, distinguished by a high headdress <note>original: "tutulo"</note>, (31) two serpents, and two wings with a globe in between, the meaning of which we have assigned elsewhere above. She holds in her hand the sistrum <note>A sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual</note> customary to her, to signify the protection of the Nile, and she has a hook attached to show the driving away of evils. By the position of her name, she displays the letters; by which she shows at the same time that she ought to be worshiped under this form to be propitiated, and that the operations of the Priests must be performed according to this. ...beyond which, a naked boy holds a staff in his hand in the shape of a handled cross <note>original: "crucis ansatæ," referring to the Ankh</note>, also distinguished by the head of a hoopoe; the Elementary World is indicated by the quadrangular gate. By the boy standing at the gate, according to the testimony of Plutarch, is meant Horus, or the mundane spirit; by his separate feet, his hidden motion into all things is shown; finally, by the staff, the <term>multiform variety of things: polymorphos</term> is indicated, which he effects by his motion within the <term>Economy of the mundane house: The organized management of the physical world</term>. Therefore, by this whole Diagram, they wished to indicate that through this ceremonial opening of the sacred <term>Enclosure: Septum</term>—made by the key-shaped hammer—that is, the dwelling of the celestial World, Osiris, and Isis—the celestial or divine moisture descends. Furthermore, they indicate that the sacred Osiris restrains and guards the bowl upon which he sits from all violent power. Again, with this Osiris acting as the president of celestial things, the material gate is opened, and the care of further matters is committed to Momphta <note>An Egyptian deity interpreted by Kircher as a creative or protective spirit</note>, whose specific role it is to actuate the moisture destined for the work of generation. Once it is actuated, he distributes it by a fourfold influx and a generous benevolence to the four terrestrial hinges, ensuring an abundance of vegetation. 

Because these things could not occur without the cooperation of the Sun and Moon, the celestial eye of Osiris and the Isiac celestial orbs—traversing the heavens in their annual path—derive the moisture through the three seasons of the year into the three lower material worlds. They do this by a provident motion into the hemisphere of the lower World. From this, they effect life (consisting in heat and moisture) in the <term>boat: Bary (from the Greek baris, an Egyptian river boat)</term> of the lower World. This life is promoted through the genital moisture of things by the hidden motion of the Divinity, leading to fertility and growth.

Because the Gods are reluctant to act unless enticed by mystical things analogous to themselves, the priests who were conscious of this secret, and now instructed in the sacred art, would wander along the Nile at certain times of the year. They used a Boat equipped with handled crosses and sistrums <note>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument used in religious ceremonies</note>, soliciting the linked Divinities with various ceremonies and the clatter of sistrums to obtain what they sought: that is, the fertile moisture which is the principle of all things. 

To ensure these ceremonies had greater efficacy and were safer against adverse powers, they carried around a mystical statue of the Nilotic Isis—that is, the president of Mundane moisture—as well as of Horus (who represents the sensible world). These statues were adorned, according to a certain secret reason, with headbands, sistrums, scepters, and similar items. Once these rites were performed, they promised themselves every favorable and fertile outcome, as will be clear from the following Reading.

### Conceptual Scheme of the Reading for the Fourth Side, Northern Context.

Through the three 1 **Elementary Worlds**, 2 **moisture** is granted; by means of the 3 **Isiac hammer** <note>original: "malleum Isiacum," a T-shaped symbol Kircher interprets as a key or tool of the goddess Isis</note>, following the 4 **enclosure** <note>original: "septum"</note> of the 5 **Bull Mnevis** <note>A sacred bull of Heliopolis, considered an avatar of Ra or Osiris</note>, it is opened to the 6 **monthly cycle** established for the course of the Moon; from which a 5 **triple life** for the triple World is poured into the 10 **bowl** of the 9 **Sun**, or **Osiris**, onto those things 7 subjected to the 8 **fourfold regions of the World**, once the 8 **destructive qualities** have been expelled. Furthermore, the all-seeing Divinity, the 19 **celestial eye of the sun**, as it moves in its 20 **orbit**, 24 **fertilizes the lower regions** of the three 21, 22, 23 **elementary Worlds**, according to the 25 **twelvefold ratio of the lunar cycle** joined to the three seasons of the year (each of which consists of a four-month period within the perpetual space of the annual course). # SCHEME V.
## Of the fourth North side.

<margin>The figure of Mophta.</margin>
It was a custom among the Egyptians that, whenever they recognized the benefits of a particular Deity, they immediately strove to invoke its kindly presence and draw it near through every possible sacred rite and ceremony. Since the preceding sections dealt with the effects of the **World-Spirit** <note>original: "spiritus mundani," the vital force that Kircher believed animated the entire universe</note>, in this place they set up a statue showing the rites for establishing it. This is performed through the garb of a Priest transformed into the 1 form of the name **Mophta** <note>A name used by Kircher to represent a creative or "hegemonic" divine intelligence</note>; he holds a staff in his hand, signifying the 2 dominion that he acquires over the Spirits through sacred acts. <margin>Gourd: Feather: Nilotic ringed vessel.</margin> There follow the sacred 2 **amulets**: the **gourd**, which they call the club of Mophta; the 3 **hawk’s feather**, which they called the "movement of Osiris"; with the amulet of the 4 **sacred urn**, which they 5 hung from the neck. To show that the World-Spirit is summoned by these sacred charms <note>original: "periaptis," from the Greek for "hanging around" or "amulet"</note>, they place the aforementioned amulets again, along with a 6 **feather**, a 7 **globe** 8 **teeming with a serpent**, and a 9 **quadrangle** placed beneath as a symbol of the lower world. This was to show that the World-Spirit does not comply except through contemplation, the movement of the mind, and the water of the super-mundane Nile, by which the soul is purified and expiated—as if being made somewhat fit and capable of receiving heavenly influxes.

<margin>Dragon-shaped butterfly.</margin>
This is followed by the 10 **dragon-shaped butterfly** <note>original: "papilio δρακοντόμορφος"</note>, a symbol of the **Multiform Genius** <note>The "Genius Polymorphus" represents the spirit that takes on many shapes in nature</note>. By this, they wished to signify that the World-Spirit, of which we spoke shortly before, exerts itself most especially in the Multiform Spirit—that is, in the variety of things. Indeed, by this 11 virtue, the earthly World shines forth, imbued with innumerable forms, as we declared in Scheme II of the Second Side. However, because all this power over the inferior 12 **material worlds** <note>original: "mundos hylæos," from the Greek "hyle" meaning matter</note> comes from the supreme triple-formed Deity and from the superior worlds, they appropriately placed 12 **three globes** between two staffs. These are followed by 13 **three quadrangles** with a 14 **right-angled scalene triangle**, which denote that the generation of things in the three material worlds proceeds only from the supreme Deity—who has descended into the sphere of generation—mediated by the World-Spirit and the Multiform Spirit.

<margin>Symbol of the reclining dog.</margin>
Next follows a 15 **dog reclining with its body prone**, which we have explained elsewhere is **Anubis**. He is the faithful guardian of the inferior things committed to **Isis** or **Hecate** <note>Kircher often synchronizes Egyptian and Greek deities; Hecate is associated here with the underworld or hidden mysteries</note>. His duty is not only to preserve created things with faithful guardianship but also to be the "fate" of the three aforementioned worlds. In these worlds, he teaches against adversity concerning what is proper to each thing, whether through astrological impressions, magical operations, or through dreams, auguries, and other types of divinations and omens of which he is the Author. All these things are indicated by the figure of the dog, by the 16 **iron of a spear**, and by 17 **three stars**. For this reason, he must be perpetually worshipped with the highest honors, which the 18 **sacred bier** <note>original: "feretrum," a portable shrine or stand for a deity</note> shows are to be offered to him. Furthermore, to achieve the stated goals with greater efficacy, they add another amulet inscribed on a sacred tablet, by whose symbol—
